name: Spring MVC

beginner.content:
Spring MVC is a web framework built on the Model-View-Controller pattern.

 Components:
 • DispatcherServlet: Front controller
 • Controller: Handles requests
 • Model: Data
 • View: Presentation
 • ViewResolver: Resolves view names

 Request Flow:
 1. Client sends request
 2. DispatcherServlet receives request
 3. Handler mapping finds controller
 4. Controller processes request
 5. Returns ModelAndView
 6. ViewResolver resolves view
 7. View renders response

Fresher Notes

  • Spring MVC is the web module of the Spring Framework; it maps HTTP requests to Java methods using a front controller called DispatcherServlet.
  • Controller classes are marked with @Controller or @RestController, and methods with @GetMapping, @PostMapping and similar.
  • Return value is either a view name (HTML page) or a body written as JSON (with @ResponseBody).

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring MVC is built around one servlet.

  • Startup: RequestMappingHandlerMapping scans all beans for @RequestMapping methods and stores them in a registry.
  • Per request: doDispatch gets the handler chain, picks a HandlerAdapter, runs interceptors, then invokes the method.
  • Arguments: resolvers read path, query, headers and body into parameters.
  • Result: a return value handler writes the body or the model and view are rendered.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options:

  • Verb shortcuts: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping.
  • Narrowing: params, headers, consumes and produces.
  • Patterns: /files/{name:.+} with a regex and /** wildcards.
  • Return types: String, ResponseEntity, ModelAndView, void, Callable.

expert.content:
DispatcherServlet: The Front Controller

Every request into a Spring MVC application passes through a single servlet - DispatcherServlet. It does not process the request itself; it coordinates a fixed pipeline of collaborator beans (HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, ViewResolver, etc.) that are auto-configured by the Spring container.

Client            DispatcherServlet     HandlerMapping     Controller     ViewResolver         View
  |                      |                     |                |               |                |
  |--- HTTP request ---->|                     |                |               |                |
  |                      |--- find handler ---->|                |               |                |
  |                      |<-- HandlerExecutionChain (controller)-|                |               |
  |                      |--- invoke via HandlerAdapter --------->|               |                |
  |                      |                     |                |-- process --   |                |
  |                      |<---------------- ModelAndView --------|                |               |
  |                      |--- resolve view name ----------------------------------->|              |
  |                      |<----------------------------------------------- View object ------------|
  |                      |--- render(model) -------------------------------------------------------->|
  |<---- HTTP response --|                     |                |               |                |

Step-by-step flow

1. Client sends an HTTP request; it hits the front controller, DispatcherServlet (mapped in web.xml / auto-configured by Spring Boot to /).
2. DispatcherServlet consults HandlerMapping to find which controller method should handle this URL + HTTP method.
3. HandlerMapping returns a HandlerExecutionChain (the controller method plus any interceptors).
4. DispatcherServlet delegates execution to a HandlerAdapter, which actually invokes the controller method, resolving method arguments (@RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestBody, etc.) along the way.
5. The controller returns a logical view name (String) or a ModelAndView object containing the view name plus model data.
6. If the return value is a view name, DispatcherServlet asks ViewResolver to resolve it to an actual View implementation (e.g. JSP under /WEB-INF/views/, or a Thymeleaf template).
7. DispatcherServlet calls view.render(model, request, response), which merges the model data into the template and writes the final HTML to the response.

For a @RestController (or a method annotated @ResponseBody) steps 6-7 are skipped entirely - the returned object is serialized directly (usually to JSON via HttpMessageConverter) straight into the HTTP response body.
codeExamples:
// web.xml style registration (classic Spring MVC, non Spring-Boot)
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet</servlet-class>
    <init-param>
        <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
        <param-value>/WEB-INF/spring-mvc-config.xml</param-value>
    </init-param>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>
<servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/</url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>
// Spring Boot auto-configures and registers this same DispatcherServlet
// for you - no XML required.

expert.content:
@Controller vs @RestController

Both are specializations of @Component and both get picked up by component scanning, but they differ in how the return value of a handler method is treated.

Aspect@Controller@RestController
Return value default meaningLogical view name, resolved by ViewResolverResponse body itself (serialized by an HttpMessageConverter)
Equivalent to@Controller (plain)@Controller + @ResponseBody on every handler method
Typical use caseTraditional server-rendered web pages (JSP/Thymeleaf)REST APIs returning JSON/XML
Need @ResponseBody explicitly?Yes, per method, if you want raw data instead of a viewNo, implied for every method in the class
Can still return a view name?Yes (default behavior)No - a String return value becomes the literal response body, not a view name

Request Mapping Annotations

@RequestMapping is the general-purpose mapping annotation; the HTTP-method-specific variants (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping) are meta-annotations built on top of it that pre-set the method attribute, making intent explicit and code shorter.

AnnotationEquivalent toTypical use
@RequestMapping@RequestMapping(method = ...) or no method restrictionClass-level base path; or when multiple HTTP methods must map to the same method
@GetMapping@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)Fetch/read a resource
@PostMapping@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.POST)Create a resource
@PutMapping@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PUT)Replace a resource entirely
@PatchMapping@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PATCH)Partially update a resource
@DeleteMapping@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.DELETE)Delete a resource

Class-level @RequestMapping combines with method-level mappings - the final URL is the concatenation of both.

Binding Request Data: @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestBody

AnnotationExtracts data fromExample URL / body
@RequestParamQuery string or form field/search?keyword=java&page=2
@PathVariableA segment of the URI template/users/42 -> id = 42
@RequestBodyThe raw HTTP request body, deserialized via an HttpMessageConverter (e.g. JSON -> POJO)POST body: {"name":"Anaji"}

Model and ModelAndView: Passing Data to the View

When a handler method returns a view name, it needs a way to hand data to that view for rendering. Spring MVC offers two equivalent styles:

• Model (an interface, usually injected as a method parameter) - you call addAttribute(name, value) and separately return the view name as a String.
• ModelAndView - a single object that bundles both the view name and the model data together, useful when you want to build and return them as one unit (e.g. from a method that may branch to different views).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the role of DispatcherServlet?It is the front controller of Spring MVC - every request enters through it, and it delegates to HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter and ViewResolver to produce the response
What is HandlerMapping?A component that maps an incoming request (URL + HTTP method) to the controller method that should handle it
Difference between @Controller and @RestController?@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody applied to every method - return values are written directly to the response body instead of being resolved as view names
What does @ResponseBody do?Tells Spring to skip view resolution and serialize the return value directly into the HTTP response body via an HttpMessageConverter
Difference between @RequestParam and @PathVariable?@RequestParam reads query-string/form parameters (?key=value); @PathVariable extracts a value from a placeholder in the URI template itself (/users/{id})
What does @RequestBody do?Binds the entire HTTP request body to a Java object, converting it (e.g. JSON to POJO) via a registered HttpMessageConverter such as Jackson
Difference between Model and ModelAndView?Model only carries attributes and is injected as a parameter while the view name is returned separately as a String; ModelAndView bundles both the view name and the attributes into a single returned object
What is a ViewResolver?A component that maps a logical view name (String) returned by a controller to an actual View implementation (JSP, Thymeleaf template, etc.)
Can one method handle multiple HTTP methods?Yes, using @RequestMapping(method = { RequestMethod.GET, RequestMethod.POST }) instead of a single HTTP-method-specific annotation
What happens if a @RestController method returns a String?Unlike @Controller, the String is NOT treated as a view name - it becomes the literal response body text (or JSON string) sent to the client

Mid-Level Notes

  • Binding: @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestBody and @ModelAttribute convert request data into Java arguments.
  • Validation: add @Valid on an argument and put constraints such as @NotBlank on the fields; failures are reported in BindingResult or as an exception.
  • Error handling: @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler gives one place for translating exceptions into responses.

Senior Notes

  • Extension points: HandlerInterceptor, HandlerMethodArgumentResolver, HttpMessageConverter and WebMvcConfigurer customize the pipeline without changing controllers.
  • Servlet stack: Spring MVC is blocking and thread-per-request, unlike Spring WebFlux which is reactive.
  • Testing: @WebMvcTest with MockMvc tests the web layer without starting a server.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong stereotype: @Controller returning a string for an API gives a missing-template error; use @RestController.
  • Missing component scan: a controller outside the main package is not found, so the URL returns 404.
  • Entity in JSON: a bidirectional JPA entity causes infinite recursion; return DTOs.
  • Ambiguous mapping: two methods with the same path and verb fail at startup.
  • Missing @RequestBody: the JSON arrives but the object stays empty.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning a Spring MVC application:

  • Thread pool: set server.tomcat.threads.max to the expected concurrency.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true for large JSON.
  • Caching: ETag and Cache-Control for static resources.
  • Async: return Callable for long work so threads are freed.
  • Template cache: keep it on in production.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.min-response-size=1024
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=7d

# OUTPUT:
# responses over 1 KB are gzipped;
static files are cached for 7 days

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A typical request in a production shop application:

  • A filter adds a trace id and Spring Security authenticates the user.
  • The controller validates the JSON, calls a service and returns a DTO.
  • A @RestControllerAdvice turns failures into a uniform error body.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MVC splits an application into three parts: the Model (data and rules), the View (what the user sees) and the Controller (handles input and connects the two).
  • Why: separation of concerns lets several people work on UI and logic at once, and each part can be tested alone.
  • Flow: the user sends a request, the controller calls the model, then picks a view that shows the model data.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Controller test with mocked model.

Practice Exercise 1

Three roles in code.

Practice Exercise 2

Tracing the three parts.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MVC is a pattern; Spring implements it with specific classes.

  • Model: Model map plus domain objects from services.
  • View: a View implementation such as ThymeleafView.
  • Controller: a handler method found by HandlerMapping.
  • Front controller: DispatcherServlet coordinates all three.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of MVC on the web:

  • Server-side MVC: controller returns a view name and HTML is rendered on the server.
  • REST MVC: controller returns data and the view is JSON.
  • MVP and MVVM: related patterns where a presenter or view-model replaces the controller, common in front-end frameworks.
  • Layered architecture: controller, service, repository on top of MVC.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Layers: in a Spring app the model side is usually split into service and repository layers below the controller.
  • Thin controller: keep business rules out of controllers; they only translate HTTP to method calls and back.
  • Variants: server-side MVC renders HTML; in a REST API the JSON body plays the role of the view.

Senior Notes

  • Front controller: MVC on the web adds one entry point (DispatcherServlet) so common work such as mapping and error handling lives in one place.
  • Anemic model: a model of only getters and setters pushes all logic into services; consider richer domain objects.
  • Coupling: the view must not call repositories, and the model must not know about HTTP classes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical architecture mistakes:

  • Fat controller: business rules in the controller; move them to a service.
  • Logic in the view: long conditionals and queries in templates.
  • Repository in the controller: skips the transaction boundary.
  • Model knows HTTP: services taking HttpServletRequest cannot be reused or tested easily.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Architecture affects speed through the layer boundaries:

  • Open Session in View: keeping the JPA session open during rendering causes lazy queries in the view; disable it with spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.
  • DTO projections: load only the fields the view shows.
  • Fragments and caching: cache expensive view fragments.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

# OUTPUT:
# no lazy loading from templates;
the service must fetch what the view needs
# (a LazyInitializationException shows a missing fetch)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A catalogue site: a request for /books goes to the controller, which asks the service for a page of books, adds them to the model and returns the view. The same service is reused by a REST controller for the mobile app.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Model is the data (and rules) the application works with, such as a Book object, plus the data handed to the view.
  • Model interface: in Spring, Model is a map-like holder; model.addAttribute("key", value) makes data available to the view.
  • ModelAndView bundles the model and the view name into one return value.

Worked Example 1

Binding a form to a model object.

Worked Example 2

Testing model content.

Practice Exercise 1

Model parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

ModelAndView.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the model is carried through a request.

  • Before the handler runs, ModelFactory invokes @ModelAttribute methods and fills a ModelAndViewContainer.
  • The Model argument is a BindingAwareModelMap, which also holds BindingResult entries.
  • After the handler, the container is turned into a ModelAndView and given to the view.
  • For redirects, the model values become query parameters unless you use flash attributes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to put data in the model:

  • Model: addAttribute(name, value).
  • ModelMap and Map: same effect.
  • ModelAndView: addObject.
  • @ModelAttribute method: shared data such as dropdown lists.
  • @SessionAttributes: keep named attributes in the session across requests.
  • RedirectAttributes: addFlashAttribute for one redirect.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @ModelAttribute on a method adds data to every request of that controller; on a parameter it binds form fields to an object.
  • Scope: model attributes live for one request; use HttpSession or @SessionAttributes to keep them longer.
  • DTO versus entity: pass a DTO to the view instead of a JPA entity to avoid lazy-loading errors and leaking fields.

Senior Notes

  • Implementation: the model is a BindingAwareModelMap inside a ModelAndViewContainer for the request.
  • Redirects: RedirectAttributes and flash attributes survive one redirect (Post-Redirect-Get).
  • Domain model: the word also means the business objects; keep them free of web types.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with the model:

  • Expecting model data after redirect: it is gone; use flash attributes.
  • BindingResult placement: it must come directly after the validated argument.
  • Mass assignment: binding a form straight to an entity lets users set fields like role; use a form object or @InitBinder allowed fields.
  • Session bloat: large objects in @SessionAttributes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance points for the model:

  • Put only the data the page needs; large lists cost memory and rendering time.
  • Use paging (Page) instead of loading all rows.
  • Prefer DTO projections over full entities.
  • Do not keep big graphs in the session on clustered servers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Registration form: show a blank form (GET), validate on POST, redisplay with errors or redirect with a success message (Post-Redirect-Get).

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • View is the part that renders the response for the user, such as an HTML page built from a template and the model data.
  • View name: a controller returns a plain string like "home"; a ViewResolver turns it into a real template.
  • Technologies: Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, Mustache and JSP; Spring Boot auto-configures the common ones.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a view name becomes HTML.

  • DispatcherServlet.render calls resolveViewName on each ViewResolver in order.
  • Boot registers ContentNegotiatingViewResolver, BeanNameViewResolver, ThymeleafViewResolver and others.
  • The resolved View receives the model map and writes to the response.
  • For @ResponseBody no view is used at all.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

View technologies and prefixes:

  • Thymeleaf: natural HTML templates, default choice in Boot.
  • FreeMarker and Mustache: alternatives.
  • JSP: needs a WAR and is poorly supported with embedded jar packaging.
  • redirect: and forward: special prefixes in view names.
  • Fragments: a view name like orders :: table returns only a fragment.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Location: Thymeleaf templates live in src/main/resources/templates and static files in static.
  • No logic: a view should only display data; avoid database calls and heavy rules in templates.
  • JSON views: with @ResponseBody there is no template, and a message converter writes the data.

Senior Notes

  • Resolution: DispatcherServlet asks each ViewResolver in order; the first non-null View renders the model.
  • Escaping: Thymeleaf th:text escapes HTML, while th:utext does not and risks XSS.
  • Redirect views: the prefixes redirect: and forward: create special views.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

View mistakes:

  • Template not found: wrong folder or name, giving a 500 error.
  • XSS: using th:utext with user input.
  • Logic in templates: hard to test and slow.
  • Stale templates in development: cache not disabled.
  • Null model value: template fails; check with th:if.

View performance:

  • Keep template caching on in production.
  • Use fragments and HTTP caching for static parts.
  • Avoid method calls that hit the database inside loops.
  • Enable gzip and cache static resources with versioned names.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A page shows the logged-in user name and a list of orders. The controller prepares all data, and the template only loops and prints.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller is a class that receives web requests, calls the business layer and chooses what to return.
  • Stereotype: @Controller is detected by component scanning; @RestController adds @ResponseBody for APIs.
  • Mapping: @RequestMapping at class level sets a prefix, and @GetMapping or @PostMapping on methods set the path and verb.

Worked Example 1

Slice test of a controller.

Worked Example 2

Bug: state in a singleton.

Practice Exercise 1

CRUD style controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Status annotation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a controller method gets called.

  • At startup RequestMappingHandlerMapping reads annotations and registers a RequestMappingInfo for each method.
  • At runtime the best match is chosen by path, verb, params, headers and media types.
  • RequestMappingHandlerAdapter uses a ServletInvocableHandlerMethod to resolve each argument and invoke the method by reflection.
  • The return value goes to a HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controller method variants:

  • Parameters: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody, @ModelAttribute.
  • Optional parameters: required=false, defaultValue or Optional.
  • Return: ResponseEntity for status and headers, plain object for 200.
  • Class-level: @RequestMapping prefix and @CrossOrigin.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Arguments: methods can take @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, Model, HttpSession and Principal.
  • Return types: String view name, ResponseEntity, a plain object, void or ModelAndView.
  • Status codes: set with ResponseEntity or @ResponseStatus.

Senior Notes

  • Handler lookup: RequestMappingHandlerMapping builds a registry of mappings at startup and RequestMappingHandlerAdapter invokes the chosen method.
  • Singleton: a controller is one shared bean, so never keep per-request state in fields.
  • Thin design: validate, call a service, map the result; transactions belong in the service layer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Controller mistakes:

  • Instance state: fields mutated per request are shared between threads.
  • Missing parameter: a required parameter that is absent gives 400.
  • Type mismatch: /users/abc for a long gives 400.
  • Swallowed exceptions: returning "error" strings with status 200 hides failures.
  • Large logic: hundreds of lines in one controller.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Controller tuning:

  • Return quickly; do slow work asynchronously with Callable or messaging.
  • Stream big downloads with StreamingResponseBody.
  • Paginate lists.
  • Set cache headers with CacheControl.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Order API with validation, service call and proper status codes, plus a global handler for not found.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request flow: the client sends a request, DispatcherServlet finds a handler, the controller runs, and a view or body is returned.
  • HandlerMapping chooses the controller method for the URL and HTTP verb.
  • ViewResolver turns a view name into a view; for REST the converter writes the body instead.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The ordered flow inside DispatcherServlet.doDispatch.

  • 1. getHandler asks each HandlerMapping and returns a HandlerExecutionChain (handler plus interceptors).
  • 2. getHandlerAdapter finds an adapter that supports the handler.
  • 3. applyPreHandle runs interceptors in order.
  • 4. ha.handle resolves arguments, invokes the method and handles the return value.
  • 5. applyPostHandle runs in reverse order.
  • 6. processDispatchResult renders the view or runs exception resolvers.
  • 7. triggerAfterCompletion runs in reverse order.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Component options in the flow:

  • HandlerMapping: RequestMappingHandlerMapping (annotations), SimpleUrlHandlerMapping, RouterFunctionMapping.
  • HandlerAdapter: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter, HttpRequestHandlerAdapter.
  • Exception resolvers: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Resolvers: ViewResolver, LocaleResolver, MultipartResolver.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: filters, then DispatcherServlet, then interceptor preHandle, then argument resolvers, controller, return value handler, then postHandle and afterCompletion.
  • HandlerAdapter knows how to call the handler and prepare arguments.
  • Exceptions thrown by the handler go to HandlerExceptionResolver beans such as @ExceptionHandler methods.

Senior Notes

  • Core method: DispatcherServlet.doDispatch runs the whole cycle; reading it is the best way to learn the flow.
  • Content negotiation: the Accept header and message converters decide JSON versus XML.
  • Async: returning Callable or DeferredResult frees the container thread while work continues.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Flow-related mistakes:

  • 404 for existing controller: not scanned, wrong path or context path.
  • 405: wrong HTTP verb.
  • 415 and 406: content type or Accept header not supported.
  • Interceptor not called: it was not registered with addInterceptors.
  • Interceptor returns false: request stops silently; set a response status.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Every step adds cost, so keep it lean.

  • Keep interceptors and filters cheap.
  • Avoid regex-heavy path patterns on hot endpoints.
  • Use OncePerRequestFilter and skip static paths.
  • Use async handlers for slow downstream calls.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Request tracing: a filter creates a trace id, an interceptor logs the handler name and duration, and an exception handler returns the trace id in the error body so support can find the logs.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring MVC is a web framework (controllers, views, mapping); Spring Boot is a tool that auto-configures and runs Spring applications.
  • Not rivals: a Boot web application uses Spring MVC inside, through spring-boot-starter-web.
  • Boot adds auto-configuration, an embedded server, starter dependencies and Actuator.

Worked Example 1

Inspecting what Boot configured.

debug=true

# OUTPUT:
# Positive matches:
#   DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration matched
#   WebMvcAutoConfiguration matched
#   ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration matched

Worked Example 2

Testing with Boot.

Practice Exercise 1

Plain Spring MVC config (Java).

Practice Exercise 2
