Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What Boot adds on top of MVC at startup.

  • @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.
  • Auto-configuration classes are listed in META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports and filtered by @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean.
  • ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration starts embedded Tomcat; DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration registers the servlet.
  • Defaults come from spring.mvc.* and server.* properties.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Boot options for MVC:

  • Starter: spring-boot-starter-web (Tomcat), swap to Jetty by excluding Tomcat.
  • Packaging: executable jar by default; WAR with SpringBootServletInitializer.
  • Properties: server.port, server.servlet.context-path, spring.mvc.static-path-pattern.
  • Customization: WebMvcConfigurer without @EnableWebMvc.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.port=9090
server.servlet.context-path=/shop
spring.mvc.static-path-pattern=/assets/**
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 9090 with context path '/shop'

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Plain MVC setup: you declare DispatcherServlet, a view resolver and a WAR for an external Tomcat; Boot does all that for you.
  • Entry point: Boot uses @SpringBootApplication and a main method.
  • Overrides: you can still define your own beans or implement WebMvcConfigurer to adjust MVC under Boot.

Senior Notes

  • Auto-config: WebMvcAutoConfiguration registers resolvers, converters, static resources and the DispatcherServlet when classes are on the classpath.
  • Conditional beans: auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean of the same kind.
  • Full control: @EnableWebMvc turns off Boot MVC defaults, which is rarely wanted.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes mixing the two:

  • @EnableWebMvc in Boot: turns off static resources, Jackson defaults and more.
  • Main class in a sub-package: component scan misses controllers.
  • Two web starters: WebFlux and MVC together make Boot choose MVC.
  • Old XML and servlet config copied: duplicate DispatcherServlet.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Boot improves startup and ops, not request speed itself.

  • Remove unused starters to cut startup time.
  • Use spring.main.lazy-initialization=true in development.
  • Use Actuator metrics to watch request timings.
  • Native images and CDS can reduce start time.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests -> count, total time, max

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A team moves a legacy WAR-based Spring MVC app to Boot: the XML and servlet initializer are replaced with @SpringBootApplication, controllers stay unchanged, and the app now runs as a jar in a container.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring Framework is the whole platform: core container (IoC, DI), AOP, data access, transactions, testing and web.
  • Spring MVC is one module of it (spring-webmvc) that handles servlet-based web requests.
  • Relationship: MVC is built on the core container, so controllers are ordinary Spring beans with injection.

Worked Example 1

Maven dependencies.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
  <version>6.1.x</version>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT: pulls spring-web, spring-context, spring-core transitively -->

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Unit test without MVC.

Practice Exercise 1

Spring Framework without MVC.

Practice Exercise 2

MVC adds the web layer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the framework modules stack.

  • spring-core and spring-beans provide the IoC container.
  • spring-context adds the application context, events and resources.
  • spring-web has the HTTP abstractions and message converters shared by MVC and WebFlux.
  • spring-webmvc adds DispatcherServlet and the MVC programming model.
  • In classic setups the ContextLoaderListener creates the root context and the DispatcherServlet a child context.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where each piece lives:

  • Core and DI: any Java program.
  • Data access: JdbcTemplate, transactions, ORM support.
  • Messaging: spring-jms, spring-messaging.
  • Web servlet: Spring MVC.
  • Web reactive: Spring WebFlux.
  • Test: spring-test with MockMvc.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Other modules: spring-jdbc, spring-tx, spring-orm, spring-aop and spring-webflux.
  • Use without web: you can use the container and transactions in a console or batch program with no MVC at all.
  • Web choice: the framework offers two web stacks, blocking Spring MVC and reactive WebFlux.

Senior Notes

  • Contexts: a root application context holds services and repositories; a child web context holds controllers and MVC beans (Boot merges them into one).
  • Jars: spring-webmvc depends on spring-web, spring-context and spring-core.
  • Boundary: MVC knows the Servlet API; the core container does not.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Confusions to avoid:

  • Saying "Spring" means MVC: interviewers expect you to separate container and web layer.
  • Putting service beans in the servlet context: they become invisible to other servlets and filters.
  • Duplicate scanning: scanning the same package in both contexts creates two copies of beans, and transactions may not apply to one of them.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Keep modules light: depend only on what you use (for example spring-context for a worker, not spring-webmvc), which reduces jar size and startup time.
codeExamples:
<!-- Worker module: no web dependencies -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-jdbc</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT: fewer jars, faster startup, no servlet API needed -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A company shares a domain and service library (plain Spring Framework) between a web application (Spring MVC) and a nightly batch job (no web), so business rules are written once.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Separation of concerns: controller, model and view are separate, so code is easier to understand and maintain.
  • Annotation-driven: @GetMapping, @RequestParam and @Valid remove much boilerplate compared with raw servlets.
  • Flexible views: works with Thymeleaf, JSP, FreeMarker or JSON REST output.

Worked Example 1

Fast web-layer test.

Worked Example 2

Global error handling.

Practice Exercise 1

Less boilerplate than a servlet.

Practice Exercise 2

Built-in validation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Why those advantages exist technically.

  • Strategy interfaces: each step (mapping, adapter, resolver, converter) is an interface, so any part can be replaced.
  • IoC: controllers get services by injection, making them easy to mock.
  • Annotation metadata: read once at startup and cached, so request handling needs little reflection lookup.
  • Data binding: WebDataBinder and ConversionService convert strings to typed values.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features that make up the advantages:

  • Binding and validation: @Valid, BindingResult.
  • Content negotiation: JSON, XML or CSV from the same method.
  • i18n: MessageSource and LocaleResolver.
  • File upload: MultipartFile.
  • CORS and security: built-in support.
  • Problem details: RFC 7807 error bodies in Spring 6.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Testability: controllers are plain classes, so MockMvc tests them without a server.
  • Integration: works with Spring Security, Data JPA, transactions and validation out of the box.
  • Extensible: interceptors, converters and argument resolvers can be swapped or added.

Senior Notes

  • Trade-offs: the servlet model is thread-per-request, so very high concurrency with slow calls needs more threads or WebFlux.
  • Learning curve: many abstractions (adapters, resolvers) make debugging harder at first; use DEBUG logging.
  • Maturity: wide community, documentation and long-term support.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Using the advantages wrongly:

  • Overusing @ModelAttribute magic: hidden data makes controllers hard to follow.
  • Binding entities directly: mass-assignment risk.
  • Ignoring validation: trusting client data.
  • Blocking calls everywhere: exhausting the thread pool.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance related strengths:

  • Mapping registry is built once, so lookup is fast.
  • Jackson converters are tuned and can be configured for streaming.
  • ETag and conditional requests are supported with ShallowEtagHeaderFilter or ResponseEntity.eTag.
  • Async support for slow calls.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A startup builds a single service that serves a web site (Thymeleaf pages) and a mobile API (JSON) with the same business layer, security rules and error handling, and tests both layers quickly with slice tests.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Lifecycle is the path of one HTTP request from arrival at the server to the response sent back to the client.
  • Main steps: filter chain, DispatcherServlet, handler mapping, controller, view or message converter, response.
  • Request scope: request-scoped beans and model attributes are created and discarded within this lifecycle.

Worked Example 1

Exception path.

Worked Example 2

Testing the response.

Practice Exercise 1

Following one request.

Practice Exercise 2

A filter before Spring.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside one request.

  • The container creates HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse and runs the filter chain.
  • DispatcherServlet stores request attributes, the locale and the web application context.
  • Arguments are resolved, the method runs, and the return value handler writes the response.
  • With @ResponseBody the converter writes bytes straight to the output stream and marks the request handled (no view).
  • The request ends; request-scoped beans are destroyed and afterCompletion runs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Lifecycle variants:

  • Normal view: model rendered through a view.
  • Body response: @ResponseBody or ResponseEntity.
  • Redirect: 302/303 and a new request.
  • Forward: same request goes to another path internally.
  • Async: Callable, DeferredResult, SSE with SseEmitter.
  • Error dispatch: container forwards to /error for unhandled errors.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Binding: before the method runs, arguments are built from path, query, headers and body; after it, the return value is processed.
  • Interceptor hooks: preHandle can stop the request, postHandle sees the model, afterCompletion always runs for cleanup.
  • Status and headers: set in the controller or via ResponseEntity; once the response is committed they cannot change.

Senior Notes

  • Argument and return handling: HandlerMethodArgumentResolver and HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler do the conversion work.
  • Exceptions: a thrown exception skips postHandle but still triggers afterCompletion.
  • Thread: the whole cycle runs on one container thread unless you return async types.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Lifecycle mistakes:

  • Reading the body twice: the input stream can be read once; use ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Writing after commit: IllegalStateException: response already committed.
  • Using request objects in other threads: the container recycles them after the request.
  • Exception in a filter: controller advice does not see it.
  • Cleanup in postHandle: use afterCompletion so errors do not skip it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Lifecycle performance:

  • Measure latency per stage (filter, controller, database) with Actuator or Micrometer timers.
  • Avoid heavy work in preHandle.
  • Do not buffer big bodies in memory; stream them.
  • Keep sessions small or stateless.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A support team gets a complaint about a slow checkout. Using a trace id added by a filter, an interceptor timing log and the error body, they find the request, see the time spent in the payment service call, and fix it with a timeout and retry.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Front Controller is a design pattern where ONE central component receives every request and then delegates to the right handler, instead of each URL having its own servlet.
  • Spring MVC implements it with DispatcherServlet, which is the single entry point for all web requests mapped to it.
  • Benefit: cross-cutting work such as security, locale, logging and error handling lives in one place instead of being repeated in every servlet.

Worked Example 1

Prove every request passes the same gate with a logging filter and a MockMvc test.

Worked Example 2

Observe the dispatcher in the logs.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal front controller idea in plain servlet code (what Spring does for you).

Practice Exercise 2

The Spring MVC version: the front controller is hidden, you only write handlers.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring implements the pattern internally.

  • Single servlet: DispatcherServlet is mapped to /, so the container sends everything to it.
  • Template method: FrameworkServlet.service calls doService, which calls doDispatch.
  • Delegation: mapping, invocation, view and error handling are strategy beans.
  • Static files: a resource handler mapping serves them through the same servlet.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options.

  • Mapping /: the default; use /api/* style paths to restrict it.
  • Multiple dispatchers: register extra DispatcherServletRegistrationBean beans.
  • Page Controller: the alternative, one handler per page, with duplicated cross-cutting code.
  • Reactive: WebFlux has its own front controller, DispatcherHandler.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Delegation: the front controller does not contain business logic; it asks HandlerMapping for a handler and HandlerAdapter to call it.
  • Servlet mapping: / sends nearly every URL to the front controller, while static files are served by the resource handler.
  • Contrast: Page Controller means one controller per page; Front Controller means one gateway for all pages.

Senior Notes

  • Extension points: interceptors, argument resolvers, converters and exception resolvers are the hooks that customize the central flow.
  • Filters versus the front controller: servlet filters run before the DispatcherServlet, interceptors run inside it and know the chosen handler.
  • Trade-off: a single entry point is a single place to fail, so keep it thin and fast and push heavy work into services.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes.

  • Business logic in filters or the front controller: keep it in services.
  • Assuming filters know the handler: they run before mapping, so use an interceptor.
  • Mapping to /*: in classic setups it also swallows JSP forwards; use /.
  • Static resources 404: check the resource handler configuration.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance points.

  • Thin entry: avoid heavy work in interceptors, they run for every request.
  • Path matching: PathPattern parsing is done once at startup.
  • Threading: use async return types for long calls so container threads are freed.
  • Static content: serve it from a CDN or reverse proxy, not the servlet.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API needs request logging, authentication and uniform error JSON for all endpoints.

  • One security filter for authentication.
  • One interceptor for request timing.
  • One @RestControllerAdvice for errors.
  • Dozens of controllers stay free of this code.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DispatcherServlet is the central servlet of Spring MVC. It receives each HTTP request, finds the matching controller method and builds the response.
  • Entry point: in Spring Boot it is registered automatically and mapped to /; you never write it yourself.
  • Helpers: it coordinates HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, ViewResolver and exception resolvers; it does the routing, they do the work.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc is built around a DispatcherServlet.

Worked Example 2

Return 404 as an exception.

Practice Exercise 1

Read it from the context.

Practice Exercise 2

Change the servlet path.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside DispatcherServlet.

  • Auto-config: DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration defines the servlet and a registration bean.
  • Properties: WebMvcProperties holds the spring.mvc.* options.
  • Context: in Boot the embedded server context hosts a single application context.
  • Request attributes: it stores the context, locale and flash maps on the request.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options you can set.

  • spring.mvc.servlet.path: the prefix.
  • spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup: eager start.
  • spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found: 404 as exception.
  • spring.mvc.dispatch-trace-request: pass TRACE requests to controllers.
  • spring.mvc.async.request-timeout: async timeout.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.servlet.path=/api
spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup=1
spring.mvc.async.request-timeout=30s
spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found=true

# OUTPUT:
# All controller URLs are served under /api, async requests time out after 30 s

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Flow: request, find handler, run interceptors, invoke controller, resolve view or write body, return response.
  • Boot auto-configuration: DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration creates the servlet and its registration bean.
  • Context: it owns a WebApplicationContext that holds controllers and web beans, and it sees the root context beans too.

Senior Notes

  • Customizing: use spring.mvc.servlet.path or a DispatcherServletRegistrationBean to change the mapping.
  • Unmatched requests: if no handler is found it returns 404; throwExceptionIfNoHandlerFound turns that into an exception you can handle.
  • Thread model: it is a singleton servlet and each request runs on a container thread, so controllers must be stateless.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes.

  • Servlet path confusion: the controller mapping does not include spring.mvc.servlet.path, the client URL does.
  • Two DispatcherServlets with overlapping mappings: requests go to the longest match.
  • Stateful controllers: fields shared across threads cause races.
  • Calling blocking code at scale: exhausts the thread pool.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning.

  • Thread pool: server.tomcat.threads.max sets request concurrency.
  • Compression and caching: enable server.compression.enabled and set cache headers for static files.
  • Virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true on Java 21 with Boot 3.2 or later.
  • Measure: use Actuator http.server.requests metrics.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.compression.enabled=true
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=7d
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=metrics

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests -> count, total time, max (varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy app has a WAR with a web.xml; migrating to Boot.

  • web.xml servlet becomes auto-configuration.
  • The URL pattern becomes spring.mvc.servlet.path.
  • Context listeners become normal beans.
  • Tests move to MockMvc slices.
codeExamples:
<!-- before: web.xml -->
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>app</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet</servlet-class>
  <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>
<servlet-mapping><servlet-name>app</servlet-name><url-pattern>/</url-pattern></servlet-mapping>

# after: application.properties
# spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup=1   (default mapping is already /)

// OUTPUT:
// Same behaviour with zero XML

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DispatcherServlet is a class that extends HttpServlet through FrameworkServlet; it is the one servlet that receives web requests in a Spring MVC application.
  • Purpose: it finds which controller method should handle a request, calls it and turns the result into an HTTP response.
  • Why needed: without it you would write one servlet per URL and parse parameters, convert data and render pages yourself.

Worked Example 1

Test that the servlet routes a request.

Worked Example 2

Check the registered servlet in a SpringBootTest.

Practice Exercise 1

The smallest working application.

Practice Exercise 2

See the class hierarchy.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it works.

  • service: FrameworkServlet.service sets up context holders and calls doService.
  • doService: adds request attributes (context, locale resolver, theme) and calls doDispatch.
  • doDispatch: finds the handler chain, applies interceptors, calls the adapter and processes the result.
  • Cleanup: it restores holders and publishes a ServletRequestHandledEvent.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants.

  • Servlet 3 style: WebApplicationInitializer.
  • Boot style: auto-configured.
  • Test style: MockMvc creates a mock servlet environment around a real DispatcherServlet.
  • Custom subclass: override doService or noHandlerFound in rare cases.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • What it does: map the URL to a handler, bind request data, call the method, then render a view or write JSON.
  • What it does not do: it holds no business logic; services and repositories do that.
  • Spring Boot: embedded Tomcat starts, the servlet is registered, and you only add @RestController classes.

Senior Notes

  • Class chain: HttpServlet, HttpServletBean, FrameworkServlet, DispatcherServlet.
  • doDispatch is the method that holds the real algorithm; everything else prepares the request for it.
  • Strategy beans: its behaviour is pluggable, because each step is a strategy interface loaded from the context.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes.

  • Missing @EnableWebMvc or Boot: plain Spring has no annotation-driven mapping until configured.
  • Component scan misses controllers: the result is a 404.
  • Mapping /* instead of /: hides static resources and JSP forwarding.
  • Adding @EnableWebMvc in Boot: turns off Boot MVC auto-configuration.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • Startup cost: scanning many controllers adds time; keep the scan narrow.
  • Per request: mapping lookup is a map and trie lookup; the body conversion usually costs more.
  • JSON: reuse the Boot-configured ObjectMapper bean.
  • Lazy init: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true lowers startup but moves the cost to first use.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.main.lazy-initialization=false
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null

# OUTPUT:
# Smaller JSON responses and predictable first-request latency

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a 404 for a URL that looks right.

  • Check the debug log for the mapped handler.
  • Check the servlet path and context path.
  • Check that the controller is in a scanned package.
  • Check the HTTP method and consumes header.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.level.org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation=TRACE
server.servlet.context-path=/shop

# OUTPUT:
# Request must be GET /shop/hello (context path + servlet path + mapping)
# TRACE RequestMappingHandlerMapping : Mapped to HelloController#hello()

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Architecture: DispatcherServlet is a coordinator that delegates each job to a strategy interface instead of doing the job itself.
  • Strategy beans: HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, HandlerExceptionResolver, ViewResolver, LocaleResolver and MultipartResolver.
  • Two contexts: a root context for services and repositories, and a web context for controllers; the web context is the child.

Worked Example 1

Test with a mocked service in the web slice only.

Worked Example 2

Inspect HandlerMapping order.

Practice Exercise 1

List the strategy beans in a running app.

Practice Exercise 2

Customize through WebMvcConfigurer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals of the architecture.

  • Defaults: DispatcherServlet.properties in the Spring jar lists default strategy classes.
  • Lookup: BeanFactoryUtils.beansOfTypeIncludingAncestors collects strategy beans from both contexts.
  • Sorting: AnnotationAwareOrderComparator orders them.
  • Fallback: getDefaultStrategies instantiates defaults if none is found.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for shaping the architecture.

  • WebMvcConfigurer: safe hook for interceptors, formatters, resolvers, CORS and resources.
  • WebMvcRegistrations: replace the mapping or adapter class in Boot.
  • Own beans: define a strategy bean to replace the default one.
  • Parent and child: classic setup with getRootConfigClasses and getServletConfigClasses.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Defaults: if you define no bean of a strategy type, Spring uses defaults from DispatcherServlet.properties.
  • Boot uses one context, but the logical split of web beans and service beans still holds.
  • Extending: add a bean of the strategy type, or implement WebMvcConfigurer to adjust the standard ones.

Senior Notes

  • initStrategies runs once at startup after the context refreshes and looks up each strategy bean by type.
  • Ordering: multiple HandlerMappings and resolvers are sorted by Ordered; the first that returns a result wins.
  • Replace with care: defining your own HandlerMapping bean in Boot can switch off defaults, so prefer WebMvcConfigurer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Duplicate beans in both contexts: controllers scanned twice, services created twice.
  • Component scan in root config picks up @Controller: exclude it.
  • Transactions not applied: services in the child context are not seen by the root proxy setup.
  • Ordering mistakes: a catch-all handler mapping with a low order hides specific ones.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • Strategy lookups happen once at startup, so the architecture costs little per request.
  • Interceptors: each one adds a call per request; restrict them with path patterns.
  • Caching: Cache-Control and ETag filters save work.
  • Conditional requests: ShallowEtagHeaderFilter saves bandwidth, not compute.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: you need audit logging of all /admin calls with the handler name.

  • An interceptor with path pattern /admin/**.
  • It reads the HandlerMethod from the handler argument.
  • Registered in a WebMvcConfigurer.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Initialization: when the servlet container starts the servlet, init() runs once, builds the web context and sets up all strategies.
  • Boot registers it with DispatcherServletRegistrationBean; by default it starts lazily on the first request unless load-on-startup is set, which Boot does.
  • Result: after init the servlet knows its handler mappings, adapters, resolvers and can serve requests.

Worked Example 1

Verify startup fails on an ambiguous mapping.

Worked Example 2

Log the init time.

Practice Exercise 1

Programmatic setup without XML.

Practice Exercise 2

Eager start in Boot.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Initialization sequence.

  • 1. init(): HttpServletBean.init binds servlet init parameters to properties.
  • 2. initServletBean(): FrameworkServlet calls initWebApplicationContext.
  • 3. Context: uses the injected one, finds an existing one or creates a new one with the root as parent.
  • 4. onRefresh(): DispatcherServlet calls initStrategies.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants.

  • web.xml: load-on-startup and contextConfigLocation.
  • Java config: AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer.
  • Boot: ServletContextInitializer and registration beans.
  • Context hierarchy: optional parent, set through ContextLoaderListener.
codeExamples:
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>app</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet</servlet-class>
  <init-param>
    <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
    <param-value>/WEB-INF/app-servlet.xml</param-value>
  </init-param>
  <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// INFO DispatcherServlet : Initializing Servlet 'app'

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Steps: init, create or find the WebApplicationContext, refresh it, then onRefresh calls initStrategies.
  • Property: spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup controls when the servlet is created (Boot default is eager with -1 meaning lazy).
  • Classic setup: in web.xml or a WebApplicationInitializer you declare the servlet and its context config.

Senior Notes

  • initStrategies calls initMultipartResolver, initLocaleResolver, initThemeResolver, initHandlerMappings, initHandlerAdapters, initHandlerExceptionResolvers, initRequestToViewNameTranslator, initViewResolvers and initFlashMapManager.
  • Detect all: by default it collects every bean of each type, including from the parent context.
  • Fail fast: a broken mapping (ambiguous handler) fails at startup, not at request time, which is why startup errors are good news.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Lazy init surprises: the first request is slow and startup errors appear late.
  • Missing config location: FileNotFoundException for app-servlet.xml.
  • Duplicate registration: two initializers register the same servlet name.
  • Blocking init: long work in a @PostConstruct of a controller delays readiness.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • Startup time: mostly component scan and bean creation, not DispatcherServlet itself.
  • Narrow scan and avoid classpath scanning of huge packages.
  • AOT and native: Spring Boot 3 supports AOT processing to speed up startup.
  • Readiness: use actuator health probes so traffic starts only when ready.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
spring.main.banner-mode=off

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/health/readiness -> {"status":"UP"}
once initialization ends

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the first user request after deploy takes 5 seconds.

  • Cause: lazy servlet init or lazy beans.
  • Fix: eager load-on-startup and no lazy initialization.
  • Verify with the startup log timestamp.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup=1
spring.main.lazy-initialization=false

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Started App in 4.1 seconds
# First GET /home -> 38 ms instead of 5 s

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request flow: request arrives, HandlerMapping picks the handler, HandlerAdapter calls it, the result becomes a view or a body, and the response goes back.
  • Controller returns either a view name (with @Controller) or data written directly (with @RestController).
  • Entry method: all of this happens in DispatcherServlet.doDispatch.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc follows the same flow.

Worked Example 2

Debug the flow.

Practice Exercise 1

Trace the steps with an interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

View versus body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The steps in doDispatch.

  • Multipart check: wraps the request if it is multipart.
  • getHandler: returns the chain from the first matching mapping.
  • getHandlerAdapter: first adapter whose supports is true.
  • applyPreHandle: interceptors run in order, and if one returns false the flow stops.
  • handle: the adapter invokes the method.
  • applyPostHandle: interceptors run in reverse order.
  • processDispatchResult: renders the view or resolves the exception, then triggers afterCompletion.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Flow variants.

  • View flow: model, view name, ViewResolver, View.render.
  • Body flow: HttpMessageConverter, no view.
  • Redirect flow: redirect: view and flash attributes.
  • Async flow: first dispatch releases the thread, a second dispatch writes the result.
  • Error flow: exception resolvers, then /error.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: mapping, interceptor preHandle, adapter invokes the method, interceptor postHandle, view rendering, afterCompletion.
  • REST: with @ResponseBody the return value is written by an HttpMessageConverter and no view is resolved.
  • Errors: an exception from the handler goes to HandlerExceptionResolver beans such as @ExceptionHandler methods.

Senior Notes

  • HandlerExecutionChain bundles the handler with its interceptors; the adapter then runs it.
  • Argument resolvers build method parameters (@RequestParam, @RequestBody); return value handlers process the result.
  • Async: a Callable or DeferredResult releases the container thread and the flow resumes with an async dispatch.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • preHandle returns false without writing a response: the client gets an empty 200.
  • Expecting postHandle on errors: use afterCompletion for cleanup.
  • Writing to the response and returning a view: causes IllegalStateException.
  • Missing content negotiation: returns 406 when the Accept header cannot be met.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • Measure each stage: mapping is cheap, body conversion and view rendering are not.
  • Skip views for APIs: return data directly.
  • Template cache: keep Thymeleaf cache on in production, spring.thymeleaf.cache=true.
  • Async: for slow downstream calls.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true

# OUTPUT:
# http.server.requests histogram shows where time is spent (varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: debug why a handler is never reached.

  • Log at TRACE for org.springframework.web.
  • Look for the mapped handler line.
  • Check that an interceptor did not return false.
  • Check security filters before the servlet.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.level.org.springframework.web=TRACE
logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# TRACE DispatcherServlet : GET "/orders/5"
# DEBUG FilterChainProxy : Securing GET /orders/5
# TRACE RequestMappingHandlerMapping : Mapped to OrderController#get(long)

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerMapping is the strategy interface that maps an incoming request to a handler (usually a controller method) plus its interceptors.
  • Main implementation: RequestMappingHandlerMapping reads @RequestMapping, @GetMapping and similar annotations.
  • Result: it returns a HandlerExecutionChain, or null if it cannot match the request.

Worked Example 1

List all mappings at runtime.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc mapping test.

Practice Exercise 1

Mapping by method, header and media type.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom URL mapping bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How RequestMappingHandlerMapping works.

  • Startup: afterPropertiesSet scans beans annotated with @Controller or @RequestMapping.
  • Registry: each method becomes a RequestMappingInfo stored in a MappingRegistry.
  • Lookup: direct path lookup first, then all conditions are tested.
  • Best match: candidates are sorted by a comparator and the first wins.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options.

  • path/value: URL patterns with {var}, * and **.
  • method: HTTP verbs, or composed annotations such as @PostMapping.
  • params and headers: require values.
  • consumes and produces: media types.
  • Programmatic: registerMapping to add routes at runtime.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Match criteria: path, HTTP method, params, headers, consumes and produces.
  • Others: BeanNameUrlHandlerMapping (bean name is the URL), RouterFunctionMapping and SimpleUrlHandlerMapping (used for static resources).
  • Order: several mappings run in order and the first non-null result wins.

Senior Notes

  • Registration: at startup all handler methods are scanned and stored in a MappingRegistry keyed by request mapping info.
  • Best match: if several mappings fit, the most specific one wins; a tie gives an ambiguous mapping error.
  • Path patterns: Spring 6 uses PathPattern by default, which is faster than the old AntPathMatcher.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Ambiguous mapping: two methods with the same path and conditions.
  • Trailing slash: in Spring 6 /items/ no longer matches /items.
  • Wrong media type: 415 for consumes, 406 for produces.
  • Class-level path forgotten: the method path is appended to it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • PathPattern: pre-parsed patterns, faster than regex or Ant matching.
  • Direct lookup: static paths use a hash map.
  • Avoid many regex-heavy mappings on hot paths.
  • Cache: the mapping lookup result is cached in a request attribute.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.pathmatch.matching-strategy=path_pattern_parser

# OUTPUT:
# Default in Boot 2.6 and later: PathPatternParser is used for request mapping

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: API versioning by header, so /orders serves v1 and v2.

  • Two methods with the same path.
  • Differentiated by a header condition.
  • Falls back to 404 or 400 when no version matches.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerAdapter is the strategy that knows how to actually invoke a handler of a certain type, so DispatcherServlet can stay independent of handler kinds.
  • Main implementation: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter invokes @RequestMapping methods.
  • Contract: supports(handler) says if it can run the handler, and handle(...) runs it and returns a ModelAndView or null.

Worked Example 1

Test the custom parameter.

Worked Example 2

Show adapters in the context.

Practice Exercise 1

A custom argument resolver.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How RequestMappingHandlerAdapter works.

  • Build: it wraps the HandlerMethod in an InvocableHandlerMethod.
  • Arguments: a composite of resolvers tries each one until supportsParameter is true.
  • Invoke: the method is called by reflection.
  • Return: a composite of return value handlers writes the result or sets the view.
  • Binder: @InitBinder and conversion are applied before binding.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Built-in resolvers and handlers.

  • @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue.
  • @RequestBody and HttpEntity use converters.
  • Model, Principal, Locale, HttpServletRequest are accepted directly.
  • Return types: String view name, ResponseEntity, void, Callable, StreamingResponseBody.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Argument resolving: the adapter fills method parameters using HandlerMethodArgumentResolver beans (for example for @RequestParam).
  • Return values: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler beans process what the method returns.
  • Conversion: HttpMessageConverter turns JSON into objects and back for @RequestBody and @ResponseBody.

Senior Notes

  • Why an adapter: handlers can be controllers, HttpRequestHandler beans or functions, and each needs a different call style.
  • Flow: DispatcherServlet loops over adapters, takes the first where supports is true and calls handle.
  • Customization: add resolvers or converters through WebMvcConfigurer instead of replacing the adapter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Missing parameter: a required @RequestParam gives 400.
  • Type mismatch: /items/abc for a long gives 400.
  • Reading the body twice: the input stream is consumed once.
  • Replacing the adapter bean: loses Boot defaults such as the JSON converter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • Reflection is cached: method metadata and parameter resolvers are looked up once per parameter.
  • Converters: Jackson is the main cost; keep payloads small.
  • Streaming: use StreamingResponseBody for large downloads.
  • Avoid reading the whole request into memory.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: inject the current tenant into controllers.

  • Annotation @Tenant on a parameter.
  • A resolver reads the tenant from a header.
  • Controllers need no boilerplate.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerExceptionResolver is the strategy that turns an exception thrown during request handling into a response, such as an error page or a JSON body.
  • Default chain: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver (for @ExceptionHandler), ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Use: you normally write @ExceptionHandler methods in a @ControllerAdvice class and let Spring wire the resolver.

Worked Example 1

Test the handler.

Worked Example 2

A custom resolver bean.

Practice Exercise 1

Global handler with a JSON body.

Practice Exercise 2

Exception with a status.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How resolution works.

  • Catch: doDispatch catches the exception and calls processHandlerException.
  • Loop: each resolver in handlerExceptionResolvers gets a chance.
  • ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver: finds an @ExceptionHandler method in the controller, then in advice beans, with the closest exception type.
  • ResponseStatusExceptionResolver: reads @ResponseStatus and ResponseStatusException.
  • DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver: maps framework exceptions to status codes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to handle errors.

  • @ExceptionHandler in the controller or advice.
  • @ResponseStatus on an exception class.
  • ResponseStatusException thrown inline.
  • ResponseEntityExceptionHandler base class for standard exceptions.
  • Custom HandlerExceptionResolver bean for special cases.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @ResponseStatus on an exception class gives it a fixed status code.
  • DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps standard Spring exceptions, for example a missing parameter becomes 400 and wrong method becomes 405.
  • ProblemDetail: Spring 6 supports RFC 7807 error bodies with ProblemDetail and ResponseEntityExceptionHandler.

Senior Notes

  • Order: resolvers are asked in order; the first returning a non-null ModelAndView (an empty one means handled) ends the search.
  • Unresolved: the exception goes to the container and, in Boot, to BasicErrorController for the /error page.
  • Scope: @ExceptionHandler in a controller applies only to it; in @ControllerAdvice it applies globally or to selected packages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Catching Exception broadly: hides bugs and wrong status codes.
  • Returning 200 with an error body: breaks clients and monitoring.
  • Leaking stack traces: keep server.error.include-stacktrace=never.
  • Handler in advice not picked: missing scan, or an earlier handler with a closer type.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and robustness.

  • Handlers should be cheap; log once, not per layer.
  • Use correlation ids in the error body.
  • Do not catch and rethrow in each controller.
  • Disable the whitelabel page for APIs.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.error.include-stacktrace=never
server.error.include-message=never
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Errors return RFC 7807 bodies without internal details

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: unified error format for a public API.

  • One advice class for the whole application.
  • Validation errors list the failing fields.
  • Unknown errors return 500 with a trace id and are logged.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ViewResolver turns a logical view name returned by a controller (such as home) into a real View object that renders the page.
  • Why: controllers stay independent of the template technology, so you can switch JSP, Thymeleaf or FreeMarker by configuration.
  • Not used for @RestController or @ResponseBody, because there is no view to render.

Worked Example 1

Test the view name and model.

Worked Example 2

Redirect after POST.

Practice Exercise 1

A controller returning a view name.

Practice Exercise 2

JSP style resolver.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How view resolution works.

  • View name: the controller returns a string or a ModelAndView.
  • Loop: resolveViewName asks each ViewResolver in order.
  • Base class: AbstractCachingViewResolver caches views by name and locale.
  • Render: View.render(model, request, response) writes the page.
  • Default name: if the controller returns nothing, RequestToViewNameTranslator derives the name from the URL.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolver types.

  • InternalResourceViewResolver: JSP and servlet forwards.
  • ThymeleafViewResolver, FreeMarkerViewResolver, MustacheViewResolver.
  • BeanNameViewResolver: view name equals a bean name.
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver: choose by Accept header.
  • XmlViewResolver and ResourceBundleViewResolver: legacy.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • InternalResourceViewResolver adds a prefix and suffix, for example /WEB-INF/views/ and .jsp.
  • Thymeleaf: Boot configures ThymeleafViewResolver with classpath:/templates/ and .html by default.
  • Properties: spring.mvc.view.prefix and spring.mvc.view.suffix change the lookup for JSP setups.

Senior Notes

  • Chain: several resolvers are ordered and the first that returns a non-null View wins; InternalResourceViewResolver accepts any name so it must be last.
  • Content negotiation: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver picks among resolvers by the requested media type.
  • Special prefixes: redirect: and forward: make UrlBasedViewResolver return a redirect or forward view.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes.

  • Wrong prefix or suffix: 404 for the template.
  • Missing starter: without spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf the name is not resolved.
  • @Controller instead of @RestController: a returned String is read as a view name.
  • JSP in an executable jar: not supported well; use Thymeleaf or a WAR.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance.

  • View cache: AbstractCachingViewResolver caches views; keep it enabled.
  • Template cache: spring.thymeleaf.cache=true in production and false in development.
  • Many resolvers: fewer resolvers means less lookup per request.
  • Fragments and gzip: reduce output size.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/templates/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Templates are parsed once and reused for later requests

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the same URL serves HTML for browsers and JSON for API clients.

  • Content negotiation picks the output.
  • The model is the shared data.
  • Tests check both representations.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • View is the V in MVC: the object that renders the model into the response, for example an HTML page, JSON or a PDF. In Spring it is the interface org.springframework.web.servlet.View.
  • Logical view name: a controller usually returns a plain string such as "home". It does not build the page itself.
  • Who renders: DispatcherServlet asks a ViewResolver to turn the name into a View, then calls view.render(model, request, response).

Worked Example 1

Registering a view resolver.

Worked Example 2

Testing the chosen view name with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Controller returning a logical view name.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect after a form post.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a view gets rendered:

  • Handler result: the controller returns a name, a View or a ModelAndView.
  • render(): DispatcherServlet.render calls resolveViewName, which loops over all ViewResolver beans in order.
  • Locale: the resolver receives the request locale, so one name can map to different templates.
  • Output: view.render(model, request, response) merges the model into request attributes (JSP) or a template context (Thymeleaf).
  • Missing view: if no resolver answers, a ServletException says "Could not resolve view with name".

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of returning a view:

  • String name: the usual choice.
  • View object: returned directly, no resolver needed.
  • redirect: and forward: special prefixes handled by UrlBasedViewResolver.
  • void: the default view name is derived from the URL.
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver: picks a view by Accept header or extension.
  • Chaining: set order on each resolver; JSP resolvers match every name, so keep them last.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ViewResolver implementations: InternalResourceViewResolver for JSP, Thymeleaf and FreeMarker resolvers, and ContentNegotiatingViewResolver to choose by media type.
  • Redirect and forward: the prefixes redirect: and forward: in a view name create a RedirectView or an internal forward.
  • @ResponseBody skips the view layer: the return value is written by an HttpMessageConverter, so no View is involved.

Senior Notes

  • Custom View: implement View or extend AbstractView to produce CSV, Excel or PDF output from the model.
  • Resolver order: several resolvers form a chain sorted by order; the first one that returns a non-null view wins.
  • Caching: resolvers cache resolved views by name, so a missing template shows up as an error at render time, not at startup.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • @Controller with a string meant as JSON: add @ResponseBody or use @RestController, or the string is treated as a view name.
  • Circular view path: a controller path equal to the view name makes a forward loop.
  • Wrong prefix: a missing slash gives 404 for the JSP.
  • Views under WEB-INF: put templates there so they cannot be requested directly.
  • Model data lost on redirect: use flash attributes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • View caching: keep the resolver cache enabled in production; turn off template caching only in development.
  • Template engine: precompile JSPs and cache Thymeleaf templates.
  • Resolver count: every resolver is tried for each miss, so register few.
  • Large pages: avoid heavy logic in templates; compute in the controller or service.
  • APIs: skip the view layer with @ResponseBody.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (Spring Boot with Thymeleaf)
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/templates/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=1d

# OUTPUT:
# templates are parsed once and reused;
static assets cached by the browser for a day

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin portal serves HTML pages and also a CSV export of orders.

  • The HTML page returns a logical name resolved by Thymeleaf.
  • The export returns a custom View that streams CSV.
  • Both read the same model attributes, so the service layer is shared.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Model is the M in MVC: a map of named attributes that carries data from the controller to the view. In Spring it is the interface org.springframework.ui.Model.
  • Adding data: call model.addAttribute("name", value) in a handler method, then the view reads name.
  • Declared as a parameter: Spring injects the model into the handler method, so you never create it yourself.

Worked Example 1

Flash attribute across a redirect.

Worked Example 2

Asserting model content in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Fill the model and read it in the view.

Practice Exercise 2

Shared attribute for all handlers.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What the model really is:

  • Creation: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter creates a ModelAndViewContainer holding a BindingAwareModelMap.
  • Injection: ModelMethodProcessor passes that map when a handler parameter is Model, ModelMap or Map.
  • Before the handler: @ModelAttribute methods run and fill the model.
  • After the handler: the model is passed to the view, and values are exposed as request attributes.
  • Binding results: BindingResult objects are stored under keys that start with org.springframework.validation.BindingResult.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for passing data:

  • Model: the common choice.
  • ModelMap: map-style helpers such as addAllAttributes.
  • Map parameter: works the same but hides intent.
  • ModelAndView: data and view together.
  • Auto-naming: addAttribute(value) without a name derives one from the type, for example a User becomes user and a List<User> becomes userList.
  • @SessionAttributes: keeps chosen attributes in the session across requests.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Types: Model is the simple interface, ModelMap is a LinkedHashMap variant, and Map<String,Object> also works as a parameter.
  • Request scope: model attributes are copied into request attributes when the view renders, so they live for one request.
  • @ModelAttribute on a method adds attributes before every handler of that controller runs.

Senior Notes

  • BindingAwareModelMap is the real class behind the parameter; it also holds BindingResult entries for validation.
  • Redirects: the model is not kept across a redirect; use RedirectAttributes and flash attributes instead.
  • Size: keep the model small, because everything in it is exposed to the view and sometimes serialized into the page.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Mutable shared objects: putting a singleton bean in the model lets a view change shared state.
  • Forgetting that the model is per request: data is gone after a redirect.
  • Large objects: loading whole entity graphs into the model slows rendering and can trigger lazy-loading errors.
  • Name clashes: two attributes with the same key overwrite each other.
  • Wrong type in the view: a mistyped attribute name gives an empty value without an error in JSP.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Keep it small: send only what the page shows.
  • Avoid session attributes: they use memory and need replication in a cluster.
  • Pagination: pass a Page, not the whole table.
  • Open-in-view: disable spring.jpa.open-in-view and use DTOs, so database sessions are not held during rendering.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

# OUTPUT:
# the connection returns to the pool before the view renders

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a product list page needs the products, the current filter and a total count.

  • The controller builds a DTO page in the service.
  • The filter is added so the form shows the chosen values.
  • A test checks the model keys, so the page contract is protected.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ModelAndView is a holder object that carries both the model data and the view (name or object) back to DispatcherServlet in one return value.
  • Creation: new ModelAndView("home", "msg", "Hi") sets the view name plus one attribute; addObject adds more.
  • Result: DispatcherServlet reads the view and model from it, resolves the view and renders it.

Worked Example 1

Exception resolver returning a ModelAndView.

Worked Example 2

Testing the returned object.

Practice Exercise 1

Return a ModelAndView.

Practice Exercise 2

Set a status code.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside ModelAndView:

  • Fields: Object view, ModelMap model, HttpStatusCode status and a cleared flag.
  • View is a String name or a View; isReference() tells which.
  • Return handler: ModelAndViewMethodReturnValueHandler copies the view and model into the ModelAndViewContainer.
  • Other types (String, View, Model) are converted to the same container, so ModelAndView is just one input form.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Constructor and helper variants:

  • new ModelAndView(): empty, fill later.
  • new ModelAndView(String viewName).
  • new ModelAndView(String viewName, String attrName, Object value).
  • new ModelAndView(String viewName, Map<String,?> model).
  • new ModelAndView(View view): an explicit view object.
  • new ModelAndView(String viewName, HttpStatusCode status): with a status.
  • setViewName, addAllObjects, clear() and RedirectView for redirects with options.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Fields: it wraps a view (a name string or a View), a ModelMap and an optional HttpStatus.
  • Common in older code and in HandlerExceptionResolver implementations, which must return a ModelAndView.
  • Modern style: returning a String plus a Model parameter does the same job with less code.

Senior Notes

  • Internally every handler result is normalized to a ModelAndView by ModelAndViewContainer and the return value handlers.
  • Empty view: new ModelAndView() without a name makes Spring use the default view name translator (the URL path).
  • Redirect: new ModelAndView("redirect:/x") works exactly like the string form.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No view and no model: an empty ModelAndView means the request is already handled, so nothing is rendered.
  • Returning null has the same effect and often gives a blank page.
  • Mixing @ResponseBody with ModelAndView: the body writer wins and the view is ignored.
  • Reusing one instance as a field makes it shared across threads; always create it per request.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • The object is cheap; one per request costs almost nothing.
  • The cost is in the model content and in the view rendering.
  • Prefer plain String returns in new code to reduce boilerplate.
  • Do not copy large maps with addAllObjects when a reference will do.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a global error page built from an exception resolver.

  • The resolver logs the error and picks a view by exception type.
  • It returns a ModelAndView with the status and a message.
  • It returns null for exceptions it does not handle, so the next resolver gets a turn.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request pipeline: the ordered steps a request passes from the servlet container to the response. DispatcherServlet is the front controller that drives them.
  • Main steps: find the handler (HandlerMapping), call it (HandlerAdapter), get a ModelAndView, resolve the view (ViewResolver), render it.
  • Extra hooks: servlet filters run before the servlet, and interceptors run around the handler.

Worked Example 1

Seeing the order with a filter and an interceptor.

Worked Example 2

Testing the pipeline.

Practice Exercise 1

Logging the pipeline with an interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it for some paths.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The flow inside DispatcherServlet.doDispatch:

  • 1. Container filters run, then FrameworkServlet.service calls doService.
  • 2. getHandler loops over HandlerMapping beans and returns a HandlerExecutionChain (handler plus interceptors).
  • 3. getHandlerAdapter finds an adapter that supports the handler.
  • 4. Interceptors preHandle; if one returns false the chain stops.
  • 5. ha.handle resolves arguments, invokes the method and handles the return value.
  • 6. postHandle, then processDispatchResult renders the view or runs exception resolvers.
  • 7. afterCompletion always runs for interceptors that returned true.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where you can plug in:

  • Filter: OncePerRequestFilter for logging, security and encoding.
  • Interceptor: HandlerInterceptor for handler-aware cross-cutting logic.
  • Argument resolver: a custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver for your own parameter types.
  • Return value handler: custom return types.
  • Advice: RequestBodyAdvice and ResponseBodyAdvice around body conversion.
  • Exception resolver: @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: Filter, DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, interceptor preHandle, argument resolvers, handler method, return value handler, postHandle, view render, afterCompletion.
  • Argument resolution: HandlerMethodArgumentResolver fills parameters such as @RequestParam and @RequestBody.
  • Errors: exceptions go to HandlerExceptionResolver beans, including @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice methods.

Senior Notes

  • doDispatch in DispatcherServlet contains the whole flow; reading it once explains most behavior.
  • Filter or interceptor: filters see every request and work at servlet level; interceptors know the handler and work at Spring level.
  • REST path: with @ResponseBody the return value handler writes the body directly and the view step is skipped.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Interceptor returns false without writing a response: the client gets an empty 200.
  • Filter order wrong: a security filter placed after the logging filter hides the user name.
  • Reading the body twice: the request stream can be read only once; wrap the request if needed.
  • Thinking interceptors see static files: that depends on the resource handler setup.
  • Handling exceptions in the interceptor instead of in @ControllerAdvice.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cheap interceptors: they run on every request, so avoid database calls.
  • Path patterns: limit interceptors to the paths they need.
  • Handler lookup is cached after startup; the mapping uses a path-pattern tree, so large controller counts are fine.
  • Async: return Callable or DeferredResult to free the container thread for slow work.
  • Measure: Micrometer exposes http.server.requests timing for every handler.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: audit every API call with the user, path, status and duration.

  • A filter wraps the request so it can read the status and time the whole chain.
  • The audit entry is written after the response, so failures are logged as well.
  • The same entry can add the handler name through an interceptor attribute.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • XML configuration defines Spring beans and MVC settings in files such as applicationContext.xml and dispatcher-servlet.xml, the original Spring style.
  • web.xml declares DispatcherServlet and the context config location, so the servlet container can start Spring.
  • Key tags: <context:component-scan>, <mvc:annotation-driven/> and a view resolver <bean>.

Worked Example 1

Static resources and interceptor in XML.
codeExamples:
<mvc:resources mapping="/static/**" location="/static/"/>
<mvc:interceptors>
  <bean class="com.example.web.TimingInterceptor"/>
</mvc:interceptors>

<!-- OUTPUT: /static/app.css is served directly; every request is timed -->

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Loading XML in a test.

web.xml wiring.

<web-app>
  <servlet>
    <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>
      org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet
    </servlet-class>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
  </servlet>
  <servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

dispatcher-servlet.xml.
codeExamples:
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:mvc="http://www.springframework.org/schema/mvc"
       xmlns:context="http://www.springframework.org/schema/context">
  <context:component-scan base-package="com.example.web"/>
  <mvc:annotation-driven/>
  <bean class="org.springframework.web.servlet.view.InternalResourceViewResolver">
    <property name="prefix" value="/WEB-INF/views/"/>
    <property name="suffix" value=".jsp"/>
  </bean>
</beans>

<!-- OUTPUT: controllers in com.example.web are found;
views map to JSPs -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the XML is processed:

  • Startup: the container reads web.xml, creates ContextLoaderListener (root context) and DispatcherServlet (child context).
  • Reader: XmlBeanDefinitionReader parses each file into BeanDefinition objects.
  • Namespaces: NamespaceHandler classes registered in META-INF/spring.handlers translate tags such as mvc:annotation-driven.
  • Refresh: AbstractApplicationContext.refresh instantiates singletons and runs post-processors.
  • Visibility: child beans see root beans, but root beans do not see child beans.
codeExamples:
<!-- web.xml: root context -->
<context-param>
  <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
  <param-value>/WEB-INF/applicationContext.xml</param-value>
</context-param>
<listener>
  <listener-class>
    org.springframework.web.context.ContextLoaderListener
  </listener-class>
</listener>

<!-- OUTPUT:
     root context = services and repositories
     dispatcher-servlet.xml = child context with controllers -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful XML options:

  • Bean wiring: constructor-arg and property elements, with ref or value.
  • Properties: context:property-placeholder loads a properties file.
  • Profiles: a nested beans profile="dev" element.
  • Imports: import resource="other.xml" splits large files.
  • Annotation config: context:annotation-config turns on @Autowired without scanning.
  • Message converters: nested elements under mvc:annotation-driven.
codeExamples:
<beans profile="dev">
  <bean id="dataSource" class="org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.DriverManagerDataSource">
    <property name="url" value="jdbc:h2:mem:test"/>
  </bean>
</beans>
<beans profile="prod">
  <bean id="dataSource" class="com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource">
    <property name="jdbcUrl" value="jdbc:postgresql://db/app"/>
  </bean>
</beans>

<!-- OUTPUT: the bean for the active profile (spring.profiles.active) is created -->

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Two contexts: a root context (services, repositories) loaded by ContextLoaderListener, and a web context (controllers) owned by the servlet.
  • Default file: a servlet named dispatcher loads /WEB-INF/dispatcher-servlet.xml unless contextConfigLocation says otherwise.
  • Resources: <mvc:resources> serves static files and <mvc:interceptors> registers interceptors.

Senior Notes

  • Parsing: namespace handlers turn each XML tag into bean definitions, so mvc:annotation-driven registers the same beans as @EnableWebMvc.
  • Trade-off: XML needs no recompile and is explicit, but it is verbose and has no compile-time checking.
  • Mixing: @ImportResource lets a Java configuration load legacy XML during migration.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Wrong XSD or namespace: tags are unknown; check the schema declarations.
  • Controllers scanned in the root context: mappings do not work in the child context; scan controllers only in the servlet file.
  • Duplicate scan: scanning the same package in both contexts creates two copies of each bean.
  • Missing mvc:annotation-driven: @RequestMapping methods return 404.
  • Typos in class names fail only at startup.
codeExamples:
<!-- root context: services only -->
<context:component-scan base-package="com.example">
  <context:exclude-filter type="annotation"
      expression="org.springframework.stereotype.Controller"/>
</context:component-scan>

<!-- servlet context: controllers only -->
<context:component-scan base-package="com.example" use-default-filters="false">
  <context:include-filter type="annotation"
      expression="org.springframework.stereotype.Controller"/>
</context:component-scan>

<!-- OUTPUT: each bean exists once, in the right context -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Startup time: classpath scanning plus big XML files slow startup; narrow base packages.
  • Lazy init: default-lazy-init="true" on the beans element postpones creation.
  • Validation: XML schema validation costs a little; it stays on in dev to catch errors.
  • Migration: moving to Java config gives IDE refactoring and faster feedback.
codeExamples:
<beans default-lazy-init="true" xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans">
  <!-- beans are created on first use -->
</beans>

<!-- OUTPUT:
     startup time drops;
     the first request pays the creation cost -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a ten-year-old WAR application moves to Java configuration step by step.

  • Create a @Configuration class that imports the old XML.
  • Convert beans one module at a time and delete their XML.
  • Replace web.xml with an initializer when no listeners remain.
  • Keep tests loading the context after each step.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Java-based configuration replaces XML with classes annotated @Configuration, so beans and MVC settings are plain, type-checked Java code.
  • Servlet setup also needs no web.xml: a class extending AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer registers DispatcherServlet.
  • MVC setup: a class with @EnableWebMvc, @ComponentScan and WebMvcConfigurer replaces mvc:annotation-driven.

Worked Example 1

A bean method.

Worked Example 2

Testing the configuration.

Practice Exercise 1

Initializer replacing web.xml.

Practice Exercise 2

Web configuration class.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Bootstrapping without XML:

  • Discovery: the servlet container finds SpringServletContainerInitializer, which calls every WebApplicationInitializer.
  • Context: the base class builds an AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext for root and servlet configs.
  • Parsing: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import and @Bean.
  • Registration: the servlet is added with ServletContext.addServlet.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options in Java configuration:

  • @Import of other configuration classes or selectors.
  • @PropertySource plus Environment to read properties.
  • @Profile and @Conditional for environment-specific beans.
  • @Bean attributes: name, initMethod, destroyMethod.
  • @Scope to change singleton to prototype or request.
  • @Lazy to delay creation.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Initializer: override getRootConfigClasses, getServletConfigClasses and getServletMappings.
  • Beans: methods annotated @Bean create objects, such as a view resolver or a DataSource.
  • Spring Boot goes one step further: auto-configuration provides most of this, so you write only what differs.

Senior Notes

  • Discovery: the container finds the initializer through ServletContainerInitializer and SpringServletContainerInitializer (Servlet 3.0 plus).
  • CGLIB: a full @Configuration class is proxied so that calls between @Bean methods return the same singleton.
  • Benefits: refactoring support, compile-time checks, conditional beans with @Profile and @Conditional.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Calling a @Bean method from a lite class: with proxyBeanMethods = false it creates a new object; pass a parameter instead.
  • Final configuration class: CGLIB cannot subclass it.
  • Wrong root and servlet split: controllers in the root config are not found by the servlet.
  • Circular dependencies between beans; use setter injection or redesign.
  • Hard-coded values: read them from the Environment.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Lite mode avoids CGLIB subclass creation and speeds startup.
  • Narrow scanning with specific packages reduces classpath work.
  • @Lazy on rarely used beans defers cost.
  • Static @Bean methods for post-processors avoid early creation of the configuration class.
  • Conditionals keep unused infrastructure out of the context.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team builds a new Spring MVC WAR without Boot for a container that is mandated by the customer.

  • An initializer replaces web.xml.
  • Root config holds services, JPA and security; web config holds MVC.
  • Tests use @SpringJUnitWebConfig and MockMvc.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @Configuration marks a class as a source of bean definitions. Spring reads its @Bean methods and registers the returned objects in the container.
  • Stereotype: it is itself meta-annotated with @Component, so component scanning picks it up.
  • Typical use: define infrastructure beans (DataSource, ObjectMapper, view resolvers) and import other configuration with @Import.

Worked Example 1

Singleton guarantee.

Worked Example 2

Testing with a slice.

Practice Exercise 1

Basic configuration class.

Practice Exercise 2

Profile-specific bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How @Configuration is processed:

  • Early parsing: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, a BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor, finds candidate classes.
  • ConfigurationClassParser handles @ComponentScan, @Import, @PropertySource and @Bean methods.
  • Enhancement: full classes are replaced by a CGLIB subclass that intercepts @Bean calls.
  • Interception: a call first checks the container for an existing singleton and creates one only if missing.
  • Loading: ConfigurationClassBeanDefinitionReader turns each @Bean method into a bean definition.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to compose configuration:

  • @Import(Other.class): pull in another configuration.
  • ImportSelector and ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar: choose or register beans programmatically (used by @Enable... annotations).
  • @ComponentScan: discover nested configuration classes.
  • @Conditional variants: @ConditionalOnProperty (Boot), @Profile.
  • @ConfigurationProperties in Boot: bind a group of properties to a typed class.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @Bean methods: the method name is the bean name; parameters are injected from the container.
  • Related: @ComponentScan, @PropertySource, @Import, @Profile and @EnableXxx annotations combine with it.
  • Boot: @SpringBootApplication includes @SpringBootConfiguration, which is a @Configuration.

Senior Notes

  • Full versus lite mode: a class with @Configuration is subclassed by CGLIB so that @Bean methods return singletons; proxyBeanMethods = false disables it.
  • Processing: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses these classes early and registers bean definitions before any bean is created.
  • Static @Bean methods are needed for BeanFactoryPostProcessor beans so that the configuration class is not created too early.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • @Configuration on a class with a constructor needing unavailable args: keep constructors simple or inject by parameters.
  • Missing @Configuration: a class with only @Bean methods (lite mode) works but without the singleton guarantee.
  • Beans defined twice by scanning and an @Import; the later definition may override or fail.
  • Non-static BeanPostProcessor beans trigger warnings that the configuration class is created too early.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • proxyBeanMethods = false on classes whose beans do not call each other.
  • Slim classes: many small configurations are easier to test and conditionally load.
  • Startup report: Boot --debug shows conditions evaluation; Actuator /actuator/beans lists the beans.
  • GraalVM: lite mode and static analysis friendly code help native images.
codeExamples:
# application.properties: list what was created
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=beans,conditions

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/beans -> JSON of every bean and its dependencies

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service needs a different HTTP client per environment.

  • A configuration reads the base URL and timeout from properties.
  • A profile switches to a stub client in tests.
  • The rest of the code only sees the PaymentClient interface.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @EnableWebMvc imports the default Spring MVC configuration (DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration), which registers handler mappings, adapters, converters and validators.
  • Where: put it on a @Configuration class in a plain Spring MVC (non Boot) application.
  • Customizing: implement WebMvcConfigurer in the same class to change parts of the defaults.

Worked Example 1

Mistake: static files break in Boot.

Worked Example 2

Test that the infrastructure is present.

Practice Exercise 1

Plain Spring MVC setup.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot: customize without the annotation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What the annotation sets up:

  • Import: @Import(DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration.class).
  • Support class: WebMvcConfigurationSupport declares the beans: RequestMappingHandlerMapping, RequestMappingHandlerAdapter, ContentNegotiationManager, HandlerExceptionResolver chain and more.
  • Delegation: the delegating subclass autowires every WebMvcConfigurer and calls them in turn.
  • Detection: Jackson, JAXB and others are added when found on the classpath.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and alternatives:

  • @EnableWebMvc + WebMvcConfigurer: standard in plain Spring.
  • Extend WebMvcConfigurationSupport: full control, override @Bean methods yourself.
  • Boot without the annotation: auto-configuration plus WebMvcConfigurer.
  • @EnableWebMvc in Boot: intentional full takeover.
  • WebMvcRegistrations: Boot hook to replace a core MVC component but keep the rest.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registers: RequestMappingHandlerMapping, RequestMappingHandlerAdapter, HandlerExceptionResolver beans, message converters (JSON if Jackson is present).
  • Not needed in Boot: Spring Boot auto-configures MVC. Adding @EnableWebMvc there switches off Boot MVC auto-configuration, including static resources and JSON settings.
  • Same as XML: it is the Java equivalent of <mvc:annotation-driven/>.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanism: the annotation uses @Import(DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration.class), which collects every WebMvcConfigurer bean and calls their methods.
  • Auto-config back-off: Boot WebMvcAutoConfiguration is @ConditionalOnMissingBean(WebMvcConfigurationSupport.class), so the import turns it off.
  • Only one: use a single @EnableWebMvc in the application; extending WebMvcConfigurationSupport has the same effect.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • @EnableWebMvc in a Boot app by habit: static files, welcome page and Boot JSON properties stop working; remove it.
  • Two @EnableWebMvc classes or a class extending the support class plus the annotation: duplicate beans.
  • Forgetting resource handling after enabling it in plain Spring: add addResourceHandlers or configurer.enable() for the default servlet.
  • No Jackson on the classpath: @ResponseBody objects fail with 406.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • The annotation itself has no runtime cost; the cost is in the registered components.
  • Remove unused message converters to shorten the search for the right one.
  • Cache static resources with setCachePeriod or a resource chain with versioned URLs.
  • Configure a single ObjectMapper bean and reuse it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy WAR migrates to Spring Boot.

  • The old @EnableWebMvc class has many customizations.
  • The annotation is removed and the class keeps only implements WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Tests with @WebMvcTest confirm the pages and JSON are unchanged.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • WebMvcConfigurer is a callback interface for customizing Spring MVC. All methods are default, so you override only what you need.
  • Typical hooks: addInterceptors, addResourceHandlers, addCorsMappings, addViewControllers and configureMessageConverters.
  • Use with: @EnableWebMvc in plain Spring, or alone in Spring Boot to keep the defaults.

Worked Example 1

Custom formatter.

Worked Example 2

Testing CORS.

Practice Exercise 1
