Interceptor, CORS and resources together.

Practice Exercise 2

View controller without a handler class.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the callbacks are used:

  • Collection: DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration.setConfigurers receives all WebMvcConfigurer beans.
  • Composite: a WebMvcConfigurerComposite loops over them for each hook.
  • Hooks: the support class calls addInterceptors, addResourceHandlers and others while it builds the MVC beans.
  • Java 8 defaults: since all methods are default, you do not need the old adapter class.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Frequently used hooks:

  • addInterceptors, addCorsMappings, addResourceHandlers.
  • addViewControllers, configureViewResolvers.
  • addArgumentResolvers, addReturnValueHandlers.
  • configureMessageConverters, extendMessageConverters.
  • addFormatters, getValidator.
  • configureContentNegotiation, configureAsyncSupport, configurePathMatch.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • CORS: registry.addMapping("/api/**").allowedOrigins("https://app.example.com").
  • Formatters: addFormatters registers converters for request parameters and path variables.
  • Resources: addResourceHandlers maps /static/** to a classpath or file location.

Senior Notes

  • Delegation: DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration autowires all WebMvcConfigurer beans and calls each one while building the MVC beans.
  • Order: several configurers are combined, in @Order order; later ones can add to earlier ones.
  • Message converters: configureMessageConverters replaces the defaults, while extendMessageConverters only adds or edits them.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • configureMessageConverters instead of extend: the defaults vanish and some content types stop working.
  • Interceptor on "/**" blocking static files: exclude resource paths.
  • CORS with credentials and wildcard origin: browsers reject it; list explicit origins.
  • Spring Security ignoring MVC CORS: enable http.cors() as well.
  • Interceptor bean not registered: an interceptor is only active after addInterceptor.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • maxAge on CORS caches preflight results in the browser.
  • Resource chain with a content hash and CachingResourceResolver reduces repeated lookups.
  • Async support: set a task executor with configureAsyncSupport for Callable returns.
  • Interceptor patterns: keep them narrow.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a single-page app on one domain calls an API on another.

  • CORS is allowed for the front-end origin only.
  • A request-ID interceptor adds a header for tracing.
  • A test checks both behaviors through MockMvc.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Component scanning makes Spring search packages for classes marked @Component (or @Controller, @Service, @Repository) and register them as beans.
  • Enable it with @ComponentScan("com.example") on a configuration class, or <context:component-scan> in XML.
  • Result: you do not write @Bean methods or XML for each class; annotating the class is enough.

Worked Example 1

Boot: scan another package.

Worked Example 2

Checking registration in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Scan configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Excluding by annotation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the scan works:

  • Parser: ComponentScanAnnotationParser creates a ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner.
  • Search: it lists .class resources under the base package (classpath*:com/example/**/*.class).
  • Metadata: the ASM-based MetadataReader reads annotations without loading the class.
  • Filter: classes with @Component (directly or as a meta-annotation) pass; abstract classes and interfaces are skipped.
  • Registration: a ScannedGenericBeanDefinition is registered with a name from AnnotationBeanNameGenerator.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = X.class): type-safe marker class instead of a string.
  • useDefaultFilters = false with includeFilters: scan only chosen types.
  • nameGenerator: custom naming.
  • lazyInit = true: scanned beans created on demand.
  • @ComponentScans or repeated @ComponentScan: several scans.
  • Boot: @SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = ...).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Stereotypes: @Controller, @Service and @Repository are specializations of @Component with extra meaning.
  • Base packages: basePackages or basePackageClasses set where to look, and sub-packages are included.
  • Filters: includeFilters and excludeFilters narrow the scan by annotation, type or regex.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanism: ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner reads class files with ASM metadata, without loading the classes, and registers bean definitions.
  • Boot: @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan for the package of the main class, so keep the main class in the root package.
  • Names: the default bean name is the decapitalized class name; @Component("x") sets it explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Class outside the scanned package: bean not found, NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
  • Main class in the default package: Boot scans everything and warns; use a named package.
  • Two beans with the same name from different packages: ConflictingBeanDefinitionException; set explicit names.
  • Annotation on an interface only: scanning ignores interfaces.
  • Scanning too wide (for example the package com) picks up library classes and slows startup.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Narrow base packages cut the number of classes read.
  • Spring Boot 3 AOT and native images do the scan at build time.
  • Index: the optional spring-context-indexer (older versions) listed candidates at build time; AOT is the modern route.
  • Lazy init postpones creation of scanned beans.
  • Measure: startup logs with logging.level.org.springframework.context.annotation=DEBUG show scanning detail.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
logging.level.org.springframework.context.annotation=DEBUG

# OUTPUT:
# faster startup;
DEBUG lines list each scanned candidate component

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a modular monolith has a shared library with its own beans.

  • The main app lives in com.shop, the library in com.shared.
  • Boot does not scan the library package by default.
  • The app lists both packages, and a test proves the library beans are present.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MVC configuration means customizing Spring MVC (formatters, converters, interceptors, resource handlers, CORS, view controllers) by implementing WebMvcConfigurer in a @Configuration class.
  • @EnableWebMvc turns on the MVC infrastructure in plain Spring; in Spring Boot it is already auto-configured, so you normally do not add it.
  • Callback methods such as addInterceptors, addViewControllers and addCorsMappings are default methods: override only what you need.

Worked Example 1

Test that the configuration is active.

Worked Example 2

Several configurers side by side.

Practice Exercise 1

Add a simple view controller (no controller class needed).

Practice Exercise 2

Add global CORS.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the configuration is assembled:

  • Collection: DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration autowires every WebMvcConfigurer bean.
  • Callbacks: it calls each configurer for interceptors, converters, resource handlers, formatters and CORS.
  • Beans produced: RequestMappingHandlerMapping, RequestMappingHandlerAdapter, ContentNegotiationManager and more.
  • Boot: WebMvcAutoConfiguration backs off when a WebMvcConfigurationSupport bean exists.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Callbacks available on WebMvcConfigurer:

  • addInterceptors, addResourceHandlers, addCorsMappings
  • addViewControllers, configureViewResolvers
  • configureMessageConverters, extendMessageConverters, addFormatters
  • configureContentNegotiation, configurePathMatch, addArgumentResolvers

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Boot and @EnableWebMvc: adding @EnableWebMvc in Boot switches off WebMvcAutoConfiguration, so static resources and JSON defaults can disappear.
  • DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration collects every WebMvcConfigurer bean and calls each one, so you can split config over many classes.
  • Order matters: interceptors run in registration order, and message converters are tried in list order.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer WebMvcConfigurer over extending WebMvcConfigurationSupport, which replaces the whole default setup.
  • Test slice: @WebMvcTest loads WebMvcConfigurer beans, so config is verified without the full context.
  • Properties first: many settings (spring.mvc.*, spring.web.resources.*) need no Java code at all.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • @EnableWebMvc in Boot: loses auto-configuration; remove it.
  • configureMessageConverters: wipes defaults; use extend instead.
  • Forgotten @Configuration: the configurer is never picked up.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Keep interceptors light and path-scoped.
  • Cache static resources and use content versioning.
  • Prefer one shared ObjectMapper bean over many converters.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=7d
spring.mvc.async.request-timeout=30s
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Static files cached 7 days;
responses gzip compressed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a company API needs a tenant interceptor, CORS for the front end, and a custom date format. The team splits one configurer per concern so each can be tested alone with @WebMvcTest.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Static resources are files such as CSS, JS and images served directly without a controller, mapped through a ResourceHttpRequestHandler.
  • Boot defaults serve /static, /public, /resources and /META-INF/resources from the classpath at the root URL.
  • addResourceHandlers in WebMvcConfigurer maps a URL pattern to one or more locations such as classpath:/assets/.

Worked Example 1

Cache busting with a version resolver.

Worked Example 2

Test a static file.

Practice Exercise 1

Serve an external folder.

Practice Exercise 2

Configure through properties only.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.web.resources.static-locations=classpath:/assets/
spring.mvc.static-path-pattern=/static/**
spring.web.resources.cache.period=3600

# OUTPUT:
# GET /static/app.css -> classpath:/assets/app.css

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internal flow for a static file:

  • A SimpleUrlHandlerMapping maps patterns like /** to a ResourceHttpRequestHandler (lowest priority).
  • The handler asks a ResourceResolver chain for the file (path, version, webjar).
  • Transformers may rewrite content, for example links in cached manifests.
  • It sets Last-Modified, ETag and cache headers and streams the file.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Properties: spring.web.resources.static-locations, spring.mvc.static-path-pattern.
  • WebJars: /webjars/** serves library files from jars.
  • Java config: several locations, tried in order, plus cache control.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cache headers: use setCacheControl or spring.web.resources.cache.* so browsers keep files.
  • Versioned URLs: a VersionResourceResolver adds a content hash so you can cache for a year and still deploy safely.
  • Welcome page: an index.html in a static location is served at /.

Senior Notes

  • Reverse proxy: in production let nginx or a CDN serve static files, not the app server.
  • Path traversal: the resource resolver rejects .. sequences; never build your own file serving with raw user input.
  • Pattern clash: /** as a static pattern can shadow controller mappings if misordered.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing trailing slash in addResourceLocations.
  • Using @EnableWebMvc and losing the default handlers.
  • Secured apps forgetting to permit static paths.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use content hashes and long max-age.
  • Enable gzip or let a CDN do it.
  • Serve big files from a proxy or object store.
codeExamples:
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.enabled=true
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.paths=/**
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=365d

# OUTPUT:
# app-9a8b7c.css served with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a portal serves user uploads from a mounted volume under /media/** with a 1-day cache while the build output stays on the classpath.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpMessageConverter reads the request body into an object and writes a return value into the response body (JSON, XML, text, bytes).
  • Selection depends on the Java type and the Content-Type or Accept header; the first converter that supports both wins.
  • configureMessageConverters replaces the defaults; extendMessageConverters keeps them and lets you add or reorder.

Worked Example 1

A minimal CSV converter.

Worked Example 2

Test content negotiation.

Practice Exercise 1

Add a custom converter.

Practice Exercise 2

Tune Jackson in Boot.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How conversion runs:

  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads @RequestBody and writes @ResponseBody values.
  • It loops over the converter list calling canRead or canWrite for the type and media type.
  • On write, the media type comes from the Accept header and the converters producible types.
  • No match raises HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException (415) or HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException (406).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Default converters in a Boot web app:

  • ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter, StringHttpMessageConverter
  • MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter (JSON) when Jackson is present
  • XML converters only if an XML library is on the classpath

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Jackson customization: in Boot use spring.jackson.* properties or a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean rather than a new converter.
  • Overriding is risky: configureMessageConverters removes the defaults, so JSON may stop working unless you re-add it.
  • 406 and 415: no producing converter gives 406 Not Acceptable, no consuming converter gives 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Senior Notes

  • Order: put specific converters (for example a CSV one) before generic ones when types overlap.
  • Custom media type: extend AbstractHttpMessageConverter and declare supported MediaType values.
  • Streaming: large payloads should use StreamingResponseBody rather than build a full object in memory.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Replacing the list and losing JSON.
  • Wrong ordering, so a generic converter swallows the type.
  • Assuming a Formatter changes JSON handling.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Reuse a single ObjectMapper; it is thread safe and costly to create.
  • Disable unused features such as FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES only when needed.
  • Stream large results.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false

# OUTPUT:
# Null fields omitted from JSON;
unknown fields ignored on input

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting API returns JSON for the web app and CSV for finance users based on the Accept header.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Formatter converts between a String and an object for web binding (for example "2026-01-15" to LocalDate) with a Locale.
  • Converter vs Formatter: a Converter maps one type to another; a Formatter<T> works only with String and is locale aware.
  • addFormatters in WebMvcConfigurer registers formatters and converters on a FormatterRegistry.

Worked Example 1

Global date pattern with properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.format.date=dd/MM/yyyy

# OUTPUT:
# ?d=15/01/2026 binds to LocalDate 2026-01-15

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Test the bad input.

Practice Exercise 1

A custom Formatter.

Practice Exercise 2

Annotation-based formatting.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • FormattingConversionService holds converters and formatters; Boot builds WebConversionService.
  • WebDataBinder uses it to convert request strings into field types.
  • Formatter annotations (@DateTimeFormat) are handled by AnnotationFormatterFactory implementations.
  • A failed conversion becomes a FieldError with code typeMismatch.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Per field: @DateTimeFormat, @NumberFormat.
  • Global: properties or addFormatters.
  • Converter: registry.addConverter(...) for non-text mapping.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Annotations: @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat format a single field without any registry code.
  • Boot properties: spring.mvc.format.date sets the default date pattern globally.
  • Where it applies: request parameters, path variables, form fields and model attributes, not JSON bodies (Jackson does that).

Senior Notes

  • Jackson separation: JSON dates use Jackson config, so a Formatter will not change @RequestBody parsing.
  • Thread safety: formatters are shared singletons, so never keep SimpleDateFormat in a field.
  • Errors: a ParseException becomes a typeMismatch binding error, shown as 400 for a request parameter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Expecting formatters to apply to JSON.
  • Keeping a non thread safe SimpleDateFormat in a field.
  • Locale ignored in tests.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: formatters are cheap, but avoid heavy work in parse, and reuse patterns (static final).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an HR form accepts dates as dd/MM/yyyy and amounts like 1,234.50; a global date pattern and a money formatter keep controllers free of parsing code.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerInterceptor hooks into request handling with preHandle, postHandle and afterCompletion, around the controller call.
  • Registration happens in addInterceptors of WebMvcConfigurer, with addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns.
  • preHandle returns boolean: false stops the chain, so you must write the response yourself.

Worked Example 1

Block requests without a header.

Worked Example 2

Test the interceptor.

Practice Exercise 1

A timing interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Register with patterns.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How interceptors run:

  • DispatcherServlet gets a HandlerExecutionChain (handler plus interceptors) from the mapping.
  • applyPreHandle calls each interceptor in order; a false triggers afterCompletion of those already run.
  • After the handler, applyPostHandle runs in reverse order.
  • triggerAfterCompletion runs even on errors.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Path based: addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns.
  • WebRequestInterceptor: servlet-independent version.
  • Handler aware: cast handler to HandlerMethod to read annotations.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: preHandle runs in registration order; postHandle and afterCompletion run in reverse.
  • Interceptor vs Filter: a filter is a servlet feature that runs before the DispatcherServlet; an interceptor is Spring MVC and knows the handler.
  • afterCompletion always runs when preHandle returned true, even after an exception, so it suits cleanup and timing.

Senior Notes

  • Async requests: use AsyncHandlerInterceptor, because normal hooks are called twice in a different shape for async dispatch.
  • Not for the body: reading the request body in an interceptor consumes the stream; use a wrapper filter instead.
  • Ordering across beans: call .order(n) on the registration to control position explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Returning false without writing a response gives an empty 200.
  • Storing request state in interceptor fields (singleton).
  • Expecting it to run for static resources or errors that bypass MVC.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: keep work per request small, avoid I/O in preHandle and narrow the path patterns so unrelated URLs skip it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a platform logs a correlation id, measures latency and rejects calls without an API key, using three small interceptors with explicit order.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ViewResolver turns a logical view name returned by a controller (such as "home") into a View that renders the response.
  • InternalResourceViewResolver uses a prefix and suffix to find JSPs, for example /WEB-INF/views/ and .jsp.
  • configureViewResolvers in WebMvcConfigurer lets you register resolvers through a ViewResolverRegistry.

Worked Example 1

Two resolvers with order.

Worked Example 2

Test the view name.

Practice Exercise 1

Configure resolvers in Java.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot property version.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/
spring.mvc.view.suffix=.jsp

# OUTPUT:
# "home" resolves to /WEB-INF/views/home.jsp

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution steps:

  • The controller returns a name, so DispatcherServlet.render loops over its viewResolvers.
  • The first resolver returning a non null View wins.
  • The view renders the model (JSP forward, Thymeleaf template, JSON view).
  • Resolvers are ordered with Ordered; InternalResourceViewResolver has lowest priority.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • JSP: prefix and suffix under WEB-INF.
  • Thymeleaf or FreeMarker: starter plus properties.
  • BeanNameViewResolver: view name equals a View bean name.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Boot properties: spring.mvc.view.prefix and spring.mvc.view.suffix set the JSP resolver; Thymeleaf is auto-configured with templates/.
  • Chain: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver asks each resolver and picks the best view for the requested media type.
  • Redirects: names starting with redirect: or forward: are handled specially, without a resolver lookup.

Senior Notes

  • Order: set setOrder on each resolver; InternalResourceViewResolver accepts every name, so it must be last.
  • Caching: resolvers cache resolved views by default; disable only in development.
  • REST apps: @RestController skips view resolution, since the return value goes to a message converter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • JSPs outside WEB-INF are reachable directly.
  • JSP in an executable jar does not work; use war or a template engine.
  • Returning a name from @RestController prints the text, not a page.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: keep view caching on in production (spring.thymeleaf.cache=true), and keep the resolver chain short.
codeExamples:
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/

# OUTPUT:
# Templates parsed once and reused

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an app serves HTML pages through Thymeleaf and a PDF export through a bean view, selected by view name.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @Controller is a stereotype annotation (a @Component) that marks a class as a Spring MVC web controller found by component scanning.
  • Return value: a String is a logical view name, and a Model carries data to the view.
  • Mapping methods use @GetMapping, @PostMapping and similar, optionally under a class-level @RequestMapping.

Worked Example 1

Slice test of a controller.

Worked Example 2

Constructor injection.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal MVC controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Mix view and body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a controller is registered and called:

  • Scan: @Controller is meta-annotated with @Component, so scanning creates the bean.
  • Detect: RequestMappingHandlerMapping checks each bean for @Controller or @RequestMapping and registers a HandlerMethod per mapping.
  • Invoke: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter resolves arguments, invokes the method and processes the return value.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @Controller plus @ResponseBody equals @RestController.
  • Class-level @RequestMapping adds a shared prefix.
  • Return ModelAndView or String for views, or void with a response argument.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Handler detection: RequestMappingHandlerMapping scans beans that have @Controller or @RequestMapping and builds the mapping table.
  • @ResponseBody on a method makes it write the return value through a message converter instead of resolving a view.
  • Arguments: parameters like Model, @RequestParam and BindingResult are filled by argument resolvers.

Senior Notes

  • Singleton: a controller is one shared bean, so keep it stateless and inject services via the constructor.
  • Thin controllers: put logic in services; controllers only translate HTTP to calls and back.
  • Slice test: @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) with @MockBean services is fast.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Mutable fields in the singleton.
  • Business logic in the controller.
  • Missing @ResponseBody so the returned text is treated as a view name.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: keep handlers short, avoid blocking calls on request threads (or return Callable or DeferredResult), and keep the model small.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin portal has page controllers (HTML) and a few AJAX endpoints. Page methods return view names, while small JSON actions use @ResponseBody, all delegating to services.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody: every method writes its return value to the response body, usually as JSON.
  • No view resolution: return values go to HttpMessageConverter instances, not to a ViewResolver.
  • Typical return: a POJO, a List, or ResponseEntity<T> when you need to set status and headers.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockMvc and JSON.

Worked Example 2

Validation failure.

Practice Exercise 1

A CRUD style endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

Restrict media types.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • @RestController is meta-annotated with @Controller and @ResponseBody.
  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor handles the return value and marks the request as handled, so no view is resolved.
  • For ResponseEntity, HttpEntityMethodProcessor writes status, headers and body.
  • Content negotiation chooses the converter.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • ResponseEntity: full control of the response.
  • @ResponseStatus: fixed status.
  • ProblemDetail: standard error body.
  • Streaming: StreamingResponseBody, SseEmitter.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status codes: use @ResponseStatus or ResponseEntity, for example 201 Created with a Location header.
  • Request body: @RequestBody parses JSON into an object, and @Valid triggers Bean Validation.
  • Error handling: pair it with @RestControllerAdvice to return consistent JSON errors.

Senior Notes

  • Content negotiation: produces and consumes on the mapping restrict media types and drive 406 or 415.
  • Problem Details: Spring 6 supports RFC 7807 through ProblemDetail for standard error bodies.
  • Never expose entities: return DTOs to avoid lazy-loading problems and leaking fields.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Returning JPA entities directly.
  • Using GET for changes.
  • No validation or no central error handler.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use pagination (Pageable) for lists.
  • Add ETag or cache headers for read-heavy resources.
  • Enable compression and keep DTOs small.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order service exposes /api/orders with validation, 201 on create, and one @RestControllerAdvice mapping errors to ProblemDetail.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller lifecycle has two parts: the bean is created once at startup as a singleton, and then each request is handled by the same instance on a different thread.
  • Request flow: DispatcherServlet finds a handler, applies interceptors, resolves arguments, calls the method, then handles the return value.
  • Bean callbacks such as @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy run once, not per request.

Worked Example 1

Trace the order with an interceptor and advice.

Worked Example 2

Request-scoped state done right.

Practice Exercise 1

Observe the lifecycle.

Practice Exercise 2

The bug of a shared field.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Full request path:

  • Startup: bean created, dependencies injected, @PostConstruct runs, mappings registered.
  • Request: servlet filters, then DispatcherServlet.doDispatch.
  • Dispatch: getHandler, preHandle, adapter invokes the method, postHandle, render, afterCompletion.
  • Shutdown: @PreDestroy runs once.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Lifecycle related options:

  • Scope: @RequestScope, @SessionScope beans injected as proxies.
  • Lazy: @Lazy or global lazy init.
  • Callbacks: InitializingBean, @PostConstruct, DisposableBean.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order per request: filters, then DispatcherServlet, preHandle, argument binding, controller method, return handling, postHandle, view render, afterCompletion.
  • Scope: controllers are singletons by default; request-scoped data should come from method arguments or scoped beans.
  • Exceptions: they go to HandlerExceptionResolver instances, including @ExceptionHandler methods.

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: no mutable instance fields; use a @RequestScope bean or local variables.
  • Lazy init: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true delays controller creation until first use, trading startup for first-request latency.
  • Proxying: AOP proxies (for example @Transactional on a controller) require a non-final class and public methods.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Instance fields holding user data.
  • Heavy work in constructors that delays startup.
  • Assuming one thread per controller; threads come from the container pool.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep construction cheap; avoid blocking work in @PostConstruct.
  • Size the Tomcat thread pool (server.tomcat.threads.max).
  • Use async return types for long calls.
codeExamples:
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
spring.main.lazy-initialization=false

# OUTPUT:
# Up to 200 requests handled in parallel by the one controller instance

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an intermittent bug where totals mix between users is traced to a controller field private double total. The fix moves it to a local variable and the test fires parallel requests.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller methods are handler methods mapped to requests with @RequestMapping or the shortcuts @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping.
  • Parameters are bound by annotations: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader, @ModelAttribute.
  • Return types include String (view), POJO (body), ResponseEntity, void and ModelAndView.

Worked Example 1

Narrow by media type.

Worked Example 2

Test missing parameter.

Practice Exercise 1

Different binding styles.

Practice Exercise 2

Form binding with validation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Method handling internals:

  • Each mapping is a RequestMappingInfo (patterns, methods, params, headers, consumes, produces).
  • InvocableHandlerMethod uses HandlerMethodArgumentResolver beans to get each argument.
  • The return value goes to a HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler.
  • Type conversion uses the WebDataBinder and conversion service.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options:

  • method, params ("debug=true"), headers.
  • consumes and produces.
  • Patterns: {id}, {id:[0-9]+}, *, **.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Mapping attributes: value, method, params, headers, consumes and produces narrow what a method accepts.
  • Special arguments: HttpServletRequest, Principal, Locale, Model, BindingResult are injected by type.
  • BindingResult must come right after the validated @ModelAttribute or @Valid argument.

Senior Notes

  • Ambiguity: two methods matching the same request cause IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping at startup.
  • Specificity: when several patterns match, the most specific one wins (exact before {var} before **).
  • Idempotency: use GET and PUT for safe or idempotent actions, POST for creation, to keep caches and retries correct.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Same mapping twice (ambiguous).
  • @RequestParam missing gives 400.
  • BindingResult after the wrong parameter.
  • Primitive parameter with absent optional value.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use specific mappings to avoid regex heavy matching.
  • Return DTOs and limit page size.
  • Use Optional or defaultValue instead of null checks.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a search endpoint takes optional filters, paging and a tenant header, returning a DTO page; tests cover each parameter combination with MockMvc.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request mapping is the rule that links an incoming HTTP request (method, URL path, and optionally headers, params and media types) to one controller method that handles it.
  • Annotations: @RequestMapping is the general one; @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping and @PatchMapping are shortcuts for one HTTP method.
  • Where it works: only on beans marked @Controller or @RestController; the mapping is read once at startup.

Worked Example 1

Two methods on different paths.

Worked Example 2

Same path, different methods.

Practice Exercise 1

Smallest mapped controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the mapping with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a request finds its handler:

  • Startup: RequestMappingHandlerMapping scans beans with @Controller and builds a RequestMappingInfo (path, method, params, headers, consumes, produces) for each handler method.
  • Registry: infos are stored in a MappingRegistry, with direct URLs in a fast map and patterns in a list.
  • Request: the DispatcherServlet asks each HandlerMapping in order; the first that returns a HandlerExecutionChain wins.
  • Choice: all matching infos are compared and the best one is used; ties throw an error.
  • Invoke: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter resolves arguments, calls the method and handles the return value.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to express a mapping:

  • Path: exact, with variables, with patterns.
  • Method: one or several HTTP methods.
  • params: params = "debug" or "mode=fast" or "!x".
  • headers: match a request header value.
  • consumes / produces: content negotiation on Content-Type and Accept.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Matching is done by RequestMappingHandlerMapping, which picks the most specific mapping when several could match.
  • No match gives 404 for an unknown path, 405 when the path exists but the method is wrong, and 415 or 406 for media type problems.
  • Ambiguity: two methods with the same condition make the application fail at startup with an IllegalStateException (Ambiguous mapping).

Senior Notes

  • Registry: all mappings live in a lookup built at startup, so matching is a fast lookup and not a reflection scan per request.
  • Design: keep URLs noun-based and let the HTTP method express the action, for example GET /orders/42.
  • Testing: use MockMvc with @WebMvcTest to prove that a URL and method reach the right handler.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Duplicate mapping: two methods with the same path and method make startup fail; change the path or add a distinguishing condition.
  • Missing controller stereotype: @RequestMapping on a plain class is ignored; add @RestController.
  • Wrong package scan: the controller is outside the component scan, so you get 404.
  • Trailing slash: in Spring 6 /a/ does not match /a.
  • Misreading 405: the path matched, only the verb is wrong.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Lookup cost: exact paths use a hash lookup; pattern paths are tested in order, so very large pattern lists cost more.
  • PathPatternParser: patterns are parsed once at startup.
  • Keep handlers thin: the mapping step is microseconds; the time goes into your code, serialization and I/O.
  • Conditions: avoid heavy custom RequestCondition logic.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop API exposes products. Reads are public, writes are for admins. Each URL and verb pair is a mapping, so security rules, metrics and documentation all line up with the same list. A startup log of mappings (or the Actuator mappings endpoint) is the first thing to check when a URL returns 404.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RequestMapping is the core Spring MVC annotation that maps requests to a class or a method; it can be placed at class level and at method level.
  • Attributes: value or path (URL), method, params, headers, consumes and produces.
  • Shortcuts: the composed annotations such as @GetMapping are just @RequestMapping(method = GET) with a shorter name.

Worked Example 1

Equivalent forms.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: no method set.

Practice Exercise 1

All attributes together.

Practice Exercise 2

Multiple paths and methods.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside @RequestMapping:

  • Annotation: attributes are aliases, value and path are the same (@AliasFor).
  • Parsing: RequestMappingHandlerMapping.createRequestMappingInfo reads the annotation and builds condition objects: PathPatternsRequestCondition, RequestMethodsRequestCondition, ParamsRequestCondition and others.
  • Matching: every condition returns a match or null; one null rejects the mapping.
  • Combining: the class info is combined with the method info.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Attribute forms: @RequestMapping("/x") is the same as path = "/x".
  • Class plus method: base path on the class.
  • consumes: restrict request Content-Type.
  • produces: restrict or choose response media type.
  • Negation: consumes = "!text/plain", params = "!debug".

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Several paths can share one method: @RequestMapping({"/a", "/b"}) is allowed.
  • Without method, the mapping accepts every HTTP method, which is rarely what you want for an API.
  • Conditions combine with AND: path, method and the other attributes must all match.

Senior Notes

  • Meta-annotation: @GetMapping is itself annotated with @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET).
  • Class plus method mappings are combined: the class path is a prefix and method conditions are merged.
  • Style: prefer the shortcuts on methods and keep plain @RequestMapping for the class-level base path.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with @RequestMapping:

  • Forgetting method: the endpoint then accepts every verb, including DELETE.
  • Mixing value and path: setting both is an error.
  • Using it on an interface only: works in recent Spring, but keep it on the implementation for clarity.
  • Class path without slash: works, but is inconsistent style.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: annotation parsing happens once at startup, not per request.
  • Many conditions: each extra condition is one more cheap check.
  • Startup time: thousands of mappings add a small startup cost; lazy initialization does not skip it for controllers that are scanned.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
# log mapping registration at startup
logging.level.org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation=TRACE

# OUTPUT:
# Mapped "{[/orders],methods=[GET]}" onto String OrderController.orders()

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy controller uses plain @RequestMapping without a verb. A security scan finds that DELETE /reports returns 200. The fix is to replace each with a verb-specific annotation, and add a MockMvc test that proves the wrong verb gives 405.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @GetMapping maps HTTP GET requests to a method; it is the shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET).
  • Use it for reads: fetching a list or one item, searching and downloading. A GET must not change server data.
  • Input comes from the path (@PathVariable) and the query string (@RequestParam), because GET has no body.

Worked Example 1

Query parameters with defaults.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: changing data in GET.

Practice Exercise 1

List and detail endpoints.

Practice Exercise 2

Test with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a GET is served:

  • Mapping: the info has a RequestMethodsRequestCondition with GET (and HEAD is accepted too).
  • Arguments: @PathVariable and @RequestParam are resolved by HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers.
  • Return value: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor writes it with a HttpMessageConverter, chosen by the Accept header.
  • Caching: a ShallowEtagHeaderFilter can compute an ETag from the body and answer 304.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options of @GetMapping:

  • path / value: one or many URLs.
  • params, headers: extra conditions.
  • produces: media type of the response, for example JSON or XML.
  • No path: inherits the class path.
  • Return types: object, ResponseEntity, Optional wrapped by you, or a view name in a @Controller.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Safe and idempotent: clients, caches and crawlers may repeat a GET, so never delete or save inside it.
  • HEAD and OPTIONS: Spring answers HEAD for a GET mapping automatically, and OPTIONS lists the allowed methods.
  • Caching: GET responses can carry ETag or Cache-Control headers.

Senior Notes

  • Conditional GET: ShallowEtagHeaderFilter or ResponseEntity.eTag allows 304 Not Modified.
  • Pagination: accept Pageable or page and size params instead of returning everything.
  • Testing: mvc.perform(get("/x")) with status and jsonPath checks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with GET:

  • Side effects: changing data in a GET.
  • Sensitive data in the URL: query strings are logged; never put passwords or tokens there.
  • Returning huge lists: use paging.
  • Type mismatch: /books/abc for an int variable gives 400.
  • Missing required param: gives 400 unless you set required = false or a default.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Pagination: use Pageable to limit rows.
  • Caching: Cache-Control, ETag and a service cache avoid repeated work.
  • Projection: return a DTO with only the needed fields.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true for large JSON.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile app lists orders and polls for updates every 30 seconds. The GET endpoint returns an ETag; when nothing changed the server answers 304 with no body, saving bandwidth and server time.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @PostMapping maps HTTP POST requests to a method; it is the shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.POST) and is used to create resources or submit forms.
  • Body: send JSON and read it with @RequestBody; for HTML forms Spring binds fields with @ModelAttribute or @RequestParam.
  • Response: a create usually returns 201 Created with a Location header.

Worked Example 1

Form post with redirect.

Worked Example 2

Validated body.

Practice Exercise 1

Create with JSON body and Location.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the POST.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a POST body is handled:

  • Mapping: POST condition plus optional consumes.
  • Reading: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks a converter from the Content-Type; JSON uses MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter.
  • Validation: with @Valid, a validator runs after binding and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException on errors.
  • Errors: that exception is translated to 400 by DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver or your @ControllerAdvice.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of POST handling:

  • JSON: @RequestBody.
  • Form: application/x-www-form-urlencoded with @RequestParam or @ModelAttribute.
  • File upload: multipart/form-data with MultipartFile.
  • Response: 201 plus Location, or 200 with a body, or a redirect.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Not idempotent: repeating a POST may create a second record, so protect important operations with an idempotency key.
  • Validation: add @Valid to the body so bad input gives 400 and not a database error.
  • Content type: use consumes to accept only JSON; other types get 415.

Senior Notes

  • Message converters: HttpMessageConverter (Jackson for JSON) turns the body into an object.
  • CSRF: with Spring Security, POST forms need a CSRF token or the call is rejected with 403.
  • Redirect after POST: for forms, redirect after success to avoid double submit on refresh.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with POST:

  • Missing @RequestBody: the parameter is then bound from form data and stays empty.
  • No default constructor or bad JSON: gives 400 (HttpMessageNotReadableException).
  • Wrong Content-Type from the client: gives 415.
  • Double submit: user refreshes a form page; use redirect after post.
  • CSRF 403 with Spring Security.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Size limits: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and server max post size.
  • Streaming: for big uploads stream to storage instead of loading into memory.
  • Idempotency key: an Idempotency-Key header lets you ignore replays.
  • Async: return Callable or use a queue for slow work and answer 202 Accepted.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a payment API must not charge twice if the client retries after a timeout. The client sends an Idempotency-Key; the server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result on a repeat.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @PutMapping maps HTTP PUT requests; it is the shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PUT) and is used to replace a whole resource.
  • Full replacement: the client sends the complete new state of the resource at a known URL such as /users/5.
  • Response: 200 OK with the body, or 204 No Content; 404 when the id does not exist.

Worked Example 1

Return 204 instead of a body.

Worked Example 2

Enable PUT from HTML forms (Boot).
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.hiddenmethod.filter.enabled=true

# form: <form method="post"> <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="put">

# OUTPUT:
# the POST is treated as PUT and reaches the @PutMapping method

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Replace a user.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the PUT.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How PUT is handled:

  • Mapping: a PUT condition; body read like POST by a message converter.
  • Semantics: the handler should replace the stored state, so the same request twice gives the same state.
  • Service layer: load by id, overwrite all fields, save in a transaction.
  • Status: 200 with the saved object, 204, or 404 when missing.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Upsert: create if missing (return 201) else update (200).
  • Conditional: If-Match header with ETag for safe updates.
  • Sub-resource: PUT /users/5/avatar to replace one part with a full value.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Idempotent: sending the same PUT twice leaves the same result, so retries are safe.
  • PUT versus PATCH: PUT replaces everything (missing fields become null); PATCH changes only the fields sent.
  • Create or update: PUT may also create a resource if the client chooses the id.

Senior Notes

  • Browsers forms send only GET and POST; HTML forms need HiddenHttpMethodFilter or Boot property spring.mvc.hiddenmethod.filter.enabled to use PUT.
  • Concurrency: use a version field or If-Match with ETag to avoid lost updates.
  • Testing: mvc.perform(put(...).contentType(...).content(...)).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with PUT:

  • Treating it as partial: missing fields silently become null.
  • Id mismatch: URL id and body id differ; trust the URL.
  • Lost update: two clients overwrite each other.
  • Form support: forms cannot send PUT without the hidden method filter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Concurrency and tuning:

  • Optimistic locking: @Version on the JPA entity throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException on conflict; map it to 409.
  • ETag: require If-Match; answer 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch.
  • Transaction: keep load and save in one @Transactional service method.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin screen edits a customer. Two admins open the same record; the second save would erase the first. Using a version number and returning 409 makes the second admin reload and merge.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @DeleteMapping maps HTTP DELETE requests; it is the shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.DELETE) and removes a resource identified by the URL.
  • Typical shape: DELETE /users/5 with the id as a @PathVariable and no request body.
  • Response: 204 No Content on success, or 404 if the resource does not exist.

Worked Example 1

With a service and exception.

Worked Example 2

Role protected delete.

Practice Exercise 1

Delete by id.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the DELETE.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How DELETE runs:

  • Mapping: DELETE condition; the id comes from the path.
  • Service: repository deleteById inside a transaction; foreign keys may block it.
  • Response: normally 204 with no body, so ResponseEntity<Void> or @ResponseStatus(NO_CONTENT).
  • Missing id: deleteById in Spring Data 3 does nothing for a missing id, so check with existsById if you need 404.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Hard delete: row removed.
  • Soft delete: set deleted = true or use Hibernate @SQLDelete with @SQLRestriction.
  • Bulk: delete by filter, for example DELETE /items?status=old.
  • Async: return 202 when deletion takes long.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Idempotent: deleting twice leaves the same state; the second call may return 404 or 204, but data is not changed further.
  • Soft delete: many systems only mark a row as deleted so history and references stay valid.
  • Security: protect it with roles, for example @PreAuthorize, and with CSRF for browser clients.

Senior Notes

  • Body on DELETE is allowed by HTTP but poorly supported, so send ids in the path or query.
  • Bulk delete: use a query like DELETE /users?ids=1,2 or a POST to a bulk endpoint, and keep it transactional.
  • Testing: mvc.perform(delete("/users/5")) and check 204.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with DELETE:

  • Deleting via GET.
  • Returning 200 with a body for no reason: 204 is cleaner.
  • Ignoring references: deleting a parent with children fails with DataIntegrityViolationException (map to 409).
  • No authorization check: any user can delete any record; verify ownership.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Bulk: deleteAllByIdInBatch issues one SQL statement.
  • Cascade: large cascades load children one by one; prefer database ON DELETE CASCADE or batch deletes.
  • Indexes: foreign key columns need indexes so deletes do not scan.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a user asks to delete their account. The API soft-deletes the account at once (204), and a nightly job removes personal data after the legal retention period, while keeping order totals.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @PatchMapping maps HTTP PATCH requests; it is the shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PATCH) and applies a partial update to a resource.
  • Only changed fields are sent, for example {"email":"new@x.com"}; all other fields stay as they are.
  • Typical use: change one field such as a status, a password or a profile detail without sending the whole object.

Worked Example 1

Patch a status field only.

Worked Example 2

Merge JSON into an entity with Jackson.

Practice Exercise 1

Update only the email.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the PATCH.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How PATCH is processed:

  • Mapping: PATCH condition and a body with only the changes.
  • Binding: into a Map, JsonNode or a DTO with nullable fields.
  • Apply: copy non-missing fields onto the loaded entity inside a transaction.
  • Dirty checking: JPA writes only the changed columns at commit if the entity is managed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patch formats:

  • Merge style: send a partial object (simple, most common).
  • JSON Patch (RFC 6902): a list of operations such as replace and remove, media type application/json-patch+json.
  • JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386): partial object where null means remove, media type application/merge-patch+json.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Not always idempotent: a patch like increment by 1 changes the result each time; a patch like set status to SHIPPED is idempotent.
  • Null handling: you must tell apart a missing field (keep) from an explicit null (clear); a plain DTO cannot, so use a Map or Optional wrapper.
  • Formats: simple merge JSON, or JSON Patch (application/json-patch+json) with operations.

Senior Notes

  • Implementation: load the entity, copy only the non-missing fields, then save in one transaction.
  • Libraries: Jackson ObjectMapper.readerForUpdating can merge JSON into an existing object.
  • Client support: some old HTTP clients and the JDK HttpURLConnection do not support PATCH; use a modern client.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with PATCH:

  • Cannot clear a field: null in a DTO means missing; use a Map or JsonNullable.
  • No validation: partial objects fail @NotNull rules, so validate after merging.
  • Using PUT semantics: overwriting unsent fields with null.
  • Unsafe field copy: allowing the client to set role or id; whitelist fields.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Smaller payloads: less data sent from mobile clients.
  • Smaller SQL: use @DynamicUpdate so Hibernate updates only changed columns.
  • One transaction: load and apply in the same transaction to avoid an extra save call.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order workflow changes a status step by step. A dedicated PATCH /orders/{id}/status with a small body keeps each change explicit, easy to audit and easy to secure per role.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP method mapping means telling Spring which verb a handler accepts: use @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping, or @RequestMapping(method = ...).
  • Meaning of verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes.
  • Wrong verb on a known path returns 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header.

Worked Example 1

Two verbs on one method.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: verb in the URL.

Practice Exercise 1

One path, all verbs, one resource.

Practice Exercise 2

Check the Allow header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the method is matched:

  • Condition: RequestMethodsRequestCondition holds the allowed verbs.
  • Path first: if the path matches but no verb does, HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException becomes 405 with an Allow header.
  • Shortcuts: the five composed annotations only set this condition.
  • Auto methods: HEAD uses the GET handler; OPTIONS is answered from collected verbs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Verb reference:

  • GET: read, safe, idempotent, cacheable.
  • POST: create or run an action, not idempotent.
  • PUT: replace, idempotent.
  • PATCH: partial change.
  • DELETE: remove, idempotent.
  • HEAD: headers only.
  • OPTIONS: capabilities and CORS preflight.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Safe and idempotent: GET is safe; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST and usually PATCH are not.
  • Same path, several methods are fine because the method is part of the mapping key.
  • Many verbs, one handler: @RequestMapping(method = {GET, POST}) handles both.

Senior Notes

  • HEAD and OPTIONS are added automatically: HEAD for each GET, OPTIONS from the registered mappings (and CORS preflight).
  • Method override: HiddenHttpMethodFilter turns a POST with _method into PUT or DELETE.
  • Design: do not tunnel everything through POST; correct verbs let caches, proxies and clients behave properly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with verbs:

  • POST for reads (breaks caching).
  • GET for changes (crawlers trigger them).
  • Verbs in URLs like /getUsers.
  • CORS: a browser preflight sends OPTIONS; if CORS is not configured, the real PUT or DELETE is blocked.
  • Security config: rules written only for GET leave other verbs open.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • GET caching gives the biggest gain: browsers, CDNs and proxies reuse responses.
  • HEAD lets clients check size or existence cheaply.
  • Preflight cache: Access-Control-Max-Age reduces OPTIONS calls.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a front end gets a CORS error only on DELETE. The cause is a missing method in allowedMethods. Reading the OPTIONS response (Allow and Access-Control-Allow-Methods headers) shows it at once.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • URL path mapping sets which request paths a handler serves: @GetMapping("/users") or @RequestMapping(path = "/users").
  • Path variables: placeholders such as /users/{id} capture part of the URL, read with @PathVariable.
  • Patterns: * matches one segment, ** matches many segments, and ? one character.

Worked Example 1

Two variables in a path.

Worked Example 2

Allow both with and without trailing slash.

Practice Exercise 1

Variables, regex and wildcard.

Practice Exercise 2

Test paths.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How paths are matched:

  • Parser: PathPatternParser compiles each pattern into a chain of nodes (literal, variable, wildcard) at startup.
  • Request: the path is parsed into segments once (RequestPath) and matched against the chain.
  • Order: PathPattern.SPECIFICITY_COMPARATOR ranks fewer wildcards and variables as more specific.
  • Variables: captured values are stored as a request attribute and then converted by the ConversionService.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Pattern options:

  • Literal: /about.
  • Variable: /users/{id}.
  • Regex variable: /users/{id:[0-9]+}.
  • Single segment wildcard: /a/*/c.
  • Capture rest: /files/{*path} puts the remaining path in a variable.
  • Trailing wildcard: /static/**.
  • Optional name: @PathVariable(required = false) with two mappings.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Several paths for one method are given as an array: @GetMapping({"/a", "/b"}).
  • Regex in variable: /users/{id:[0-9]+} restricts the variable to digits so other values do not match.
  • Specific wins: /users/me beats /users/{id} when both match.

Senior Notes

  • PathPattern: since Spring 5.3 the default matcher is PathPatternParser, which is faster than the old AntPathMatcher; ** is only allowed at the end of a pattern.
  • Trailing slash: in Spring 6 /users/ no longer matches /users by default, so clients must use the exact path.
  • Encoding: path variables are URL-decoded; semicolon content (matrix variables) is disabled by default.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with paths:

  • Variable name mismatch: {id} with @PathVariable String userId fails unless you name it or compile with -parameters.
  • Dots in variables: a value like a.b is kept in Spring 6 (suffix matching is off), but old code relied on extension stripping.
  • Encoded slash: %2F is rejected by Tomcat by default.
  • Pattern after **: /a/**/b is not allowed with PathPatternParser.
  • Trailing slash: mapping and call must agree.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and design:

  • Prefer literals: exact paths use a direct map lookup.
  • Avoid broad patterns like /{a}/{b} at the root; they match too much and slow ranking.
  • Short stable URLs: nouns, plural, lowercase, hyphens.
  • Pre-parsed patterns: do not build a PathPattern per request in your own code.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a documentation site serves pages at /docs/{section}/{page} and a single download handler for any file under /downloads. Regex limits sections to known names so typos give a clean 404 and not a database call.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Class-level mapping puts @RequestMapping("/base") on the controller class so every handler method inherits that path as a prefix.
  • Method paths are added to it: class /users plus method /{id} gives /users/{id}.
  • Benefit: no repeated prefix, and the whole controller can be moved by changing one line.

Worked Example 1

Shared produces on the class.

Worked Example 2

Global prefix without editing classes.

Practice Exercise 1

Controller with base path.

Practice Exercise 2

Test with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How class and method are merged:

  • Build: RequestMappingHandlerMapping.getMappingForMethod creates info for the method, then the type-level info, and returns typeInfo.combine(methodInfo).
  • Paths: combined with the pattern parser, so one slash is placed between parts.
  • Other conditions: methods and params are unioned; consumes and produces on the method override the class.
  • Prefix: a configured global prefix is applied last.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options at class level:

  • path: one or several base paths.
  • produces / consumes: default media types.
  • headers / params: a condition for the whole controller.
  • method: a default verb (rare).
  • Interfaces: mapping annotations on a controller interface are inherited by implementations in Spring 5.1 and later.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Shared conditions: produces, consumes and headers on the class apply to all methods; a method can narrow them.
  • Method only: a method annotation with no path maps to exactly the class path, for example list at /users.
  • Slashes: Spring joins the parts correctly, so "users" and "/users" both work, but keep the leading slash for clarity.

Senior Notes

  • Combination: RequestMappingInfo.combine merges class and method info; patterns are concatenated, methods and params are unioned.
  • Versioning: one class per version, for example /api/v1/users, keeps old clients working.
  • Global prefix: PathMatchConfigurer.addPathPrefix("/api", ...) adds a prefix to all matching controllers without editing each class.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with class-level mapping:

  • Double prefix: class has /api/users and a global prefix /api adds it again, giving /api/api/users.
  • Duplicate paths: two controllers share the same base and the same method path.
  • Class method condition: a class-level method = GET blocks POST handlers inside it.
  • Expecting inheritance of class paths in security rules: rules must use the full path.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and structure:

  • No runtime cost: the merge is done at startup.
  • Cohesion: one controller per resource with one base path keeps classes small.
  • Versions: use separate packages or classes per API version.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team moves an API from /api/v1 to /api/v2 for a few resources. Each v2 controller declares its own class-level path, so v1 clients keep working. A MockMvc test for each version guards against accidental breaks.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Method-level mapping binds a single handler method to a URL and HTTP method with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping or @RequestMapping(method = ...).
  • Combined with the class: a class-level @RequestMapping("/users") gives a prefix, and each method adds its own path to it.
  • Shortcut annotations are composed annotations: @GetMapping is just @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET).

Worked Example 1

Same path with different verbs.

Worked Example 2

Narrowing a mapping with params.

Practice Exercise 1

Write a controller with a class prefix and three methods (list, get one, create).

Practice Exercise 2

Test the mapping with MockMvc, including the wrong verb.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Method mappings are collected once at startup.

  • Scan: RequestMappingHandlerMapping finds beans annotated with @Controller or @RequestMapping.
  • Combine: for each method a RequestMappingInfo is built and merged with the class-level one (paths joined, conditions combined).
  • Lookup: per request the registry returns the matching infos and the best one is chosen by comparator.
  • Invoke: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter resolves arguments, calls the method and handles the return value.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of a method-level mapping:

  • Shortcuts: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.
  • Generic: @RequestMapping(value, method, params, headers, consumes, produces).
  • Multiple verbs: method = {GET, HEAD}.
  • Empty path: a method with no path maps to the class prefix itself.
  • Version header: headers = "X-API-Version=2" selects between versions.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Same path, different verbs: GET /users/{id} and DELETE /users/{id} can be two methods without conflict.
  • Narrowing: besides path and method, a mapping can be narrowed by params, headers, consumes and produces.
  • Wrong verb gives 405 Method Not Allowed, an unknown path gives 404.

Senior Notes

  • Registry: at startup RequestMappingHandlerMapping builds a map of RequestMappingInfo to HandlerMethod.
  • Ambiguity: two methods with the same conditions fail at startup with IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping.
  • Specificity: the most specific match wins, for example /users/me beats /users/{id}.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing slash or double slash: Spring joins paths, but a typo like "users" without prefix slash still works while hiding bugs; keep one style.
  • Ambiguous mapping: two methods with equal conditions fail at startup; add params or change the path.
  • Using @Controller without @ResponseBody: a returned string is treated as a view name and gives a 404 or a template error.
  • Wrong verb in clients: a form can only send GET and POST, so use hidden-method filters or fetch.
  • Mapping on interface only: works, but keep annotations in one place.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Mapping lookup is cheap, but keep it simple:

  • Direct path: literal paths are looked up in a hash map first, patterns are tried afterwards.
  • Pattern count: thousands of wildcard patterns slow matching; prefer literal paths.
  • Startup: mapping scan time grows with controller count, which is rarely a problem.
  • Observe: Actuator /actuator/mappings lists all mappings.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=mappings
logging.level.org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation=TRACE

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/mappings -> JSON with every handler, pattern and method (varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a REST API for a library with a class prefix and verbs that match CRUD. Keep one controller per resource, put the shared prefix on the class, and test every mapping with @WebMvcTest so a refactor cannot silently change a URL.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Multiple URL mappings let one handler method answer several paths, written as an array: @GetMapping({"/home", "/index"}).
  • Use cases: aliases, old and new URLs during a migration, and a trailing or alternative path for the same page.
  • Same method: every listed path runs the same code and returns the same view or body.

Worked Example 1

Class and method arrays multiply.

Worked Example 2

Pattern with a wildcard.

Practice Exercise 1

Home page with three aliases.

Practice Exercise 2

MockMvc test over all aliases.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

One handler, many patterns.

  • Model: RequestMappingInfo holds a PathPatternsRequestCondition with a set of patterns.
  • Matching: a request matches if any pattern matches; the best one is recorded in a request attribute.
  • Combination: class patterns and method patterns are combined as a cross product.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to expose several URLs:

  • Array of paths: @GetMapping({"/a", "/b"}).
  • Wildcards: * for one segment, ** for many, ? for one character.
  • Optional segment: map two paths, one with the variable and one without.
  • View controller: registry.addViewController("/old").setViewName("home") for static aliases.
  • Redirect: registry.addRedirectViewController("/old", "/new").

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Array syntax: both value and path accept String[], and curly braces are needed for more than one path.
  • Patterns: each entry can be a pattern such as /files/* or /docs/**.
  • Class level: a class-level array multiplies with method paths, so two prefixes and two paths give four URLs.

Senior Notes

  • Many registrations: Spring registers one RequestMappingInfo holding all patterns, not several handlers.
  • Trailing slash: since Spring Framework 6 /home/ no longer matches /home by default, so list both if you need it.
  • Redirects: for old URLs a redirect: or a 301 is often better than a silent alias.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forgetting curly braces: @GetMapping("/a", "/b") does not compile; use an array.
  • Overlap with another method: a wildcard alias that also matches another handler may be ambiguous.
  • Trailing slash assumption: in Spring 6 add both /x and /x/ if clients use either.
  • Too many aliases: duplicate URLs hurt SEO and caching; redirect instead.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Aliases cost almost nothing at runtime because they are only extra patterns in one condition. The real cost is operational: each alias is another URL to document, secure and cache. Secure all aliases with the same rule, preferably by pattern in the security configuration.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a site moves from /products to /catalog. During the migration both URLs are served by one handler; later the old one becomes a permanent redirect and finally disappears.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • consumes is a mapping condition that limits a handler to requests whose Content-Type header matches, such as consumes = "application/json".
  • Purpose: pick the right method for the body format the client sends, for example JSON versus XML versus form data.
  • Mismatch: a request with another content type gets 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Worked Example 1

Two methods on one path.

Worked Example 2

Form data endpoint.

Practice Exercise 1

A JSON-only endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

MockMvc test for the 415.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Request conditions are evaluated during mapping lookup.

  • Parse: ConsumesRequestCondition parses the request Content-Type into a MediaType.
  • Compare: it checks the media type against the declared expressions, including wildcards and negation.
  • Fail: if the path matches but the type does not, HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException becomes 415.
  • Read: a converter such as MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter deserializes the body.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Exact type: "application/json".
  • Wildcard: "application/*" or "*/*".
  • Negation: "!text/plain".
  • List: {"application/json", "application/xml"}.
  • Multipart: MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE for uploads.
  • Class level: shared default for all methods; a method value replaces it.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Constants: use MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE instead of raw strings to avoid typos.
  • Negation: consumes = "!text/plain" accepts everything except plain text.
  • Only for bodies: it checks Content-Type, so it matters for POST, PUT and PATCH, not for a plain GET.

Senior Notes

  • Matching: ConsumesRequestCondition compares the request media type with the declared ones.
  • Body conversion: after the match an HttpMessageConverter such as Jackson reads the body for @RequestBody.
  • Class level: a class-level consumes is overridden, not merged, by a method-level one.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing Content-Type from the client: curl with -d sends form-encoded, not JSON; add -H "Content-Type: application/json".
  • Confusing with Accept: consumes is about the request, produces about the response.
  • Using consumes on GET: there is no body, so the condition is meaningless.
  • Charset in value: application/json;charset=UTF-8 in consumes can reject plain application/json.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

consumes adds almost no cost. Tuning is about the body: set a maximum size, avoid reading huge JSON into memory and prefer streaming for large uploads.

  • Size limits: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size.
  • Jackson: reuse one ObjectMapper bean.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB

# OUTPUT:
# upload over 5MB -> 413 / MaxUploadSizeExceededException (handled by an advice)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an import API accepts JSON from web clients and CSV from batch tools. Two methods share a path and differ only by consumes, so each has simple code and its own tests.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • produces is a mapping condition that declares the media type a handler returns, such as produces = "application/json".
  • Content negotiation: Spring compares the request Accept header with produces; no match gives 406 Not Acceptable.
  • Response header: the chosen type is written into the response Content-Type.

Worked Example 1

Both consumes and produces.

Worked Example 2

Plain text with charset.

Practice Exercise 1

JSON and plain text variants.

Practice Exercise 2

MockMvc test of negotiation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Content negotiation steps:

  • Filter: ProducesRequestCondition keeps handlers whose produces list is compatible with Accept.
  • Pick: the most specific acceptable type is stored in the request attribute PRODUCIBLE_MEDIA_TYPES_ATTRIBUTE.
  • Write: the return value handler asks the converters in order for one that can write that type.
  • Fail: no match gives HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException and 406.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Constants: MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE.
  • Multiple: several types, client chooses by Accept quality.
  • XML: add jackson-dataformat-xml to support application/xml.
  • Vendor types: application/vnd.shop.v2+json for API versioning.
  • Streaming: text/event-stream for server-sent events.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • consumes vs produces: consumes looks at the request Content-Type, produces looks at the request Accept and sets the response type.
  • Charset: add it when needed, for example text/plain;charset=UTF-8.
  • Several types: produces = {"application/json", "application/xml"} lets the client choose with Accept.

Senior Notes

  • Condition: ProducesRequestCondition filters candidate handlers by Accept.
  • Converter: HttpMessageConverter instances that can write the chosen type serialize the return value.
  • Default: without produces Spring negotiates from the Accept header and the available converters.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Browser Accept: browsers send text/html,...,*/*;q=0.8, so JSON still matches thanks to the wildcard.
  • Missing converter: producing XML without the XML library gives 406.
  • Hardcoded string typos: "application/jason" fails at runtime; use constants.
  • Returning String as JSON: a String is written as is; with produces JSON you must supply valid JSON yourself or return an object.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Cacheable: send Vary: Accept (Spring adds it) so caches keep one copy per type.
  • Compression: enable server.compression.enabled=true for text types.
  • Avoid duplicate work: do not build both JSON and XML models when only one is asked for.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,application/xml,text/plain
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# OUTPUT:
# Response > 1KB with Accept-Encoding: gzip -> Content-Encoding: gzip

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an API serves JSON to apps and a CSV export to analysts from the same URL, selected by Accept. Tests assert both outputs and the 406 case.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP request is the message a client sends: a request line (method, URL, version), headers, and an optional body.
  • In Spring MVC it reaches your code as HttpServletRequest or, more conveniently, as typed method arguments.
  • Parts: path, query string, headers, cookies, session, and body all can be injected with annotations.

Worked Example 1

RequestEntity gives method, URL, headers and body.

Worked Example 2

Cookie and client address.

Practice Exercise 1

Read several parts of a request.

Practice Exercise 2

Test headers and body with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Journey of a request:

  • Container: Tomcat parses the bytes into an HttpServletRequest and calls the servlet.
  • Dispatch: DispatcherServlet asks HandlerMapping for a handler and HandlerAdapter to run it.
  • Arguments: each parameter is filled by a HandlerMethodArgumentResolver.
  • Body: converters turn the stream into objects; a HandlerInterceptor can inspect the request before and after.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to access request data:

  • Annotations: @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody, @RequestAttribute, @SessionAttribute.
  • Types: HttpServletRequest, WebRequest, Locale, Principal, HttpMethod.
  • Wrappers: HttpEntity, RequestEntity.
  • Static helper: RequestContextHolder for code outside controllers.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Annotations: @RequestParam (query or form), @PathVariable (URL path), @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody.
  • Raw access: declare HttpServletRequest or WebRequest as an argument when you need everything.
  • HttpEntity: HttpEntity<T> or RequestEntity<T> gives headers and body together.

Senior Notes

  • Resolution: the DispatcherServlet calls HandlerMethodArgumentResolver beans, one per argument type or annotation.
  • Body: @RequestBody is read by RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor with an HttpMessageConverter.
  • One read: the body stream can be read only once, so avoid reading it in a filter without a caching wrapper.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Reading body twice: a filter that reads the stream leaves nothing for @RequestBody; use ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Trusting headers: X-Forwarded-For can be forged unless set by your proxy.
  • Storing request in a field: controllers are singletons, so never keep the request in a field.
  • Case in headers: header names are case-insensitive, so use the API and not string maps with exact case.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Limits: cap header and body sizes (server.max-http-request-header-size).
  • Large bodies: stream with InputStream or @RequestPart instead of loading a String.
  • Logging: avoid logging full bodies in production.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.max-http-request-header-size=16KB
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB
spring.mvc.log-request-details=false

# OUTPUT:
