# header larger than 16KB -> 431 or connection closed (varies by server)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an audit feature records who called which endpoint. An interceptor or filter reads method, URI, user and a correlation id from headers, and puts the id in the logging context.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP response is what the server returns: a status line, headers and an optional body.
  • In Spring MVC you shape it with return values, ResponseEntity, @ResponseStatus or the raw HttpServletResponse.
  • Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error; choose them on purpose, for example 201 Created after a POST.

Worked Example 1

Status annotation and error response.

Worked Example 2

Write directly to the response.

Practice Exercise 1

Return 201 with a Location header.

Practice Exercise 2

Test status and header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the response is produced:

  • Return handler: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler beans decide what to do with the value.
  • Body: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks a converter and writes to the output stream.
  • View: ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler sends a name to the ViewResolver.
  • Exceptions: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver maps them to a response.
  • Commit: after the first flush status and headers can not change.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Response options:

  • ResponseEntity: builders such as ok(), created(uri), noContent(), notFound().
  • @ResponseStatus: fixed status on a method or exception class.
  • ResponseStatusException: throw it to set status and reason.
  • Streaming: StreamingResponseBody and SseEmitter.
  • Files: Resource with Content-Disposition.
  • Redirect: return redirect:/path from a view controller.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @ResponseBody (or @RestController) writes the return value to the body through an HttpMessageConverter.
  • ResponseEntity<T> controls status, headers and body in one object.
  • Views: a plain @Controller returning a String names a view, which a ViewResolver renders as HTML.

Senior Notes

  • Handling: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor or ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler processes the return value.
  • Errors: exceptions go to HandlerExceptionResolver beans, such as @ExceptionHandler and ResponseStatusException.
  • Committed: once the response is committed (flushed), you cannot change status or headers any more.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Always 200: returning an error object with status 200 hides failures; use 4xx and 5xx.
  • Null body: a null return from a @ResponseBody method gives an empty 200; return 404 or 204 on purpose.
  • Entity leaks: returning JPA entities exposes internal fields and may trigger lazy loading; use DTOs.
  • Writing after commit: setting headers after flushing is ignored.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning the response:

  • Compression: gzip text responses.
  • Caching: ETag and Cache-Control; ShallowEtagHeaderFilter saves bandwidth.
  • Streaming: avoid building a huge list in memory.
  • Small payloads: return only needed fields.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a consistent error format. A @RestControllerAdvice converts exceptions to the same JSON shape with the right status code, so clients can rely on it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request parameters are name-value pairs sent in the query string (?page=2&size=10) or in a form-encoded body.
  • Binding: Spring MVC copies them into method arguments, usually with @RequestParam, or into an object with @ModelAttribute.
  • Always text: they arrive as strings and Spring converts them to int, boolean, enums, dates and so on.

Worked Example 1

Bind parameters to an object.

Worked Example 2

Multi-value and map forms.

Practice Exercise 1

Search with paging.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the 400 and the defaults.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where parameters come from and how they are bound.

  • Container: the servlet container parses the query string and, for form content types, the body into one parameter map.
  • Resolver: RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver handles simple types; ModelAttributeMethodProcessor binds objects.
  • Binder: WebDataBinder converts text with ConversionService, applies formatters and collects BindingResult errors.
  • Unannotated: a simple type without annotation is treated as @RequestParam, a complex type as @ModelAttribute.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to read parameters:

  • @RequestParam: one value, list, or map.
  • Object binding: record or class with matching field names, nested as address.city.
  • HttpServletRequest: getParameter, getParameterValues, getParameterMap.
  • Formats: @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat.
  • Params condition: params = "mode=fast" selects a method by value.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Optional or default: use required = false, defaultValue or Optional<T>.
  • Many values: ?tag=a&tag=b binds to a List<String> or array.
  • All at once: @RequestParam Map<String,String> collects every parameter.

Senior Notes

  • Conversion: WebDataBinder and the ConversionService convert strings to target types.
  • Errors: a missing required parameter gives MissingServletRequestParameterException (400); a bad type gives MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException (400).
  • Not for secrets: query strings end up in logs and browser history.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Primitive with missing value: int page without a default gives 400; use Integer or a default.
  • No bounds: accepting size=1000000 invites denial of service; clamp it.
  • Mass assignment: binding to an entity lets callers set fields like role; bind to a DTO or use setAllowedFields.
  • Date format: without @DateTimeFormat a date string fails with 400.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Paging: always limit page size.
  • Query efficiency: pass parameters to the database as bound values, never as concatenated SQL.
  • Max parameters: the container limits their count (server.tomcat.max-parameter-count).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a product search page with filters. Parameters carry the filter, sort and paging, so every result page is a bookmarkable URL.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RequestParam binds a query-string or form parameter to a controller method argument: @RequestParam("name") String name.
  • Attributes: value/name (parameter name), required (default true) and defaultValue.
  • Missing: a required parameter that is absent returns 400 Bad Request.

Worked Example 1

List of ids.

Worked Example 2

Enum and date conversion.

Practice Exercise 1

Required, optional and default.

Practice Exercise 2

Type mismatch test.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution of one parameter:

  • Pick: RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver supports arguments with @RequestParam and simple types.
  • Read: it looks up the name in request.getParameterValues (or multipart parts).
  • Missing: it uses defaultValue or throws MissingServletRequestParameterException.
  • Convert: WebDataBinder.convertIfNecessary turns the text into the target type.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Annotation attributes and types:

  • value/name: parameter name.
  • required: default true.
  • defaultValue: text used when missing or empty; it implies required false.
  • Types: String, numbers, boolean, enum, LocalDate, UUID, List, Optional, MultipartFile.
  • MultiValueMap: keeps all values per name.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Name inference: the name can be omitted when the code is compiled with -parameters (Spring Boot does this by default).
  • Optional: @RequestParam Optional<String> or required = false gives null when absent.
  • Collections: List, arrays, and Map<String,String> are supported.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver reads request.getParameter and converts the value.
  • Empty vs missing: ?name= is present but empty, and defaultValue also replaces an empty value.
  • Multipart: for file uploads @RequestParam MultipartFile is resolved by the same family of resolvers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Primitive and optional: @RequestParam(required = false) int x fails because null cannot be an int; use Integer or a default.
  • Name mismatch: the client sends userId while the code expects user_id.
  • Commas in lists: a single value a,b splits into two list items, which can surprise when values contain commas.
  • Wrong place: an @RequestParam does not read JSON; JSON needs @RequestBody.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Notes for performance and safety:

  • Validation: add @Validated on the class plus constraints such as @Min and @Max on the parameters.
  • Limits: clamp numbers that drive queries.
  • Failures: handle ConstraintViolationException in an advice to return 400.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a log viewer endpoint filtered by level and time range. Parameters are optional, typed and validated, and the same URL can be shared by support staff.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Path variables are values placed inside the URL path itself, written as template segments such as /users/{id}.
  • RESTful style: they identify a resource (/orders/17), while query parameters filter or sort.
  • Binding: Spring extracts the segment and passes it to the method with @PathVariable.

Worked Example 1

Regex restriction.

Worked Example 2

Collect all variables in a map.

Practice Exercise 1

Nested resource.

Practice Exercise 2

Test with URI variables.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How template variables work.

  • Parse: at startup PathPatternParser compiles /users/{id} into a pattern object.
  • Match: per request PathPattern.matchAndExtract returns the variables.
  • Store: they go into the request attribute URI_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES_ATTRIBUTE.
  • Bind: PathVariableMethodArgumentResolver reads that attribute and converts the text.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Pattern features:

  • Regex: {id:[0-9]+}.
  • Mixed segments: /files/{name}.{ext} or /v{version}/users.
  • Multi-segment capture: {*rest} at the end captures the remaining path.
  • Wildcards: * and ** alongside variables.
  • Matrix variables: /cars;color=red with @MatrixVariable (needs enabling).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Several variables: /users/{userId}/orders/{orderId} works with two arguments.
  • Regex: {id:[0-9]+} restricts a variable, so /users/abc gives a 404 instead of a conversion error.
  • Type conversion: the segment is converted to int, long, UUID, enum and more.

Senior Notes

  • Matching: PathPattern (the default parser) matches the URL and fills the URI template variables.
  • Storage: values are kept in the request attribute HandlerMapping.URI_TEMPLATE_VARIABLES_ATTRIBUTE.
  • Specificity: literal segments win over variable ones, so /users/me beats /users/{id}.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Dot in the last variable: older versions cut the suffix; in Spring 6 suffix pattern matching is off, but encode special characters anyway.
  • Encoded slash: %2F is rejected by default for safety.
  • Sensitive ids: sequential ids invite guessing; also check ownership, not only existence.
  • Ambiguous patterns: /a/{x} and /a/{y} in two methods with the same verb conflict.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Notes:

  • Cost: pattern matching is fast; literal paths are looked up directly.
  • Caching: path-based URLs cache better in CDNs than query-based ones.
  • Parser: the default PathPatternParser is faster than the old AntPathMatcher.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (usually the default, shown for clarity)
spring.mvc.pathmatch.matching-strategy=path-pattern-parser

# OUTPUT:
# PathPatternParser is used;
patterns are precompiled once at startup

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nested REST resource where the URL shows ownership. The service checks the parent-child relation, and a missing child returns 404.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @PathVariable binds a URI template variable to a method argument: @GetMapping("/users/{id}") with @PathVariable Long id.
  • Name matching: the argument name must equal the placeholder, or be given explicitly, as in @PathVariable("id") Long userId.
  • Required: by default the variable is required; a missing one means the mapping did not match.

Worked Example 1

Validate the variable.

Worked Example 2

Test the type mismatch.

Practice Exercise 1

Basic and renamed binding.

Practice Exercise 2

Optional variable with two mappings.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

@PathVariable internals:

  • Supports: PathVariableMethodArgumentResolver handles arguments annotated with @PathVariable (and Map form via PathVariableMapMethodArgumentResolver).
  • Lookup: reads the template variables attribute set by the matched mapping.
  • Convert: the text is decoded and converted with the binder.
  • Missing: throws MissingPathVariableException, which is a server error because it usually means a coding mistake.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Usage forms:

  • Default name: argument name equals the placeholder.
  • Explicit name: @PathVariable("id").
  • Optional: required = false or Optional with two mappings.
  • Map: all variables.
  • Types: UUID, enums, LocalDate (with @DateTimeFormat), or your own class through a Converter.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Optional: required = false or Optional<T> works only when another mapping covers the shorter path.
  • Map form: @PathVariable Map<String,String> receives all variables.
  • Conversion: a failing conversion (for example text for a Long) gives 400 Bad Request.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: PathVariableMethodArgumentResolver reads the template variables saved by the handler mapping.
  • Encoding: values are URL-decoded, and a dot or a slash needs care because suffix and path handling changed in Spring 6.
  • Security: validate the value (type, range, regex) before using it in a query or a file path.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Renamed variable: placeholder and argument differ, and -parameters is missing, so binding fails.
  • Optional without second mapping: required = false alone does not make /users/ match.
  • No validation: ids from the path are untrusted input.
  • Using for filters: /products/red/under50 is awkward; use query parameters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and safety:

  • Regex: restrict early so bad input gives 404 without reaching your code.
  • Validation: @Validated with @Min or @Pattern.
  • Identifiers: UUIDs avoid guessing and enumeration.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a document service identifies files by UUID and tests the controller slice, including the invalid UUID case.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request headers are name-value pairs the client sends before the body, such as Accept, Content-Type, Authorization and User-Agent; they describe the client and the request.
  • Reading them in Spring MVC: use @RequestHeader, a HttpHeaders parameter, RequestEntity or HttpServletRequest.getHeader().
  • Case-insensitive: content-type and Content-Type are the same header, and Spring treats them so.

Worked Example 1

Test a header with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Iterate over all headers.

Practice Exercise 1

Read two headers.

Practice Exercise 2

Select a handler by header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a header reaches your method:

  • The servlet container parses the header lines into the request.
  • DispatcherServlet finds a handler, and RequestMappingHandlerAdapter runs its argument resolvers.
  • RequestHeaderMethodArgumentResolver calls request.getHeader and converts the text.
  • RequestHeaderMapMethodArgumentResolver handles Map and HttpHeaders parameters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants for headers:

  • Single value: @RequestHeader("X") String.
  • List: @RequestHeader("Accept") List<String> for comma separated values.
  • Map and HttpHeaders: all headers; MultiValueMap keeps repeated names.
  • Mapping conditions: headers, consumes, produces.
  • WebRequest: request.getHeader without the servlet API.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Use cases: content negotiation (Accept), authentication tokens (Authorization), API versions and correlation ids (X-Request-Id).
  • Mapping by header: @GetMapping(headers = "X-Api-Version=2") or consumes and produces choose a handler by header.
  • Multi-value: one header name can appear more than once; HttpHeaders.get(name) returns a list.

Senior Notes

  • Never trust client headers such as X-Forwarded-For unless a trusted proxy sets them; configure forwarded header handling on purpose.
  • Do not log Authorization or cookie headers in plain text.
  • Cross-cutting headers (request id, tenant) belong in a filter or interceptor, not in every controller method.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Required header missing: clients get 400; add required = false or a default.
  • Spaces in header names: header names use hyphens, so copy them exactly.
  • Reading Authorization manually: use Spring Security instead.
  • Plain Map with repeated headers: only the first value is kept; use MultiValueMap.
  • Custom headers blocked by CORS: list them in allowed and exposed headers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Header reads are cheap, a map lookup in the container.
  • Binding all headers copies them into a new map, so only do it when needed.
  • Large headers (big cookies or tokens) cost bandwidth on every request.
  • Container limits such as server.max-http-request-header-size reject oversized headers early.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.max-http-request-header-size=16KB
server.tomcat.max-http-response-header-size=16KB

# OUTPUT:
# requests with headers above 16KB get HTTP 431 Request Header Fields Too Large

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: every request carries X-Request-Id. A filter reads it, creates one when absent, puts it in the logging MDC and echoes it in the response, so logs from many services can be matched.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RequestHeader binds an HTTP request header to a controller method parameter, for example @RequestHeader("Accept-Language") String lang.
  • Required by default: a missing header gives 400; set required = false or defaultValue to relax it.
  • Type conversion: the header text is converted to the parameter type (int, Locale, Date) like any request value.

Worked Example 1

Test missing and present header.

Worked Example 2

Optional parameter.

Practice Exercise 1

Defaults and optional headers.

Practice Exercise 2

Typed header value.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the binding:

  • AbstractNamedValueMethodArgumentResolver is the base class; it resolves the name, applies the default value and checks required.
  • The header text goes through WebDataBinder and the ConversionService to the target type.
  • When nothing is found and the value is required, MissingRequestHeaderException is thrown.
  • The exception is turned into 400 by DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver (or ResponseEntityExceptionHandler).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attributes of the annotation:

  • value / name: the header name.
  • required: true by default.
  • defaultValue: used when missing or empty; it also makes the header not required.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Aggregates: bind Map<String,String>, MultiValueMap or HttpHeaders to get every header.
  • Optional: Optional<String> is the clean way to say "may be absent".
  • Name inference: with the -parameters compiler flag the parameter name can be the header name, but explicit names are safer.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: RequestHeaderMethodArgumentResolver reads the header and runs the ConversionService.
  • Missing header raises MissingRequestHeaderException, which becomes a 400 response.
  • Secrets: do not echo Authorization back in responses or logs; use security filters for auth.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing header gives 400: decide if it is truly required.
  • Header name typo: the value is then always missing; use constants.
  • Primitive with missing header: int with required = false fails on null; use Integer or a default.
  • Conversion error: a bad number gives 400 (MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: binding a header costs almost nothing. Avoid heavy parsing in the controller; for a token that needs parsing on every call, do it once in a filter. Keep custom headers short because they are repeated in every call, including preflight and proxy hops.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: API versioning by header. Clients send X-Api-Version; the controller gives each version its own handler, and a default handles clients that send nothing.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • A cookie is a small name-value pair that the server sets with the Set-Cookie response header; the browser returns it in the Cookie request header on later requests.
  • Purpose: keep state over stateless HTTP, such as a session id, a language choice or a remember-me token.
  • Attributes control behaviour: Path, Max-Age, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.

Worked Example 1

Delete a cookie.

Worked Example 2

Test cookies with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Set a cookie.

Practice Exercise 2

Read all cookies.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The cookie round trip:

  • The server sends Set-Cookie: name=value; attributes.
  • The browser stores it and sends Cookie: name=value on later requests that match domain, path and flags.
  • The container parses the header into Cookie[], which @CookieValue reads.
  • The session id cookie is created by the container (or Spring Session) in the same way.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attributes and APIs:

  • Path / Domain: where the cookie is sent.
  • Max-Age / Expires: lifetime; without them it is a session cookie.
  • HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite: security flags.
  • APIs: ResponseCookie (Spring, supports SameSite), Cookie (servlet), CookieGenerator style helpers in older code.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Read with @CookieValue or request.getCookies(); write with ResponseCookie or jakarta.servlet.http.Cookie.
  • HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, which limits theft by XSS; Secure sends it only over HTTPS.
  • SameSite (Lax or Strict) reduces CSRF risk; the servlet Cookie class has no direct SameSite setter, so use ResponseCookie.

Senior Notes

  • Size: browsers allow about 4 KB per cookie, and every cookie travels on every request to the path, so keep them small.
  • Never store secrets or trusted data (roles, prices) in a plain cookie; sign or encrypt it, or store it server side.
  • Session cookie JSESSIONID is created by the container; tune it with server.servlet.session.cookie.* properties.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Forgot HttpOnly or Secure: add both for session-like cookies.
  • Wrong path: a cookie set on /a is not sent to /b; use / when needed.
  • Deleting with a different path: the browser keeps it; match name, path and domain and set Max-Age 0.
  • Non-ASCII values: encode them (for example Base64 or URL encoding).
  • Trusting cookie data: sign or encrypt, or keep it on the server.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cookies are sent on every request to the path, including images, so large cookies slow pages.
  • Serve static files from a cookie-free domain or path.
  • Keep each cookie small (browser limit is about 4 KB).
  • Tune the container session cookie with properties.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a "remember language" feature. The first visit stores the chosen language in a cookie, later visits read it and fall back to the browser default.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @CookieValue binds the value of a named request cookie to a controller method parameter, for example @CookieValue("theme") String theme.
  • Required by default: a missing cookie gives 400 (MissingRequestCookieException); use required = false or defaultValue.
  • Type conversion applies, so you can bind int, boolean or Optional<String>.

Worked Example 1

Test required cookie.

Worked Example 2

Cookie bound to a number.

Practice Exercise 1

Optional cookie with default.

Practice Exercise 2

Get the Cookie object.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the argument is resolved:

  • ServletCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver extends AbstractCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver, which extends the named-value base class.
  • It uses WebUtils.getCookie(request, name) to find the cookie.
  • If the parameter type is Cookie, the object is passed; otherwise the value is URL-decoded and converted.
  • Missing and required throws MissingRequestCookieException.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • String / primitive / wrapper: converted value.
  • Cookie: the full servlet object (the browser only sends name and value, so path and age are null or -1).
  • Optional: absent means empty.
  • defaultValue: used when absent.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cookie object: declare the parameter as jakarta.servlet.http.Cookie to get name, path and age, not only the value.
  • Name comes from value or name; do not rely on the parameter name alone.
  • Only reads: it cannot set cookies; use ResponseCookie or HttpServletResponse for writing.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: ServletCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver finds the cookie through the request and converts it.
  • Trust: the value is client input, so validate it like any parameter and never treat it as proof of identity.
  • Browsers send only cookies whose path, domain and Secure flag match the request.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Assuming the cookie exists: first-time visitors do not have it; give a default.
  • Expecting Cookie path or max-age: the browser never sends them back.
  • Number parsing: a tampered value gives 400; handle it centrally.
  • Using it for identity: use the security session or a signed token.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: reading is cheap because cookies are already parsed once per request. The cost is the size of the cookie header sent on every call, so store only ids and small flags.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a cookie-based A/B test. A cookie holds the bucket; if absent, the server assigns one and sets it for next time.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • The request body is the payload after the headers, used by POST, PUT and PATCH to send JSON, XML, form data or files.
  • Spring reads it through HttpMessageConverter objects, chosen by the Content-Type header; JSON uses Jackson.
  • Bind it with @RequestBody to a Java object, String or byte[]; the stream can be read only once.

Worked Example 1

Test a JSON body.

Worked Example 2

Wrong content type.

Practice Exercise 1

Receive JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

Raw text body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the body is read:

  • The adapter calls RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor for a @RequestBody parameter.
  • It wraps the request as an HttpInputMessage and reads Content-Type.
  • It asks each HttpMessageConverter if it canRead(type, mediaType); the first match reads the stream.
  • Jackson converter: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter; text: StringHttpMessageConverter; bytes: ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter.
  • No match gives HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException (415).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Body types you can bind:

  • Object / record: JSON or XML.
  • String: raw text.
  • byte[] / InputStream / Reader: raw data.
  • Map / List: generic JSON.
  • HttpEntity or RequestEntity: body plus headers.
  • Multipart: use @RequestPart or MultipartFile.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Content-Type decides: application/json goes to Jackson, text/plain to the String converter; an unknown type gives 415.
  • Form data (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) is not read with @RequestBody; use @RequestParam or @ModelAttribute.
  • GET and DELETE normally have no body, so do not design APIs that depend on one.

Senior Notes

  • Size limits: cap body size (servlet container or gateway) to stop memory abuse.
  • Validate the bound object with @Valid and never trust fields such as ids or roles.
  • Single read: a filter that reads the stream must wrap the request (for example ContentCachingRequestWrapper) or later binding fails.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing Content-Type header: gives 415; set application/json.
  • Reading the stream in a filter: later binding sees an empty body; use a caching wrapper.
  • Sending form data to @RequestBody: use @ModelAttribute.
  • Date formats: configure Jackson or use ISO strings.
  • Entity as body: use a DTO.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • JSON parsing cost grows with body size; the converter reads the stream in one pass.
  • Set limits: Tomcat server.tomcat.max-swallow-size and max-http-form-post-size, and gateway limits.
  • For very large uploads or feeds, stream with InputStream instead of binding a big object.
  • Enable HTTP compression only where it helps.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order API. The client posts an order document; the server validates it, saves it and returns 201 with a Location header.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RequestBody tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and convert it to the method parameter using an HttpMessageConverter.
  • With JSON and Jackson on the classpath, the body is deserialized into a record, class or Map.
  • Add @Valid to run Bean Validation; failures raise MethodArgumentNotValidException and a 400 response.

Worked Example 1

Test validation failure.

Worked Example 2

Handle bad JSON.

Practice Exercise 1

Validated DTO.

Practice Exercise 2

Optional body and list.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The annotation at work:

  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor.resolveArgument calls readWithMessageConverters.
  • Then it creates a WebDataBinder and, if the parameter has @Valid or @Validated, runs the validator.
  • A RequestBodyAdvice bean can inspect or change the body before and after conversion.
  • Errors become MethodArgumentNotValidException.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • required: default true.
  • Records, classes with setters, and @JsonCreator constructors all work.
  • Control fields with Jackson annotations such as @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnoreProperties, @JsonFormat.
  • Groups: @Validated(Create.class) for different rules per operation.
  • @RequestBody is not needed in @RestController for return values, only for parameters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Required by default: an empty body gives 400; use required = false to allow it (the parameter is then null).
  • Generics: @RequestBody List<Book> works because Spring keeps the generic type of the parameter.
  • Bad JSON raises HttpMessageNotReadableException (400); a wrong media type raises 415.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads the body and also handles @ResponseBody.
  • Mass assignment: binding straight into an entity lets clients set fields like id or role; use a request DTO.
  • Unknown fields: Spring Boot disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES by default, so extra JSON fields are ignored.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • No @Valid: constraints are ignored; add it.
  • Binding an entity: clients can set the id or role; use a DTO.
  • Primitive fields for optional JSON values: a missing field becomes 0 or false; use wrapper types when you must tell absent from zero.
  • Date text not parsed: add @JsonFormat or send ISO dates.
  • Missing no-arg constructor on a plain class: use a record or setters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Reuse the Spring-managed ObjectMapper; do not create a new one per request.
  • Use spring.jackson.* properties for global date and null handling.
  • Reject oversized collections with @Size.
  • Prefer records for small immutable payloads.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# unknown JSON fields now cause HTTP 400 with an RFC 7807 problem body

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a payment webhook posts JSON signed with a header. The controller needs the raw bytes to verify the signature and the object to process, so it takes both.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpServletRequest (jakarta.servlet.http) is the servlet API object that holds everything about the incoming request: method, URL, headers, parameters, cookies, body stream and session.
  • Spring injects it into controller methods when you add it as a parameter; there is one object per request.
  • Prefer annotations such as @RequestParam and @RequestHeader for simple needs, and use the raw request only for what they cannot do.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockHttpServletRequest.

Worked Example 2

Read the raw body once.

Practice Exercise 1

Inspect the request.

Practice Exercise 2

Pass data with an attribute.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the object comes from:

  • The container (Tomcat) creates a request object per call, and filters may wrap it.
  • RequestContextHolder keeps it in a thread local for the current thread.
  • The argument resolver ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver passes it into your method.
  • Spring also supports WebRequest, HttpMethod, Locale and InputStream as parameters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful groups of methods:

  • URL: getRequestURL, getContextPath, getServletPath, getQueryString.
  • Client: getRemoteAddr, getScheme, isSecure, getLocale.
  • Data: getParameterMap, getHeaderNames, getParts.
  • Security: getUserPrincipal, isUserInRole.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Common methods: getMethod(), getRequestURI(), getParameter(), getHeader(), getRemoteAddr(), getCookies().
  • Attributes: setAttribute and getAttribute share data inside one request, for example between a filter and a controller.
  • Body: getInputStream() or getReader() read it once, and you cannot use both on the same request.

Senior Notes

  • Coupling: using the servlet API ties the method to a servlet container and makes tests need a mock request.
  • Client IP: getRemoteAddr() shows the proxy behind a load balancer; configure forwarded headers instead of parsing them by hand.
  • Not thread safe to share: never store the request in a field or pass it to another thread after the request ends.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Calling both getReader and getInputStream: throws IllegalStateException.
  • Reading the body after a form parameter call: getParameter may consume form bodies.
  • Using the request in an async thread: it can be recycled; copy needed values first.
  • Old javax imports: Spring Boot 3 uses jakarta.servlet.
  • Trusting remote address behind a proxy: configure forwarded headers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: parameter and header lookups are cheap. Avoid parsing the full parameter map when you need one value. Use server.forward-headers-strategy so scheme, host and client address are right behind a proxy, which avoids bad redirects.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.forward-headers-strategy=framework
server.tomcat.remoteip.remote-ip-header=x-forwarded-for
server.tomcat.remoteip.protocol-header=x-forwarded-proto

# OUTPUT:
# getRemoteAddr() and getScheme() now reflect the real client and HTTPS

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an audit interceptor records who called which endpoint. It uses the request for method, path, client address and user.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpServletResponse (jakarta.servlet.http) represents the outgoing response: status code, headers, cookies and the body stream or writer.
  • Spring injects it when it is a controller parameter, letting you write the response yourself.
  • Use it rarely: return values, ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus are cleaner for most responses.

Worked Example 1

Test the response.

Worked Example 2

Redirect and error.

Practice Exercise 1

Write status, header and body.

Practice Exercise 2

CSV download.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the response is produced:

  • The container creates a response with a buffer; headers and body are held until the buffer fills or is flushed.
  • Committed: once flushed, status and headers are fixed.
  • If a handler returns a value, HttpMessageConverter writes it to the same output stream.
  • If you write the response yourself, return void (or mark it handled) so Spring does not add output.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to send a response:

  • Return value / ResponseEntity: preferred.
  • Raw writer or stream: custom formats.
  • StreamingResponseBody: large output on a separate thread.
  • SseEmitter: server-sent events.
  • Redirect: sendRedirect (302) or RedirectView.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Common methods: setStatus, setHeader, addCookie, sendRedirect, sendError, getWriter, getOutputStream.
  • Streaming: write a large file or CSV directly to getOutputStream() to avoid loading it into memory (or use StreamingResponseBody).
  • Writer or stream: call one of getWriter or getOutputStream, not both.

Senior Notes

  • Committed: once headers and some body are flushed, you cannot change the status or headers; late errors cannot become a clean error page.
  • Void methods: if a handler writes the response itself, return void so Spring does not try to render a view.
  • Download safety: set Content-Disposition and a correct Content-Type, and never put unchecked user input in the file name.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Setting a header after commit: it is ignored; set headers before writing.
  • Using both writer and output stream: IllegalStateException.
  • Returning a value too: a non-void return after writing causes double output or errors.
  • Missing Content-Type or charset: garbled text; set it.
  • Unsafe file name in Content-Disposition: sanitize it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Stream large payloads instead of building them in memory.
  • Enable compression for text content with server.compression.enabled=true.
  • Set cache headers on static or stable data (Cache-Control, ETag).
  • Flush only when you need progressive output.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,text/csv,text/html
server.compression.min-response-size=1KB

# OUTPUT:
# responses above 1KB of those types are sent with Content-Encoding: gzip

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: export a large report as CSV. The controller streams rows from the database cursor straight to the client, with a download file name.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpSession is a server-side object that stores data for one user across several requests; the browser holds only the session id in the JSESSIONID cookie.
  • Get it by adding HttpSession as a controller parameter (it is created when first used), or with request.getSession(false) to avoid creating one.
  • Store data with setAttribute and getAttribute; values should be serializable and small.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockHttpSession.

Worked Example 2

Read without creating.

Practice Exercise 1

Count visits.

Practice Exercise 2

Logout.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the session:

  • The container keeps a Map of session id to HttpSession (in Tomcat, a StandardManager).
  • On first use it creates the object and sends Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID.
  • Each request with the cookie looks the session up and updates the last accessed time.
  • A background task removes sessions idle past their timeout.
  • Listeners (HttpSessionListener) can react to create and destroy.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Spring helpers around sessions:

  • @SessionAttributes("cart"): keeps a model attribute in the session for one controller.
  • @SessionAttribute("user"): reads one attribute into a parameter.
  • @SessionScope bean: one bean instance per session.
  • SessionStatus.setComplete() clears @SessionAttributes data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Timeout: the container expires idle sessions; set it with server.servlet.session.timeout or setMaxInactiveInterval.
  • Logout: call session.invalidate() to remove all data.
  • @SessionAttributes and @SessionAttribute are Spring helpers built on the same session.

Senior Notes

  • Scaling: sessions live in server memory, so multiple instances need sticky sessions or shared storage such as Spring Session with Redis.
  • Session fixation: change the id after login (changeSessionId); Spring Security does this by default.
  • Memory: do not keep large objects or entities in the session; keep ids and load data when needed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Creating sessions for everyone (bots included): use getSession(false) where no state is needed.
  • Storing big or non-serializable objects: keep ids, not entities.
  • No invalidation on logout: call invalidate().
  • Not renewing the id on login: allows session fixation.
  • Concurrent updates to the same attribute: sessions are not locked; synchronize or avoid shared mutable state.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep session data small, it is held in memory and may be replicated.
  • Set a reasonable timeout, since idle sessions cost memory.
  • For several servers use Spring Session so any instance can serve the user.
  • Prefer stateless tokens for pure APIs.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.timeout=20m
spring.session.store-type=redis
spring.session.redis.namespace=myapp:sessions

# OUTPUT:
# sessions are stored in Redis, and any application instance can read them

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shopping flow. The cart lives in the session until checkout, then the session data is cleared after the order is saved.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Principal (java.security.Principal) represents the authenticated user; its getName() returns the username.
  • Spring MVC injects it as a controller parameter; it is null when no one is logged in and no security is configured.
  • With Spring Security the real object is an Authentication (a Principal) holding authorities and details.

Worked Example 1

Test with a mock user.

Worked Example 2

Own data only.

Practice Exercise 1

Principal parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

@AuthenticationPrincipal.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the Principal comes from:

  • Spring Security filters authenticate the request and store an Authentication in SecurityContextHolder.
  • SecurityContextHolderAwareRequestFilter wraps the request so getUserPrincipal() returns it.
  • MVC's ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver then passes request.getUserPrincipal() into a Principal parameter.
  • @AuthenticationPrincipal is handled by AuthenticationPrincipalArgumentResolver.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to reach the current user:

  • Principal: just the name.
  • Authentication: authorities and details.
  • @AuthenticationPrincipal: your user object; expression can pick a field.
  • SecurityContextHolder: anywhere in code, same thread.
  • JWT: @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt with a resource server.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Richer access: use Authentication or @AuthenticationPrincipal to get your own user type instead of only a name.
  • Servlet API: request.getUserPrincipal() and request.isUserInRole() expose the same identity.
  • Authorization belongs in security config or @PreAuthorize, not in manual Principal checks.

Senior Notes

  • Source: the principal comes from the SecurityContext, filled by the security filter chain before MVC runs.
  • Never accept a user id from the request when the Principal already tells you who is calling; that prevents acting on other accounts.
  • Async threads: the security context does not follow plain new threads, so pass the user explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Principal is null: the endpoint is public or security is off; require authentication.
  • Taking user id from the request: use the Principal.
  • Using the Principal in a new thread: the context is not copied; use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or pass values.
  • Casting the Principal to your class blindly: use @AuthenticationPrincipal.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: the Principal is already in memory, so reading it is free. Cost lies in authentication; cache user lookups, use stateless tokens to avoid session lookups, and avoid loading the full user entity on each call when the name or id is enough.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a "my account" API plus an audit field. Controllers use the Principal to scope data to the caller and to record who changed a record.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Locale is the language and region (for example en_US or fr_FR) that Spring MVC works out for each request, so messages, dates and numbers can be shown in the user language.
  • Controller argument: declare a java.util.Locale parameter and Spring fills it with the current request locale.
  • Default source: the Accept-Language header sent by the browser is used unless another LocaleResolver is configured.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Use LocaleContextHolder in a service.

Practice Exercise 1

Locale as a controller argument.

Practice Exercise 2

Format a date for the locale.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The locale is resolved once per request by DispatcherServlet.

  • doService: it stores the resolver as a request attribute and calls buildLocaleContext.
  • Lookup: the LocaleResolver bean must be named localeResolver.
  • Argument: ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver fills a Locale parameter from the resolver.
  • Thread: FrameworkServlet sets LocaleContextHolder for the request thread and clears it afterwards.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolver choices:

  • AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver: default, read-only; setLocale throws an exception.
  • SessionLocaleResolver: stores the locale in the HTTP session.
  • CookieLocaleResolver: stores it in a cookie; works across sessions.
  • FixedLocaleResolver: always one locale.
  • LocaleChangeInterceptor: reads a parameter such as lang and calls setLocale.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • LocaleResolver decides the locale: AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver (default), SessionLocaleResolver, CookieLocaleResolver and FixedLocaleResolver.
  • MessageSource turns a key plus a locale into text from messages_fr.properties style files.
  • LocaleContextHolder gives the current locale anywhere in the thread, even outside a controller.

Senior Notes

  • Bean name: a resolver bean must be named localeResolver, or DispatcherServlet ignores it.
  • Thread binding: the locale is stored in a thread-local, so it is not visible in new threads you start yourself.
  • Testing: use MockMvc with .locale(Locale.FRANCE) or an Accept-Language header.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong bean name: a method called resolver() is ignored; name it localeResolver.
  • Language switch ignored: the default header resolver cannot change locale, so use Session or Cookie.
  • Missing fallback: a locale with no bundle should fall back to the base file.
  • Wrong thread: @Async code does not see the request locale.
  • Default JVM locale: set a default so servers behave the same everywhere.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning points:

  • Cost: the header resolver is cheap and stateless, so it scales well.
  • Session resolver: adds memory and sticky-session needs; a cookie resolver avoids that.
  • MessageSource: set setCacheSeconds or rely on the default cache, and avoid reloading bundles on every request.
  • Formatters: reuse DateTimeFormatter instances per locale.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.messages.basename=messages
spring.messages.cache-duration=3600s
spring.messages.fallback-to-system-locale=false

# OUTPUT:
# bundles are cached for an hour;
unknown locales fall back to messages.properties

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A shop supports English, French and German. Choose a cookie resolver so the choice persists, show prices with locale-aware formatting, and test each language with MockMvc.

  • Cookie: keeps the language between visits.
  • Switch link: ?lang=de in the page header.
  • Test: one test per supported language.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request attributes are named objects stored on the current HttpServletRequest with setAttribute; they live only until the response is finished.
  • Read them in a handler with @RequestAttribute, or with request.getAttribute(name).
  • Typical use: a filter or interceptor computes something (user id, trace id) and the controller reads it later in the same request.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc supplies the attribute.

Worked Example 2

Interceptor passes the user id.

Practice Exercise 1

Filter sets, controller reads.

Practice Exercise 2

Optional attribute.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Attributes are stored in the servlet container request object.

  • Storage: setAttribute writes to a map on the request; there is no copy to the client.
  • Binding: RequestAttributeMethodArgumentResolver calls request.getAttribute(name, SCOPE_REQUEST).
  • Required: a missing required value throws ServletRequestBindingException.
  • Lifetime: the container discards them after the response; wrappers and forwards share them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @RequestAttribute: read a request-scope value.
  • @SessionAttribute: read a session value without creating a session.
  • @SessionAttributes: keep model attributes in the session for a controller.
  • RequestContextHolder: read attributes outside a controller.
  • @RequestScope: a bean that lives for one request.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Not parameters: request parameters come from the client; attributes are set by server code, so users cannot forge them.
  • @RequestAttribute is required by default; use required = false or a default value when it may be missing.
  • Scope: request attributes differ from session attributes (@SessionAttribute) and from model attributes, which are for the view.

Senior Notes

  • Forward: attributes survive a forward: because it is the same request, but they are lost on a redirect:.
  • Name clashes: use namespaced names such as com.shop.userId to avoid overwriting framework attributes.
  • Testing: use MockMvc with .requestAttr(name, value) to supply the attribute.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using a parameter name: the value was set as an attribute, so @RequestParam returns nothing.
  • Type mismatch: setting a String and reading a Long fails with a conversion error.
  • Redirect loss: data set before redirect: is gone; use flash attributes.
  • Filter order: the filter must run before the handler, so check its order.
  • Trusting input: never copy client input into a trusted attribute name.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Request attributes cost almost nothing: they are in-memory map entries.

  • Compute once: a filter that parses a token once and stores the result avoids repeating the work in each handler.
  • Keep small: store ids or small objects, not large payloads.
  • Prefer @RequestScope beans when many classes need the same value, to avoid passing the request around.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A multi-tenant API resolves the tenant from the host name in a filter and stores it for the whole request.

  • Filter: reads the host, validates the tenant, sets the attribute.
  • Controller: uses @RequestAttribute to stay clean.
  • Test: supply the attribute with requestAttr.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Model is the Spring MVC interface that carries data from the controller to the view; you add named objects and the view reads them while rendering.
  • Declare it as a handler parameter: String list(Model model); Spring creates it and passes it in.
  • Add data with model.addAttribute("name", value) and return the view name as a String.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc checks the model.

Worked Example 2

Model is not session data.

Practice Exercise 1

A controller filling the Model.

Practice Exercise 2

Derived attribute name.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The model is created by the framework before the handler runs.

  • Container: ModelAndViewContainer holds a BindingAwareModelMap for the request.
  • Argument: ModelMethodProcessor passes that map as the Model parameter.
  • After handler: the container's model plus the view name become a ModelAndView.
  • Render: the view copies the map into request attributes or template context.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to use the model:

  • Model: the standard interface with addAttribute.
  • Map<String,Object>: a plain map parameter works too.
  • ModelMap: the map subclass.
  • ModelAndView: return value with view and model.
  • @ModelAttribute: method or parameter for shared and bound data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Per request: the model is created for each request and discarded after the view renders.
  • Implementation: the argument is really a BindingAwareModelMap, a map of attribute names to values.
  • Model or ModelMap or ModelAndView: all hold the same kind of data; Model is the simplest and most common choice.

Senior Notes

  • Exposed to the view: attributes are copied to request attributes (or template variables) by the View.
  • Name by type: addAttribute(value) without a name derives one, such as userList from a List<User>.
  • Testing: MockMvc checks it with model().attribute(name, value).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning the model: a Model return type is not a view name.
  • @RestController: the model is ignored because the return value is the body.
  • Large objects: adding whole entity graphs causes lazy loading and big pages.
  • Expecting persistence: the model is gone after the request.
  • Name clash: two attributes with the same name overwrite each other.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Keep the model small and ready for display.

  • DTOs: add view objects, not full entities.
  • Paging: add one page of data, not the whole table.
  • Lazy loading: load what the page needs inside the service, because open-in-view hides extra queries.
  • Caching: cache reference data used by shared @ModelAttribute methods.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A product list page shows a title, a page of products and a filter list.

  • Handler: adds only these three attributes.
  • Test: checks each attribute and the view name.
  • Template: loops over products.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ModelMap is a LinkedHashMap<String, Object> subclass in Spring that holds model attributes and keeps the order in which you added them.
  • Use it as a handler parameter: String show(ModelMap map), then map.addAttribute("k", v).
  • Same job as Model: both pass data to the view; ModelMap just exposes the map methods as well.

Worked Example 1

One model, two parameters.

Worked Example 2

Test the ModelMap data.

Practice Exercise 1

Fill a ModelMap.

Practice Exercise 2

Use the map methods.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The class is small and sits in org.springframework.ui.

  • Hierarchy: ModelMap extends LinkedHashMap<String, Object>.
  • addAttribute: asserts the name is not null, then calls put.
  • Runtime type: the injected object is a BindingAwareModelMap, which extends ExtendedModelMap and implements both Model and the map.
  • Ordering: insertion order is kept for predictable output.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful methods:

  • addAttribute(name, value): add one.
  • addAttribute(value): name derived from the type.
  • addAllAttributes: from a map or collection.
  • mergeAttributes: add only names not present.
  • containsAttribute: existence check.
  • getAttribute: read a value.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Chaining: addAttribute returns the map, so you can write map.addAttribute("a", 1).addAttribute("b", 2).
  • Map methods: get, containsKey, putAll and mergeAttributes are available.
  • Null values: addAttribute accepts a null value but the name must not be null.

Senior Notes

  • Which to pick: prefer Model for new code because it is an interface; use ModelMap when you need map behaviour.
  • Same instance: Spring passes the same BindingAwareModelMap whichever of the two types you declare.
  • Pitfall: do not declare both Model and ModelMap and expect separate data; they share one model.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Empty collection name: addAttribute(emptyList) cannot derive a name and fails.
  • Null name: throws IllegalArgumentException.
  • Two parameter types: using Model and ModelMap together does not create two models.
  • Mutating a shared map: storing a ModelMap in a field leaks request data between users.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance is the same as a LinkedHashMap: constant-time puts and gets. Tuning notes:

  • Small: a request model has few entries, so size is not a concern.
  • Values: avoid heavy objects.
  • No sharing: never keep it in a singleton field; it is per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A report page builds many ordered attributes and a helper method fills them.

  • Helper: accepts the ModelMap and fills a section.
  • Order: preserved for debugging output.
  • Test: checks each key.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ModelAndView is a single object that holds both the view (a name or a View) and the model data a handler wants rendered.
  • Create it as new ModelAndView("viewName") and add data with addObject(name, value).
  • Return it from the handler method; DispatcherServlet then picks the view and renders it with the model.

Test the returned object.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The class stores a view and a model together.

  • Fields: view (a name string or a View object), a ModelMap and an optional HttpStatusCode.
  • Handling: ModelAndViewMethodReturnValueHandler puts the name and model into the container.
  • Render: DispatcherServlet.render resolves the name with the ViewResolver chain.
  • Reference flag: a name starting with redirect: is handled as a redirect view.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Constructors and helpers:

  • new ModelAndView(): empty; set later.
  • (String viewName): name only.
  • (String, String, Object): name plus one attribute.
  • (String, Map): name plus a model map.
  • (String, HttpStatusCode): name plus status.
  • clear(): removes view and model.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Constructors: ModelAndView(String viewName), (String, String, Object) for one attribute, and (String, Map).
  • Extras: setStatus(HttpStatus) sets the response status and setViewName changes the view later.
  • Redirect: new ModelAndView("redirect:/home") works just like returning a redirect string.

Senior Notes

  • Model plus view in one return value is handy when the view depends on logic, but a plain String plus Model is simpler.
  • Inspect: getModel() and getViewName() help in tests and in HandlerInterceptor.postHandle.
  • Empty: returning null means the handler handled the response itself.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Null return: returning null from a controller without writing the response gives an empty page.
  • Wrong controller type: inside a @RestController the object is serialised as JSON instead of rendered.
  • No view: an empty ModelAndView falls back to the path-derived name and may fail with a missing template.
  • Mixing: do not both return a ModelAndView and write directly to the response.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Overhead is one small object per request. Tuning points:

  • Interceptor cost: postHandle work runs on every page, so keep it light.
  • Model size: add only what the view shows.
  • Reuse nothing: a new instance per request is correct and cheap.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A checkout controller returns different views by result.

  • Success: redirect to the receipt page.
  • Validation failure: same form view with errors and status 422.
  • Test: one test per outcome.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Adding data means putting named values into the model so the view can show them; the main call is model.addAttribute(name, value).
  • Many at once: addAllAttributes(Map) or addAllAttributes(Collection) adds several values.
  • Shared data: a method annotated with @ModelAttribute runs before every handler and adds data for all of them.

Worked Example 1

Global data in a ControllerAdvice.

Worked Example 2

Verify in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

addAttribute and addAllAttributes.

Practice Exercise 2

Shared data with @ModelAttribute.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Data reaches the model in a fixed order.

  • 1: ModelFactory.initModel runs the @ModelAttribute methods.
  • 2: @SessionAttributes values are merged in.
  • 3: the handler runs and adds its own attributes.
  • 4: after the handler, updateModel adds BindingResult objects for bound attributes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • addAttribute(name, value): explicit name.
  • addAttribute(value): derived name.
  • addAllAttributes: map or collection.
  • mergeAttributes: do not overwrite existing.
  • @ModelAttribute method: per controller.
  • @ControllerAdvice: global.
  • RedirectAttributes: for redirects.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @ModelAttribute method: @ModelAttribute("countries") List<String> countries() fills a dropdown on each request.
  • Form binding: a @ModelAttribute parameter is created, filled from request parameters and added to the model by name.
  • @ControllerAdvice: put @ModelAttribute methods in an advice class to add data to every controller.

Senior Notes

  • Order: @ModelAttribute methods run before the handler, so the handler may overwrite their values.
  • Cost: a shared @ModelAttribute method runs on every request of that controller, so keep it cheap or cache the result.
  • Do not add secrets: anything in the model may be rendered or leaked by a template mistake, so add only what the view needs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Overwriting by name: two sources using the same name replace each other.
  • Heavy shared method: a database call in @ModelAttribute runs for every handler.
  • Redirect parameters: simple values in the model are added to the redirect URL; use RedirectAttributes.
  • Mutable cached lists: a template or handler changing a shared list affects other users.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Make shared data cheap.

  • Cache: use @Cacheable for reference data.
  • Scope: use a controller-specific method, not a global advice, if only some pages need it.
  • Lazy: add data only in the handlers that need it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A registration page needs dropdown lists, a blank form object and a title.

  • @ModelAttribute methods: countries and roles.
  • Handler: adds the blank form and title.
  • Test: asserts all four attributes.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Reading model data happens in the view: a template uses the attribute name to show the value the controller added.
  • In a controller you can read model data already added with model.getAttribute, containsAttribute or asMap().
  • Parameters: @ModelAttribute on a handler parameter reads an object that an earlier @ModelAttribute method or a redirect flash put in the model.

Worked Example 1

Read the model in a test.

Worked Example 2

A template typo fails silently.

Practice Exercise 1

Read inside a handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Flash attribute across a redirect.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Reading depends on where you are.

  • View: the View.render method receives the model map and merges it into the template or request attributes.
  • Handler: the Model argument is the live map, so reads see earlier additions.
  • After redirect: FlashMapManager keeps flash values in the session, then puts them into the next request model.
  • Interceptor: postHandle reads mav.getModel().

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to read:

  • Template: by attribute name.
  • Model methods: getAttribute, containsAttribute, asMap.
  • @ModelAttribute parameter: flash or earlier data.
  • RequestContextUtils.getInputFlashMap: direct flash access.
  • MockMvc: model() matchers.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • View side: Thymeleaf, JSP and FreeMarker all read the model by attribute name; in JSP the values are exposed as request attributes.
  • Flash attributes: RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute keeps data for one redirect, and the next handler reads it from the model.
  • Missing name: a template usually shows an empty value when the attribute does not exist, so typos fail silently.

Senior Notes

  • Testing: use model().attribute, model().attributeExists and result.getModelAndView().getModel().
  • Types: read with the correct type; getAttribute returns Object and needs a cast.
  • Scope: model data is not available after the view renders; use the session or a database for data that must last longer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Direct access to a flash page: the flash value is missing, so a @ModelAttribute String is created empty or fails.
  • Refresh loses data: flash lasts for one redirect only.
  • Casting: a wrong cast from getAttribute gives ClassCastException.
  • Name typos: silent empty values in the page.
  • Unescaped output: showing model text with an unsafe tag allows script injection; use the escaping tag.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Reading is free, but what you stored matters.

  • Eager data: load before rendering, not inside the template.
  • Lazy collections: touching them in the view can start extra queries.
  • Large lists: page them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Post-Redirect-Get with a success message is the classic case.

  • POST: saves and sets a flash message.
  • GET: reads it from the model and shows it once.
  • Test: checks flash().attribute.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Returning a view name means the handler returns a String such as "home"; Spring treats it as a logical view name, not as the response text.
  • ViewResolver turns the logical name into a real view, for example home into /templates/home.html with Thymeleaf.
  • @Controller needed: with @RestController or @ResponseBody the string is written to the body instead.

Worked Example 1

Test view name and redirect.

Worked Example 2

RestController returns text.

Practice Exercise 1

Return a view name.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect and forward.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The String return is handled by ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler.

  • Step 1: it sets the view name on the ModelAndViewContainer.
  • Step 2: a name that starts with redirect: marks it as a redirect and ignores the default model.
  • Step 3: DispatcherServlet.resolveViewName loops over the resolvers.
  • Step 4: the chosen View renders.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Return forms:

  • String name: "home".
  • redirect: a 302 to another URL.
  • forward: internal forward.
  • void: view name from the request path.
  • View object: return a View directly.
  • Fragment name: Thymeleaf allows "page :: section".

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefixes: redirect:/path sends a 302 to a new URL and forward:/path forwards inside the server.
  • void return: a void handler uses the request path as the view name by default.
  • Model together: the view name plus the Model argument gives the view its data.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver chain: DispatcherServlet asks each ViewResolver in order until one returns a view.
  • Post-Redirect-Get: redirect after a successful POST so a browser refresh does not submit the form twice.
  • Testing: MockMvc checks the name with view().name("home"), and redirects with redirectedUrl.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • @RestController: the name is returned as text.
  • Missing template: a typo gives a 500 (Thymeleaf) or a 404 (JSP).
  • Leading slash: "/home" may resolve to a wrong path; use "home".
  • Redirect without PRG: returning a view after POST allows duplicate submits.
  • Open redirect: do not build redirect: from user input without checks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Notes:

  • Template cache: keep spring.thymeleaf.cache=true in production.
  • Resolver count: fewer resolvers mean faster lookup.
  • Fragments: return a fragment for partial page updates to send less HTML.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/templates/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html

# OUTPUT:
# templates are parsed once and cached for later requests

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A form flow: show form, validate, then redirect.

  • GET: returns the form view.
  • POST invalid: returns the form view again.
  • POST valid: redirects to a success page.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Returning ModelAndView means the handler gives back one object holding the view and the data; Spring renders that view with that model.
  • Build it: new ModelAndView("view") then addObject("key", value), and return mav;.
  • Return type of the method is ModelAndView; the class must be a @Controller, not a @RestController.
