Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Handling happens in ModelAndViewMethodReturnValueHandler.

  • Null: marks the request as handled, so no view is rendered.
  • View name: if it is a reference, it sets the name; otherwise it sets the View object.
  • Model: the attributes are merged into the container model.
  • Redirect: a redirect name switches the container to redirect scenario.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Name: logical view.
  • View object: new ModelAndView(new RedirectView("/x")).
  • Status: setStatus.
  • Redirect with attributes: use RedirectView with flash map or RedirectAttributes.
  • JSON view: MappingJackson2JsonView renders the model as JSON.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Choose the view at run time: set the name from logic, such as mav.setViewName(isAdmin ? "admin" : "user").
  • Status: mav.setStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) sets the response code with the page.
  • Empty result: new ModelAndView() without a name makes Spring use the default view name from the path.

Senior Notes

  • Handler return handler: ModelAndViewMethodReturnValueHandler copies the object into the request ModelAndViewContainer.
  • Exception resolvers: a HandlerExceptionResolver can also return a ModelAndView to show an error page.
  • Style: modern code usually returns a view name plus Model; use ModelAndView when you need its extra control.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting to return: building the object and returning null shows no page.
  • RestController: leads to unexpected JSON.
  • Duplicate name: adding the same attribute twice keeps the last value.
  • Mixing responses: writing to HttpServletResponse and returning a view causes "response already committed".

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Notes:

  • Object cost: trivial per request.
  • View choice: avoid looking up expensive data just to choose a view.
  • Testing speed: @WebMvcTest loads only web beans, so tests stay fast.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A legacy admin app returns different views by user type and also exposes a JSON view for export.

  • HTML: normal pages through a template engine.
  • JSON view: export of the same model.
  • Interceptor: adds the logged in user name to every model.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • View rendering is the last step of a request: DispatcherServlet resolves the view name to a View object and calls view.render(model, request, response).
  • ViewResolver maps the logical name to a view: ThymeleafViewResolver, InternalResourceViewResolver for JSP, and so on.
  • Result: the view merges the model data into the template and writes the HTML to the response.

Worked Example 1

Test the rendered HTML.

Worked Example 2

Custom View object.

Practice Exercise 1

Boot templates and a view.

Practice Exercise 2

Configure JSP style resolver.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Rendering starts after the handler and interceptors.

  • processDispatchResult: checks for exceptions, then calls render if a ModelAndView exists.
  • resolveViewName: loops through viewResolvers and returns the first non-null view.
  • view.render: merges the model with the template and writes the response.
  • Locale: the resolved locale is set on the response before rendering.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common view technologies:

  • Thymeleaf: HTML templates, Boot default for server pages.
  • FreeMarker, Mustache: other template engines.
  • JSP: needs InternalResourceViewResolver and a WAR style setup.
  • MappingJackson2JsonView: JSON from the model.
  • BeanNameViewResolver: views registered as beans.
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver: chooses by Accept header or extension.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Flow: handler returns name and model, DispatcherServlet.render asks resolvers, the first non-null View renders.
  • Spring Boot auto-configures resolvers for Thymeleaf, FreeMarker and others when the library is on the classpath; templates live in src/main/resources/templates.
  • Content negotiation: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver picks a view that matches what the client accepts, such as HTML or JSON.

Senior Notes

  • Order: several resolvers can exist; set setOrder so the right one runs first, because a catch-all resolver can swallow names.
  • Errors: a missing template gives a TemplateInputException (Thymeleaf) and a 500 response.
  • Testing: MockMvc does not run a real template engine for JSP, so check the view name; use @SpringBootTest to test real HTML output.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Template not found: wrong folder or suffix; Boot expects templates/name.html.
  • Resolver order: an internal resource resolver accepts every name and blocks later ones; give it the lowest priority.
  • Wrong path in JSP: files must be under WEB-INF to avoid direct access.
  • Disabled cache in production: slows every request.
  • Unescaped output: use the escaping attribute to prevent XSS.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rendering time often dominates a page request.

  • Template cache: keep it on in production.
  • Compression: enable server.compression.enabled for HTML.
  • Fragments: cache parts with a cache layer.
  • Avoid logic: keep heavy loops and queries out of templates.
  • Streaming: large output can be written in chunks.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=text/html,text/css,application/json

# OUTPUT:
# smaller responses and no repeated template parsing

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A storefront renders the same data as HTML for browsers and JSON for API clients.

  • Browser: view name plus model.
  • API: a separate @RestController path, or content negotiation.
  • Test: a full test checks the HTML title.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • View resolution is the step where Spring MVC turns the logical view name returned by a controller (such as "home") into a real View object that renders the response.
  • Who does it: the DispatcherServlet asks each registered ViewResolver in order until one returns a view.
  • Why it exists: controllers stay free of file paths and technology, so JSP can be swapped for Thymeleaf without touching them.

Worked Example 1

Test the logical view name with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Inspect the registered resolvers.

Practice Exercise 1

Return a logical name from a controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Write the name through ModelAndView.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

View resolution happens inside DispatcherServlet.render.

  • The handler adapter returns a ModelAndView (or the name is converted into one).
  • If the view is a name, resolveViewName loops through the viewResolvers list.
  • The first non-null View is used, otherwise a ServletException is thrown.
  • The locale from the LocaleResolver is passed to the resolver.
  • Finally view.render(model, request, response) writes the output.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to name a view:

  • String: return "home".
  • ModelAndView: a name plus model in one object.
  • View instance: skips resolution completely.
  • void: name derived from the URL path.
  • Prefixes: redirect: and forward:.
  • Bean name: BeanNameViewResolver finds a View bean with that name.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Flow: handler returns a name or ModelAndView, then resolveViewName, then view.render(model, request, response).
  • Order: resolvers are sorted by their order value, and the first non-null result wins.
  • No view name: if a handler returns void, the name is derived from the request URL by RequestToViewNameTranslator.

Senior Notes

  • Content negotiation: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver picks among candidate views by the requested media type.
  • Not for REST: with @ResponseBody or @RestController no view resolution happens; a message converter writes the body.
  • Failure mode: if no resolver finds a view you see a 404 or a ServletException: Could not resolve view.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical problems:

  • Circular view path: a controller mapped to /home returns "home" with no resolver prefix, so it forwards to itself.
  • Wrong order: a catch-all resolver placed first hides others.
  • Missing template: returns 404 or an error page.
  • @ResponseBody forgotten or added: a name is printed as text, or a page is expected but text arrives.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Resolvers cache created views by name and locale (cache limit 1024 by default).
  • Keep the number of resolvers small; each one is asked in turn.
  • Put cheap, specific resolvers first and the catch-all last.
  • Disable caching only in development.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=false

# OUTPUT:
# production: views and templates cached;
development: set cache=false

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin portal serves HTML pages, a PDF report and JSON from the same controller methods. A ContentNegotiatingViewResolver chooses the PDF view for .pdf requests and the HTML template otherwise, while REST endpoints use @ResponseBody and bypass views entirely.

  • Pages: Thymeleaf resolver.
  • Reports: bean-name resolver.
  • API: message converters.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ViewResolver is an interface with one method, View resolveViewName(String viewName, Locale locale), that returns a View or null.
  • Purpose: it decouples the controller from the view technology (JSP, Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, PDF).
  • With ModelAndView: the view name you put in ModelAndView is exactly the string given to the resolver.

Worked Example 1

Return a ModelAndView with a name and model.

Worked Example 2

Assert resolution with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

A tiny custom ViewResolver.

Practice Exercise 2

Register through configurer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The contract is small.

  • ViewResolver.resolveViewName(String, Locale) returns a View or null.
  • View.render(Map model, request, response) writes the response.
  • AbstractCachingViewResolver keeps a cache keyed by name and locale and calls loadView only on a miss.
  • UrlBasedViewResolver adds the prefix and suffix and handles redirect: and forward:.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common ModelAndView forms:

  • new ModelAndView("name").
  • new ModelAndView("name", "key", value) for one attribute.
  • new ModelAndView("name", map) for many.
  • new ModelAndView(view) for a ready View.
  • setStatus to change the HTTP status.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Null means pass: returning null lets the next resolver in the chain try.
  • View object: a controller can also set a concrete View in ModelAndView, which skips resolution.
  • Common types: InternalResourceViewResolver, ThymeleafViewResolver, BeanNameViewResolver, ContentNegotiatingViewResolver.

Senior Notes

  • Caching: AbstractCachingViewResolver caches views by name and locale; disable it in development.
  • Custom resolver: implement the interface and implement Ordered so it runs before the catch-all one.
  • Registration: expose a @Bean or use WebMvcConfigurer.configureViewResolvers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Returning null from a custom resolver for everything: no view is ever found.
  • Returning a View for every name: hides the resolvers after it.
  • Forgetting Ordered: custom resolver runs last, after the catch-all.
  • Mutating a cached View: views are shared between requests and must be thread-safe.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Leave caching on; it avoids creating views per request.
  • Raise setCacheLimit only if many distinct names exist.
  • Use setCache(false) only for dynamic names such as per-tenant views.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a multi-tenant portal shows the tenant theme by view name tenantA/home. A custom resolver maps the first path segment to a template directory and falls back to default/home when the tenant has no override.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • InternalResourceViewResolver maps a logical name to a server resource such as a JSP by adding a prefix and a suffix.
  • Example: prefix /WEB-INF/views/ plus name home plus suffix .jsp gives /WEB-INF/views/home.jsp.
  • Result: it creates an InternalResourceView (or JstlView when JSTL is on the classpath) that forwards to that path.

Worked Example 1

Test the forwarded URL.

Worked Example 2

Typical mistake: wrong prefix.

Practice Exercise 1

Java configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/
spring.mvc.view.suffix=.jsp

# OUTPUT:
# controller returns "home" -> Tomcat forwards to /WEB-INF/views/home.jsp

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it works:

  • It extends UrlBasedViewResolver; buildView sets the URL as prefix + name + suffix.
  • The created view is InternalResourceView, or JstlView when JSTL is present.
  • On render the view copies model entries to request attributes and calls RequestDispatcher.forward.
  • If the page was already included, it uses include instead.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • setPrefix, setSuffix.
  • setViewClass (JstlView).
  • setExposeContextBeansAsAttributes to read beans from EL.
  • setAlwaysInclude to use include.
  • setRequestContextAttribute to expose a RequestContext.
  • The registry shortcut registry.jsp(prefix, suffix).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Why WEB-INF: files under it cannot be requested directly by a browser, so pages are only reachable through controllers.
  • Boot properties: spring.mvc.view.prefix and spring.mvc.view.suffix configure it automatically.
  • Catch-all: it resolves any name, so it must be the last resolver in the chain.

Senior Notes

  • View class: setViewClass(JstlView.class) exposes JSTL locale and message bundles.
  • Packaging: JSP with embedded Tomcat needs war packaging or extra jasper libraries; Thymeleaf avoids this.
  • Missing page: a wrong path gives a 404 from the container, not a Spring exception.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Prefix without a trailing slash: add the slash.
  • Blank suffix and a name with an extension: be consistent.
  • Resolver placed before others: set the lowest priority.
  • Boot executable jar: JSP not found; use war or Thymeleaf.
  • Missing jasper: the JSP is downloaded as text or gives 404.
codeExamples:
# WRONG in a Boot jar: JSP files in src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/WEB-INF
# RIGHT: war packaging and src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/views

# OUTPUT:
# jar: 404 for every JSP;
war on external or embedded Tomcat: pages render

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • JSP compile cost occurs once per page; precompile (JspC) for production wars.
  • Disable development mode for Jasper so it does not poll for changes.
  • Keep pages small and move logic into the controller.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (embedded Tomcat with Jasper)
server.servlet.jsp.init-parameters.development=false
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/
spring.mvc.view.suffix=.jsp

# OUTPUT:
# Jasper no longer checks timestamps on each request

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy WAR with 200 JSPs migrates to Spring MVC. The team keeps all pages under /WEB-INF/views, configures a single InternalResourceViewResolver and moves scriptlet logic into controllers one page at a time, and later adds a Thymeleaf resolver with a lower order for new pages.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Redirect tells the browser to make a new request to another URL: the server answers with status 302 or 303 and a Location header.
  • Effect: the address bar changes and the model and request attributes are lost, because it is a brand new request.
  • Use it after a successful POST (Post-Redirect-Get) so that refreshing the page does not submit the form again.

Worked Example 1

Test the redirect with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: reading a model value after redirect.

Practice Exercise 1

Post-Redirect-Get with a flash message.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect with RedirectView.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internally:

  • RedirectView.renderMergedOutputModel builds the target URL, adds the context path and query parameters.
  • It then calls sendRedirect, which sets the status and Location header.
  • With RedirectAttributes, flash attributes are saved by FlashMapManager (in the session) and picked up by the next request that matches the target URL.
  • Flash maps expire after a short time.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • redirect:/path (302).
  • RedirectView with setStatusCode (301, 303, 307, 308).
  • ResponseEntity.status(...).location(uri).build().
  • HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect.
  • Use UriComponentsBuilder to build safe URLs.
  • redirect:/users/{id} expands path variables from the model.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Ways to redirect: return "redirect:/users", return a RedirectView, or return ResponseEntity with a Location header.
  • Flash attributes: RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute keeps a value for exactly one following request.
  • Path variables: addAttribute adds values to the redirect URL as query parameters.

Senior Notes

  • Exposed model: Spring may append simple model attributes to the redirect URL; set ignoreDefaultModelOnRedirect=true to stop that.
  • Status code: 303 See Other is the cleanest for POST redirects; 302 is the default of redirect:.
  • Open redirect: never redirect to a URL taken from user input without validating it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Model data after redirect: use flash attributes.
  • Using redirect for an API: clients may not follow it; return 201 with Location.
  • Open redirect: check the target against an allow list.
  • Redirect loop: redirecting to a URL that redirects back.
  • Relative URL surprises: start with a slash.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Costs and tuning:

  • A redirect adds one round trip, so use forward for purely internal routing.
  • 301 and 308 are cached by browsers; 302 and 303 are not.
  • Flash attributes use the session, which affects clustered setups (use sticky sessions or shared sessions).
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.ignore-default-model-on-redirect=true

# OUTPUT:
# redirect URLs no longer carry model attributes as query parameters

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a checkout form posts an order. The controller saves it, then redirects to the order confirmation page with a flash message, so a browser refresh shows the confirmation again instead of creating a duplicate order.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Forward hands the same request to another resource on the server, using RequestDispatcher.forward; the browser does not know it happened.
  • Effect: the URL in the address bar stays the same, and request attributes and the model are still available.
  • Use it to reuse another handler, or to render a JSP, without an extra round trip.

Worked Example 1

Test the forward with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: forward after commit.

Practice Exercise 1

Forward to another handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Forward with the servlet API.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a forward works:

  • RequestDispatcher.forward resets the response buffer and dispatches inside the container.
  • The request path attributes (jakarta.servlet.forward.request_uri and others) keep the original URL.
  • Filters registered for DispatcherType.FORWARD run; others skip it.
  • Spring handles forward: by creating an InternalResourceView.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • return "forward:/path".
  • request.getRequestDispatcher(path).forward.
  • include merges the output of another resource.
  • The ViewControllerRegistry.addViewController("/x").setViewName("forward:/y") shortcut.
  • @RequestAttribute reads the data set before forwarding.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Same request: there is only one HTTP request, so the forwarded target sees the same parameters and attributes.
  • Server-side only: a forward cannot go to another application or external site.
  • Default for views: InternalResourceView renders a JSP by forwarding to it.

Senior Notes

  • Refresh problem: after a forwarded POST a browser refresh submits the form again, unlike with a redirect.
  • Dispatcher type: filters can be registered for FORWARD dispatches separately from REQUEST.
  • Response committed: a forward fails with IllegalStateException if the response is already committed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forward after POST: refresh repeats it; use redirect.
  • Forward loop: check the target mapping.
  • Forward after writing output: response is committed.
  • Assuming a new request: request-scoped data is shared.
  • Forward to a path blocked by security: the filter may apply again.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: a forward is cheaper than a redirect because there is no extra browser round trip, and the request object, parameters and body are reused. Use it for internal routing and error handling, and keep chains short because each forward re-enters the filter and handler pipeline.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the root URL / shows the home page without a redirect, so the address bar stays clean. A view controller forwards / to /home, and a custom error page forwards 404 requests to a friendly template.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • redirect: is a prefix on a view name, as in new ModelAndView("redirect:/users"); Spring turns it into a RedirectView.
  • Handled by UrlBasedViewResolver (and its subclasses), which checks the prefix before applying prefix and suffix.
  • Result: an HTTP 302 response with a Location header; no template is rendered.

Worked Example 1

Disable model exposure.

Worked Example 2

Test it.

Practice Exercise 1

ModelAndView with redirect:.

Practice Exercise 2

Model attributes become query parameters.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Under the hood:

  • UrlBasedViewResolver.createView checks viewName.startsWith("redirect:").
  • It strips the prefix and builds a RedirectView with contextRelative=true and http10Compatible set from the resolver.
  • The RedirectView expands URI template variables from the model, appends remaining simple attributes as query parameters, then encodes and sends the redirect.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants:

  • redirect:/abs context relative.
  • redirect:rel relative to the current URL.
  • redirect:http://host/x absolute.
  • redirect:/users/{id} template variable filled from the model.
  • redirect:/list?x=1 with a manual query string.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Context path: a path beginning with / is relative to the application context, so the context path is added automatically.
  • Model to query: with ModelAndView, model attributes of simple types are appended to the URL as query parameters.
  • Absolute URL: redirect:https://example.com redirects outside the app.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid exposing data: call setExposeModelAttributes(false) on RedirectView or use RedirectAttributes instead of a bare model.
  • Relative paths: redirect:list resolves relative to the current request URL, which surprises many developers.
  • Status: to get 301 or 303 use a RedirectView with setStatusCode.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Relative path without slash: resolves against the current URL.
  • Large model: non-simple objects are skipped, but strings can make URLs very long.
  • Forgetting the status: redirect: always gives 302.
  • User data in the query: sensitive values appear in logs and history.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: avoid query strings from large models; set ignoreDefaultModelOnRedirect; use 303 for POST responses and 301 or 308 only for permanent moves, because browsers cache them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy URL scheme moves from /items?id=5 to /products/5. A controller keeps the old URL working with a permanent redirect so search engines update their links.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • forward: is a prefix on a view name, as in new ModelAndView("forward:/home"); Spring creates an InternalResourceView that forwards the request.
  • Handled by UrlBasedViewResolver, which detects the prefix before adding the configured prefix and suffix.
  • Result: the same request is dispatched to another path, and the model is exposed as request attributes.

Worked Example 1

Test the forward.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: forward loop.

Practice Exercise 1

ModelAndView with forward:.

Practice Exercise 2

Target controller reads the attribute.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Under the hood:

  • UrlBasedViewResolver.createView checks viewName.startsWith("forward:").
  • It strips the prefix and builds an InternalResourceView for the remaining URL.
  • When rendered, the model is exposed as request attributes and forward is called.
  • The prefix and suffix of the resolver are not applied to a forward: name.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • forward:/path to a controller or resource.
  • forward:/WEB-INF/views/x.jsp straight to a JSP.
  • Use a ModelAndView to pass data as request attributes.
  • Use RedirectView instead for an outside URL.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Target: any path the container can dispatch to, including another controller mapping or a JSP.
  • Model: model entries are copied to request attributes, so the target can read them with request.getAttribute.
  • URL unchanged: the browser still shows the original address.

Senior Notes

  • Re-entering the DispatcherServlet: forwarding to a controller path runs the handler mapping again, including filters set for FORWARD.
  • Loops: forwarding to the same path leads to an infinite loop and a stack overflow or container error.
  • Prefer redirect after POST; use forward for internal routing and error pages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Expecting prefix and suffix: they are skipped.
  • Expecting a new request: POST body and method stay the same, so the target must accept that method.
  • Forward loops.
  • Using forward: to external URLs: not possible.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: forwards avoid network round trips, but each one passes through the dispatcher pipeline again. Keep the chain to one hop, and avoid forwarding large uploaded request bodies repeatedly.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a front controller inspects the request and forwards to a handler by device type, for example forward:/m/home for mobile clients, keeping one public URL.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSP (Jakarta Server Pages) is a template technology where HTML mixes with tags and Expression Language; the container compiles each page into a servlet on first use.
  • In Spring MVC the controller returns a logical name, InternalResourceViewResolver maps it to the JSP, and the JSP renders the model.
  • Location: keep pages under /WEB-INF/views/ so they are only reachable through controllers.

Worked Example 1

Test the view name (JSP is not rendered by MockMvc).

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: unescaped output.
codeExamples:
<%-- unsafe: the value is written as raw HTML --%>

Hi ${param.name}

<%-- safe --%>

Hi

// OUTPUT: // ?name=

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Controller and JSP.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot dependencies for JSP.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml: packaging war -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.tomcat.embed</groupId>
    <artifactId>tomcat-embed-jasper</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

// OUTPUT:
// JSP pages under src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/views are compiled and served by Tomcat

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Lifecycle of a JSP:

  • Jasper translates greet.jsp to a servlet class (greet_jsp.java) and compiles it.
  • The container loads the servlet and calls _jspService per request.
  • Spring forwards to the JSP, so request attributes hold the model.
  • Template text is written with out.write and EL is evaluated by the EL resolver.
codeExamples:
<%-- greet.jsp --%> <%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>

Hello,

// OUTPUT: // generated servlet: greet_jsp._jspService(request, response) writes the HTML

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features:

  • Directives: page, include, taglib.
  • EL: expressions for model data.
  • Standard actions: jsp:include.
  • Tag files and custom tags for reuse.
  • Spring tags: spring:message, spring:url, form tags.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="form" uri="jakarta.tags.form" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="spring" uri="jakarta.tags.spring" %>
<form:form modelAttribute="user" method="post">
  <spring:message code="user.name"/>
  <form:input path="name"/> <form:errors path="name"/>
  <button>Save</button>
</form:form>

// OUTPUT:
// <form method="post"> ... <input name="name" value="..."/> ... error message if invalid

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Model access: model attributes are request attributes, so a JSP reads them with Expression Language.
  • Tags: use JSTL and the Spring form tag library instead of scriptlets (<% %> Java code).
  • Spring Boot: embedded Tomcat needs tomcat-embed-jasper and war packaging; JSP is not supported in executable jars.

Senior Notes

  • Compile step: the first request of a JSP is slower because Jasper translates and compiles it.
  • Security: output must be escaped with c:out or fn:escapeXml to prevent XSS.
  • Limits: JSPs are not natural templates and are hard to test, which is why many teams move to Thymeleaf.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Scriptlets: use EL and JSTL instead.
  • Unescaped output: XSS risk.
  • JSP in a Boot jar: not served.
  • Missing taglib directive: tags print as text.
  • Database access from a JSP: belongs in the service layer.
codeExamples:
<%-- WRONG: logic in the page --%>
<% List<User> us = new UserDao().findAll();
%>
<%-- RIGHT: controller adds users to the model, page only displays --%>

// OUTPUT:
// untestable page with SQL access; fix by moving logic to controller and service

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Precompile JSPs at build time (JspC) to avoid first-request delay.
  • Turn off development mode in production.
  • Use <%@ page session="false" %> when the page needs no session.
  • Avoid huge pages; split with jsp:include.
codeExamples:
<%@ page session="false" trimDirectiveWhitespaces="true" %>

// OUTPUT:
// no HttpSession is created just for rendering, and blank lines from directives are removed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an intranet app has existing JSP pages. Controllers prepare data, JSPs show it with JSTL, a shared header uses jsp:include, and the war is deployed to Tomcat. New features use Thymeleaf so the team can leave JSP gradually.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSTL (Jakarta Standard Tag Library) is a set of tags for JSP that replace scriptlets: c:if, c:forEach, c:out, fmt:formatDate.
  • Declare it at the top of the page with a taglib directive, usually with the prefix c for the core library.
  • Why: logic like loops and conditions stays readable and free of Java code in the page.

Worked Example 1

Controller feeding the page, tested with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: old taglib URI.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core" %>

// OUTPUT:
// Works only with the old javax JSTL; with Spring 6 use uri="jakarta.tags.core"

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Loop over a list.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
// OUTPUT: //
  • Abaji
  • Raoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Condition and empty check.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<c:choose>
  <c:when test="${empty users}
">No users found</c:when>
  <c:otherwise>Total: <c:out value="${users.size()}
"/></c:otherwise>
</c:choose>

// OUTPUT:
// Total: 2   (or "No users found" for an empty list)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How JSTL works:

  • The taglib directive maps a prefix to a TLD (tag library descriptor) inside the JSTL jar.
  • Jasper turns each tag into calls on a tag handler class (for example ForEachTag).
  • Tag attributes use EL, evaluated against page, request, session and application scopes.
  • c:out calls an escape routine, so characters such as < become <.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>

// OUTPUT: //

a < b

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Libraries and URIs (Jakarta EE 10):

  • core: jakarta.tags.core, prefix c.
  • fmt: jakarta.tags.fmt, numbers, dates, messages.
  • fn: jakarta.tags.functions, string and collection functions.
  • sql and xml: exist but are discouraged.
codeExamples:
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="fmt" uri="jakarta.tags.fmt" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="fn" uri="jakarta.tags.functions" %>
<fmt:formatNumber value="${price}
" type="currency" currencyCode="INR"/>
<c:out value="${fn:toUpperCase(name)}
"/>
<c:url value="/orders" var="ordersUrl"/>

// OUTPUT:
// price=1999.5 name=abaji -> "₹1,999.50 ABAJI", ordersUrl=/shop/orders

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Core tags: c:out (escapes output), c:if, c:choose, c:forEach, c:url, c:set.
  • Other libraries: fmt for numbers, dates and messages; fn for string functions.
  • Dependency: add the Jakarta JSTL API and implementation; the URI for Jakarta EE 10 is jakarta.tags.core.

Senior Notes

  • Escaping: c:out escapes XML characters by default, which protects against XSS.
  • Scopes: tags read page, request, session and application attributes in that order of lookup.
  • JstlView: with InternalResourceViewResolver and JstlView the JSTL locale and message bundles follow Spring.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Old URI: http://java.sun.com/... with Jakarta servlets.
  • Mixing javax and jakarta JSTL jars: tags fail to load.
  • Raw EL output: no escaping.
  • Missing JSTL jar: The absolute uri cannot be resolved.
  • Using c:forEach on a null: prints nothing; check with empty.
codeExamples:
<%-- error when the JSTL jar is missing --%>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>

// OUTPUT:
// org.apache.jasper.JasperException: The absolute uri: [jakarta.tags.core] cannot be resolved
// Fix: add org.glassfish.web:jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl and jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl-api

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use varStatus instead of manual counters.
  • Use begin, end and step for paging instead of looping all items.
  • Do not call methods with side effects from EL.
  • Prepare data in the controller; keep loops short.
codeExamples: <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> // OUTPUT: // first ten rows with alternating row classes

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order list page shows rows with a currency format, an empty-state message and a link per row built with c:url, so the context path is always correct.
codeExamples: <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> <%@ taglib prefix="fmt" uri="jakarta.tags.fmt" %> # // OUTPUT: // #17 $120.00 (link /shop/orders/17)

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Thymeleaf is a server-side template engine that writes logic as HTML attributes such as th:text and th:each, so templates open correctly in a browser.
  • In Spring MVC the controller returns a name, ThymeleafViewResolver finds templates/name.html and renders it with the model.
  • Spring Boot auto-configures it when spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf is on the classpath, with no extra setup.

Worked Example 1

Test the model and view.

Worked Example 2

Pitfall: unescaped user text.
codeExamples:
x

x

// OUTPUT: // comment=hi: first line shows bold text (XSS risk), second shows the tags as text

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Controller and template.

Practice Exercise 2

Starter and properties.
codeExamples:
# build.gradle: implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf'
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=false
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/templates/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html

# OUTPUT:
# templates are reloaded on every request (development setting)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the integration works:

  • ThymeleafAutoConfiguration creates SpringResourceTemplateResolver, SpringTemplateEngine and ThymeleafViewResolver.
  • The resolver returns a ThymeleafView for a name (it must be before the default resolver in order).
  • On render, the model plus request data become a Thymeleaf Context.
  • The engine parses the template, runs attribute processors in order and writes the result.
  • Spring expressions (SpEL) are used for variable expressions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common syntax:

  • th:text, th:utext, th:value, th:href.
  • th:each, th:if, th:unless, th:switch.
  • th:object and th:field for forms.
  • th:fragment and th:replace for layouts.
  • Message expressions read messages.properties.
codeExamples:
Title

All users
error
// OUTPUT: //

User Manager

All users

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Default location: src/main/resources/templates/ with the suffix .html.
  • Key attributes: th:text (escaped), th:utext (not escaped), th:each, th:if, th:href with @{...} link expressions.
  • Expression types: variable expressions (dollar sign and braces), selection, message (#{...}), link (@{...}) and fragment (~{...}).

Senior Notes

  • Natural templates: the static text inside a tag is a prototype shown when the file is opened directly, and replaced when rendered.
  • Escaping: th:text escapes HTML by default; use th:utext only for trusted content.
  • Caching: set spring.thymeleaf.cache=false in development to see changes without restart.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Template not found: wrong folder or name (error TemplateInputException).
  • Missing @Controller: using @RestController returns the name as text.
  • th:utext with user input.
  • Null property access: use ?. safe navigation.
  • Case-sensitive file names on Linux servers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep template caching on in production.
  • Use fragments to reuse markup instead of repeating it.
  • Avoid heavy logic and database calls in expressions.
  • Use spring.thymeleaf.cache=false only for development.
  • Enable HTTP caching for static assets, not for rendered pages with user data.
codeExamples:
# application-dev.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=false
spring.web.resources.cache.period=0

# application-prod.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.web.resources.cache.period=86400

# OUTPUT:
# dev: changes visible on browser refresh;
prod: parsed templates are reused

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a company site renders product pages on the server for search engines. Controllers add a product to the model, the template shows it, and a shared layout fragment supplies header and footer. Security expressions and form binding work through the same engine.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • FreeMarker is a server-side template engine: you write a .ftlh file with placeholders and directives, and Spring MVC merges it with the model into HTML.
  • Setup: add spring-boot-starter-freemarker; templates live in src/main/resources/templates and the controller returns the view name without the suffix.
  • Directives start with <#, for example <#list items as i>, <#if> and <#include>; user macros use <@name/>.

Worked Example 1

A reusable macro.
codeExamples: <#-- templates/macros.ftlh --> <#macro badge text> ${text} <#-- templates/page.ftlh --> <#import "macros.ftlh" as m> <@m.badge text="New"/> // New

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Escaping on .ftlh.

Practice Exercise 1

Create the starter page: a controller that fills the model and a template that lists names.

Practice Exercise 2

Show a default when a value is missing.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

FreeMarker renders in two phases: parse the template once into an object tree, then process it with a data model.

  • Config: Boot creates a FreeMarkerConfigurer that owns the FreeMarker Configuration and the template loader path.
  • Resolver: FreeMarkerViewResolver builds a FreeMarkerView for a view name plus the suffix.
  • Render: the view merges model, request and session attributes, then calls template.process on the response writer.
  • Cache: parsed templates are cached and refreshed after templateUpdateDelay in development.
codeExamples:
# Boot auto-configuration (FreeMarkerAutoConfiguration) in short:
# 1. FreeMarkerConfigurer  -> Configuration, loader path classpath:/templates/
# 2. FreeMarkerViewResolver -> suffix .ftlh, content type text/html
# 3. view.render(model) -> template.process(model, response.getWriter())

# OUTPUT:
# "hello" -> templates/hello.ftlh -> HTML written to the response

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options and syntax:

  • Properties: spring.freemarker.suffix, template-loader-path, cache, charset, settings.*.
  • Directives: list, if/elseif/else, assign, macro, import, include.
  • Built-ins: ?upper_case, ?size, ?string("0.00"), ?date, ?has_content.
  • Request data: enable expose-request-attributes and expose-session-attributes when needed.
codeExamples:
<#assign total = 0> <#list items as i> <#assign total = total + i.price>

${i.name?upper_case} -${i.price?string("0.00")}

<#if items?has_content>Total ${total?string("0.00")} <#else>Empty # OUTPUT: #

PEN - 2.50

#

BOOK - 10.00

# Total 12.50

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Auto-escaping: the .ftlh extension turns on HTML escaping for interpolations, so user text is safe by default; the older .ftl does not escape.
  • Beans: Boot configures FreeMarkerConfigurer (loads templates) and FreeMarkerViewResolver (maps view names to templates); both can be tuned with spring.freemarker.*.
  • Null handling: a missing value fails the render unless you write a default, as in name!"guest", or test with name??.

Senior Notes

  • Caching: FreeMarker caches parsed templates; in production keep spring.freemarker.cache=true and turn it off only in development.
  • Security: never use ?no_esc on user data and avoid exposing the whole Configuration to templates, because template authors could then reach internals.
  • Choosing: FreeMarker has richer logic (macros, functions, built-ins) than Mustache, but Thymeleaf keeps templates valid HTML, which is why it is the Boot default choice.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing variable: an undefined name stops rendering; use ! or ??.
  • Wrong extension: .ftl gives no escaping, so XSS is possible; use .ftlh.
  • Suffix in the view name: returning "hello.ftlh" looks for hello.ftlh.ftlh.
  • Number formatting: 1,234 is printed by default; use ?c for machine output such as ids.
  • Entity access: lazy collections in templates fail after the session is closed; map to DTOs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cache on: parsing is the expensive part, so keep spring.freemarker.cache=true in production.
  • Keep logic out: prepare totals and flags in Java instead of heavy template computation.
  • Output size: add <#compress> or enable gzip compression at the server.
  • Fail fast: set template_exception_handler=rethrow so errors give a clear 500, not half a page.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (production)
spring.freemarker.cache=true
spring.freemarker.settings.template_exception_handler=rethrow
spring.freemarker.settings.number_format=0.##
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Templates parsed once;
errors surface as a 500 with a stack trace in the log.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order confirmation page and an invoice email share the same engine.

  • The same FreeMarker Configuration renders the web page and an HTML email.
  • A shared macro file keeps the address and price blocks identical.
  • A MockMvc test checks the page; a unit test processes the email template with a sample model.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Mustache is a logic-less template engine: templates contain only tags such as {{name}} and sections, no real code.
  • Setup: add spring-boot-starter-mustache; templates go in templates/ with the .mustache suffix and the controller returns the name without it.
  • Tags: {{name}} prints an escaped value, {{{html}}} prints raw, {{#list}}...{{/list}} loops, and {{^list}}...{{/list}} shows when empty.

Worked Example 1

Partials for a shared header.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Mustache templates are compiled by JMustache into a tree of text and tag nodes.

  • Config: MustacheAutoConfiguration creates a Mustache.Compiler and a MustacheViewResolver.
  • Lookup: a name is searched in the current context, then its parents, then the model map.
  • Sections: a collection repeats, a boolean true shows once, false or empty hides, and an object becomes the new context.
  • Output: the compiled template executes against the model and writes to the response.
codeExamples:
# MustacheAutoConfiguration in short:
# Mustache.Compiler (JMustache) + TemplateLoader classpath:/templates/
# MustacheViewResolver -> suffix .mustache

# OUTPUT:
# "users" -> templates/users.mustache compiled once, executed per request

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax summary:

  • Variable: {{name}} escaped, {{{name}}} or {{&name}} raw.
  • Section: {{#x}}...{{/x}}; inverted {{^x}}...{{/x}}.
  • Partial: {{> file}}.
  • Comment: {{! note }}.
  • Dot: {{.}} is the current item in a list of simple values.
codeExamples:
{{! a comment, not printed }}
    { {#tags} }
  • { {.} }
    • { {/tags} }
{{^tags}}No tags { {/tags} } // OUTPUT: //

  • spring

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Escaping: double braces escape HTML; triple braces do not, so use them only for trusted markup.
  • Context lookup: inside a section the current item becomes the context, and Mustache falls back to the parent context when a name is not found.
  • Partials: {{> header}} includes header.mustache, which is the basis for layouts.

Senior Notes

  • Logic-less by design: conditions and formatting must be prepared in Java (view model or DTO), which keeps templates simple and testable.
  • Engine: Boot uses JMustache; settings live under spring.mustache.*, for example suffix and servlet.expose-request-attributes.
  • Trade-off: tiny and fast, and the same syntax works in JavaScript, but there are no expressions, so complex pages need more view-model code.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing key: JMustache throws for an undefined variable by default; set spring.mustache.check-template-location and provide defaults in the model, or configure the compiler to default to empty.
  • Wanting if/else: compute a boolean in Java and use a section.
  • Raw output of user text: triple braces open an XSS hole.
  • Formatting dates: format in Java; there are no functions in templates.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cheap: compilation is quick and the compiled template is cached.
  • Small models: pass flat records so lookups stay short.
  • Dev reload: set spring.mustache.servlet.cache=false only while developing.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mustache.servlet.cache=true
spring.mustache.suffix=.mustache
spring.mustache.servlet.expose-request-attributes=false

# OUTPUT:
# Templates are compiled once and reused for every request.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a small status page that must also render in a JavaScript front end.

  • The same .mustache file is used on the server and in the browser.
  • Java prepares a view record with labels and flags.
  • A MockMvc test checks the HTML for each state.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTML template: an HTML file with placeholders that Spring MVC fills with model data on the server before sending the page to the browser.
  • Flow: the controller returns a view name, the ViewResolver finds the template, and the engine renders it with the Model.
  • Engines: Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, Mustache and JSP all plug into the same flow; only the template syntax differs.

Worked Example 1

Test the view.

Worked Example 2

Conditional markup.

Practice Exercise 1

Render a greeting with Thymeleaf.

Practice Exercise 2

Iterate a list.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Rendering an HTML template involves several Spring components.

  • DispatcherServlet: finds the handler, runs it and receives the view name and model.
  • ViewResolver: turns the name into a View.
  • View.render: the engine merges the model into the template and writes to the response.
  • Boot: the matching auto-configuration (Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, Mustache) registers the resolver when its library is on the classpath.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to supply model data:

  • Model parameter: model.addAttribute.
  • ModelAndView: return view and data together.
  • @ModelAttribute method: data added for every handler in the controller.
  • @ControllerAdvice: data shared by all controllers, such as the current user.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Model data: Model, ModelMap and ModelAndView carry attributes to the template; @ModelAttribute methods add shared data.
  • Natural templates: Thymeleaf pages open correctly in a browser without a server because directives are attributes, such as th:text.
  • Location: Boot reads templates from classpath:/templates/; the path is not served directly, only through a controller.

Senior Notes

  • Escaping: use the escaping output form (th:text) for user data; unescaped output (th:utext) is an XSS risk.
  • Caching: set spring.thymeleaf.cache=false only in development; production keeps parsed templates in memory.
  • Separation: pass small view objects to the template instead of entities, so lazy loading and sensitive fields never leak into rendering.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forgetting @Controller: @RestController writes the view name as text.
  • Template in wrong folder: a 500 with TemplateInputException.
  • th:utext with user data: XSS risk.
  • Entities with lazy fields: LazyInitializationException during render.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Keep template caching on in production.
  • Avoid database calls inside templates; load data in the service layer.
  • Enable gzip and long cache headers for assets, not for dynamic pages.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=text/html,text/css,application/javascript

# OUTPUT:
# HTML responses are compressed;
template parsing happens once.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a product list page.

  • The service returns a list of small view records.
  • The controller adds it to the model and returns the view name.
  • A @WebMvcTest with a mocked service checks the HTML.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Static HTML is a plain file served as it is, with no model and no rendering; Boot serves such files from src/main/resources/static.
  • URL mapping: static/about.html is reachable at /about.html; the folder name is not part of the URL.
  • Welcome page: an index.html in a static folder answers the root URL /.

Worked Example 2

# application.properties
spring.mvc.static-path-pattern=/assets/**
spring.web.resources.static-locations=classpath:/static/

# OUTPUT:

# GET /css/app.css        -> 404

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Static files are served by a resource handler, not by controllers.

  • Registration: WebMvcAutoConfiguration adds a ResourceHttpRequestHandler for /** with the static locations.
  • Order: RequestMappingHandlerMapping is asked first; the resource mapping has the lowest priority.
  • Response: the handler resolves the file, sets content type, Last-Modified and ETag, and supports conditional requests (304).
  • Welcome page: WelcomePageHandlerMapping maps / to index.html or an index template.
codeExamples:
# Request flow for GET /css/app.css
# 1. RequestMappingHandlerMapping -> no controller matches
# 2. SimpleUrlHandlerMapping(/**) -> ResourceHttpRequestHandler
# 3. found classpath:/static/css/app.css -> 200 + ETag

# OUTPUT:
# HTTP/1.1 200
# Content-Type: text/css
# ETag: "0a1b2c" (varies)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Folders: spring.web.resources.static-locations.
  • Prefix: spring.mvc.static-path-pattern.
  • Caching: spring.web.resources.cache.period and cachecontrol.*.
  • Versioning: spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.enabled=true.
  • Disable: spring.web.resources.add-mappings=false for an API-only app.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=7d
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.enabled=true
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.paths=/**

# OUTPUT:
# Cache-Control: max-age=604800 on static responses

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Locations: Boot checks /static, /public, /resources and /META-INF/resources on the classpath.
  • Handler: ResourceHttpRequestHandler serves these files, after controllers had no matching mapping.
  • Static or template: use static for fixed pages, CSS, JS and images; use a template when the page needs model data.

Senior Notes

  • Caching: set spring.web.resources.cache.period or use versioned URLs with ResourceUrlProvider so browsers cache assets safely.
  • Custom mapping: spring.mvc.static-path-pattern and spring.web.resources.static-locations change the URL prefix and folders.
  • Security: Spring Security protects static files too, so permit /css/** and /js/** explicitly for a login page.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • /static in the URL: the folder name is not part of the path.
  • Static file in templates folder: it is not served directly.
  • Stale cache after deploy: use content-versioned URLs.
  • Security blocks CSS: permit the asset paths on the login page.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Long cache periods plus content hashes in the URL.
  • Serve big assets through a CDN or reverse proxy such as nginx.
  • Enable compression for text assets.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.min-response-size=1024
spring.web.resources.cache.period=365d

# OUTPUT:
# Browser reuses assets for a year;
URL changes when content changes.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a marketing landing page next to a dynamic app.

  • static/index.html is the public home page.
  • Dynamic pages use templates and controllers.
  • Assets are versioned and cached, and a test confirms the welcome page.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Template resolution is the step that turns the view name returned by a controller into a real template file.
  • Two steps: Spring MVC first picks a ViewResolver to create a View, then the engine finds the template file using prefix and suffix.
  • Defaults: for Thymeleaf in Boot, prefix classpath:/templates/ and suffix .html, so "home" becomes templates/home.html.

Worked Example 1

Render one fragment only.

Worked Example 2

Test the resolved view.

Practice Exercise 1

See how names map to files.

Practice Exercise 2

Customize prefix and suffix.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/views/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html

# OUTPUT:
# return "home" -> classpath:/views/home.html

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution happens in two layers.

  • Spring layer: DispatcherServlet.resolveViewName loops over viewResolvers sorted by order.
  • Engine layer: for Thymeleaf, ThymeleafViewResolver makes a ThymeleafView; SpringResourceTemplateResolver adds prefix and suffix and loads the resource.
  • Special names: redirect: and forward: are handled before the engine.
  • Default order: content negotiation, bean name, then the engine resolvers.
codeExamples:
# resolveViewName("admin/list")
# ContentNegotiatingViewResolver -> asks the others
# BeanNameViewResolver           -> no bean named admin/list
# ThymeleafViewResolver          -> templates/admin/list.html

# OUTPUT:
# View: ThymeleafView[admin/list]

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Plain MVC: InternalResourceViewResolver with prefix /WEB-INF/views/ and suffix .jsp.
  • Fragments: name :: fragment or a selector like name :: #id.
  • Custom view: a bean implementing View found by BeanNameViewResolver.
  • Order: spring.thymeleaf.servlet.produce-partial-output-while-processing and resolver setOrder for tuning.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Resolver chain: DispatcherServlet asks each ViewResolver in order; the first one that returns a view wins.
  • Prefixes: redirect:/x sends a 302 and forward:/x forwards inside the server; both skip template lookup.
  • No view name: a void handler gets a name from the URL through RequestToViewNameTranslator, which is a common surprise.

Senior Notes

  • Ordering: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver comes first and asks the others; set order when you add several engines.
  • Thymeleaf inside: SpringResourceTemplateResolver loads the file, and fragment expressions such as "page :: part" render only a piece.
  • Failure: a missing template ends in TemplateInputException and a 500 page, so cover each view name with a MockMvc test.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Leading slash or suffix in the name: "/home.html" misses the file.
  • Void handler: the view name comes from the URL, which may not exist.
  • Wrong case: file lookups are case sensitive on Linux.
  • Resolver order clash: a catch-all resolver (JSP) swallows names meant for another engine.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Resolved views are cached by ViewResolver cache (setCache, default on).
  • Fewer resolvers means fewer lookups per request.
  • Use spring.thymeleaf.check-template-location=true to fail early in development.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.check-template-location=true
spring.thymeleaf.view-names=pages/*,admin/*

# OUTPUT:
# Only names under pages/ and admin/ are handled by Thymeleaf.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: migrating a legacy JSP area while new pages use Thymeleaf.

  • Thymeleaf handles view-names=new/*.
  • The JSP resolver has a higher order number and takes the rest.
  • Tests assert view().name() for both groups.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Layout: a shared page frame (header, menu, footer) written once and reused by every page, so you do not copy markup.
  • Thymeleaf fragments: define with th:fragment="header" and use with th:replace or th:insert.
  • Other engines: FreeMarker uses <#include> and macros, and Mustache uses partials such as {{> header}}.

Worked Example 1

codeExamples:
<!-- templates/base.html -->
<html xmlns:layout="http://www.ultraq.net.nz/thymeleaf/layout">
<body>
  <header>My App</header>
  <section layout:fragment="content">default</section>
</body></html>
<!-- templates/page.html -->
<html layout:decorate="~{base}">
<body><section layout:fragment="content">Page body</section></body>
</html>

// OUTPUT:
// <header>My App</header><section>Page body</section>

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Fragments are resolved at render time by the engine.

  • Expression: ~{file :: name} loads another template and selects the element with a matching th:fragment or id.
  • replace: the host element is removed and the fragment takes its place.
  • Layout dialect: the decorator page is processed first, then the content page fills the slots of the base.
  • Caching: each template file is parsed once; fragment selection runs per request.
codeExamples:
(c) Shop
//
(c) Shop

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Layout techniques:

  • Fragment with content: pass markup as a parameter using a fragment expression.
  • Optional parameters: use th:with or null checks.
  • Head merging: layout:title-pattern builds page titles.
  • FreeMarker: <#macro layout><#nested></#macro> wraps page content.
codeExamples:
<!-- layout.ftlh -->
<#macro page title>
<html><head><title>${title}
</title></head>
<body><header>Shop</header><#nested><footer>2026</footer></body></html>
</#macro>
<!-- page.ftlh -->
<#import "layout.ftlh" as l>
<@l.page title="Home">Welcome</@l.page>

// OUTPUT:
// <title>Home</title> ... <header>Shop</header>Welcome<footer>2026</footer>

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • replace or insert: th:replace swaps the host tag with the fragment; th:insert puts the fragment inside the host tag.
  • Parameters: a fragment can take arguments, as in th:fragment="nav(active)", to highlight the current menu item.
  • Layout dialect: the thymeleaf-layout-dialect library adds layout:decorate, so a page fills the slots of a base layout.

Senior Notes

  • Content slots: pass the page body as a fragment parameter or use the layout dialect, so one base template controls head, scripts and footer.
  • Cost: each fragment lookup is parsed once and cached; deep nesting is cheap, but a missing fragment fails at render time, not at startup.
  • Testing: assert that shared markup (for example the nav) appears in the response of several pages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong path: ~{fragments :: header} without the folder if the file is in a subfolder.
  • Fragment name typo: fails only at render time.
  • replace versus insert: an extra wrapper tag appears when you use insert by mistake.
  • Missing dialect dependency: layout:decorate is ignored without the library.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Fragments cost almost nothing once templates are cached.
  • Do not call services from fragments; pass data in the model.
  • Cache rarely changing fragments such as the footer with an HTTP cache if the whole page is static.
codeExamples:
# production settings
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Layout and fragments are parsed once and reused.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin portal with 30 pages.

  • One base.html holds the head, menu and scripts.
  • Each page only supplies its content slot and title.
  • A test checks that the menu appears on several pages.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form binding copies the submitted form fields into the properties of a Java object, so you work with an object instead of many strings.
  • How: the field name must match the property name; a field email is set through setEmail on the @ModelAttribute object.
  • Both ways: on GET the object is put in the model to fill the form; on POST Spring creates it from the request and passes it to the handler.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Handle a conversion error.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

The Thymeleaf side.
codeExamples:
<form th:object="${registerForm}
" th:action="@{/register}
" method="post">
  <input type="text" th:field="*{name}">
  <input type="number" th:field="*{age}">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// <input type="text" id="name" name="name" value="">

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Binding is performed by a WebDataBinder for each request.

  • Argument resolver: ModelAttributeMethodProcessor creates the object (or takes it from the model), then calls binder.bind(request).
  • Property access: request parameters are matched to bean properties, including nested ones like address.city.
  • Conversion: ConversionService converts strings; failures add a FieldError with code typeMismatch.
  • Validation: if @Valid is present, the validator runs after binding.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Binding options:

  • Formats: @DateTimeFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd"), @NumberFormat.
  • Custom type: register a Converter or Formatter in WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters.
  • Lists: repeated names or indexed names such as items[0].name.
  • Binder rules: @InitBinder with allowed, disallowed and required fields.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Thymeleaf: th:object names the form bean, and th:field="*{email}" sets id, name and value in one step.
  • Conversion: strings become numbers, dates and enums using converters and formatters; @DateTimeFormat controls date patterns.
  • Errors: a failed conversion or validation is stored in BindingResult, which must come right after the bound parameter.

Senior Notes

  • Mass assignment: a client can post extra fields such as admin=true; bind to a form class (DTO) or restrict with @InitBinder and setAllowedFields.
  • Engine: WebDataBinder does the work using ConversionService; custom types need a Converter or Formatter.
  • Empty strings: register StringTrimmerEditor(true) so blank input becomes null and validation like @NotNull works as expected.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • BindingResult in the wrong place: it must follow the model parameter immediately.
  • No setters: properties stay empty without setters or field access.
  • Binding an entity: users can set id or role.
  • Date format mismatch: use the pattern the HTML input sends (yyyy-MM-dd for type date).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Binding is reflective but fast; the cost is small compared with I/O.
  • Limit collection growth with setAutoGrowCollectionLimit to stop huge indexes like items[100000].
  • Use form classes with only the needed fields.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a profile edit page.

  • GET loads the user into ProfileForm with only name, phone and birthday.
  • POST binds, validates and copies the fields back to the entity.
  • The role field is never bindable.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Server-side rendering (SSR) means the server builds the complete HTML page and sends it, so the browser only displays it.
  • In Spring MVC: a @Controller returns a view name, a template engine fills the page, and the response body is HTML.
  • Compare: client-side rendering sends mostly JavaScript and JSON and builds the page in the browser; SSR needs no JavaScript to show content.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SSR in Spring MVC follows the normal request cycle.

  • Handler: the controller prepares the model.
  • View: ThymeleafView (or another engine view) writes HTML into the response.
  • Session: state such as login lives in the HttpSession and is sent back by a cookie.
  • Each click: a new request returns a full document, unless a fragment endpoint is used.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Full pages: @Controller plus a template.
  • Fragments: "page :: part" for htmx or fetch.
  • Mixed: an HTML page plus a @RestController for the data a widget needs.
  • Errors: templates/error/404.html and 500.html are used by Boot automatically.
codeExamples:
Page not found

Back home @GetMapping("/products/{id}") String one(@PathVariable long id, Model m) { m.addAttribute("p", service.find(id) .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND))); return "product"; } // OUTPUT: // GET /products/999 -> 404 with the custom error page

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Benefits: fast first paint, good for SEO and simple to secure because logic and data stay on the server.
  • Post/Redirect/Get: after a successful form POST, redirect to a GET page, so a browser refresh does not submit the form again.
  • Flash attributes: RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute carries a success message across the redirect once.

Senior Notes

  • Partial updates: return only a fragment ("page :: part") for libraries such as htmx, to refresh a part of the page without a full SPA.
  • Scaling: rendering costs CPU on the server; cache fragments, enable gzip, and keep sessions small or stateless.
  • Controller or REST: @Controller returns views; @RestController returns data. Mixing them by accident (missing @ResponseBody) gives a missing-template error.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No redirect after POST: refresh repeats the action.
  • Large session: storing lists in the session hurts scaling.
  • Mixing @RestController: returns text instead of a page.
  • Flash with forward: flash attributes only work with redirect.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Rendering cost grows with template size; keep pages light and paginate lists.
  • Compress HTML and cache static assets.
  • Use ETag filters or HTTP caching for pages that rarely change.
  • Keep the session small, or use Spring Session for several instances.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an internal admin application built only with SSR.

  • Thymeleaf pages with a shared layout and Spring Security form login.
  • htmx loads table rows as fragments for sorting and paging.
  • MockMvc tests cover each page and each redirect.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTML form: a <form> element groups inputs and sends them to the server when the user submits.
  • Main attributes: action is the URL and method is get or post; each input needs a name because the name is the request parameter key.
  • Spring side: read single values with @RequestParam or bind many values to an object with @ModelAttribute.

Practice Exercise 2

A search form with GET.
codeExamples:
<form action="/search" method="get"><input name="q"></form>
@GetMapping("/search")
String search(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "") String q, Model m) {
    m.addAttribute("q", q);
    return "results";
}

// OUTPUT:
// GET /search?q=spring -> view "results", q = "spring"

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens when a form is submitted.

  • Browser: collects named, enabled controls into name=value pairs and URL-encodes them.
  • GET: pairs go in the query string; POST: in the body with application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart.
  • Servlet: the container parses them into request parameters.
  • Spring: @RequestParam and @ModelAttribute read those parameters; a HiddenHttpMethodFilter can change the method.
codeExamples:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

user=abaji&pass=secret%21&remember=on

# OUTPUT:
# request.getParameter("pass") = "secret!"   (decoded by the container)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • enctype: urlencoded (default), multipart/form-data, text/plain.
  • Multiple values: several checkboxes with the same name bind to a List or array.
  • Buttons: name on the submit button tells which one was pressed.
  • Hidden method: _method field for PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
codeExamples:
<form method="post" action="/files" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="doc">
  <input type="checkbox" name="tags" value="a"><input type="checkbox" name="tags" value="b">
  <button name="action" value="save">Save</button>
</form>
@PostMapping("/files")
String up(@RequestParam MultipartFile doc, @RequestParam List<String> tags,
          @RequestParam String action) { return "ok"; }

// OUTPUT:
// doc = report.pdf, tags = [a, b], action = save

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • GET or POST: GET puts values in the URL and suits searches; POST puts them in the body and suits changes.
  • Input types: text, email, number, date, checkbox, radio, select and textarea; unchecked checkboxes are not sent at all.
  • Browsers only send GET and POST: for PUT or DELETE add a hidden _method field and enable spring.mvc.hiddenmethod.filter.enabled=true.

Senior Notes

  • File upload: use enctype="multipart/form-data" and a MultipartFile parameter; limits are in spring.servlet.multipart.*.
  • CSRF: with Spring Security every POST form needs the CSRF token; Thymeleaf adds it automatically when you use th:action.
  • Validation twice: HTML attributes such as required help the user, but only server-side validation protects the application.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing name: field not sent.
  • Missing enctype for upload: file arrives empty.
  • POST without CSRF token: 403 with Spring Security.
  • Required parameter absent: 400 MissingServletRequestParameterException.
codeExamples:
<!-- WRONG -->
<form action="/upload" method="post"><input type="file" name="doc"></form>
<!-- RIGHT -->
<form action="/upload" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="doc">
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// WRONG -> doc.isEmpty() is true ; RIGHT -> file bytes received

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and limits:

  • Set upload limits to protect memory and disk.
  • Stream large files instead of reading them into memory.
  • Use GET for safe, cacheable searches.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB

# OUTPUT:
# A 6 MB upload fails with MaxUploadSizeExceededException (HTTP 413 or 400).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a contact form on a company site.

  • HTML form posts name, email and message.
  • The controller validates, saves and redirects to a thank-you page.
  • A hidden honeypot field stops simple bots.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring MVC form: the usual flow is GET shows an empty form backed by an object, POST receives the filled object, validates it and either shows errors or redirects.
  • Pieces: a form class, a GET handler that adds it to the model, a POST handler with @Valid and BindingResult, and a template that shows fields and errors.
  • Views: Thymeleaf uses th:object and th:field; JSP uses the Spring tag library <form:form modelAttribute="user">.

Worked Example 1

Test validation errors.

Worked Example 2

Custom error message.
codeExamples:
# messages.properties
NotBlank.userForm.name=Please enter your name
Email.userForm.email=Enter a valid email address

# OUTPUT:
# The page shows "Please enter your name" for an empty name.
