beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A full Spring MVC form request passes through these steps.

  • GET: handler adds an empty form bean to the model; the view renders it with th:object.
  • POST: ModelAttributeMethodProcessor binds and, with @Valid, validates through LocalValidatorFactoryBean.
  • Errors: collected in BindingResult and exposed to the view as #fields.
  • Success: service call, then redirect.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features:

  • Groups: validation groups through @Validated(Group.class).
  • Class-level rules: a custom constraint for password and confirm password.
  • JSP tags: <form:form>, <form:input path="name"/>, <form:errors path="name"/>.
  • Select options: a list in the model with th:each on option.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Validation: put Jakarta annotations such as @NotBlank, @Email and @Size on the form class and add @Valid on the parameter.
  • Order rule: BindingResult must come immediately after the @Valid parameter, or Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException instead.
  • Show errors: th:errors="*{email}" prints messages and #fields.hasErrors('email') can change CSS classes.

Senior Notes

  • Post/Redirect/Get: redirect after success so refresh does not resubmit; return the view directly (no redirect) on errors so the entered values and messages stay.
  • Messages: field errors use codes like NotBlank.form.name, which you can override in messages.properties for friendly, translated text.
  • Edit forms: load the entity into a form object on GET and copy only allowed fields back on POST; never bind straight to a JPA entity.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong model attribute name: th:object="${form}" must match the name in the model (default is the class name in camelCase).
  • Redirect on errors: loses the errors and typed values.
  • No GET model object: the form page fails with a missing bean error.
  • Forgetting @Valid: annotations on the class are never checked.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and robustness:

  • Avoid database checks in plain annotations; do uniqueness checks in the service and add the error with br.rejectValue.
  • Guard against double submit with Post/Redirect/Get and a disabled button.
  • Cache lookup lists for select boxes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: user registration.

  • Form class with name, email, password and confirm password.
  • Controller validates, checks for duplicates, hashes the password and redirects to login.
  • MockMvc tests cover valid, invalid and duplicate cases.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form submission is the browser sending the field values of an HTML <form> to the server as a request, usually application/x-www-form-urlencoded through POST.
  • Spring MVC flow: the DispatcherServlet picks a handler, binds the parameters to an object, validates it and then returns a view or a redirect.
  • Two handlers are typical: a @GetMapping that shows the empty form and a @PostMapping that receives it.

Worked Example 1

Flash message after redirect.

Worked Example 2

Plain HTML form with CSRF (Thymeleaf).
codeExamples:
<form th:action="@{/register}" method="post">
    <input type="text" name="name"/>
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT: rendered HTML -->
// <form action="/register" method="post">
//   <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="a1b2..."/>   (token varies)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Show a form and receive it.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the submission with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens between the browser click and your method:

  • The servlet container parses the urlencoded body into parameters.
  • DispatcherServlet asks RequestMappingHandlerMapping for the handler method.
  • RequestMappingHandlerAdapter runs the argument resolvers; ModelAttributeMethodProcessor creates and binds the form object.
  • The handler returns a view name or redirect:; a ViewResolver renders it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of submitting a form:

  • Urlencoded: default for a simple form.
  • Multipart: add enctype="multipart/form-data" for files.
  • Method override: hidden _method field with spring.mvc.hiddenmethod.filter.enabled=true.
  • Fetch or AJAX: send JSON and use @RequestBody instead.
  • Consumes: restrict a handler with consumes = "application/x-www-form-urlencoded".

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Post-Redirect-Get: after a successful POST return redirect:/... so a browser refresh does not submit the form twice.
  • Flash attributes (RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute) carry a one-time message across the redirect.
  • Content types: a plain form sends urlencoded data, a file form needs multipart/form-data.

Senior Notes

  • CSRF: Spring Security rejects a POST without the token, so Thymeleaf forms add a hidden _csrf field automatically.
  • Hidden method: browsers only send GET and POST, so PUT or DELETE from a form needs HiddenHttpMethodFilter or a JavaScript call.
  • Double submit: besides PRG, disable the button on click or use an idempotency token for payments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No redirect after success: refresh creates a duplicate; use PRG.
  • Forgot the CSRF token: 403 on every POST.
  • Missing empty object on GET: template error because the form object is not in the model.
  • Field name differs from the property: value stays null.
  • Missing setters: binding silently skips the field.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Binding is cheap; keep the form small and avoid binding large graphs.
  • Set server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size and multipart limits to block huge bodies.
  • Use PRG so the heavy page is a cacheable GET.
  • Enable compression for rendered pages with server.compression.enabled=true.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=1MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=6MB
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# POST with an 8 MB file -> 413 / MaxUploadSizeExceededException

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a sign-up page.

  • GET shows the form; POST validates, saves and redirects with a welcome flash message.
  • A duplicate email is shown as a field error.
  • A MockMvc test covers valid, invalid and CSRF-less requests.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Data binding copies request parameters into the fields of a Java object by name, converting each text value to the field type.
  • Name match: a parameter age=30 goes to setAge(int); nested names such as address.city reach nested objects.
  • Binder: the work is done by WebDataBinder with a ConversionService; a failed conversion becomes a field error, not a crash.

Worked Example 1

Bind a list of items.

Worked Example 2

Binding error is kept, not thrown.

Practice Exercise 1

Bind nested and date fields.

Practice Exercise 2

Restrict bound fields.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Binding internals:

  • A WebDataBinder is created per attribute by ServletRequestDataBinderFactory.
  • Request parameters become MutablePropertyValues.
  • A BeanWrapper sets each property and uses the ConversionService (or PropertyEditors) to convert strings.
  • Failures are stored as FieldError with the rejected value; the binder never throws for them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • Setter binding: default with a no-arg constructor.
  • Constructor binding: records or one constructor with parameter names.
  • @InitBinder: custom editors, allowed fields, validators.
  • Formatter: a global Formatter<T> bean for a type.
  • Prefix: @ModelAttribute("a") with parameters named a.field is not required; names are plain.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lists and maps: items[0].name binds into a List; the list grows automatically up to a limit (autoGrowCollectionLimit).
  • @InitBinder registers custom editors, formatters or allowed fields for one controller.
  • @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat on a field tell the binder how to parse dates and numbers.

Senior Notes

  • Mass assignment: binding a JPA entity directly lets a client set fields like role; bind a DTO or call setAllowedFields.
  • Constructor binding: with records or a single constructor Spring 6 binds through the constructor, so objects can be immutable.
  • typeMismatch errors keep the rejected value, so the form can show what the user typed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Binding entities: mass assignment risk.
  • Missing setters or getters: value stays null.
  • Primitive for optional field: empty input gives a typeMismatch; use the wrapper type.
  • Date without format: parsing fails for ISO strings in some locales.
  • Ignoring BindingResult: conversion errors become a 400.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and limits:

  • Auto-grow limit for collections defaults to 256 elements, which stops memory attacks via items[100000].
  • Tune it with binder.setAutoGrowCollectionLimit.
  • Prefer shallow DTOs to keep reflection cost low.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order form with several lines.

  • Line items are bound to a list in a DTO.
  • Dates and money use formatting annotations.
  • Only whitelisted fields are accepted.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @ModelAttribute marks a method parameter that Spring binds from request data and adds to the model, or a method that adds data to the model before every handler.
  • On a parameter: @ModelAttribute("form") RegisterForm form creates the object, binds the parameters and exposes it to the view under the name form.
  • Default name: without a name Spring uses the decapitalized class name, so RegisterForm becomes registerForm.

Worked Example 1

Dropdown data shared by two handlers.

Worked Example 2

Implicit model attribute.

Practice Exercise 1

Parameter and method usage.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the model with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it works:

  • Before the handler, RequestMappingHandlerAdapter invokes every @ModelAttribute method of the controller (and its advice) and fills the ModelAndViewContainer.
  • For a parameter, ModelAttributeMethodProcessor first looks in the model (or session attributes), else creates the object by constructor.
  • It binds, optionally validates, then adds the object and its BindingResult to the model.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @ModelAttribute("name") sets the model name.
  • binding = false adds the attribute without binding request data.
  • A method can return void and write into Model.
  • @ControllerAdvice + @ModelAttribute shares data across controllers.
  • @SessionAttributes keeps the attribute between requests.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • On a method: a @ModelAttribute method runs before each handler of the controller and puts its return value in the model, good for dropdown lists.
  • Optional annotation: a non-simple parameter type with no annotation is treated as @ModelAttribute by default.
  • Not for JSON: @ModelAttribute reads form parameters; use @RequestBody for a JSON body.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: ModelAttributeMethodProcessor (servlet version) creates, binds and validates the object.
  • Order: the controller @ModelAttribute methods run first, then the handler, so a handler can rely on the shared data.
  • Session reuse: with @SessionAttributes the object survives between requests, which suits multi-step wizards.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using it for JSON: fields stay null; use @RequestBody.
  • Heavy work in a @ModelAttribute method: it runs for every handler, even those that do not need it.
  • Name clash: two attributes with the same name overwrite each other.
  • BindingResult in wrong place.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: keep @ModelAttribute methods cheap, cache lookup lists (countries, roles) and prefer explicit loading for large data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a create/edit product form with category dropdown.

  • @ModelAttribute method supplies categories to both GET and POST views.
  • The POST handler returns the form with errors and the dropdown still works.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Command object (form-backing object) is a plain Java class whose fields mirror the form fields; Spring fills it from the request and the view reads it back.
  • Round trip: the GET handler puts an empty (or pre-filled) command object in the model, the form binds to it, and the POST handler receives it filled.
  • Plain bean: it needs a default constructor and getters and setters, or a record or a constructor Spring can bind to.

Worked Example 1

Pre-filled edit form.

Worked Example 2

Thymeleaf binding.
codeExamples:
<form th:object="${form}
" th:action="@{/users}
" method="post">
    <input type="text" th:field="*{name}"/>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT: rendered -->
// <input type="text" id="name" name="name" value="Abaji"/>

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Command object and controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Record as command object.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • The GET handler stores the object in the model under a name.
  • The view engine binds fields with th:field, which reads the property value for display.
  • On POST a new instance is created and bound; for @SessionAttributes the stored instance is reused and updated.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Class with setters.
  • Record with constructor binding.
  • Class with a constructor having parameters named like the fields (compile with -parameters, default in Spring Boot plugin).
  • Nested command objects for grouped fields.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Pre-fill for edit: load an entity, copy its values into the command object and add it to the model, so the form shows current data.
  • Validation: put Bean Validation annotations on the command object and use @Valid on the parameter.
  • Thymeleaf link: th:object names the command object and th:field binds each input to a property.

Senior Notes

  • Separate from the entity: a command object shaped for the screen avoids exposing database fields and lazy-loading problems.
  • Records work as immutable command objects with constructor binding in Spring 6.
  • Scope: the object lives for one request unless you add @SessionAttributes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Putting an entity with lazy relations in the form.
  • Not initializing nested objects, which gives NullPointerException in the view.
  • Sharing one object between users by storing it in a field of the controller (controllers are singletons).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: command objects are short-lived, so keep them small; avoid large session attributes since sessions are held in memory.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.timeout=15m

# OUTPUT:
# abandoned wizard objects are released after 15 minutes of inactivity

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: profile edit page.

  • GET loads the user and fills a command object.
  • POST validates it and updates only allowed fields.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form DTO is a data transfer object designed only for one form: it holds just the fields the user may send and the rules to check them.
  • Why: it separates the web layer from the entity, so the screen can change without touching the database model.
  • Mapping: the controller or a service copies the DTO into an entity; the DTO itself has no persistence annotations.

Worked Example 1

Mass assignment blocked.

Worked Example 2

Separate update DTO.

Practice Exercise 1

A record DTO with rules.

Practice Exercise 2

Map DTO to entity.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals and layers:

  • Controller binds and validates the DTO.
  • Service maps it to the entity inside a transaction.
  • The reverse mapping (entity to DTO) fills the edit form.
  • Binding uses only the DTO properties, so no unexpected setter is reachable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Hand-written mapper method.
  • MapStruct interface generated at compile time.
  • ModelMapper (reflection based, slower and less safe).
  • Class-level constraints for cross-field rules.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Validation lives here: @NotBlank, @Email and @Size on the DTO describe form rules.
  • Different DTOs for create and update are common, because update has an id and may skip the password.
  • Mapping tools: write a small mapper by hand, or use MapStruct for many fields.

Senior Notes

  • Security: a DTO without role or enabled makes mass assignment impossible.
  • Cross-field rules (password equals confirm) use a class-level constraint or a check in the service.
  • Records keep DTOs short and immutable; validation annotations go on the record components.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Reusing one DTO for request and response, leaking fields.
  • Putting JPA annotations on the DTO.
  • Trusting a hidden id field from the form.
  • Mapping nulls over existing data on update.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: DTOs add a copy, which is negligible; MapStruct avoids reflection. Use projections for read-only list pages instead of loading entities.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: user registration.

  • SignupForm carries name, email, password and confirm.
  • The service creates the User with a hashed password and default role.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • BindingResult holds the result of binding and validating one model attribute: the field errors, the global errors and the rejected values.
  • Position rule: declare it immediately after the model attribute parameter, for example (@Valid Form f, BindingResult br).
  • Without it a binding or validation failure throws MethodArgumentNotValidException (or BindException) and the user gets a 400 page.

Worked Example 1

Wrong order causes failure.

Worked Example 2

Global error.

Practice Exercise 1

Check errors in the handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Add a business error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • BindingResult is implemented by BeanPropertyBindingResult, created by the WebDataBinder.
  • The resolver puts it in the model under org.springframework.validation.BindingResult. + the attribute name, which is how views find it.
  • If the next parameter is an Errors or BindingResult, the processor passes it; otherwise it throws on errors.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

API summary:

  • hasErrors(), hasFieldErrors("f"), getErrorCount()
  • getFieldError("f"), getFieldErrors(), getGlobalErrors()
  • rejectValue(field, code, msg) and reject(code, msg)
  • getRawFieldValue("f"), getFieldValue("f")

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • hasErrors() tells whether anything failed; getFieldErrors() lists each field problem.
  • rejectValue adds your own field error, for example a duplicate email found in the database.
  • reject adds a global (object-level) error that is not tied to a field.

Senior Notes

  • Error codes: each error has codes like NotBlank.form.name that a MessageSource turns into text.
  • Rejected value is kept so the form can redisplay what the user typed.
  • Errors is the parent interface; BindingResult adds access to the target object and the model.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong parameter order.
  • One BindingResult for two form objects (each needs its own).
  • Returning a redirect when errors exist.
  • Calling rejectValue with a field that does not exist (NotReadablePropertyException).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: errors are small objects; the cost is in message resolution, which is cached by MessageSource (set spring.messages.cache-duration in production).
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.messages.basename=messages
spring.messages.cache-duration=1h

# OUTPUT:
# message files are re-read at most once per hour

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: signup with a database uniqueness check that must appear on the form.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form validation checks the submitted data against rules before the application uses it; in Spring MVC rules are Bean Validation annotations and @Valid triggers them.
  • Common annotations: @NotBlank, @NotNull, @Size, @Min, @Max, @Email and @Pattern.
  • Dependency: add spring-boot-starter-validation, which brings Hibernate Validator as the implementation.

Worked Example 2

Messages file.
codeExamples:

NotBlank.productForm.name=Please enter the product name
Min.productForm.price=Price must be 1 or more

# OUTPUT:
# the form shows "Please enter the product name" instead of the default text

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Annotated form and handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Test validation failure.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • ModelAttributeMethodProcessor calls binder.validate() when @Valid or @Validated is present.
  • The binder delegates to SpringValidatorAdapter which wraps the Hibernate Validator Validator.
  • Each ConstraintViolation becomes a FieldError in the BindingResult.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Groups: @Validated(OnCreate.class).
  • Cascade: @Valid on nested field or list.
  • Class level: constraint on the class for cross-field checks.
  • Method validation: @Validated on the class and constraints on parameters (Spring 6.1 validates handler arguments too).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Namespace: in Spring Boot 3 the annotations are in jakarta.validation.constraints.
  • Groups let one DTO have different rules for create and update, selected with @Validated(Group.class).
  • Custom constraint: write an annotation plus a ConstraintValidator for rules such as a unique username.

Senior Notes

  • Trigger: the argument resolver validates after binding; failures go to BindingResult.
  • Client validation is not enough: always validate on the server, since requests can skip the browser.
  • Messages come from messages.properties using keys like NotBlank.form.name, which supports other languages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing starter, so annotations are silently ignored.
  • Using javax.validation imports in Boot 3.
  • Using @NotNull on strings and expecting blank rejection.
  • Forgetting @Valid on nested objects.
  • Only client-side validation.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: the validator is created once and is thread safe; constraint metadata is cached per class. Avoid database calls inside validators unless needed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: checkout form with address, card number and consent.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • GET form sends the field values in the URL query string (/search?q=spring); it is used for reading and searching, never for changing data.
  • Safe and idempotent: the result can be bookmarked, shared and repeated without side effects.
  • Handler: a @GetMapping method reads the values with @RequestParam or a form object.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

HTML GET form.

<form action="/search" method="get">
    <input type="text" name="q"/>
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT: browser requests -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Search form handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Bind a query into an object.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • The browser builds ?name=value&... from the inputs, URL-encoding each value.
  • The servlet container decodes it into parameters.
  • @RequestParam uses RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver; an object parameter uses the model attribute resolver.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @RequestParam Map<String,String> for all parameters.
  • @RequestParam List<String> for repeated names (tag=a&tag=b).
  • Pageable for page, size and sort.
  • @RequestParam Optional<String>.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Show a form also uses GET: the handler only adds an empty object to the model and returns the view name.
  • Optional parameters: @RequestParam(required = false) or defaultValue help with search boxes and paging.
  • Encoding: browsers URL-encode the values, and Spring decodes them before binding.

Senior Notes

  • No secrets: URLs end up in logs, history and the Referer header, so passwords never go in GET.
  • Length limits: servers and proxies limit the URL size, so use POST for long input.
  • Caching: GET responses can be cached, so add Cache-Control if the page must always be fresh.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sensitive data in the URL.
  • Required parameter missing gives 400; use a default.
  • Using GET to delete or update.
  • Not encoding values when building links by hand; use UriComponentsBuilder or th:href with parameters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: GET results can be cached by browser and proxies; add paging and indexes behind search queries and limit the maximum page size.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100
spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size=20

# OUTPUT:
# size=100000 is capped to 100

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: product search with filters, kept in the URL so users can bookmark results.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • POST form sends the values in the request body and is used to create or change data, such as registration, login or payment.
  • Not idempotent: repeating a POST can repeat its effect, so apply Post-Redirect-Get after success.
  • Handler: a @PostMapping method takes a form object, validates it and returns a view or a redirect.

Worked Example 1

File upload form.

Worked Example 2

PRG in action.

Practice Exercise 1

Complete POST handler.

Practice Exercise 2

MockMvc with CSRF.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • The body is read once by the container (urlencoded) or by MultipartResolver (multipart).
  • With Spring Security the CsrfFilter checks the token before the dispatcher runs.
  • The handler result decides the response: view render (200) or redirect (302/303).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Urlencoded form object.
  • Multipart with @RequestPart or MultipartFile.
  • Redirect with RedirectView or redirect: prefix.
  • Status 303 See Other via RedirectView with setStatusCode.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Error path: on validation errors return the form view directly (status 200) so the entered values stay; on success redirect.
  • Body encoding: urlencoded for simple forms, multipart/form-data for file upload with MultipartFile.
  • Hidden fields such as the id or CSRF token travel with the form but can be edited by a user, so never trust them.

Senior Notes

  • CSRF: Spring Security expects the token on every POST; test with .with(csrf()) in MockMvc.
  • Size limits: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and the server post size limit protect memory.
  • Authorization: check that the user may change the record, not only that the form is valid.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning the view after success (duplicate on refresh).
  • Redirecting after errors (errors lost).
  • Wrong enctype for files: file arrives empty.
  • Trusting hidden fields and client-supplied ids.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: stream large uploads to disk or storage, set size limits, and move heavy work (image processing, email) out of the request thread with @Async or a queue.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: order checkout.

  • Validated POST, transaction in the service, unique order number.
  • PRG to the confirmation page.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form error handling means showing the user what went wrong in a submitted form, next to the field, while keeping the values they typed.
  • Flow: binding or validation fails, errors go into BindingResult, the handler returns the form view again and the template prints the errors.
  • Thymeleaf: th:errors="*{email}" prints the messages of a field and #fields.hasErrors(...) checks for them.

Worked Example 2

Test error display.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • Errors live in the BindingResult that is stored in the model.
  • Thymeleaf's th:errors and #fields read it through the form-backing object name set by th:object.
  • Messages are resolved by the MessageSource from error codes, most specific first: Code.object.field, Code.field, Code.type, Code.

NotBlank.email=Email is required (generic)
NotBlank=This field is required

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Display options:

  • Per field: th:errors="*{field}".
  • All errors: #fields.allErrors() in a th:each loop.
  • Global: #fields.hasGlobalErrors().
  • Summary: th:errors="*".
  • JSP: form:errors tag.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Re-display: return the same view name, not a redirect, so the model with the errors is still available.
  • Global errors are shown with #fields.globalErrors() or th:errors="*{global}".
  • CSS class: th:errorclass="error" adds a class to invalid inputs for red borders.

Senior Notes

  • Unexpected exceptions are handled by @ExceptionHandler or @ControllerAdvice, not by BindingResult.
  • Type mismatch messages use keys like typeMismatch.age in messages.properties.
  • Never leak stack traces or SQL errors to the page; map them to a friendly global error.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Redirecting on error loses the errors; use flash attributes only if you really redirect.
  • Form attribute name differs from th:object.
  • Showing raw exception messages.
  • Not handling MethodArgumentNotValidException for JSON endpoints.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: message lookups are cached; keep error pages light and do not run extra queries when rendering errors.

# application.properties
spring.messages.cache-duration=-1
spring.messages.fallback-to-system-locale=false
