no surprise language fallback

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: one handler advice that turns validation failures into a consistent JSON error for the API and HTML re-display for the web form.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Redirect after POST means that after a form POST succeeds, the controller returns redirect:/somewhere instead of rendering a view, so the browser makes a new GET request.
  • Why: if the POST response is a page, pressing refresh re-sends the POST and can create a duplicate order or payment.
  • Syntax: return the string "redirect:/orders/42" from the handler, and Spring sends an HTTP 302 with a Location header.

Worked Example 1

addAttribute versus flash.

Worked Example 2

Redirect with a 303 status.

Practice Exercise 1

A controller that redirects after saving.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the redirect with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a redirect travels through Spring MVC:

  • The handler returns the string redirect:/orders/42.
  • ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler stores it as the view name.
  • UrlBasedViewResolver sees the prefix and builds a RedirectView.
  • RedirectView writes the flash attributes to the FlashMapManager, builds the URL and calls sendRedirect.
  • On the next request, DispatcherServlet reads the flash map and puts it into the model.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Redirect variants:

  • redirect: prefix: relative to the application context path.
  • RedirectView: lets you set contextRelative, http10Compatible and the status.
  • ResponseEntity: full control, for example 303 or 301.
  • forward: prefix: a server-side forward, no new request.
  • RedirectAttributes: query parameters versus flash attributes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • RedirectAttributes: use addAttribute for URL query parameters and addFlashAttribute for one-time data kept in the session.
  • Flash attributes survive exactly one redirect, so a success message shows once and disappears on refresh.
  • Redirect view: the redirect: prefix is handled by UrlBasedViewResolver, which creates a RedirectView.

Senior Notes

  • Status code: 302 is the default; use RedirectView or ResponseEntity with 303 See Other when you want a strict GET after POST.
  • Model leakage: by default model attributes can be appended to the redirect URL, so set ignoreDefaultModelOnRedirect=true to avoid this.
  • Testing: with MockMvc assert status().is3xxRedirection(), redirectedUrl(...) and flash().attributeExists(...).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Model data lost: model attributes do not survive a redirect; use flash attributes.
  • Ugly URLs: model values leaking into the query string; set spring.mvc.ignore-default-model-on-redirect (true by default in Boot).
  • Redirect to user input: an open redirect vulnerability when you redirect to a URL taken from a parameter; validate it.
  • Missing slash: redirect:orders is relative to the current path.
  • Flash on non-redirect: flash data is for the next request only.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • A redirect costs one extra round trip; that is acceptable for a POST but avoid it for every GET.
  • Flash attributes use the HTTP session, so keep them small.
  • For stateless services, put the id in the URL instead of a flash attribute.
  • Use a 303 status so clients always switch to GET.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an online shop checkout. The POST charges the card once, then redirects to an order confirmation page that is safe to refresh, bookmark and email.

  • The POST creates the order and returns the order id.
  • The GET page loads the order by id.
  • A unique order token in the form blocks double clicks.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • PRG stands for Post/Redirect/Get: the browser POSTs a form, the server answers with a redirect, and the browser then GETs a result page.
  • Problem solved: the browser history keeps the final GET, so refresh or the back button never re-submits the form.
  • Three steps: a @PostMapping handler processes the data, returns redirect:/url, and a @GetMapping handler renders the page.

Worked Example 1

Without PRG (the bug).

Worked Example 2

Fixed with PRG.

Practice Exercise 1

Full PRG with validation.

Practice Exercise 2

MockMvc test of both paths.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

PRG works with HTTP and the browser history, not with a Spring trick.

  • A browser remembers the last navigation request. After a POST that returns 200, that entry is the POST, so refresh re-sends it.
  • After a 302 or 303, the history entry is the GET of the new URL.
  • Spring just returns the redirect; DispatcherServlet and RedirectView do the rest.
  • The state needed by the GET page is either in the database (read by id) or in a flash attribute.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of the pattern:

  • Redirect to the created resource: /users/{id}.
  • Redirect to a list with a flash message.
  • Redirect back to the form with errors flashed, using BindingResult as a flash attribute.
  • REST APIs: return 201 Created with a Location header instead of a redirect.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Validation errors are the exception: when BindingResult.hasErrors() is true, return the form view directly (no redirect) so the errors are shown.
  • Success message: pass it with addFlashAttribute, because model data is lost at a redirect.
  • Idempotent GET: the page you redirect to must be safe to load many times.

Senior Notes

  • Double submit: PRG does not stop a user who clicks the button twice quickly; add a token or a unique constraint as well.
  • Flash and validation: to keep errors across a redirect you must also flash the BindingResult, which is rarely worth the effort.
  • Testing: one MockMvc test for the invalid path (200 with the form) and one for the valid path (redirect).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Redirecting on validation errors: the messages disappear.
  • Using model.addAttribute instead of flash attributes before a redirect.
  • Doing work in the GET page such as saving data; GET must stay safe.
  • Forgetting the form token: PRG alone does not stop two quick clicks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • PRG adds one cheap request; the GET page can often be served from a cache.
  • Prefer reading by id from the database over keeping a large object in a flash attribute.
  • With several servers, flash attributes need a shared session or sticky routing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a registration form in a school portal. The POST validates and saves the student, then redirects to a welcome page. Invalid input stays on the form with messages; valid input never causes a duplicate account on refresh.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Data binding is the automatic copying of request values (form fields, query parameters, path variables) into Java objects, with type conversion.
  • Purpose: you write save(UserForm form) instead of calling request.getParameter for every field.
  • Names match: a parameter called name is copied into the setter setName of the target object.

Worked Example 1

Binding errors.

Worked Example 2

Path and query binding.

Practice Exercise 1

Binding a form to an object.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the binding.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside a request:

  • RequestMappingHandlerAdapter prepares the argument list through HandlerMethodArgumentResolver objects.
  • ModelAttributeMethodProcessor creates the target object (default constructor, or the primary constructor for records).
  • A WebDataBinder is made by the binder factory, which applies @InitBinder methods.
  • The binder takes the request parameters as MutablePropertyValues and binds them with BeanWrapper.
  • Each value goes through the ConversionService or a PropertyEditor.
  • Validation runs, then errors and the target form the BindingResult.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Binding sources and options:

  • @RequestParam: one parameter.
  • @PathVariable: URI template value.
  • @ModelAttribute: many parameters into one object.
  • @RequestHeader, @CookieValue: headers and cookies.
  • @RequestBody: the body, JSON by Jackson.
  • @RequestPart: multipart files and parts.
  • @SessionAttribute: session data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Sources: @ModelAttribute binds request parameters to an object, while @RequestBody uses message converters (JSON) instead.
  • Conversion: the string "25" becomes an int, and "2024-05-01" can become a LocalDate with @DateTimeFormat.
  • Errors: a failed conversion does not throw; it is stored in BindingResult as a field error.

Senior Notes

  • Engine: a WebDataBinder created per request does the work through BeanWrapper and a ConversionService.
  • Security: binding to an entity can let a client set fields you did not intend (mass assignment), so bind to a form or DTO class.
  • Testing: send parameters with MockMvc param(...) and assert on the model with model().attribute(...).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Binding straight to a JPA entity: mass assignment; use a DTO.
  • Missing getters and setters: nothing is bound and no error appears.
  • No BindingResult right after the object: a bad value throws an exception.
  • Wrong parameter name: HTML field name and property name differ.
  • Date format: no @DateTimeFormat, so the date does not convert.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Binding uses reflection but is cached by BeanWrapper and is rarely a bottleneck.
  • Keep form classes small and avoid large nested graphs.
  • Limit list growth with setAutoGrowCollectionLimit.
  • Use setAllowedFields to ignore unwanted input early.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a job application form with personal data, an address and a list of skills. One DTO gets all fields; validation messages come back on the same page.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Property binding means mapping one request parameter to one property of a bean through its setter, such as address.city to getAddress().setCity().
  • Property path: dots reach nested objects, brackets reach lists and maps, as in items[0].name or tags[red].
  • Requirement: the bean needs a public setter (or a field set up for direct access) for each bound property.

Worked Example 1

Map binding.

Worked Example 2

Field access without setters.

Practice Exercise 1

Nested and indexed properties.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the nested binding.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The path items[0].name is handled by BeanWrapperImpl:

  • It splits the path into tokens: items, index 0, then name.
  • It reads getItems(); if the value is null and auto-grow is on, it creates a new list.
  • It grows the list to size 1 and creates an Item instance using its default constructor.
  • It calls setName with the converted value.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax summary:

  • name: simple property.
  • address.city: nested property.
  • items[0] or items[0].name: list or array index.
  • tags[color]: map key.
  • skills=a&skills=b: repeated parameter into a list or array.
  • _flag prefix (_subscribe): marker for unchecked checkboxes.
  • !field prefix: default value when the field is absent.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Nested objects are created automatically when autoGrowNestedPaths is true, which is the default.
  • Collections grow as needed up to autoGrowCollectionLimit, which is 256 by default.
  • Name rule: the name is the property name, so setFirstName binds the parameter firstName.

Senior Notes

  • Engine: BeanPropertyBindingResult wraps a BeanWrapperImpl that resolves each path segment.
  • Direct field access: call initDirectFieldAccess() in an @InitBinder to bind private fields without setters.
  • Pitfall: unknown parameters are ignored silently unless ignoreUnknownFields is set to false.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Null nested object when auto-grow is disabled, giving NullValueInNestedPathException.
  • Missing default constructor on the list element class.
  • Index gaps: items[5] creates five empty items.
  • Property name case: setURL maps to URL, not url.
  • Typos in names are silently ignored.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Large indexes allocate many objects; cap them with autoGrowCollectionLimit.
  • Prefer a flat form class for simple forms.
  • Direct field access avoids setter calls but skips setter logic.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an invoice form where the user can add lines dynamically. JavaScript names the inputs lines[0].product, lines[0].qty, lines[1].product and so on, and Spring builds the list.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Automatic binding is what Spring MVC does without extra code: any controller argument that is not a simple type or a special type is bound from the request as a model attribute.
  • Implicit @ModelAttribute: save(UserForm form) works exactly like save(@ModelAttribute UserForm form).
  • Simple types (int, String, and so on) are treated as @RequestParam by default, with the parameter name taken from the argument name.

Worked Example 1

Simple type defaults.

Worked Example 2

Safe version.

Practice Exercise 1

Implicit binding and the model.

Practice Exercise 2

Constructor binding with a record.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Argument resolution order in RequestMappingHandlerAdapter:

  • Annotation-based resolvers first (@RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestBody, ...).
  • Type-based resolvers next (Model, HttpServletRequest, Principal, Locale).
  • Custom resolvers you registered.
  • Catch-all resolvers last: simple types become @RequestParam, everything else becomes @ModelAttribute.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Automatic does not mean fixed. You can change it:

  • @ModelAttribute("name") to change the model name.
  • @ModelAttribute method to preload data into every request.
  • @RequestParam(required = false) or Optional for optional values.
  • Custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver to bind your own argument type, such as CurrentUser.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Argument resolvers: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter asks each HandlerMethodArgumentResolver in turn; ServletModelAttributeMethodProcessor handles the bean case.
  • Parameter names are available because Spring Boot compiles with -parameters; without it use @RequestParam("name").
  • Missing values leave the property at its default (null or 0) instead of failing.

Senior Notes

  • Order of work: create the object, bind parameters, run validation if @Valid is present, then call the method.
  • Pitfall: a record or constructor-bound class is built through its constructor, so a missing primitive parameter can throw instead of defaulting.
  • Testing: test the binding with @WebMvcTest and check both the model and the returned view.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • int instead of Integer for optional input: absent value gives an error.
  • Compiling without -parameters (non-Boot builds) so names are lost.
  • Two beans with the same attribute name clashing in the model.
  • Mutable shared form objects kept as fields in the controller; controllers are singletons.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Resolver lookup is cached per parameter.
  • Do not do database access inside argument resolvers on hot paths unless it is cached.
  • Use records for immutable, small form objects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a search page. Filters (text, category, page, sort) arrive as query parameters and are bound in one object, which is then passed to a service.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom data binding means teaching Spring MVC how to convert a request string into your own type, such as a Money or Email class.
  • Ways to do it: a Converter, a Formatter, a PropertyEditor, or a type with a single-string constructor or valueOf.
  • Why: without it the binder cannot convert and records a typeMismatch error.

Worked Example 1

Registering manually.

Worked Example 2

Per-field formats.

Practice Exercise 1

A Money converter.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the converter and the endpoint.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a custom type is bound:

  • The binder asks its TypeConverterDelegate to convert the String to your target type.
  • Order of attempts: custom PropertyEditor on the binder, then the ConversionService (your Converter or Formatter), then default editors, then a constructor or valueOf taking a String.
  • If nothing works, a TypeMismatchException becomes a field error.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Converter for one direction.
  • Formatter for text in both directions with a Locale.
  • AnnotationFormatterFactory for your own format annotation, such as @Phone.
  • ConditionalGenericConverter to decide by field annotations.
  • HttpMessageConverter for bodies, not parameters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Converter: Converter<String, Money> converts one way and is registered in WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters.
  • Formatter: Formatter<T> converts both ways (text to object and object to text) and supports a Locale.
  • Annotations: @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat customize built-in types per field without any class.

Senior Notes

  • Scope: a global converter applies everywhere; an @InitBinder applies to one controller only.
  • Error handling: throw IllegalArgumentException from the converter to produce a clean field error.
  • Testing: unit test the converter alone, then one MockMvc test to prove it is registered.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning null on bad input, so the field is silently empty.
  • Forgetting to register the converter (plain class, no @Component).
  • Using the wrong generic types: Converter<Object, Money> may clash with others.
  • Shared editor instances used from many threads.
  • Expecting JSON bodies to use it: Jackson needs its own deserializer.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Converters are singletons, so keep them stateless and cheap.
  • Cache expensive lookups, for example String to entity, or avoid converting to entities and pass the id instead.
  • Prefer the built-in @DateTimeFormat over hand-written parsing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a finance screen with amounts like 12,50 in one locale and 12.50 in another. A Formatter using the request Locale parses and prints both consistently.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • WebDataBinder is the object that binds request parameters onto a target object, converts types, and (optionally) validates the result.
  • One per attribute: Spring creates a new binder for each @ModelAttribute or @RequestBody argument that needs it.
  • Results: it fills the target and keeps all problems in a BindingResult that you can receive as the next method argument.

Worked Example 1

Using the binder by hand.

Worked Example 2

Registering a formatter.

Practice Exercise 1

Protecting fields.

Practice Exercise 2

Test that the role is ignored.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Class structure and flow:

  • DataBinder holds the target, a BindingResult, validators and conversion settings.
  • WebDataBinder adds web features: the _ and ! field prefixes and multipart support.
  • ServletRequestDataBinder reads parameters from a ServletRequest.
  • bind() checks allowed and disallowed fields, checks required fields, then calls applyPropertyValues.
  • Errors are stored as FieldError objects with codes used for message lookup.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Main configuration methods:

  • setAllowedFields / setDisallowedFields: whitelist or blacklist, patterns allowed.
  • setRequiredFields: must be present.
  • setIgnoreInvalidFields, setIgnoreUnknownFields.
  • setFieldMarkerPrefix and setFieldDefaultPrefix.
  • setValidator / addValidators.
  • setConversionService, registerCustomEditor.
  • setBindEmptyMultipartFiles.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Key settings: setAllowedFields, setDisallowedFields, setRequiredFields and setIgnoreUnknownFields.
  • Registering conversion: registerCustomEditor adds a PropertyEditor, and addCustomFormatter adds a Formatter.
  • Customizing: use @InitBinder methods in a controller or @ControllerAdvice to configure it.

Senior Notes

  • Creation: DefaultDataBinderFactory builds the binder and applies the WebBindingInitializer and all @InitBinder methods.
  • Class hierarchy: WebDataBinder extends DataBinder, which uses BeanWrapper and a ConversionService.
  • Security: set allowed fields to stop mass-assignment attacks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting to disallow sensitive fields: id, role, price.
  • Setting a validator with setValidator that replaces the default bean validator; use addValidators.
  • Using the same editor instance in every request.
  • Reading BindingResult before binding finishes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • A binder is created per argument per request; its cost is small but not zero, so keep @InitBinder methods light.
  • Use patterns in allowed fields to avoid long lists.
  • Do not create a new SimpleDateFormat per call outside the binder scope; they are not thread-safe.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an admin profile edit page. The form is bound to the user entity, so the binder protects fields that must not be changed from the browser.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @InitBinder marks a controller method that customizes the WebDataBinder before binding starts for each request.
  • Typical uses: register custom editors or formatters, trim strings, and allow or block fields.
  • Signature: the method returns void and takes a WebDataBinder (and optionally a WebRequest or Locale).

Worked Example 1

Scoped to one attribute.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc check.

Practice Exercise 1

Trim strings and format dates.

Practice Exercise 2

Global version.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Discovery and execution:

  • RequestMappingHandlerAdapter scans the controller class (and every @ControllerAdvice) for methods annotated with @InitBinder and caches them.
  • When an argument needs binding, ServletRequestDataBinderFactory creates the binder.
  • InitBinderDataBinderFactory invokes each matching method, filtering by the optional attribute names.
  • Methods from advice run first, then those of the controller.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @InitBinder: all attributes in this controller.
  • @InitBinder("a", "b"): named attributes only.
  • In @ControllerAdvice: all controllers, or narrowed by basePackages or assignableTypes.
  • Extra arguments: WebRequest, Locale, HttpServletRequest.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Scope: inside a controller it affects only that controller; inside a @ControllerAdvice it affects all controllers.
  • Limit names: @InitBinder("user") applies only to the model attribute or parameter called user.
  • Trim example: StringTrimmerEditor(true) turns blank input into null, which is handy for optional fields.

Senior Notes

  • Run time: it runs for every binder created in a request, so keep it fast and free of database calls.
  • Pitfall: it does not run for @RequestBody JSON, because Jackson does that conversion, not the binder.
  • Testing: check the effect with MockMvc, for example that " Abaji " arrives as "Abaji".

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong return type: a non-void method fails at startup.
  • Name mismatch: @InitBinder("user") but the attribute is userForm, so it never runs.
  • Expecting it to run for @RequestBody.
  • Heavy work such as database calls in the method.
  • Trimming passwords globally by accident.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • The method list is cached, so the cost is one invocation per binder.
  • Create editors with new instances only when they are not thread-safe.
  • Put shared rules in one advice class instead of repeating them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a student portal where every text field must be trimmed and empty strings stored as null, and the id and createdBy fields must never come from a browser. One advice class covers all controllers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • PropertyEditor is the older java.beans API that converts a String to an object and back; Spring MVC still supports it for data binding.
  • How to write one: extend PropertyEditorSupport, override setAsText to parse and getAsText to print.
  • Register it in an @InitBinder method with binder.registerCustomEditor(Type.class, editor).

Worked Example 1

Built-in date editor.

Worked Example 2

Trimming blanks to null.

Practice Exercise 1

A custom editor.

Practice Exercise 2

Unit test of the editor.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the binder:

  • PropertyEditorRegistrySupport keeps default editors (numbers, booleans, Class, Locale, ...) and custom editors.
  • TypeConverterDelegate looks up a custom editor by type or by type plus property path.
  • It calls setAsText, then getValue to get the result.
  • For output (for example in a form tag), getAsText is used.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Registration variants:

  • registerCustomEditor(Type.class, editor): for every property of that type.
  • registerCustomEditor(Type.class, "field", editor): for one property path.
  • PropertyEditorRegistrar: a reusable set of editors shared by many binders.
  • CustomCollectionEditor: converts a comma list or array into a collection.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Built-in editors: Spring ships CustomDateEditor, StringTrimmerEditor, CustomNumberEditor and many more.
  • Call setValue: inside setAsText you must call setValue(object) with the parsed result.
  • Thread safety: editors are stateful, so create a new one for each binder instead of sharing one instance.

Senior Notes

  • Why Converters won: editors are not thread-safe, only convert from String, and are tied to the binder, so modern code prefers Converter and Formatter.
  • Order: the binder tries a custom editor first, then the ConversionService, then default editors.
  • Testing: an editor is plain Java, so unit test it by calling setAsText and getValue.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Not calling setValue, so the property stays null.
  • Sharing one editor in a static field across threads.
  • Lenient SimpleDateFormat: 31-02 becomes 03-03; call setLenient(false).
  • Throwing the wrong exception: use IllegalArgumentException for bad text.
  • Using editors for new code where a Converter is better.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • An editor is created for each binder, so keep construction cheap.
  • Prefer thread-safe converters and formatters to avoid allocation on each request.
  • Use DateTimeFormatter-based formatters instead of SimpleDateFormat.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: maintaining an old Spring MVC application that has a BirthDateEditor in many controllers. The migration plan moves them to one global Formatter registered in WebMvcConfigurer.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Converter is the Spring interface Converter<S, T> with one method, T convert(S source), that turns one type into another.
  • Use in MVC: it converts request parameters, path variables and headers (strings) into your own types before a controller runs.
  • Stateless and thread-safe, so one instance can be shared across all requests.

Worked Example 1

ConverterFactory for all enums.

Worked Example 2

Manual registration.

Practice Exercise 1

String to enum, case-insensitive.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the endpoint.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The conversion machinery:

  • GenericConversionService stores converters in a map keyed by ConvertiblePair (source type, target type).
  • Lookup walks the class hierarchy of both types and picks the closest registered pair, with a cache.
  • Converter is adapted to a GenericConverter internally.
  • Spring Boot builds a WebConversionService and adds all Converter, GenericConverter and Formatter beans.
  • The binder, @RequestParam, @PathVariable and @Value all use it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Converter types:

  • Converter<S,T>: one pair.
  • ConverterFactory<S,R>: one source, a family of targets.
  • GenericConverter: several pairs and access to TypeDescriptor with annotations.
  • ConditionalConverter: decide at run time with matches.
  • Built-in: String to numbers, enums, dates, collections, Optional.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registering: in Spring Boot, expose the converter as a @Component; otherwise override addFormatters in WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Variants: ConverterFactory for a family of types (for example all enums) and GenericConverter for several type pairs.
  • Returning null from a converter means "no value", so handle bad input by throwing IllegalArgumentException instead.

Senior Notes

  • ConversionService: WebConversionService (a FormattingConversionService) holds all converters and is used by the binder and by @Value.
  • Lookup: it searches by source and target type, walking class hierarchies to the closest match.
  • Testing: call convert in a unit test and add one MockMvc test to prove the endpoint uses it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Not a bean in a Boot app, so it is never used.
  • Ambiguous converters for overlapping types.
  • Returning null for bad data.
  • Hidden database calls in a converter without caching.
  • Expecting it for JSON bodies: Jackson does not use the Spring ConversionService.
  • @WebMvcTest without the converter: import it with @Import.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • The conversion lookup is cached; converting is cheap for simple types.
  • Keep converters stateless so one instance serves every thread.
  • Avoid converting to entities in the converter on high-traffic endpoints; pass the id and load in the service.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an API that accepts ?status=active and ?since=2025-01-31. One converter maps text to an enum, and @DateTimeFormat handles the date; both are covered by a single MockMvc test.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Formatter: a Spring SPI (org.springframework.format.Formatter<T>) that converts between a String and an object, in both directions, using the request Locale.
  • Built-in formatters handle dates, numbers and currency through @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat on fields and parameters.
  • Why not only converters: a converter is locale-free, while a formatter parses and prints text for humans, such as 12/05/2026 or 1,234.50.

Worked Example 1

Global date format in Boot.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.format.date=dd/MM/yyyy
spring.mvc.format.date-time=dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm

# OUTPUT:
# every LocalDate parameter now accepts 05/03/2026 without annotations

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Test the binding with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Format a date request parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

Format a number field.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Spring MVC builds a FormattingConversionService that holds converters and formatters.
  • Each Formatter is wrapped by an adapter so it appears as String to T and T to String converters.
  • During binding, WebDataBinder asks the service to convert the request String to the target type.
  • Annotations such as @DateTimeFormat are found through AnnotationFormatterFactory beans (JSR-310 and Joda factories).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • @DateTimeFormat(iso = ISO.DATE) uses the ISO form 2026-03-05.
  • @DateTimeFormat(style = "S-") uses the locale short date style.
  • @NumberFormat(style = Style.CURRENCY) or Style.PERCENT for money and percent.
  • Boot properties spring.mvc.format.date, time and date-time set global patterns.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registration: formatters are added to the FormatterRegistry by overriding addFormatters in WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Annotation driven: @DateTimeFormat(pattern = "dd/MM/yyyy") works on LocalDate, Date and Calendar without any extra code.
  • Print side: formatters also render values in views, for example the Thymeleaf double-brace syntax or the JSP spring:eval tag.

Senior Notes

  • ConversionService: Spring MVC uses FormattingConversionService, which holds both converters and formatters behind one API.
  • Boot defaults: the spring.mvc.format.date property sets a global date pattern, so you avoid repeating annotations.
  • Scope: formatters apply to request parameters, path variables and form binding, but not to JSON bodies, which Jackson handles.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Using formatters on JSON: they are ignored; use @JsonFormat or Jackson modules.
  • No pattern given: a LocalDate parameter then needs the locale default style and often fails with 400.
  • Wrong pattern case: MM is month, mm is minutes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Formatters are singletons; avoid creating DateTimeFormatter per call, since it is immutable and can be cached.
  • Do not use SimpleDateFormat in a shared formatter, because it is not thread safe.
  • Heavy parsing inside a formatter (database lookups) should move to a converter plus caching.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A booking form accepts dd/MM/yyyy dates from users in India and shows them back in the same style.
  • One global property sets the format, so no field needs an annotation.
  • The REST API uses ISO dates through Jackson for machine clients.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom Formatter: your own class implementing Formatter<T> with two methods, parse(String, Locale) and print(T, Locale).
  • Use it when a value has a human text form that built-in formatters do not know, such as a phone number, a money amount with currency or a product code.
  • Register it in WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters; after that the type binds automatically from text.

Worked Example 1

Controller using the formatter.

Worked Example 2

Bad input handled.

Practice Exercise 1

A formatter for Money like 12.50 USD.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Registry call addFormatter(f) reads the generic type T of the formatter and registers a Printer and a Parser for it.
  • On binding, the parser is invoked with the String and the current Locale from LocaleContextHolder.
  • A ParseException or IllegalArgumentException becomes a conversion failure.
  • The printer runs when a view renders the value through the conversion service.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Plain Formatter bean in Boot or addFormatter in a configurer.
  • addFormatterForFieldType(Class, Printer, Parser) for separate print and parse logic.
  • AnnotationFormatterFactory for options such as @Phone(region = "IN").

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Throw ParseException from parse for bad input; Spring turns it into a binding error (typeMismatch) instead of a 500.
  • Annotation based: implement AnnotationFormatterFactory to create @PhoneNumber-style annotations that carry options.
  • Be stateless: a formatter is a shared singleton, so keep no per-request fields and do not use non thread safe classes like SimpleDateFormat.

Senior Notes

  • Round trip: print(parse(s)) should equal s; test that property because forms re-display values.
  • Component scanning: in Spring Boot a Formatter bean is auto registered, no configurer needed.
  • Locale: use the passed Locale, never the JVM default, or users in other countries see wrong output.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Returning null on bad input hides errors; throw ParseException.
  • Using the default locale instead of the argument.
  • Forgetting to register: the binding then fails with no converter found.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Keep parsing allocation free: precompiled Pattern constants.
  • Do not call remote services in parse; it runs on the request thread for every bind.
  • Cache lookup results if you must resolve codes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A logistics app receives shipment codes like ABC-1234 in query strings.
  • A Code formatter converts them once; controllers just declare a Code parameter.
  • Invalid codes give a clean 400 with no manual parsing in controllers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Converter: an interface Converter<S, T> with one method T convert(S source) that turns a source type into a target type.
  • Use it to bind simple request text, such as an id or a code, to a domain object like Country or an enum with a custom spelling.
  • Register with registry.addConverter in WebMvcConfigurer, or expose it as a Spring Boot bean.

Worked Example 1

Register in plain Spring MVC.

Worked Example 2

Unit test the converter.

Practice Exercise 1

String id to Country.

Practice Exercise 2

Use it as a parameter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • GenericConversionService stores converters in a map keyed by ConvertiblePair(source, target).
  • For a request it walks the class hierarchy of source and target to find the closest match.
  • The found converter is cached per type pair for the next call.
  • A Converter is wrapped in ConverterAdapter; its generics are resolved by ResolvableType.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Converter<S,T>: one pair.
  • ConverterFactory<S,R>: all subtypes of R, for example every enum.
  • GenericConverter: several pairs and access to field annotations through TypeDescriptor.
  • ConditionalConverter: add a matches check.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Not locale aware: a converter has no Locale, so choose Formatter for user facing text and Converter for technical conversions.
  • ConverterFactory converts to a family of types (one factory for all enums of a base type); GenericConverter handles collections and several pairs.
  • Null and empty: decide what an empty string means; return null deliberately and never throw for empty input unless required.

Senior Notes

  • Lookup: GenericConversionService searches converters by source and target type hierarchy, so the most specific match wins.
  • Lambda trap: addConverter(s -> ...) loses generic types, so use an anonymous class or a named class.
  • Failure: an exception inside convert becomes a ConversionFailedException and finally HTTP 400 or a binding error.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Lambda registration loses generics and throws an exception at startup.
  • Returning null for unknown ids makes controllers fail later with NullPointerException.
  • Hitting the database per element when binding a list.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Converters should be fast and side effect free.
  • For database lookups, cache the table or fetch ids in one query in the service.
  • Prefer binding an id and loading the entity in the service to keep transactions clear.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • An admin screen shows countries as dropdown with code values.
  • A converter turns the posted code into a Country object inside the form bean.
  • Unknown codes yield a typeMismatch error rather than a null pointer.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Type conversion turns request text (always String) into method parameter types such as int, LocalDate, enums or your own classes.
  • Who does it: WebDataBinder uses the ConversionService first, then falls back to PropertyEditor instances.
  • Failure gives a MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException (HTTP 400) for parameters or a typeMismatch field error for form objects.

Worked Example 1

Controller-local trimming with @InitBinder.

Worked Example 2

Test a mismatch.

Practice Exercise 1

Built-in conversions.

Practice Exercise 2

Failed conversion.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Argument resolvers (for example RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver) create a WebDataBinder.
  • The binder calls convertIfNecessary on a TypeConverterDelegate.
  • Order: custom PropertyEditor, ConversionService, default editors, then constructor or string based fallback.
  • Failure raises TypeMismatchException, wrapped into MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException for parameters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Primitives and wrappers, enums, UUID, Locale, Currency, Optional wrapping are built in.
  • Collections from comma separated Strings; arrays likewise.
  • Id to entity via DomainClassConverter in Spring Data web support.
  • @InitBinder with setDisallowedFields or custom editors for one controller.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: custom editors from @InitBinder, then the ConversionService, then default editors for primitives, arrays and collections.
  • @InitBinder customizes one controller: binder.registerCustomEditor or binder.addCustomFormatter.
  • Collections: a=1,2,3 converts to List<Integer> through the built-in String to Collection converter.

Senior Notes

  • Enum binding is case sensitive by default; add a converter to accept lower case values.
  • Exception path: TypeMismatchException is mapped to 400 by DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Prefer ConversionService: it is thread safe and shared, while PropertyEditor is stateful and created per binder.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Primitive and empty value: int a with a= fails; use Integer.
  • Enum case: ?status=active fails against ACTIVE.
  • Expecting JSON conversion from the ConversionService.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Conversion is cheap, but avoid exceptions for control flow in custom converters.
  • Reuse the shared ConversionService bean rather than creating one per request.
  • Prefer typed parameters over parsing Strings in the controller.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A search endpoint takes ids=1,2,3, a status enum and a date range.
  • All types come straight from the query string with no manual parsing.
  • Bad values give 400 and a clear message from the error handler.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring Validation checks incoming data before business logic runs, using the Validator interface or Bean Validation annotations.
  • Two styles: implement org.springframework.validation.Validator by hand, or annotate fields with @NotBlank, @Size and trigger with @Valid.
  • Results are stored in an Errors / BindingResult object, which the view uses to show messages next to fields.

Worked Example 1

Attach a validator to a controller.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Manual validator.

Practice Exercise 2

Annotation style.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Spring core defines Validator and Errors; MVC wires them through WebDataBinder.
  • When the binder finishes binding, binder.validate() calls every registered validator.
  • Boot provides LocalValidatorFactoryBean, an adapter that exposes Bean Validation as a Spring Validator.
  • Error codes are resolved by DefaultMessageCodesResolver into a list from most to least specific.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Manual Validator with ValidationUtils.
  • Annotation based through LocalValidatorFactoryBean.
  • SmartValidator adds validate(target, errors, hints...) for groups.
  • Both styles can run together on one binder.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Validator contract: supports(Class) says which types it handles and validate(Object, Errors) records problems.
  • ValidationUtils has helpers like rejectIfEmptyOrWhitespace to keep manual validators short.
  • Messages come from a MessageSource by error code such as NotBlank.user.name, which allows internationalization.

Senior Notes

  • Boot auto configures a LocalValidatorFactoryBean when a Bean Validation provider (Hibernate Validator) is on the classpath.
  • Combine both: binder.addValidators(new MyValidator()) in @InitBinder runs your code together with annotations.
  • Layering: validate shape in the web layer, and enforce business rules (uniqueness) in the service and the database.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • setValidator replaces the default validator, so annotations stop working; use addValidators.
  • Missing starter: no Hibernate Validator means annotations are ignored silently in some setups.
  • Validator supports wrong class and never runs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Validation is CPU cheap; cost comes from extra database checks.
  • Run expensive checks (uniqueness) only after cheap field checks pass.
  • The validator factory is created once and reused; never build it per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A signup form: annotations check shape, a validator checks that password and confirm match.
  • Messages are internationalized through messages_hi.properties.
  • The database unique index remains the final guard.
codeExamples:
# messages.properties
NotBlank.form.name=Please enter your name
Size.form.password=Password needs 8 to 30 characters
password.mismatch=Passwords do not match

# OUTPUT:
# form shows the three messages next to the fields

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Bean Validation is the standard (JSR 380 / Jakarta Validation) for declaring constraints as annotations on fields, getters and parameters.
  • Common constraints: @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Min, @Max, @Email, @Pattern.
  • Implementation: the spec is only an API; Hibernate Validator is the reference provider that Spring Boot pulls in with spring-boot-starter-validation.

Worked Example 1

Validate programmatically.

Worked Example 2

Cascade with @Valid.

Practice Exercise 1

Annotated DTO.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom constraint.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • A constraint is an annotation marked with @Constraint; its ConstraintValidator holds the logic.
  • Validator.validate(obj) builds a metadata model of the class and runs each validator.
  • Results are ConstraintViolation objects with path, message and invalid value.
  • Spring adapts the result to FieldError entries in the BindingResult.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Strings: @NotBlank, @Size, @Pattern, @Email.
  • Numbers: @Min, @Max, @Positive, @DecimalMin, @Digits.
  • Dates: @Past, @Future, @PastOrPresent.
  • Collections: @NotEmpty, @Size, container element constraints such as List<@NotBlank String>.
  • Class level constraints for cross field rules.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Differences: @NotNull rejects null only, @NotEmpty also empty, @NotBlank also whitespace only (Strings).
  • Custom constraint: define an annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy = ...) and a class implementing ConstraintValidator.
  • Nested objects: put @Valid on the field to cascade into the inner object or each element of a collection.

Senior Notes

  • Groups let one class have different rules for create and update, selected with @Validated(Create.class).
  • Messages: set message on each constraint or use ValidationMessages.properties and Spring MessageSource.
  • Starter: since Spring Boot 2.3 the validation starter is no longer inside the web starter, so add it explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • @NotNull on a String lets empty text pass; use @NotBlank.
  • @Size on a number is invalid; use @Min and @Max.
  • Primitives can never be null, so @NotNull on int is useless.
  • Missing @Valid on the parameter, so nothing is checked.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • The validator factory is thread safe and costly to create; Spring creates one.
  • Use failFast in Hibernate Validator to stop at the first violation for large graphs.
  • Avoid database calls inside ConstraintValidator unless needed; they run for every request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A product API shares a DTO across create and update with groups.
  • An @UniqueSku constraint calls the service to check the database.
  • Error responses list each field and message in JSON.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Jakarta Validation is the same Bean Validation API after its move from javax.validation to the jakarta.validation packages (Jakarta EE 9+).
  • Spring Boot 3 and Framework 6 require the Jakarta names, so imports use jakarta.validation.constraints.*.
  • Same annotations: @NotNull, @Size, @Valid behave as before; only the package prefix changed.

Worked Example 1

Detect the wrong import.

Worked Example 2

Verify it works.

Practice Exercise 1

Boot 3 imports.

Practice Exercise 2

Maven dependency.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
<!-- adds hibernate-validator and the jakarta.validation API -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Jakarta EE 9 renamed all javax.* specs to jakarta.*; behavior stayed the same.
  • Spring Framework 6 and Boot 3 are built on Jakarta EE 9/10, so they look for jakarta.validation only.
  • The provider (Hibernate Validator 8) reads annotations from the jakarta packages.
  • Annotations from javax.validation are just unknown annotations and are skipped.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Versions: Jakarta Validation 3.0 (EE 9/10) uses jakarta names; 2.0 (javax) was Java EE 8.
  • Boot 2.x uses javax; Boot 3.x uses jakarta.
  • Spring specific @Validated does not change.
codeExamples:
# Dependency check
./mvnw dependency:tree | grep validat

# OUTPUT: (versions vary)
# org.hibernate.validator:hibernate-validator
# jakarta.validation:jakarta.validation-api

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Migration: replace javax.validation with jakarta.validation in imports; Boot 3 projects will not compile with the old names.
  • Provider: use Hibernate Validator 8 (Jakarta Validation 3.0) with Boot 3; Hibernate Validator 6 and 7 are for older stacks.
  • Mixed classpath: an old library with javax annotations is silently ignored, so constraints seem to do nothing.

Senior Notes

  • Expression Language: Hibernate Validator needs an EL implementation (Boot starter includes Tomcat Embed EL) for message interpolation.
  • Tooling: OpenRewrite and the Spring Boot Migrator automate the javax to jakarta rename.
  • Spring type: @Validated is Spring specific and stays in org.springframework.validation.annotation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Partial rename: some imports changed, others not, giving mixed errors.
  • Old shared library compiled with javax annotations: constraints silently ignored.
  • Missing EL gives HV000183 style startup errors.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • No runtime cost for the rename; startup scans the same metadata.
  • Use OpenRewrite recipes to migrate large code bases in one pass.
  • Run the full test suite after migration, because ignored constraints do not fail compilation.
codeExamples:
# Maven (OpenRewrite)
./mvnw org.openrewrite.maven:rewrite-maven-plugin:run -Drewrite.activeRecipes=org.openrewrite.java.migrate.jakarta.JavaxMigrationToJakarta

# OUTPUT:
# imports rewritten from javax.* to jakarta.*  (check the diff)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A team upgrades a Boot 2.7 service to Boot 3.
  • Controller tests for 400 responses suddenly fail because a shared DTO jar still uses javax constraints.
  • Upgrading the jar (or rewriting its imports) restores the validation.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @Valid (jakarta.validation.Valid) tells Spring to run Bean Validation on a method argument, such as a form object or a @RequestBody.
  • Failure: with @RequestBody it throws MethodArgumentNotValidException (400); with @ModelAttribute and a following BindingResult you handle errors yourself.
  • Cascade: placed on a field, it validates the nested object or the elements of a collection too.

Worked Example 1

Return field errors as JSON.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test.

Practice Exercise 1

Validate a JSON body.

Practice Exercise 2

Form with BindingResult.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • ModelAttributeMethodProcessor and RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor create a binder for the argument.
  • They check for @Valid or @Validated through ValidationAnnotationUtils and call binder.validate().
  • If the next parameter is a BindingResult the errors go there, otherwise an exception is thrown.
  • MethodArgumentNotValidException is mapped to 400 by DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • On @RequestBody, @ModelAttribute, plain model parameters and HttpEntity.
  • On a field or collection element for cascading.
  • Combined with @Validated on the class for simple parameters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Placement rule: the BindingResult parameter must come immediately after the validated argument.
  • No groups: @Valid cannot select groups; use @Validated for that.
  • Bad request body: the response comes from DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver, or from your @ExceptionHandler returning field messages as JSON.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanism: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor and ModelAttributeMethodProcessor call WebDataBinder.validate() when they see the annotation.
  • Order: binding and conversion run first; validation runs only on the bound object.
  • Not for simple params: @Valid on @RequestParam does nothing; put @Validated on the class instead.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • BindingResult in the wrong place, causing the exception even though a result exists.
  • @Valid on @RequestParam has no effect.
  • Forgetting cascade: nested object constraints are skipped without @Valid on the field.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Validation runs once per argument, which is cheap for small DTOs.
  • Large collections: use @Size(max=...) to cap input before deep cascade.
  • Limit request body size so a huge payload is rejected early.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A REST API returns a uniform error body listing every invalid field.
  • A @RestControllerAdvice converts MethodArgumentNotValidException to JSON.
  • The client highlights fields by the keys returned.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @Validated (org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated) is Spring own variant of @Valid that also supports validation groups.
  • On a class, it enables method validation, so constraints on @RequestParam, @PathVariable and service arguments are checked.
  • Failure on method parameters throws ConstraintViolationException (not a binding error), which you map to 400 yourself.

Worked Example 1

Map the exception to 400.

Worked Example 2

Service level validation.

Practice Exercise 1

Groups for create and update.

Practice Exercise 2

Validate path and query values.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • @Validated on a class marks it for MethodValidationPostProcessor, which creates an AOP proxy.
  • The proxy calls MethodValidationInterceptor, which uses the Jakarta ExecutableValidator for parameters and return values.
  • Violations become ConstraintViolationException.
  • On a parameter, @Validated(Group.class) is read by the MVC argument resolvers to select groups.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Class level: enables method validation.
  • Parameter level with groups: @Validated(Create.class).
  • Group sequences with @GroupSequence to order cheap and expensive checks.
  • Return value constraints validate what a method returns.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Groups: @Validated(OnCreate.class) on a parameter checks only constraints with that group.
  • Simple params: @Validated on the controller plus @Min(1) on @PathVariable long id validates path values.
  • Service layer: put @Validated on a bean class and constraints on its method arguments to validate non web calls.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanism: MethodValidationPostProcessor wraps the bean in an AOP proxy with MethodValidationInterceptor.
  • Proxy limits: self invocation and private or final methods skip validation.
  • Spring 6.1: built-in method validation for controllers can raise HandlerMethodValidationException instead; check your version before writing handlers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Self invocation: calling this.deposit(-1) skips the proxy.
  • Missing class annotation: parameter constraints on a controller do nothing.
  • Expecting BindingResult: method validation raises an exception instead.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • One proxy interceptor per call; overhead is small compared to I/O.
  • Do not put heavy checks in constraints on frequently called methods.
  • Use groups to avoid running create rules on update.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A paged API checks page >= 0 and size <= 100 on query parameters.
  • A handler for ConstraintViolationException returns 400 with the messages.
  • The same constraints also protect service methods called from batch jobs.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • BindingResult holds the outcome of data binding and validation for one model object: field errors, global errors and the rejected values.
  • Position: it must be declared right after the @Valid or @ModelAttribute parameter, or Spring throws an exception instead of filling it.
  • Use: check result.hasErrors() and redisplay the form; the view reads the errors, for example with th:errors or form:errors.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • BindingResult is implemented by BeanPropertyBindingResult, created by the WebDataBinder.
  • It stores ObjectError and FieldError lists and the original rejected values.
  • Argument resolvers add it to the model so views can read it.
  • Type mismatches add a FieldError with code typeMismatch.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • rejectValue(field, code, message) and reject(code, message).
  • hasErrors(), hasFieldErrors(field), getErrorCount().
  • Model attribute name must match the form object name for the view to find errors.
  • Use RedirectAttributes flash attributes to carry errors across a redirect.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Add your own error: result.rejectValue("email", "email.taken", "Already used") for a field, result.reject(...) for the whole object.
  • Read errors: getFieldErrors(), getFieldError("name") and getAllErrors().
  • Rejected value is kept (getRejectedValue), so the form can show what the user typed, even when conversion failed.

Senior Notes

  • Model key: the result is stored in the model as org.springframework.validation.BindingResult.<name> and shares the object with the same attribute name.
  • Redirect pitfall: errors are lost on redirect; use forward (return the view) or flash attributes for the result.
  • REST: for @RequestBody a BindingResult parameter suppresses the exception, so you must return the 400 yourself.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Wrong parameter order.
  • Ignoring errors: forgetting hasErrors() and saving invalid data.
  • Different attribute names so the view cannot find the errors.
  • Redirect after errors without flash attributes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Errors are small objects created per request; the cost is negligible.
  • Avoid database checks before hasFieldErrors short circuits.
  • Keep messages in a MessageSource, which caches loaded bundles.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A signup page shows an error beside each field and a summary on top.
  • A global error from reject says that the account could not be created.
  • A test confirms field errors with MockMvc model() assertions.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Validator is the Spring interface org.springframework.validation.Validator that checks an object and records problems in an Errors object.
  • Two methods: supports(Class) says which types it can check, and validate(Object, Errors) does the checking.
  • Use it by registering it in @InitBinder with binder.addValidators(...) or by calling it by hand.

Worked Example 1

Unit test without Spring.

Worked Example 2

Calling a validator by hand.

Practice Exercise 1

A Validator for a Person.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it on a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The DataBinder owns the validators and calls them after binding.

  • Binding: request params are bound to the target, then binder.validate() runs.
  • Loop: each registered Validator is called with the target and the BindingResult.
  • Global validator: Boot registers LocalValidatorFactoryBean, which runs Bean Validation.
  • Check: addValidators calls supports first and fails fast if the type is wrong.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of Validator usage.

  • @InitBinder: per controller, optional model name filter.
  • setValidator: replaces the default one instead of adding.
  • SmartValidator: adds validate(target, errors, hints) for groups.
  • Manual: call validate in a service.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ValidationUtils has helpers such as rejectIfEmptyOrWhitespace that keep validate() short.
  • Bean Validation bridge: LocalValidatorFactoryBean is a Spring Validator that runs jakarta.validation annotations.
  • Order: validators added in @InitBinder run when the model attribute is bound, before the handler body.

Senior Notes

  • supports() must be exact; a wrong class makes the binder throw IllegalStateException on addValidators.
  • Combine annotations for simple rules and a Validator for cross-field or database rules.
  • Testing: a Validator is a plain class, so unit test it with BeanPropertyBindingResult and no Spring context.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes.

  • Wrong supports: using equals instead of isAssignableFrom breaks proxies.
  • No @InitBinder name: the validator is applied to every model attribute and fails supports().
  • Null target: forgetting null checks in validate.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Cheap: a Validator is a plain object with no reflection cost.
  • Reuse: make it stateless and share one instance.
  • Database checks: avoid a query per field; do one lookup and report it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a booking form needs a rule that the room is free. Annotations cover required fields, and a Validator calls the booking service once and rejects the dates when taken.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom validator means your own constraint: an annotation plus a ConstraintValidator class that holds the rule.
  • Annotation needs message, groups and payload attributes and @Constraint(validatedBy=...).
  • Use it like any built-in constraint: put it on a field and add @Valid to the controller parameter.

Worked Example 1

Class-level match rule.

Worked Example 2

Test the validator alone.

Practice Exercise 1

A @StrongPassword constraint.

Practice Exercise 2

Use it in a DTO.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a custom constraint is resolved.

  • Scan: Hibernate Validator reads @Constraint(validatedBy) on your annotation.
  • Create: SpringConstraintValidatorFactory builds the validator as a bean-like object, so injection works.
  • Init: initialize(annotation) receives attribute values once.
  • Call: isValid runs for each validation and returns true or false.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for a custom constraint.

  • Field or parameter: choose with @Target.
  • Composed: combine existing constraints into one annotation using @ReportAsSingleViolation.
  • Cross-parameter: @SupportedValidationTarget for methods.
  • Repeatable: add a container annotation.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • isValid receives the value and a context; treat null as valid and let @NotNull handle it.
  • Spring beans can be injected into a ConstraintValidator, because Spring creates it through its own factory.
  • Class-level constraints (target TYPE) compare several fields, for example password and confirm.

Senior Notes

  • Custom node: use context.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(...).addPropertyNode(...) to put the error on the right field.
  • Cost: a validator that calls the database runs on every request, so keep it cheap or cache.
  • Testing: test the ConstraintValidator directly, and the whole path with @WebMvcTest.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Missing groups or payload: the provider throws a ConstraintDefinitionException.
  • Null returns false: optional fields fail; return true for null.
  • Not discovered: forgetting @Retention(RUNTIME).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Compile regex once: store a Pattern field, not matches per call.
  • Remote calls: a database check in isValid runs on each request.
  • Thread safety: validators must be stateless after initialize.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: usernames must be unique. A @UniqueUsername constraint injects the repository and checks existence, so every DTO that uses it gets the same rule.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Errors is the Spring interface org.springframework.validation.Errors that stores binding and validation problems for one target object.
  • Methods include reject (object error), rejectValue (field error), hasErrors and getFieldError.
  • BindingResult extends Errors and is the type you declare in a handler to receive the problems.

Worked Example 1

Read errors.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc check.

Practice Exercise 1

Use BindingResult.

Practice Exercise 2

Add errors by hand.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The Errors hierarchy.

  • Implementation: BeanPropertyBindingResult (or BindException) holds lists of ObjectError and FieldError.
  • Binder: the DataBinder creates it and adds type mismatches and validator results.
  • Argument resolver: ModelAttributeMethodProcessor passes it to the BindingResult parameter.
  • No parameter: it throws MethodArgumentNotValidException when errors exist.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful Errors API.

  • Check: hasErrors, hasFieldErrors(name), hasGlobalErrors.
  • Read: getAllErrors, getFieldValue(field).
  • Nested: pushNestedPath and popNestedPath.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Position: the BindingResult parameter must come right after the model attribute it describes.
  • Missing it makes Spring throw MethodArgumentNotValidException or BindException instead of calling the method.
  • Nested path: pushNestedPath("address") lets a validator report errors on a sub-object.

Senior Notes

  • Model key: errors live in the model under BindingResult.MODEL_KEY_PREFIX + name, so a redirect loses them.
  • Codes: each error carries several message codes from specific to general for message lookup.
  • Counting: getErrorCount, getFieldErrors and getGlobalErrors help build custom responses.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Wrong order: a parameter between the model attribute and BindingResult causes an exception.
  • Redirect: returning redirect with errors loses them.
  • Ignoring errors: not checking hasErrors saves bad data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Lazy messages: message lookup happens at render time.
  • Large forms: stop early with hasErrors in a multi-step validator.
  • Memory: errors are request scoped, so cost is small.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin screen validates a user form. The handler checks BindingResult, adds a global error when the account is locked, and shows both field and global messages.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • FieldError is an ObjectError subclass for a problem with one property, such as a blank name.
  • Data: it holds the object name, field, rejectedValue, codes, arguments and a default message.
  • Created by @Valid constraint failures, type mismatches and errors.rejectValue(...).

Worked Example 1

Show in Thymeleaf.
codeExamples: Error // Invalid email shown next to the input

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Type mismatch.

Practice Exercise 1

Read a FieldError.

Practice Exercise 2

Create one manually.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a FieldError appears.

  • Constraint: SpringValidatorAdapter converts each ConstraintViolation into a FieldError.
  • Codes: DefaultMessageCodesResolver builds codes such as NotBlank.user.name.
  • Arguments: include a DefaultMessageSourceResolvable for the field name, then the annotation attributes.
  • Message: the MessageSource formats the first matching code.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Constructors and options.

  • Short: new FieldError(object, field, message).
  • Full: adds rejectedValue, bindingFailure, codes, arguments.
  • rejectValue: the simplest way inside a Validator.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Get them with getFieldErrors() or getFieldError("age") from the BindingResult.
  • bindingFailure is true when the error came from type conversion (for example "abc" into an int), not from a constraint.
  • Views show them with Thymeleaf th:errors or the JSP form tag form:errors.

Senior Notes

  • Rejected value lets the form show what the user typed; never log it for passwords.
  • JSON APIs: map each FieldError to field plus message in your own error body.
  • Codes order: for field age on object user: Min.user.age, Min.age, Min.int, Min.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Wrong field name: an unknown property throws NotReadablePropertyException.
  • Leaking input: echoing rejected passwords.
  • Mixed lists: casting every ObjectError to FieldError throws ClassCastException.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Message lookup is cached by the MessageSource per locale.
  • Many errors: mapping thousands of FieldErrors for an API is cheap but cap the list size.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a form shows the user own wrong entry in the input and a message below it. Thymeleaf uses the FieldError rejected value and message; a CSS class is added with th:errorclass.
codeExamples: // input keeps "5" and shows: must be greater than or equal to 18

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ObjectError is a validation problem about the whole object, not one field, also called a global error.
  • FieldError extends ObjectError, so getAllErrors() returns both kinds.
  • Created by errors.reject("code", "message") or by class-level constraints.

Worked Example 1

Date range rule.

Worked Example 2

Test it.

Practice Exercise 1

Add a global error.

Practice Exercise 2

List all errors.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How global errors arise.

  • Direct: errors.reject(code) creates an ObjectError with the object name.
  • Class-level constraint: a violation with an empty property path becomes an ObjectError.
  • Codes: built as code.objectName then code.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants.

  • With args: reject(code, args, defaultMessage).
  • Class constraint: @ScriptAssert or your own TYPE-level annotation.
  • Move to field: addPropertyNode in the validator context.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Examples: passwords do not match, end date before start date, the account is blocked.
  • Read them with getGlobalErrors() from BindingResult.
  • Views: Thymeleaf shows them with #fields.hasGlobalErrors() and loop over #fields.globalErrors().

Senior Notes

  • Class-level constraints produce an ObjectError unless the validator moves the violation to a property node.
  • Design: attach to a field when the user can fix that field; use global errors for rules without one clear field.
  • API output: give global errors a separate list or a null field in your error body.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Not displayed: forgetting to render global errors in the view.
  • Wrong type: using reject when the field is known.
codeExamples: // lists each global error message above the form

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Order: run cheap field checks first and global checks only if no field errors.
  • Cost: global rules often touch several fields or a service, so guard them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a transfer form with source, target and amount. Fields are checked first; then a global error is added when source equals target.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Validation messages are the texts users see for failed rules; they come from the annotation message or from a properties file.
  • Placeholders such as {min} and {max} are filled from the annotation attributes.
  • Keys in curly braces, like message = "{user.name.required}", are looked up in ValidationMessages.properties.

Worked Example 1

Spring config for both.

Worked Example 2

Test a locale.

Practice Exercise 1

Messages in a properties file.

Practice Exercise 2

Annotation with key.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Message resolution flow.

  • Violation: Hibernate Validator interpolates the template, replacing {min} and resolving keys from ValidationMessages.
  • Adapter: Spring wraps the result in a FieldError with codes and the interpolated default message.
  • Render: the view calls the Spring MessageSource with the codes and locale.
  • Fallback: if no code matches, the default message is used.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration.

  • Basename: spring.messages.basename=messages,errors.
  • Locale: AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver by default, or a session or cookie resolver.
  • Fallback: spring.messages.fallback-to-system-locale.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.messages.basename=messages
spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8
spring.messages.cache-duration=PT10M

# OUTPUT:
# messages reload at most every 10 minutes

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Two sources: Bean Validation reads ValidationMessages.properties; Spring MVC reads its MessageSource with codes like NotBlank.user.name.
  • Locale: add messages_fr.properties and the LocaleResolver picks the file per request.
  • Boot sets the basename with spring.messages.basename.

Senior Notes

  • One source: make Bean Validation use the Spring MessageSource through LocalValidatorFactoryBean.setValidationMessageSource.
  • Encoding: set spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8 for non-Latin text.
  • Never hardcode user text in annotations on a product with several languages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Two systems: keys in messages.properties not applied to annotation braces, since those use ValidationMessages.
  • Wrong placeholder order: Spring uses positional numbers, Bean Validation uses names.
  • Cache: edits not visible until restart.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Caching: ResourceBundleMessageSource caches bundles; set a cache duration in development only.
  • Interpolation: Bean Validation caches parsed templates.
codeExamples:
# production: cache forever (default);
development: short cache
spring.messages.cache-duration=-1

# OUTPUT:
# bundles loaded once

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an app in English and Hindi. messages_en and messages_hi hold the same keys, the locale comes from a lang parameter via LocaleChangeInterceptor, and the same form shows translated errors.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Validation groups let one class have different rule sets by use case, for example create versus update.
  • A group is just an empty marker interface, like interface OnCreate {}.
  • Selecting a group in a controller uses @Validated(OnCreate.class) instead of @Valid.

Worked Example 1

GroupSequence.

Worked Example 2

Test groups.

Practice Exercise 1

Define and use groups.

Practice Exercise 2

Controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How groups are applied.

  • Selection: @Validated(Group.class) is read by the argument resolver and passed as hints to SmartValidator.validate.
  • Filter: Hibernate Validator runs only constraints whose groups match.
  • Inheritance: a group interface extending another includes the parent constraints.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants.

  • Several groups: groups = {A.class, B.class}.
  • Combine with Default: @Validated({Default.class, OnCreate.class}).
  • Sequence: @GroupSequence on a class redefines Default.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Constraints name their groups: @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class) on the id field.
  • Default group: a constraint without groups belongs to Default, which does not run when you select another group.
  • Extend Default in your marker (interface OnCreate extends Default) to run both.

Senior Notes

  • @Valid cannot choose a group; only the Spring @Validated can.
  • Order: @GroupSequence runs groups one after another and stops at the first failing group, useful to avoid costly checks.
  • Design: often separate DTOs for create and update are simpler than groups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • @Valid used: groups ignored; switch to @Validated.
  • Default skipped: plain constraints not checked when a custom group is selected.
  • Nested: cascaded objects also need matching groups.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Fewer checks: groups skip irrelevant constraints per request.
  • Sequences: put cheap groups first so expensive checks run only when needed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: one Employee payload used for POST and PUT. Create must have no id, update must have one; groups keep one class and two clear rules.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form validation in Spring MVC checks submitted form data and, on errors, shows the same form again with messages.
  • Flow: bind request params to a form object, validate it with @Valid, test BindingResult.hasErrors().
  • Success redirects (Post-Redirect-Get); failure returns the form view name.

Thymeleaf form.
