Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The request path for a form post.

  • Mapping: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter invokes the handler method.
  • Resolver: ServletModelAttributeMethodProcessor creates the object and binds the params.
  • Validate: it calls the validators when @Valid or @Validated is present.
  • Result: the BindingResult is put in the model so the view can read it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Form options.

  • Names: @ModelAttribute("form") sets the model key.
  • Allowed fields: binder.setAllowedFields blocks mass assignment.
  • Trimming: StringTrimmerEditor turns blanks into null.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Form object is a plain class with constraints like @NotBlank and @Email.
  • View uses th:field and th:errors so values and messages are kept.
  • GET form must put an empty object in the model, for example model.addAttribute("user", new UserForm()).

Senior Notes

  • PRG: never return a view after a successful POST, or a refresh submits again.
  • Server rules always matter; HTML required attributes are only hints and are easy to bypass.
  • Testing: use MockMvc with .param() and check the model errors and view name.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Return view after success: double submit.
  • No empty object on GET: template error.
  • @NotNull on strings: empty text passes; use @NotBlank.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Validate once: avoid calling validate again in the service for the same data.
  • Binding limits: setAutoGrowCollectionLimit protects against huge lists.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a registration page. The GET shows an empty form, the POST validates, shows errors in place, and on success redirects with a flash message.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • REST request validation checks a JSON body or parameters: put @Valid on a @RequestBody and constraints on the DTO.
  • Failure throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring turns into 400 Bad Request by default.
  • Parameters: constraints on @RequestParam and @PathVariable need @Validated on the class.

Worked Example 1

WebMvcTest.

Worked Example 2

Parameter validation.

Practice Exercise 1

Validated REST endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

Error body from an advice.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens for a JSON body.

  • Convert: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads JSON with Jackson.
  • Validate: it runs the validator when the parameter has @Valid.
  • Fail: it throws MethodArgumentNotValidException with the BindingResult.
  • Resolve: DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver sends 400, or your advice handles it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants.

  • Lists: List<@Valid Item> or a wrapper with @Valid on the list.
  • Params: @RequestParam @NotBlank String q with class-level @Validated.
  • Groups: @Validated(Group.class) on the body.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Java records work well as DTOs: record CreateUser(@NotBlank String name).
  • Custom body: handle the exception in @RestControllerAdvice and return a list of field errors.
  • Param violations throw ConstraintViolationException (or HandlerMethodValidationException in Spring 6.1+).

Senior Notes

  • Bad JSON (wrong types, broken syntax) throws HttpMessageNotReadableException, a different path from constraint errors.
  • Nested objects need @Valid on the nested field and on list elements to be checked.
  • Security: validate size limits (@Size) so clients cannot send huge payloads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Missing @Valid: no check at all.
  • Primitive defaults: a missing int becomes 0 and may pass; use Integer with @NotNull.
  • Leaking details: returning stack traces.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Limit sizes: @Size(max=...) and a server max request size.
  • Fail fast: Hibernate Validator can stop on the first violation with the hibernate.validator.fail_fast property.
  • Cheap rules first: avoid database lookups in constraints.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=2MB
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB

# OUTPUT:
# oversized request rejected before validation

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public orders API returns a uniform error list. The advice maps field errors to {field, message}, so clients can highlight the right input.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Exception handling in Spring MVC turns exceptions thrown by controllers into proper responses instead of a raw error page.
  • @ExceptionHandler marks a method that handles a given exception type in one controller.
  • @ControllerAdvice (or @RestControllerAdvice) shares such handlers across all controllers.

Worked Example 1

ProblemDetail.

Worked Example 2

Test the handler.

Practice Exercise 1

Global JSON handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Annotated exception.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How an exception is resolved.

  • Catch: DispatcherServlet.processHandlerException receives the exception.
  • Chain: it asks each HandlerExceptionResolver in order.
  • 1: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver finds @ExceptionHandler methods, controller first, then advice.
  • 2: ResponseStatusExceptionResolver handles @ResponseStatus and ResponseStatusException.
  • 3: DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps Spring exceptions to statuses such as 405 and 400.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to handle errors.

  • Local: @ExceptionHandler inside the controller.
  • Global: @ControllerAdvice, optionally limited by basePackages or annotations.
  • Status only: @ResponseStatus on the exception class.
  • Programmatic: ResponseStatusException.
  • Standard body: extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status: set it with @ResponseStatus, ResponseEntity or throw ResponseStatusException.
  • Resolvers: the DispatcherServlet asks HandlerExceptionResolver beans, such as ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, in order.
  • Unhandled exceptions go to the servlet container error page; Boot maps it to /error.

Senior Notes

  • ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, Spring 6) is the standard JSON error body; extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler to customize built-in errors.
  • Specific first: the most specific exception type wins, so put a generic Exception handler last.
  • Logging: log the stack trace once in the advice and send only a safe message to clients.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes.

  • Catch-all first: a general handler hides specific ones in the same class only if types are ambiguous; keep it specific.
  • Swallowing: returning 200 with an error text.
  • Handler throws: an exception inside a handler goes unhandled.
  • Lost status: returning a plain object gives 200; use ResponseEntity.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes.

  • Stack traces: creating them is costly; override fillInStackTrace for high-volume business exceptions.
  • Not control flow: prefer checking conditions to throwing in hot paths.
  • Logging: log once, at the advice, with the right level (warn for client errors).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop API. Domain exceptions (not found, out of stock) are thrown by services. One advice maps them to 404 and 409 with a ProblemDetail, logs unexpected errors with a correlation id, and returns a safe 500.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @ExceptionHandler marks a controller method that handles exceptions thrown by handler methods, so you can turn an exception into a response.
  • Scope: declared inside a controller it applies only to that controller; declared in a @ControllerAdvice class it applies to all controllers.
  • Arguments: the method can take the exception, HttpServletRequest, Model and similar, and can return a view, a body or a ResponseEntity.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a handler is found and called:

  • Catch: DispatcherServlet.processHandlerException loops over its resolver list.
  • Resolver: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver builds an ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver per controller class and caches it.
  • Matching: it picks the mapped exception type with the shortest depth to the thrown class.
  • Invoke: the method is run through ServletInvocableHandlerMethod, so argument resolvers and return value handlers work as in normal handlers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Supported method arguments and results:

  • Arguments: the exception, WebRequest, HttpServletRequest, HandlerMethod, Model, Locale, Principal.
  • Not allowed: @RequestBody and BindingResult are not available.
  • Results: String view name, ModelAndView, ResponseEntity, a body object with @ResponseBody, or void when the response is written directly.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Most specific wins: if several handlers match, Spring picks the one whose exception type is closest to the thrown type.
  • Status: add @ResponseStatus or return ResponseEntity, otherwise a handled exception answers with 200.
  • Several types: @ExceptionHandler({A.class, B.class}) maps many exceptions to one method.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver finds and calls the method through HandlerMethod machinery.
  • Cause matching: Spring also tries the cause of a wrapped exception when no handler matches the outer one.
  • Thrown after the response is committed: the handler cannot change the status any more.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • 200 on error: a handler that returns a body but no status answers 200; add @ResponseStatus.
  • Too broad: a local handler for Exception hides specific advice handlers.
  • Ambiguous mapping: two methods for the same exception type in one class cause an IllegalStateException at the first error.
  • Wrong scope: expecting a controller-local handler to catch another controller exceptions.
  • Swallowed cause: returning a message without logging the exception.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Cheap lookup: mappings are cached per class, so matching costs a map lookup.
  • Stack traces: the cost of an error path is mostly building the trace; do not use exceptions for routine branches.
  • Logging: log expected client errors at warn or debug without a trace, and unexpected ones at error with a trace.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order API throws OrderNotFoundException from the service. The controller owns a handler for it that also records a metric. Other controllers use the global advice.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @ControllerAdvice is a Spring component that shares @ExceptionHandler, @ModelAttribute and @InitBinder methods across many controllers.
  • Purpose: keep error handling in one class instead of copying it into every controller.
  • Registration: it is a @Component, so component scanning finds it; no other configuration is needed.

Worked Example 2

Test that advice applies (slice test).

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Startup and request flow:

  • Scan: ControllerAdviceBean.findAnnotatedBeans finds all beans annotated with @ControllerAdvice.
  • Sort: they are ordered by @Order or Ordered.
  • Cache: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver keeps an ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver per advice bean.
  • Request: the controller class is checked first, then each advice whose selector matches the handler.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Selectors and what the class can hold:

  • basePackages / basePackageClasses: choose by package.
  • assignableTypes: choose by controller type or interface.
  • annotations: choose controllers carrying an annotation.
  • Methods: @ExceptionHandler, @ModelAttribute, @InitBinder.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Narrowing: use basePackages, assignableTypes or annotations to limit which controllers are advised.
  • Ordering: several advices are ordered with @Order; the lowest value is asked first.
  • REST: @RestControllerAdvice is @ControllerAdvice plus @ResponseBody.

Senior Notes

  • Discovery: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver collects all advice beans through ControllerAdviceBean at startup.
  • Lookup order: handlers in the controller come first, then the advice beans by order.
  • Advices for requests: RequestBodyAdvice and ResponseBodyAdvice are separate hooks that also use this annotation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Not scanned: advice in a package outside component scanning is ignored.
  • Missing ResponseBody: with @ControllerAdvice a returned String is a view name; use @RestControllerAdvice for JSON.
  • Order surprise: a catch-all Exception handler with a high precedence hides specific ones.
  • Test slice: @WebMvcTest loads advice automatically, but a plain standalone setup needs setControllerAdvice.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Singleton: advice beans are created once and method lookup is cached.
  • Keep it light: @ModelAttribute methods run for every request of the advised controllers, so avoid database calls there.
  • Selectors: narrow scope so work is not repeated for unrelated controllers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a company has a public API and an admin site. Two advices keep their error formats separate by package.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RestControllerAdvice is a global advice class whose handler methods write their return value straight to the response body (it equals @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody).
  • Use: build JSON error responses for REST APIs in one place.
  • Return types: a plain object, a ResponseEntity, or ProblemDetail are all serialized by message converters.

Worked Example 1

Test the JSON body.

Worked Example 2

Advice for annotated controllers only.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it works:

  • Meta-annotation: @RestControllerAdvice carries @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody.
  • Handler: the result goes through RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor.
  • Converter: the Accept header picks an HttpMessageConverter, usually Jackson.
  • Not acceptable: if no converter matches, an error response cannot be written and a 406 may result.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • ResponseEntity: full control of status and headers.
  • ProblemDetail: RFC 7807 body, content type application/problem+json.
  • ErrorResponse: a Spring 6 interface that built-in exceptions implement, giving them a ProblemDetail.
  • ResponseEntityExceptionHandler: base class with handlers for MVC exceptions.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status codes: set them with @ResponseStatus or ResponseEntity, otherwise the status is 200.
  • ProblemDetail: Spring Framework 6 supports RFC 7807 style bodies through the ProblemDetail class.
  • ResponseEntityExceptionHandler: extend it to get ready handlers for standard MVC exceptions.

Senior Notes

  • Content negotiation: the body is written by an HttpMessageConverter, chosen from the Accept header.
  • No view resolution: because of @ResponseBody, a returned String is the body, not a view name.
  • Selectors: the same basePackages and annotations filters as in @ControllerAdvice.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Two beans handle the same exception: a class extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler plus another advice with the same handler gives an ambiguous mapping error.
  • Returning 200: forgetting the status.
  • Leaking text: returning e.toString().
  • Serialization failure: returning an entity with lazy proxies; return a DTO.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Small bodies: error records are cheap to serialize.
  • Reuse: Jackson caches serializers per class, so use stable record types.
  • Log once: log in the advice only, not again in the service, to avoid duplicate large traces.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile client needs one error format for every endpoint, including validation errors.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Global exception handling means one central place that converts every uncaught exception from controllers into a proper HTTP response.
  • Tools: @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods is the standard way; HandlerExceptionResolver is the low-level mechanism.
  • Benefit: controllers stay free of try/catch, and all errors share one format and one logging policy.

Worked Example 1

Verify the catch-all.

Worked Example 2

Trace id for support.

Practice Exercise 1

A layered global handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Controller stays clean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution pipeline:

  • 1: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver runs controller and advice @ExceptionHandler methods.
  • 2: ResponseStatusExceptionResolver handles @ResponseStatus and ResponseStatusException.
  • 3: DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps Spring exceptions to codes (for example 405, 415, 400).
  • 4: if none resolves, the exception propagates and the container dispatches to /error.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design options:

  • Advice only: simplest for REST.
  • Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler: one hook covering all standard MVC exceptions.
  • Boot ErrorController: covers errors that never reach MVC (filters, unknown paths).
  • Filter: an outer filter can catch exceptions thrown by other filters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Layers: specific handlers (business, validation) first, then a catch-all Exception handler returning 500.
  • Do not leak: never return stack traces or internal messages to the client; log them instead.
  • Errors outside MVC: filter errors and 404 for unknown URLs are handled by the servlet container or Boot error page, not by advice (unless configured).

Senior Notes

  • Chain: DispatcherServlet asks ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, then ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, then DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Fallback: if nothing resolves the exception it is rethrown and the container forwards to /error.
  • Boot: BasicErrorController serves that fallback as JSON or HTML.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Catch-all swallows security: a handler for Exception also catches AccessDeniedException thrown inside controllers, turning 403 into 500; add a specific handler or rethrow.
  • Leaking details: returning messages from unknown exceptions.
  • No logging: handled errors vanish silently.
  • Different formats: advice JSON but Boot errors HTML.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and operations:

  • Metrics: count errors by status to alert on spikes.
  • Log levels: client errors low level, server errors error level.
  • Rate of logs: a flood of failing requests can fill disks; avoid full traces for expected errors.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team of ten developers adds endpoints daily. One global advice guarantees every error has the same JSON and gets logged.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerExceptionResolver is the Spring MVC interface with one method, resolveException, that turns an exception into a ModelAndView (or an empty one if it wrote the response).
  • Built-in: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Role: the DispatcherServlet calls the resolvers in order until one returns non-null.

Worked Example 1

List the resolvers at runtime.

Worked Example 2

Test a custom resolver directly.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom resolver writing a response.

Practice Exercise 2

Map exceptions to views.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the DispatcherServlet:

  • Catch: doDispatch catches the exception and calls processHandlerException.
  • Loop: it calls each HandlerExceptionResolver in order.
  • Result: the first non-null ModelAndView wins, even an empty one meaning the response is done.
  • Nothing: if all return null the exception is rethrown.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to plug in:

  • Bean: a HandlerExceptionResolver bean is picked up in Spring Boot and added to the list.
  • extendHandlerExceptionResolvers: add to the list while keeping defaults.
  • configureHandlerExceptionResolvers: replace the defaults completely (rarely wanted).
  • AbstractHandlerExceptionResolver: base class with handler matching and setOrder.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Return value: returning null means "not mine, try the next resolver".
  • Custom resolver: implement the interface and register it as a bean, or add it through WebMvcConfigurer.extendHandlerExceptionResolvers.
  • SimpleMappingExceptionResolver: maps exception class names to view names, handy for classic pages.

Senior Notes

  • Composite: Spring builds a HandlerExceptionResolverComposite holding the list.
  • Ordering: custom resolvers with Ordered run by their order value.
  • Prefer annotations: most code needs only @ExceptionHandler, which is built on this interface.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning an empty ModelAndView by habit: it ends the chain; return null for exceptions you do not handle.
  • Resolver order: a custom resolver added last never sees what built-in ones handled.
  • Replacing defaults: configureHandlerExceptionResolvers removes @ExceptionHandler support.
  • Not seeing filter exceptions: resolvers only see exceptions from the DispatcherServlet.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Order: put cheap, frequently matching resolvers first.
  • Exit early: check instanceof before doing work.
  • Only on errors: resolvers run only on the failure path, so they do not slow normal requests.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy module throws its own exceptions in places where annotations cannot be used (a third-party base controller). A resolver bean maps them.

  • Custom error pages are friendly views shown for HTTP errors (404, 500) instead of the default container or whitelabel page.
  • Spring Boot way: place error/404.html, error/500.html or error/4xx.html under templates or static.
  • Mechanism: the container forwards the failed request to /error, which Boot serves with BasicErrorController.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The error dispatch:

  • 1: the controller throws, no resolver handles it, or sendError is called.
  • 2: the container forwards to /error (Boot registers an error page for it).
  • 3: BasicErrorController builds the model with ErrorAttributes.
  • 4: for HTML it asks ErrorViewResolver for a view; for other types it returns JSON.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options:

  • Files: templates/error/404.html, static/error/5xx.html.
  • Own controller: implement ErrorController and map /error.
  • Properties: server.error.path, include-message, include-binding-errors, include-stacktrace, include-exception.
  • Plain Spring MVC: register an error page in the container (web.xml or a Servlet registration).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lookup order: an exact code file (404.html) beats a series file (4xx.html).
  • Model attributes: error templates can read status, error, path and timestamp.
  • Whitelabel: switch it off with server.error.whitelabel.enabled=false only if you supply your own page.

Senior Notes

  • ErrorViewResolver: DefaultErrorViewResolver turns the status into a view name like error/404.
  • ErrorAttributes: DefaultErrorAttributes collects the data; show message and trace with the server.error.include-* properties.
  • Content type: BasicErrorController returns HTML for browsers and JSON for API clients.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong folder: templates/404.html is ignored; it must be under error/.
  • Secured /error: with Spring Security, /error must be permitted or users see 401 instead of 404.
  • Details shown: turning on trace output for production.
  • Static page uses model: a static HTML file cannot read the error attributes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Static error pages are the cheapest; use templates only when you need data.
  • Caching: static error files can be cached by the browser.
  • Bots: scanners hit many 404s; keep the error page light and avoid database calls.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP error responses tell the client a request failed: 4xx means the client made a mistake, 5xx means the server failed.
  • Common codes: 400 bad request, 401 unauthorized, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable, 500 server error.
  • Ways to set them: @ResponseStatus, ResponseEntity, ResponseStatusException or an exception handler.

Worked Example 1

ResponseEntity with headers.

Worked Example 2

Test the status code.

Practice Exercise 1

Status with ResponseStatusException.

Practice Exercise 2

Status on an exception class.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Three internal paths produce an error status:

  • ResponseEntity or setStatus: writes the status directly, the body is yours.
  • sendError (annotation or ResponseStatusException): marks the response as error and the container dispatches to /error.
  • Exception resolvers: the three default resolvers choose between these for each exception.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful status codes:

  • 400: malformed or invalid request.
  • 401 / 403: not authenticated / not allowed.
  • 404: unknown resource.
  • 405 / 415 / 406: wrong method, content type, accept.
  • 409: state conflict, duplicates.
  • 422: semantically invalid data.
  • 429: too many requests.
  • 500 / 502 / 503: server, upstream, unavailable.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ResponseStatusException: throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "no user") for a quick error without a custom class.
  • @ResponseStatus on an exception class gives it a fixed status and reason.
  • Pick the right code: do not answer 200 with an error message in the body.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: ResponseStatusExceptionResolver reads the annotation or exception and calls sendError or sets the status.
  • sendError: it triggers the container error dispatch to /error, which adds the Boot JSON body.
  • ResponseEntity: writes status and headers directly with no error dispatch.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • 200 with error text: clients and monitoring cannot see the failure.
  • 500 for client mistakes: missing parameter handled by a catch-all gives 500 instead of 400.
  • 401 vs 403 mixed up.
  • ResponseStatus with reason: the reason uses sendError and may replace your JSON body.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and caching notes:

  • Cheap errors: return early with a status and no heavy body.
  • Retry-After: tell clients when to try again for 429 and 503 to reduce retry storms.
  • Cache: 404 and 410 responses can carry cache headers when the answer is stable.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a payments API must return distinct codes so mobile apps can react.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom error response is a fixed JSON shape (for example code, message, time, path) that every failure in your API returns.
  • Why: clients can parse every error the same way instead of guessing between HTML, text and different JSON forms.
  • How: define a small class or record and return it from @RestControllerAdvice handler methods.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the body comes from:

  • Handler return value: your record is serialized by Jackson.
  • Boot fallback: DefaultErrorAttributes builds a map with timestamp, status, error, path.
  • ErrorResponse: Spring 6 exceptions like MethodArgumentNotValidException implement it and expose a ProblemDetail.
  • RFC 7807: the media type is application/problem+json.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Record: a plain record for your own contract.
  • ProblemDetail: standard, supports extra properties.
  • Boot ErrorAttributes: change what the default error JSON contains.
  • Locale text: use MessageSource to translate messages.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Fields: keep status, a machine-readable code, a human message, a timestamp and the path; add field errors for validation.
  • Standard: ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) is the built-in standard shape; use it unless you have your own contract.
  • Safe messages: never copy raw exception text from the database or framework.

Senior Notes

  • Path: take it from HttpServletRequest.getRequestURI() or WebRequest.getDescription(false).
  • Dates: Jackson with the Java time module writes Instant as ISO text when timestamps are disabled.
  • Boot errors: for errors outside advice, customise ErrorAttributes so the shape matches.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Several shapes: advice returns one format, but Boot defaults return another.
  • Instant as number: without ISO settings the time is a number; set spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false.
  • Null noise: fields set to null clutter the JSON; use @JsonInclude(NON_NULL).
  • Untranslated messages for international users.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Small records serialize quickly.
  • Avoid heavy fields: never embed entities, collections or stack traces.
  • Static messages: look up message bundles once per locale, which Spring caches.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: front-end developers want one JSON contract documented in the API spec, with a trace id to quote when raising support tickets.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Validation exceptions are thrown when request data breaks constraints such as @NotBlank or @Min.
  • Body validation: @Valid @RequestBody failing throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which carries a BindingResult.
  • Parameter validation: constraints on @RequestParam or @PathVariable need @Validated on the class and throw ConstraintViolationException.

Worked Example 1

Parameter constraints.

Worked Example 2

Test invalid body.

Practice Exercise 1

Request DTO and controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where each exception comes from:

  • @RequestBody: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor validates after reading the body and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • @ModelAttribute: ModelAttributeMethodProcessor throws BindException (or MethodArgumentNotValidException in Spring 6) when no BindingResult follows.
  • @Validated class: an AOP proxy with MethodValidationInterceptor throws ConstraintViolationException.
  • Bad JSON: HttpMessageNotReadableException, also a 400.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • Groups: validate different rules for create and update with @Validated(OnCreate.class).
  • Custom constraint: an annotation plus a ConstraintValidator.
  • Cascade: put @Valid on nested fields.
  • Messages: ValidationMessages.properties or a custom MessageSource.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Form binding: for @ModelAttribute the exception is BindException unless you declare a BindingResult parameter right after.
  • Default status: these exceptions give 400 Bad Request unless you handle them.
  • Collect errors: loop over getFieldErrors() to build a field-to-message map.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps them to 400 if no handler exists.
  • Spring 6.1: method validation raises HandlerMethodValidationException for controller parameters in newer setups.
  • Validator: Hibernate Validator runs through LocalValidatorFactoryBean, and messages come from message bundles.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No starter: constraints are silently ignored without spring-boot-starter-validation.
  • Missing @Valid: the body is never checked.
  • Missing @Validated for parameter constraints.
  • ConstraintViolationException unhandled: becomes 500.
  • BindingResult in wrong place: it must come right after the validated argument.
  • @NotNull on String: use @NotBlank to reject empty text.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Validator is thread-safe: one shared instance is reused.
  • Order: cheap checks first; avoid database lookups in constraints on hot endpoints.
  • Fail fast: Hibernate Validator can stop at the first violation with hibernate.validator.fail_fast.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a signup form API returns all field errors to the front end in one response.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Business exceptions are your own exceptions that express a broken business rule, such as InsufficientFundsException or OrderNotFoundException.
  • Design: extend RuntimeException so services stay free of throws clauses, and name them after the rule.
  • Mapping: a global advice turns each business exception into a suitable HTTP status and message.

Worked Example 1

Service throwing the rule.

Worked Example 2

Test the service rule.

Practice Exercise 1

Exceptions and service.

Practice Exercise 2

Handler that maps by type.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the flow works:

  • Service: checks a rule and throws a domain exception.
  • Transaction: the proxy sees an unchecked exception and rolls back.
  • Controller: does not catch it, the exception passes through.
  • Advice: maps the type to an HTTP status and body.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design variants:

  • Base class with code: one handler for all business errors.
  • Enum of errors: an enum holds code, status and message key.
  • Checked exceptions: force callers to deal with it, but clutter signatures; add rollbackFor if used with transactions.
  • Result objects: return a result type for expected failures to avoid exceptions.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Hierarchy: create a base BusinessException with a code, then subclasses; one handler can cover the whole family.
  • Transactions: unchecked exceptions roll back a @Transactional method by default; checked ones do not.
  • Not for flow control: do not use exceptions for ordinary branches that happen often.

Senior Notes

  • Layers: services throw domain exceptions, and only the web layer (advice) knows about HTTP statuses.
  • Cost: creating a stack trace is the expensive part; for very hot paths override fillInStackTrace or use a constructor that disables it.
  • Message keys: store an error code and look the text up from a message bundle for translation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Catch and ignore in the service: the rule failure is lost.
  • Checked exception without rollbackFor: data is committed despite the error.
  • HTTP types in the service: ResponseStatusException in domain code couples layers.
  • Generic RuntimeException: the handler cannot tell rules apart.
  • Wrapping and losing the cause: always pass the cause to the constructor.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Stack trace cost: exceptions used for expected, frequent outcomes can be costly; disable the stack trace for them.
  • Validate early: cheap checks before database work.
  • Logging: log business failures at info or warn without a trace.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a banking service turns three business rules into clear, testable API answers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style where a server exposes resources identified by URLs and clients act on them with HTTP methods.
  • Representations such as JSON travel between client and server; the resource itself stays on the server.
  • Stateless: every request carries everything the server needs, so no HTTP session is required.

Worked Example 1

Stateless check with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Created with Location header.

Practice Exercise 1

Tiny resource API: list and get.

Practice Exercise 2

Verb to action mapping.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A REST call in Spring MVC passes through these components:

  • DispatcherServlet receives every request (front controller).
  • HandlerMapping finds the controller method from URL and HTTP method.
  • HandlerAdapter resolves arguments (@RequestBody, @PathVariable) and invokes the method.
  • HttpMessageConverter reads the request body and writes the return value.
  • Exception resolvers turn thrown exceptions into error responses.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

REST architectural constraints and what they mean in practice:

  • Client-server: UI and data storage are separate.
  • Stateless: no server session between calls.
  • Cacheable: responses declare whether they can be cached.
  • Uniform interface: resources, representations, standard verbs.
  • Layered system: proxies, gateways and load balancers sit between client and server.
  • Code on demand: optional.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Uniform interface: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes.
  • Layers in Spring: DispatcherServlet routes to a controller, the service holds logic, the repository talks to the database.
  • Status codes carry the result: 200, 201, 204, 400, 404, 409, 500.

Senior Notes

  • Scalability: statelessness lets you add servers behind a load balancer without sticky sessions.
  • Caching: safe GET responses can use Cache-Control and ETag.
  • HATEOAS (links inside responses) is the highest REST maturity level, but most APIs stop at level 2 (resources plus verbs).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common architecture mistakes:

  • Server session state: breaks horizontal scaling; use tokens.
  • Verbs in URLs: use nouns plus HTTP methods.
  • Always returning 200: use proper codes.
  • POST for everything: loses caching and idempotency.
  • Chatty APIs: too many tiny calls; offer aggregate endpoints.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tuning for REST services:

  • HTTP caching with ETag and ShallowEtagHeaderFilter saves bandwidth.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true.
  • Pagination for large collections.
  • Avoid N+1 queries behind the API with fetch joins.
  • Keep-alive and HTTP/2 reduce connection cost.
codeExamples:
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.min-response-size=1024
server.http2.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# JSON responses over 1 KB are gzip compressed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an order service behind an API gateway.

  • The gateway validates the JWT and forwards the request.
  • Any instance can answer, because nothing is stored in a session.
  • The controller maps to DTOs; the service runs in a transaction.
  • Errors return ProblemDetail JSON with the right status.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • RESTful API design means modelling your domain as resources with clear URLs, correct HTTP methods and meaningful status codes.
  • Use nouns in URLs: /api/orders, not /api/getOrders; the HTTP method is the verb.
  • Plural collections and nesting: /api/users/5/orders reads as the orders of user 5.

Worked Example 1

Missing resource returns 404.

Worked Example 2

Test the contract.

Practice Exercise 1

CRUD design table in code.

Practice Exercise 2

Bad and good URLs.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How design decisions map to Spring internals:

  • URL and verb are matched by RequestMappingInfo conditions (path, method, consumes, produces).
  • Status comes from ResponseEntity, @ResponseStatus or an exception resolver.
  • Paging parameters are bound to Pageable by PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver (Spring Data).
  • Errors are produced by ResponseEntityExceptionHandler or your advice.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design variants worth knowing:

  • Versioning: path, header (X-API-Version) or media type.
  • Sub-resources: /orders/5/items; keep nesting to two levels.
  • Actions: model as sub-resource, for example POST /orders/5/cancellation.
  • Filtering: query parameters; sorting with sort=price,desc.
  • Bulk: POST an array, return a per-item result.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status codes: 201 with a Location header on create, 204 on delete, 404 when missing, 400 for bad input.
  • Filtering and paging use query parameters: ?page=0&size=20&sort=name.
  • Versioning through the path (/api/v1) or a header keeps old clients working.

Senior Notes

  • Consistent errors: return one error shape everywhere, ideally RFC 7807 ProblemDetail, via @RestControllerAdvice.
  • DTOs keep the API contract separate from JPA entities, so schema changes do not break clients.
  • Idempotency: make PUT and DELETE safe to retry; use an idempotency key for POST payments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Frequent design mistakes:

  • Exposing entities: use DTOs.
  • 200 with error text: use correct status codes.
  • Inconsistent naming: pick one case style (camelCase) everywhere.
  • Unbounded lists: always page.
  • Breaking changes in place: add fields, do not remove or rename without a new version.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning API design for speed:

  • Sparse fields: let clients ask for only the fields they need.
  • Conditional GET with ETag returns 304 without a body.
  • Cursor paging beats offset paging on big tables.
  • Limit page size with a maximum to protect the database.
codeExamples:
spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100
spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size=20

# OUTPUT:
# GET /api/users?size=5000 is capped at 100 rows

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an e-commerce catalogue API.

  • Public GET endpoints are cacheable and paged.
  • Write endpoints need a JWT and validate input.
  • A v2 path is introduced when the price object changes shape.
  • Contract tests (MockMvc) lock the JSON shape for each version.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • REST controller is a Spring bean that handles HTTP requests and writes the return value straight into the response body (usually JSON) instead of rendering a view.
  • Declare it with @RestController and map methods with @GetMapping, @PostMapping and friends.
  • Return values are converted by an HttpMessageConverter, normally Jackson for JSON.

Worked Example 1

Slice test.

Worked Example 2

Controller with a service.

Practice Exercise 1

Hello REST controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Path variable and status.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens when a REST controller method runs:

  • RequestMappingHandlerAdapter builds an InvocableHandlerMethod.
  • Argument resolvers fill parameters (@PathVariable, @RequestBody).
  • The method is invoked by reflection.
  • Return value handlers pick RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor because of @ResponseBody.
  • The processor selects a converter by Accept header and writes the body.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controller method options:

  • Return types: object, ResponseEntity, void with @ResponseStatus, Optional (not unwrapped specially), reactive or Callable for async.
  • Mapping attributes: path, method, params, headers, consumes, produces.
  • Shortcuts: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Inputs: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody and @RequestHeader.
  • ResponseEntity lets you control status code, headers and body in one object.
  • Thin controller: only translate HTTP to a service call and back; keep business logic in services.

Senior Notes

  • Content negotiation: produces and consumes plus the Accept header pick the converter.
  • Validation: add @Valid on the body; failures raise MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • Testing: use @WebMvcTest with MockMvc and a @MockBean service for fast slice tests.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • @Controller instead of @RestController: add the right annotation.
  • Business logic in the controller: move it to a service.
  • Returning entities: return DTOs.
  • Catching exceptions in each method: use one @RestControllerAdvice.
  • Field injection: use constructor injection for testability.
  • Missing @RequestBody: the parameter is then bound from form or query data and stays empty.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips for controllers:

  • Keep methods short and non-blocking in logic.
  • Use Callable or virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true in Boot 3.2+) for blocking calls under load.
  • Avoid reading the body twice.
  • Return DTOs with only needed fields.
  • Cache read-heavy responses with Cache-Control.
codeExamples:
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
server.tomcat.threads.max=200

# OUTPUT:
# Request handling uses virtual threads on Java 21

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a payments controller.

  • Validates the body with @Valid.
  • Delegates to PaymentService inside a transaction.
  • Returns 201 with a Location header.
  • Domain errors become 409 or 422 through the advice.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @RestController is a stereotype annotation equal to @Controller plus @ResponseBody on every method.
  • Effect: return values are written to the HTTP response body through message converters, never resolved as a view name.
  • Component scanning registers it as a bean, so it also works with constructor injection.

Worked Example 1

Test returns JSON.

Worked Example 2

Single method override.

Practice Exercise 1

Equivalent forms.

Practice Exercise 2

Wrong annotation pitfall.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The annotation is defined like this in the framework:

  • @RestController is meta-annotated with @Controller and @ResponseBody.
  • Spring checks for @ResponseBody on the method or declaring class when it selects a return value handler.
  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor supports the return type, so ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler is skipped.
  • Component scanning picks the class up because @Controller is a @Component.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and combinations:

  • Class level path: @RequestMapping("/api").
  • Bean name: @RestController("orders").
  • ResponseEntity still works and wins for status and headers.
  • Mixed controller: @Controller with @ResponseBody on single methods.
  • @RestControllerAdvice is the matching annotation for global error handling.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Compare: @Controller returns view names for Thymeleaf or JSP, while @RestController returns data.
  • Mixing: if one class needs both, use @Controller and add @ResponseBody only on data methods.
  • Combine with @RequestMapping on the class for a shared base path.

Senior Notes

  • Meta-annotation: it is annotated with @Controller and @ResponseBody, which is why it works with all their features.
  • Return types that bypass conversion: String goes through StringHttpMessageConverter as plain text, not JSON.
  • Void and null return an empty body with status 200 unless you set another status.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wanting a view from a @RestController: it returns the view name as text; use @Controller.
  • String returns expected as JSON: a String is plain text.
  • Forgetting the Jackson dependency: then no converter exists and you get 406 or 500.
  • Null body: returns an empty 200; return 404 explicitly.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance note: the annotation costs nothing at run time beyond a handler lookup, since metadata is cached at startup. What matters is the converter work.

  • Return a String or byte[] to skip Jackson when you already have the payload.
  • Stream large results with StreamingResponseBody or ResponseBodyEmitter.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a hybrid app with Thymeleaf pages and a JSON API.

  • Page controllers use @Controller and return view names.
  • API controllers use @RestController under /api.
  • A @RestControllerAdvice limited by basePackages formats errors for the API only.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSON request means the client sends a JSON document in the HTTP body, usually with POST or PUT and the header Content-Type: application/json.
  • @RequestBody tells Spring to read that body and convert it into a Java object.
  • Conversion is done by Jackson; field names in JSON map to properties of the class.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Bad JSON.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a user from JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

List body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the request body is bound:

  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor resolves the @RequestBody argument.
  • It checks the Content-Type against each converter's canRead.
  • MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter calls ObjectMapper.readValue on the input stream.
  • If @Valid is present, a validator runs and may throw MethodArgumentNotValidException.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Request body variants:

  • DTO or record for objects.
  • List or Map for arrays and free-form JSON.
  • JsonNode for dynamic structure.
  • String for the raw body.
  • HttpEntity to read body and headers together.
  • @RequestPart for JSON inside multipart requests.
  • required = false makes an empty body allowed.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Class shape: a record or a class with a no-args constructor and getters and setters works best.
  • Validation: add @Valid with @NotBlank or @Size on the fields.
  • Unknown fields are ignored by default in Spring Boot, because FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is off.

Senior Notes

  • Errors: malformed JSON gives HttpMessageNotReadableException (400); a wrong content type gives 415.
  • Body is read once; to read it twice (for logging) wrap the request in a caching wrapper.
  • Lists and generics work as @RequestBody List<Item> because Spring keeps the generic type.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing Content-Type: add the header in the client.
  • No default constructor in a plain class: add one, or use a record.
  • Single quotes or trailing commas: invalid JSON gives 400.
  • Mixing @RequestBody and @ModelAttribute for the same data.
  • Date format mismatch: send ISO text like 2026-10-08.
  • Reading getInputStream after @RequestBody: the stream is already consumed.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety for request bodies:

  • Limit body size at the server or gateway, for example server.tomcat.max-swallow-size and proxy limits.
  • Avoid huge arrays in one request; use batches.
  • Prefer records for lower boilerplate and immutability.
  • Use streaming parsing (JsonParser) for very large uploads.
codeExamples:
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB

# OUTPUT:
# Oversized requests are rejected early instead of exhausting memory

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a signup endpoint.

  • Client posts JSON with name, email and password.
  • Server validates, hashes the password and saves.
  • Validation failures return field errors in a standard body.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSON response is a JSON document written into the HTTP response body with header Content-Type: application/json.
  • Return an object from a @RestController method and Spring serializes it with Jackson automatically.
  • Collections and records work too: a List becomes a JSON array, a record becomes an object.

Worked Example 1

Assert JSON with jsonPath.

Worked Example 2

Hide a field.

Practice Exercise 1

Object to JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

ResponseEntity with header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a JSON response is produced:

  • The handler returns an object.
  • RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads the Accept header and the possible produces types.
  • It picks the first converter that canWrite the type and media type, normally Jackson.
  • The converter calls ObjectMapper.writeValue into the response stream and sets Content-Type.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Response variants:

  • Plain object with 200.
  • ResponseEntity with status, headers, body.
  • @ResponseStatus for a fixed status.
  • Optional handling with map and orElse.
  • ProblemDetail for errors.
  • Streaming with ResponseBodyEmitter or Server-Sent Events.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ResponseEntity sets the status and headers together with the body.
  • Content type can be forced with produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE.
  • Error bodies should also be JSON, built by @RestControllerAdvice or ProblemDetail.

Senior Notes

  • Hide fields with @JsonIgnore and rename with @JsonProperty.
  • Never return entities with lazy relations directly; map to DTOs to avoid lazy-loading errors and data leaks.
  • Dates become ISO strings when WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS is false (the Spring Boot default).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • LazyInitializationException: map to DTOs in the service layer.
  • Infinite recursion: break cycles with DTOs.
  • Leaking fields (passwords): use DTOs or @JsonIgnore.
  • Empty bean error: a class without getters causes FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS; add getters or use a record.
  • Dates as numbers: register JavaTimeModule (Boot does it) and disable timestamps.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips:

  • Return only the fields needed (DTO projections).
  • Enable response compression for large JSON.
  • Use NON_NULL inclusion to cut size.
  • Cache stable responses with ETag.
  • Stream huge lists instead of building them in memory.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json

# OUTPUT:
# Smaller payloads: null fields are dropped and the body is gzip compressed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a paged product list for a mobile app.

  • Response wraps items with paging metadata.
  • Prices are formatted as numbers, dates as ISO strings.
  • An ETag lets the app skip unchanged pages.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Jackson is the JSON library Spring Boot uses by default to turn Java objects into JSON and back.
  • Modules: jackson-databind does the mapping, and add-ons such as jackson-datatype-jsr310 handle Java time types.
  • Spring Boot includes it through spring-boot-starter-web and configures it automatically.

Worked Example 1

Customizer bean.

Worked Example 2

JSON slice test.

Practice Exercise 1

Annotations in action.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot properties.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true

# OUTPUT:
# firstName is written as first_name, nulls are skipped

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Jackson is built from three core modules and Spring wires it in:

  • jackson-core: streaming parser and generator.
  • jackson-annotations: the @Json... annotations.
  • jackson-databind: the ObjectMapper that binds objects.
  • Spring Boot adds JacksonAutoConfiguration, which creates the mapper from a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder, registers every Module bean and applies spring.jackson.*.
  • Spring MVC wraps it in MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful Jackson options:

  • Naming: spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy (SNAKE_CASE, KEBAB_CASE).
  • Inclusion: default-property-inclusion.
  • Features: spring.jackson.serialization.* and deserialization.* and mapper.*.
  • Date: spring.jackson.date-format and time zone.
  • Mixins add annotations to classes you cannot change.
  • Other formats: XML, YAML and CSV via extra data format modules.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false
spring.jackson.time-zone=Asia/Kolkata
spring.jackson.mapper.accept-case-insensitive-properties=true

# OUTPUT:
# LocalDateTime is written as "2026-10-08T10:15:30" and keys match any case

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonInclude, @JsonFormat and @JsonCreator.
  • Properties: spring.jackson.* in application.properties tunes the shared mapper.
  • Records are supported out of the box in Jackson 2.12 and later.

Senior Notes

  • Auto-configuration: JacksonAutoConfiguration builds one ObjectMapper bean and registers modules found on the classpath.
  • Customizing: define a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean instead of creating your own mapper.
  • Security: avoid default typing on untrusted input, because polymorphic deserialization can be exploited.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Own ObjectMapper bean replaces Boot default: modules and properties are lost; customize instead.
  • Version mismatch between Jackson modules: let the Spring Boot BOM manage versions.
  • Annotations from the wrong package: use com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.
  • Missing JavaTimeModule outside Spring: register it manually.
  • Ambiguous constructors: mark one with @JsonCreator.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tuning:

  • Reuse one mapper; it caches serializers and deserializers.
  • Use the Afterburner or Blackbird module to speed up reflection access.
  • Prefer streaming API for very large documents.
  • Avoid convertValue in hot paths.
  • Smaller models (DTOs) mean less work.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a service that must expose snake_case JSON and ISO dates, and hide internal fields.

  • Set naming strategy and date options in properties.
  • Annotate DTOs, not entities.
  • Add a @JsonTest to guard the JSON contract.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ObjectMapper is the central Jackson class: writeValueAsString converts an object to JSON and readValue converts JSON to an object.
  • Thread safe once configured, so share one instance instead of creating a new one per call.
  • In Spring Boot you simply inject the auto-configured bean with @Autowired or constructor injection.

Worked Example 1

Inject and use.

Worked Example 2

Generic list.

Practice Exercise 1

Write and read.

Practice Exercise 2

Tree model.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside ObjectMapper:

  • It holds caches: SerializerProvider keeps serializers per class, DeserializationContext keeps deserializers.
  • The first use of a type builds and caches them; later calls are fast.
  • Configuration (features, modules, mixins) is read while building those; changing it after use is unsafe.
  • Spring Boot builds the bean with Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

API variants:

  • writeValueAsString, writeValue(File/OutputStream, obj), writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter().
  • readValue for String, File, InputStream, byte[].
  • readTree and JsonNode, createObjectNode() to build JSON.
  • convertValue, valueToTree, treeToValue.
  • copy() to create a separately configurable mapper.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Generics need a TypeReference: readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<User>>() {}).
  • Tree model: readTree gives a JsonNode for dynamic JSON without a class.
  • Conversion: convertValue maps one object type to another, such as a Map to a DTO.

Senior Notes

  • Checked exception: methods throw JsonProcessingException, so wrap them or declare throws.
  • Configuration: configure(DeserializationFeature...) and modules like JavaTimeModule must be set before first use.
  • Reuse: ObjectReader and ObjectWriter are cheaper, immutable views for repeated work.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • new ObjectMapper() per call: wasteful and misconfigured; inject the bean.
  • Mutating the shared bean at run time: use copy() for variations.
  • Raw List.class: returns maps, not your type; use TypeReference.
  • Ignoring JsonProcessingException: handle or translate it.
  • Parsing untrusted JSON to huge trees: set stream read constraints.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tuning:

  • One shared instance; build ObjectReader and ObjectWriter once per type.
  • Prefer readValue(byte[]) and streams over building Strings.
  • Avoid the tree model when a class exists.
  • Check JsonFactory constraints for large input.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: store a flexible audit payload as JSON text in a database column.

  • Serialize the event with the injected mapper.
  • Save the string; on read, use readTree when the structure varies.
  • Wrap checked exceptions in an unchecked one.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Serialization is turning a Java object into JSON text; in Spring MVC it happens when a controller returns an object.
  • Property discovery: Jackson uses public getters (or record components) to find properties and their names.
  • Result: nested objects become nested JSON objects and collections become arrays.

Worked Example 1

Custom serializer.

Worked Example 2

Assert the JSON.

Practice Exercise 1

Rename, skip, order.

Practice Exercise 2

Date format.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Jackson serializes:

  • BeanSerializerFactory inspects the class once and builds a BeanSerializer with a list of property writers.
  • Properties come from getters, public fields and record components; annotations adjust names and visibility.
  • Each writer reads the value and writes it with the serializer for its type.
  • The result is cached for the next call.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Serialization options:

  • @JsonValue writes a whole object as one value (good for enums).
  • @JsonSerialize(using = ...) per property serializer.
  • @JsonUnwrapped flattens a nested object.
  • @JsonView field groups.
  • Enums write their name by default; change with WRITE_ENUMS_USING_TO_STRING.
  • Maps become objects; keys must be strings or convertible.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Control output with @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonInclude and @JsonPropertyOrder.
  • Dates: use @JsonFormat(pattern = ...) or keep the ISO default from the Boot mapper.
  • Custom serializer: extend JsonSerializer (or use @JsonComponent) for special types such as money.

Senior Notes

  • Cycles: bidirectional JPA relations cause infinite recursion; use DTOs, @JsonManagedReference or @JsonIgnore.
  • Lazy proxies can fail with Hibernate; map to DTOs inside the transaction.
  • Views: @JsonView chooses different field sets per endpoint without more classes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Bidirectional entities: StackOverflowError; use DTOs.
  • Hibernate lazy proxy: fetch inside the transaction or use a DTO.
  • Getter side effects: any getX() method is treated as a property; rename it or add @JsonIgnore.
  • Double precision surprises: use BigDecimal with a formatter for money.
  • Time zones: store UTC and let clients convert.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips:

  • Smaller DTOs, fewer nested levels.
  • Skip nulls and empty values.
  • Reuse the mapper so serializers stay cached.
  • Use streaming (JsonGenerator) for huge collections.
  • Avoid pretty printing in production.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an API that returns different detail by audience.

  • Public view: id and name.
  • Admin view: adds email and audit fields.
  • Use @JsonView on the DTO and the controller method.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Deserialization is turning JSON text into a Java object; in Spring MVC it happens for @RequestBody parameters.
  • How: Jackson creates the object through a constructor (or no-args constructor) and fills properties by name.
  • Mapping: JSON keys match Java property names; types are converted, for example a number to int.

Worked Example 1

Strict unknown fields.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true

# OUTPUT:
# POST {"user":"a","extra":1}
-> 400 Unrecognized field "extra"

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Type mismatch test.

Practice Exercise 1

Record deserialization.

Practice Exercise 2

Creator and alias.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Jackson deserializes:

  • BeanDeserializerFactory picks a creator: default constructor, annotated @JsonCreator, or the canonical record constructor.
  • The parser reads tokens; for each field name it finds the property and its deserializer.
  • Values are set through setters, fields or constructor arguments.
  • Unknown fields follow the configured feature (ignored by default in Boot).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Deserialization options:

  • @JsonCreator and @JsonProperty for immutable classes.
  • @JsonSetter, @JsonAlias, @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true).
  • @JsonDeserialize(using = ...) custom logic.
  • Features: ACCEPT_SINGLE_VALUE_AS_ARRAY, READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL, FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES.
  • Polymorphism with @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonSubTypes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Records and constructors: records work directly; for classes use @JsonCreator with @JsonProperty parameters.
  • Different names: @JsonProperty("user_name") or @JsonAlias accept alternative keys.
  • Unknown fields are ignored in Spring Boot unless you enable FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES.

Senior Notes

  • Errors: bad syntax or a type mismatch (text for a number) raises HttpMessageNotReadableException and a 400 response.
  • Polymorphism: use @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonSubTypes with a whitelist, never open default typing.
  • Custom deserializer: extend JsonDeserializer for odd formats such as "12,50" money strings.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • No usable constructor: add a no-args constructor or @JsonCreator.
  • Compiled without -parameters: constructor names are lost; Boot parent POM enables it, otherwise annotate.
  • Primitive and missing field: becomes 0; use wrapper types if absence matters.
  • Enum mismatch: unknown value fails; enable lenient enum reading.
  • Number as string: Jackson may coerce "5" to 5, hiding bad clients.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Reuse ObjectReader for a known type.
  • Set limits on nesting depth, string length and document size (StreamReadConstraints).
  • Never enable default typing for untrusted data.
  • Validate after binding with Bean Validation.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a webhook receiver.

  • The third-party adds new fields over time; ignoring unknown fields keeps you working.
  • The event type decides the class (polymorphism).
  • Signature is verified on the raw body first, then JSON is parsed.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpMessageConverter is the Spring interface that turns an HTTP request body into a Java object and a Java object into a response body.
  • Where it is used: @RequestBody, @ResponseBody, @RestController, HttpEntity and ResponseEntity all go through converters.
  • Selection depends on the Java type and the media type, such as application/json or text/plain.

Worked Example 1

Extend the converters.

Worked Example 2

Test the conversion with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

A tiny controller that relies on converters.

Practice Exercise 2

List the registered converters.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The interface HttpMessageConverter<T> lives in org.springframework.http.converter.

  • Interface: canRead(Class, MediaType), canWrite(Class, MediaType), getSupportedMediaTypes(), read(...), write(...).
  • Argument side: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor loops over converters and calls the first that can read.
  • Return side: it computes producible types, picks the best match with Accept, and writes with the first capable converter.
  • Registration: WebMvcConfigurationSupport builds the default list, Boot adds its own through HttpMessageConverters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to register converters:

  • configureMessageConverters: replaces all defaults.
  • extendMessageConverters: modifies the default list.
  • Boot bean: declare a converter or HttpMessageConverters bean.
  • RestTemplate and RestClient: have their own converter lists.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Key methods: canRead, canWrite, getSupportedMediaTypes, read and write.
  • Defaults: Spring MVC registers String, byte array, Resource, form and (when on the classpath) Jackson JSON and XML converters.
  • Not for views: converters bypass the ViewResolver; the body is written straight to the response.

Senior Notes

  • Order matters: the first converter whose canWrite returns true wins, so a broad custom converter can hide the Jackson one.
  • Customizing: use extendMessageConverters in WebMvcConfigurer to keep defaults, and configureMessageConverters only when you want to replace them.
  • Errors: no reader gives 415, no writer gives 406, and an unreadable body gives 400.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • configureMessageConverters used by accident: JSON stops working because defaults are gone; use extend.
  • Broad canWrite: a converter that supports Object intercepts everything.
  • Missing Content-Type: the request gets 415.
  • Forgetting to close or read the stream twice: the body can be read only once.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Converter lookup is a linear scan of a short list, which is negligible.
  • Cost is in serialization, so reuse the thread-safe ObjectMapper.
  • Large bodies: stream, or use StreamingResponseBody.
  • Compression: enable server.compression.enabled for text payloads.
codeExamples:
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,text/csv
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# OUTPUT:
# Content-Encoding: gzip on responses above 1 KB

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting API serves JSON to a web app and CSV to finance. A small converter plus the Accept header lets one endpoint handle both without extra URLs.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter is the converter that reads and writes JSON using the Jackson ObjectMapper.
  • Media types: it supports application/json and application/*+json.
  • Automatic: it is registered when Jackson is on the classpath, and Spring Boot gives it a pre-configured ObjectMapper.

Worked Example 1

Define your own converter bean.

Worked Example 2

Test the JSON output.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom field names and ignored fields.

Practice Exercise 2

Boot properties for Jackson.
