spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false

# OUTPUT:
# {"first_name":"Abaji","created_at":"2024-05-01T10:15:30"}
(null fields omitted)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The converter extends AbstractJackson2HttpMessageConverter and wraps an ObjectMapper.

  • canRead: asks ObjectMapper.canDeserialize for the target type.
  • read: builds a Jackson JavaType from the generic parameter and calls readValue.
  • write: uses an ObjectWriter with a JsonGenerator and the chosen charset.
  • Boot: JacksonAutoConfiguration builds the mapper and HttpMessageConvertersAutoConfiguration wraps it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • Boot properties: spring.jackson.* for naming, inclusion, dates, features.
  • Customizer bean: Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer.
  • Annotations: @JsonView, @JsonInclude, @JsonAlias, @JsonCreator.
  • Modules: any Module bean is registered automatically.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Read side: @RequestBody JSON is deserialized into the target type, and bad JSON gives 400.
  • Write side: the return value is serialized, with Content-Type: application/json.
  • Customizing: use annotations like @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonFormat, or Boot properties under spring.jackson.

Senior Notes

  • Shared ObjectMapper: the same bean is used for the converter, so register modules (such as JavaTimeModule) as beans and Boot picks them up.
  • Unknown properties: Boot disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, plain Spring does not.
  • Lazy entities: serializing JPA proxies can fail or trigger queries, so return DTOs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • new ObjectMapper() in code: it ignores Boot settings; inject the bean.
  • No default constructor: deserialization fails; use records or @JsonCreator.
  • Bidirectional entities: infinite recursion; use DTOs or @JsonManagedReference.
  • Dates as numbers: turn off WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Reuse the mapper; creating one is expensive and it caches serializers.
  • Afterburner or Blackbird modules can speed up access.
  • Smaller output: exclude nulls and use DTOs with only needed fields.
  • Streaming: for large lists write with a JsonGenerator.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the mobile app expects snake_case and ISO dates, while the code uses camelCase. Two Boot properties fix it for the whole API with no code change.
codeExamples:
spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false

# OUTPUT:
# {"order_id":5,"created_at":"2024-05-01T10:15:30"}

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ResponseEntity represents the whole HTTP response: status code, headers and body, returned from a controller method.
  • Use it when the status or headers depend on the result, for example 201 with a Location header or 404 when nothing is found.
  • Generic: ResponseEntity<T> where T is the body type, and the body is converted by an HttpMessageConverter.

Worked Example 1

Custom headers.

Worked Example 2

Test status and headers.

Practice Exercise 1

Create returns 201 and Location.

Practice Exercise 2

Find returns 200 or 404.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

ResponseEntity<T> extends HttpEntity<T> and adds a status.

  • Handler: HttpEntityMethodProcessor supports it as a return type.
  • Steps: copy headers, set status, then write the body through a converter chosen by Accept.
  • Empty body: with build() no converter is used.
  • Conditional: for ETag or Last-Modified the processor can return 304 on its own for GET and HEAD.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Shortcuts: ok, created, accepted, noContent, badRequest, notFound.
  • HeadersBuilder: build() for no body, BodyBuilder.body() for a body.
  • Files: ResponseEntity<Resource> with contentType and contentLength.
  • ETag: .eTag("v1").
  • RestTemplate: also returns it, via getForEntity.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Builders: ResponseEntity.ok(body), created(uri), noContent(), notFound() and status(code).
  • Headers: add them with .header(name, value) or HttpHeaders.
  • Versus @ResponseBody: plain @ResponseBody always returns 200 unless you use @ResponseStatus.

Senior Notes

  • Handled by HttpEntityMethodProcessor, which writes status and headers, then the body through a converter.
  • Optional: map it with optional.map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build()).
  • Prefer exceptions with @ControllerAdvice for errors, so success paths stay clean.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Body with 204: a 204 must not have a body.
  • Raw type: ResponseEntity without a type loses documentation; use ResponseEntity<Void> for no body.
  • Everywhere ResponseEntity: routine 200 responses are simpler as plain return values.
  • Returning null instead of 404.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Cost is negligible; the body conversion dominates.
  • Caching: cacheControl and eTag save bandwidth.
  • Large files: return a Resource or StreamingResponseBody, not a byte array.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a payment endpoint returns 202 with a status URL while the job runs, then clients poll that URL.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers that tell the client the result: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
  • Common REST codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 500 Internal Server Error.
  • In Spring set them with ResponseEntity, @ResponseStatus or ResponseStatusException, using the HttpStatus enum.

Worked Example 1

Map exceptions to statuses.

Worked Example 2

Assert statuses in tests.

Practice Exercise 1

Set a status with an annotation.

Practice Exercise 2

ResponseStatusException.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring models status codes with HttpStatusCode and the enum HttpStatus.

  • Set by: ResponseEntity, @ResponseStatus, ResponseStatusException, or exception resolvers.
  • Resolvers: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver run in that order.
  • Default mapping: missing parameter 400, no handler 404, wrong method 405, unsupported media 415.
  • Fallback: unhandled exceptions become 500 via /error in Boot.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Quick reference by use case:

  • Read: 200, 304, 404.
  • Create: 201, 202 for async, 409 for duplicates.
  • Update and delete: 200 or 204, 404, 409, 412 for failed preconditions.
  • Validation: 400 or 422.
  • Security: 401, 403, 429 for rate limiting.
  • Server: 500, 502, 503, 504.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • 401 versus 403: 401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but not allowed.
  • 400 versus 422: 400 for malformed requests, 422 for well-formed but invalid data; many APIs use 400 for both.
  • 204 is the usual answer to a successful DELETE or PUT with no body.

Senior Notes

  • Defaults: validation failure gives 400, missing converter gives 415 or 406, unknown URL gives 404, wrong method gives 405.
  • Central mapping: translate exceptions to statuses in one @RestControllerAdvice.
  • HttpStatus is an enum; in Spring 6 HttpStatusCode also allows custom numeric codes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • 200 with an error message: clients cannot detect failure.
  • 500 for client errors: an uncaught validation exception should be 400.
  • 404 for authorization failure without a reason; fine for hiding existence, wrong otherwise.
  • Mixing 401 and 403.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Operational notes:

  • Monitoring: alert on 5xx rate; 4xx spikes show client or contract problems.
  • Retry: clients retry 502, 503, 504 and 429, never 400.
  • 429 and Retry-After help clients back off.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order API maps domain exceptions to statuses in one advice, so controllers contain only the happy path.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • API versioning lets you change an API without breaking existing clients, by serving old and new behavior side by side.
  • Common strategies: URI path (/api/v1/users), request parameter, custom header, and media type (content negotiation).
  • Spring MVC has no single built-in switch in older releases; you map versions with @RequestMapping attributes such as params, headers and produces.

Worked Example 1

Media type versioning.

Worked Example 2

Test both versions.

Practice Exercise 1

URI versioning.

Practice Exercise 2

Header versioning.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Versioning works through request mapping conditions that RequestMappingHandlerMapping evaluates.

  • Conditions: patterns, params, headers, consumes, produces.
  • Most specific wins: if several mappings match, Spring compares the conditions and picks the best.
  • No match: 404, 400 for missing params, 406 or 415 for media types.
  • Custom: a RequestCondition can implement version ranges.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Strategy comparison:

  • URI: easy, cacheable, visible; not pure REST.
  • Query param: easy to test; may be dropped by caches.
  • Header: clean URLs; harder to test by hand.
  • Media type: most RESTful; complex for clients.
  • Newer Spring: recent releases add first-class API versioning support; check your Spring version documentation before relying on it.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • URI versioning is the simplest and cache friendly, but the version becomes part of the resource address.
  • Header versioning: @GetMapping(path = "/users", headers = "X-API-VERSION=2").
  • Media type versioning: produces = "application/vnd.app.v2+json", matched against the Accept header.

Senior Notes

  • Only break when needed: adding fields is backward compatible; removing or renaming is a new version.
  • Share logic: keep one service and map to different DTOs per version, so controllers stay thin.
  • Deprecation: announce it, add a Deprecation or Sunset header, and track traffic before removal.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Versioning too early or too often: prefer additive changes.
  • Copy-pasting controllers: bugs get fixed in one version only.
  • No default version: clients without the header fail.
  • Never retiring old versions.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Operational notes:

  • Measure traffic per version (a metrics tag) before deleting one.
  • Signal deprecation with Deprecation and Sunset headers.
  • Document each version in OpenAPI groups.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: v1 returned a single name field; the new mobile app needs first and last name. v2 is added, v1 stays for old apps for six months, then is removed after traffic drops to zero.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • REST best practices make an API predictable: nouns for resources, HTTP methods for actions, and correct status codes.
  • Naming: plural nouns like /users, no verbs in the path, and nesting only one or two levels such as /users/5/orders.
  • Methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates partly, DELETE removes.

Worked Example 1

ProblemDetail error body.

Worked Example 2

Test the contract.

Practice Exercise 1

A clean resource controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Validation with a DTO.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Most practices map to a Spring feature.

  • Resources and verbs: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.
  • Validation: @Valid triggers Bean Validation before the method runs.
  • Errors: @RestControllerAdvice and ProblemDetail (RFC 9457).
  • Pagination: Pageable resolved by PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver in Spring Data.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants worth knowing:

  • PUT vs PATCH: PUT is full replacement and idempotent.
  • Filtering: ?status=active&sort=name,asc.
  • HATEOAS: optional links with Spring HATEOAS.
  • Bulk operations: a dedicated endpoint such as POST /orders/batch.
  • Long tasks: return 202 and a status URL.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status codes: 201 with Location for create, 204 for delete, 404 for missing, 400 for invalid input.
  • Use DTOs instead of exposing entities, and validate input with @Valid.
  • Consistent errors: one JSON error shape for the whole API.

Senior Notes

  • Idempotency: GET, PUT and DELETE should be safe to repeat; POST is not, so use an idempotency key for payments.
  • Pagination, sorting, filtering through query parameters, with Pageable and a bounded page size.
  • Security and caching: HTTPS, authentication, ETag or Cache-Control, rate limiting, and versioning from day one.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Verbs in URLs: /getUser instead of GET /users/1.
  • Entities as responses: leaks data and lazy loading errors.
  • Unbounded lists: always paginate.
  • Inconsistent errors and wrong status codes.
  • Returning stack traces: set server.error.include-stacktrace=never.
codeExamples:
# Wrong: POST /api/createUser, GET /api/getUsers
# Right
# POST /api/v1/users       -> 201
# GET  /api/v1/users       -> 200 (paged)
# GET  /api/v1/users/5     -> 200 or 404

server.error.include-stacktrace=never
server.error.include-message=never

# OUTPUT:
# errors no longer expose internals

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and robustness:

  • Cap page size with spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size.
  • Caching: ETag and Cache-Control on read endpoints.
  • Compression for JSON.
  • Timeouts and rate limits to protect the server.
  • N+1 queries: fetch DTO projections.
codeExamples:
spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100
spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size=20
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# size=10000 request is clamped to 100

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team reviews an API before launch with a checklist: plural nouns, status codes, validation, ProblemDetail errors, pagination, versioning, security and OpenAPI documentation.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • What it is: an HttpMessageConverter<T> reads the HTTP body into an object of type T and writes an object of type T to the body.
  • Why it exists: controllers should work with Java objects, not raw bytes, so Spring hides the parsing and formatting.
  • Negotiation: the Content-Type header picks the reader and the Accept header picks the writer.

Worked Example 1

Trace a failed negotiation.

Worked Example 2

Test negotiation.

Practice Exercise 1

Same method, two formats.

Practice Exercise 2

Raw text body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The conversion pipeline for a request and a response:

  • Request: DispatcherServlet finds the handler, then RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor resolves the @RequestBody argument by trying converters against Content-Type.
  • Response: after the handler returns, the same processor collects producible media types, intersects them with Accept, sorts by quality, and writes.
  • Advice: RequestBodyAdvice and ResponseBodyAdvice can wrap this step.
  • No view: the ModelAndView is marked handled, so no ViewResolver runs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controlling the negotiation:

  • consumes / produces on the mapping.
  • Accept header from the client, with quality values such as q=0.8.
  • Path extension and parameter strategies are off by default in modern Spring; use headers.
  • HttpEntity gives access to headers and body together.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request flow: Content-Type and the parameter type choose a converter for @RequestBody.
  • Response flow: the return type and Accept choose a converter for @ResponseBody.
  • Built in: String, byte[], Resource, form data, JSON (Jackson or Gson), XML (JAXB or Jackson XML).

Senior Notes

  • Processor: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor asks each converter canRead or canWrite.
  • Producible types: produces on the mapping narrows what the server offers.
  • Tell apart: converters handle bodies; Converter and Formatter handle parameters, and HandlerMethodArgumentResolver handles argument binding.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong Content-Type from the client: 415.
  • Reading the body twice in a filter, which breaks @RequestBody; wrap the request with ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Mixing @Controller and String returns without @ResponseBody.
  • Assuming JSON when XML is on the classpath.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • Keep the converter list short: remove unused XML libraries.
  • Set produces to skip negotiation work and make behavior explicit.
  • Avoid body logging for large payloads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy partner sends XML while the new web app sends JSON. One endpoint accepts both through consumes and returns the format asked for in Accept.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSON converter is the HttpMessageConverter that maps JSON text to Java objects and back; in Spring it is Jackson by default.
  • Request: @RequestBody with Content-Type: application/json deserializes into the parameter type.
  • Response: returning an object from a @RestController serializes it to JSON.

Worked Example 1

Handle bad JSON.

Worked Example 2

Test with jsonPath.

Practice Exercise 1

Receive and return a list.

Practice Exercise 2

A record body.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Reading JSON with Jackson inside Spring:

  • Type resolution: the method parameter generic type becomes a Jackson JavaType.
  • Binding: Jackson uses setters, fields or a constructor (records and @JsonCreator).
  • Errors: JsonProcessingException is wrapped in HttpMessageNotReadableException.
  • Writing: getters or record accessors are serialized; null handling follows the inclusion setting.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful variants:

  • JsonNode / Map for dynamic payloads.
  • @JsonView to expose different fields to different callers.
  • @JsonAnySetter for unknown fields.
  • Gson as an alternative converter.
  • JSON Patch and Merge Patch media types for PATCH.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Classes: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) or GsonHttpMessageConverter (Gson).
  • Records and classes both work; fields need getters or be public, and a constructor Jackson can use.
  • Generic bodies: List<User> works because Spring keeps the generic type of the parameter.

Senior Notes

  • Dates: add jackson-datatype-jsr310 (Boot includes it) and turn off timestamps for ISO dates.
  • Polymorphism: use @JsonTypeInfo carefully; untrusted type names are a security risk.
  • Large payloads: Jackson reads the whole body; for huge data stream with JsonParser or a streaming response.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Lombok or class without accessors: empty JSON {}.
  • Unknown property errors outside Boot; configure FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES.
  • Wrong date format or timestamps.
  • Enum mismatch: a bad value gives 400.
  • Primitive vs wrapper: a missing int becomes 0, a missing Integer becomes null.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Smaller DTOs mean less serialization.
  • Avoid serializing deep lazy graphs.
  • Reuse the ObjectMapper.
  • Compress large JSON.
  • Set limits on body size: spring.servlet.multipart and server max sizes.
codeExamples:
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# large JSON responses are gzip compressed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile client sends a batch of events as a JSON array, and the API returns a summary object with counts, with bad JSON mapped to a clean 400.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • XML converter is an HttpMessageConverter that maps XML to Java objects and back, so an endpoint can speak application/xml.
  • Two options: MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter (needs jackson-dataformat-xml) or Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter (needs JAXB annotations).
  • Activation: add the dependency and Spring registers it; the Accept header then chooses XML or JSON.

Worked Example 1

Force XML only.

Worked Example 2

Test XML.

Practice Exercise 1

Dependency.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-dataformat-xml</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter is registered automatically

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

An XML model.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

XML support depends on what is on the classpath.

  • Jackson XML: MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter is added when jackson-dataformat-xml exists, using an XmlMapper.
  • JAXB: Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter needs @XmlRootElement and a JAXB runtime such as Jakarta XML Bind.
  • Media types: application/xml, text/xml, application/*+xml.
  • Selection: same canRead and canWrite loop as for JSON.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Attributes: @JacksonXmlProperty(isAttribute = true).
  • Lists: @JacksonXmlElementWrapper(localName = "items").
  • Namespaces: namespace on @JacksonXmlProperty.
  • Pretty print: SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT.
  • Per endpoint: produces = application/xml.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Jackson XML reuses Jackson annotations plus @JacksonXmlRootElement and @JacksonXmlProperty.
  • JAXB needs @XmlRootElement and the Jakarta JAXB runtime, which is not in the JDK any more.
  • Both formats: once XML is on the classpath, clients without an Accept header may start receiving XML, so set produces when it matters.

Senior Notes

  • Security: parse untrusted XML with external entities disabled to avoid XXE attacks.
  • Order: Jackson JSON usually comes before XML, so a browser sending Accept: */* gets whichever is first.
  • Collections: a wrapper element is needed for lists; use @JacksonXmlElementWrapper.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing dependency: requests for XML return 406.
  • JAXB on a modern JDK: the runtime is no longer bundled; add Jakarta XML Bind and an implementation.
  • Unexpected XML responses after adding the library.
  • XXE: parsing untrusted XML with a permissive parser.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • XML is bigger and slower than JSON; use it only when a partner needs it.
  • Limit sizes and disable DTDs.
  • Streaming parsers (StAX) for large documents.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a government partner posts invoices as XML, while the internal web app uses JSON. Both hit the same controller and service.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • StringHttpMessageConverter reads and writes plain text bodies and supports text/plain and */*.
  • Read: @RequestBody String body gives the raw request text.
  • Write: a method returning String under @ResponseBody or @RestController writes the text directly, not a view name.

Worked Example 1

Set the charset in config.
codeExamples:
server.servlet.encoding.charset=UTF-8
server.servlet.encoding.force=true

# OUTPUT:
# Content-Type: text/plain;
charset=UTF-8

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Test text output.

Practice Exercise 1

Echo text.

Practice Exercise 2

Raw JSON as a String.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

StringHttpMessageConverter extends AbstractHttpMessageConverter<String>.

  • Supports: only the String class and all media types by default.
  • Charset: uses the charset of the Content-Type, or a default (ISO-8859-1 for response unless set).
  • Position: it is second in the default list, so Strings are written as text before Jackson sees them.
  • Accept-Charset: it can add the header Accept-Charset; Boot turns that off.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Plain text: produces = text/plain.
  • HTML snippet: produces = text/html.
  • JSON string: build the JSON yourself or return an object.
  • Fixed charset: use produces with ;charset=UTF-8.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Charset: it defaults to ISO-8859-1 for write unless the content type says otherwise; Spring Boot sets UTF-8 through server.servlet.encoding.
  • JSON strings: returning a String from a JSON endpoint is not quoted, because the String converter comes before Jackson.
  • Raw JSON: you can receive JSON as a String and parse it yourself.

Senior Notes

  • Order: it sits before the JSON converter, so a String return value never becomes a JSON string literal.
  • Content type: set produces = "text/plain;charset=UTF-8" to be explicit.
  • Gotcha: with @Controller and no @ResponseBody, a returned String is a view name.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Garbled characters: charset not UTF-8.
  • Expecting quotes around a returned String in a JSON API.
  • Returning String from @Controller and getting a view name lookup.
  • Large String bodies held fully in memory.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Cheap: no parsing, just charset decoding.
  • Large text: stream with StreamingResponseBody or Resource.
  • Compression helps text responses.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a webhook endpoint receives a signed payload. The signature is computed over the raw bytes, so the controller takes the body as a String, verifies it, then parses JSON.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter is the built-in converter that reads and writes a raw byte[] body, with no JSON or XML mapping at all.
  • Media types: it supports application/octet-stream and */*, so it is the usual choice for file downloads such as PDFs and images.
  • Minimal use: a controller returns byte[] or ResponseEntity<byte[]> and Spring writes the bytes straight to the response.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test for a download.

Worked Example 2

Force a download with a file name.

Practice Exercise 1

Return a small file as bytes.

Practice Exercise 2

Receive raw bytes.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a byte[] body travels through Spring MVC:

  • Write path: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor asks each converter canWrite(byte[].class, mediaType).
  • Match: ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter supports byte[] for application/octet-stream and */*.
  • Order: it is first in the default list, so it wins before Jackson.
  • Read path: readInternal copies the input stream into an array.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to send binary content:

  • byte[]: simplest, whole body in memory.
  • Resource: handled by ResourceHttpMessageConverter, supports range requests.
  • InputStreamResource: for streams of unknown length.
  • StreamingResponseBody: writes directly to the output from another thread.
  • HttpServletResponse: manual control.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Content-Type: set it yourself in the ResponseEntity (for example MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF), otherwise the browser sees a generic octet-stream.
  • Download header: add Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=... to make the browser save the file instead of showing it.
  • Request side: @RequestBody byte[] data reads the whole upload into memory, so it suits small payloads only.

Senior Notes

  • Memory: a byte array holds the entire file in the heap; for large files return a Resource or StreamingResponseBody instead.
  • Order: the converter is registered early in the default list, so byte[] never reaches Jackson.
  • Testing: with MockMvc assert on content().bytes(...) and the Content-Type header.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing Content-Type: a PDF served as octet-stream is downloaded with no hint of its type.
  • Large file in byte[]: causes OutOfMemoryError under load.
  • Returning byte[] with produces JSON: mismatched type leads to 406 or odd output.
  • Unsafe file names: never build a path from user input without validation.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning binary responses:

  • Prefer Resource for files; it uses zero-copy paths and supports Range headers.
  • Set Content-Length and cache headers (ETag, Cache-Control).
  • Let a CDN or static handler serve big files.
  • Compression is wasted on already compressed formats like JPEG or ZIP.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an invoice service generates a PDF with a library and returns it for download.

  • Generate to a byte array (small, short lived).
  • Return with the right Content-Type and file name.
  • Test status, type and the PDF header bytes.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • FormHttpMessageConverter reads and writes HTML form data (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) and multipart forms (multipart/form-data).
  • Java type: it maps the body to MultiValueMap<String, String>, where one key can carry several values.
  • Minimal use: @RequestBody MultiValueMap<String, String> form hands you every submitted field.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc form post.

Worked Example 2

Client posting a form.

Practice Exercise 1

Read a form as a map.

Practice Exercise 2

Bind a form to an object.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals of form handling:

  • Read: FormHttpMessageConverter parses the body into a MultiValueMap, splitting on & and URL-decoding names and values.
  • Write: it encodes the map back to a=1&b=2; for multipart it writes boundaries and parts.
  • Supported types: MultiValueMap for form types; it does not read multipart into a map.
  • Servlet interplay: for urlencoded POST, request.getParameter triggers body parsing by the container.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Three ways to read the same form:

  • @RequestParam: one field, with defaults and conversion.
  • @ModelAttribute: binds to an object and supports validation.
  • @RequestBody MultiValueMap: raw access to all fields.
  • @RequestParam Map: only the first value per key.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Usual alternative: for forms most code uses @RequestParam or @ModelAttribute, which read request parameters, not this converter.
  • Client side: RestTemplate uses this converter to send a MultiValueMap as a form post.
  • Multipart: this converter can write multipart requests, but for reading uploads use MultipartFile or @RequestPart.

Senior Notes

  • Servlet quirk: for urlencoded POST the container may already consume the body into parameters, which is why @RequestBody and @RequestParam should not be mixed.
  • Charset: default is UTF-8 in Spring 6; a wrong charset gives garbled field values.
  • Testing: use contentType(APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED) and param(...) or formField in MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sending JSON to a form endpoint: gives 415 or empty fields.
  • Missing Content-Type on the client, so the body is not treated as a form.
  • Mixing @RequestBody and @RequestParam on the same urlencoded request.
  • Wrong encoding of special characters such as plus or ampersand in hand-built bodies.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Form tuning and limits:

  • Limit size with server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size.
  • Large uploads: set spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size.
  • Use HiddenHttpMethodFilter (or Boot form-content filter) only when you need PUT and DELETE from forms.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB

# OUTPUT:
# larger form posts are rejected before reaching the controller

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy HTML page posts a login form and a mobile app calls the same logic with JSON.

  • Two mappings, one per Content-Type.
  • Both delegate to the same service.
  • Tests cover both bodies.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Jackson is the default JSON library; MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses an ObjectMapper to turn Java objects into JSON and back.
  • Auto-config: with spring-boot-starter-web a configured ObjectMapper bean and the converter are registered for you.
  • Minimal use: @RestController methods returning a record or POJO produce application/json with no extra code.

Worked Example 1

Test JSON with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Customize the shared mapper.

Practice Exercise 1

JSON in and out.

Practice Exercise 2

Shape output with annotations.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Jackson is wired:

  • Boot: JacksonAutoConfiguration builds an ObjectMapper using Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder and registers modules found on the classpath (java.time, Jdk8, parameter names).
  • MVC: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter gets that mapper and handles application/json and application/*+json.
  • Read: the converter calls readValue; write: writeValue to the output stream.
  • Boot defaults: unknown properties ignored, dates as ISO strings.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options:

  • Properties: spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy, default-property-inclusion, serialization.*, deserialization.*.
  • Annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonAlias, @JsonIgnoreProperties, @JsonView, @JsonCreator.
  • Mixins: annotate classes you cannot edit.
  • Custom (de)serializers: @JsonComponent.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
spring:
  jackson:
    property-naming-strategy: SNAKE_CASE
    default-property-inclusion: non_null
    serialization:
      indent-output: true

# OUTPUT:
# {
#   "first_name" : "Ann"
# }

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Properties: tune it with spring.jackson.*, for example default-property-inclusion and serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps.
  • Annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonFormat and @JsonInclude shape the output per class or field.
  • Dates: java.time types work through the JavaTimeModule, which Boot registers automatically.

Senior Notes

  • One shared mapper: inject the Boot ObjectMapper instead of calling new ObjectMapper(), otherwise your settings are lost.
  • Customizing: define a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean to keep Boot defaults and add changes.
  • Failures: bad JSON gives HttpMessageNotReadableException, which becomes 400 by default.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Missing default constructor for classes (records and @JsonCreator fix it).
  • Lazy Hibernate proxies serialized directly; return DTOs instead.
  • Infinite recursion from bidirectional entities; use DTOs or @JsonIgnore.
  • Date as array when the JavaTimeModule is missing in a hand-built mapper.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • The ObjectMapper is thread safe and costly to create, so share one.
  • Return small DTOs and use @JsonView or projections to avoid large payloads.
  • Consider the Afterburner or Blackbird module for speed, and gzip for large bodies.
  • Use streaming (JsonGenerator) for huge lists.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json
server.compression.min-response-size=2048

# OUTPUT:
# responses over 2 KB are gzip compressed (Content-Encoding: gzip)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API must return snake_case JSON with ISO dates, hide internal fields and still accept camelCase input from an old client.

  • Naming strategy in properties.
  • @JsonAlias for the old names.
  • A slice test locks the contract.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom converter: a class that teaches Spring MVC to read or write a Java type in a media type it does not know, such as CSV.
  • Base class: extend AbstractHttpMessageConverter<T> and implement supports, readInternal and writeInternal.
  • Registration: add it in WebMvcConfigurer.extendMessageConverters so the default converters stay in place.

Worked Example 1

Controller serving both formats.

Worked Example 2

Test the CSV output.

Practice Exercise 1

A CSV converter for Book.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens at runtime:

  • Write: the return value processor loops converters, calls canWrite(type, mediaType); AbstractHttpMessageConverter checks supports and the media type list.
  • Headers: the base class sets Content-Type and optionally Content-Length (getContentLength).
  • Read: canRead is checked against the request Content-Type before readInternal.
  • List building: Spring starts with defaults, then calls your configureMessageConverters or extendMessageConverters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • AbstractHttpMessageConverter<T>: one concrete class.
  • AbstractGenericHttpMessageConverter: generic types.
  • HttpMessageConverters bean (Boot): add converters and keep defaults.
  • Fully custom: implement HttpMessageConverter directly.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Media type: pass the supported MediaType to the super constructor; Spring matches it against Accept and Content-Type.
  • extend or configure: extendMessageConverters adds to the defaults, while configureMessageConverters replaces them all.
  • Controller: nothing changes; a method with produces = "text/csv" returns the object and your converter writes it.

Senior Notes

  • Order: the first converter that can handle the type and media type wins, so use converters.add(0, ...) to take priority.
  • Generic variant: GenericHttpMessageConverter is needed when you must see generic types such as List<Book>.
  • Testing: send Accept: text/csv in MockMvc and compare the body string.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • configureMessageConverters removes all defaults, so JSON stops working.
  • supports always true, which hijacks every type.
  • Not closing or flushing: use the stream given and do not close it.
  • Charset ignored: encode with an explicit charset.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Write straight to the output stream; avoid building big strings.
  • Keep converters stateless and thread safe.
  • Put frequently used converters first, but only if supports is narrow and cheap.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting API lets analysts download text/csv from the same endpoint that serves JSON to the web app.

  • Same controller, two media types.
  • Converter registered once.
  • Tests per Accept header.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Content negotiation is how Spring MVC decides the response format (JSON, XML, CSV) when a resource can be served in several.
  • Default strategy: the Accept request header; Spring picks the best match from what the controller can produce.
  • Result: if nothing matches, the response is 406 Not Acceptable.

Worked Example 1

Test 406.

Worked Example 2

Test both formats.

Practice Exercise 1

One URL, two formats.

Practice Exercise 2

Enable the format parameter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Steps in the pipeline:

  • 1: ContentNegotiationManager asks its strategies for requested media types (header by default, parameter if enabled).
  • 2: the producible types come from produces or from converters that can write the return type.
  • 3: both lists are matched and sorted by specificity and quality.
  • 4: the first compatible pair picks the converter, else HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException (406).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Strategies:

  • Header: default, uses Accept.
  • Parameter: ?format=json via favorParameter.
  • Fixed default: defaultContentType when none is requested.
  • Custom: implement ContentNegotiationStrategy.
  • Path extension: removed in Spring 6.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ContentNegotiationManager holds the strategies and returns the list of acceptable media types for a request.
  • Query parameter: enable it with configurer.favorParameter(true) and a map such as ?format=xml; it is off by default.
  • Path extensions like .json are no longer supported in Spring 6, so do not rely on them.

Senior Notes

  • Selection: the acceptable types are intersected with the producible types from produces and the registered converters.
  • Configuration: override configureContentNegotiation in a WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Testing: call the same URL with different Accept headers and assert each Content-Type.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Expecting .json URL suffix to work in Spring 6.
  • Missing the XML library, so XML is never offered (add Jackson XML).
  • Returning a String and expecting JSON: the String converter writes it as plain text.
  • Browsers send XML-friendly Accept headers, so JSON may become XML unexpectedly.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Negotiation is cheap, but each extra format needs tests.
  • Expose only formats you support; use produces to keep the list small.
  • Cache by Vary: Accept or give each format its own URL.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API serves JSON to apps and XML to a partner who cannot change headers, so the partner uses ?format=xml.

  • Enable the parameter strategy.
  • Keep JSON as default.
  • Test all three paths.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Accept is a request header that tells the server which response media types the client can handle, for example Accept: application/json.
  • Quality values: q ranks choices, as in application/xml;q=0.5, application/json; higher q wins and the default is 1.0.
  • Server side: Spring compares Accept with the produces of mappings and the converters that can write the type.

Worked Example 1

Mismatch test.

Worked Example 2

Quality value test.

Practice Exercise 1

Two methods, one URL.

Practice Exercise 2

Read the header directly.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Processing steps:

  • Parse: MediaType.parseMediaTypes splits the header into media types with q values.
  • Sort: MimeTypeUtils.sortBySpecificity: specific beats wildcard, then higher q.
  • Map: ProducesRequestCondition on each mapping matches the sorted list.
  • Fail: no match gives HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException, status 406.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms of the header:

  • Accept: application/json exact.
  • Accept: application/*+json structured suffix.
  • Accept: */* anything.
  • Accept: text/html, application/json;q=0.9 list with q.
  • Negation: produces = "!application/xml".

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • produces: @GetMapping(produces = "application/json") narrows the mapping; a mismatch gives 406 Not Acceptable.
  • Wildcards: */* means any type, which browsers often send, so the first producible type is used.
  • Not the same as Content-Type: Accept describes the response wanted, while Content-Type describes the body sent.

Senior Notes

  • Resolution: HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy parses and sorts the header by specificity and quality.
  • Vary: when the response depends on Accept, caches need Vary: Accept; Spring adds it for negotiated responses.
  • Testing: MockMvc.accept(...) sets the header and content().contentType checks the result.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Treating 406 as a server bug; the client asked for an unsupported type.
  • Hard-coding Accept in tests instead of using accept(...).
  • Confusing Accept with Content-Type in a POST.
  • Ignoring wildcard requests from browsers and curl.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and caching:

  • Parsing the header is cheap.
  • Different representations at one URL need Vary: Accept for correct caching.
  • Many formats multiply cache entries; consider separate URLs for hot resources.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: one endpoint serves a web app (JSON) and a spreadsheet export (CSV) chosen by the Accept header.

  • Declare both types in produces.
  • Test both and the 406 case.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Content-Type says what format the message body is in, for example Content-Type: application/json on a POST request.
  • Request side: Spring uses it to choose the converter that reads @RequestBody.
  • Response side: it also tells the client how to parse the body Spring sends back.

Worked Example 1

Test 415.

Worked Example 2

Test the happy path.

Practice Exercise 1

A JSON-only endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

Different bodies on one path.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the request path:

  • Mapping: ConsumesRequestCondition compares Content-Type with consumes; mismatch gives HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException (415).
  • Argument: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks a converter via canRead.
  • Response: the chosen converter sets Content-Type on output, with charset when relevant.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • consumes = "application/json" single type.
  • Several types in an array.
  • MediaType constants such as APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE.
  • Negation with !.
  • Class-level consumes, overridden per method.
  • Multipart: @RequestPart with multipart/form-data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • consumes: @PostMapping(consumes = "application/json") restricts a mapping to that request type.
  • 415: if the type is missing or not supported, Spring answers 415 Unsupported Media Type.
  • Charset: application/json is UTF-8 by default; for text types add ;charset=UTF-8 if needed.

Senior Notes

  • Converter choice: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor loops over converters and picks the first with canRead(type, contentType).
  • Missing header: Spring assumes application/octet-stream, which usually matches no converter for objects.
  • Testing: contentType(...) in MockMvc sets the request header; forgetting it is the top cause of 415 in tests.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Test or client without Content-Type, then 415.
  • Sending form data to a JSON endpoint.
  • Wrong charset in header for non-UTF-8 text.
  • Putting @RequestBody and @RequestParam for the same form.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and safety:

  • Accept only the types you handle; fewer converters means less attack surface.
  • Limit body size (server.tomcat.max-swallow-size, spring.servlet.multipart.*).
  • Reject early with consumes before parsing starts.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB

# OUTPUT:
# oversize bodies are rejected before the controller runs

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a webhook endpoint receives JSON from one partner and XML from another.

  • Two methods on one URL, split by consumes.
  • Unknown formats receive 415 automatically.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Interceptor: a Spring MVC component that runs code before and after a controller method, for cross-cutting work such as logging, timing or authorization checks.
  • Where it runs: inside the DispatcherServlet, around the handler; filters run earlier, outside Spring MVC.
  • How to use: implement HandlerInterceptor and register it with InterceptorRegistry in a WebMvcConfigurer.

Worked Example 1

Test through MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Trace the order.

Practice Exercise 1

A timing interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where interceptors sit in the flow:

  • DispatcherServlet.doDispatch finds a handler and its HandlerExecutionChain (handler plus matching interceptors).
  • applyPreHandle loops in order and stops at the first false, then triggers afterCompletion for those already passed.
  • handle invokes the controller through a HandlerAdapter.
  • applyPostHandle runs in reverse, then the view renders, then triggerAfterCompletion.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Registration options:

  • addPathPatterns / excludePathPatterns: ant-style or PathPattern URLs.
  • order(int): explicit ordering.
  • Built-ins: LocaleChangeInterceptor, ThemeChangeInterceptor, ConversionServiceExposingInterceptor.
  • WebRequestInterceptor: servlet-independent variant.
  • Boot: use a WebMvcConfigurer bean; no extra setup.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Three hooks: preHandle before the controller, postHandle after it, afterCompletion after the view or response.
  • Path rules: addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns choose which URLs get the interceptor.
  • Beans: the interceptor can be a Spring bean, so it can inject services and be unit tested.

Senior Notes

  • Chain: interceptors form a HandlerExecutionChain; preHandle runs in order, postHandle and afterCompletion in reverse.
  • Versus filters: interceptors know the handler method and Spring context; filters see raw servlet requests and can wrap them.
  • Versus AOP: interceptors work on web requests, AOP on any bean method.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Instance created with new inside the registry, so no injection; use a bean.
  • Wrong pattern: /api/* misses deeper paths.
  • Expecting interceptors for static files or servlet filters.
  • Heavy work in preHandle blocks every request.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Interceptors run on every matched request, so keep them cheap.
  • Narrow path patterns to avoid needless calls.
  • Do slow work (remote calls) with caches, not in each request.
  • Use afterCompletion for timing; postHandle is skipped on errors.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: audit logging of every API call with user, URL, status and duration.

  • Start time in preHandle.
  • Log in afterCompletion (always runs).
  • Exclude health and static paths.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerInterceptor is the Spring MVC interface (org.springframework.web.servlet) with three callbacks around handler execution.
  • Methods: preHandle returns a boolean; postHandle and afterCompletion return nothing; all three have default empty implementations.
  • Minimal use: implement only the methods you need and register the class with InterceptorRegistry.

Worked Example 1

Unit test without Spring.

Worked Example 2

Check cleanup runs after errors.

Practice Exercise 1

Log all three phases.

Practice Exercise 2

Annotation-driven check.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Contract and call order:

  • preHandle: called by HandlerExecutionChain.applyPreHandle in order; false stops.
  • postHandle: called in reverse after the handler, with the ModelAndView (null for @ResponseBody).
  • afterCompletion: called in reverse for each interceptor that passed preHandle, with the exception if any.
  • Defaults: since Spring 5 all methods are Java default methods, so implement only what you need.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Related types:

  • HandlerInterceptor: servlet based, common.
  • AsyncHandlerInterceptor: adds afterConcurrentHandlingStarted.
  • WebRequestInterceptor: request abstraction, no way to stop the chain.
  • MappedInterceptor: wraps an interceptor with path patterns (Boot beans of this type are picked up).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • postHandle runs after the controller but before the view is rendered, and can change the ModelAndView; it is skipped if the handler throws.
  • afterCompletion always runs for interceptors whose preHandle returned true, even after an exception; use it for cleanup.
  • handler argument: usually a HandlerMethod, which gives access to the controller class, method and annotations.

Senior Notes

  • @ResponseBody caveat: the response may already be committed when postHandle runs, so changing headers there is unreliable.
  • Async: for async requests use AsyncHandlerInterceptor, whose afterConcurrentHandlingStarted is called instead.
  • Static resources: the handler is a ResourceHttpRequestHandler, not a HandlerMethod, so check the type before casting.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Changing response headers in postHandle for @ResponseBody: already committed.
  • Casting handler to HandlerMethod without checking.
  • Throwing from afterCompletion: it is logged and ignored.
  • Storing request data in fields: interceptors are singletons.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Call overhead is tiny; the cost is what you do inside.
  • Check the handler type first and return fast for unrelated requests.
  • Cache reflection results (annotation lookups) in a map.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a multi-tenant API reads X-Tenant and stores it for the request, then clears it.

  • Set in preHandle.
  • Clear in afterCompletion to avoid leaking between pooled threads.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • preHandle() is the HandlerInterceptor method that runs before the controller; its signature is boolean preHandle(request, response, handler).
  • Return value: true continues the chain to the next interceptor and the controller; false stops it.
  • Typical use: authentication, rate limiting, request logging and setting request attributes.

Test the rejection.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Simple API key check.

Practice Exercise 2

Pass a value to the controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where preHandle is called:

  • DispatcherServlet.doDispatch calls mappedHandler.applyPreHandle(request, response).
  • The loop records interceptorIndex after each success.
  • On false it calls triggerAfterCompletion for the interceptors already passed and returns without calling the controller.
  • An exception goes the same way and then to the HandlerExceptionResolver chain.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common ways to end the request from preHandle:

  • response.sendError(code): goes to the error page or JSON error handling.
  • response.setStatus(code) and write the body.
  • response.sendRedirect(url): for example to a login page.
  • Throw an exception handled by @ControllerAdvice.
  • Forward with request.getRequestDispatcher(...).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • When returning false: you must write the response yourself, for example response.sendError(401) or set a status and body; otherwise the client gets an empty 200.
  • handler: the matched target, usually a HandlerMethod, so you can read annotations.
  • Passing data: use request.setAttribute to hand values to the controller or to afterCompletion.

Senior Notes

  • Chain behavior: if interceptor 2 returns false, interceptor 1 still gets afterCompletion, but 2 and later get nothing and the controller never runs.
  • Exceptions: an exception thrown in preHandle goes to the exception resolvers, such as @ControllerAdvice.
  • Body reading: do not read the request body here without a caching wrapper, because the controller needs it too.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Returning false with no response written: empty 200.
  • Forgetting return true on the normal path, so no endpoint ever works.
  • Doing database calls for every request without a cache.
  • Reading the body stream.
  • Using an interceptor for CORS preflight; the handling must come from the CORS support.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • preHandle is on the hot path: no blocking calls without timeouts.
  • Use cheap checks first (header present) before expensive ones (token validation).
  • Cache validated tokens briefly.
  • Exclude static and health URLs with excludePathPatterns.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: simple rate limiting per client IP, with a 429 response when exceeded.

  • Counter per IP in a concurrent map.
  • Return false with Retry-After.
  • Test with repeated MockMvc calls.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • postHandle() is a HandlerInterceptor callback that runs after the controller method returned but before the view is rendered.
  • It receives the ModelAndView, so you can add shared model attributes (such as the current year or the user name) for every page.
  • It is skipped when the controller throws an exception or when preHandle() returned false.

Order of callbacks.

Worked Example 2

postHandle skipped on exception.

Practice Exercise 1

Add a shared attribute after the handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Test it with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • DispatcherServlet.doDispatch() gets a HandlerExecutionChain from the HandlerMapping.
  • It calls applyPreHandle, then the HandlerAdapter runs the controller and returns a ModelAndView.
  • applyPostHandle loops over the interceptors from the last to the first, then processDispatchResult renders the view.
  • If the handler throws, control jumps to exception resolution and applyPostHandle is never called.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Signature has four parameters; modelAndView is null for @ResponseBody methods and for handlers that return a view name only in some cases, so null-check it.
  • Extend HandlerInterceptor default methods: all three callbacks have default implementations, override only what you need.
  • AsyncHandlerInterceptor adds afterConcurrentHandlingStarted for async requests.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Signature: void postHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler, ModelAndView mav); mav can be null.
  • @ResponseBody: for REST controllers the body is already written when postHandle runs, so changing headers or the body there has no effect.
  • Reverse order: with several interceptors, postHandle runs in the reverse of the registration order.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer advice: use @ControllerAdvice with @ModelAttribute for shared model data; use postHandle only when you need the handler or request context.
  • Not for cleanup: because it is skipped on exceptions, put cleanup in afterCompletion(), never here.
  • Async requests: for async handlers use AsyncHandlerInterceptor, as the callbacks run on the initial and the dispatched thread.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: cleaning resources in postHandle. Fix: use afterCompletion.
  • Mistake: setting a header for a JSON response. Fix: set it in preHandle, or use a filter or ResponseBodyAdvice.
  • Mistake: using mav without a null check, giving NullPointerException.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • postHandle is cheap, but heavy work (database calls for menus) on every request slows all pages.
  • Cache shared model data (menu, footer) with @Cacheable instead of loading it per request.
  • Restrict the interceptor to HTML paths so API calls do not pay for it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A site needs the logged-in user name and cart size in the header of every page.
  • A postHandle adds both to the model once, so no controller repeats the code.
  • The team later moves the data to @ControllerAdvice to ease testing.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • afterCompletion() is the last HandlerInterceptor callback; it runs after the view is rendered, or after an exception was handled.
  • It is called whenever preHandle() of that interceptor returned true, even if the controller threw an exception.
  • The Exception ex parameter is non-null when the handler failed and no resolver has already handled it.

Worked Example 1

Guaranteed even on failure.

Worked Example 2

Test the cleanup.

Practice Exercise 1

Clean up a ThreadLocal.

Practice Exercise 2

Log status and failure.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • After processDispatchResult renders the view, triggerAfterCompletion is invoked.
  • HandlerExecutionChain keeps an index interceptorIndex of the last interceptor whose preHandle returned true.
  • triggerAfterCompletion loops from that index down to 0, which is why only the passed interceptors are cleaned up and in reverse order.
  • Exceptions thrown by an interceptor here are caught and logged, so the loop continues.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • The ex argument is set only for exceptions that no resolver handled, plus view rendering errors.
  • For @ExceptionHandler handled errors, check res.getStatus() instead.
  • For async requests it is called once, after the async dispatch finishes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cleanup: release resources opened in preHandle, such as ThreadLocal values, MDC keys and timers.
  • Exception argument: exceptions handled by @ExceptionHandler do not show up in ex, so it is null in that case.
  • Reverse order: it runs only for interceptors whose preHandle passed, in reverse order.

Senior Notes

  • ThreadLocal leaks: servlet threads are pooled; forgetting remove() here leaks data into the next request.
  • Do not throw: an exception thrown here is only logged by Spring, it cannot change the response which is already sent.
  • Status code: use res.getStatus() to log the final HTTP status, which is known at this point.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: forgetting ThreadLocal.remove(). Fix: always remove in afterCompletion.
  • Mistake: expecting it for an interceptor whose preHandle returned false. Fix: do not rely on it for that interceptor, and clean up before returning false.
  • Mistake: trying to change the response here. Fix: the response is already committed.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • The cost is tiny, but a slow afterCompletion (remote audit call) delays the thread release.
  • The response is usually already sent, yet the servlet thread stays busy; send audit data to a queue or @Async method.
  • A leaked ThreadLocal in a pool of 200 threads can hold large objects for a long time.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A multi-tenant app sets the tenant id in a ThreadLocal in preHandle.
  • Production showed users seeing another tenant data: the id was never removed.
  • Adding the cleanup in afterCompletion fixed it; a test now asserts the ThreadLocal is empty.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Registration means telling Spring MVC about your interceptor: implement WebMvcConfigurer and override addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry).
  • An interceptor class alone does nothing; it must be added with registry.addInterceptor(new MyInterceptor()).
  • Choose the URLs with addPathPatterns("/admin/**") and exclude some with excludePathPatterns.

Worked Example 1

Two ways to build the interceptor.

Worked Example 2

Order set explicitly.

Practice Exercise 1

Register one interceptor for /admin.

Practice Exercise 2

Verify with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • Spring Boot auto-configures WebMvcAutoConfiguration, which collects all WebMvcConfigurer beans through DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration.
  • Each addInterceptors call fills an InterceptorRegistry.
  • The registry builds MappedInterceptor objects (interceptor plus include and exclude patterns) sorted by order.
  • The RequestMappingHandlerMapping receives them and, for each request, adds those whose patterns match to the HandlerExecutionChain.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • addPathPatterns(String...) and a List overload.
  • excludePathPatterns wins over include patterns.
  • pathMatcher(...) switches the matching strategy; the default uses PathPatternParser in Spring 6.
  • order(int) sets position; WebRequestInterceptor can be added via addWebRequestInterceptor.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Default: with no path pattern the interceptor applies to every request that reaches the DispatcherServlet.
  • order(): registration.order(1) sets the position; lower numbers run first.
  • Spring Boot: put the @Configuration class with WebMvcConfigurer in your app and do not add @EnableWebMvc, which turns off Boot auto-configuration.

Senior Notes

  • Dependency injection: make the interceptor a @Component and inject it into the config class; new gives no injected fields.
  • Static resources: patterns also match static resource requests, so exclude /css/** and /js/** when needed.
  • Filters differ: a Servlet filter is registered through FilterRegistrationBean, not here.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: new interceptor with @Autowired fields gives NullPointerException. Fix: inject the bean through the config constructor.
  • Mistake: @EnableWebMvc in Boot hides auto-configured static resources and JSON settings. Fix: remove it.
  • Mistake: pattern /admin/* misses /admin/a/b. Fix: use /admin/**.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Matching runs on every request for every mapped interceptor; keep the list short and patterns simple.
  • Narrow patterns avoid the interceptor cost for static files.
  • Interceptor beans are singletons and must be thread safe.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A team has three cross-cutting needs: request id, authentication, audit.
  • One WebConfig registers all three with explicit order and path rules, and an integration test checks the chain for /api, /login and /css.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Interceptor chain: all registered interceptors that match the URL form a HandlerExecutionChain around the handler.
  • preHandle runs in registration order (1, 2, 3); postHandle and afterCompletion run in the reverse order (3, 2, 1).
  • If one preHandle returns false, the chain stops: the handler and later interceptors are skipped.

Worked Example 1

Order enforced with order().

Worked Example 2

Test the short circuit.

Practice Exercise 1

Print the order.

Practice Exercise 2

Short circuit in B.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • HandlerExecutionChain.applyPreHandle loops forward and increments interceptorIndex after each true result.
  • When one returns false, it calls triggerAfterCompletion itself and returns false to the dispatcher.
  • applyPostHandle loops backward from the last interceptor.
  • So the chain is a stack: first in, last out for the closing callbacks.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Order is decided by order() first, then by registration order for equal values.
  • Different interceptors can use different path patterns, so the chain differs per URL.
  • To share data between interceptors use request attributes with constant names.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Short circuit: when interceptor 2 returns false, only afterCompletion of interceptor 1 runs afterwards.
  • Response duty: an interceptor that returns false must write the response itself (error status, redirect), or the client gets an empty 200.
  • Ordering rule: put cheap and generic interceptors (logging, request id) first and expensive ones (auth lookups) later.

Senior Notes

  • Hidden dependencies: if interceptor B reads a request attribute set by A, document and enforce the order with order().
  • Cost: every interceptor adds work on each request; limit each to the paths where it is needed.
  • Filters first: servlet filters run before the whole interceptor chain and after it on the way out.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: relying on bean scan order for the sequence. Fix: set order().
  • Mistake: returning false without a response. Fix: send the error or redirect first.
  • Mistake: assuming afterCompletion runs for all interceptors. Fix: only those with passed preHandle.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Put the most likely to reject interceptor (authentication) early so later work is skipped.
  • Avoid per-request object creation and remote calls inside preHandle; use caches.
  • Merge small related interceptors if they always apply to the same paths.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • An API has request id, logging, authentication and rate limiting.
  • Order: request id, logging (so rejected requests are logged too), authentication, rate limit.
  • An integration test calls with and without a token and checks status and headers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Logging interceptor: an interceptor that logs every request (method, URL, status, duration) in one place instead of in each controller.
  • Log the start in preHandle() and the result in afterCompletion(), where the status and the exception are known.
  • Use a unique request id in the log lines so you can follow one request through many log entries.

Worked Example 1

Mask sensitive headers.

Worked Example 2

Verify the interceptor does not change responses.

Practice Exercise 1

A simple logging interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Log pattern with MDC.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss}
[%X{requestId}] %-5level %msg%n

# OUTPUT:
# 10:15:02 [a1b2c3d4] INFO  --> GET /products

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • The interceptor is a singleton called by the container thread of the request, so MDC (a ThreadLocal map in SLF4J) is safe.
  • Logback reads MDC values when formatting each line with %X{key}.
  • With a servlet filter before the interceptor, you can put the id there to also cover error pages.
  • Async work on other threads does not inherit MDC unless you copy it (for example with a task decorator).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Levels: log start at DEBUG and failures at ERROR to control volume.
  • Structured logging: Spring Boot 3.4 and later can output JSON; otherwise use a Logback JSON encoder.
  • Choose what to log: method, path, status, duration, user id; avoid full query strings with secrets.
codeExamples:
log.atInfo()
   .addKeyValue("method", q.getMethod())
   .addKeyValue("path", q.getRequestURI())
   .addKeyValue("status", s.getStatus())
   .log("request done");

# OUTPUT:
# {"msg":"request done","method":"GET","path":"/products","status":200}

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • MDC: MDC.put("requestId", id) in preHandle and MDC.clear() in afterCompletion; the log pattern prints %X{requestId}.
  • Logger: use SLF4J (LoggerFactory.getLogger), not System.out.
  • Skip noise: exclude health checks and static resources with excludePathPatterns.

Senior Notes

  • Sensitive data: never log passwords, tokens or full request bodies; mask headers such as Authorization.
  • Body logging: reading the body in an interceptor consumes the stream; use ContentCachingRequestWrapper in a filter if you really need it.
  • Alternative: CommonsRequestLoggingFilter is a ready-made filter for simple request logging.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: logging Authorization or passwords. Fix: mask or skip them.
  • Mistake: not clearing MDC. Fix: clear in afterCompletion.
  • Mistake: reading getInputStream() to log the body, so the controller gets an empty body. Fix: use a caching wrapper in a filter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Use parameterized logging (log.info("{}", x)) so strings are built only when the level is on.
  • Log at DEBUG for noisy endpoints and sample high traffic ones.
  • Async appenders keep slow disks away from request threads.
codeExamples:
<appender name="ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">
    <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
    <queueSize>1024</queueSize>
</appender>

// OUTPUT:
// request threads hand log events to a queue instead of writing to disk

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • Support receives: "order 42 failed at 10:15". With the request id in every line, an engineer greps one id and sees the whole story.
  • The id is also returned in the X-Request-Id response header, so the user can quote it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Authentication interceptor: checks in preHandle() that the caller is logged in and rejects the request otherwise.
  • For session apps check a session attribute and redirect to /login; for APIs check a token header and reply 401 Unauthorized.
  • Return false after sending the redirect or error, so the controller is never reached.

Worked Example 1

Registration with public paths.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test with a session.

Practice Exercise 1

Session-based check.

Practice Exercise 2

Token check for an API.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • The preHandle runs after servlet filters but before the controller, with the HttpSession managed by the container (cookie JSESSIONID).
  • getSession(false) only looks up the existing session by the cookie.
  • Rejecting means writing the response in the interceptor and returning false; the dispatcher then skips the handler.
  • Spring Security does this earlier, in a servlet filter chain (FilterChainProxy), which also protects non-MVC resources.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Session variant: redirect to login. Token variant: 401 JSON body.
  • Remember me or API keys: validate in a service, cache the result briefly.
  • Return the original URL after login by storing it in the session.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Session check: request.getSession(false) returns null when there is no session; avoid creating one by accident.
  • Public URLs: exclude /login, /register and static files with excludePathPatterns, or you cause a redirect loop.
  • Status codes: 401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

Senior Notes

  • Use Spring Security for real applications: it handles sessions, password hashing, CSRF and token validation; a hand-made interceptor is fine for learning or small internal tools.
  • Token validation: verify signature and expiry on every request; never trust a header only because it exists.
  • Return to page: store the original URL before redirecting to login so you can send the user back after login.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: redirect loop because /login is protected. Fix: exclude it.
  • Mistake: returning true after sendRedirect, causing IllegalStateException later. Fix: return false.
  • Mistake: trusting a role or userId request parameter. Fix: use server-side data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Session lookups are in memory and cheap; remote token validation is not, so cache validated tokens for a short time.
  • Avoid creating sessions for anonymous traffic (getSession(false)).
  • For many servers use stateless tokens or a shared session store (Spring Session).
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.timeout=30m
spring.session.store-type=redis

# OUTPUT:
# sessions shared between instances and expire after 30 minutes

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • An internal admin tool needs a quick login gate for 20 pages and has no security library yet.
  • One interceptor checks the session user; later the team migrates to Spring Security without touching controllers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Authorization interceptor: after the user is known, it checks whether the user has the role or permission needed for the requested handler.
  • The handler is passed as Object handler; cast it to HandlerMethod to read annotations on the controller method.
  • Reply with 403 Forbidden and return false when the user lacks the permission.

Worked Example 1

Test both outcomes.

Worked Example 2

Class level plus method level.

Practice Exercise 1

Annotation-driven roles.

Practice Exercise 2

Use it on a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • For controller methods, the handler argument is a HandlerMethod, which exposes the bean type, method and annotations.
  • For static resources it is a ResourceHttpRequestHandler, so the cast needs a guard.
  • getMethodAnnotation finds annotations on the method, including meta annotations.
  • The role comes from earlier authentication (session or request attribute).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Allow several roles: String[] value() in the annotation.
  • Permission checks can use a service: permissionService.can(user, action).
  • Spring Security equivalents: @PreAuthorize, @Secured, requestMatchers(...).hasRole(...).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom annotation: define @RequiresRole("ADMIN") with @Retention(RUNTIME) and read it with handlerMethod.getMethodAnnotation(...).
  • instanceof check: static resources use a different handler type, so test handler instanceof HandlerMethod first.
  • Order: run it after the authentication interceptor, since it needs the user.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer Spring Security: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") with method security does the same with far more features.
  • Class and method: check the annotation on both the method and the class (getBeanType()).
  • Never trust the client: take roles from the server side session or verified token, not from a request parameter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: forgetting RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME, so the annotation is invisible. Fix: add it.
  • Mistake: ClassCastException on static resources. Fix: use instanceof.
  • Mistake: 401 instead of 403 for a logged-in user. Fix: send 403.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Reflection lookups per request are fast but can be cached in a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by method.
  • Permission service calls to a database should be cached per user.
  • Do the cheap role check before any heavy query.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A back office has USER, MANAGER and ADMIN. Report pages need MANAGER or ADMIN; user deletion needs ADMIN.
  • Annotations on controller methods document the rule next to the code, and a MockMvc test per role guards it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request tracking means giving each request an id and recording counts or timings so one call can be followed across logs and services.
  • An interceptor reads the X-Request-Id header or generates a UUID in preHandle() and sets it on the request and response.
  • Keep the id in the MDC so every log line of that request shows it.

Worked Example 1

Read the id in a controller.

Worked Example 2

Test that the header is returned.

Practice Exercise 1

Assign and echo a request id.

Practice Exercise 2

Count hits per path.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • The interceptor creates or reads the id in preHandle, stores it as an attribute and in MDC, and echoes it in the response header.
  • Outgoing calls (RestClient, WebClient) add the header from MDC.
  • Logs of all services then share the id, so a log tool can join them.
  • Micrometer Tracing standardizes this with trace and span ids (W3C traceparent).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Counters: LongAdder is faster than AtomicLong under heavy contention.
  • Per-user or per-path stats: bounded maps only, or Micrometer tags with a small number of values.
  • Use the route template (/orders/{id}), not the raw URL, as a key.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Propagation: when your service calls another service, send the same X-Request-Id header so logs can be joined.
  • Counters: use AtomicLong or a ConcurrentHashMap for hit counts; plain HashMap is not thread safe.
  • Request attribute: request.setAttribute("requestId", id) makes the id available to controllers.

Senior Notes

  • Use real tools: Micrometer and Micrometer Tracing give metrics and distributed trace ids; hand-made counters are only for learning.
  • Memory growth: do not store one map entry per request or per raw URL with ids inside; the map grows without limit.
  • Trust: validate an incoming request id (length, characters) before logging it to avoid log injection.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: raw URLs as map keys give unbounded memory. Fix: use the pattern.
  • Mistake: logging the incoming id unchecked. Fix: validate with a regex.
  • Mistake: using a plain HashMap across threads. Fix: ConcurrentHashMap.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Tracking cost is small; unbounded keys and synchronized blocks are the real risk.
  • UUID generation is fast, but avoid SecureRandom blocking by using UUID.randomUUID() as usual.
  • Prefer Micrometer for metrics so you get aggregation and export for free.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.tracing.sampling.probability=0.1

# OUTPUT:
# 10 percent of requests are traced, lowering overhead

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A checkout call passes through gateway, order service and payment service.
  • One failed payment is found in seconds by searching its request id in the central log tool.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes
