  • Performance monitoring with an interceptor measures how long each request takes, from preHandle() to afterCompletion().
  • Store the start time as a request attribute in preHandle and compute the difference in afterCompletion.
  • Log slow requests with a warning when the duration is above a threshold, such as 500 ms.

Worked Example 1

Use Actuator instead.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests
# {
    "name":"http.server.requests","measurements":[{"statistic":"COUNT","value":42.0}]
}

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Test the header.

Practice Exercise 1

Timing interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Add the time as a response header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • The interceptor instance is shared, so per-request state lives in the request (attributes) or on the stack.
  • preHandle stores System.nanoTime(); afterCompletion subtracts it.
  • Spring Boot Actuator does the same through WebMvcMetricsFilter (a filter) feeding a Micrometer Timer.
  • Because a filter wraps the interceptors, Actuator numbers include more work than an interceptor measures.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Use a Micrometer Timer for percentiles instead of manual logs.
  • Tag with route template and status, never with raw URL or user id.
  • @Timed on controller methods is another option.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Clock: use System.nanoTime() for durations; currentTimeMillis() can jump when the clock changes.
  • No instance field: an interceptor is a singleton shared by all threads, so a start time field would be overwritten by other requests.
  • Scope: the measured time covers the handler and view rendering, but not time spent in servlet filters before the interceptor.

Senior Notes

  • Real metrics: Spring Boot Actuator with Micrometer already records http.server.requests timers; prefer it over hand-made code.
  • Percentiles: averages hide slow requests; track p95 and p99 with histograms.
  • Overhead: measuring is cheap, but logging every request at INFO adds I/O; log only slow ones or sample them.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: storing start time in a field. Fix: request attribute.
  • Mistake: timing with currentTimeMillis. Fix: nanoTime.
  • Mistake: calling postHandle to measure, missing failed requests. Fix: use afterCompletion.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Alert on p95 and p99 latency and error rate, not on the average.
  • Slow request logs help find the cause; add a trace id for details.
  • Do not call remote systems in the measuring code.
codeExamples:
# Prometheus style query
# histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

# OUTPUT:
# 0.42  (seconds, varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • After a release the report page became slow only for large customers.
  • The slow request warning in the log named the URL and duration; a trace pointed to an N+1 query, fixed with a fetch join.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Servlet filter: a class implementing jakarta.servlet.Filter that runs before a request reaches the servlet and again after the response is produced.
  • It works at the servlet container level, before the DispatcherServlet, so it knows nothing about controllers or handlers.
  • Its method doFilter(request, response, chain) must call chain.doFilter(request, response) to continue; skipping it blocks the request.

Worked Example 1

Block a request in a filter.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc (filters added explicitly in slice tests).

Practice Exercise 1

A timing filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Register with a pattern and order.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

  • The servlet container (Tomcat) builds a FilterChain per request from the registered filters and the target servlet.
  • Spring Boot registers every Filter bean (and FilterRegistrationBean) with the embedded container.
  • Each doFilter calls chain.doFilter, which runs the next filter and finally the DispatcherServlet.
  • Code after chain.doFilter runs on the way back, after the response is produced.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Plain Filter (init, doFilter, destroy) or OncePerRequestFilter with doFilterInternal.
  • Skip logic: override shouldNotFilter(request).
  • Async and error dispatches: shouldNotFilterAsyncDispatch() and shouldNotFilterErrorDispatch().
  • Wrappers: HttpServletRequestWrapper and ContentCachingResponseWrapper to change or capture data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registration: annotate with @Component in Spring Boot, or use FilterRegistrationBean to set URL patterns and order.
  • OncePerRequestFilter: the Spring base class guarantees one execution per request, even across forwards and error dispatches.
  • Filter vs interceptor: filters wrap everything and can replace the request or response (wrappers); interceptors see the handler and the model.

Senior Notes

  • Typical uses: encoding, CORS, security (Spring Security is a filter chain), compression and request body caching.
  • Order: setOrder(...) on the registration bean or @Order on the class; lower runs first.
  • Exceptions: exceptions thrown in a filter are not handled by @ControllerAdvice because MVC has not started; use a HandlerExceptionResolver or write the response in the filter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Mistake: forgetting chain.doFilter, so every request hangs or returns empty. Fix: call it on the allowed path.
  • Mistake: expecting @ControllerAdvice to handle filter exceptions. Fix: catch and write the response, or delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Mistake: registering the same filter twice (bean plus FilterRegistrationBean). Fix: use only one.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Filters run for every request including static files; use URL patterns or shouldNotFilter.
  • Do not buffer whole bodies in memory for large uploads.
  • Keep the number of filters small; each adds a call level to the stack.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

  • A service must accept only requests with a valid API key and log all rejects, even for URLs with no controller.
  • A filter is the right place: it runs before MVC, covers every path, and can reject early and cheaply.
  • Per-controller rules (roles) stay in interceptors or Spring Security.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Filter is a servlet-container component (jakarta.servlet.Filter) that runs before the request reaches DispatcherServlet.
  • Interceptor is a Spring MVC component (HandlerInterceptor) that runs inside the DispatcherServlet, around the controller method.
  • Rule of thumb: use a filter for cross-cutting web concerns (security, CORS, encoding, logging); use an interceptor when you need to know which handler will run.

Worked Example 1

Show the call order.

Worked Example 2

Test the interceptor with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Register a simple interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

A filter doing the same job.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The two sit at different layers of the stack.

  • Filter: Tomcat builds an ApplicationFilterChain and the last element calls the servlet.
  • Interceptor: DispatcherServlet.doDispatch gets a HandlerExecutionChain from the HandlerMapping.
  • preHandle runs in order; if one returns false the rest are skipped and afterCompletion runs for those that passed.
  • postHandle runs in reverse order after the handler but before view rendering.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • Filter: Filter, OncePerRequestFilter, GenericFilterBean.
  • Interceptor: HandlerInterceptor and AsyncHandlerInterceptor.
  • Registration: addPathPatterns, excludePathPatterns and order for interceptors.
  • Alternatives: AOP for service-layer concerns and @ControllerAdvice for responses.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Handler access: an interceptor receives the handler object (for example a HandlerMethod), a filter only sees raw request and response.
  • Three callbacks: preHandle, postHandle and afterCompletion; a filter has just doFilter with code before and after chain.doFilter.
  • Scope: a filter can touch every request including static files and non-Spring servlets; an interceptor only sees requests mapped to the DispatcherServlet.

Senior Notes

  • Exceptions: an exception thrown by a controller can be handled by @ControllerAdvice before an interceptor runs afterCompletion, but a filter sees it only if it propagates out.
  • Body wrapping: only a filter can replace the request or response with a wrapper (for example caching the body), because it controls what goes down the chain.
  • Spring Security is itself a filter chain (DelegatingFilterProxy or FilterChainProxy), which is why authentication belongs in filters.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using an interceptor for security: static resources and error pages can bypass it; use a filter or Spring Security.
  • Forgetting to return true in preHandle, so the controller never runs.
  • Reading the body in an interceptor: the stream is consumed; wrap it in a filter instead.
  • Interceptor not applied: it was not registered through WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Modifying the response in postHandle after it is committed has no effect.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning points:

  • Keep both cheap; they run on every request.
  • Narrow interceptors with path patterns instead of checking the URL inside.
  • Avoid blocking calls (remote auth checks) without caching.
  • Use filters only for what must happen before MVC.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real project layout:

  • Filters: request id, logging, CORS, JWT authentication.
  • Interceptors: tenant resolution from the handler annotation, audit of admin actions, locale change.
  • Reason: auth needs to cover every path, while audit needs controller metadata.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Filter is a servlet component implementing jakarta.servlet.Filter that inspects or changes a request and response before and after the servlet runs.
  • doFilter is the only method you must write: do pre-work, call chain.doFilter(req, res) to continue, then do post-work.
  • Typical jobs: logging, authentication, CORS headers, character encoding, compression and rate limiting.

Worked Example 1

Control URL pattern and order.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal filter that adds a response header.

Practice Exercise 2

Blocking requests without a header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a filter runs in the container:

  • Container reads filter declarations (annotations, web.xml or Boot registration beans) at startup and calls init.
  • For each request it matches URL patterns and dispatcher types and builds a chain.
  • Each doFilter gets the same request and response objects, or wrappers it passes on.
  • When the chain ends the servlet (DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC) is invoked.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to create a filter:

  • @Component: maps to /*, simplest.
  • FilterRegistrationBean: patterns, order, init params, dispatcher types.
  • @WebFilter with @ServletComponentScan.
  • DelegatingFilterProxy: bridges a servlet filter to a Spring bean in non-Boot apps.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registration in Spring Boot: declare the filter as a @Component or define a FilterRegistrationBean for URL patterns and order.
  • Short circuit: do not call chain.doFilter and write the response yourself (for example 401) to stop the request.
  • Lifecycle: init once at startup, doFilter per request, destroy at shutdown; the latter two have default methods since Servlet 4.

Senior Notes

  • Singleton: one filter instance serves many threads, so keep it stateless or thread safe.
  • Wrappers: use HttpServletRequestWrapper or ContentCachingRequestWrapper to read the body more than once.
  • Async and dispatch types: filters run for REQUEST by default; ASYNC, ERROR and FORWARD dispatches need extra registration or OncePerRequestFilter care.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No chain.doFilter on the normal path: request hangs or returns blank.
  • Reading the body without a wrapper: controller gets an empty body.
  • Storing state in fields: race conditions.
  • Swallowing exceptions so errors become empty 200 responses.
  • Casting to HttpServletRequest without checking when the filter may see other types.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Filters run for every request, including images and CSS; restrict patterns.
  • Avoid blocking IO and heavy parsing.
  • Wrapping and copying bodies costs memory; set a maximum length.
  • Prefer static immutable fields (patterns, config) created once.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API needs an API key check, a request id and a response compression rule.

  • Request id filter first, so every log has an id.
  • API key filter on /api/* only.
  • Rate limit counters held in a thread-safe cache, not in the filter instance.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • OncePerRequestFilter is a Spring base class that guarantees doFilterInternal runs only one time per request, even with forwards or error dispatches.
  • You override doFilterInternal(request, response, filterChain) and call filterChain.doFilter yourself to continue.
  • Why use it: a plain Filter can run twice when a request is forwarded internally; this class marks the request with an attribute to skip repeats.

Worked Example 1

Show the double-run problem avoided.

Worked Example 2

Test the header.

Practice Exercise 1

A request id filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Skip health checks.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside OncePerRequestFilter.doFilter:

  • Computes an attribute name from getAlreadyFilteredAttributeName(): the filter bean name plus .FILTERED.
  • If the attribute exists, or shouldNotFilter is true, it just calls chain.doFilter.
  • Otherwise sets the attribute, calls doFilterInternal, and removes the attribute in a finally block.
  • Async and error dispatch types have their own skip methods.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Overridable hooks:

  • shouldNotFilter(request): skip by URL or header.
  • shouldNotFilterAsyncDispatch(): default true, skips ASYNC.
  • shouldNotFilterErrorDispatch(): default true, skips ERROR.
  • getAlreadyFilteredAttributeName(): custom attribute key.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • shouldNotFilter lets you skip URLs, for example /health or static resources.
  • Casting done for you: arguments are already HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse, no manual casts.
  • Async: override shouldNotFilterAsyncDispatch and shouldNotFilterErrorDispatch to control those dispatch types.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanism: it stores an attribute named from the filter bean name plus .FILTERED on the request and checks it on the next dispatch.
  • Bean name matters: two instances of the same class with different names are treated as different filters.
  • Security: Spring Security filters such as BasicAuthenticationFilter extend it, so custom auth filters follow the same pattern.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Extending Filter directly and then seeing duplicated work after a forward.
  • Forgetting to call filterChain.doFilter inside doFilterInternal.
  • Expecting the filter to run on error pages; the default skips ERROR.
  • Doing post-processing for an async controller in the wrong dispatch.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance is almost free: one attribute read and write per request. Gains come from shouldNotFilter skipping static files, actuator and health endpoints.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a tenant filter reads the X-Tenant header and stores it in a ThreadLocal, which must be cleared after one run.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request logging filter is a filter that records method, URL, status and duration of every request in one central place.
  • Spring built-in: CommonsRequestLoggingFilter logs request details at DEBUG level of its own logger.
  • Custom version: extend OncePerRequestFilter, measure time around chain.doFilter and log after the response is produced.

Worked Example 1

Add a request id to MDC.

Worked Example 2

Test that the filter does not break the request.

Practice Exercise 1

Built-in filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom timing logger.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the built-in CommonsRequestLoggingFilter works (it extends AbstractRequestLoggingFilter):

  • Its doFilterInternal calls beforeRequest and, after the chain, afterRequest.
  • With payload logging it wraps the request in ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Messages are built from prefix, URI, query, client, session, headers and payload, then sent to the logger only if DEBUG is on.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • setIncludeQueryString, setIncludeClientInfo, setIncludeHeaders, setIncludePayload.
  • setMaxPayloadLength limits payload size.
  • setHeaderPredicate chooses which headers are shown.
  • Prefix and suffix text through setBeforeMessagePrefix and similar.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Enable the built-in filter by declaring it as a bean and setting the logger org.springframework.web.filter.CommonsRequestLoggingFilter to DEBUG.
  • Options: setIncludeQueryString, setIncludePayload, setIncludeHeaders and setMaxPayloadLength.
  • Correlation: put a request id into the MDC so every log line of that request can be linked.

Senior Notes

  • Body logging needs ContentCachingRequestWrapper; the payload is only available after the controller has read it.
  • Sensitive data: never log passwords, tokens or card numbers; mask headers such as Authorization.
  • MDC cleanup: always call MDC.clear() in a finally block because threads are reused.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Logger level not DEBUG, so nothing is printed.
  • Logging the payload before the controller reads it: always empty.
  • Logging the Authorization header or password fields.
  • MDC not cleared.
  • Using the same filter in the security chain and as a bean: double logs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Use parameterized logging so strings are built only if the level is on.
  • Cap payload length and skip binary or upload types.
  • Use async appenders for heavy traffic.
  • Sample (for example 1 percent) when volume is huge.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: support asks why one customer got a 500. Each log line has a request id from the MDC, so the whole request can be found with one search.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Authentication filter is a filter that finds credentials in a request (header, cookie, token), verifies them and marks the request as authenticated or rejects it.
  • In Spring Security the filter puts an Authentication object into the SecurityContextHolder so later code can call getPrincipal.
  • Failure returns 401 Unauthorized before the controller runs.

Worked Example 1

Reject bad token directly.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc and a user.

Practice Exercise 1

A simple token filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Add it to the security chain.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Typical internal flow of a token authentication filter:

  • Extract the credential from the request.
  • Create an unauthenticated token and pass it to the AuthenticationManager, or validate directly.
  • On success build an authenticated Authentication and store it in SecurityContextHolder.
  • Continue the chain; later AuthorizationFilter checks roles.
  • On failure call an AuthenticationEntryPoint to send 401.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Basic: BasicAuthenticationFilter.
  • Form login: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.
  • Bearer or JWT: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter in the resource server module, or a custom filter.
  • API key: custom filter with a fixed header.
  • Pre-authenticated: AbstractPreAuthenticatedProcessingFilter for gateway headers.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom filter usually extends OncePerRequestFilter and is added with http.addFilterBefore(filter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class).
  • Typical flow: read the Authorization: Bearer header, validate the token, build UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, set the context, continue the chain.
  • Built-ins: BasicAuthenticationFilter and UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter already handle Basic auth and form login.

Senior Notes

  • Do not register twice: a filter bean that is also added to the security chain runs outside and inside it; disable the servlet registration with FilterRegistrationBean.setEnabled(false).
  • Stateless APIs set SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS and rebuild the context on every request.
  • Clear the context: Spring Security clears it after each request; custom code should never keep it in static fields.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Registering the filter as a bean as well as in the security chain (runs twice).
  • Never clearing or setting the context in a stateless app, so stale users appear.
  • Returning 403 for bad credentials instead of 401.
  • Comparing secrets with equals (timing attack): use MessageDigest.isEqual.
  • Placing the filter after AuthorizationFilter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cache validated tokens or use signature-only JWT checks to avoid a database call on each request.
  • Skip public paths with shouldNotFilter.
  • Do not load full user entities each request unless needed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile app sends a JWT. The filter validates it, loads roles from claims, and controllers use @PreAuthorize and Principal.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule: a page from one origin may call another origin only if the server sends allowing headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • CORS filter is a filter (Spring provides CorsFilter) that answers the browser preflight OPTIONS request and adds those headers.
  • Origin means scheme, host and port together; http://localhost:3000 and http://localhost:8080 are different origins.

Worked Example 1

With Spring Security.

Worked Example 2

Test the preflight.

Practice Exercise 1

Global config with WebMvcConfigurer.

Practice Exercise 2

CorsFilter bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How CORS processing works:

  • Browser sends Origin; for non-simple requests it first sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method.
  • CorsFilter asks a CorsConfigurationSource for a configuration for the path.
  • DefaultCorsProcessor validates origin, method and headers, and adds response headers.
  • For a valid preflight it returns immediately without calling the chain; for a normal request it adds headers and continues.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options:

  • allowedOrigins or allowedOriginPatterns.
  • allowedMethods, allowedHeaders, exposedHeaders.
  • allowCredentials and maxAge.
  • Per controller: @CrossOrigin(origins = ..., maxAge = ...).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Simple way: annotate a controller with @CrossOrigin or configure addCorsMappings in WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Filter way: register CorsFilter with a UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource so CORS runs before security and MVC.
  • Preflight: for methods like PUT, DELETE or custom headers the browser first sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method.

Senior Notes

  • Credentials: with allowCredentials(true) you cannot use the wildcard * for origins; list them or use origin patterns.
  • Spring Security: enable http.cors(...), otherwise the security filters reject the preflight before MVC CORS runs.
  • Not a security feature: CORS only protects browsers; curl or other servers ignore it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wildcard origin with credentials: Spring throws an error at startup.
  • Security blocks preflight (no http.cors).
  • Missing OPTIONS in allowed methods in a custom filter.
  • Trailing slash or wrong port in the origin string.
  • Believing CORS blocks server-to-server calls.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning: set maxAge so browsers cache the preflight result and skip repeat OPTIONS calls; limit allowed paths to the API.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a React app on port 3000 calls a Spring Boot API on port 8080 with cookies. Configure the exact origin, allow credentials, enable http.cors.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CharacterEncodingFilter is a Spring filter that sets the character encoding (usually UTF-8) on the request, and optionally the response, so text is decoded correctly.
  • Without it form data and request bodies may be read as ISO-8859-1, giving broken text such as unreadable symbols for non-English names.
  • Spring Boot registers it automatically with UTF-8 through server.servlet.encoding properties.

Worked Example 1

Controller that echoes a form field.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Boot properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.encoding.charset=UTF-8
server.servlet.encoding.enabled=true
server.servlet.encoding.force=true

# OUTPUT:
# POST name=Zoë -> controller receives "Zoë" (not "ZoÃ«")

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Manual bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it works:

  • Extends OncePerRequestFilter.
  • If encoding is set and (forceRequestEncoding or the request has no encoding), it calls request.setCharacterEncoding.
  • If forceResponseEncoding is on it calls response.setCharacterEncoding.
  • Then it continues the chain.
  • Boot configures it in HttpEncodingAutoConfiguration from the server.servlet.encoding properties.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options in Boot:

  • server.servlet.encoding.charset (default UTF-8).
  • server.servlet.encoding.force, force-request, force-response.
  • server.servlet.encoding.mapping maps locales to encodings.
  • Classic: AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer.getServletFilters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Properties: server.servlet.encoding.charset=UTF-8, enabled=true and force=true.
  • force makes the filter overwrite the encoding even if the request already declares one; forceRequest and forceResponse are separate switches.
  • Classic Spring MVC: declare the filter in web.xml or in a WebApplicationInitializer with setEncoding("UTF-8").

Senior Notes

  • Order: it must run first (before any code calls getParameter), because after parameters are parsed the request encoding cannot be changed.
  • Implementation: it extends OncePerRequestFilter and calls request.setCharacterEncoding when none is set or force is on.
  • JSON is always UTF-8 by default in Jackson, so the filter matters mostly for form posts and query strings.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Filter registered late: getParameter already ran in an earlier filter.
  • Different charset on the HTML page, database connection and filter.
  • Setting encoding in a controller after reading parameters.
  • Using ISO-8859-1 by default in old projects.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The filter is nearly free (two setter calls). The real cost is in debugging mismatches, so standardize on UTF-8 everywhere: filter, <meta charset>, JDBC URL and file encoding.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost/app?characterEncoding=UTF-8
server.servlet.encoding.charset=UTF-8

# OUTPUT:
# Names with accents round-trip browser -> controller -> database -> browser

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a registration form accepts names in many languages. After enabling UTF-8 and the forced filter, saved names display correctly.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • FilterChain is the object passed to doFilter that represents the remaining filters and finally the servlet.
  • Calling chain.doFilter(req, res) hands control to the next element; code before the call runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way out.
  • Like layers of an onion: the first filter wraps all the others and sees the response last.

Worked Example 1

Catch downstream errors.

Worked Example 2

Test filter order.

Practice Exercise 1

Two filters showing the flow.

Practice Exercise 2

Stopping the chain.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Servlet container chain:

  • Tomcat: ApplicationFilterFactory.createFilterChain collects filter maps whose URL and dispatcher type match.
  • Spring Security: FilterChainProxy.doFilter finds the first SecurityFilterChain whose matcher accepts the request and runs a VirtualFilterChain over its filters, then continues the outer chain.
  • Each wrapper object created along the way is what later filters see.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for building chains:

  • Several SecurityFilterChain beans with securityMatcher and @Order.
  • Servlet filters through FilterRegistrationBean.
  • Dispatcher types (REQUEST, FORWARD, INCLUDE, ERROR, ASYNC).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order is decided by FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder or @Order; lower numbers run first.
  • Skipping: if a filter does not call the chain, later filters and the servlet never run.
  • Spring Security adds a single springSecurityFilterChain filter that itself holds an inner list of security filters.

Senior Notes

  • Container implementation: Tomcat builds an ApplicationFilterChain per request holding the matching filters in order and an index to the next one.
  • Multiple chains: FilterChainProxy picks one SecurityFilterChain by request matcher, so /api and /admin can have different rules.
  • Exceptions propagate back through the chain; a filter can catch them in a try/catch around chain.doFilter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Not calling the chain on the happy path.
  • Calling the chain twice (duplicate responses).
  • Writing to the response and then calling the chain.
  • Catching exceptions and hiding them.
  • Putting a catch-all SecurityFilterChain first so later ones never match.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Chain length adds cost to every request. Remove unused filters, narrow URL patterns, and put cheap rejecting filters (rate limit, auth) early so expensive work is skipped.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: debugging "why is my header missing". Print the filter chain in order from the startup log or the Boot actuator /actuator/mappings and check position of the filter.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Filter ordering decides which filter runs first; lower order value means earlier on the way in and later on the way out.
  • In Spring Boot set it with @Order(n) on the filter component or setOrder(n) on a FilterRegistrationBean.
  • Constants: Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE is the smallest int and runs first; LOWEST_PRECEDENCE runs last.

Worked Example 1

Place a filter in the security chain.

Worked Example 2

Assert order in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Order with annotations.

Practice Exercise 2

Order with registration bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Ordering internals:

  • Boot collects Filter beans and FilterRegistrationBean beans in ServletContextInitializerBeans.
  • It sorts them with AnnotationAwareOrderComparator, which reads Ordered or @Order.
  • The sorted list is registered in the servlet context in that order, and the container keeps registration order for the chain.
  • Inside security, FilterOrderRegistry assigns a number to each known filter class and custom filters are placed relative to them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to control order:

  • @Order on a filter bean.
  • Implement Ordered.
  • FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder.
  • addFilterBefore, addFilterAfter, addFilterAt in security.
  • Constants from OrderedFilter such as REQUEST_WRAPPER_FILTER_MAX_ORDER in Boot.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Default: a filter without order gets LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, and ties have no guaranteed order.
  • Boot built-ins have fixed orders, for example the character encoding filter is early and Spring Security default filter order is -100 (SecurityProperties.DEFAULT_FILTER_ORDER).
  • Inside security the order is defined by the position in SecurityFilterChain; use addFilterBefore, addFilterAfter or addFilterAt.

Senior Notes

  • @Order on a plain @Component works for Boot-detected filters, but @WebFilter classes ignore it unless wrapped in a registration bean.
  • Typical sequence: encoding, request id and logging, CORS, security, then rate limiting and business filters.
  • Debug with logging.level.org.springframework.boot.web.servlet=DEBUG or the startup log of mapped filters to confirm order.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Same order number for two filters: unpredictable.
  • Placing a logging filter after security, so 401 requests are not logged.
  • Placing a CORS filter after security, so preflight gets 401.
  • Using @Order on a filter created with new inside a configuration (not a bean).
  • Assuming @Order on @WebFilter works.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Place cheap rejecting filters before expensive ones, and keep an ordering table in your documentation. Leave gaps (10, 20, 30) so new filters can be inserted without renumbering.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: logs show requests rejected with 401 but no request id. The request id filter was ordered after the security filter; moving it to HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE fixes it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Servlet is a Java class (extending jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet) that runs inside a container such as Tomcat and handles HTTP requests, producing responses.
  • Container creates the servlet, calls init once, calls service (which dispatches to doGet, doPost and so on) per request, and calls destroy at shutdown.
  • Spring MVC is built on one servlet: DispatcherServlet receives every request and routes it to your controllers.

Worked Example 1

Sessions and attributes.

Worked Example 2

Test a servlet with MockMvc-style mocks.

Practice Exercise 1

Hello servlet.

Practice Exercise 2

Register in Spring Boot.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the container runs a servlet:

  • Container (Tomcat) loads the class, creates one instance and calls init(ServletConfig).
  • A connector thread parses the HTTP request into HttpServletRequest and calls service.
  • HttpServlet.service picks doGet, doPost and so on by the HTTP method.
  • When the response is complete the thread returns to the pool.
  • On shutdown destroy is called.
  • In Spring MVC the single DispatcherServlet does the above and then uses HandlerMapping to find your controller.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Servlet features:

  • Methods: doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete.
  • Reading input: getParameter, getHeader, getInputStream, getReader.
  • Output: setStatus, setHeader, sendRedirect, getWriter.
  • Forwarding: RequestDispatcher.forward and include.
  • Other: @MultipartConfig for uploads, startAsync for async.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request and response: HttpServletRequest gives parameters, headers and body; HttpServletResponse sets status, headers and writes output.
  • Mapping with @WebServlet("/hello") or in web.xml; in Boot use @ServletComponentScan or ServletRegistrationBean.
  • Scopes: request attributes, HttpSession and the ServletContext (application scope).

Senior Notes

  • Threading: one servlet instance serves all requests concurrently, so instance fields are shared; keep servlets stateless.
  • Jakarta: since Servlet 5 (Spring 6, Boot 3) packages are jakarta.servlet, not javax.servlet.
  • Layers: filters wrap servlets; DispatcherServlet then adds handler mapping, adapters, view resolvers and exception resolvers on top.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Storing request data in instance fields (shared by all threads).
  • Using javax.servlet imports with Boot 3.
  • Calling getWriter and getOutputStream on the same response.
  • Forwarding or redirecting after the response is committed.
  • Forgetting @ServletComponentScan, so @WebServlet is ignored in Boot.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Tomcat thread pool: server.tomcat.threads.max (default 200).
  • Do not block request threads for long; use async or a separate executor.
  • Enable compression with server.compression.enabled.
  • Use loadOnStartup so the first request is not slow.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.tomcat.accept-count=100
server.compression.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 8080;
up to 200 concurrent request threads

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy servlet endpoint must live next to Spring MVC controllers. Register it with a ServletRegistrationBean on a path outside the dispatcher.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Servlet lifecycle is the set of stages the container drives for a servlet: load and instantiate, init(), many service() calls, then destroy().
  • One instance of a servlet normally serves all requests, each on a different thread, so init() and destroy() run once while service() runs per request.
  • service() looks at the HTTP method and calls doGet, doPost and the like in HttpServlet.

Worked Example 1

Unsafe shared field.

Worked Example 2

Test the servlet with Spring mocks.

Practice Exercise 1

Log each stage.

Practice Exercise 2

Count requests safely.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container controls the whole life of a servlet.

  • Load: the class is loaded and one instance is created, lazily or at startup.
  • init: called once with a ServletConfig; the servlet is not in service until it returns.
  • service: called on a worker thread for each request; HttpServlet.service dispatches by method.
  • destroy: called once, after the servlet stops accepting work.
  • Spring: DispatcherServlet builds its context during init and handles every request in doService.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options that affect the lifecycle:

  • Eager start: loadOnStartup with a number; lower numbers start first.
  • Single thread model: the old SingleThreadModel is removed; use stateless code or locks.
  • Boot property: spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup, where the default -1 means lazy.
  • Async: a request can leave service and finish later with AsyncContext.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lazy or eager loading: by default the container creates the servlet on its first request, while load-on-startup (or loadOnStartup) creates it at deployment.
  • Thread safety: instance fields are shared by all request threads, so keep servlets stateless or guard shared state.
  • DispatcherServlet is a normal servlet: Spring builds its web application context in init().

Senior Notes

  • Init failure: if init() throws ServletException, the servlet is not put into service and requests get an error.
  • Graceful shutdown: destroy() is the place to release pools and threads, but it can run while requests are still finishing.
  • Spring Boot registers DispatcherServlet through DispatcherServletRegistrationBean and the property spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup controls early init.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Mutable fields: instance fields shared between threads cause data mix-ups.
  • Heavy work in init: a slow or failing init delays or blocks the first requests.
  • Not closing resources: forgetting to release pools in destroy.
  • Calling service by hand: bypasses the container.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Eager init moves the cost of context creation from the first user to startup.
  • Thread pool: request throughput is limited by container threads, not by the number of servlets.
  • Keep service short: offload long work to async or an executor.
  • Avoid synchronized on the whole service method.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a payment service needs its HTTP client pool created once and closed on shutdown. With a plain servlet you do it in init and destroy; in Spring you make it a bean with @PreDestroy and let DispatcherServlet handle the rest.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Servlet container (web container) is the server part that runs servlets: it listens on a port, parses HTTP into request and response objects and calls your servlets.
  • Examples are Tomcat, Jetty and Undertow; they implement the Jakarta Servlet specification.
  • Container services include the lifecycle, threading, sessions, security, URL mapping and deployment.

Worked Example 1

Mixing javax and jakarta.

Worked Example 2

Run the container in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Switch to Jetty in Maven.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

// OUTPUT:
// Jetty started on port 8080 (http/1.1) with context path '/'

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Show which container runs.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A container turns sockets into servlet calls.

  • Connector: accepts connections and parses HTTP.
  • Pipeline: engine, host, context and wrapper valves pass the request to the right servlet.
  • Thread pool: one worker thread per active request (NIO poller plus workers).
  • Boot: ServletWebServerApplicationContext asks a ServletWebServerFactory to create and start the server during refresh.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Tomcat: default, widest use.
  • Jetty: light, good for embedding.
  • Undertow: non-blocking core, low memory.
  • WAR: extend SpringBootServletInitializer and mark the container starter as provided.
  • Reactive: WebFlux uses Netty and not a servlet container by default.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Embedded vs external: Spring Boot embeds the container in the jar and starts it with SpringApplication.run; classic apps ship a WAR to an external server.
  • Thread pool: the container owns the request threads, so a slow controller occupies one of them.
  • Switching the embedded container means excluding spring-boot-starter-tomcat and adding spring-boot-starter-jetty or the Undertow starter.

Senior Notes

  • Boot wiring: ServletWebServerFactory creates the container and ServletContextInitializer beans register servlets and filters.
  • WAR deployment needs a SpringBootServletInitializer subclass and a provided-scope container starter.
  • Jakarta: Servlet 5 and later moved from javax.servlet to jakarta.servlet; Spring Boot 3 requires the new package.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Two containers on the classpath (Tomcat and Jetty) without exclusion.
  • Packaging WAR without making the embedded starter provided, causing class conflicts.
  • javax imports with Boot 3.
  • Hard-coded port in tests; use RANDOM_PORT.
codeExamples:
<!-- WAR build: embedded Tomcat must not be packaged -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Without provided scope, duplicate servlet classes may break deployment

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Threads: size for blocking time; default 200 is often too many for a small machine.
  • Keep-alive and compression: reduce connection cost.
  • Access log costs I/O; enable only when needed.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21 and Boot 3.2) can serve blocking code with a small pool, enabled by spring.threads.virtual.enabled.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=100
server.tomcat.accept-count=50
server.compression.enabled=true
server.http2.enabled=true

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 8080 (http, h2c) with context path ''

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a team moves from an external Tomcat that hosts five WARs to one jar per service in containers. Each service embeds its server, sets its own thread limits and shuts down gracefully when the orchestrator stops it.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s

# OUTPUT:
# Commencing graceful shutdown. Waiting for active requests to complete
# Graceful shutdown complete

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Tomcat is the Apache open-source servlet container; it implements the Jakarta Servlet, JSP and WebSocket specifications and is the default server in spring-boot-starter-web.
  • Connector and engine: a connector accepts HTTP connections (default port 8080) and passes requests to the engine, which finds the host and the web application.
  • Deployment: classic Tomcat runs WAR files from its webapps folder, while Boot embeds Tomcat inside the jar.

Worked Example 1

Port already in use.

Worked Example 2

Check the server in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Tune Tomcat in properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.port=9090
server.servlet.context-path=/shop
server.tomcat.threads.max=100
server.shutdown=graceful

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 9090 (http) with context path '/shop'

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Customize the connector in code.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Tomcat is built from nested components.

  • Server and Service: top-level objects.
  • Connector: protocol handler, NIO by default.
  • Engine, Host, Context: the Context is one web application.
  • Wrapper: one per servlet.
  • Valves: pipeline steps such as the access log valve.
  • Embedded: Boot builds this tree in code, with TomcatServletWebServerFactory, instead of server.xml.
codeExamples:
<!-- standalone conf/server.xml (shortened) -->
<Server port="8005" shutdown="SHUTDOWN">
  <Service name="Catalina">
    <Connector port="8080" protocol="HTTP/1.1" connectionTimeout="20000"/>
    <Engine name="Catalina" defaultHost="localhost">
      <Host name="localhost" appBase="webapps"/>
    </Engine>
  </Service>
</Server>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Catalina: Server startup in [1520] milliseconds (varies)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful Boot properties:

  • server.port, server.address
  • server.servlet.context-path
  • server.tomcat.threads.max and threads.min-spare
  • server.tomcat.max-connections and accept-count
  • server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size
  • server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled
  • server.ssl.* for HTTPS
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.port=8443
server.ssl.enabled=true
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-password=changeit
server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled=true
server.tomcat.basedir=target/tomcat

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 8443 (https) with context path ''

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Properties such as server.port, server.servlet.context-path and server.tomcat.threads.max tune the embedded server.
  • Thread pool: the default maximum is 200 request threads; more concurrent slow requests than that queue up.
  • Logs: embedded Tomcat writes to the application log, and access logs can be switched on with server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled.

Senior Notes

  • Class loading: each web app has its own class loader in a standalone Tomcat, but an embedded one has a single application.
  • Customizing through a WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> bean gives code-level control of connectors.
  • Graceful shutdown is enabled with server.shutdown=graceful so running requests can finish.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Port clash with another process.
  • Large upload fails because of the multipart and post size limits.
  • Context path forgotten in URLs after setting it.
  • Memory leaks on redeploy in standalone Tomcat from threads or drivers that are not stopped.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=20MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=25MB

# OUTPUT:
# Without these limits, a 5 MB file works but a 2 GB file gives
# MaxUploadSizeExceededException (HTTP 413 or 500, varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Measure first: expose tomcat.threads.busy via Actuator metrics.
  • Threads: raise only if the CPU is idle while requests queue.
  • Timeouts: server.tomcat.connection-timeout frees stuck connections.
  • Compression and HTTP/2 reduce bandwidth.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: during a sale, requests get slower. Metrics show all 200 threads busy waiting for a slow database. The fix is to optimize queries and add a pool timeout, not to raise the thread count.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=30
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=2000
server.tomcat.threads.max=200

# OUTPUT:
# Callers fail fast after 2 s instead of piling up on Tomcat threads

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpServletRequest is the object that represents one incoming HTTP request: method, URL, headers, parameters, cookies and body.
  • Reading data uses getParameter for query and form values, getHeader for headers and getInputStream for the body.
  • Request attributes (setAttribute and getAttribute) carry data between filters, servlets and views within one request.

Worked Example 1

Reading the body twice.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Read request details.

Practice Exercise 2

Share data using attributes.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the request object is built.

  • The connector parses the request line, headers and creates a Request object.
  • The container hands your code a RequestFacade that limits access to internals.
  • Parameters are parsed lazily on the first getParameter call, from the query string and, for form posts, the body.
  • Spring wraps it in ServletWebRequest and stores it in RequestContextHolder.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Main reading options:

  • Line: getMethod, getRequestURI, getQueryString.
  • Headers: getHeader, getHeaders, getHeaderNames.
  • Parameters: getParameter, getParameterValues, getParameterMap.
  • Body: getReader or getInputStream.
  • Other: getCookies, getSession, getPart for multipart.
  • Spring annotations cover most cases.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Spring MVC hides it: @RequestParam, @RequestHeader and @PathVariable read values for you, but you can still declare HttpServletRequest as a method argument.
  • Body is read once: the stream can be consumed only one time, so wrap it with ContentCachingRequestWrapper when a filter must also read it.
  • Encoding: form data is decoded with the request character encoding; Boot sets UTF-8 through CharacterEncodingFilter.

Senior Notes

  • Container object: Tomcat creates a Request facade per call and recycles it, so never keep a reference after the request ends.
  • Async: after startAsync() the request stays valid until completion, which Spring uses for DeferredResult and Callable.
  • Client address: getRemoteAddr() shows the proxy behind a load balancer, so configure forwarded headers handling.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • NullPointerException from a missing parameter; check null or use @RequestParam(required = false).
  • Body consumed by a filter, so the controller sees nothing.
  • Trusting client headers such as X-Forwarded-For without a trusted proxy.
  • Keeping the request in a background thread.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Do not log full bodies for large uploads.
  • Limit size: post size and multipart limits protect memory.
  • Avoid getParameterMap copies in hot paths.
  • Stream big bodies instead of reading all bytes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: an audit filter records method, path, user and a request id for every call. It reads headers only, adds the id as an attribute and as a log context entry, and never touches the body.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpServletResponse is the object you fill to answer a request: status code, headers, cookies and the body.
  • Body writing uses getWriter() for text or getOutputStream() for bytes; you may use only one of the two per response.
  • Status and type are set with setStatus, sendError and setContentType before any body is written.

Worked Example 1

Header after the body.

Worked Example 2

Test the response.

Practice Exercise 1

Write plain text and a header.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the response is produced.

  • You write to a buffered output; nothing reaches the socket until the buffer flushes.
  • The response is committed when the status line and headers are sent.
  • Spring message converters write @ResponseBody values to this stream.
  • After the handler returns, the container flushes and completes the response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Status: setStatus(201) or sendError(404).
  • Headers: setHeader, addHeader, setDateHeader.
  • Cookies: addCookie or ResponseCookie for SameSite.
  • Spring style: ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus.
  • Download: Content-Disposition header.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Spring MVC normally builds the response for you from @ResponseBody, ResponseEntity and view rendering.
  • Committed response: once the buffer is flushed, headers and status cannot change and sendRedirect throws IllegalStateException.
  • Redirect: sendRedirect sends a 302 with a Location header, and the browser makes a new GET request.

Senior Notes

  • Buffering: the container buffers (about 8 KB in Tomcat) so that headers can still be changed until the buffer fills or flushBuffer runs.
  • Streaming: large downloads should use StreamingResponseBody or ResponseEntity<Resource> instead of building bytes in memory.
  • sendError hands control to the container error page, which Boot maps to /error and BasicErrorController.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Writer and stream both used raises IllegalStateException.
  • Missing content type or encoding gives garbled characters.
  • Redirect after commit.
  • Writing after a controller already returned a view or body.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Stream large bodies in chunks.
  • Compression with server.compression.enabled.
  • Caching headers (Cache-Control, ETag) avoid repeat transfers.
  • Buffer size via setBufferSize before writing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a reporting endpoint exports a million rows as CSV. It streams rows from the database cursor straight to the response with a download header, so the server never builds the whole file in memory.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpSession stores per-user data across several requests, because HTTP itself is stateless.
  • Session id: the container creates a session and sends its id in the JSESSIONID cookie; the browser returns it with every request.
  • API: request.getSession() creates or returns the session, setAttribute and getAttribute store values, and invalidate() ends it (for example on logout).

Worked Example 1

Using a session with no cookie.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc session.

Practice Exercise 1

Count visits in a session.

Practice Exercise 2

Log out.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How sessions work inside the container.

  • The container keeps a map from session id to HttpSession (Tomcat StandardManager).
  • On the first getSession() it creates a random id and sends Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID.
  • On later requests it reads the cookie and finds the object.
  • A background task removes sessions idle past the timeout.
  • Spring Session replaces the container manager by a filter that stores data in Redis or a database.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Timeout in properties or code.
  • Cookie settings: server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only, secure, same-site.
  • Tracking mode: cookie only is safest.
  • @SessionAttributes keeps model values in the session for a controller.
  • Spring Session for external storage.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Timeout: an idle session expires after 30 minutes by default; set server.servlet.session.timeout or call setMaxInactiveInterval.
  • Spring MVC offers @SessionAttributes and @SessionAttribute, and you can inject HttpSession into a handler method.
  • Serializable: values should implement Serializable so sessions can be persisted or replicated.

Senior Notes

  • Clustering: in-memory sessions live on one server, so use sticky sessions or Spring Session with Redis or JDBC to share them.
  • Security: change the session id after login (session fixation protection) and mark the cookie HttpOnly and Secure.
  • Memory: big objects in a session multiply by the number of users, so store ids, not entities.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Storing large objects or JPA entities.
  • No invalidate on logout.
  • Creating sessions for every request (for example bots), which wastes memory.
  • Non-serializable values in a replicated session.
  • Concurrent modification of the same session from parallel calls.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Short timeout frees memory.
  • Use getSession(false) where a session is not needed.
  • Stateless APIs with JWT avoid session memory entirely.
  • External store adds latency but lets you scale out.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a shopping cart is kept in the session for guests. With three app servers behind a load balancer the cart disappears, so the team adds Spring Session with Redis and the cart survives server changes.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.properties
spring.session.store-type=redis
spring.session.timeout=30m

# OUTPUT:
# Sessions are stored in Redis under spring:session:sessions:...

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ServletContext represents the whole web application; there is exactly one per application (per container deployment).
  • Shared state: attributes set with setAttribute are visible to every servlet, filter and user, so it works like application scope.
  • Information: it gives the context path, init parameters, resource access with getResourceAsStream and the server info.

Worked Example 1

Non thread-safe shared value.

Worked Example 2

Test with a mock context.

Practice Exercise 1

Application-wide counter.

Practice Exercise 2

Context information.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

One ServletContext object (a Tomcat ApplicationContext facade) exists per deployed web application.

  • It holds an attribute map shared by all components.
  • It knows the registered servlets and filters and allows dynamic registration while the app starts.
  • Spring stores the root context under the attribute WebApplicationContext.ROOT_WEB_APPLICATION_CONTEXT_ATTRIBUTE.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Capabilities:

  • Attributes: setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute.
  • Parameters: getInitParameter.
  • Resources: getResource, getResourceAsStream.
  • Logging: log().
  • Dynamic registration: addServlet, addFilter, addListener during startup.
  • Dispatch: getRequestDispatcher.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Get it by request.getServletContext(), getServletContext() in a servlet, or by injecting it as a Spring bean in a web application.
  • Thread safety: attributes are shared by all threads, so store thread-safe or immutable objects.
  • Spring link: the root WebApplicationContext is stored as a ServletContext attribute, and ServletContextAware beans receive the object.

Senior Notes

  • Boot: the context is created by the embedded server, and ServletContextInitializer beans can register servlets and filters on it.
  • Scope: a Spring bean in application scope is stored in the ServletContext.
  • Resources: getRealPath may return null in a packaged jar, so prefer getResourceAsStream or Spring Resource.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Global mutable state that is not thread-safe.
  • Using it as a cache without limits or eviction.
  • getRealPath in a packaged jar.
  • Storing user data there, where it leaks to other users.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Prefer Spring beans (singleton scope) over ServletContext attributes for shared objects.
  • Use concurrent collections for shared caches.
  • Use a real cache such as Caffeine for size limits.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: legacy code stores a configuration map in the ServletContext at startup. During migration to Boot the team moves it to a @ConfigurationProperties bean, so values are typed, validated and injectable.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ServletConfig holds the configuration of ONE servlet: its name, its init parameters and a reference to the ServletContext.
  • Passed to init() by the container; GenericServlet stores it so you can call getInitParameter.
  • Per servlet: unlike ServletContext (one per application), every servlet declaration gets its own ServletConfig.

Worked Example 1

Confusing config and context.

Worked Example 2

Test it with mocks.

Practice Exercise 1

Servlet with an init parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

Register in Spring Boot.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container creates one ServletConfig per servlet registration and passes it to init(ServletConfig).

  • GenericServlet keeps it and calls the no-argument init() as a convenience.
  • HttpServletBean.init() turns init parameters into bean properties of DispatcherServlet.
  • FrameworkServlet then creates the web application context.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to supply init parameters:

  • Annotation: @WebInitParam.
  • web.xml: init-param elements.
  • Boot: ServletRegistrationBean.addInitParameter.
  • Spring MVC WAR: AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer configures the dispatcher in code.
codeExamples:
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet</servlet-class>
    <init-param>
        <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
        <param-value>/WEB-INF/dispatcher-config.xml</param-value>
    </init-param>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Initializing Servlet 'dispatcher'

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Declare init parameters with @WebServlet(initParams = @WebInitParam(...)) or in web.xml under init-param.
  • DispatcherServlet reads its own settings, such as contextConfigLocation, from the ServletConfig.
  • Context vs config: context-param is shared by the whole app; init-param belongs to a single servlet.

Senior Notes

  • Boot: with ServletRegistrationBean you call addInitParameter to fill the ServletConfig.
  • HttpServletBean: Spring maps init parameters onto bean properties of DispatcherServlet using ServletConfigPropertyValues.
  • Prefer Spring @Value and properties for your own settings; ServletConfig is mostly a framework concern now.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong object: reading a context parameter from the config.
  • Using config before init: it is null in the constructor.
  • Overriding init(ServletConfig) without calling super, which loses the config.
  • Typos in parameter names return null silently.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance is not affected by ServletConfig; the cost is only at init.

  • Read values once in init and keep them in final fields.
  • Do not call getInitParameter on every request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a legacy admin servlet gets its upload folder from an init parameter. During migration the team replaces it with a property bound through @Value, so each environment can change it with an environment variable.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Filter is a component that sits in front of servlets and can inspect or change the request and the response, then pass control on with chain.doFilter(request, response).
  • Typical uses: logging, authentication, CORS, compression, character encoding and request timing.
  • Lifecycle: init() once, doFilter() for each matching request and destroy() once.

Worked Example 1

Forgetting the chain call.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Timing filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Register for one URL pattern.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container builds a FilterChain for each request from the matching filters, then the servlet is the last element.

  • Each doFilter call moves to the next link, so code before it runs on the way in, and code after it on the way out.
  • Matching uses URL patterns and servlet names; dispatcher types (REQUEST, FORWARD, ERROR, ASYNC) decide when a filter applies.
  • Boot registers filter beans in order and Spring Security sits at order -100 by default.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Plain Filter interface.
  • OncePerRequestFilter with shouldNotFilter.
  • @WebFilter with @ServletComponentScan.
  • FilterRegistrationBean for patterns, order and dispatcher types.
  • GenericFilterBean gives access to filter config as bean properties.
  • CorsFilter, ForwardedHeaderFilter and CharacterEncodingFilter are ready-made.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order matters: filters form a chain, and each one runs before the next and again after it on the way back.
  • Boot: a filter that is a @Component is registered for all URLs; use FilterRegistrationBean for URL patterns and order.
  • OncePerRequestFilter is the Spring base class that guarantees one execution per request, even with forwards.

Senior Notes

  • Filter vs interceptor: filters belong to the servlet container and see every request; HandlerInterceptor belongs to Spring MVC and knows the handler method.
  • Spring Security is a chain of filters inside DelegatingFilterProxy or FilterChainProxy.
  • Skipping the chain: if you do not call doFilter, the request stops there, which is how a filter can block or short-circuit.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No doFilter call.
  • Wrong order, for example logging before the encoding filter.
  • Filter as @Component also registered manually, so it runs twice.
  • Heavy work in every request.
  • Exceptions thrown in filters bypass @ControllerAdvice; handle them with a HandlerExceptionResolver or write the response.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Limit patterns to the URLs that need the filter.
  • Keep it cheap: avoid reading bodies and heavy lookups.
  • Cache token or key checks.
  • Do not buffer whole bodies for logging of large uploads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a gateway-style filter adds a correlation id to every request, copies it to the response header and to the log context, so one request can be traced across services.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Listener is a servlet component that gets a callback when something happens in the web application, such as startup, shutdown, a session being created or a request arriving.
  • Interfaces: ServletContextListener, HttpSessionListener, ServletRequestListener and the matching attribute listeners.
  • Registration: use @WebListener, web.xml, or in Spring Boot a ServletListenerRegistrationBean or a bean that implements the interface.

Worked Example 1

Listener not registered.

Worked Example 2

Test the listener directly.

Practice Exercise 1

Context listener.

Practice Exercise 2

Count active sessions in Boot.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How listeners are called.

  • The container finds listeners from annotations, web.xml or programmatic registration before the app starts.
  • Context listeners run in declaration order at startup and in reverse order at shutdown.
  • Session listeners are triggered by the session manager on create, expire or invalidate.
  • In Boot, ServletContextInitializerBeans collects listener beans and registers them on the ServletContext.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Interfaces:

  • ServletContextListener and ServletContextAttributeListener
  • HttpSessionListener, HttpSessionAttributeListener, HttpSessionIdListener
  • ServletRequestListener and ServletRequestAttributeListener
  • Spring equivalents: @EventListener, ApplicationListener, SmartLifecycle.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Startup hook: contextInitialized runs when the application starts, and contextDestroyed when it stops.
  • Session counting: HttpSessionListener sees sessionCreated and sessionDestroyed, a classic way to count active users.
  • Spring way: for most startup work use ApplicationRunner, @EventListener or ContextRefreshedEvent instead of servlet listeners.

Senior Notes

  • Boot detection: beans implementing the servlet listener interfaces are registered automatically by ServletContextInitializerBeans.
  • ContextLoaderListener is the classic listener that creates the root Spring context in a web.xml application.
  • Threading: session listeners are called from request threads, so shared counters need atomic types.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • @WebListener ignored without @ServletComponentScan.
  • Slow work in contextInitialized delays startup.
  • Using Spring beans in a listener created by the container (no injection); register it as a bean instead.
  • Unbalanced counters when sessions expire.
  • Exceptions in a startup listener fail the deployment.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep callbacks short; session listeners run on request threads.
  • Use atomic counters, not locks.
  • Do startup tasks after readiness, with ApplicationRunner, when they are slow.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: an operations dashboard shows the number of logged-in users. A session listener updates a Micrometer gauge, so the metric appears in Prometheus without extra queries.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DispatcherServlet is the front controller of Spring MVC: one servlet that receives every request and hands it to the right controller.
  • Servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) accepts the HTTP connection, builds HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse and calls the servlet.
  • Flow: container, filters, DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, controller, view or message converter, response.

Worked Example 1

Test the full dispatch path with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Change the servlet path.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.servlet.path=/api
server.servlet.context-path=/shop

# OUTPUT:
# GET http://localhost:8080/shop/api/hello  -> 200 hi
# GET http://localhost:8080/shop/hello      -> 404

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Print the dispatcher bean and its mapping in a Boot app.

Practice Exercise 2

Log every step with a filter and a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container and the servlet share the work:

  • Container: accepts the socket, parses HTTP, picks a pool thread, runs the filter chain, then calls service() on the servlet.
  • doService: DispatcherServlet stores request attributes and calls doDispatch.
  • Lookup: getHandler asks each HandlerMapping, and getHandlerAdapter picks the adapter.
  • Invoke: interceptors preHandle, the adapter runs the method with argument resolvers, and return value handlers write the result.
  • Finish: postHandle, view rendering, then afterCompletion; exceptions go to HandlerExceptionResolver beans.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to set it up:

  • Boot: auto-configured, mapped to /; change with spring.mvc.servlet.path.
  • Java config: extend AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer and return root and servlet config classes.
  • Several servlets: add ServletRegistrationBean with its own context.
  • Startup: spring.mvc.servlet.load-on-startup=1 initializes it early.
  • Unmatched 404: spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found turns it into an exception.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Registration: Spring Boot registers it through DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration mapped to /; a classic app uses web.xml or AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer.
  • Strategies: it delegates to beans such as HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, ViewResolver and HandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Contexts: the servlet owns a WebApplicationContext, which can have a parent root context holding services and repositories.

Senior Notes

  • Threading: the container uses one thread per request from its pool, so controllers must be stateless or thread-safe.
  • Embedded vs external: Boot embeds Tomcat and runs a jar; a WAR is deployed into an external container through SpringBootServletInitializer.
  • Tuning: server.tomcat.threads.max and spring.mvc.servlet.path change capacity and the mapping.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Component scan misses controllers: controllers outside the main package give 404; scan the package or move the class.
  • Mapping /* instead of /: static files and JSPs stop working.
  • Per-user fields in a controller: singletons are shared by threads; keep state in the session or a database.
  • Slow work in the request thread: starves the pool; use async return types.
  • Double context: beans defined in both root and servlet context get created twice.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning the container and servlet:

  • Threads: server.tomcat.threads.max (default 200) and accept-count.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true.
  • Keep-alive: reuse connections to reduce handshakes.
  • Virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true on Java 21 with a supported Boot version.
  • Async: return Callable, DeferredResult or CompletableFuture to free the container thread.
  • Lean filters: every filter and interceptor adds work to every request.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=100
server.tomcat.accept-count=50
server.compression.enabled=true
server.http2.enabled=true

@GetMapping("/report")
Callable<String> report() {
    return () -> { Thread.sleep(500); return "done"; };   // container thread freed
}

# OUTPUT:
# slow requests no longer pin a container thread while the Callable runs

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API returns 404 for a valid URL after an upgrade.

  • Check logs: DEBUG on the DispatcherServlet shows which mapping matched.
  • Check scan: the controller is in a sub-package of the main class.
  • Check path: a changed servlet.path or context-path shifts all URLs.
  • Check filters: a filter that does not call chain.doFilter ends the request early.
  • Interview angle: explain the request path from socket to controller.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP session is server-side memory that remembers one user across several requests, because HTTP itself is stateless.
  • Session id: the server creates a random id and sends it to the browser, usually in the JSESSIONID cookie; the browser returns it on each request.
  • Data lives on the server: only the id travels over the network, never the stored objects.

Worked Example 1

Test a session with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Inspect the cookie with curl.
codeExamples:
curl -i -c jar.txt http://localhost:8080/visits
curl -b jar.txt http://localhost:8080/visits

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=7F3A91...;
Path=/;
HttpOnly
# visit 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Count visits per user.

Practice Exercise 2

Invalidate on logout.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a container session works:

  • Creation: request.getSession() asks the session manager to build a StandardSession with a random id.
  • Id delivery: the response gets Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID.
  • Lookup: on later requests the container reads the cookie, finds the session in a concurrent map and attaches it to the request.
  • Expiry: a background thread checks idle time and destroys old sessions, firing listener events.
  • Persistence: Tomcat can write sessions to disk at restart if they are serializable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Session options:

  • Request-scoped access: HttpSession parameter or RequestContextHolder.
  • Session-scoped bean: @SessionScope with a scoped proxy.
  • Model attributes: @SessionAttributes.
  • Redirect data: RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute uses the session for one redirect.
  • Spring Session: external store for the same API.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lifecycle: created on first getSession(), kept alive by each request, destroyed by invalidate() or by timeout.
  • Typical use: login state, shopping cart, wizard steps and flash data between pages.
  • Container managed: Tomcat keeps a session manager with a map from id to session object.

Senior Notes

  • Memory: each session costs heap, so store small ids and not big object graphs.
  • Scaling: with several servers use sticky sessions or a shared store such as Spring Session with Redis.
  • Security: use HTTPS, HttpOnly and Secure cookies and a new id after login.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Large objects in the session: memory grows with users; store ids.
  • Non-serializable attributes: fail on replication or restart.
  • Mutating a stored object without setAttribute: some stores do not notice the change; call it again.
  • Creating sessions for bots: use getSession(false) where possible.
  • Using session state in a REST API that must scale out.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning sessions:

  • Keep them small and short-lived.
  • Shorter timeout for anonymous traffic.
  • Spring Session Redis: choose a flush mode and a serializer such as JSON.
  • Avoid sticky-only designs if you need rolling restarts.
  • Measure: active sessions through Micrometer (Tomcat exposes session metrics).
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.timeout=20m
spring.session.store-type=redis
spring.session.redis.flush-mode=on-save
spring.session.timeout=20m

# OUTPUT:
# metrics: tomcat.sessions.active.current (varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: users are logged out randomly in production behind two servers.

  • Cause: the load balancer sends requests to different nodes, each with its own memory.
  • Fix 1: sticky sessions at the balancer.
  • Fix 2: Spring Session with Redis so all nodes share data.
  • Interview angle: explain trade-offs of sticky versus shared sessions.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
// spring-session-data-redis and spring-boot-starter-data-redis

@EnableRedisHttpSession
class SessionConfig {}

// OUTPUT:
// node A creates the session; node B reads the same SESSION cookie data from Redis

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpSession is the servlet API interface (jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession) that represents one user session.
  • Get it by adding it as a controller parameter, or call request.getSession().
  • Main methods: setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute, invalidate, getId and setMaxInactiveInterval.

Worked Example 1

Session listener that counts active sessions.

Worked Example 2

Test that login stores the user.

Practice Exercise 1

Store and read a user object.

Practice Exercise 2

Do not create sessions for anonymous reads.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the interface:
