  • Implementation: Tomcat uses StandardSession wrapped by StandardSessionFacade, which hides internals from your code.
  • Attributes live in a ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Access time updates at the start and end of each request.
  • Events: adding or removing an attribute fires binding and attribute listeners.
  • Argument resolution: Spring uses ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver to inject HttpSession in a handler method.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

API variants:

  • Create or get: getSession() and getSession(true).
  • Get only: getSession(false).
  • New id: request.changeSessionId() keeps data and swaps the id.
  • Attribute names: getAttributeNames().
  • Servlet context: getServletContext() for application-wide data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • getSession(false) returns null instead of creating a session, which avoids useless sessions for anonymous users.
  • Metadata: getCreationTime, getLastAccessedTime and isNew describe the session.
  • Listeners: HttpSessionListener and HttpSessionAttributeListener react to creation, destruction and attribute changes.

Senior Notes

  • Serializable: attributes should implement Serializable so they survive persistence and replication.
  • Thread safety: one user may send parallel requests, so guard mutable attributes with synchronization or use immutable values.
  • Binding events: an attribute implementing HttpSessionBindingListener is told when it is added or removed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Casting without a null check: getAttribute may return null.
  • Using the session as a cache for shared data; use a real cache.
  • Race conditions: two parallel requests do read-modify-write on a counter.
  • Forgetting to invalidate on logout.
  • Keeping entities from a closed persistence context; store ids.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Every setAttribute may cost a write to Redis or JDBC stores.
  • Batch changes and write once per request.
  • Small immutable values serialize quickly.
  • Avoid getSession() on static resources.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: remember a logged-in user and show a welcome message.

  • Login stores a small LoginUser record.
  • Interceptor checks the attribute and redirects guests.
  • Logout invalidates.
  • Real apps use Spring Security rather than hand-made checks.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @SessionAttributes on a controller class lists model attribute names that Spring keeps in the HTTP session between requests.
  • @SessionAttribute (singular) on a method parameter reads one existing session attribute, for example @SessionAttribute("user") User u.
  • SessionStatus: call status.setComplete() to remove the attributes that @SessionAttributes stored.

Worked Example 1

Test with sessionAttr.

Worked Example 2

Check that the attribute is in the session.

Practice Exercise 1

Multi-step form with a session-held object.

Practice Exercise 2

Read a value set at login.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How @SessionAttributes works:

  • Before the handler: ModelFactory.initModel copies the named attributes from the session into the model.
  • After the handler: updateModel copies the listed attributes from the model back into the session.
  • Store: DefaultSessionAttributeStore prefixes names with a constant and calls WebRequest.setAttribute in session scope.
  • Complete: SessionStatus.setComplete() marks the handler done, and the attributes are removed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • By name: @SessionAttributes("order") or names = {...}.
  • By type: types = Order.class stores any model attribute of that type.
  • Read: @SessionAttribute on a parameter or WebRequest.getAttribute(name, SCOPE_SESSION).
  • Reset: SessionStatus or WebRequest.removeAttribute.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Scope: @SessionAttributes only applies to the controller that declares it; it does not read attributes set elsewhere.
  • Wizard pattern: keep a form object across several pages, then complete it on the last step.
  • required: @SessionAttribute(required = false) gives null instead of an exception when the attribute is missing.

Senior Notes

  • Handled by SessionAttributesHandler and the SessionAttributeStore inside RequestMappingHandlerAdapter.
  • Pitfall: data stays until setComplete() or timeout, so forgotten cleanup leaks memory.
  • Alternative: for a plain value use HttpSession directly or a session-scoped bean.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No cleanup: the object stays in the session for 30 minutes or more.
  • Expecting sharing across controllers.
  • Back button and two tabs: both tabs edit the same session object.
  • Missing @ModelAttribute factory: a form post then fails with HttpSessionRequiredException.
  • Binding too much: a posted form can overwrite fields; use @InitBinder to allow only certain fields.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Small objects only; each wizard keeps its form data in memory per user.
  • Complete early to free memory.
  • With Redis sessions the object is serialized, so keep it Serializable and compact.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a three-step checkout wizard.

  • Step 1 collects the address, step 2 the payment, step 3 confirms.
  • Session holds one Checkout object.
  • Confirm saves and calls setComplete.
  • Alternative: Spring Web Flow, or a hidden-field approach for stateless designs.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Session timeout is the number of idle seconds after which the container destroys a session; each request resets the clock.
  • Spring Boot property: server.servlet.session.timeout=30m.
  • Per session: session.setMaxInactiveInterval(seconds) overrides the default; a negative value means never expire.

Worked Example 1

Test the configured interval.

Worked Example 2

Listener logs expiry.

Practice Exercise 1

Set the timeout in properties and in code.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect after expiry with Spring Security.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How timeout is enforced:

  • Tracking: each session stores lastAccessedTime and maxInactiveInterval.
  • Check: Tomcat ManagerBase runs a background process about every 10 seconds and expires idle sessions; a lookup also checks validity.
  • Expiry: listeners are called, attributes unbound and the session removed.
  • Reset: the access time is refreshed when a request enters.
  • Redis store: uses key expiry plus Spring Session cleanup.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to configure:

  • Boot: server.servlet.session.timeout with units such as 90s or 30m.
  • Code: setMaxInactiveInterval.
  • Web.xml: minutes.
  • Spring Session: spring.session.timeout or maxInactiveIntervalInSeconds.
  • Remember-me cookie gives long-lived login without a long session.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Default: the servlet default is 30 minutes, and Tomcat rounds the value to whole minutes.
  • web.xml: session-config / session-timeout takes minutes, not seconds.
  • After expiry: getSession(false) is null, and the user must log in again.

Senior Notes

  • Spring Security: configure sessionManagement().invalidSessionUrl(...) to redirect users whose session expired.
  • Token-based apps use token expiry instead of a server session.
  • UX: warn the user before expiry or refresh the session with a periodic call.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Seconds versus minutes: web.xml uses minutes.
  • Sub-minute values in Tomcat are rounded up to a minute.
  • Ajax calls that keep the session alive unintentionally.
  • Not handling expiry in Ajax: the login page HTML comes back as a 200 for a JSON call; return 401.
  • Infinite timeout (negative) leaks memory.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and cost:

  • Shorter timeouts free memory sooner.
  • Long timeouts help users but raise memory and security exposure.
  • Choose by risk: banking minutes, shopping hours.
  • Absolute timeout (maximum session age) needs custom code or a filter.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: users complain that long forms are lost.

  • Diagnose: the idle timeout is 5 minutes and typing sends no requests.
  • Fix: a small script pings the server every few minutes while the form is open, or autosave drafts.
  • Balance against security needs.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Cookie-based session means the browser stores only a session id cookie (such as JSESSIONID) while the real data stays on the server.
  • Round trip: the server answers with Set-Cookie; the browser sends Cookie: JSESSIONID=... on each later request to that site.
  • Default: the container prefers cookies for session tracking and falls back to URL rewriting only if cookies are off.

Worked Example 1

Test that the cookie is set.

Worked Example 2

Inspect with curl.

Practice Exercise 1

Harden the session cookie.

Practice Exercise 2

Show the cookie exchange.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The mechanism:

  • Response: the container adds Set-Cookie built by SessionConfig and its cookie settings.
  • Request: Tomcat parses the Cookie header and matches the session id.
  • Boot customization: server.servlet.session.cookie.* maps to the servlet SessionCookieConfig.
  • Spring Session: CookieSerializer (DefaultCookieSerializer) writes a base64 session id in the SESSION cookie.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Domain and path: restrict to a subdomain or path.
  • Max-age: persistent session cookie, rarely wanted.
  • Header-based id: HeaderHttpSessionIdResolver.xAuthToken() for APIs.
  • Cookie prefix: __Host- names enforce Secure and path of slash.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cookie flags: HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript, Secure sends it only over HTTPS, SameSite limits cross-site sending.
  • Boot properties: server.servlet.session.cookie.name, .http-only, .secure, .same-site and .max-age.
  • Tracking modes: server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie turns off URL rewriting.

Senior Notes

  • Client-side sessions (signed cookies holding data) remove server memory but are limited to about 4 KB and need signing or encryption.
  • CSRF: because browsers attach the cookie automatically, state-changing requests need a CSRF token.
  • Spring Session replaces the container manager and can use a cookie or a header to carry the id.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No Secure flag in production.
  • SameSite=None without Secure is rejected by browsers.
  • Cookie set on the wrong domain or path so it is not sent.
  • Cross-origin Ajax without credentials: include and CORS allowCredentials.
  • Missing CSRF protection for forms.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Small cookie: only the id, a few dozen bytes.
  • Path scoping stops cookies being sent with static asset requests; serve static files from a cookie-free domain.
  • Lookup cost: one map or Redis read per request.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.cookie.path=/app
server.servlet.session.cookie.max-age=-1

# OUTPUT:
# requests to /static/* carry no session cookie

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: security audit flags the session cookie.

  • Findings: missing Secure and SameSite.
  • Fix: set the properties and force HTTPS.
  • Verify with browser dev tools or curl.
  • Interview angle: why HttpOnly does not stop CSRF but helps against XSS theft.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • URL rewriting keeps the session id in the URL, for example /cart;jsessionid=ABC123, for browsers that block cookies.
  • Encode links: call response.encodeURL(url); it appends the id only when the container needs it.
  • Fallback only: containers use cookies first and add the id to URLs when no cookie came back.

Worked Example 1

Test that no id is appended.

Worked Example 2

Redirect with encoding.

Practice Exercise 1

Encode a link manually.

Practice Exercise 2

Switch rewriting off.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie

# OUTPUT:
# /cart   (never carries jsessionid; cookie-less clients lose the session)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How rewriting works:

  • Decision: encodeURL calls the request isRequestedSessionIdFromCookie; if the cookie is not confirmed, the id is added.
  • Format: a path parameter ;jsessionid=ID after the path and before the query string.
  • Incoming: Tomcat parses the path parameter and finds the session.
  • First request: the server cannot know whether cookies work yet, so it rewrites links once.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls:

  • Tracking modes: COOKIE, URL, SSL.
  • Java config: servletContext.setSessionTrackingModes(EnumSet.of(SessionTrackingMode.COOKIE)).
  • Boot: property server.servlet.session.tracking-modes.
  • JSTL: c:url also encodes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Redirects: use encodeRedirectURL for sendRedirect targets.
  • Security risk: the id appears in logs, history, bookmarks and the Referer header, so it can leak and enable hijacking.
  • Spring Security rejects URLs with ;jsessionid through StrictHttpFirewall.

Senior Notes

  • Disable it in Boot with server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie.
  • Thymeleaf link expressions encode URLs automatically, which is how the id can appear unexpectedly.
  • Modern practice: avoid rewriting; use cookies or tokens in a header.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Leaving it on in a public site: ids in URLs get shared.
  • Only encoding some links so the session is lost on others.
  • SEO duplicates: search engines index jsessionid URLs.
  • Security firewall errors for semicolon URLs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost of rewriting:

  • Cache busting: unique URLs hurt caches.
  • More CPU to encode every link.
  • Longer URLs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: Google shows pages with jsessionid in results.

  • Cause: crawlers send no cookies, so every link gets an id.
  • Fix: cookie-only tracking and a canonical link tag.
codeExamples:
server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie

# OUTPUT:
# crawler gets clean URLs;
users keep sessions through cookies

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Session management covers how an app creates, protects, limits and ends user sessions.
  • Spring Security configures it through http.sessionManagement(...): creation policy, fixation protection and concurrency limits.
  • Creation policy: IF_REQUIRED (default), ALWAYS, NEVER or STATELESS.

Worked Example 1

Test fixation protection.

Worked Example 2

Stateless API policy.

Practice Exercise 1

Limit concurrent sessions.

Practice Exercise 2

List active sessions of a user.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside Spring Security:

  • SessionManagementFilter / strategies: a composite SessionAuthenticationStrategy runs after login.
  • Parts: ChangeSessionIdAuthenticationStrategy, ConcurrentSessionControlAuthenticationStrategy and RegisterSessionAuthenticationStrategy.
  • Repository: HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository saves the SecurityContext in the session.
  • ConcurrentSessionFilter checks whether the session was marked expired.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Policies:

  • Fixation: changeSessionId (default), newSession, migrateSession, none.
  • Creation: ALWAYS, IF_REQUIRED, NEVER, STATELESS.
  • Concurrency: maximumSessions, maxSessionsPreventsLogin.
  • Expired handling: expiredUrl or expiredSessionStrategy.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Fixation protection: by default Security changes the session id after login (changeSessionId).
  • Concurrent sessions: maximumSessions(1) limits one user to a number of sessions, and maxSessionsPreventsLogin(true) blocks the new login.
  • Registry: SessionRegistry and an HttpSessionEventPublisher bean track active sessions.

Senior Notes

  • Cluster: Spring Session stores sessions in Redis or a database so any node can serve the user.
  • Logout: invalidate the session, clear the cookie and clear the SecurityContext.
  • Audit: log session creation, expiry and forced logout for security review.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing HttpSessionEventPublisher: logged-out sessions still count toward the limit.
  • Missing equals/hashCode on a custom principal: the registry cannot match the same user.
  • Disabling fixation protection.
  • Mixing STATELESS and form login.
  • Not clearing cookies at logout.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • SessionRegistry is in memory; use a Spring Session backed one in a cluster.
  • Every authenticated request loads the SecurityContext from the session; keep the principal light.
  • Stateless tokens remove this load but need revocation design.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a banking app must allow one active session and end the old one.

  • Config: maximumSessions(1) with newest login winning.
  • Admin tool: expire a user session through the registry.
  • Audit: log events.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Stateful servers remember the client between requests (for example an HTTP session); stateless servers keep nothing, and each request carries all it needs.
  • Stateless example: a REST call with an Authorization: Bearer token that the server validates each time.
  • Stateful example: a login that stores the user in HttpSession.

Worked Example 1

Test the stateless endpoint.

Worked Example 2

Check no session is created.

Practice Exercise 1

Stateful counter versus stateless echo.

Practice Exercise 2

Make Security stateless with a bearer token.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where state can live:

  • Server memory: fast, lost on restart, tied to one node.
  • Shared store: Redis or a database; any node can serve.
  • Client: a token or cookie with signed data.
  • Stateless server: verifies the signature and reads claims, no lookup.
  • Spring Security: with STATELESS, the SecurityContext is rebuilt on every request by a filter such as BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design variants:

  • Sticky stateful: simple, weak on failover.
  • Shared session: stateful for the user, stateless servers.
  • JWT: self-contained token.
  • Opaque token: random string looked up in a store.
  • Hybrid: short access token plus a refresh token.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Scaling: stateless servers are easy to clone behind a load balancer; stateful ones need sticky sessions or a shared store.
  • Resilience: if a stateless node dies, the next request just goes to another node.
  • Trade-off: stateless requests are larger, because they repeat tokens and parameters.

Senior Notes

  • Not totally stateless: state moves to the client (token) or to a database or cache.
  • Spring: SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS tells Security not to create or use an HttpSession.
  • Controller beans are singletons, so they must not hold per-user fields in either style.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Claiming REST while using sessions.
  • Singleton fields holding user data.
  • Long-lived tokens that cannot be revoked.
  • Tokens in local storage exposed to XSS; prefer HttpOnly cookies when possible.
  • Forgetting CSRF when a stateless API still uses cookies.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance trade-offs:

  • Stateless: more CPU per request (signature check), less memory and no shared store.
  • Stateful: small requests, but memory and store costs.
  • Cache parsed keys such as the JWK set.
  • Short tokens keep payloads small.
codeExamples:
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=https://auth.example.com/jwks

# OUTPUT:
# keys fetched once and cached;
each request verifies locally in microseconds (varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP cookie is a small name-value pair that the server asks the browser to store and send back on later requests.
  • Set with the Set-Cookie response header; the browser returns it in the Cookie request header.
  • Read in Spring with @CookieValue("theme") String theme; write with jakarta.servlet.http.Cookie or ResponseCookie.

Worked Example 1

Test reading a cookie.

Worked Example 2

Test the cookie is set.

Practice Exercise 1

Remember a theme.

Practice Exercise 2

Delete a cookie.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How cookies work internally:

  • Wire format: Set-Cookie: name=value; Path=/; Max-Age=3600; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax.
  • Browser jar: keyed by name, domain and path; sent when the request URL matches and flags allow.
  • Spring: @CookieValue is resolved by ServletCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver from request.getCookies().
  • Writing: HttpServletResponse.addCookie or a Set-Cookie header built by ResponseCookie.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Cookie class: setHttpOnly, setSecure, setMaxAge; recent servlet versions also allow attributes through setAttribute.
  • ResponseCookie: fluent builder with sameSite.
  • CookieValue options: required and defaultValue.
  • Prefixes: __Host- and __Secure-.
  • CookieLocaleResolver stores the locale in a cookie.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Attributes: Path, Domain, Max-Age, Expires, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
  • Session vs persistent: without Max-Age the cookie dies when the browser closes.
  • Deleting: send the same name, path and domain with Max-Age=0.

Senior Notes

  • Size limits: about 4 KB per cookie, and every matching cookie is sent with every request, so keep them small.
  • Never store secrets or trust cookie values without a signature; the user can edit them.
  • Privacy: tracking cookies need user consent in many regions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Sensitive data in cookies such as passwords.
  • Spaces or semicolons in values: encode them.
  • Wrong path on delete: the cookie stays.
  • Forgetting HttpOnly for auth cookies.
  • Required cookie missing gives 400; use a default.
  • Trusting a role cookie.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Every cookie is sent with every matching request, including images.
  • Keep names and values short.
  • Use Path and Domain to limit scope.
  • Serve static files from a cookieless host.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: remember the chosen language and a consent choice.

  • Language: CookieLocaleResolver with a one-year cookie.
  • Consent: a small cookie consent=yes; set tracking only when present.
  • Test with MockMvc cookie() assertions.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Cookie: a small name-value pair the server sends in a Set-Cookie response header; the browser stores it and returns it in the Cookie request header on later requests.
  • Create one with new Cookie(name, value) and add it using response.addCookie(cookie) on the HttpServletResponse.
  • Set the path with setPath("/") and a lifetime with setMaxAge; without a max age it is a session cookie that dies when the browser closes.

Worked Example 1

Test that the cookie is created.

Worked Example 2

Create two cookies in one response.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a cookie with the servlet API.

Practice Exercise 2

Create a cookie with ResponseCookie.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A cookie is only a header exchange; the servlet container writes it.

  • addCookie: HttpServletResponse.addCookie turns the Cookie object into a Set-Cookie header when the response is built.
  • Browser: stores it by name, Path and Domain, and decides later which requests get it.
  • Next request: the browser adds a Cookie: name=value header and the container parses it into getCookies().
  • ResponseCookie: is an immutable Spring class that builds the same header text, including SameSite.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to create a cookie:

  • Servlet Cookie: simple, with setPath, setMaxAge, setHttpOnly, setSecure, setDomain.
  • ResponseCookie: fluent builder with sameSite and Duration.
  • Session cookie: no max age, so it ends with the browser session.
  • Persistent cookie: has Max-Age or Expires.
  • Boot properties: only for the session cookie.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ResponseCookie: the Spring builder (ResponseCookie.from(name, value)) supports sameSite, maxAge(Duration) and more, and is sent through HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE.
  • Attributes: Path, Domain, Max-Age, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite decide where and how the browser sends the cookie.
  • Size limit: a cookie is about 4 KB and a browser keeps only a limited number per domain, so store ids, not data.

Senior Notes

  • Never trust the value: the user can edit any cookie, so sign it or keep only an opaque id that maps to server-side data.
  • Defaults: always set HttpOnly, Secure and a SameSite value on cookies that identify a user.
  • Privacy: cookies that track users need consent under laws such as GDPR; keep the lifetime as short as the feature needs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Illegal characters: spaces, commas and semicolons in a value; encode the value (URL or Base64) first.
  • Missing path: the cookie is scoped to the creating URL directory and is not seen elsewhere; set Path=/.
  • Seconds vs milliseconds: setMaxAge takes seconds.
  • Storing secrets: never put passwords or full user data in a cookie.
  • Setting after commit: a cookie added after the response is already written is lost.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cookies travel on every request to the matching path, so they cost bandwidth.

  • Keep them small: only ids and flags.
  • Narrow Path: scope big cookies to the paths that need them.
  • Static files: serve images and scripts from a cookieless domain.
  • Lifetime: short lifetimes limit stale data and risk.
  • Count: avoid many cookies; combine small values server-side.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop remembers the language and the cart id of an anonymous visitor.

  • Language: a persistent, non-sensitive cookie.
  • Cart id: an opaque id cookie with HttpOnly and Secure; the cart itself lives in the database.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @CookieValue: @CookieValue("theme") String theme binds a request cookie to a controller parameter.
  • Default: if the cookie is missing the request fails with a 400 error, so use required = false or defaultValue.
  • All cookies: request.getCookies() returns an array of Cookie objects, or null when the request has none.

Worked Example 1

Test reading with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Optional cookie and a typed cookie.

Practice Exercise 1

Read one cookie with a default.

Practice Exercise 2

Read all cookies.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a cookie reaches your method:

  • Container: parses the Cookie header into Cookie objects.
  • DispatcherServlet: picks the handler method through RequestMappingHandlerAdapter.
  • Resolver: ServletCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver (an AbstractNamedValueMethodArgumentResolver) finds the cookie by name.
  • Conversion: the value goes through ConversionService to the parameter type.
  • Missing: if required and absent, MissingRequestCookieException is thrown, resolved to 400.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options of @CookieValue:

  • value / name: the cookie name; if omitted, the parameter name is used when compiled with -parameters.
  • required: default true.
  • defaultValue: used when absent; also makes it not required.
  • Types: String, numbers, Optional, or the Cookie object itself.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Conversion: @CookieValue uses the normal type converters, so an int or Long parameter works if the text is a valid number.
  • Only name and value: the browser sends just the name and value; the server never sees Path, Max-Age or HttpOnly of a request cookie.
  • Optional: Optional<String> also works as a parameter type for an optional cookie.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver: ServletCookieValueMethodArgumentResolver reads the cookie by name; a missing required cookie raises MissingRequestCookieException.
  • Validate every cookie value because it is user input: check length, format and allowed values before using it.
  • Duplicates: two cookies with the same name but different paths can both arrive, and the first one wins in @CookieValue.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting null: getCookies() can return null.
  • Wrong type: a text cookie bound to int gives 400 (type mismatch).
  • Trusting the value: do not use it in SQL, file paths or HTML without checking.
  • Expecting attributes: getMaxAge() on a request cookie is always -1.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Reading is cheap, but keep these points in mind:

  • Header size: all cookies are parsed on every request; fewer, smaller cookies are faster.
  • Utility: WebUtils.getCookie(request, name) avoids writing the loop each time.
  • Caching: responses that depend on a cookie need Vary: Cookie to stay safe in shared caches.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: choose the page theme from a cookie, with a safe whitelist.

  • Validate: accept only known values.
  • Default: fall back to light.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • No update call: HTTP has no "edit cookie" command; you update a cookie by sending a new Set-Cookie with the same name, path and domain.
  • Same identity: a cookie is identified by name plus Path plus Domain; if any of them differs, the browser keeps two separate cookies.
  • Refresh the lifetime the same way: send the cookie again with a new Max-Age to extend it (a sliding expiry).

Worked Example 1

Test the update.

Worked Example 2

Wrong: a different path creates a second cookie.

Practice Exercise 1

Visit counter updated on every request.

Practice Exercise 2

Change the theme only when it differs.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Updating is overwriting at the browser.

  • Key: the browser stores cookies in a jar keyed by name, domain and path.
  • Set-Cookie: when a response has the same key, the stored cookie is replaced, including its expiry.
  • Different key: a different Path or Domain makes a second cookie, and both may be sent.
  • Order: when two cookies match, the browser sends the longer path first.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to update:

  • Replace value: new value, same attributes.
  • Slide expiry: same value, new Max-Age on each request.
  • Change flags: send a cookie with the new flags and the same key.
  • Interceptor or filter: refresh a cookie across all requests.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Read then write: read the old value with @CookieValue, compute the new value and add the cookie to the response.
  • Attributes must match: set the same Path and Domain as when you created it, or you create a duplicate.
  • Counter pattern: a visit counter reads the cookie, adds one and writes it back on every request.

Senior Notes

  • Race: two parallel requests can both read the same old value and both write the same new value, so a lost update happens; use the server for exact counters.
  • Change detection: write the cookie only when the value changed to avoid extra header bytes on every response.
  • Signed values: when a cookie carries a signed value, re-sign it on every update.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Path or Domain mismatch: creates duplicates.
  • Flags dropped: the update omits HttpOnly or Secure, so a safe cookie becomes unsafe.
  • Update after commit: the response is already sent.
  • Reading your own write: the new value is only visible on the next request, not in the same request.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Updates add bytes to every response; reduce them:

  • Write on change: skip the header when the value is the same.
  • Throttle sliding expiry: refresh only when the cookie is older than a threshold.
  • Server state: keep frequently changing data in the session, not a cookie.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: remember-me style sliding login that lasts 14 days after the last visit.

  • Each visit refreshes the lifetime.
  • Inactive users expire naturally.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Delete by expiring: send the cookie again with Max-Age=0 (setMaxAge(0)) and the browser removes it at once.
  • Match the identity: use the same name, Path and Domain as the original, or the browser will not find the cookie to delete.
  • Value does not matter when deleting; an empty string is common.

Worked Example 1

Test the deletion.

Worked Example 2

Delete every cookie of the request.

Practice Exercise 1

Delete a cookie with the servlet API.

Practice Exercise 2

Logout deletes the cookie and the session.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Deleting is an expiry instruction.

  • Max-Age=0 or a past Expires date tells the browser to drop the cookie matching name, domain and path.
  • Container: the servlet container writes both Max-Age=0 and an old Expires for compatibility.
  • No match: if the key differs, nothing is deleted and the old cookie lives on.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Servlet: setMaxAge(0).
  • ResponseCookie: maxAge(0), or Duration.ZERO.
  • Spring Security: .logout(l -> l.deleteCookies("JSESSIONID")).
  • Clear-Site-Data: HeaderWriterLogoutHandler with ClearSiteDataHeaderWriter can clear cookies and storage.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Negative max age: setMaxAge(-1) means a session cookie, not a delete; use 0 to delete.
  • ResponseCookie: ResponseCookie.from("name", "").maxAge(0).path("/").build() produces the delete header.
  • Logout: logging out should delete the login cookie and invalidate the session on the server.

Senior Notes

  • Security attributes: send the same Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite flags on the delete cookie, since some browsers compare them.
  • HttpOnly cookies cannot be deleted from JavaScript, so provide a server endpoint such as /logout.
  • Delete is a hint: the server cannot verify the deletion, so never rely on the client to forget sensitive data.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Different Path or Domain: the delete is ignored.
  • Using -1: that means session cookie, not delete.
  • JavaScript delete of HttpOnly: not possible.
  • Client-only logout: deleting the cookie but not the server session leaves a valid session id.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Deleting is cheap. The concern is cleaning up:

  • Server state: remove session or token records so storage does not grow.
  • Many cookies: clear only the cookies your app owns, not all of them.
  • Domain cookies: subdomain cookies need the same Domain to be deleted.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: logout that removes the session, the remember-me cookie and the CSRF cookie.

  • Server: invalidate the session.
  • Browser: send three expiring cookies.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Secure flag: a cookie with Secure is sent by the browser only over HTTPS, so it cannot leak on plain HTTP.
  • Set it with cookie.setSecure(true) or ResponseCookie.from(...).secure(true).
  • Secure cookie in practice means three flags together: Secure, HttpOnly and a SameSite value.

Worked Example 1

Test the flags.

Worked Example 2

Force HTTPS with Spring Security.

Practice Exercise 1

Secure cookie with all three flags.

Practice Exercise 2

Session cookie settings in application.properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The browser enforces the Secure flag; the server only sets it.

  • Browser rule: a Secure cookie is stored only when it comes from an HTTPS response and is sent only on HTTPS requests.
  • Spring Boot: reads server.servlet.session.cookie.* into the servlet SessionCookieConfig.
  • Proxy: with TLS termination, request.isSecure() depends on forwarded headers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Related settings:

  • Boot properties: secure, http-only, same-site, name, max-age, path, domain.
  • Cookie prefixes: __Secure- needs Secure; __Host- needs Secure, Path=/ and no Domain.
  • HSTS: forces HTTPS for later visits.
  • Proxy headers: server.forward-headers-strategy (native or framework).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Needs HTTPS: a Secure cookie is ignored by the browser on a plain HTTP page (except for localhost in modern browsers), so local tests may differ.
  • Session cookie: configure it with server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true in Spring Boot.
  • Prefixes: the name prefix __Host- forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, which blocks subdomain tricks.

Senior Notes

  • Behind a proxy: when TLS ends at a load balancer, set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework so the app knows the request was HTTPS.
  • HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) makes the browser use HTTPS always, which complements Secure cookies.
  • Secure is not encryption of the value: it protects transport only, so still keep secrets out of cookie values.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Secure on local HTTP: the cookie never comes back, so login appears broken in development; use a profile for dev.
  • Proxy hides HTTPS: the cookie is not marked Secure or redirects loop.
  • Mixed content: one HTTP page of the site can expose non-Secure cookies.
  • Secure value inside: a Secure flag does not encrypt a cookie value.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

HTTPS has a cost, but small:

  • TLS sessions: resumption and HTTP/2 make the cost low.
  • HSTS preload: removes the first insecure redirect.
  • Cookie size: flags add a few bytes only.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: production deployment behind a load balancer that ends TLS.

  • Proxy sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https.
  • App trusts it so cookies and redirects use HTTPS.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpOnly is a cookie flag that hides the cookie from JavaScript, so document.cookie cannot read it.
  • Purpose: it limits the damage of an XSS attack, because an injected script cannot steal the session cookie.
  • Set it with cookie.setHttpOnly(true) or ResponseCookie.from(...).httpOnly(true).

Worked Example 1

Test the HttpOnly flag.

Worked Example 2

A readable cookie must not be HttpOnly.

Practice Exercise 1

HttpOnly cookie.

Practice Exercise 2

HttpOnly for the Boot session cookie.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HttpOnly is enforced inside the browser.

  • Storage: the cookie jar marks the cookie as http-only.
  • JavaScript: document.cookie returns only cookies without the flag, and a script write to an HttpOnly name is ignored.
  • Network: the cookie is still attached to requests by the browser itself.
  • Spring Boot: sets the session cookie HttpOnly by default.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where to set it:

  • Cookie: setHttpOnly(true).
  • ResponseCookie: httpOnly(true).
  • Session: server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only.
  • Spring Security CSRF: CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() for script-readable tokens, and new CookieCsrfTokenRepository() defaults to HttpOnly true.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Still sent: the browser keeps sending an HttpOnly cookie with every matching request; only scripts are blocked.
  • Session cookie: the servlet container marks JSESSIONID HttpOnly by default in Spring Boot; confirm with server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only.
  • Trade-off: if your own JavaScript must read a value (a theme, for example), that cookie cannot be HttpOnly.

Senior Notes

  • Not a full defence: HttpOnly does not stop an XSS script from sending requests as the user, so also escape output and use a Content-Security-Policy.
  • CSRF token cookies for single-page apps are an exception: they must be readable by script, so they are not HttpOnly.
  • Attribute only: it is enforced by the browser, so it does not affect server code or tools like curl.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting the flag on auth cookies.
  • Thinking it stops XSS: it only stops cookie theft.
  • HttpOnly on a cookie JS needs: the front end cannot read it, so features break.
  • Debugging confusion: the cookie is hidden from document.cookie but visible in browser developer tools.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

There is no performance cost. A review checklist:

  • Audit: list all cookies and mark which scripts need them.
  • Default: HttpOnly unless a script truly needs the value.
  • Test: a MockMvc test per auth cookie keeps the flag from being lost.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: single-page app with a cookie session and CSRF.

  • Session cookie: HttpOnly, hidden from the script.
  • CSRF cookie: readable, copied into a header.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • SameSite tells the browser whether to send a cookie on cross-site requests; it is the main browser defence against CSRF.
  • Three values: Strict (never cross-site), Lax (only top-level GET navigation) and None (always, but requires Secure).
  • Default: modern browsers treat a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax.

Worked Example 1

Test the header.

Worked Example 2

Cross-site front-end needs None plus Secure.

Practice Exercise 1

SameSite with ResponseCookie.

Practice Exercise 2

SameSite with the servlet Cookie (Servlet 6).

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The browser decides per request.

  • Site: scheme plus registrable domain (eTLD+1); ports and subdomains do not matter for "same site".
  • Strict: cookie sent only when the request starts from the same site.
  • Lax: also sent for top-level navigations using safe methods such as GET.
  • None: always sent, but only if Secure.
  • Framework: ResponseCookie.sameSite only writes the attribute; Tomcat writes it for the session cookie from the Boot property.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

How to choose:

  • Strict: banking style apps where an extra login after an external link is fine.
  • Lax: good default for normal sites.
  • None + Secure: embedded widgets, payment frames, separate API domain.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Set it with ResponseCookie.from(...).sameSite("Lax"); the servlet Cookie needs setAttribute("SameSite", "Lax") on Servlet 6.
  • Session cookie: server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax configures it in Spring Boot.
  • None is needed for embedded or cross-site flows such as an iframe or a third-party widget, and must come with Secure.

Senior Notes

  • Site, not origin: "same site" means the same registrable domain (for example shop.example.com and api.example.com are same-site), which differs from CORS origins.
  • Strict breaks links: a user following a link from email to your site arrives without the cookie, so they look logged out on the first page.
  • Not enough alone: keep CSRF tokens for state-changing requests, because SameSite is a browser feature and older browsers ignore it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • None without Secure: rejected by modern browsers.
  • Strict on the login cookie: external links appear logged out.
  • Relying on it only: keep CSRF tokens.
  • Mixing up site and origin: CORS settings are separate from SameSite.
  • Typo in value: lax and Lax are accepted, but a wrong word is ignored by the browser.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

No runtime cost, but check the effect on behaviour:

  • Test browsers: verify flows in current versions of Chrome, Firefox and Safari.
  • Logging: log missing-cookie rates after a change.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the web app is on app.example.com and the API on api.example.com.

  • Same site: both share example.com, so Lax works for fetch calls from the app.
  • Different site: needs None, Secure and CORS credentials.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Idea: after login the server sends a cookie holding a session id or token; the browser returns it on each request, and the server uses it to know who the user is.
  • Session-based: the usual form is JSESSIONID; the cookie holds only an id and the user data stays in HttpSession on the server.
  • Flow: login with credentials, server checks them, creates a session, sends the cookie; later requests carry the cookie and are treated as logged in.

Worked Example 1

Test a protected endpoint with a session.

Worked Example 2

Test Spring Security form login.

Practice Exercise 1

Minimal login with HttpSession.

Practice Exercise 2

Form login with Spring Security.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring Security handles a cookie session:

  • Filter chain: SecurityContextHolderFilter loads the SecurityContext from the session (via HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository).
  • Login: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter calls the AuthenticationManager, then a session strategy changes the session id.
  • Next request: the JSESSIONID cookie finds the session, and the stored Authentication becomes the current user.
  • Authorization: AuthorizationFilter checks rules against it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of cookie authentication:

  • Server session: default; the cookie holds only the id.
  • Remember-me: rememberMe() adds a long-lived cookie with a token hash.
  • Signed token cookie: a JWT in an HttpOnly cookie, so scripts cannot read it.
  • Spring Session: stores sessions in Redis or a database, and can use a header instead of a cookie.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cookie flags: the login cookie should be HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, and have a limited lifetime.
  • Spring Security does this for you: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter authenticates and SecurityContextHolder plus the session keep the login.
  • Stateless variant: the cookie can hold a signed token (such as a JWT) so the server keeps no session, at the cost of harder revocation.

Senior Notes

  • Session fixation: always change the session id after login; Spring Security does this by default (changeSessionId).
  • CSRF: cookies are sent automatically, so state-changing requests need CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies.
  • Scaling: session data must be shared across servers (sticky sessions or Spring Session with Redis) when you run several instances.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Storing the user or password in the cookie instead of an id.
  • No CSRF protection on state-changing endpoints.
  • Not changing the session id at login.
  • Logout only client side: the server session still works.
  • Plain HTTP: the cookie can be sniffed.
  • Long, never expiring sessions.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Scaling and tuning:

  • Timeout: server.servlet.session.timeout=30m frees memory.
  • Small sessions: store the user id, not big objects.
  • Shared store: Spring Session with Redis for many instances.
  • Stateless: signed token cookies avoid the shared store but need a revocation plan.
codeExamples:
server.servlet.session.timeout=30m
spring.session.store-type=redis
spring.session.timeout=30m
spring.data.redis.host=localhost

# OUTPUT:
# Any server instance can read the session by its cookie id from Redis

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an internal admin web app with login, role checks, logout and a test.

  • Config: form login, secure cookie flags, CSRF on.
  • Test: MockMvc with Spring Security test support.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Multipart request: an HTTP request with Content-Type: multipart/form-data that carries several parts (text fields and files) separated by a boundary string.
  • Use: file upload forms need enctype="multipart/form-data" and method="post"; a normal form encoding cannot carry files.
  • In Spring: a MultipartResolver parses the request, and the controller receives MultipartFile parameters or @RequestPart values.

Worked Example 1

Test a multipart request with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

JSON part plus file with @RequestPart.

Practice Exercise 1

Controller that accepts a field and a file.

Practice Exercise 2

HTML form.
codeExamples:
<form action="/upload" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
    <input type="text" name="title">
    <input type="file" name="file">
    <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT:
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data;
boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX
(one part per field, each starting with the boundary line) -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Anatomy and processing:

  • Format: the body is split by a boundary; each part has its own headers (Content-Disposition: form-data; name=..., optional filename and Content-Type).
  • Detection: DispatcherServlet.checkMultipart asks the MultipartResolver if the request is multipart.
  • Wrapping: StandardServletMultipartResolver wraps it in a StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest using the container Part API.
  • Binding: argument resolvers fill MultipartFile and @RequestPart parameters.
  • Cleanup: temp files are deleted when the request finishes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Binding options:

  • @RequestParam MultipartFile: one file by part name.
  • @RequestParam List<MultipartFile>: many files with one name.
  • @RequestParam Map<String, MultipartFile>: all files by part name.
  • @RequestPart: JSON or XML part converted by message converters.
  • @ModelAttribute: a form object with a MultipartFile field.
  • Part: the raw servlet jakarta.servlet.http.Part.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @RequestParam binds a simple field or a file by part name; @RequestPart also converts a JSON part with an HttpMessageConverter.
  • consumes: add consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE to the mapping to accept only multipart requests.
  • Limits: set spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size to cap uploads.

Senior Notes

  • Parsing: Spring Boot registers StandardServletMultipartResolver and the servlet container (Tomcat) parses the parts; small parts stay in memory and big ones go to a temp file.
  • Too large: exceeding a limit raises MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which you should handle with @ExceptionHandler and return 413.
  • Security: treat file names, content type and content as untrusted; check size, type and store files outside the web root.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No enctype on the HTML form: the file name arrives as text and the file is not uploaded.
  • Setting Content-Type by hand in fetch or Postman: the boundary is lost; let the client set it.
  • Wrong part name: the name must match the parameter, otherwise 400.
  • JSON part without content type: @RequestPart needs the part to say application/json.
  • Size limits left at default: 1 MB file and 10 MB request in Spring Boot.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning the multipart handling:

  • file-size-threshold: parts above it are written to disk; below it they stay in memory.
  • location: the temp directory, which needs free space.
  • Streaming: for huge files read getInputStream() and write straight to storage.
  • Proxy limits: nginx client_max_body_size and Tomcat max-swallow-size also apply.
codeExamples:
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=50MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=60MB
spring.servlet.multipart.file-size-threshold=2MB
spring.servlet.multipart.location=/var/tmp/uploads
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=100MB

# OUTPUT:
# Parts under 2 MB are kept in memory;
bigger parts go to /var/tmp/uploads

Scenario: a profile screen sends the user data as JSON and a photo in one request.

  • Test with MockMultipartFile for both parts.

  • Save a file with file.transferTo(target); the temporary data is deleted after the request, so you must copy it if you want to keep it.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What is behind the interface:

  • Implementation: StandardMultipartFile (inside StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest) wraps the servlet Part.
  • Storage: the container keeps small content in memory and larger content in a temp file.
  • transferTo: moves or copies the temp file to your target, and may be called once for some implementations.
  • Lifetime: temp data is removed when the request ends, so do not use the object in a background thread without copying.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to store and read a file:

  • transferTo(Path): simplest and efficient.
  • Files.copy(getInputStream(), target): streaming, with REPLACE_EXISTING option.
  • getBytes(): for small files and databases (BLOB).
  • Download: return a Resource with Content-Disposition.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Check first: call isEmpty() and verify size and content type before saving.
  • Many files: use MultipartFile[] or List<MultipartFile> with the same part name.
  • Streams: getInputStream() lets you process a large file without loading it all with getBytes().

Senior Notes

  • Path traversal: the original file name is user input and may contain ../; generate your own name or clean it with StringUtils.cleanPath and check it.
  • Content type comes from the client and can be false; inspect the real content (magic bytes) for strict checks.
  • Memory: getBytes() loads the whole file into memory, so avoid it for big files and set size limits.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Trusting the file name: allows path traversal.
  • Trusting the content type: an attacker can rename a script to .png.
  • getBytes() for large files: out-of-memory risk.
  • Relative transferTo path: resolves against the temp location for some containers; use an absolute Path.
  • Using the file after the request: the temp file is gone.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and capacity:

  • Stream big files and write them in chunks.
  • Async processing: save quickly, then process (thumbnails, virus scan) in a queue, passing the saved path, not the MultipartFile.
  • Object storage: for many users, store files in S3-style storage instead of the app disk.
  • Disk: monitor temp space and clean old files.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a document upload endpoint with checks, a database record and tests.

  • Checks: not empty, size, allowed type.
  • Record: store metadata and the generated name.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a multipart upload flows through Spring MVC:

  • Request: the browser sends multipart/form-data with a boundary string; each field or file is one part.
  • Parsing: DispatcherServlet.checkMultipart asks the MultipartResolver (Boot: StandardServletMultipartResolver) to wrap the request in a MultipartHttpServletRequest.
  • Container: the servlet container (Tomcat) parses the parts and decides memory or temp file by file-size-threshold.
  • Binding: RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver or RequestPartMethodArgumentResolver gives the controller a MultipartFile.
  • Cleanup: after the response, cleanupMultipart deletes temp files.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Binding variants for uploads:

  • @RequestParam: file by part name.
  • @RequestPart: a part with its own content type, such as JSON read by a message converter.
  • @ModelAttribute: a form object with a MultipartFile field.
  • Optional: required = false or Optional<MultipartFile> for a skipped input.
  • Part: the servlet type jakarta.servlet.http.Part also works.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • MultipartResolver: Spring Boot registers StandardServletMultipartResolver, which wraps the servlet container parsing and wraps each part as a MultipartFile.
  • Limits are set with spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size (defaults are 1MB and 10MB).
  • Mixed parts: use @RequestPart to receive a JSON part and a file part in one request.

Senior Notes

  • Never trust the file name: it can contain ../ (path traversal), so generate your own name and resolve it against a fixed folder.
  • Store outside the web root or in object storage, and stream with getInputStream() rather than getBytes() for big files.
  • Temporary storage: parts above file-size-threshold are written to disk and removed after the request.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical upload mistakes:

  • Missing enctype: the form sends text only, so the file is null or empty. Fix: add enctype="multipart/form-data".
  • Wrong part name: MissingServletRequestPartException; match the name attribute.
  • Relative path with transferTo: it resolves against the temp directory in some containers; use an absolute path.
  • Using the original name as the path: traversal risk.
  • Reading the file twice: getInputStream() can be called again, but save once and reuse the stored copy.
  • Setting Content-Type header by hand in a client: the boundary is then missing.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning uploads:

  • Threshold: keep file-size-threshold small enough to protect heap, large enough to avoid disk for tiny files.
  • Streaming: copy with Files.copy rather than reading all bytes.
  • Temp disk: put location on fast storage with space.
  • Thread usage: uploads hold a request thread for the whole transfer, so use timeouts.
  • Compression: do not gzip already compressed formats such as JPEG or ZIP.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a profile photo endpoint. It should check size and type, store the image under a generated name, save only the generated name in the database, and serve it later through a controlled download endpoint.

  • Service: validate, store, return a public id.
  • Database: keep id, original name, type, size and path.
  • Serving: by id, never by path.

  • Multiple upload sends several files in one request; bind them as MultipartFile[] or List<MultipartFile>.
  • HTML side: add the multiple attribute to the file input, or repeat inputs with the same name.
  • Loop over the files, skip those where isEmpty() is true, and save each one.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internally every file is its own part in the multipart body.

  • Parsing: the container produces a list of Part objects; the resolver converts them into a MultiValueMap<String, MultipartFile>.
  • Binding: for List<MultipartFile> or arrays, RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver reads getFiles(name).
  • Order: files keep the order sent by the client.
  • Temp files: each part over the threshold has its own temp file, all removed at the end.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to bind several files:

  • List or array with one shared name.
  • Map: @RequestParam Map<String, MultipartFile> gets one file per distinct name.
  • MultiValueMap: all files grouped by name.
  • Form object: a field List<MultipartFile> files with @ModelAttribute.
  • Different names: separate parameters, such as cv and photo.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Same name for all parts: @RequestParam("files") List<MultipartFile> files collects every part named files.
  • Grouped by name: MultipartHttpServletRequest.getMultiFileMap() returns a map of part name to list of files.
  • Request size: max-request-size limits the sum of all files, while max-file-size limits each file.

Senior Notes

  • All or nothing: decide whether one bad file fails the whole request, or return a per-file result list.
  • Count limit: the container also caps part count (Tomcat maxPartCount style limits), so cap the number of files in code too.
  • Clean up: if the third file fails, delete the first two so you do not leave orphans.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using Map<String, MultipartFile> with a shared name: only one file per name is kept; use a list.
  • Not skipping empty slots: a blank input still sends an empty part.
  • Total limit confusion: each file passes max-file-size yet the request fails on max-request-size.
  • One failure leaves earlier files saved. Track saved paths and delete them in a catch block.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips for batches:

  • Cap the count to bound work per request.
  • Parallel saves help only with slow storage; disk copies are usually IO bound.
  • Stream each file instead of reading bytes.
  • Return early with a job id for heavy processing such as thumbnails, then process in the background.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a document portal where a user attaches several PDFs to a claim. The API returns a result per file so the UI can show which ones succeeded.

  • Result record: name, status, message.
  • Status: 207-style body or 200 with details.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • File validation checks an upload before you store it: not empty, allowed size, allowed type and a safe name.
  • Why: a client can send anything, so the server must verify, because browser side accept filters are only a hint.
  • Where: do quick checks in the controller or a service, or write a custom ConstraintValidator for reuse.

Worked Example 1

Custom constraint annotation.

Worked Example 2

Test the bad request.

Practice Exercise 1

A small validation method.

Practice Exercise 2

Map failures to 400.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How validation fits the request lifecycle:

  • Before the controller: the container and resolver enforce size limits.
  • Argument resolution: a null or missing part raises MissingServletRequestPartException unless optional.
  • Bean Validation: with @Valid on a model object, a custom constraint on a MultipartFile field runs through ConstraintValidator.
  • Method validation: with @Validated on the controller class, constraints on parameters are checked by an AOP proxy and raise ConstraintViolationException (Spring 6.1 also has built-in method validation raising HandlerMethodValidationException).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Validation options:

  • Manual checks in a service: simple and explicit.
  • Custom annotation with ConstraintValidator: reusable, with attributes such as max size or allowed types.
  • Spring Validator interface for form pages with BindingResult.
  • Library: Apache Tika for content detection.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • No built-in annotation: Bean Validation has nothing for MultipartFile, so write your own, for example @ValidFile.
  • Custom constraint: an annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy = ...) plus a class implementing ConstraintValidator.
  • Errors: return 400 with a clear message, using @ControllerAdvice or a BindingResult for form pages.

Senior Notes

  • Content sniffing: do not trust the Content-Type header or extension; inspect the first bytes (magic numbers).
  • Name safety: use StringUtils.cleanPath and reject names containing ...
  • Defense in depth: store outside the web root, never execute uploads, and scan for malware when risk is high.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Trusting browser accept: add server checks.
  • Checking only content type: add magic byte or Tika detection.
  • Forgetting @Valid: the custom constraint never runs.
  • Leaking internal paths in error messages: return short generic messages.
  • Dropping the check after refactoring: cover with tests.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: validation should be cheap and happen before expensive work.

  • Order checks: empty, size, declared type, then content sniffing.
  • Read few bytes: magic numbers need only the first bytes, not the whole file.
  • Avoid re-reading: pass the verified stream or path on.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: KYC document upload. Rules: PDF or JPEG, up to 5MB, detected from content, stored with a generated name, and every rejection logged with the reason (not the file content).

  • Layers: properties for hard limits, a validator for rules, an advice class for the response shape.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Size validation limits how large an upload may be, to protect disk, memory and bandwidth.
  • Global limits: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size (each file) and max-request-size (whole request).
  • Violation raises MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which you should map to HTTP 413 Payload Too Large.

Worked Example 1

Properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=2MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=6MB

# OUTPUT:
# 3 MB file -> MaxUploadSizeExceededException -> 413

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Test the limit.

Practice Exercise 1

Per-endpoint limit in code.

Practice Exercise 2
