Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the size limit is enforced:

  • Servlet container: Spring Boot turns the properties into a MultipartConfigElement given to the DispatcherServlet registration; Tomcat counts bytes while parsing.
  • On breach: the container throws IllegalStateException, which StandardServletMultipartResolver wraps as MaxUploadSizeExceededException.
  • Timing: parsing is lazy by default in the standard resolver, so the exception can appear when the argument is resolved.
  • Tomcat extras: maxSwallowSize controls how much of an aborted body it reads.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Size units and options:

  • Properties: 1MB, 512KB, 2GB, or plain bytes; -1 means no limit.
  • Unit helper: DataSize.ofMegabytes(2).toBytes().
  • Per-endpoint limit: compare getSize() to a configured constant.
  • Type specific: small for avatars, bigger for videos.
  • Custom property: bind with @ConfigurationProperties for easy changes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Per-endpoint limit: check file.getSize() in code when one endpoint needs a stricter limit than the global one.
  • Handler: @ExceptionHandler(MaxUploadSizeExceededException.class) inside @RestControllerAdvice.
  • DataSize: write limits as 5MB or 512KB in properties; Spring converts them to DataSize.

Senior Notes

  • Container limits too: a reverse proxy (nginx client_max_body_size) or Tomcat may reject before Spring sees it.
  • getSize() is client declared per part, but the container enforces real counting; still re-check after saving if you must be strict.
  • Unlimited is possible with -1, but dangerous without another guard.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Raising only the Spring limit: a proxy still returns 413; raise nginx client_max_body_size too.
  • Handler not applied: the exception is thrown before binding, so make sure the advice class is a bean.
  • Confusing KB and MB strings: 1M and 1MB both parse, but be explicit.
  • Returning 500: unhandled MaxUploadSizeExceededException gives a generic error.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Reject early: a Content-Length check at the proxy saves bandwidth.
  • Streaming limit: for raw bodies, wrap the stream with a counting guard (Apache Commons IO BoundedInputStream or your own) so a lying client cannot send more.
  • Quota: also limit total storage per user.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an image gallery with an avatar limit of 2MB and a gallery photo limit of 10MB, behind nginx. Configure container limits at the larger value, enforce the small limit in code, and set the proxy limit slightly above the container limit.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=10MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=12MB
app.upload.avatar-max=2MB

# nginx
# client_max_body_size 12m;

# OUTPUT:
# avatar 3MB  -> 400 Avatar too large (from code)
# photo 11MB  -> 413 (from Spring)
# photo 13MB  -> 413 (from nginx)

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Type validation allows only chosen kinds of files, such as images (image/png, image/jpeg) or PDFs.
  • Check file.getContentType() against an allow-list; prefer an allow-list over a block-list.
  • Also check the extension of the name, because the declared content type is sent by the client.

Worked Example 1

Extension plus type.

Worked Example 2

Test a rejected type.

Practice Exercise 1

Allow-list check.

Practice Exercise 2

Magic number check for PNG.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How type information reaches you:

  • Part header: the client writes Content-Type inside each part; the container exposes it via Part.getContentType() and Spring via MultipartFile.getContentType().
  • Not verified: neither the container nor Spring inspects bytes.
  • File name: getOriginalFilename() is also client supplied.
  • Detection: only your code (magic bytes, Tika, URLConnection.guessContentTypeFromStream) knows the real format.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Allow-list styles:

  • Set of MIME types for simple cases.
  • Extension map: extension to expected MIME type, compare both.
  • Tika: new Tika().detect(inputStream) covers hundreds of formats.
  • Annotation attributes: types in a custom constraint.
  • MediaType matching: MediaType.IMAGE_PNG.includes(parsed) or wildcards like image/*.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Magic numbers: read the first bytes (PNG starts with 89 50 4E 47, PDF with %PDF) to confirm real content.
  • Tika: Apache Tika detects the real type from content, if you add the dependency.
  • Response: return 415 Unsupported Media Type or 400 with a message listing allowed types.

Senior Notes

  • Polyglot files: a file can be a valid image and a script at once, so also serve uploads with a fixed safe Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
  • Image re-encoding: decoding and re-writing an image with ImageIO strips hidden payloads.
  • Never save with the client extension into an executable location such as a script folder.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Block-list: attackers use a type you forgot; use an allow-list.
  • Case sensitivity: .PNG versus .png; lower-case with Locale.ROOT.
  • Double extension: shell.php.png may be executed by a misconfigured server; rename on store.
  • Serving user files from your own origin with their own type allows stored XSS (an uploaded HTML or SVG); serve from a separate domain or force download.
  • SVG: it is XML that can hold scripts; avoid or sanitize.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Read only the header: magic numbers need a few bytes.
  • Tika: reuse one Tika instance, it is thread safe.
  • Image decoding for re-encoding costs CPU; do it only for images that are shown to others, and limit dimensions to avoid decompression bombs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a resume upload that accepts PDF and DOCX only. The service detects the type, compares it with an allow-list, stores under a generated name and returns 415 for everything else.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • File download sends a stored file to the client; the controller returns bytes with Content-Type and Content-Disposition: attachment.
  • Simplest form: return ResponseEntity<Resource> built from a FileSystemResource or UrlResource.
  • attachment makes the browser save the file; inline lets it show the file (for example a PDF) in the tab.

Worked Example 1

Traversal attempt is blocked.

Worked Example 2

Test the download.

Practice Exercise 1

Download endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

Download bytes directly.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens on a download request:

  • Mapping: RequestMappingHandlerMapping finds the method; RequestMappingHandlerAdapter calls it.
  • Return value: HttpEntityMethodProcessor handles ResponseEntity, writes status and headers, then picks a converter for the body.
  • Converter: ResourceHttpMessageConverter copies the resource stream to the response output stream in a buffer; content type defaults from the file name if not given.
  • Ranges: if a Range header exists and the body is a Resource, the entity processor converts to ResourceRegion and replies 206.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to send a file:

  • ResponseEntity<Resource>: best default.
  • byte[]: only for small content.
  • StreamingResponseBody: for generated or huge output.
  • HttpServletResponse: manual control, return void.
  • Static handler: ResourceHandlerRegistry maps a URL to a folder without a controller.
  • Disposition: attachment versus inline.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Handled by ResourceHttpMessageConverter (and ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter for ranges), selected by the return type.
  • Header helper: ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name).build() encodes the file name correctly.
  • Media type: use Files.probeContentType or MediaTypeFactory.getMediaType(resource), with application/octet-stream as the fallback.

Senior Notes

  • Path traversal: resolve the requested name against a base directory, call normalize(), and check startsWith(base).
  • Not found: return 404 when the file is missing, instead of a 500.
  • Caching: add ETag or Last-Modified, and Content-Length, so clients and proxies behave well.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Path traversal: never concatenate user input into a path; normalize and check.
  • Wrong filename encoding: non-ASCII names break; use ContentDisposition.
  • Loading bytes for big files: use Resource.
  • Returning 500 for missing files: return 404.
  • Header injection: a name with a newline; the builder encodes it, manual strings may not.
  • Authorization: checking login but not ownership of the file.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Zero copy: the servlet container may use sendfile for static files.
  • HTTP caching: ETag, Last-Modified and Cache-Control avoid repeat transfers; ShallowEtagHeaderFilter adds ETags but needs the full body in memory.
  • Compression: not for already compressed files.
  • CDN: offload public files.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: invoice PDFs. The user must be logged in and must own the invoice; the file is found by invoice id (not by a path) and sent as attachment.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Streaming response writes data to the client as it is produced, instead of building the whole body in memory first.
  • Main tool: return StreamingResponseBody, a functional interface whose writeTo(OutputStream) runs on an async thread.
  • Use for big files, generated exports (CSV) and long running output, where holding everything in a byte[] would waste memory.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test for streaming.

Worked Example 2

Async configuration.

Practice Exercise 1

Stream a generated CSV.

Practice Exercise 2

Server sent events.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a StreamingResponseBody request runs:

  • Return handler: StreamingResponseBodyReturnValueHandler wraps the body in a WebAsyncTask.
  • Async start: startAsync() is called on the servlet request, so the container thread is released.
  • Worker thread: a TaskExecutor runs writeTo(outputStream); output goes directly to the servlet response.
  • Completion: when writeTo returns, Spring completes the async context; on error it dispatches an error.
  • Timeout: spring.mvc.async.request-timeout (default depends on the container) ends a slow stream.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Streaming options:

  • StreamingResponseBody: raw bytes.
  • ResponseBodyEmitter: many objects, written as JSON items over time.
  • SseEmitter: text/event-stream for browsers.
  • Flux (WebFlux): reactive streaming, a separate stack.
  • Servlet output stream: synchronous writing in the request thread.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • How: Spring MVC starts async processing, frees the request thread, and a task executor runs your writeTo code.
  • Other types: SseEmitter (server sent events) and ResponseBodyEmitter push many items over time.
  • Executor: configure spring.mvc.async.request-timeout and a TaskExecutor via WebMvcConfigurer.configureAsyncSupport.

Senior Notes

  • Headers first: status and headers are committed on the first flush, so you cannot change them after output starts.
  • Errors mid-stream cannot become a clean 500; the client sees a truncated body, so log and design for it.
  • Transactions and open sessions do not span the async thread by default, so avoid lazy loading inside writeTo.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Not flushing: data sits in buffers; flush after logical chunks.
  • Using a request scoped bean or lazy entity inside writeTo; the request context and session are not available the same way.
  • Unbounded default executor: the simple async executor may create many threads; configure a pool.
  • Not closing resources: use try-with-resources inside the body.
  • Ignoring client disconnect: an IOException on write means stop work.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Memory: constant, only the buffer size.
  • Threads: each stream uses a worker for its whole life, so size the pool for concurrent streams.
  • Flush frequency: too often costs syscalls; too rarely delays the client.
  • Proxy buffering: nginx may buffer responses; set X-Accel-Buffering: no for live streams.
  • Database: use fetch size or a cursor, not a full list.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: exporting a million order rows as CSV without loading them. The query is streamed from the database, rows are written one by one, and the browser starts the download immediately.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Resource is Spring abstraction (org.springframework.core.io.Resource) for any readable content: a file, classpath entry, URL or byte array.
  • Common types: ClassPathResource, FileSystemResource, UrlResource, ByteArrayResource and InputStreamResource.
  • Key methods: exists(), getInputStream(), getFile(), contentLength() and getFilename().

Worked Example 1

Resource types.

Worked Example 2

Test with a test resource.

Practice Exercise 1

Inject and read a resource.

Practice Exercise 2

ResourceLoader and patterns.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring resolves a resource:

  • ResourceLoader: the ApplicationContext is itself a ResourceLoader.
  • Prefix rule: classpath: gives ClassPathResource, file: and URLs give FileUrlResource or UrlResource; no prefix depends on the context (a web context uses ServletContextResource).
  • Conversion: ResourceEditor and the conversion service turn a string in @Value into a Resource at injection time.
  • Handle only: creating a Resource does not open anything; I/O starts at getInputStream().

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resource types at a glance:

  • ClassPathResource: packaged with the app, read-only in a JAR.
  • FileSystemResource / PathResource: files on disk, writable via WritableResource.
  • UrlResource: remote or file URL.
  • ByteArrayResource: in memory bytes.
  • InputStreamResource: one shot stream.
  • ServletContextResource: file under the web application root.
  • Pattern lookups: classpath*:META-INF/*.xml.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefixes pick the type: classpath:, file:, http:; no prefix uses the context type.
  • Injection: @Value("classpath:data/seed.json") Resource seed or the ResourceLoader interface (getResource).
  • Patterns: ResourcePatternResolver with classpath*: and Ant patterns finds many resources at once.

Senior Notes

  • getFile() fails for resources inside a JAR, because they are not files; use getInputStream() instead.
  • InputStreamResource can be read only once, and has no length, so it is a poor choice for downloads that need Content-Length.
  • Close streams with try-with-resources; the Resource itself is just a handle, the stream is what you must close.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • getFile() inside a JAR: throws FileNotFoundException (resource "cannot be resolved to absolute file path"). Use getInputStream().
  • Wrong prefix: classpath:/x and classpath:x are fine, but a leading wrong folder is not.
  • Forgetting to close streams.
  • Reading an InputStreamResource twice fails with IllegalStateException.
  • Using new File("src/main/resources/..."): works in the IDE only.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cache content: read static resources once at startup, not per request.
  • Pattern scans over the whole classpath are slow; do them at startup.
  • Buffered reads: use readAllBytes for small files, buffers for large.
  • Remote URLs: set timeouts; UrlResource alone has none, so prefer RestClient for HTTP.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: loading a seed JSON file at startup to insert default data, then letting an admin download generated reports through ResponseEntity<Resource>. Both use the same abstraction, so tests can swap the location for a test file.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ResponseEntity<Resource> returns a file or stream together with the status code and headers you choose.
  • Why it fits downloads: you control Content-Type, Content-Disposition, Content-Length and caching headers, plus 404 for missing files.
  • Build with ResponseEntity.ok().headers(...).contentType(...).body(resource).

Worked Example 1

Generated content with ByteArrayResource.

Worked Example 2

Test a range request.

Practice Exercise 1

Full download method.

Practice Exercise 2

Inline display with cache.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals of returning ResponseEntity<Resource>:

  • Processor: HttpEntityMethodProcessor.handleReturnValue copies your headers to the response.
  • Range check: if the body is a Resource and the request has a Range header, it builds HttpRange to ResourceRegion and uses the region converter; status 206.
  • Otherwise ResourceHttpMessageConverter writes the whole resource, defaulting the type from the file name.
  • Headers added: Accept-Ranges: bytes and, when known, Content-Length.
  • Invalid range: 416 Range Not Satisfiable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Builder options:

  • Status: ok(), status(...), notFound().
  • Type: contentType, contentLength.
  • Disposition: ContentDisposition.attachment() or inline().
  • Cache: cacheControl, eTag, lastModified.
  • Resource kinds: FileSystemResource, UrlResource, ClassPathResource, ByteArrayResource, InputStreamResource.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Converter: ResourceHttpMessageConverter writes the resource, and ResourceRegionHttpMessageConverter serves ranges (206 Partial Content).
  • Content length is taken from resource.contentLength(), so use FileSystemResource or UrlResource rather than InputStreamResource.
  • Range requests work automatically when the body is a Resource and the client sends Range.

Senior Notes

  • Missing file: check resource.exists() && resource.isReadable() and return ResponseEntity.notFound().build().
  • Name encoding: ContentDisposition.filename(name, UTF_8) handles non-ASCII names with the right encoding.
  • Caching: add cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(...)) and eTag for static downloads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Not checking exists(): a missing file leads to an exception and 500.
  • Closing the stream yourself: Spring closes it after writing.
  • Path traversal through @PathVariable names.
  • Wrong media type guess: set it explicitly when you know it.
  • Mapping name with dots: /files/{name} may cut the extension off in older setups; use {name:.+} if needed.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Use FileSystemResource: length and last modified are cheap; ranges allow seeking in video.
  • Add caching headers to avoid repeat transfers.
  • Avoid ByteArrayResource for big data: it is held in memory.
  • Static files: prefer the resource handler or a CDN for public content.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a video endpoint. Browsers send Range requests when users seek. Returning a FileSystemResource inside ResponseEntity lets Spring answer with partial content, so seeking works without extra code.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Large files must be handled as streams, because loading a whole file into a byte[] can exhaust the heap.
  • Upload side: use getInputStream() and copy in chunks, or transferTo(), never getBytes().
  • Download side: return a Resource or StreamingResponseBody so data flows from disk to socket in small buffers.

Worked Example 1

Stream a large download in chunks.

Worked Example 2

Properties for large uploads.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=2GB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=2GB
spring.servlet.multipart.file-size-threshold=2MB
spring.servlet.multipart.location=/data/tmp

# OUTPUT:
# Parts above 2MB spool to /data/tmp, then are removed after the request

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Stream an upload to disk.

Practice Exercise 2

Raw body upload with PUT.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Memory paths for large data:

  • Upload: the container spools big parts to a temp file; the controller sees a MultipartFile backed by that file, so memory stays low if you stream.
  • Danger zone: getBytes(), MultipartFile to byte[], and JSON/Base64 bodies load everything.
  • Download: Resource and StreamingResponseBody copy in 8 KB style buffers.
  • Request thread: a slow upload or download occupies a thread for the whole time unless you go async.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Strategies:

  • Multipart streaming: simple, fine up to hundreds of MB.
  • Raw body with PUT: skips multipart parsing.
  • Chunked upload: client sends numbered parts, server tracks and merges.
  • Pre-signed URL: client talks to S3 or similar directly.
  • Resumable (tus-like): uses offsets so a broken upload continues.
  • Download ranges: Resource supports Range.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Multipart temp files: parts above spring.servlet.multipart.file-size-threshold go to disk; set location to a disk with enough space.
  • Limits: raise max-file-size and max-request-size deliberately, and match proxy limits.
  • Chunked or resumable uploads split a file into pieces that the client sends one by one and the server joins.

Senior Notes

  • Bypass multipart parsing: for very big uploads, accept the raw body (InputStream or HttpServletRequest) with PUT and stream it to storage.
  • Offload: let clients upload straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL, so your app does not carry the bytes.
  • Timeouts and threads: slow clients hold a request thread; use async handling, timeouts and a bounded pool.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forgetting the proxy limit: nginx and load balancers have their own body limits and timeouts.
  • Temp directory full: the default temp location may be small; set spring.servlet.multipart.location.
  • Short timeouts: a slow client needs larger idle timeouts.
  • Compute on the request thread: hashing or virus scanning a big file blocks the response; do it asynchronously.
  • No cleanup: abandoned chunks pile up; run a scheduled cleanup.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning checklist:

  • Buffers: 8 to 64 KB chunks are usual.
  • Threads: bound concurrent transfers with a pool or a semaphore.
  • Checksums: compute while copying (a DigestInputStream), not in a second pass.
  • Disk: use fast storage for temp and target.
  • Virtual threads: on Java 21 with Spring Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true makes blocking IO cheaper per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a video platform. Large uploads go straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL. The app only issues the URL and records metadata, so no gigabytes pass through the Spring servers; downloads use a CDN, with Range support as a fallback.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Internationalization (i18n) means designing an application so it can be adapted to many languages and regions without changing the code; the 18 stands for the letters between i and n.
  • Texts move out of code: labels and messages live in messages_xx.properties files and are looked up by a key.
  • Three Spring pieces: a MessageSource finds the text, a LocaleResolver decides the current locale, and a LocaleChangeInterceptor lets the user switch it.

Worked Example 1

Test the French text.

Worked Example 2

Minimal Boot setup.

Practice Exercise 1

Create the bundle files.

Practice Exercise 2

Read a message in a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

i18n in Spring MVC is a chain of small steps in the request cycle.

  • Locale step: the DispatcherServlet calls the LocaleResolver and stores the result in the request, also available through LocaleContextHolder.
  • Text step: the controller, view or validator asks the MessageSource for a key and locale.
  • Bundle step: the source loads messages_xx.properties through a ResourceBundle and caches it.
  • Format step: MessageFormat fills {0} placeholders using the locale.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for supplying messages:

  • Boot properties: spring.messages.basename, encoding, cache-duration.
  • Java config: a MessageSource bean named messageSource.
  • Views: #{key} (Thymeleaf) or spring:message (JSP).
  • Validation: message codes like Size.user.name.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.messages.basename=messages,errors
spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8
spring.messages.cache-duration=10m
spring.messages.fallback-to-system-locale=false

# OUTPUT:
# Boot logs nothing;
a MessageSource bean named messageSource is created.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Locale-aware data: i18n also covers dates, numbers and currency, not only text, and Spring formatting uses the request locale.
  • Fallback chain: messages_fr_CA, then messages_fr, then messages; the last file is the default.
  • Encoding: set UTF-8 on the message source, otherwise accented and non-Latin text is garbled.

Senior Notes

  • Design for expansion: translated text is often longer, so layouts must not depend on fixed widths.
  • Never concatenate sentences from pieces; use one message with placeholders such as {0} because word order differs by language.
  • Test with MockMvc by sending an Accept-Language header or a lang parameter and asserting the text.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Wrong bean name: naming it messages instead of messageSource.
  • Wrong encoding: garbled letters; set UTF-8.
  • Hard-coded text left in templates.
  • Sentence building from fragments.
  • Missing base file: unknown locale then fails.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Message lookup is cheap, but a few points matter:

  • Cache: bundles are cached; reloading in production is rarely needed.
  • Reloadable source: use only in development with a short cache time.
  • Hot path: avoid resolving the same message in a tight loop; resolve once per request.
  • MessageFormat is not thread-safe, Spring handles this internally.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an online shop for India and France.

  • Files messages.properties, messages_fr.properties, messages_hi.properties.
  • A cookie resolver keeps the choice for 30 days.
  • A test checks all key sets are equal before each release.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Localization (l10n) is the work of adapting an internationalized application to one specific locale: translating text and choosing local formats for dates, numbers and currency.
  • i18n versus l10n: i18n is the one-time design that makes translation possible; l10n is the per-language work done on top of it.
  • In Spring localization means adding a messages_xx.properties file per language and letting the framework pick it.

Worked Example 1

Localized date in a controller.

Worked Example 2

Check all languages have all keys.

Practice Exercise 1

Add Hindi next to English.

Practice Exercise 2

Format a number by locale.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Localization uses the same machinery as i18n but supplies locale-specific data.

  • Text: resolved from the most specific bundle first (fr_CA then fr then base).
  • Formats: JDK classes (NumberFormat, DateTimeFormatter) read patterns from CLDR locale data.
  • Spring formatters: FormattingConversionService picks a formatter per field and uses the current locale from LocaleContextHolder.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Localization variants:

  • Language only: messages_fr.
  • Language and country: messages_fr_CA overrides only the keys that differ.
  • Script and variant tags exist but are rare.
  • Formatting styles: SHORT, MEDIUM, LONG, FULL.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Beyond text: dates, numbers, plurals, images, colours and even layout direction (right to left) can differ.
  • Formatting: @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat use the request locale when no pattern is given.
  • Region variants: en_US and en_GB can differ in a few words while sharing messages_en.

Senior Notes

  • Translation workflow: keep keys stable, give translators context, and fail the build when a key is missing in a language.
  • Plurals: simple messages cannot express them in every language; use MessageFormat choice patterns or avoid counts in text.
  • Content localization: user-generated or database content needs its own translated columns or tables, not property files.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common localization mistakes:

  • Parsing user input with the server locale instead of the request locale.
  • Hard-coded date patterns such as MM/dd/yyyy.
  • Storing formatted values in the database; store raw numbers and dates.
  • Upper-casing without a locale (the Turkish i problem).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Format objects: DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe and can be cached per locale; NumberFormat is not thread-safe.
  • Locale list: restrict supported locales so no time is spent on unsupported ones.
  • Static content: translate images and large text once and serve from a CDN with a locale key.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: invoices for several countries.

  • Amount and date use the customer locale.
  • Legal text comes from message files.
  • The invoice PDF job receives the stored customer locale.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Locale is the java.util.Locale object that holds a language and an optional country, such as fr or en_GB; it tells Java which language and format rules to use.
  • Created with Locale.of("fr", "CA") (Java 19+), new Locale("fr", "CA") or Locale.forLanguageTag("fr-CA").
  • In a controller declare a Locale method parameter and Spring injects the locale chosen by the LocaleResolver.

Worked Example 1

Locale in a service.

Worked Example 2

Test with a fixed locale.

Practice Exercise 1

Create and inspect locales.

Practice Exercise 2

Locale in a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the locale travels through a request:

  • DispatcherServlet.buildLocaleContext asks the LocaleResolver.
  • The result is placed in LocaleContextHolder (a thread-local) for the whole request.
  • The argument resolver for Locale method parameters reads the same value.
  • After the response, the holder is reset.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to obtain a locale:

  • Method parameter: Locale locale.
  • Request: RequestContextUtils.getLocale(request).
  • Holder: LocaleContextHolder.getLocale().
  • Factory: Locale.forLanguageTag, Locale.of (Java 19+), Locale.Builder.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Parts: language (ISO 639), country (ISO 3166) and variant; getLanguage() and getCountry() read them.
  • Locale.getDefault() is the server JVM locale; do not use it for web users, use the request locale instead.
  • LocaleContextHolder.getLocale() gives the current request locale anywhere, even in a service class.

Senior Notes

  • Thread-bound: LocaleContextHolder stores the locale in a thread-local, so it is lost in new threads and async tasks unless copied.
  • Language tags: prefer forLanguageTag("fr-CA"), the BCP 47 form; toString() gives fr_CA.
  • Never store the locale as a plain string in business logic without validating it against the supported list.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with locales:

  • Default locale in server code: String.format without a locale.
  • Parsing tags by hand: splitting on an underscore fails for new tags.
  • Async loss: the locale is missing in worker threads.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • A Locale is immutable and cheap, but getDisplayName loads locale data on first use.
  • Use Locale.ROOT for technical case conversion and formatting of keys.
  • A TaskDecorator can copy the locale to async threads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a welcome email after sign-up.

  • The locale is read once in the controller.
  • It is saved in the user record.
  • The mail job reads it from the record, never from the thread.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • LocaleResolver is the Spring MVC interface that decides the locale of each request; the DispatcherServlet calls it first and exposes the result.
  • Built-in types: AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver (default, reads Accept-Language), SessionLocaleResolver, CookieLocaleResolver and FixedLocaleResolver.
  • Bean name matters: the bean must be called localeResolver, otherwise the DispatcherServlet does not find it.

Worked Example 1

Custom resolver from a query parameter.

Worked Example 2

Test the cookie.

Practice Exercise 1

Register a cookie resolver.

Practice Exercise 2

Limit accepted languages.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The interface has two methods: resolveLocale(request) and setLocale(request, response, locale).

  • DispatcherServlet.initLocaleResolver looks for a bean named localeResolver; if none, it creates AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver.
  • On each request buildLocaleContext calls resolveLocale (or a LocaleContextResolver, which can also give a time zone).
  • SessionLocaleResolver stores the locale in a session attribute; CookieLocaleResolver writes a cookie in setLocale.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolver options:

  • AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver: stateless, no switching.
  • SessionLocaleResolver: per session, simple.
  • CookieLocaleResolver: persistent, cookie name, max age, path, secure flags.
  • FixedLocaleResolver: always one locale, useful for tests.
  • Custom: read from user, subdomain or path.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Header resolver is read-only: it cannot change the locale, so setLocale throws UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Session resolver keeps the choice in the HTTP session; the cookie resolver keeps it in a cookie and survives restarts.
  • Default locale: setDefaultLocale is used when nothing was chosen yet.

Senior Notes

  • Stateless APIs should keep the header resolver or a custom one, since sessions break horizontal scaling.
  • Custom resolver: implement resolveLocale(HttpServletRequest), for example to read the locale from a JWT claim or a user profile.
  • Supported list: AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver.setSupportedLocales avoids using a locale you have no texts for.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common problems:

  • Bean named wrongly so it is ignored.
  • Header resolver plus interceptor gives UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Cookie flags: cookie missing because of Secure on plain HTTP in development.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and design:

  • Header and cookie resolvers are stateless on the server and scale freely.
  • The session resolver adds session memory and needs sticky or shared sessions.
  • A custom resolver that loads the user from a database should cache the value in the request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: logged-in users keep their language across devices.

  • The profile stores the locale.
  • The resolver prefers the profile, then the cookie, then the header.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • LocaleChangeInterceptor is a HandlerInterceptor that reads a request parameter (default name locale) and calls setLocale on the LocaleResolver.
  • Usage: a link such as /home?lang=fr switches the language for the following requests.
  • Needs a writable resolver: it works with session or cookie resolvers, not with the header resolver.

Worked Example 1

Test the switch.

Worked Example 2

Ignore bad values.

Practice Exercise 1

Register the interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Pair it with a session resolver.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The class extends HandlerInterceptorAdapter-style behavior through HandlerInterceptor.preHandle.

  • It reads request.getParameter(paramName).
  • It gets the resolver with RequestContextUtils.getLocaleResolver(request); if none, it throws IllegalStateException.
  • It parses the value with StringUtils.parseLocale and calls setLocale.
  • It always returns true, so the chain continues.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • setParamName: parameter name.
  • setHttpMethods: allowed methods (all by default).
  • setIgnoreInvalidLocale: swallow bad values.
  • setLanguageTagCompliant: parse BCP 47 tags such as fr-CA when true.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Register it in WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors; a bean alone is not enough.
  • setParamName("lang") changes the parameter name; setHttpMethods can limit it to POST or GET.
  • Order: it runs in preHandle, before the controller, so the new locale is already active for that request.

Senior Notes

  • Invalid values: set setIgnoreInvalidLocale(true) so a bad parameter does not give a 500 error.
  • Security: the parameter is user input; it only selects a locale and is never written to a file or query, but still validate it against a supported list.
  • Caching: pages that change with a parameter must vary the cache key, or a CDN may serve the wrong language.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Not registered: only a bean, never added to the registry.
  • Header resolver still active.
  • Lowercase vs tag: fr_CA versus fr-CA confusion; enable the language tag mode if you send tags.
  • Caching by proxies ignoring the parameter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • The cost is one parameter read per request, almost nothing.
  • Limit it with addPathPatterns to page routes, not static files or APIs.
  • For caches add Vary: Accept-Language or include the parameter in the cache key.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: switch with a safe redirect and a test.

  • The parameter changes the cookie.
  • The cookie is checked in the test response.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MessageSource is the Spring interface that resolves a message key to text for a given Locale, with optional arguments and a default message.
  • Main method: getMessage(String code, Object[] args, Locale locale); overloads accept a default message or a MessageSourceResolvable.
  • Every ApplicationContext is a MessageSource and delegates to the bean named messageSource.

Worked Example 1

Controller with MessageSource.

Worked Example 2

Test the missing key.

Practice Exercise 1

Use getMessage with arguments.

Practice Exercise 2

Default message and fallback.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the framework:

  • AbstractMessageSource.getMessage first tries resolveCodeWithoutArguments when args are empty, otherwise resolveCode that returns a cached MessageFormat.
  • If not found it asks the parent source, then uses the default message, then throws.
  • Formats are cached per message and locale.
  • AbstractApplicationContext.initMessageSource picks the bean named messageSource or creates an empty delegating one.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to call it:

  • Inject MessageSource.
  • Implement MessageSourceAware.
  • Use MessageSourceAccessor to avoid passing a locale.
  • Use a MessageSourceResolvable such as DefaultMessageSourceResolvable with several candidate codes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Placeholders: welcome=Hello, {0} is filled from the args array using java.text.MessageFormat.
  • Implementations: ResourceBundleMessageSource (classpath bundles) and ReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource (re-reads files, can use external paths).
  • Missing key: throws NoSuchMessageException unless you pass a default message or set setUseCodeAsDefaultMessage(true).

Senior Notes

  • Hierarchy: a message source can have a parent through setParentMessageSource, searched when the key is missing.
  • Validation: Bean Validation messages can use the same source if you register a LocalValidatorFactoryBean with setValidationMessageSource.
  • Single quote trap: in MessageFormat a single quote hides placeholders, so write two quotes in properties files.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Passing null locale.
  • Forgetting the args array so {0} stays in the text.
  • Number formatting in args: 1234 becomes 1,234; pass a String if you want it plain.
  • Single quote problem.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Parsed MessageFormat objects are cached, so repeated calls are cheap.
  • Messages with no args skip the format step.
  • Large bundles: split by feature with several basenames.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service that builds user-facing error text.

  • Business code throws a coded exception.
  • An advice translates the code using the request locale.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ResourceBundleMessageSource is the standard MessageSource built on java.util.ResourceBundle; it loads basename_xx.properties files from the classpath.
  • Configure with setBasename("messages") or setBasenames("messages", "errors") and setDefaultEncoding("UTF-8").
  • Lookup order: messages_fr_CA, messages_fr, then the system locale file, then messages.

Worked Example 1

Reloadable version for development.

Worked Example 2

Lookup order check.

Practice Exercise 1

Java configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Spring Boot properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.messages.basename=messages,errors
spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8
spring.messages.fallback-to-system-locale=false
spring.messages.use-code-as-default-message=true

# OUTPUT:
# Boot builds the same ResourceBundleMessageSource from these values.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it loads text:

  • It calls ResourceBundle.getBundle(basename, locale, classLoader, control) with a control that reads properties in the chosen encoding.
  • Candidate locales are tried from specific to general.
  • Bundles are kept in a map keyed by basename and locale, so each file is read once.
  • A MessageFormat per message and locale is cached too.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of configuration:

  • setBasename or setBasenames.
  • setDefaultEncoding and per-file setFileEncodings.
  • setFallbackToSystemLocale.
  • setUseCodeAsDefaultMessage: return the key instead of throwing.
  • setParentMessageSource.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Bean name must be messageSource; with Spring Boot you can instead set spring.messages.basename.
  • fallbackToSystemLocale: by default the JVM locale file is tried before the base file; set it to false to make the base file the only fallback.
  • Caching: bundles are cached forever by default; setCacheSeconds is only supported by the reloadable variant.

Senior Notes

  • Classpath only: files must be on the classpath (for example src/main/resources); use ReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource for file: paths.
  • Encoding: the old ISO-8859-1 default breaks non-Latin text; set UTF-8 explicitly.
  • Common messages: setCommonMessages supplies shared properties for all bundles.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Path style basename: use i18n/messages or dots, not classpath: (that prefix belongs to the reloadable class).
  • File not copied to target/classes because it sits outside resources.
  • Wrong file name case on Linux.
  • Editing in IDE without a rebuild.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep bundles in the jar; classpath reads are fast and cached.
  • Do not use the reloadable class in production unless you need live editing.
  • Keep the base file complete to avoid repeated failed lookups.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: unit test without starting Spring.

  • Build the source by hand.
  • Assert the lookup order.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Language properties files are plain text files of key=value lines, one file per language, named messages_xx.properties where xx is the language code.
  • Base file messages.properties is the default used when no language file matches.
  • Same keys must exist in every file; only the values are translated.

Worked Example 1

Test that keys match.

Worked Example 2

Use in Thymeleaf.
codeExamples:
Sign in

Welcome back

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Two files, same keys.

Practice Exercise 2

Apostrophe rule.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A properties file is parsed by java.util.Properties.load into a map.

  • Lines with # or ! start comments.
  • The first =, : or space separates key and value.
  • A trailing backslash continues a value on the next line.
  • The message source then wraps each value in a MessageFormat when args are given.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants:

  • Placeholders: {0}, with types such as {0,number,#.##} or {1,date,short}.
  • Choice: {0,choice,0#no items|1#one item|1<{0} items}.
  • Unicode escapes: \u0928.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Naming: messages_fr.properties for French, messages_pt_BR.properties for Brazilian Portuguese.
  • Placeholders {0}, {1} are filled with arguments; a literal single quote is written as two quotes.
  • Key style: group keys with dots such as login.title and login.error.badPassword.

Senior Notes

  • Encoding: Java 9+ reads properties as UTF-8 by default for bundles, but Spring still needs setDefaultEncoding("UTF-8"); save the files as UTF-8.
  • Escapes: older tools write \u0928 style escapes; both forms work, but UTF-8 text is easier to review.
  • Review: a build check that compares key sets of all files catches missing translations early.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Frequent mistakes:

  • Missing key in one language.
  • Trailing spaces are kept in values.
  • Quotes: don't loses the placeholder after it.
  • Duplicate keys: the last one wins silently.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and maintenance:

  • Files are read once and cached; size has little effect.
  • Keep one file per feature for large apps.
  • Sort keys and review them in pull requests.
  • Use a translation tool or service that exports properties files.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - split by feature
spring.messages.basename=i18n/common,i18n/orders,i18n/admin

# src/main/resources/i18n/orders_fr.properties
order.title=Commandes

# OUTPUT:
# Smaller files, fewer merge conflicts between translators.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: release gate that checks all languages.

  • The test lists every messages_*.properties file.
  • It fails when a key is missing or has an empty value.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • A multi-language application serves the same pages in several languages and lets the user choose; in Spring MVC it combines message files, a LocaleResolver and a language switch.
  • Recipe: messages_xx.properties files, a MessageSource, a CookieLocaleResolver or SessionLocaleResolver, and a LocaleChangeInterceptor.
  • In views use #{key} in Thymeleaf or spring:message in JSP; never hard-code visible text.

Worked Example 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The full request flow of a multi-language page:

  • Interceptor: LocaleChangeInterceptor may change the locale.
  • Controller: builds the model; texts may come from MessageSource.
  • View: ThymeleafView uses the request locale for #{...} keys, formats and the #locale object.
  • Errors: the BindingResult resolves field error codes through the same source.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design variants:

  • Parameter and cookie: simplest.
  • Path prefix: /fr/..., best for SEO.
  • Subdomain: fr.example.com.
  • Header only: best for APIs.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Language switcher: links such as ?lang=en and ?lang=fr in the page header.
  • Validation messages also need translating: messages.properties can define NotBlank.user.name style keys that Spring finds for field errors.
  • Default: always keep a complete base file so unknown languages still show readable text.

Senior Notes

  • URL strategy: a locale in the path (/fr/products) is cache and SEO friendly; a parameter or cookie is simpler but hides the language from crawlers.
  • Email and PDF output run outside the request, so pass the user locale explicitly to templates.
  • Content: product names and articles usually need translated database columns, not property files.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Untranslated images or buttons with text inside the picture.
  • Fixed-width layouts.
  • Language list in code repeated in many places.
  • Forgetting error pages and emails.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep pages cacheable by including the language in the URL or the cache key.
  • Load only needed bundles per module.
  • Use the Content-Language header and lang attribute for correctness.
codeExamples:
<html th:lang="${#locale.language}
">
<head><link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" th:href="@{/fr/home}"></head>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
<!-- <html lang="fr"> and alternate links help browsers and search engines -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a learning portal in English, French and Hindi.

  • UI text in message files.
  • Course titles in a translation table.
  • Locale stored in the cookie and the profile.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Dynamic language switching lets a user change the language at run time, with no restart or redeploy, usually by clicking a link or a drop-down.
  • How: the link sends ?lang=fr; LocaleChangeInterceptor calls setLocale on a SessionLocaleResolver or CookieLocaleResolver, and later requests use it.
  • Needs a writable resolver; the default header resolver cannot switch dynamically.

Worked Example 1

Test persistence.

Worked Example 2

Safe redirect target.

Practice Exercise 1

Switch and return to the same page.

Practice Exercise 2

Dropdown in Thymeleaf.
codeExamples:
<select onchange="location.href='?lang=' + this.value">
  <option value="en" th:selected="${#locale.language == 'en'}
">English</option>
  <option value="fr" th:selected="${#locale.language == 'fr'}
">Francais</option>
</select>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
<!-- choosing Francais requests ?lang=fr and the same page reloads in French -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Step by step:

  • 1. The user clicks ?lang=fr.
  • 2. LocaleChangeInterceptor.preHandle parses the value.
  • 3. The resolver stores it (session attribute or Set-Cookie).
  • 4. For this request the locale holder is updated, so the page already renders in French.
  • 5. Later requests read the stored value in resolveLocale.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to trigger a switch:

  • Link or form with a parameter.
  • Dedicated endpoint that stores the locale and redirects.
  • JavaScript that sets a cookie and reloads.
  • REST API that updates the user profile locale.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order of events: request arrives, interceptor reads the parameter, resolver stores the locale, controller and view use it.
  • Persistence: a cookie keeps the choice between visits; a session keeps it only until the session ends.
  • Redirect back: after switching, send the user to the same page using the Referer header or a return path.

Senior Notes

  • Post-switch redirect must validate the target to avoid an open redirect; allow only local paths.
  • Logged-in users: store the chosen locale in the user profile and read it in a custom resolver on the next login.
  • Single page apps: send the locale in a header such as Accept-Language and let the API return text for it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Page not reloaded after a JavaScript switch.
  • Cached HTML served in the old language.
  • Open redirect after switching.
  • Locale lost after login because the session id changes; the cookie resolver avoids this.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use a cookie so no session memory is needed.
  • Add Vary: Cookie or Vary: Accept-Language on cacheable pages.
  • Prefer a path prefix when pages are cached by a CDN.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: end-to-end test of the switch in a Boot application.

  • First request switches to Spanish.
  • Second request, with the returned cookie, stays Spanish.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Theme means a named set of static resources (CSS, images) that changes the look of a page without changing its logic. Classic Spring MVC (5.x) had built-in theme support for this.
  • Three pieces made it work: a ThemeSource (finds the theme properties), a ThemeResolver (picks the theme per request) and a ThemeChangeInterceptor (switches it from a request parameter).
  • Important: built-in theme support was removed in Spring Framework 6.0, so on Spring Boot 3 you use CSS variables, a cookie and a template attribute instead.

Worked Example 1

Controller that reads the theme cookie.

Worked Example 2

Testing the model attribute.

Practice Exercise 1

Legacy Spring 5 configuration (for reading old code).

Practice Exercise 2

Modern theme with CSS variables.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How theme support worked in Spring 5 and what replaces it.

  • Request flow: DispatcherServlet called the ThemeResolver bean in doService and stored it as a request attribute.
  • View access: the spring:theme tag used the resolver and the ThemeSource to get a Theme and then the message for a key.
  • Removal: Spring Framework 6.0 removed these classes, so a Boot 3 app has no such beans.
  • Now: the choice is a plain request or cookie value that you expose to the view.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants available today:

  • CSS variables + data-theme: the simplest and fastest.
  • Separate stylesheets: link to light.css or dark.css chosen on the server.
  • Class on body: a theme-dark class, easy to combine with utility CSS.
  • Per-tenant themes: pick the stylesheet from the subdomain or tenant record.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Properties file: in 5.x a theme was a file such as dark.properties that mapped keys like styleSheet to a CSS path.
  • View side: JSP used the spring:theme tag, which looked the key up for the current theme and printed the value.
  • Modern replacement: ship one stylesheet that reads CSS custom properties, and set data-theme on the html element.

Senior Notes

  • Migration: when upgrading from Spring 5 to 6, delete the theme beans and the interceptor, or the application fails to compile.
  • Persistence: store the choice in a cookie (anonymous users) or in the user profile (logged-in users), not in the session only.
  • Caching: if the server renders the theme into the HTML, add Vary: Cookie or the shared cache serves the wrong theme.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Keeping Spring 5 theme beans after the upgrade: the classes are gone, so remove them.
  • Trusting the cookie value and writing it into HTML or a file path: whitelist it.
  • Duplicating CSS for every theme instead of using variables.
  • Theme only in session: the user loses it on logout or timeout.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Static assets: serve CSS with long cache headers and a content hash in the name.
  • One stylesheet for all themes means one request and one cache entry.
  • Server-rendered theme: adds Vary: Cookie, which lowers shared cache hits.
  • Client-side: keeps the HTML identical for everyone.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.enabled=true
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.paths=/**
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=365d

# OUTPUT:
# /css/app.css  is served as /css/app-3f9a1c.css with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a company portal needs light and dark modes and a corporate high-contrast mode for accessibility.

  • Store the choice in the user profile for logged-in users and in a cookie for visitors.
  • An advice reads either source and gives the view one value.
  • The stylesheet uses variables, so a new theme is a new block of colors.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ThemeResolver is the Spring 5 interface that answers one question per request: which theme name is active? It has resolveThemeName and setThemeName.
  • Implementations: FixedThemeResolver (always one theme), SessionThemeResolver (stores it in the session) and CookieThemeResolver (stores it in a cookie).
  • Bean name: the DispatcherServlet looked for a bean named themeResolver; it was removed in Spring Framework 6.0.

Worked Example 1

Setting the cookie.

Worked Example 2

Testing the endpoint.

Practice Exercise 1

Legacy resolver beans (Spring 5).

Practice Exercise 2

Own resolver as a plain class (works in Spring 6).

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the Spring 5 resolver.

  • Interface: resolveThemeName(HttpServletRequest) returns a String; setThemeName changes it.
  • Abstract base: AbstractThemeResolver holds the default theme name (default theme).
  • Cookie variant: CookieThemeResolver reads the cookie, validates it and caches the value in a request attribute.
  • Removal: gone in Spring Framework 6.0.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolver choices:

  • Fixed: one theme, cannot change.
  • Session: per session, lost on expiry.
  • Cookie: per browser, with cookie name, path and max age settings.
  • Custom: user profile, tenant or A/B test group.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Fixed is the default and is fine for a site with a single look.
  • Session loses the choice when the session ends, while cookie remembers it across visits.
  • Same idea as LocaleResolver: the resolver reads the request and returns a small value; the interceptor changes it.

Senior Notes

  • Custom resolver: implement the interface to pick the theme from the user profile or from the subdomain.
  • Thread safety: resolvers are singletons, so keep no per-request state in fields.
  • Today: write a small HandlerInterceptor or a @ControllerAdvice that returns the same decision.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong bean name: a bean called anything other than themeResolver was ignored.
  • Resolver state in fields: shared across users.
  • Missing interceptor: the resolver alone never changes the theme.
  • Unvalidated theme name: it selects a file, so check it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Resolution costs one cookie scan per request; keep it simple.
  • Do not hit the database in a resolver without a cache.
  • For profile themes, load the preference once into the security principal or session.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a multi-tenant SaaS shows each customer its own colors.

  • The tenant is read from the host name.
  • A resolver maps tenant id to a theme name.
  • Unknown tenants get the default.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ThemeSource is the Spring 5 interface that turns a theme name into a Theme object, which holds a MessageSource with the theme keys.
  • Default implementation: ResourceBundleThemeSource, which loads a properties file named after the theme, such as dark.properties.
  • Removed in Spring Framework 6.0 together with the other theme classes.

Worked Example 1

Using the properties.

Worked Example 2

Test with a property override.

Practice Exercise 1

Legacy source bean (Spring 5).

Practice Exercise 2

Modern version with configuration properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the Spring 5 source.

  • Interface: ThemeSource.getTheme(String themeName), returning null if unknown.
  • Resource bundle: ResourceBundleThemeSource creates a SimpleTheme around a ResourceBundleMessageSource per theme and caches it.
  • Context: the web application context itself implements ThemeSource and delegates to a bean named themeSource.
  • Removal: gone in Spring Framework 6.0.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Basename prefix: where the files live, such as themes..
  • Default encoding: set to UTF-8 for non-ASCII text.
  • Parent source: a fallback theme.
  • Modern equivalent: a map in configuration properties, or a database table.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Theme file content looked like styleSheet=/css/dark.css; the key names were chosen by the application.
  • Lookup: the view tag asked the Theme for a key and the bundle returned the value for the active theme name.
  • Basename prefix: setBasenamePrefix("themes.") placed the files in a package or folder.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver plus source: the resolver gives the name, the source gives the values; they were deliberately separate.
  • Replacement: a plain properties class bound with @ConfigurationProperties, or a map of theme name to CSS path.
  • Static content: with CSS variables you need no per-theme lookup at runtime.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Properties file not on the classpath under the prefix.
  • Missing key in one theme: add a default or fail fast at startup.
  • Non-UTF-8 files garble text; set the encoding.
  • Null theme from an unknown name used without a check.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Load definitions once at startup into an immutable map.
  • Avoid reading files per request.
  • If themes live in the database, cache them with a short expiry.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: marketing wants to add a seasonal theme without a release.

  • Themes are rows in a table with CSS path and logo.
  • An admin screen adds a row and clears the cache.
  • The cookie value is checked against the table.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Theme configuration is wiring the pieces together: a theme source, a resolver, an interceptor, and the theme files. In Spring 5 this was Java config or XML; Spring 6 removed the classes.
  • Order of setup: register the ThemeResolver bean, add the ThemeChangeInterceptor through WebMvcConfigurer, and put the theme properties on the classpath.
  • Modern setup: one CSS file with variables, a cookie, and a few lines in a @ControllerAdvice.

Worked Example 1

Registering the interceptor.

Worked Example 2

Test the configuration.

Practice Exercise 1

Modern configuration class.

Practice Exercise 2

Interceptor that sets the cookie from a parameter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the pieces connect in modern configuration.

  • Properties binding: Boot binds app.theme.* into a record at startup and fails fast on a bad value.
  • Interceptor chain: HandlerExecutionChain runs the interceptor before the controller.
  • Model: an advice adds the theme to every model before the view renders.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration variants:

  • Properties or YAML: per environment.
  • Java config: beans and interceptors.
  • Legacy XML or Java (Spring 5): the same set of theme beans.
  • Profiles: different defaults for dev and prod.
codeExamples:
# application-prod.yml
app:
  theme:
    default-name: dark
    allowed: [light, dark, contrast]

# application-dev.yml
app:
  theme:
    default-name: light
    allowed: [light, dark]

# OUTPUT:
# --spring.profiles.active=prod -> default dark, three allowed themes

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Bean names mattered: themeResolver and themeSource were found by name in the web application context.
  • Interceptor param: setParamName("theme") chose the request parameter, with ?theme=dark as the usual call.
  • Spring Boot never auto-configured themes, so you always added them by hand.

Senior Notes

  • Validate input: a theme name from the URL must be checked against known values before it is stored.
  • Cookie flags: set Path, Max-Age and SameSite; a theme cookie holds no secret, so it needs no HttpOnly if the script reads it.
  • Testing: use MockMvc with a cookie and assert the model or the rendered attribute.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forgetting @EnableConfigurationProperties (or scanning) so the record is not a bean.
  • Interceptor not registered because the config class does not implement WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Path patterns: the interceptor also runs for static files unless you exclude them.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: interceptors run on every request, so keep them cheap.

  • No database calls.
  • Exclude static resources.
  • Use set lookups, not lists.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: moving a Spring 5 application to Spring Boot 3.

  • Delete ThemeResolver, ThemeSource and ThemeChangeInterceptor beans and the theme properties files.
  • Replace spring:theme tags with a CSS file chosen by the model value.
  • Keep the same ?theme= URL so bookmarks and links still work.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Dynamic theme means the user can change the look at runtime, for example with a dark mode toggle, and the choice is remembered.
  • Flow: the user clicks a toggle, the browser or server stores the name in a cookie, and the next page renders with that name on the html element.
  • Two styles: client-side (JavaScript and localStorage) and server-side (cookie read by a @ControllerAdvice).

Worked Example 1

Server-rendered attribute with Thymeleaf attribute th:attr (no expressions shown).

Worked Example 2

Test the toggle.

Practice Exercise 1

Toggle endpoint and cookie.

Practice Exercise 2

Client-side switch.
codeExamples:
<script>
  const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
  const sys = matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches;
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = saved || (sys ? "dark" : "light");
  function toggle() {
    const t = document.documentElement.dataset.theme === "dark" ? "light" : "dark";
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t;
    localStorage.setItem("theme", t);
  }
</script>

// OUTPUT:
// first visit on a dark OS -> data-theme="dark"
// after toggle()          -> data-theme="light", saved for next visit

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a dynamic switch works end to end.

  • Client-side: a script sets data-theme on the html element and writes localStorage; the CSS cascade does the rest.
  • Server-side: a request carries the cookie, an advice puts it in the model, the template prints it.
  • Hybrid: the script also writes a cookie so the server can render the right value on the next request.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Toggle button for two modes.
  • Select box for many themes.
  • Follow system: matchMedia listener updates when the OS changes.
  • Server API: PUT /api/me/theme saves to the profile.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • CSS variables let one stylesheet serve every theme; only the values under [data-theme] change.
  • prefers-color-scheme: use the media query as the default when the user has not chosen yet.
  • Legacy way: ?theme=dark handled by ThemeChangeInterceptor in Spring 5.

Senior Notes

  • Flash of wrong theme: render the attribute on the server or set it from an inline script before the page paints.
  • Caching: server-rendered themes need Vary: Cookie; a client-side toggle keeps the HTML cacheable.
  • User profile: for logged-in users save the theme in the database so it follows them across devices.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Flash of wrong theme: the script runs after the page paints.
  • Cached HTML with a baked-in theme served to everyone.
  • No CSRF thought: a state-changing theme endpoint with cookie auth should still use POST and a token if it changes profile data.
  • Untrusted value printed into HTML without escaping.
codeExamples:
<!-- put in head, before the stylesheet, to avoid the flash -->
<script>
  (function () {
    var t = localStorage.getItem("theme");
    if (t) document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t;
  })();
</script>

// OUTPUT:
// the correct theme is applied before first paint

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Switching an attribute repaints once; avoid loading a new stylesheet for each switch.
  • Use transition only on a few properties.
  • Keep the cookie small and scoped to /.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: dashboard with an admin who works on several machines.

  • The toggle calls an API that saves the theme in the profile.
  • On login the server sends the saved value in the first page.
  • The cookie is only a fallback for the login page.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Content negotiation is how the server and client agree on the representation of a resource, such as JSON or XML, for one URL.
  • Strategies: Spring MVC looks at the Accept header first. Older options were a path extension or a query parameter, and the parameter strategy is still available if you enable it.
  • Who does it: ContentNegotiationManager picks the media types, and an HttpMessageConverter writes the body.

Worked Example 1

Reading the negotiated type in a test.

Worked Example 2

406 test.

Practice Exercise 1

One method, two formats.

Practice Exercise 2

Configuring defaults.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a request is negotiated inside Spring MVC.

  • Mapping phase: RequestMappingHandlerMapping matches path, method, consumes and produces.
  • Manager: ContentNegotiationManager runs its strategies (parameter, header) to get the requested types.
  • Return value: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks the best producible type, then the first HttpMessageConverter that can write it.
  • Failure: no match throws HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Header: default.
  • Parameter: optional.
  • Default content type: used when the client sends no preference.
  • Per method: produces and consumes.
  • Manual: return ResponseEntity with an explicit content type.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • produces on @GetMapping lists what a method can return, and consumes lists what it accepts.
  • Failure codes: 406 Not Acceptable when nothing matches the Accept header; 415 Unsupported Media Type when the request body type is not accepted.
  • Default: Spring Boot registers a Jackson JSON converter, so JSON is returned unless you add an XML converter.

Senior Notes

  • Quality values: Accept: application/xml;q=0.9, application/json ranks types; the highest q wins.
  • Vary: responses that depend on Accept should send Vary: Accept for correct caching.
  • Configure with configureContentNegotiation in WebMvcConfigurer, or Boot properties under spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No converter for a type listed in produces: results in 406 or 500.
  • Confusing 406 and 415: 406 concerns the response type, 415 the request body type.
  • Returning a String when you want JSON: it is written as plain text.
  • Missing getters make Jackson produce empty objects or an error.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Narrow produces so mapping resolution is cheap.
  • Reuse one ObjectMapper; Boot already does.
  • Send Vary: Accept so caches stay correct.
  • Use compression (server.compression.enabled) for large bodies.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,application/xml,text/csv
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# OUTPUT:
# responses larger than 1 KB are gzipped when the client sends Accept-Encoding: gzip

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API serves a JavaScript front end (JSON) and a partner system (XML).

  • One controller and one record serve both.
  • The partner is told to send Accept: application/xml.
  • A test per format guards the contract.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a light text format of objects, arrays, strings, numbers and booleans. XML is a tag-based format with attributes, namespaces and schemas.
  • Spring support: JSON through Jackson (MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter), XML through jackson-dataformat-xml or JAXB.
  • Default choice: JSON for web and mobile APIs because it is shorter and maps easily to objects; XML where partners or standards (SOAP, SAML, some banking APIs) require it.

Worked Example 1

Parsing with a small test.

Worked Example 2

Hardening XML input (JAXB style factory).

Practice Exercise 1

Same record in both formats.

Practice Exercise 2

XML attribute.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How each format is handled internally.

  • JSON: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses ObjectMapper to bind JSON to Java objects through getters, setters or record components.
  • XML: MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter uses XmlMapper from jackson-dataformat-xml; the same annotations mostly apply.
  • Order: converters are tried in order, and Boot places the XML converter next to the JSON one once the library is on the classpath.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml: enables XML in Boot -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-dataformat-xml</artifactId>
</dependency>

// OUTPUT:
// startup registers MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter
// requests with Accept: application/xml now succeed

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Comparison points:

  • Verbosity: XML is longer.
  • Schema: XSD for XML; JSON Schema for JSON.
  • Mixed content and attributes: XML only.
  • Types: JSON has numbers and booleans; XML values are text.
  • Tooling: JSON is native in browsers.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Size: the same data is usually smaller in JSON, since XML repeats closing tags.
  • Features: XML has attributes, comments, namespaces and XSD validation; JSON has none of these but has native arrays and numbers.
  • Annotations: @JsonProperty and @JacksonXmlProperty rename fields for each format.

Senior Notes

  • Security: XML parsers need XXE protection (disable external entities); JSON parsers need limits on depth and size.
  • Same model: one record can serve both formats, so content negotiation decides at runtime.
  • Evolution: ignore unknown properties (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off, Boot default) to keep clients compatible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • XXE through unsafe parsers.
  • Date formats: dates become timestamps unless WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS is disabled (Boot disables it).
  • Lists in XML: a wrapper element name is needed to control output.
  • Null handling differs: JSON writes null; XML may write an empty tag.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • JSON parsing is usually faster and allocates less than XML.
  • Reuse mappers (they are thread-safe once configured).
  • Stream large payloads with JsonGenerator or StreamingResponseBody.
  • Compress both formats; text compresses well.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a bank exposes JSON for its mobile app and XML for an older partner.

  • Same service layer and DTO.
  • XML needs a namespace and attribute for the partner schema; use annotations only on the DTO.
  • Contract tests validate XML against the XSD.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Accept header is a request header where the client lists the media types it can handle, for example Accept: application/json.
  • Spring behavior: HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy reads it and the handler mapping matches it against produces; this is the default strategy.
  • Result: a match gives the body in that type; no match gives 406 Not Acceptable.

Worked Example 1

Reading the header manually.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Two methods, one URL, different produces.

Practice Exercise 2

Weighted Accept.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Matching Accept to produces in detail.

  • Parse: MediaType.parseMediaTypes splits the header and reads q values.
  • Sort: MimeTypeUtils.sortBySpecificity puts concrete types before wildcards and higher quality first.
  • Mapping: ProducesRequestCondition keeps only handlers whose produces is compatible; more specific conditions win ties.
  • Ambiguity: two methods that both match raise IllegalStateException (ambiguous mapping) at startup or at request time.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of the header and of mappings:

  • Negation: produces = "!text/plain" excludes a type.
  • Wildcard: produces = "application/*".
  • Vendor types: application/vnd.shop.v2+json for versioning.
  • Class level: produces on the controller applies to all methods.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Quality factor: q values from 0 to 1 rank types; a missing q means 1.
  • Wildcards: */* and application/* match many types; browsers usually send a long list ending in */*.
  • Accept vs Content-Type: Accept describes the response you want; Content-Type describes the body you send.

Senior Notes

  • Most specific wins at the same q, so application/json beats application/*.
  • Order of produces: if the client accepts */*, the first type in your produces list is used.
  • Errors: a custom @ExceptionHandler for HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException should return a type the client accepts, or a plain text fallback.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Browser sends */* and gets the first produces type, which may surprise you.
  • Ambiguous mappings from two methods with the same path and overlapping produces.
  • Custom error body in a type the client did not accept, which causes a second 406.
  • Ignoring Accept by setting the content type manually in the controller.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Header parsing is cheap and cached per request.
  • Fewer overlapping mappings mean faster matching.
  • Add Vary: Accept only where the output really depends on it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: API versioning by media type.

  • Clients ask for application/vnd.shop.v2+json.
  • Old clients keep v1.
  • Tests send both Accept values.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Content-Type is a header that tells the receiver the media type of the body, such as application/json or multipart/form-data. It is sent on a request that has a body and on every response with a body.
  • Request side: Spring picks the HttpMessageConverter that reads the body into your @RequestBody parameter based on it.
  • Mapping: consumes on @PostMapping restricts accepted types; a wrong type gives 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Worked Example 1

Test the 415.

Worked Example 2

Sending JSON from a client.

Practice Exercise 1

consumes and produces together.

Practice Exercise 2

Setting the response type.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the request Content-Type is used.

  • Mapping: ConsumesRequestCondition compares it with consumes; a mismatch throws HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException (415).
  • Reading: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor.readWithMessageConverters finds a converter with canRead(targetClass, contentType).
  • Default: a body without Content-Type is treated as application/octet-stream.
  • Forms: x-www-form-urlencoded and multipart are read by the servlet container or special converters, not by @RequestBody JSON.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common Content-Type values and handling:

  • JSON: @RequestBody.
  • Form: @RequestParam or a model attribute.
  • Multipart: @RequestPart or MultipartFile.
  • Plain text: @RequestBody String.
  • Binary: byte[] or InputStream.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Response side: produces or ResponseEntity.contentType(...) sets the response Content-Type, and the charset is added for text types.
  • Common types: application/json, application/xml, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/plain.
  • Not the same as Accept: Content-Type describes what is being sent; Accept describes what is wanted back.

Senior Notes

  • Missing header: a POST with a JSON body but no Content-Type fails with 415 on a consumes mapping.
  • Charset: JSON is UTF-8 by default; do not rely on ISO-8859-1 defaults for text types.
  • Security: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers from guessing a different type for your response.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes
