Mistakes:

  • Client forgets the header: curl -d sends form encoding, not JSON; add -H "Content-Type: application/json".
  • Wrong annotation: @RequestParam does not read a JSON body.
  • Charset assumptions for non-JSON text.
  • Trusting an upload type: the header is client-controlled, so check the file content too.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Limit request sizes (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size, server max post size).
  • Reject unexpected types early with consumes.
  • Stream large uploads instead of loading them in memory.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB
server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size=2MB

# OUTPUT:
# a 6 MB upload fails with 413 / MaxUploadSizeExceededException

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an endpoint accepts either JSON or XML orders and answers in the format that was sent.

  • Both types appear in consumes.
  • The response type follows Accept, defaulting to the request type.
  • Tests send each type.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • URL-based negotiation chooses the representation from the URL instead of the Accept header: a path extension such as /users.json, or a parameter such as ?format=xml.
  • Current status: since Spring 5.3 the path extension strategy is off and deprecated; the parameter strategy is still supported if you enable it.
  • Why use it: it is easy to try in a browser address bar, where you cannot set an Accept header.

Worked Example 1

Test the parameter.

Worked Example 2

Unknown format value.

Practice Exercise 1

Boot properties.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=true
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.parameter-name=format
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.xml=application/xml
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.json=application/json

# OUTPUT:
# GET /users/1?format=xml  -> XML
# GET /users/1?format=json -> JSON

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Java configuration.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the strategies chain together.

  • ParameterContentNegotiationStrategy: reads the query parameter and maps its value through a registered keyword table.
  • HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy: reads Accept.
  • FixedContentNegotiationStrategy: default type when nothing else decided.
  • Order: the manager asks them in that order and uses the first answer.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • parameterName: default is format.
  • mediaType(key, type): add keywords.
  • ignoreAcceptHeader: force URL-only negotiation.
  • defaultContentType: fallback.
  • Separate URLs: two methods at /users/json and /users/xml need no negotiation at all.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Enable the parameter: favorParameter(true) or the Boot property spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=true.
  • Name and mapping: parameterName("format") and mediaType("xml", APPLICATION_XML) bind keywords to types.
  • Order: strategies are tried in order, parameter first, then the header.

Senior Notes

  • Cache and links: each format has its own URL, which is easy to cache and share, unlike the header approach.
  • REST purity: the same resource having several URLs is debated; many teams keep the header as the main method and the parameter only as a helper.
  • Extension risk: suffix patterns caused security problems (reflected file download), which is why they were removed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Using a path extension on Spring 5.3 or later and wondering why .json returns 404 or 406.
  • Forgetting to register the keyword, so an unknown value gives 406.
  • Parameter name clash with a business parameter called format.
  • Missing converter for the type behind a keyword.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and caching:

  • URL-selected formats cache naturally, since each URL is distinct.
  • Do not send Vary: Accept when you ignore the header.
  • Allow only a small set of keywords.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a report page where analysts paste links into spreadsheets and email.

  • They need a link that returns CSV or JSON without custom headers.
  • The parameter strategy gives /reports/7?format=csv.
  • Browsers and spreadsheet tools can open it directly.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Parameter-based negotiation lets the client choose the response format with a query parameter such as /users?format=json instead of the Accept header.
  • Why use it: a browser address bar or a plain link cannot set the Accept header, but it can add a query parameter.
  • Enable it with configurer.favorParameter(true) in configureContentNegotiation; the default parameter name is format.

Worked Example 1

Test the parameter with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Unknown value gives 406.

Practice Exercise 1

Enable the format parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

Controller that serves both formats.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring resolves the response format through a ContentNegotiationManager.

  • Strategies: the manager holds an ordered list; ParameterContentNegotiationStrategy reads the request parameter and maps the value through a registered table.
  • Selection: AbstractMessageConverterMethodProcessor asks for the requested types, intersects them with the produces types, then finds a converter that can write the return value.
  • Result: the chosen type becomes the Content-Type of the response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • favorParameter: turns the strategy on.
  • parameterName: renames the parameter.
  • mediaType: adds a key to type mapping.
  • defaultContentType: used when nothing is requested.
  • ignoreAcceptHeader: makes the parameter the only source.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Mapping: register values with mediaType("json", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) and mediaType("xml", MediaType.APPLICATION_XML); an unknown value gives 406.
  • Parameter name can be changed with parameterName("type").
  • Precedence: when the parameter strategy is on it is asked first, then the Accept header strategy.

Senior Notes

  • Strategy class: it is ParameterContentNegotiationStrategy, held inside ContentNegotiationManager.
  • Path extensions like /users.json were removed in Spring Framework 6, so the parameter is the supported URL based option.
  • Caching: different formats share one URL path, so make sure proxies cache by the full query string.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgot the mapping: ?format=xml returns 406 because no key was registered.
  • No XML converter: add jackson-dataformat-xml, or the type has no writer.
  • Using path extensions: /users.json no longer works in Spring 6.
  • Missing produces: a method that only produces JSON cannot answer ?format=xml.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: resolving is a map lookup, so it is negligible.
  • Caching: use the full URL, including the query string, as the cache key, or the wrong format can be served.
  • Fewer formats: expose only the formats you test and support.
  • Serialization: XML is heavier than JSON, so keep it for clients that need it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting API where analysts download data in a browser. A link with ?format=csv is easier than setting headers, while API clients keep using Accept.

  • Both strategies stay on, so each client style works.
  • A custom converter writes CSV.
  • Tests cover each format.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Header-based negotiation is the default: the client sends an Accept header and Spring picks the matching HttpMessageConverter.
  • Response: the chosen type is written to the Content-Type header of the reply.
  • No match means 406 Not Acceptable; a wrong request body type means 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Worked Example 1

Test with the Accept header.

Worked Example 2

No acceptable type.

Practice Exercise 1

Two formats from one method.

Practice Exercise 2

Different method per type.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the Accept header is processed:

  • Parse: HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy reads Accept and sorts by quality.
  • Mapping match: produces conditions filter handlers; ambiguity between handlers leads to the best match by specificity.
  • Write: the first converter whose canWrite succeeds writes the body.
  • Failure: no compatible type throws HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException, which becomes 406.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants:

  • produces array: several types on one method.
  • Negation: produces = "!text/html".
  • Wildcards: application/*+json.
  • Request side: consumes for the body type.
  • ResponseEntity: set contentType(...) yourself.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • produces in @GetMapping(produces = "application/json") narrows which requests a method accepts based on Accept.
  • consumes does the same for the request Content-Type header.
  • Quality values: Accept: application/xml;q=0.9, application/json ranks types; the highest q wins.

Senior Notes

  • Strategy class: HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy reads the Accept header.
  • Vary header: caches must key on Accept, so send Vary: Accept when one URL has several formats.
  • Spring Boot adds Jackson for JSON and, if jackson-dataformat-xml is on the classpath, XML too.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Confusing 406 and 415: 406 is about the response type, 415 about the request body.
  • Browser default Accept: browsers send text/html,...,*/*, so a JSON-only endpoint still answers.
  • No Vary header: proxies may serve the wrong format.
  • Testing without accept: MockMvc without accept() means */*.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Negotiation cost: small; the main cost is serialization.
  • Fewer candidates: an explicit produces avoids scanning all converters.
  • Caching: use Vary: Accept with Cache-Control.
  • Compression: enable server.compression.enabled for large JSON.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,application/xml
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# OUTPUT:
# Content-Encoding: gzip for responses of 1 KB or more

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API serves a web app (JSON) and a legacy partner (XML) on the same URLs.

  • Keep header negotiation as the one rule.
  • Document the supported Accept values.
  • Return 406 with a helpful body through @ExceptionHandler.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom content negotiation means you replace or extend how Spring decides the response media type, by writing your own ContentNegotiationStrategy.
  • Typical need: choose the format from a custom header (for example X-Api-Version), a cookie, the host name or the user agent.
  • Register it with configurer.strategies(List.of(...)) in configureContentNegotiation.

Worked Example 1

Test the custom header.

Worked Example 2

Unit test the strategy alone.

Practice Exercise 1

A header-driven strategy.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it with the default header strategy as fallback.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The manager chains strategies.

  • Loop: ContentNegotiationManager.resolveMediaTypes asks each strategy in order and stops at the first result that is not */*.
  • Resolvers: optional MediaTypeFileExtensionResolver objects are used only to look up extensions.
  • Failure mode: if no strategy has an opinion the result is */* and the first usable converter wins.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Other custom sources:

  • Cookie or session: a user preference.
  • Host name: xml.api.shop.com.
  • User agent: mobile clients get compact JSON.
  • Fixed strategy: FixedContentNegotiationStrategy for a default.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Interface: implement resolveMediaTypes(NativeWebRequest) and return a list of MediaType; return MEDIA_TYPE_ALL_LIST to mean "no opinion".
  • Vendor types such as application/vnd.shop.v2+json are a common way to version an API through negotiation.
  • Custom converter: for a brand-new format also add an HttpMessageConverter through extendMessageConverters.

Senior Notes

  • Order: strategies in ContentNegotiationManager run in list order and the first non-empty result wins.
  • Replacing defaults: calling strategies(...) replaces the built-in header and parameter strategies, so add them back if you still need them.
  • Keep it cheap: the strategy runs for every request that writes a body, so do no I/O in it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning an empty list: use MEDIA_TYPE_ALL_LIST for no opinion.
  • Dropping Accept support: add HeaderContentNegotiationStrategy back.
  • No matching produces: the vendor type must also appear in produces.
  • Throwing for unknown values: throw HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException only when you truly cannot serve.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • No I/O: read request data only, never call a database.
  • Stateless: make the strategy a thread-safe singleton.
  • Parse once: pre-build the MediaType constants instead of parsing each request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile app and a web app share an API; the mobile app sends X-Api-Version: 2 and receives the new response shape while old clients keep v1.

  • Two handlers with different produces.
  • One strategy chooses between them.
  • Tests pin both versions.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism where a server uses HTTP headers to say which other origins may read its responses.
  • Purpose: browsers block JavaScript on http://localhost:3000 from reading a response from http://localhost:8080 unless the server allows it.
  • Server side: Spring adds headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin; the browser, not the server, enforces the rule.

Worked Example 1

Test a CORS header with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

A disallowed origin.

Practice Exercise 1

The failing call and its fix.

Practice Exercise 2

Inspect headers with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a CORS check works end to end:

  • Browser: adds Origin to the cross-origin request.
  • Spring: the handler mapping builds a CorsConfiguration; DefaultCorsProcessor.processRequest compares origin, method and headers.
  • Allowed: response headers are added and the request continues.
  • Rejected: status 403 with the text Invalid CORS request.
  • Browser again: compares the response headers and either shows the data to the script or hides it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Response headers at a glance:

  • Allow-Origin: which origin may read.
  • Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers: what the real request may use.
  • Allow-Credentials: permits cookies.
  • Expose-Headers: extra headers JavaScript can read.
  • Max-Age: preflight cache time.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Not a security tool for the server: tools like curl and Postman ignore CORS, so it never replaces authentication.
  • Spring options: @CrossOrigin, a global addCorsMappings, or a CorsFilter.
  • Common error: "has been blocked by CORS policy: No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header" in the browser console.

Senior Notes

  • Processing: DispatcherServlet asks the HandlerMapping for a CorsConfiguration and applies it through DefaultCorsProcessor.
  • Credentials: with cookies, the origin cannot be *; list exact origins or patterns.
  • With Spring Security: enable http.cors(...) so the CORS check runs before the security filters reject the request.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wildcard with credentials: * and allowCredentials(true) together throw an exception; use patterns.
  • Trailing slash in origin: http://localhost:3000/ never matches.
  • Fixing it in the browser: the fix is always on the server.
  • Treating CORS as security: it only protects browser users.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • maxAge: a larger value means fewer preflights.
  • Narrow mappings: apply rules only to /api/**.
  • Same origin: serving the UI and API from one origin removes CORS cost entirely.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a React single-page app on localhost:3000 calls a Spring Boot API. The team starts with a global mapping for the dev origin and moves the production origin into a property.

  • Dev: allow the local origin.
  • Prod: allow only the real domain.
  • Tests assert the headers.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is a browser rule: a page may freely read data only from the same origin, meaning the same scheme, host and port.
  • Origin parts: https://shop.com:443 differs from http://shop.com (scheme), https://api.shop.com (host) and https://shop.com:8443 (port).
  • Why it exists: without it a malicious site could read your bank page using your logged-in cookies.

Worked Example 1

Same origin needs no CORS header.

Worked Example 2

Dev proxy instead of CORS.

Practice Exercise 1

Compare origins in code.

Practice Exercise 2

Spring sends the opt-in header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SOP is implemented inside the browser.

  • Origin tuple: scheme, host, port.
  • Reads blocked: script access to cross-origin responses, DOM of other-origin frames and their storage.
  • Writes allowed: links, form submits and image loads can still send requests.
  • Spring role: none; Spring only provides CORS headers as the opt-in.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways around SOP, safest first:

  • Same origin: serve the SPA from Spring static resources.
  • Reverse proxy: one host routes / and /api.
  • CORS: explicit server opt-in.
  • JSONP: legacy and unsafe; avoid.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • What is blocked: reading cross-origin responses from fetch or XMLHttpRequest; sending the request itself is often still allowed.
  • What is allowed: embedding images, scripts and stylesheets from other origins, and form posts.
  • CORS relaxes SOP: the server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

Senior Notes

  • Simple requests still reach the server, so SOP does not stop CSRF; use CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
  • Dev setup: React on port 3000 and Spring on 8080 are different origins; use CORS config or a dev proxy.
  • Server code: Spring does not enforce SOP; it only supplies the CORS headers the browser checks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Disabling it with a browser flag: hides the problem only on your machine.
  • Allow-Origin * for private data: any site can read public responses; combine with auth carefully.
  • Trusting the Origin header: only browsers send it honestly; non-browser clients can fake it.
  • Port confusion: localhost:3000 and localhost:8080 are different origins.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance angle:

  • Same origin saves preflights, so it is the fastest option.
  • Proxy: adds one hop but removes preflight round trips.
  • Static hosting: bundle the SPA in src/main/resources/static for small apps.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.web.resources.static-locations=classpath:/static/
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=1d

# OUTPUT:
# GET /index.html and GET /api/items share one origin: no preflight

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a developer sees a CORS error from localhost:3000 and wants to find the cause.

  • Compare scheme, host, port.
  • Check the Network tab for the OPTIONS call.
  • Add a mapping for the origin on the server.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Cross-origin request is a request from a page on one origin to a URL on another, for example React on :3000 calling Spring on :8080.
  • Two kinds: simple requests (GET, HEAD, POST with basic content types) go straight out; others trigger a preflight OPTIONS request first.
  • Headers: the browser sends Origin; the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin and related headers.

Worked Example 1

Simulate a cross-origin request.

Worked Example 2

Wrong origin is rejected.

Practice Exercise 1

A cross-origin POST with JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

Expose a custom response header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Request classification and handling:

  • Detect: CorsUtils.isCorsRequest checks for an Origin that differs from the host.
  • Preflight check: CorsUtils.isPreFlightRequest checks for OPTIONS plus Access-Control-Request-Method.
  • Apply: DefaultCorsProcessor adds headers for an actual request and answers a preflight directly.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Client-side options (fetch):

  • mode: cors is the default for cross-origin.
  • credentials: include sends cookies.
  • no-cors: returns an opaque response you cannot read.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Non-simple requests include PUT, DELETE, a JSON Content-Type and custom headers like Authorization.
  • Reading headers: JavaScript sees only safe response headers unless exposedHeaders lists others.
  • Cookies: fetch needs credentials: "include" and the server needs allowCredentials(true).

Senior Notes

  • Spring flow: the handler mapping builds the CORS config, DefaultCorsProcessor validates the origin, method and headers and writes the response headers.
  • Rejected requests get 403 Invalid CORS request from Spring.
  • Vary: Spring adds Vary: Origin so caches keep separate copies per origin.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing allowedHeaders: the Authorization header triggers a failed preflight.
  • Hidden response header: forgot exposedHeaders.
  • Redirects: a redirect on the preflight URL fails the check.
  • Error responses without CORS headers: the browser then reports a CORS error instead of the real 500.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Avoid preflights: use simple requests where possible.
  • Cache preflights: maxAge.
  • Batch calls: fewer cross-origin calls mean fewer round trips.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order form on app.shop.com posts JSON to api.shop.com.

  • The browser sends a preflight.
  • Spring approves it.
  • The POST runs with the order data.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @CrossOrigin is an annotation that enables CORS for one controller method or a whole controller class.
  • Attributes: origins, methods, allowedHeaders, exposedHeaders, allowCredentials and maxAge.
  • Default: with no attributes it allows all origins (patterns) and the methods mapped on the handler, so name the origins you trust.

Worked Example 1

Test allowed origin.

Worked Example 2

Test blocked origin.

Practice Exercise 1

Class-level and method-level.

Practice Exercise 2

Credentials with patterns.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the annotation becomes a rule:

  • Scan: RequestMappingHandlerMapping.initCorsConfiguration reads @CrossOrigin from class and method.
  • Merge: CorsConfiguration.combine joins the class and method values.
  • Apply: the combined config is attached to the handler and processed by DefaultCorsProcessor.
  • Defaults: origin patterns *, mapped methods, all headers, maxAge 1800 seconds; credentials are off.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attribute reference:

  • origins and originPatterns: who may call.
  • methods: allowed HTTP methods.
  • allowedHeaders and exposedHeaders: request and response headers.
  • allowCredentials: a string value "true" or "false".
  • maxAge: preflight cache seconds.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Class and method: a class-level annotation applies to every method; method-level values are combined with it.
  • Pattern support: originPatterns = "https://*.shop.com" allows subdomains and works with credentials.
  • maxAge sets how many seconds the browser may cache the preflight answer (default 1800).

Senior Notes

  • Processing: RequestMappingHandlerMapping reads the annotation into a CorsConfiguration for that handler.
  • Scale: repeating it on many controllers is error-prone; use the global configuration for shared rules.
  • Security: with Spring Security you still need http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wide open default: a bare @CrossOrigin allows every origin; always list origins.
  • Credentials with origins star: use originPatterns.
  • Only on the GET method: the DELETE method in the same controller stays blocked.
  • Spring Security 401 on OPTIONS: the annotation alone is not enough.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • The annotation is read once at startup, so it costs nothing per request.
  • Use maxAge to cut preflight traffic.
  • Prefer the global config when many controllers share the same rules.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a small internal tool has one controller used by a single front end. A class-level annotation with the exact origin is simple and clear.

  • One origin from a property.
  • Credentials allowed.
  • Test for allowed and blocked origins.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Global CORS configuration defines CORS rules for many URL paths in one place by overriding addCorsMappings in a WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Example: registry.addMapping("/api/**").allowedOrigins("http://localhost:3000").
  • Benefit: controllers stay clean and the rules are easy to audit and change per environment.

Worked Example 1

Test with @WebMvcTest.

Worked Example 2

Path outside the mapping.

Practice Exercise 1

Global rules.

Practice Exercise 2

Origins from properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Registry internals:

  • Registry: CorsRegistry.addMapping returns a CorsRegistration holding a CorsConfiguration with defaults applied.
  • Map: path pattern to config, handed to HandlerMapping through setCorsConfigurations.
  • Match: at request time the best matching pattern is combined with any handler-level @CrossOrigin.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Several mappings: different rules per path.
  • Boot property style: none; CORS is configured in code.
  • Spring Security: CorsConfigurationSource bean.
  • WebFlux: CorsWebFilter is the reactive equivalent.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Options on the registration: allowedMethods, allowedHeaders, exposedHeaders, allowCredentials, maxAge.
  • allowedOriginPatterns supports wildcards like https://*.shop.com and is the right choice with credentials.
  • Per environment: read allowed origins from a property so test and production differ.

Senior Notes

  • Mechanics: CorsRegistry builds path-pattern keyed CorsConfiguration objects used by AbstractHandlerMapping.
  • Merging: global config is combined with any @CrossOrigin on the handler.
  • Security: MVC config is not seen by Spring Security filters; add http.cors() so it reuses this configuration.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Pattern too narrow: /api/* misses nested paths; use /api/**.
  • @WebMvcTest without the config: import the class.
  • Forgetting Security: add http.cors().
  • Two sources: a filter and a mapping with different rules confuse debugging.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Lookup is a path match on each request, which is cheap.
  • Set maxAge high to cut preflights.
  • Keep the list of origins short and exact.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: dev, test and prod each allow different origins.

  • Origins come from a profile property.
  • One config class serves all environments.
  • A test checks the dev setting.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CorsFilter is a servlet filter (org.springframework.web.filter.CorsFilter) that applies CORS rules before the request reaches the DispatcherServlet.
  • Build it from a CorsConfiguration registered in a UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource and expose it as a @Bean.
  • When to use: when you need CORS to apply before other filters, or the app uses Spring Security without MVC-level config.

Worked Example 1

Test the filter with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Disallowed origin.

Practice Exercise 1

A CorsFilter bean.

Practice Exercise 2

With Spring Security.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Filter internals:

  • Class: CorsFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter.
  • Flow: look up the config from the source, call processor.processRequest, and if it returns false stop; for a preflight stop as well.
  • Otherwise: continue with filterChain.doFilter.
  • Spring MVC: DefaultCorsProcessor is shared, so the headers match the annotation approach.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Registration options:

  • FilterRegistrationBean: control order and URL patterns.
  • Plain @Bean CorsFilter: Boot registers it for all paths.
  • Spring Security: http.cors() with a CorsConfigurationSource bean.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: register with FilterRegistrationBean and a high precedence so it runs first.
  • Source: source.registerCorsConfiguration("/**", config) maps path patterns to configurations.
  • Short circuit: for a valid preflight it answers directly and does not call the rest of the chain.

Senior Notes

  • Security: with Spring Security a CorsConfigurationSource bean plus http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) installs the same CorsFilter early.
  • Processor: it delegates to DefaultCorsProcessor, the same class MVC uses.
  • Duplication: avoid both a filter and MVC config with different rules; pick one source of truth.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Low filter order: a security filter runs first and rejects the preflight.
  • Duplicate headers: a filter plus MVC config can add the same header twice; keep one.
  • Wildcard with credentials: use patterns.
  • Path pattern: /api/* instead of /api/**.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • The filter runs on every request, but the lookup is a cheap path match.
  • A valid preflight ends in the filter and never reaches MVC.
  • Restrict the path pattern to /api/**.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a gateway service uses Spring Security with JWT. The front end on another origin sends an Authorization header, so every call is preflighted.

  • CORS source bean allows the header.
  • http.cors() runs before the JWT filter.
  • The preflight passes without a token.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Preflight request is an automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request, to ask the server for permission.
  • Headers sent: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers.
  • Server reply: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers and Access-Control-Max-Age.

Worked Example 1

Test the preflight with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

A method that is not allowed.

Practice Exercise 1

What the browser sends and gets.

Practice Exercise 2

Send a preflight with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring answers a preflight:

  • Detect: CorsUtils.isPreFlightRequest is true for OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method.
  • Map: AbstractHandlerMapping.getHandler swaps the handler for a PreFlightHandler built from the CORS config.
  • Reply: DefaultCorsProcessor writes the Allow headers with status 200, or 403 if the request is not allowed.
  • Controller: never invoked, and handler interceptors still run.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Preflight related settings:

  • allowedMethods and allowedHeaders: must cover the planned request.
  • maxAge: caching of the answer.
  • allowPrivateNetwork: for private network access, set with care.
  • Spring Security: permit OPTIONS only through CORS handling, not blanket permit.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Triggers: methods like PUT and DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, or custom headers such as Authorization.
  • Result: if the answer allows the request, the browser sends the real call; otherwise it blocks it and logs a CORS error.
  • Caching: maxAge lets the browser skip repeated preflights for that URL.

Senior Notes

  • Spring handling: AbstractHandlerMapping detects a preflight and returns a PreflightHandler, so your controller method is not called.
  • Security: the preflight carries no credentials, so Spring Security must let it pass (use http.cors()).
  • Debug: look at the OPTIONS call in the browser Network tab; a 401, 403 or missing header explains most failures.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • 401 or 403 on OPTIONS: authentication runs before CORS.
  • Header list mismatch: the planned headers are not allowed.
  • Custom OPTIONS controller: hand-written handlers often miss headers; let Spring do it.
  • Redirect on OPTIONS: browsers reject redirected preflights.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Every non-simple call can cost an extra round trip.
  • A maxAge such as 3600 or more removes most of them.
  • Reduce custom headers and prefer simple content types when possible.
  • Browsers cap the cache (for example, Chromium limits it to a few hours).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a front end shows a CORS error on a DELETE call, but the server logs show no controller call.

  • Open the Network tab and find the OPTIONS request.
  • Check status and the Allow-Methods header.
  • Add DELETE to the allowed methods.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • OPTIONS is an HTTP method that asks a server which methods and headers a URL supports; it changes nothing and has no body.
  • Preflight: before a cross-origin call that is not simple (for example JSON POST or PUT), the browser sends an automatic OPTIONS request first.
  • Answer: the server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and the browser then sends the real request.

Worked Example 1

Global CORS configuration.

Worked Example 2

Read the Allow header from a real OPTIONS call.

Practice Exercise 1

Test a preflight with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 2

Allow origin on a controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A preflight is handled before your controller is chosen.

  • Detection: CorsUtils.isPreFlightRequest checks for method OPTIONS, an Origin header and Access-Control-Request-Method.
  • Handler mapping: AbstractHandlerMapping returns a special preflight handler when CORS configuration matches the path.
  • Processing: DefaultCorsProcessor validates origin, method and headers and writes the response headers.
  • Result: status 200 with Access-Control-Allow-* headers, or 403 with the text Invalid CORS request.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to configure what answers a preflight:

  • @CrossOrigin on a class or method.
  • WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings for global rules.
  • CorsFilter bean for servlet-level control.
  • CorsConfigurationSource bean for Spring Security.
  • Properties: exposedHeaders, allowedHeaders, maxAge, allowCredentials.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request headers: the preflight carries Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers, and never carries cookies or the Authorization header.
  • Spring handling: DispatcherServlet answers a preflight through the CorsProcessor without calling your controller method when CORS is configured.
  • Caching: Access-Control-Max-Age tells the browser how long to remember the answer so it skips repeat preflights.

Senior Notes

  • Security order: with Spring Security, enable http.cors() so the CorsFilter runs before authentication; otherwise the preflight gets 401 or 403.
  • Explicit OPTIONS: @RequestMapping(method = OPTIONS) is rarely needed; the default handling also adds an Allow header for real OPTIONS calls.
  • Debugging: a preflight failure shows in the browser console as a CORS error, but the real cause is visible in the Network tab on the OPTIONS row.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Security blocks OPTIONS: add http.cors() instead of permitting all OPTIONS blindly.
  • Missing header: a custom header such as X-Token not listed in allowed headers fails the preflight.
  • Redirects: a preflight that gets 301 or 302 fails; the server must answer directly.
  • Wildcard and credentials: not allowed together.
  • Wrong layer: a gateway or proxy may add its own CORS headers and create duplicates.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Preflight costs one extra round trip per call.

  • maxAge: browsers cap the cache (often 2 hours in Chrome), so a value like 3600 helps.
  • Same origin: serve the front end and API from one origin or a reverse proxy to avoid preflight entirely.
  • Simple requests: GET with standard headers needs no preflight.
  • Fewer headers: avoid custom headers when a query parameter is enough.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a React app on port 3000 calls a Spring API on port 8080 with a JSON POST and a bearer token. The browser sends OPTIONS first. The team enabled CORS in Spring Security and the preflight now returns 200; the real call then needs the token.

  • Allow the Authorization and Content-Type headers.
  • Keep the origin list per environment in properties.
  • Test the preflight in a MockMvc test so a security change cannot break it unnoticed.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that blocks a page from reading responses of another origin unless that server allows it.
  • Origin means scheme, host and port together, so http://localhost:3000 and http://localhost:8080 are different origins.
  • Not a server firewall: CORS protects the user browser only; tools such as curl or Postman ignore it, so it never replaces authentication.

Worked Example 1

Wrong: wildcard with credentials.

Worked Example 2

Right: pattern for subdomains.

Practice Exercise 1

CORS in the Spring Security chain.

Practice Exercise 2

Rejected origin.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The same-origin policy is enforced by the browser; CORS relaxes it with response headers.

  • Simple request: the browser sends it and then checks Access-Control-Allow-Origin before giving the response to JavaScript.
  • Preflight: non-simple requests are first checked with OPTIONS.
  • Spring: CorsFilter or the MVC handler mapping applies CorsConfiguration through DefaultCorsProcessor.
  • Vary header: Spring adds Vary: Origin so caches do not mix answers for different origins.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options of CorsConfiguration:

  • allowedOrigins and allowedOriginPatterns.
  • allowedMethods and allowedHeaders.
  • exposedHeaders: headers that scripts may read, such as Location.
  • allowCredentials: cookies and Authorization.
  • maxAge: preflight cache time in seconds.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Whitelist exact origins with allowedOrigins; avoid * for APIs that use cookies or sessions.
  • Credentials: allowCredentials(true) lets the browser send cookies, and then the origin must be explicit, not *.
  • Spring Security: add http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) with a CorsConfigurationSource bean so CORS runs inside the security chain.

Senior Notes

  • Filter order: CorsFilter must run before the authentication filters, or preflight calls fail with 401.
  • Patterns: use allowedOriginPatterns for wildcard subdomains when credentials are on.
  • CSRF is a separate protection: CORS does not stop a forged form post, so keep CSRF tokens for cookie-based sessions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Security mistakes:

  • Reflecting Origin: copying any request origin into the header with credentials gives every site access.
  • Trusting null origin: sandboxed pages send Origin: null; do not allow it.
  • Regex errors: a pattern like example.com may also match evilexample.com.
  • Thinking CORS is authentication: a direct call without a browser ignores it.
  • Missing CSRF: cookie sessions still need CSRF protection.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and operations:

  • Preflight cache: use maxAge.
  • Reverse proxy: set CORS in one place only, to avoid duplicate headers that browsers reject.
  • Vary: keep Vary: Origin so CDNs cache correctly.
  • Logging: log rejected origins at debug level to find configuration errors.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.level.org.springframework.web.cors=DEBUG

# OUTPUT:
# DefaultCorsProcessor : Reject: 'https://evil.example.com' origin is not allowed

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin portal at one domain calls an API at another. The team allows only the portal origin with credentials, adds CSRF tokens to cookie requests, and writes tests for allowed and rejected origins.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring Security is a framework that protects a Spring application with a chain of servlet filters for authentication, authorization and attack protection.
  • Integration: add spring-boot-starter-security and every endpoint is secured at once, with a generated password printed at startup for the user user.
  • Configure by declaring a SecurityFilterChain bean with HttpSecurity, which replaces the old WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter.

Worked Example 1

Test with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Read the principal.

Practice Exercise 1

Minimal secured application.

Practice Exercise 2

In-memory users.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring Boot auto-configures security when the starter is on the classpath.

  • Registration: SecurityFilterAutoConfiguration registers DelegatingFilterProxy named springSecurityFilterChain.
  • Dispatch: FilterChainProxy finds the first SecurityFilterChain whose matcher fits the request.
  • Typical filters, in order: SecurityContextHolderFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter.
  • Errors: ExceptionTranslationFilter turns authentication errors into the entry point and access errors into 403.
codeExamples:
# application.properties: print the filter chain at startup
logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG

# OUTPUT:
# Will secure any request with filters: DisableEncodeUrlFilter, WebAsyncManagerIntegrationFilter,
# SecurityContextHolderFilter, HeaderWriterFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter,
# UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter,
# BasicAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of integration:

  • Lambda DSL: the standard style since Spring Security 6.
  • Multiple chains: split API and web.
  • WebSecurityCustomizer: ignore static resources, though permitAll is often preferred.
  • Method security: @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured.
  • Properties: spring.security.user.name and spring.security.user.password for a quick demo user.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Filter chain: DelegatingFilterProxy hands each request to FilterChainProxy, which picks a SecurityFilterChain and runs its filters in order.
  • SecurityContext: after login the Authentication object is stored in SecurityContextHolder and is available in controllers with @AuthenticationPrincipal.
  • Defaults: form login, HTTP Basic, CSRF protection, session fixation protection and security headers are all enabled out of the box.

Senior Notes

  • Method security: @EnableMethodSecurity turns on @PreAuthorize checks on service methods.
  • Multiple chains: use securityMatcher and @Order to give /api/** a stateless chain and the web pages a session chain.
  • Testing: spring-security-test gives @WithMockUser and SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors for MockMvc tests.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Old adapter: extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter no longer compiles in Spring Security 6.
  • antMatchers and mvcMatchers: replaced by requestMatchers.
  • Disabling CSRF everywhere: only do it for stateless APIs.
  • Plain passwords: no PasswordEncoder gives "There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id null".
  • Missing import in tests: @WebMvcTest does not load your config unless you import it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Filters run on every request: keep custom filters light and avoid database calls for public paths.
  • BCrypt strength: the default cost of 10 balances safety and speed; raise it carefully.
  • Session lookups: external session stores add network time.
  • Method security: proxies add small overhead; avoid it in tight loops.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an existing MVC shop adds security. Public catalogue pages stay open, the cart needs a login, and the admin area needs the ADMIN role. The team adds the starter, one chain, a database UserDetailsService, and MockMvc tests for each rule.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Authentication answers the question "who are you?": the system checks credentials such as a password, token or certificate and proves the caller identity.
  • Result: on success Spring Security builds an Authentication object holding the principal, the authorities and an authenticated flag.
  • Different from authorization, which decides what an already identified user may do.

Worked Example 1

Expose the AuthenticationManager bean.

Worked Example 2

Test authentication failure.

Practice Exercise 1

Authenticate programmatically.

Practice Exercise 2

Database users.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Authentication is a pipeline of small objects.

  • Filter: builds an unauthenticated Authentication (for example UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken).
  • ProviderManager: asks each AuthenticationProvider whether it supports that token type.
  • DaoAuthenticationProvider: calls UserDetailsService, checks account flags, then PasswordEncoder.matches.
  • Result: a new token with authorities and authenticated=true, stored in the SecurityContext; credentials are erased.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Form, Basic, Bearer token, OAuth2 login, SAML, LDAP, certificates.
  • UserDetails flags: enabled, accountNonLocked, accountNonExpired, credentialsNonExpired.
  • PasswordEncoder: DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores an id such as {bcrypt} to allow upgrades.
  • Custom provider for non-password credentials.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • AuthenticationManager receives an Authentication request and returns a fully filled one; the usual implementation is ProviderManager.
  • AuthenticationProvider: DaoAuthenticationProvider loads the user from a UserDetailsService and compares the password with a PasswordEncoder.
  • Failure throws an AuthenticationException such as BadCredentialsException, which becomes a 401 or a redirect to the login page.

Senior Notes

  • Password storage: always hash with BCryptPasswordEncoder or DelegatingPasswordEncoder; never store plain text.
  • Custom provider: implement AuthenticationProvider for API keys, LDAP or an external identity service.
  • Stateless tokens: a JWT filter validates the token on each request and fills SecurityContextHolder without a session.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Revealing which part is wrong: "user not found" versus "wrong password" helps attackers.
  • Weak hashing: MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords; use BCrypt, Argon2 or SCrypt.
  • Not clearing the context: in tests or threads the context may leak; use SecurityContextHolder.clearContext().
  • Locked or disabled accounts: not mapped to a clear message.
  • Thread pools: new threads do not inherit the context unless a strategy such as MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL or a delegating executor is used.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • BCrypt cost is deliberate; do not lower it for speed, cache sessions or tokens instead.
  • User lookup: index the username column and cache UserDetails with CachingUserDetailsService only when changes are rare.
  • Token validation for JWT is local and fast, with no database read per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a company portal authenticates employees. Passwords are BCrypt hashed, five failed logins lock the account for a time, and the lock is reported through AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent listeners.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do, for example who may open /admin or delete an order.
  • Authorities and roles: a role is an authority with the prefix ROLE_, so hasRole("ADMIN") checks for ROLE_ADMIN.
  • Two levels: URL rules in authorizeHttpRequests and method rules with @PreAuthorize.

Worked Example 1

Test roles.

Worked Example 2

Custom access denied response.

Practice Exercise 1

URL based rules.

Practice Exercise 2

Method security.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring Security 6 uses AuthorizationManager.

  • URL level: AuthorizationFilter asks an AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext>; the first matching rule decides.
  • Method level: an AOP interceptor calls AuthorizationManager<MethodInvocation> before the method runs.
  • Decision: granted, or AccessDeniedException handled by ExceptionTranslationFilter.
  • Authorities come from the Authentication object.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Expression options:

  • hasRole, hasAnyRole, hasAuthority, hasAnyAuthority.
  • permitAll, denyAll, authenticated, anonymous.
  • access: custom AuthorizationManager or a SpEL expression.
  • @PostAuthorize checks the returned object; @PreFilter and @PostFilter filter collections.
  • Role hierarchy: ADMIN implies USER.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • URL rules are checked in order, so put specific matchers first and anyRequest() last.
  • Method security: add @EnableMethodSecurity, then use @PreAuthorize("hasRole("ADMIN")") on service methods.
  • Denied: an anonymous user gets 401 (or login redirect) and an authenticated user without permission gets 403 through AccessDeniedHandler.

Senior Notes

  • Ownership checks: use SpEL such as @PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id") to protect a single record.
  • AuthorizationManager is the Spring Security 6 interface behind these rules; you can write a custom one for complex logic.
  • Defense in depth: secure the URL and the service method, because other callers may reach the method directly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • ROLE_ prefix confusion: hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") works but hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks a different string.
  • Rule order: anyRequest().permitAll() placed first.
  • Only hiding links: a hidden button does not protect the endpoint.
  • Self invocation: method security is skipped within the same class.
  • Path mismatch: /admin versus /admin/; use requestMatchers with the MVC mapping.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cheap checks first: URL rules are fast string matches.
  • Expensive checks: a database lookup in a custom manager runs on every call; cache the permissions.
  • Load authorities once at login rather than on each request.
  • Avoid @PostFilter on huge lists; filter in the query.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a hospital system. Doctors read and write notes of their own patients, nurses read, and auditors only read the log. The team uses roles for broad areas and a custom AuthorizationManager for patient-level checks.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Login is the step where a user sends credentials so the application can authenticate them and start a session or issue a token.
  • Page and processing: the login page shows the form, and a security filter handles the POST /login request; your controller does not process the password.
  • Outcome: success redirects to the saved or default page, and failure redirects to /login?error.

Worked Example 1

JSON login for a single-page app.

Worked Example 2

Test a login.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom login page and controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Thymeleaf login form.
codeExamples:
<form th:action="@{/login}" method="post">
    <input type="text" name="username" />
    <input type="password" name="password" />
    <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// The rendered form contains a hidden _csrf input added by Thymeleaf.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The login request path inside Spring Security:

  • Page: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter renders the built-in page, or your /login controller is used.
  • Processing: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter matches POST /login, creates the token and calls the manager.
  • Success: session strategy changes the session id, the context is saved, and the success handler redirects.
  • Failure: context cleared, failure handler redirects to /login?error.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Login styles:

  • Default page for quick starts.
  • Custom page with loginPage.
  • JSON endpoint with your own controller calling AuthenticationManager and returning a token.
  • OAuth2 login with oauth2Login().
  • Success options: defaultSuccessUrl(url, alwaysUse) and successHandler.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom page: call formLogin(f -> f.loginPage("/login").permitAll()) and serve your own view from a controller.
  • Parameter names default to username and password; change them with usernameParameter and passwordParameter.
  • CSRF token: the login form must include the hidden CSRF field, which Thymeleaf adds automatically for th:action.

Senior Notes

  • Handlers: successHandler and failureHandler return JSON for single-page apps instead of redirecting.
  • Brute force: add rate limiting or account lockout; keep the error message generic.
  • Session fixation: Spring changes the session id after login by default; keep that protection on.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Login page blocked: forget permitAll() and get a redirect loop.
  • Missing CSRF field: 403 on post.
  • Form field names differ from the configured parameters.
  • Detailed errors: telling which of user or password is wrong.
  • HTTP instead of HTTPS: passwords visible on the network.
  • Open redirect: using an unchecked redirect parameter after login.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and protection:

  • Throttle: limit attempts per IP and per account.
  • Hash cost: BCrypt slows guessing but also uses CPU on every login.
  • Lightweight page: serve static assets with caching.
  • Multi-factor: add a second step for sensitive apps.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a ticket system with a custom page. Users who open a deep link are sent to login and then back to the same ticket. The team verifies that with a MockMvc test and logs every failed attempt.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Logout ends the authenticated session: Spring invalidates the HTTP session, clears the SecurityContext and can delete cookies.
  • Default: POST /logout with a CSRF token, then a redirect to /login?logout.
  • Filter: LogoutFilter runs a list of LogoutHandler objects and then a LogoutSuccessHandler.

Worked Example 1

REST logout returning 200.

Worked Example 2

Test logout.

Practice Exercise 1

Logout configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Logout button.
codeExamples:
<form th:action="@{/logout}" method="post">
    <button type="submit">Logout</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Clicking the button posts to /logout with the hidden CSRF token.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Logout internals:

  • LogoutFilter matches POST /logout and calls CompositeLogoutHandler.
  • Handlers: SecurityContextLogoutHandler invalidates the session and clears the context; CookieClearingLogoutHandler deletes cookies; CsrfLogoutHandler clears the CSRF token.
  • Success handler: SimpleUrlLogoutSuccessHandler redirects.
  • The session id is gone on the server, so the old cookie is useless.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • logoutUrl or logoutRequestMatcher (to allow GET, only when CSRF risk is accepted).
  • addLogoutHandler for custom cleanup.
  • clearAuthentication and invalidateHttpSession.
  • OIDC logout: OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler signs out of the identity provider.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Configure with http.logout(l -> l.logoutUrl("/logout").logoutSuccessUrl("/login?bye")).
  • Cookies: deleteCookies("JSESSIONID") removes the session cookie in the browser.
  • Why POST: with CSRF enabled, a GET logout link is not allowed because a third-party site could log users out.

Senior Notes

  • Stateless apps have no session to destroy; JWT logout needs a token blacklist or short token lifetime.
  • Success handler can return 200 JSON for a front-end app: HttpStatusReturningLogoutSuccessHandler.
  • Single sign-out with OAuth or SAML needs extra configuration to end the identity provider session too.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Logout link with GET while CSRF is on gives a 404 or login page.
  • Forgetting the CSRF token in the logout form.
  • Stale JWT: the client logs out but the token stays valid until it expires.
  • Remember-me cookie not cleared, so the user returns logged in.
  • Caching: the browser back button shows protected pages; Spring sends no-cache headers by default, keep them.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and scale:

  • Invalidating a session frees server memory at once.
  • With Spring Session, the logout deletes the entry in Redis.
  • Use short session timeouts for sensitive apps so abandoned sessions disappear.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.timeout=15m

# OUTPUT:
# Idle sessions expire after 15 minutes;
the next request redirects to /login

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shared computer in a bank branch. The team logs out on a button and on idle timeout, deletes cookies, clears the cache headers, and checks with a test that a protected page redirects after logout.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Form login is authentication through an HTML form: the user types a username and password and the server answers with a session cookie.
  • Enable it with http.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults()); Spring then generates a login page at /login.
  • Flow: an anonymous request is redirected to the login page, the credentials are posted, and the user returns to the page first requested.

Worked Example 1

Test form login.

Worked Example 2

Anonymous redirect.

Practice Exercise 1

Full form login setup.

Practice Exercise 2

Form for the custom parameter.
codeExamples:
<form th:action="@{/do-login}" method="post">
    <input name="email" type="email" />
    <input name="password" type="password" />
    <label><input type="checkbox" name="remember-me" /> Remember me</label>
    <button>Login</button>
</form>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Posting with remember-me checked also sets the remember-me cookie.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Form login builds on a chain of cooperating parts.

  • Config: FormLoginConfigurer adds UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter and sets an AuthenticationEntryPoint that redirects to the login page.
  • Entry point: LoginUrlAuthenticationEntryPoint is triggered by ExceptionTranslationFilter when an anonymous user hits a protected URL.
  • Request cache: HttpSessionRequestCache stores the original request.
  • Success: session id changes and the saved request is replayed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options of formLogin:

  • loginPage, loginProcessingUrl, failureUrl.
  • defaultSuccessUrl(url, true) forces that page, ignoring the saved request.
  • successForwardUrl and failureForwardUrl forward instead of redirecting.
  • authenticationDetailsSource to store extra data such as the IP address.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Components: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter reads the form and calls the AuthenticationManager.
  • Saved request: RequestCache remembers the original URL so SavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler can send the user back.
  • Options: loginPage, loginProcessingUrl, defaultSuccessUrl, failureUrl and usernameParameter.

Senior Notes

  • Best for server-rendered web apps with sessions; APIs and mobile apps usually prefer tokens.
  • Remember me: rememberMe adds a long-lived cookie; use the persistent token approach for better safety.
  • HTTPS is required, because the form sends the password in the request body.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Writing a controller for POST /login: the filter handles it and your method is never reached.
  • Plain-text passwords in test users.
  • Static resources blocked so the login page has no CSS.
  • Stateless config with form login: the session is needed to keep the user logged in.
  • Open redirect via a custom redirect parameter.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Cache static files of the login page.
  • Limit attempts and add a delay after failures.
  • Remember me avoids repeated BCrypt checks, but uses a long-lived token.
  • Session size: store only the principal id and not large objects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an internal HR portal with Thymeleaf pages. The team uses form login with a branded page, role based menus, and a test suite that checks anonymous redirect, success, failure and logout.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP Basic authentication sends the credentials in every request in the header Authorization: Basic base64(user:password).
  • Challenge: when the header is missing the server answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Basic, and the browser shows a login dialog.
  • Enable it with http.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults()); it is simple and good for tools, scripts and internal services.

Worked Example 1

Test with httpBasic.

Worked Example 2

JSON 401 entry point.

Practice Exercise 1

Stateless Basic API.

Practice Exercise 2

Build the header by hand.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Basic works on the wire and in Spring:

  • 1: the client sends a request without credentials.
  • 2: BasicAuthenticationEntryPoint answers 401 and WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm".
  • 3: the client repeats it with the Authorization header.
  • 4: BasicAuthenticationFilter decodes it, builds a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken and calls the manager.
  • 5: on success the context is filled; with sessions it may also be saved.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Realm name: httpBasic(b -> b.realmName("Shop API")).
  • Custom entry point for JSON errors.
  • Client side: RestTemplate or WebClient with setBasicAuth.
  • Mixed: Basic for internal paths, form login for browser pages.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Base64 is not encryption: anyone who sees the header can decode it, so Basic must only run over HTTPS.
  • Filter: BasicAuthenticationFilter reads the header and calls the AuthenticationManager on every request.
  • Stateless: combine with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS so no session is created for API clients.

Senior Notes

  • Cost: the password is checked on every call, so a slow BCrypt hash adds latency; cache authentication or use tokens for high traffic.
  • Entry point: set authenticationEntryPoint to return a JSON 401 instead of the browser dialog.
  • Logout is not really possible, because the browser keeps sending the cached credentials.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using HTTP: credentials can be read by anyone on the path.
  • Leaving CSRF on for a stateless API: POST calls return 403.
  • Keeping a session: without STATELESS, a session is created and may behave unexpectedly.
  • Logging the header in access logs or tracing.
  • Hardcoded credentials in the source code.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Hash cost per request: BCrypt on every call limits throughput; this is why tokens are used for high-volume APIs.
  • Connection reuse: keep-alive reduces TLS cost.
  • Service accounts: use a faster hash only if the secret is long and random, such as an API key.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a nightly job calls an internal reporting API. The team uses Basic over HTTPS with a service account, reads the password from an environment variable, and restricts the account to one role.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Session authentication keeps the logged-in user on the server: after login the SecurityContext is stored in the HttpSession and the browser sends the JSESSIONID cookie.
  • Flow: login creates a session, each later request carries the cookie, and SecurityContextHolderFilter restores the user from the session.
  • Stateful: the server holds memory per user, unlike token approaches where the client carries the proof.

Worked Example 1

Inspect the session in a test.

Worked Example 2

Count active sessions.

Practice Exercise 1

Session management settings.

Practice Exercise 2

Session cookie properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Session handling internals:

  • Login: after success, SessionAuthenticationStrategy runs (fixation, concurrency), then HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository saves the context under an attribute.
  • Next request: SecurityContextHolderFilter loads it from the session into SecurityContextHolder lazily.
  • Concurrency: ConcurrentSessionControlAuthenticationStrategy consults the SessionRegistry.
  • End of request: the holder is cleared from the thread.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Session creation policies:

  • IF_REQUIRED (default), ALWAYS, NEVER, STATELESS.
  • Session fixation: changeSessionId, newSession, migrateSession, none.
  • Invalid session URL and expired URL for friendly redirects.
  • Spring Session: Redis, JDBC or Hazelcast stores with @EnableRedisHttpSession.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cookie flags: set HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite (server.servlet.session.cookie.*) to protect the cookie.
  • Timeout: server.servlet.session.timeout=30m expires idle sessions.
  • Fixation protection: Spring issues a new session id after login (changeSessionId) by default.

Senior Notes

  • Concurrency: maximumSessions(1) limits one user to a number of sessions and can block or expire the older one.
  • Scaling: with several servers use sticky sessions or Spring Session with Redis or JDBC so any node can read the session.
  • CSRF protection is needed because the browser sends the cookie automatically.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Large objects in the session increase memory and replication cost.
  • Non-serializable attributes break external session stores.
  • Disabled fixation protection.
  • Missing Secure and HttpOnly flags.
  • Load balancer without sticky sessions or shared store: the user keeps being logged out.
  • Ignoring concurrent logins: sharing accounts.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and scaling:

  • Memory: each session uses heap; set a timeout and keep data small.
  • Shared store: Redis gives horizontal scaling at the cost of a network call per request; use lazy writes.
  • Cookie only: disable URL rewriting with server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.servlet.session.tracking-modes=cookie
spring.session.store-type=redis
spring.session.timeout=30m

# OUTPUT:
# Sessions are stored in Redis and shared by every application instance.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an online exam site must allow only one active login per student and must end the session on timeout. The team uses maximumSessions(1), a session registry to show online users, and a 20 minute idle timeout.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Security filter chain: Spring Security protects a web app with an ordered list of servlet filters that run before the DispatcherServlet and decide whether a request may continue.
  • Entry point: a servlet filter named DelegatingFilterProxy (or FilterChainProxy in Boot) hands each request to the security chain.
  • Configuration: you declare a SecurityFilterChain bean and use HttpSecurity to switch filters on, such as login, CSRF and CORS.

Worked Example 1

A custom logging filter.

Worked Example 2

Testing with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

A minimal chain bean.

Practice Exercise 2

Printing the filters.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring Security is built only from servlet filters.

  • Registration: Boot registers DelegatingFilterProxy named springSecurityFilterChain with the servlet container.
  • FilterChainProxy: that bean holds the list of SecurityFilterChain objects and picks the first one whose request matcher matches.
  • Virtual chain: the selected filters run as one chain, then control returns to the real servlet chain and reaches the DispatcherServlet.
  • Failure handling: ExceptionTranslationFilter catches AuthenticationException and AccessDeniedException and starts the login or sends 403.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to shape the chain:

  • Several chains: securityMatcher plus @Order; the most specific chain gets the lowest order.
  • Add filters: addFilterBefore, addFilterAfter, addFilterAt.
  • Disable parts: csrf, formLogin, httpBasic, logout each take a customizer or disable().
  • Sessions: sessionManagement sets stateless or stateful mode.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order matters: filters like SecurityContextHolderFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter and AuthorizationFilter run in a fixed order.
  • Several chains: you can define more than one SecurityFilterChain and pick one per URL with securityMatcher, for example one for /api/** and one for the web pages.
  • Custom filter: add your own with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter, for example a JWT filter before the login filter.

Senior Notes

  • Bypass: web.ignoring() skips the whole chain (no headers, no context), so prefer permitAll() for public URLs.
  • OncePerRequestFilter: extend it so your filter runs once per request even after forwards.
  • Debugging: set logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG to see the filters of every request.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Wrong order: a chain without a securityMatcher placed first catches every URL; give it the highest order number.
  • Bean filter registered twice: a filter declared as a @Component is also added to the servlet container and runs twice; extend OncePerRequestFilter or disable the extra registration.
  • web.ignoring for static files only: using it for APIs removes security headers.
  • Old API: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is removed in Spring Security 6; use the bean style.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cheap filters: every request pays for each filter, so avoid database calls in custom filters; cache or use a signed token.
  • Shorter chain: disable features you do not use (form login on a pure API).
  • Password hashing: BCrypt strength is deliberately slow; do not run it on every request, only at login.
  • Observe: Boot Actuator and the DEBUG log show time spent per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop has a browser site and a mobile API.

  • The site uses form login, sessions and CSRF.
  • The API uses JWT, no session and no CSRF.
  • Two chains separate these rules, so one set of changes cannot break the other.
  • A test per chain protects the rules.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is an attack where a malicious page makes the browser of a logged-in user send a request to your site, using the cookies the browser attaches automatically.
  • Defense: Spring Security gives every session a secret token and rejects state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) that do not send it back.
  • Default: CSRF protection is on by default for browser apps; GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are not checked.

Worked Example 1

Testing with the csrf() post processor.

Worked Example 2

Disabling CSRF for a stateless API chain only.

Practice Exercise 1

Default form with Thymeleaf.
codeExamples:
<form th:action="@{/transfer}" method="post">
    <input name="amount" />
    <button>Send</button>
    <!-- Thymeleaf adds: <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="..."/> -->
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// POST /transfer with _csrf  -> 200
// POST /transfer without it  -> 403 Forbidden

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Cookie repository for a single page app.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the protection works (synchronizer token pattern):

  • Create: CsrfFilter asks the CsrfTokenRepository (session based by default) for a token and stores it as a request attribute.
  • Send: the view puts it into a hidden field or header.
  • Check: on unsafe methods the filter compares the submitted token with the stored one; a mismatch calls AccessDeniedHandler and gives 403.
  • Why it works: an attacker page can make the browser send cookies but cannot read your token.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Repositories: HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository (default), CookieCsrfTokenRepository.
  • Handlers: XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler (default, BREACH protection) and CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler for simple SPA setups.
  • Ignoring paths: ignoringRequestMatchers("/webhooks/**") for server-to-server calls with their own signature.
  • Disable: csrf(c -> c.disable()).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Token in forms: Thymeleaf adds a hidden _csrf field to forms automatically when the form uses th:action.
  • Token in AJAX: send the token in the X-CSRF-TOKEN header, or use CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() so JavaScript can read an XSRF-TOKEN cookie.
  • 403 Forbidden: a missing or wrong token on a POST gives 403, the most common reason a new login form or REST call fails.

Senior Notes

  • Stateless APIs: pure token APIs (JWT in the Authorization header, no cookies) may disable CSRF with csrf(c -> c.disable()); never disable it for cookie sessions.
  • SameSite cookies: SameSite=Lax or Strict is a good second layer but does not replace the token.
  • Spring Security 6: the token is loaded lazily and can be BREACH-protected with XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Disabling CSRF to fix a 403: add the token instead.
  • Form without th:action: a plain action attribute gets no hidden token.
  • Logout by GET: logout must be POST when CSRF is on.
  • SPA reads the cookie but the cookie is HttpOnly: use withHttpOnlyFalse() for the token cookie only.
  • Token in the URL: it leaks through logs and referrers; use a header or body.
codeExamples:
<!-- wrong: no token is added -->
<form action="/transfer" method="post">...</form>

<!-- right: Thymeleaf adds the hidden _csrf input -->
<form th:action="@{/transfer}" method="post">...</form>

// OUTPUT:
// wrong form -> 403 ; right form -> 200

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and cost:

  • Session tokens need session storage; with many nodes use a shared session store or the cookie repository.
  • Deferred tokens: Spring Security 6 loads the token only when needed, so pages that never render a form do not create a session.
  • Cookie attributes: set Secure and SameSite for the session cookie as an extra layer.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a banking page transfers money with a POST form.

  • An attacker site hides a form that posts to /transfer.
  • The victim is logged in, so the browser sends the session cookie.
  • Without a token the transfer would succeed; with CSRF protection the attacker has no token, so the server answers 403.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) lets a browser page from one origin call an API on another origin when the server sends the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers.
  • With Security: the CORS preflight (OPTIONS) request carries no credentials, so Spring Security must handle CORS before it checks authentication.
  • One call: enable it with http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) plus a CorsConfigurationSource bean.

Worked Example 1

Testing the preflight with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Rejected origin.

Practice Exercise 1

Security plus CORS bean.

Practice Exercise 2

Checking a preflight with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Order of events for a cross-origin call:

  • Preflight: for a non-simple request the browser first sends OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method.
  • CorsFilter: with http.cors() Spring Security inserts a CorsFilter before authentication; it answers the preflight itself using the CorsConfigurationSource.
  • Actual request: goes through the normal chain, and the CORS headers are added to the response.
  • Without http.cors(): the preflight reaches AuthorizationFilter with no credentials and fails.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options of CorsConfiguration:

  • allowedOrigins exact origins; allowedOriginPatterns for patterns like https://*.example.com.
  • allowedMethods, allowedHeaders, exposedHeaders.
  • allowCredentials for cookies and Authorization.
  • maxAge to cache preflight.
  • MVC level alternatives: @CrossOrigin and WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Why @CrossOrigin alone fails: if the security chain rejects the preflight with 401 or 403, the MVC annotation never runs.
  • CorsConfigurationSource: define allowed origins, methods and headers once and register it for /** with UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource.
  • Credentials: with allowCredentials(true) you cannot use the wildcard * for origins; list the exact origins.

Senior Notes

  • CorsFilter: http.cors() adds a CorsFilter early in the chain, so preflights are answered before authorization.
  • Preflight cache: set maxAge so browsers skip repeated preflights.
  • Not a security control: CORS only instructs browsers; tools like curl ignore it, so you still need authentication.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wildcard with credentials: * plus allowCredentials(true) is rejected at startup or by the browser.
  • Only @CrossOrigin: Security blocks the preflight first.
  • Missing Authorization in allowed headers: the preflight fails for token calls.
  • Duplicate headers: configuring CORS in a gateway and in the app sends the header twice, which browsers reject.
  • Treating CORS as security: it is only browser policy.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Set maxAge to cut preflight traffic (browsers cap it, often at a few hours).
  • Keep the allowed lists short and explicit.
  • Use one place (a gateway or the app) for CORS, not both.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a React app on port 3000 calls a Spring API on port 8080 with a bearer token.

  • The browser sends a preflight because of the Authorization header.
  • The security chain has http.cors() and the origin list contains http://localhost:3000.
  • The call succeeds; a call from another origin is blocked by the browser.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Role-based authorization allows or denies access depending on the roles of the logged-in user, such as USER or ADMIN.
  • URL rules: write them in the chain with requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN"); the first matching rule wins.
  • ROLE_ prefix: hasRole("ADMIN") checks the authority ROLE_ADMIN; hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks the exact text.

Worked Example 1

Test roles with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Role hierarchy.

Practice Exercise 1

URL rules by role.

Practice Exercise 2

In-memory users for a demo.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a role check runs:
