  • Login: UserDetails.getAuthorities() returns GrantedAuthority objects such as ROLE_ADMIN; they are stored in the Authentication.
  • Request: AuthorizationFilter asks the AuthorizationManager built from your matchers whether this request is allowed.
  • Decision: hasRole("ADMIN") becomes an AuthorityAuthorizationManager that checks for ROLE_ADMIN.
  • Denied: an anonymous user starts the login, a known user gets 403 from AccessDeniedHandler.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • hasRole / hasAnyRole add the prefix; hasAuthority does not.
  • access(...) with a custom AuthorizationManager for rules like "owner or admin".
  • HTTP method rules: requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/items/**").
  • Prefix change: a GrantedAuthorityDefaults bean changes or removes ROLE_.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Rule order: put specific rules first and anyRequest() last, or a broad rule hides the narrow ones.
  • Helpers: hasAnyRole, authenticated, permitAll, denyAll and access(...) with an AuthorizationManager.
  • Results: an anonymous user gets 401 (or a redirect to login); a logged-in user without the role gets 403.

Senior Notes

  • Role hierarchy: a RoleHierarchy bean lets ADMIN imply USER so you do not repeat roles.
  • Roles versus permissions: roles are coarse; fine-grained permissions (order:write) as authorities scale better.
  • Data from the database: UserDetailsService maps stored roles to GrantedAuthority objects.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Storing ROLE_ADMIN and calling hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN"): works in Spring Security 6 only by accident of prefix handling; store plain ADMIN in roles() and use hasRole("ADMIN").
  • anyRequest().permitAll() first: everything is public.
  • Hiding a button only in the UI: the server must enforce the rule.
  • No default deny: end with anyRequest().authenticated() or denyAll().

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Authorities are loaded once at login and kept in the session, so a role change applies at the next login unless you reload them.
  • For JWT, put roles in a claim and map them with a converter, so no database call is needed per request.
  • Keep the number of URL rules small; use method security for detail.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an HR app with three groups.

  • EMPLOYEE sees own data, MANAGER sees the team, ADMIN manages everything.
  • A role hierarchy ADMIN > MANAGER > EMPLOYEE keeps rules short.
  • Tests cover each URL for each role, so a refactor cannot open a hole.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Method security puts authorization rules directly on service or controller methods with annotations such as @PreAuthorize.
  • Enable it: add @EnableMethodSecurity to a configuration class; in Spring Security 6 @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize are on by default with it.
  • Example: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") blocks the call before the method body runs and throws AccessDeniedException.

Worked Example 1

Testing a service rule.

Worked Example 2

Custom permission bean.

Practice Exercise 1

Enable and use.

Practice Exercise 2

PostAuthorize on the result.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Method security uses Spring AOP.

  • Proxy: @EnableMethodSecurity registers an advisor; beans with secured methods get a proxy (CGLIB for classes).
  • Interceptor: AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor runs before the call and AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor after it.
  • Expression: the SpEL is evaluated with authentication, method arguments (#name) and returnObject.
  • Context: it reads the Authentication from the SecurityContextHolder of the current thread.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Annotations and switches:

  • @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @PreFilter, @PostFilter are on by default.
  • @EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled = true) turns on @Secured; jsr250Enabled = true turns on @RolesAllowed.
  • Class-level annotations apply to all methods; a method annotation overrides them.
  • Meta-annotations let you create @IsAdmin to avoid repeating strings.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • SpEL: rules are expressions, so you can use method arguments: @PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id").
  • @PostAuthorize: checks after the method returns, using returnObject, for example to allow only the owner of the result.
  • Other annotations: @PreFilter and @PostFilter filter collections; @Secured and JSR-250 @RolesAllowed are simpler role checks.

Senior Notes

  • Proxy based: security is applied by an AOP proxy, so a self-call inside the same class (this.method()) skips the check.
  • Where to put it: protect the service layer, because a service may be called from several controllers, jobs or messages.
  • Custom beans: call a bean in SpEL, @PreAuthorize("@perm.canEdit(#id)"), to keep complex rules testable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Self-invocation: calling a secured method from another method of the same class skips the proxy.
  • Private or final methods: they cannot be proxied.
  • Forgetting @EnableMethodSecurity: annotations are silently ignored.
  • Old annotation: @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity is deprecated; use @EnableMethodSecurity.
  • PostFilter on large lists: loads everything then filters; filter in the query instead.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • SpEL is parsed once and cached; keep expressions simple.
  • Calling a bean from SpEL that hits the database on every call is costly; cache the result per request or load needed data once.
  • Prefer a query condition (where owner = :user) over @PostFilter for large data sets.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a document service.

  • Any user may list their documents; only the owner or an admin may delete one.
  • The URL rule only requires login; the service rule checks the owner.
  • The same rule protects REST, scheduled jobs and message handlers that call the service.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • SecurityContext is the object that holds the Authentication of the current user (who is logged in and with which authorities).
  • SecurityContextHolder gives access to it from anywhere: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().
  • Per thread: by default the context is stored in a ThreadLocal, so it belongs to the thread handling the current request.

Worked Example 1

Propagating to another thread.

Worked Example 2

Setting a test context.

Practice Exercise 1

Reading the context.

Practice Exercise 2

Programmatic login.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Lifecycle of the context in one web request:

  • Start: SecurityContextHolderFilter asks the SecurityContextRepository to load the context (from the session) and sets it in the holder.
  • Authentication: a login filter or token filter puts an Authentication into it.
  • Use: filters, controllers, services and method security read it.
  • End: the holder is cleared in a finally block, so the pooled thread is clean.
  • Strategy: SecurityContextHolderStrategy chooses the storage: MODE_THREADLOCAL (default), inheritable or global.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Strategies: MODE_THREADLOCAL, MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL, MODE_GLOBAL (only for desktop-like apps).
  • Repositories: HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository, RequestAttributeSecurityContextRepository (stateless), DelegatingSecurityContextRepository.
  • Wrappers: DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable, Callable and the executor wrappers.
  • Bean injection: a SecurityContextHolderStrategy bean can replace static calls.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Loaded per request: SecurityContextHolderFilter loads the context from the session at the start and clears it at the end.
  • Authentication parts: principal (the user), credentials (cleared after login), authorities and the authenticated flag.
  • Anonymous: a user who is not logged in has an AnonymousAuthenticationToken, not null.

Senior Notes

  • Async code: a new thread does not inherit the context; use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or the MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL strategy.
  • Repository: SecurityContextRepository decides where the context is saved between requests (session by default, nothing for stateless).
  • Explicit save: in Spring Security 6 you must save the context yourself when you authenticate manually in a controller.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Static access in business code: hard to test; inject the user or the strategy.
  • Threads: an @Async method or a new Thread sees no user.
  • Not saving the context in Security 6: after manual authentication the next request is anonymous.
  • Reading when anonymous: casting the principal to your user class fails with ClassCastException.
  • Leaking: never keep the Authentication in a static field.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • The default ThreadLocal strategy is cheap.
  • Deferred context loading in Security 6 avoids touching the session until the user is actually read.
  • With virtual threads, ThreadLocal still works per virtual thread, but do not copy large objects into it.
  • Stateless APIs use a request-scoped repository, so no session memory is used.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: audit logging.

  • An AuditorAware bean reads the user from the security context so every saved entity gets createdBy.
  • Background jobs set a system user explicitly in the context before work starts and clear it after.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Principal is the identity of the logged-in user; in Spring Security it is the object returned by Authentication.getPrincipal(), usually a UserDetails.
  • In a controller: add a Principal parameter and Spring MVC fills it, so principal.getName() gives the username.
  • Better: use @AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails user to get your own user type directly.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the Principal comes from:

  • Authentication: after login the provider builds an Authentication whose principal is the UserDetails from your UserDetailsService.
  • Request wrapper: SecurityContextHolderAwareRequestFilter wraps the request so getUserPrincipal() returns that authentication.
  • Argument resolvers: MVC uses ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver for Principal; Security adds AuthenticationPrincipalArgumentResolver for @AuthenticationPrincipal.
  • Types: the principal object depends on the login type (UserDetails for forms, a Jwt for resource servers, an OidcUser for OAuth2 login).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Principal p gives only getName().
  • Authentication a adds authorities and details.
  • @AuthenticationPrincipal MyUser u gives your class; add errorOnInvalidType = true to fail on a wrong type.
  • @CurrentSecurityContext(expression = "authentication.name") reads any part of the context.
  • A custom meta-annotation @CurrentUser hides the expression.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Parameter options: Principal, Authentication, @AuthenticationPrincipal and HttpServletRequest.getUserPrincipal() all give the same user.
  • Anonymous: for a page that anyone can open, the principal may be null (plain Principal) or the string anonymousUser (from the holder).
  • Thymeleaf: sec:authentication="name" prints the username in a view (needs the springsecurity extras dialect).

Senior Notes

  • How it is resolved: ServletRequestMethodArgumentResolver handles Principal; AuthenticationPrincipalArgumentResolver handles the annotation.
  • Custom principal: have your UserDetailsService return a class that extends User with an id field, then read the id without a database call.
  • SpEL: @AuthenticationPrincipal(expression = "id") injects a single property.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong type: @AuthenticationPrincipal AppUser receives null when the principal is a different class (or the string anonymousUser).
  • Trusting a user id from the request: take the id from the principal, not from a parameter, or any user can read others (IDOR).
  • Using the principal in an unprotected URL: it is null; protect the URL.
  • Password in the principal: Spring clears credentials after login; do not keep them in your own class.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Keep the principal small (id, name, roles); it is serialized into the session.
  • Make it Serializable if sessions are replicated.
  • Load extra profile data lazily from a cache, not at every login.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a user can only see their own invoices.

  • The controller takes the id from the principal and passes it to the service.
  • The repository query includes the owner id, so even a bug in the URL cannot expose other data.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring MVC + JDBC means a controller calls a service, and the service uses JdbcTemplate to run plain SQL against a relational database.
  • JdbcTemplate opens the connection, runs the statement, maps the rows and closes everything, so you write only the SQL and the mapping.
  • Layers: controller handles HTTP, service holds business rules and transactions, repository holds the SQL.

Worked Example 1

Testing with @JdbcTest.

Worked Example 2

Controller test with a mocked repository.

Practice Exercise 1

Repository with JdbcTemplate.

Practice Exercise 2

Controller and properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What JdbcTemplate does for one query:

  • Gets a connection from the DataSource (the transaction connection if one is active, else from the pool).
  • Creates a PreparedStatement, binds the arguments, executes it.
  • Calls your RowMapper for each row of the ResultSet.
  • Closes resources and translates SQLException into the unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.
  • Returns the connection to the pool (or keeps it until the transaction ends).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • JdbcTemplate: positional ? parameters.
  • NamedParameterJdbcTemplate: :name parameters.
  • SimpleJdbcInsert: insert with generated keys and no SQL.
  • KeyHolder: read generated ids.
  • JdbcClient (Spring 6.1): fluent API over both styles.
  • BeanPropertyRowMapper: maps columns to bean properties by name.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Query: jdbcTemplate.query(sql, rowMapper, args) returns a list; queryForObject returns one row or throws EmptyResultDataAccessException.
  • Update: update(sql, args) runs insert, update and delete and returns the number of rows changed.
  • Parameters: always use ? placeholders (or NamedParameterJdbcTemplate) and never join user text into the SQL, to prevent SQL injection.

Senior Notes

  • DataSource: Boot auto-configures a pooled HikariDataSource from spring.datasource.*.
  • Transactions: put @Transactional on service methods; the transaction manager binds one connection to the thread.
  • Batching: batchUpdate sends many rows in one round trip, much faster than a loop of inserts.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • String concatenation in SQL: SQL injection; use placeholders.
  • queryForObject for optional rows: throws on empty; use query and take the first element.
  • Missing @Transactional: two updates that must succeed together run in separate transactions.
  • Column name mismatch: BeanPropertyRowMapper needs matching names (snake_case is converted).
  • Catching SQLException: JdbcTemplate throws DataAccessException.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Pool: size Hikari maximum-pool-size to the database capacity, not to the number of threads.
  • Batch: batchUpdate for many rows.
  • Fetch size: set jdbc.setFetchSize for large reads.
  • Indexes: add them for columns in where clauses and check the plan with explain.
  • Select only needed columns.
codeExamples:
jdbc.batchUpdate("insert into users(name) values (?)",
    List.of("a", "b", "c"), 100,
    (ps, n) -> ps.setString(1, n));

# application.properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10

# OUTPUT:
# one round trip per 100 rows instead of one per row

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting page with a hand-tuned SQL join.

  • JDBC gives full control over the SQL and avoids ORM overhead.
  • The service is transactional and read-only; a @JdbcTest checks the SQL and a @WebMvcTest checks the JSON.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring MVC + JPA means controllers use services that read and write objects through JPA entities and a JpaRepository, without writing SQL by hand.
  • Entity: a class marked @Entity with an @Id field maps to one table row per object.
  • Spring Data JPA: you declare an interface that extends JpaRepository<User, Long> and Spring creates the implementation at startup.

Worked Example 1

Testing with @DataJpaTest.

Worked Example 2

Fixing N+1 with an entity graph.

Practice Exercise 1

Entity, repository and controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Paging.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a Spring Data JPA call works:

  • Startup: Spring creates a proxy for your repository interface; SimpleJpaRepository implements the standard methods.
  • Derived query: the method name is parsed into a JPQL criteria query once at startup.
  • Call: the proxy uses the shared EntityManager; the repository methods are transactional by default (reads are read-only).
  • Persistence context: loaded entities are tracked until the transaction ends.
  • MVC link: @Transactional belongs on the service, so one request can group several repository calls.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Query options:

  • Derived: findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThan.
  • @Query: JPQL or native SQL with named parameters.
  • Projections: interface or record projections load only some columns.
  • Specifications / Querydsl: dynamic filters.
  • @Modifying: bulk update and delete queries.
  • Pageable and Sort: built-in paging.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Derived queries: a method like findByEmail(String email) becomes SQL from its name; use @Query for custom JPQL.
  • DTOs: return DTOs (records) from controllers, not entities, to avoid exposing columns and lazy-loading errors.
  • Paging: accept a Pageable parameter in the controller and return Page<T>.

Senior Notes

  • Lazy loading: a lazy association read after the transaction ends causes LazyInitializationException; fetch what you need inside the service or with join fetch.
  • N+1 problem: looping over parents and touching a lazy child list runs one query per parent; fix with @EntityGraph or join fetch.
  • Open Session In View: Boot keeps the session open during the request by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view); many teams turn it off to keep database work in the service.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning entities with lazy collections from controllers: JSON serialization triggers lazy loading errors or loops; use DTOs.
  • N+1 selects: fix with join fetch or @EntityGraph.
  • Fetching a whole table: always page large results.
  • @Transactional on the controller or on private methods: put it on public service methods.
  • equals/hashCode on generated id: breaks sets before the entity is saved.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Open in view off: spring.jpa.open-in-view=false releases the connection after the service.
  • Batch inserts: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size; note that IDENTITY ids disable insert batching, so use a sequence for bulk work.
  • Read-only: @Transactional(readOnly = true) skips dirty checking.
  • Indexes on query columns; check generated SQL.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true

# OUTPUT:
# 1000 inserts -> about 20 batches instead of 1000 statements

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a product catalog with search and paging.

  • Controller accepts q and Pageable.
  • Service calls the repository and maps to DTOs.
  • A @DataJpaTest checks the query and a @WebMvcTest checks the JSON shape.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Hibernate is the JPA implementation that Spring Boot uses by default; it turns entity objects into SQL and manages their state in a persistence context.
  • Session: Hibernate works through a Session (JPA: EntityManager); inside a transaction, changes to loaded entities are saved automatically at commit (dirty checking).
  • With MVC: the controller calls a @Transactional service, which uses a repository or the EntityManager.

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside Hibernate:

  • SessionFactory: built once at startup from the entity metadata and the DataSource.
  • Session: one per transaction (or per request with open-in-view); holds the first-level cache and the entity snapshots.
  • Action queue: inserts, updates and deletes are queued and sent at flush.
  • Dirty checking: at flush each managed entity is compared with its snapshot.
  • Proxies: lazy associations are bytecode proxies that load data on first access.
  • Spring link: JpaTransactionManager binds the EntityManager to the thread for the duration of @Transactional.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options worth knowing:

  • Id strategies: IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, UUID.
  • Relations: @OneToMany(mappedBy), @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY), @ManyToMany with a join table.
  • Cascade and orphanRemoval: propagate save and delete to children.
  • Enums and dates: @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING).
  • Optimistic locking: @Version.
  • Embeddables: value objects with @Embeddable.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Entity states: transient (new), managed (tracked), detached (session closed) and removed.
  • DDL setting: spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto accepts none, validate, update, create and create-drop; use validate or a migration tool in production.
  • See the SQL: spring.jpa.show-sql=true and logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG help find slow or repeated queries.

Senior Notes

  • First-level cache: inside one session the same id returns the same object without a second query.
  • Flush: Hibernate sends SQL at commit, before a query that needs it, or on flush(), not at each setter.
  • Fetch plan: associations are lazy by default for collections; @ManyToOne is eager by default, so set it to LAZY when you do not always need it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Eager @ManyToOne everywhere: loads extra tables; set LAZY.
  • ddl-auto=update in production: unreviewed schema changes; use Flyway or Liquibase.
  • Missing owning side update: for bidirectional relations set both sides with a helper method.
  • Detached entity save: merging a stale object overwrites newer data; use @Version.
  • Large persistence context: loading thousands of entities in one transaction; clear the session or stream in chunks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Turn on hibernate.generate_statistics in a test to count queries.
  • Use join fetch or @EntityGraph for known read paths.
  • default_batch_fetch_size reduces N+1 cheaply.
  • Use projections for read-only lists.
  • Second-level cache only for rarely changing reference data.
  • For bulk work use StatelessSession or JDBC batching, and clear the session every few hundred rows.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order screen is slow.

  • The log shows 101 selects for 100 orders (N+1).
  • The team adds an entity graph for the items and a query-count assertion in a test.
  • The page now uses 1 select; the test fails if the count grows again.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Repository layer is the part of the application that talks to the database; it hides queries behind methods such as findById and save.
  • Spring Data JPA lets you write only an interface that extends JpaRepository<User, Long>; Spring generates the implementation at startup.
  • Derived queries: a method name like findByEmail is parsed into a query, so simple lookups need no SQL.

Worked Example 1

@DataJpaTest for a repository.

Worked Example 2

Interface projection.

Practice Exercise 1

Repository interface with derived queries.

Practice Exercise 2

Paged custom query.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A Spring Data repository is a JDK proxy created at startup.

  • Scanning: @EnableJpaRepositories (auto-configured in Boot) finds interfaces extending Repository.
  • Factory: JpaRepositoryFactoryBean builds a proxy backed by SimpleJpaRepository.
  • Query methods: PartTree parses names like findByEmailAndActiveTrue into JPA Criteria queries once at startup, so a bad property name fails fast.
  • Transactions: built-in methods are already transactional; reads are readOnly.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Repository interface choices:

  • CrudRepository: basic create, read, update, delete.
  • ListCrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository: lists and paging.
  • JpaRepository: adds flush, batch deletes and JPA extras.
  • Query forms: derived names, @Query JPQL, native queries, Specification for dynamic filters.
  • Modifying: @Modifying for update and delete queries.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @Query holds JPQL or native SQL when the method name would be too long or the query is complex.
  • Paging: pass a Pageable and return Page<T> so the database does the limiting.
  • Stereotype: @Repository marks a class as persistence code and translates vendor exceptions into DataAccessException.

Senior Notes

  • Projections: return interfaces or records with only the needed columns to avoid loading whole entities.
  • N+1 problem: lazy associations loaded in a loop fire one query each; fix with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
  • Testing: use @DataJpaTest, which starts only the JPA slice with an in-memory database and rolls back each test.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical repository mistakes:

  • Wrong property name in a derived method fails at startup with PropertyReferenceException.
  • Returning an entity with a lazy collection to the web layer causes LazyInitializationException.
  • findAll() on big tables loads everything; page it.
  • @Modifying without @Transactional throws TransactionRequiredException.
  • Optional ignored: calling .get() without checking.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning repository access:

  • N+1: use JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size.
  • Projections read only needed columns.
  • Paging: prefer Slice when the total count is not needed, since it skips the count query.
  • Read-only transactions let Hibernate skip dirty checking.
  • Bulk updates with @Modifying instead of loading and saving in a loop.
  • Index the columns used in derived finders.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an admin screen lists orders with the customer name, 20 per page.

  • Entity list would trigger N+1 for customers.
  • A DTO projection fetches exactly the columns shown.
  • A Pageable from the request drives limit and sort.
  • Whitelist sortable fields to avoid errors and information leaks.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Service layer holds the business rules of the application: it sits between controllers and repositories and decides what happens.
  • @Service is a stereotype annotation that registers the class as a Spring bean and documents its role.
  • Constructor injection gives the service its repositories, which keeps the class easy to test with mocks.

Worked Example 1

Coordinating two repositories.

Worked Example 2

Mapping to a DTO.

Practice Exercise 1

A service with a business rule.

Practice Exercise 2

Service unit test with Mockito.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A service bean is normally wrapped by a proxy that adds cross-cutting behaviour.

  • Creation: component scanning registers @Service classes as singleton beans.
  • Proxy: @Transactional triggers an AOP proxy (CGLIB for classes) with a TransactionInterceptor.
  • Call flow: controller calls the proxy, the interceptor opens a transaction, the real method runs, then commit or rollback.
  • Singleton: keep services stateless so threads do not share mutable fields.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Service design variants:

  • Concrete class (most common in Boot apps).
  • Interface plus impl when you need alternatives, such as a mock payment gateway.
  • Read and write split: a query service with readOnly = true and a command service.
  • Facade service to orchestrate several smaller services.
  • Events: publish ApplicationEvent for side effects such as email.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Transaction boundary: put @Transactional on service methods so several repository calls succeed or fail together.
  • Entities in, DTOs out: the service maps between entities and DTOs so controllers never touch persistence classes.
  • Exceptions: throw meaningful business exceptions such as UserNotFoundException instead of returning null.

Senior Notes

  • Interface plus implementation is optional; use it only when you really have several implementations.
  • Self-invocation: calling a @Transactional method from the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts.
  • Unit tests use Mockito with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), with no Spring context at all.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Service layer mistakes:

  • Self-invocation: this.save() inside the class skips the proxy.
  • Private or final methods cannot be proxied.
  • Stateful fields such as a current user stored in a singleton.
  • Returning entities that the controller then touches lazily.
  • Catching and hiding exceptions so rollback never happens.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning the service layer:

  • Short transactions: do not call remote HTTP services inside a transaction, because connections stay locked.
  • readOnly = true on queries.
  • Batch work in chunks, flushing and clearing the persistence context.
  • Caching: @Cacheable for rarely changing lookups.
  • Async: @Async for slow side effects such as sending email.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: user registration sends a welcome email, but a slow mail server must not block or undo the signup.

  • The service saves the user in a transaction.
  • It publishes an event after the commit.
  • @TransactionalEventListener sends the email only if the commit succeeded.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller layer receives HTTP requests, calls the service layer and returns a view name or a response body.
  • @Controller returns view names for HTML pages; @RestController returns data (usually JSON) written straight to the response.
  • Mapping annotations such as @GetMapping and @PostMapping connect URLs and HTTP methods to methods.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test.

Worked Example 2

Validation failure.

Practice Exercise 1

A REST controller.

Practice Exercise 2

MVC controller returning a view.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a request reaches a controller method.

  • DispatcherServlet receives every request.
  • HandlerMapping (RequestMappingHandlerMapping) finds the method from path, verb and content type.
  • HandlerAdapter resolves arguments with HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers and invokes the method.
  • Return value is handled by a HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler: a view name goes to ViewResolver, a body goes to an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson for JSON).
  • Errors go to HandlerExceptionResolvers such as @ExceptionHandler.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Argument and return options:

  • Inputs: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @RequestBody, @ModelAttribute for forms, @CookieValue.
  • Narrowing: consumes, produces, params and headers on the mapping.
  • Outputs: a DTO, ResponseEntity, a view name, void with @ResponseStatus.
  • Shortcuts: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Binding: @PathVariable reads the URL, @RequestParam reads query parameters and @RequestBody reads the JSON body.
  • Validation: add @Valid on the argument and Bean Validation annotations on the DTO.
  • Thin controllers: no business logic and no repository calls; only translate between HTTP and the service.

Senior Notes

  • DispatcherServlet finds the method through HandlerMapping and calls it through HandlerAdapter.
  • Status codes: use ResponseEntity or @ResponseStatus to return 201, 204 and so on.
  • Testing: @WebMvcTest with MockMvc loads only the web slice and a mocked service.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical controller mistakes:

  • @Controller returning an object without @ResponseBody: Spring looks for a view with that name and gives 404.
  • Missing @RequestBody: the DTO fields stay null.
  • Wrong content type: posting JSON without the header gives 415.
  • Business logic inside the method.
  • Always 200: returning error text with status 200 instead of proper codes.
  • Missing @Valid: constraints are silently ignored.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Controller performance points:

  • Keep it thin; slow work belongs in services that you can cache or make async.
  • Return pages, not entire tables.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true for big JSON.
  • ETag and caching headers for static-like responses.
  • Async: return Callable or CompletableFuture to free the servlet thread during long work.
  • Avoid serializing deep entity graphs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API for products with consistent errors.

  • Versioned base path /api/v1.
  • DTOs with validation.
  • Location header on create.
  • One @RestControllerAdvice for all errors.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DAO (Data Access Object) is a class that holds all database access for one entity, so the rest of the code never sees SQL or JDBC.
  • Typical methods are findById, findAll, insert, update and delete.
  • @Repository marks a DAO class and enables translation of SQL errors into Spring DataAccessException.

Worked Example 1

@JdbcTest for the DAO.

Worked Example 2

Injection-safe search.

Practice Exercise 1

A JdbcTemplate DAO.

Practice Exercise 2

Insert with generated key.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the Spring JDBC DAO works inside.

  • JdbcTemplate gets a connection from the DataSource (usually a HikariCP pool), creates a PreparedStatement, executes it and always closes resources.
  • Transactions: the connection is bound to the thread by DataSourceTransactionManager, so several DAO calls in one service method share it.
  • Exceptions: SQLException is translated by SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslator into DataAccessException subclasses.
  • RowMapper is called once per row.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Spring JDBC variants:

  • JdbcTemplate: positional ? parameters.
  • NamedParameterJdbcTemplate: :name parameters.
  • SimpleJdbcInsert: insert without writing SQL.
  • JdbcClient (Spring 6.1 and later): a fluent API over the same engine.
  • BeanPropertyRowMapper: maps columns to bean properties by name.
  • batchUpdate: many rows in one round trip.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • JdbcTemplate removes boilerplate: it opens connections, runs the SQL, maps rows and closes resources.
  • RowMapper converts one ResultSet row into an object.
  • DAO or Spring Data: a hand-written DAO gives full control; a Spring Data repository generates the same code for you.

Senior Notes

  • Interface first: define UserDao and an implementation, so you can swap JDBC for JPA or a test stub.
  • Named parameters (NamedParameterJdbcTemplate) are safer and clearer than positional question marks, and prevent SQL injection.
  • Testing: run the DAO against an embedded H2 database with @JdbcTest.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

DAO mistakes:

  • String concatenation in SQL: injection risk.
  • queryForObject with no row throws EmptyResultDataAccessException; use query and check the list.
  • Leaking ResultSet or connections when using raw JDBC.
  • Missing @Repository: no exception translation.
  • Business logic in the DAO instead of the service.
  • SELECT * with a RowMapper that misses new columns.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

DAO tuning:

  • Batching with batchUpdate and JDBC batch settings.
  • Pool size: HikariCP maximum-pool-size matched to database capacity.
  • fetchSize for large reads, and stream with queryForStream inside a transaction.
  • Indexes on filtered columns; read the execution plan.
  • Select only needed columns.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a legacy reporting query with window functions that JPA cannot express well.

  • Keep entities and repositories for normal CRUD.
  • Add a small DAO for the report with JdbcClient or JdbcTemplate.
  • Return a record per row to the service.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a simple object that carries data between layers or across the network; it has fields and no business logic.
  • Why: it exposes only the fields a client needs, so the database schema and internal entity details stay hidden.
  • Java records are a compact way to write immutable DTOs: record UserDto(Long id, String name) {}.

Worked Example 1

JSON shape produced.

Worked Example 2

Mass assignment blocked.

Practice Exercise 1

Request and response DTOs with a mapper.

Practice Exercise 2

DTO straight from a query.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A DTO has no framework magic: it is a plain class, and the framework only converts it.

  • Request: HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) reads JSON into the DTO, then @Valid runs Hibernate Validator.
  • Response: Jackson writes the DTO fields to JSON.
  • Records: Jackson supports them as constructors since 2.12 (Spring Boot 3 includes this).
  • Mapping between entity and DTO is your own code or a generated MapStruct class.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

DTO styles:

  • Records: short and immutable.
  • Classes with Lombok when you need builders or setters.
  • Separate DTOs per use case: CreateUser, UpdateUser, UserSummary, UserDetail.
  • MapStruct: an interface with @Mapper(componentModel = "spring") that generates the mapping.
  • Jackson annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonInclude to shape JSON.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Separate request and response DTOs: a create request has no id, a response has one; do not reuse one class for both.
  • Validation goes on request DTOs with @NotBlank, @Email and @Size.
  • Mapping: write it by hand for small apps or use MapStruct to generate mappers at compile time.

Senior Notes

  • Mass assignment: binding JSON straight onto an entity lets a client set fields like role; a DTO blocks this.
  • Lazy loading: serializing an entity can trigger lazy queries or infinite loops in bidirectional relations; DTOs avoid both.
  • Projections: Spring Data can return DTO records straight from a query, skipping the entity.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

DTO mistakes:

  • One DTO for everything leads to nullable fields and unclear rules.
  • Entity inside a DTO brings the persistence model back.
  • Validation on the entity only: the request DTO is the right place for input rules.
  • Manual mapping errors: forgetting a new field; MapStruct with unmappedTargetPolicy = ERROR catches this.
  • Mutable DTOs shared across threads.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

DTO performance:

  • Projection queries avoid loading and then discarding columns.
  • Compile-time mapping (MapStruct) is faster than reflection mappers.
  • Smaller payloads mean less serialization and network time.
  • Avoid mapping inside loops that trigger lazy queries; fetch needed data first.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the public API must not expose internal flags.

  • The entity has passwordHash, role and deleted.
  • The public DTO has only id, name and avatar.
  • An admin DTO adds role.
  • Two mappers keep the views apart, and tests assert that secrets never appear in JSON.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Entity mapping tells JPA how a Java class maps to a database table: @Entity marks the class and @Table names the table.
  • Primary key: @Id marks the key field and @GeneratedValue lets the database create values.
  • Columns: fields map to columns by name; use @Column to set the name, length and nullability.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Bidirectional one-to-many.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What JPA does with a mapped entity.

  • Metadata: at startup Hibernate reads annotations into a metamodel and checks the schema if validate is on.
  • Persistence context: the EntityManager tracks managed entities by id (first-level cache).
  • Dirty checking: at flush Hibernate compares fields to a snapshot and issues UPDATEs, so no explicit save is needed inside a transaction.
  • Lazy proxies: lazy associations are replaced by proxies that load on first access.
  • Entity states: transient, managed, detached, removed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options:

  • Id strategies: IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, UUID; SEQUENCE allows insert batching.
  • Value types: @Embeddable and @Embedded for groups like Address.
  • Inheritance: SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, TABLE_PER_CLASS.
  • Many to many: @ManyToMany with @JoinTable, or an explicit join entity when the link has data.
  • Others: @Lob, @Transient, @CreatedDate with auditing, @Version.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Relationships: @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @OneToOne and @ManyToMany describe foreign keys.
  • Owning side: the side with @JoinColumn owns the relation; the other side uses mappedBy.
  • Enums: use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) so reordering the enum does not corrupt data.

Senior Notes

  • Fetch type: @ManyToOne is eager by default, collections are lazy; prefer lazy and fetch explicitly when needed.
  • equals and hashCode: base them on a business key or the id carefully, never on lazy collections.
  • Schema: use Flyway or Liquibase in production and keep ddl-auto at validate or none.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mapping mistakes:

  • EAGER everywhere causes huge joins.
  • @OneToMany without mappedBy creates an extra join table.
  • Lombok @Data on entities: toString and hashCode walk relations and loop forever.
  • List for @ManyToMany makes removal delete and reinsert all links; use a Set.
  • EnumType.ORDINAL default.
  • No no-arg constructor: JPA needs one (protected is fine).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Mapping and performance:

  • Lazy by default, then fetch with JOIN FETCH when needed.
  • Batch inserts: SEQUENCE ids plus hibernate.jdbc.batch_size.
  • @BatchSize on collections to cut N+1.
  • Indexes declared in @Table(indexes = ...) and managed through migrations.
  • Open session in view: set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false so lazy loading does not leak into the web layer.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an online shop with customers, orders and order lines.

  • Customer has many orders; order has many lines (cascade and orphan removal).
  • Order total is calculated by the aggregate root.
  • Money uses BigDecimal.
  • Schema comes from Flyway, validated by Hibernate.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Transaction is a group of database operations that either all succeed (commit) or all undo (rollback); it follows ACID rules.
  • @Transactional on a method makes Spring open a transaction before it runs and commit when it returns normally.
  • Rollback: by default Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error), not on checked exceptions.

Worked Example 1

Test that rollback happens.

Worked Example 2

Swallowed exception bug.

Practice Exercise 1

Atomic money transfer.

Practice Exercise 2

Checked exception rollback.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Declarative transactions run through AOP.

  • Setup: Boot auto-configures @EnableTransactionManagement and a PlatformTransactionManager (JpaTransactionManager with JPA).
  • Interceptor: TransactionInterceptor reads the attribute, asks the manager for a transaction, calls the method and then commits or rolls back.
  • Thread binding: the connection or EntityManager is stored in TransactionSynchronizationManager thread locals, so repositories join the same transaction.
  • Rollback-only: an unchecked exception in an inner joined method marks the whole transaction rollback-only.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attributes of @Transactional:

  • propagation: REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, SUPPORTS, MANDATORY, NOT_SUPPORTED, NEVER, NESTED.
  • isolation: DEFAULT, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE.
  • readOnly and timeout (seconds).
  • rollbackFor and noRollbackFor.
  • Programmatic: TransactionTemplate for fine-grained control.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Propagation says what to do when a transaction already exists: REQUIRED (default) joins it, REQUIRES_NEW starts a new one.
  • readOnly = true is a hint for query-only methods; it can skip dirty checking and help the database.
  • rollbackFor: use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) to also roll back on checked exceptions.

Senior Notes

  • Proxy based: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, so calls from the same class (self-invocation) and private methods are not transactional.
  • Isolation levels (READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE) trade consistency against concurrency.
  • Swallowed exceptions: catching the exception inside the method means Spring never sees it and commits anyway.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Transaction mistakes:

  • Self-invocation and private methods: no proxy, no transaction.
  • Catching exceptions so Spring never sees them.
  • Checked exceptions without rollbackFor.
  • @Transactional on the controller or on a final class method.
  • Using the wrong annotation: prefer Spring @Transactional or the Jakarta one consistently.
  • Inner REQUIRED failure: caller sees UnexpectedRollbackException.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning transactions:

  • Keep them short: no remote calls, file work or user waits inside.
  • readOnly = true for queries.
  • Lower isolation only when the rules allow.
  • Lock carefully: optimistic with @Version first, pessimistic (@Lock) for hot rows.
  • Pool sizing: a long transaction holds a pooled connection.
  • Timeouts to avoid stuck locks.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: place an order, charge the card and write an audit record.

  • Order and stock changes share one transaction.
  • The audit log uses REQUIRES_NEW so failures are recorded too.
  • The remote payment call happens after commit using an event, to keep the transaction short.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DataAccessException is Spring unchecked root exception for all database errors, so your code is not tied to JDBC or Hibernate exception types.
  • Translation: classes marked @Repository get vendor exceptions converted into subclasses like DuplicateKeyException.
  • Common ones: DataIntegrityViolationException (constraint broken) and EmptyResultDataAccessException (expected a row, found none).

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test of the handler.

Worked Example 2

Catch at the right place.

Practice Exercise 1

Global handler for database errors.

Practice Exercise 2

Optimistic locking.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring converts and delivers database errors.

  • Translation: PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor wraps @Repository beans; Hibernate and JDBC exceptions become DataAccessException subtypes.
  • Hierarchy: NonTransientDataAccessException (do not retry) versus TransientDataAccessException (may retry).
  • Spring Data repositories are translated automatically.
  • Web side: an uncaught exception reaches ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, which looks for a matching @ExceptionHandler method.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Commonly used exception types:

  • DuplicateKeyException: unique key broken (JDBC).
  • DataIntegrityViolationException: any constraint failure (also JPA).
  • EmptyResultDataAccessException and IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException.
  • OptimisticLockingFailureException and PessimisticLockingFailureException.
  • CannotAcquireLockException and QueryTimeoutException (transient).
  • Handler styles: controller-local @ExceptionHandler, @RestControllerAdvice, ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) in Spring 6.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler turns exceptions into clean HTTP responses in one place.
  • Mapping: duplicate or constraint errors usually become 409 Conflict, missing data 404 Not Found.
  • Do not leak SQL text, table names or stack traces in the response body; log them on the server instead.

Senior Notes

  • Optimistic locking: with @Version a concurrent update throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException; map it to 409 and let the client retry.
  • Timing: with JPA the constraint error may appear at flush or commit time, outside your try block.
  • Transaction state: after a database exception the transaction is marked rollback-only, so catching it inside the same transaction does not save the work.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Returning e.getMessage() to clients leaks SQL and table names.
  • Catching Exception broadly so rollback is lost.
  • Expecting the error at save() when the flush is delayed.
  • Catching and continuing in the same transaction after a failed statement; the session may be unusable.
  • Treating every error as 500 when 404 or 409 is correct.
  • No logging of the root cause.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Resilience and tuning:

  • Retry transient errors (deadlocks, lock timeouts) with @Retryable from Spring Retry, with backoff and a limit.
  • Check before insert for friendly messages, but still handle the constraint error because of race conditions.
  • Query timeouts via @Transactional(timeout = ...) or jakarta.persistence.query.timeout.
  • Metrics: count failures per type.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: sign-up with a unique email under concurrent requests.

  • The service checks existsByEmail for a friendly path.
  • Two simultaneous requests can both pass the check.
  • The unique index is the real guard; the loser gets DataIntegrityViolationException.
  • The service converts it into a domain exception, and the advice returns 409.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller is the top layer of a layered application: it is the entry point for web requests and talks only to the service layer below.
  • Layer rule: the flow is Controller, then Service, then Repository, and each layer only calls the one directly below it.
  • Responsibility: parse the request, validate input, call one service method and shape the response; nothing more.

Worked Example 1

Layered flow trace.

Worked Example 2

Web slice test.

Practice Exercise 1

Controller delegating to the layer below.

Practice Exercise 2

Fat controller versus thin controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where the controller sits at runtime.

  • Servlet container (Tomcat) hands the request to DispatcherServlet after filters run.
  • Interceptors (HandlerInterceptor) run before and after the controller method.
  • Controller is a singleton bean; its method runs on a request thread.
  • Layer calls: controller to service proxy to repository proxy to DataSource.
  • Response: converters write the body, then filters see the response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Layering styles:

  • Classic three layers: controller, service, repository.
  • Package by feature (user, order) instead of by layer, each with its own controller, service and repository.
  • Hexagonal: controllers are one adapter around a core of use cases and ports.
  • ArchUnit tests can enforce the allowed dependencies.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Separation of concerns lets you change the UI or API style without touching business rules or the database code.
  • Dependencies point downward; a repository must never call a controller, and a service must not use HttpServletRequest.
  • Error handling is centralized in @ControllerAdvice rather than repeated in every controller.

Senior Notes

  • Anti-patterns: fat controllers with business logic, controllers calling repositories directly, and entities exposed in responses.
  • Constructor injection keeps dependencies explicit and makes controller tests simple.
  • Testing by layer: @WebMvcTest for controllers, plain Mockito for services, @DataJpaTest for repositories.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Layer violations to avoid:

  • Controller to repository shortcuts.
  • Business rules in the controller, such as price or permission logic.
  • Service using HttpServletRequest, HttpSession or ResponseEntity.
  • Entities in JSON.
  • Duplicated error handling in every method with try and catch.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Layer-aware testing keeps the suite fast.

  • @WebMvcTest loads only controllers, advice and converters.
  • Mockito tests services in milliseconds.
  • @DataJpaTest tests repositories.
  • @SpringBootTest only for a few end to end flows.
  • Use @MockBean sparingly; many of them slow down context caching.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: mobile and web clients share the same business rules.

  • An OrderController serves JSON to the mobile app.
  • An MVC OrderPageController serves HTML to the website.
  • Both call the same OrderService, so rules stay identical.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Service layer is the middle layer of a layered application: it contains business logic and is called by controllers and other services.
  • Position: it uses the repository layer below it for data and knows nothing about HTTP or views above it.
  • @Service registers the class as a bean; the real work is the business methods, usually one per use case.

Worked Example 1

Mockito test of the use case.

Worked Example 2

Reuse from a scheduler.

Practice Exercise 1

Use case spanning two repositories.

Practice Exercise 2

Domain exception mapped by the web layer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The service layer is where the transaction and the use case meet.

  • Entry: the controller calls a Spring proxy of the service bean.
  • Transaction: the proxy opens it, the method runs, the proxy commits.
  • Collaborators: the method calls repositories (joining the same transaction) and other services.
  • Output: returns DTOs or values; failures are exceptions.
  • The persistence context lives for the transaction, so entities are managed inside the service and detached outside it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to organise services:

  • One service per aggregate (OrderService, CustomerService).
  • Per use case classes (PlaceOrderService) for large apps.
  • Domain services for rules spanning several entities.
  • Application services that orchestrate and own transactions.
  • Port interfaces for outside systems such as PaymentGateway.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Use case methods such as placeOrder and cancelOrder are better names than generic save and update.
  • Transactions start here: annotate use case methods with @Transactional so the whole use case is atomic.
  • Reuse: several controllers, schedulers or message listeners can call the same service method.

Senior Notes

  • Service calling service is fine, but avoid circular dependencies; extract a third class if two services need each other.
  • Domain exceptions express business failures; the web layer maps them to HTTP codes.
  • Anemic model: if services only shuffle getters and setters, move rules into the entities where they belong.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Service layer mistakes:

  • God service with 50 methods; split by aggregate or use case.
  • Pass-through services that only call the repository with no value; acceptable only if rules are expected to grow.
  • Remote calls inside a transaction.
  • Circular injection between two services.
  • Returning null instead of Optional or an exception.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Service layer performance and safety:

  • Short transactions and readOnly for reads.
  • Cache stable lookups with @Cacheable and evict on change.
  • Async or events for slow side effects.
  • Idempotency: make operations safe to retry using request ids.
  • Avoid per-row service calls in loops; add a bulk method.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: cancel an order. Rules: only NEW or PAID orders, refund if paid, restore stock, notify the customer.

  • One service method owns the rule order.
  • Entity guards its own state change.
  • Refund and stock restore happen in the same transaction.
  • The email is sent after commit.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Repository layer is the part of the app that stores and loads data; services call it and never write SQL themselves.
  • Spring Data JPA lets you declare an interface that extends JpaRepository, and Spring generates the implementation at startup.
  • Annotation: @Repository marks the bean and translates persistence exceptions into DataAccessException.

Worked Example 1

Repository test with @DataJpaTest.

Worked Example 2

Service uses the repository.

Practice Exercise 1

A first repository.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom query with paging.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring Data builds repositories at startup, with no class written by you.

  • Scanning: @EnableJpaRepositories (auto-configured in Boot) finds interfaces that extend Repository.
  • Proxy: each interface gets a JDK proxy whose target is SimpleJpaRepository.
  • Query methods: PartTree parses names like findByEmailAndActiveTrue into JPQL criteria.
  • Interceptors: a chain handles transactions (read-only by default for finders) and exception translation.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of repository interfaces:

  • CrudRepository: basic save, find, delete.
  • ListCrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository: lists and paging.
  • JpaRepository: adds flush and batch delete.
  • @Query: JPQL or native SQL.
  • @Modifying: for update and delete queries.
  • Specifications and Querydsl: dynamic filters.
  • Projections: interface or record results.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Derived queries: a method such as findByEmailIgnoreCase becomes a query from its name; use @Query when the name gets too long.
  • Transactions belong to the service layer, so one business action can call several repositories in one commit.
  • Return types: use Optional<T> for single results and Page<T> for paged lists.

Senior Notes

  • Test slice: @DataJpaTest loads only JPA beans and an embedded database, which makes repository tests fast.
  • N+1 selects: lazy associations loaded in a loop; fix with @EntityGraph or a join fetch query.
  • Projections: return interfaces or records instead of full entities when a screen needs only a few columns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Business logic in the repository: keep it in services.
  • Transaction on the repository only: two saves then run in two commits; put @Transactional on the service.
  • Misspelled property in a method name: fails at startup with PropertyReferenceException.
  • Returning null checks: use Optional.
  • Loading all rows: use paging.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning repositories:

  • Page, do not list: Pageable avoids loading whole tables.
  • N+1: use @EntityGraph or join fetch.
  • Projections: select only needed columns.
  • Batching: set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size for many inserts.
  • Read-only: @Transactional(readOnly = true) skips dirty checking.
  • Indexes: match the columns in your finders.
