Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a customer list screen with search and paging.

  • The controller receives page and q.
  • The service calls repo.search(q, pageable) in a read-only transaction.
  • The repository returns a projection, so only id and name are read.
  • An index on name keeps the query fast at a million rows.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DAO (Data Access Object) is a class that holds all database access code for one entity, so the rest of the app never sees JDBC or SQL.
  • Purpose: change the database or the query style by editing only the DAO, not the service or the controller.
  • Spring support: mark a DAO class with @Repository and use JdbcTemplate or EntityManager inside it.

Worked Example 1

Testing a DAO with an embedded database.

Worked Example 2

Catching the translated exception.

Practice Exercise 1

DAO interface and JDBC implementation.

Practice Exercise 2

Batch insert.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How JdbcTemplate serves a DAO internally:

  • Connection: taken from DataSource through DataSourceUtils, so it joins an active transaction.
  • Template method: it prepares the statement, runs it, calls your RowMapper and always closes resources.
  • Translation: SQLExceptionTranslator maps vendor error codes to DataAccessException types.
  • @Repository: a post processor adds translation for DAOs that use JPA directly.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to write a DAO in Spring:

  • JdbcTemplate: simple SQL.
  • NamedParameterJdbcTemplate: named parameters.
  • SimpleJdbcInsert: inserts with generated keys.
  • JdbcClient (Spring 6.1): a fluent API over the same engine.
  • EntityManager: JPA and JPQL.
  • Spring Data: interface only.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Interface plus class: an interface UserDao and an implementation JdbcUserDao let you swap and mock the storage.
  • JdbcTemplate opens and closes connections for you and maps rows with a RowMapper.
  • Exceptions: Spring turns SQLException into unchecked DataAccessException subclasses.

Senior Notes

  • DAO versus repository: with Spring Data you often need no hand-written DAO; keep a DAO for complex SQL, reports and batch work.
  • Parameters: always bind with ? or named parameters to avoid SQL injection.
  • Batching: batchUpdate sends many rows in few round trips.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common DAO mistakes:

  • String concatenation: opens SQL injection.
  • queryForObject on no row: throws EmptyResultDataAccessException.
  • Manual connection handling: leaks connections; let the template do it.
  • Catching and hiding exceptions: the service never learns of a failure.
  • Business rules in the DAO: keep it to storage.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning a DAO:

  • Connection pool: HikariCP is the Boot default; size it to the database, not the thread count.
  • batchUpdate: far fewer round trips.
  • fetchSize: stream large results with a larger fetch size.
  • Select only needed columns.
  • Indexes on filtered columns.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a nightly report that sums sales per region across millions of rows.

  • A Spring Data derived query cannot express the grouping well.
  • A ReportDao runs one tuned SQL with group by and returns small row objects.
  • The service calls it inside a read-only transaction.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Entity is a Java class mapped to a database table; each object is one row and each field is a column.
  • Annotations: @Entity, @Table, @Id and @GeneratedValue describe the mapping.
  • Domain model: the entity layer holds the data and the rules that belong to the data, and it is not the same as the JSON sent to clients.

Worked Example 1

Entity mapping test.

Worked Example 2

Constraint violation.

Practice Exercise 1

A simple entity.

Practice Exercise 2

One to many relation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What the persistence provider (Hibernate) does with entities:

  • Metamodel: at startup it reads the annotations and builds the table mapping.
  • Persistence context: a first-level cache of entities per transaction; the same id returns the same object.
  • Dirty checking: at flush it compares loaded state with current state and writes UPDATEs for changed fields.
  • Proxies: lazy associations are subclasses created at runtime, which is why entity classes should not be final.
  • States: new, managed, detached and removed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options:

  • Id strategies: IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, UUID.
  • @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING): store enum names.
  • @Embedded and @Embeddable: reuse value objects like Address.
  • @Version: optimistic locking.
  • Auditing: @CreatedDate with @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class).
  • Inheritance: SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Columns: @Column(nullable = false, length = 100) sets constraints that the schema and validation can use.
  • Relations: @OneToMany and @ManyToOne link entities; the owning side holds the foreign key.
  • No-arg constructor: JPA needs one (it may be protected) to create objects when it loads rows.

Senior Notes

  • equals and hashCode: base them on a business key or the id carefully, because entities live in sets and persistence contexts.
  • Lazy loading: touching a lazy field after the session closes gives LazyInitializationException.
  • Do not expose entities from controllers: it leaks columns and causes infinite JSON loops with bidirectional links.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common entity mistakes:

  • EnumType.ORDINAL: breaks when enum order changes.
  • Eager everywhere: loads too much; default to lazy.
  • Lombok @Data on entities: equals and toString touch lazy fields and cause loops.
  • Bidirectional JSON: infinite recursion; use DTOs.
  • Setting only the inverse side: the foreign key is not saved.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning entities:

  • Lazy by default and fetch what you need with entity graphs.
  • SEQUENCE with allocation size allows insert batching; IDENTITY disables it.
  • Read-only queries with projections avoid managed entities.
  • Second-level cache only for rarely changed data.
  • Keep entities small; split rarely used big columns.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order system with Order and OrderItem.

  • Order is the aggregate root with cascade = ALL over its items.
  • A @Version field prevents two users from overwriting each other.
  • The API exposes DTOs only, so schema changes stay internal.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a plain object that carries data between layers or across the network, without behavior or database mapping.
  • Why: it lets the API show only the fields a client needs and hides the entity structure.
  • Java records are a short way to write DTOs: record UserDto(Long id, String name) {}.

Worked Example 1

Validation of a DTO with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Hidden field is not leaked.

Practice Exercise 1

Request and response records.

Practice Exercise 2

Query straight into a DTO.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a DTO travels through Spring MVC:

  • Incoming: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor picks a converter by Content-Type; Jackson builds the record or class.
  • Validation: with @Valid the processor runs the Bean Validation Validator and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • Outgoing: the return value is written by a converter chosen from Accept.
  • Records: Jackson uses the canonical constructor.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

DTO design options:

  • Records: concise and immutable.
  • Classes with Lombok: mutable, familiar.
  • @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore: control JSON names.
  • @JsonInclude(NON_NULL): skip nulls.
  • Nested DTOs: for related data.
  • Validation groups: different rules for create and update.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request and response DTOs are separate: a create request has no id, while a response has one.
  • Validation: put @NotBlank and @Email on request DTO fields and use @Valid in the controller.
  • Versioning: you can change entities without breaking clients when the DTO stays stable.

Senior Notes

  • Mass assignment: binding input straight to an entity lets a client set fields such as role; a DTO blocks this.
  • Projections: query directly into a DTO with an interface projection or a constructor expression to skip loading full entities.
  • Immutability: records are immutable and work well with Jackson 2.12 and later.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common DTO mistakes:

  • One DTO for everything: create, update and read need different fields.
  • Entity in the request: mass assignment risk.
  • Missing @Valid: annotations are ignored.
  • Mutable shared DTO: hard to reason about.
  • DTOs with logic: keep them as data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Projection to DTO in the query reads fewer columns.
  • Avoid mapping huge lists in memory; page them.
  • Jackson is fast; reuse the auto-configured ObjectMapper.
  • Compression (server.compression.enabled=true) helps big JSON.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API for products while the table has cost and supplier columns.

  • The entity keeps cost and supplierId.
  • The response DTO exposes only id, name and price.
  • Adding a column later does not change the API.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Mapper layer converts objects from one shape to another, mostly entity to DTO and DTO to entity.
  • Why: it keeps conversion code in one place so controllers and services stay clean.
  • MapStruct is a popular tool: you write an interface with @Mapper and it generates the implementation at compile time.

Worked Example 1

Plain unit test of a mapper.

Worked Example 2

Update an existing entity.

Practice Exercise 1

MapStruct mapper.

Practice Exercise 2

Manual mapper without a library.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How MapStruct works:

  • Annotation processor: at compile time it reads the @Mapper interface.
  • Generated class: UserMapperImpl with plain getter and setter calls, no reflection.
  • Spring bean: with componentModel = "spring" the class gets @Component.
  • Build checks: unmapped target properties produce warnings, or errors if configured.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping features:

  • @Mapping: rename, ignore, constant, expression.
  • uses: reuse other mappers.
  • @MappingTarget: update in place.
  • @BeanMapping: null strategies.
  • @Named: choose a custom method.
  • Collections: list methods are generated automatically.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • componentModel: use @Mapper(componentModel = "spring") so the generated class is a Spring bean you can inject.
  • Field names that match are copied automatically; use @Mapping(source, target) for different names.
  • Manual mapping with a small static method or a record constructor is fine for tiny projects.

Senior Notes

  • Compile-time safety: MapStruct reports unmapped fields during the build, unlike reflection tools such as ModelMapper.
  • Update methods: @MappingTarget updates an existing entity, which suits PUT and PATCH.
  • Null handling: use NullValuePropertyMappingStrategy.IGNORE for partial updates.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mapper mistakes:

  • Lombok order: add lombok-mapstruct-binding and keep Lombok before MapStruct in processor paths.
  • Mapping lazy collections outside a transaction.
  • Silent unmapped fields: set the policy to ERROR.
  • Mapping logic with side effects: mappers should be pure.
  • Mapping ids on create: ignore the id.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml annotation processor order -->
<annotationProcessorPaths>
    <path><groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId><artifactId>lombok</artifactId></path>
    <path><groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
          <artifactId>lombok-mapstruct-binding</artifactId></path>
    <path><groupId>org.mapstruct</groupId>
          <artifactId>mapstruct-processor</artifactId></path>
</annotationProcessorPaths>

// OUTPUT:
// with this order, mappers see Lombok getters and setters

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • MapStruct is as fast as hand-written code.
  • ModelMapper and reflection tools cost more per call.
  • Avoid deep graphs: map only what the screen needs.
  • Use projections to skip mapping entirely.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: order API where Order has nested customer and items.

  • The mapper uses CustomerMapper and ItemMapper.
  • Money is converted with a @Named method to cents.
  • A unit test checks the full mapping once, so changes are caught.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Utility layer holds small helper classes with reusable logic that does not belong to any one layer, such as date formatting or string checks.
  • Static helpers: a final class with a private constructor and static methods, for example DateUtils.
  • Not business logic: rules of the domain belong in services; utilities only help.

Worked Example 1

Unit test of a static helper.

Worked Example 2

Fixed clock in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

Static utility class.

Practice Exercise 2

Bean with a Clock for testing.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Utilities and the Spring container:

  • Static class: loaded by the class loader, never managed by Spring, no injection.
  • Bean utility: created once as a singleton and injected like any service.
  • Static access to the context: avoid ApplicationContextAware holders; they hide dependencies.
  • Time: Clock is a bean you can replace in tests.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where to find ready helpers:

  • Spring: StringUtils, CollectionUtils, Assert, ObjectUtils.
  • JDK: Objects, Optional, Collections, java.time.
  • Libraries: Apache Commons Lang, Guava.
  • Custom: only for rules specific to your app.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Static or bean: pure functions can be static; code that needs configuration or other beans should be a @Component.
  • Existing libraries: prefer StringUtils, Objects and Apache Commons before writing your own.
  • Stateless: a utility must be thread-safe, so keep no mutable shared fields.

Senior Notes

  • Hard to mock: static calls cannot be replaced easily in tests, so wrap time and random in a bean such as Clock.
  • Dumping ground: a giant Utils class is a smell; group by purpose and name clearly.
  • Thread safety: SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe, so use DateTimeFormatter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Static state: shared mutable fields cause race conditions.
  • Static calls to now(): tests become time-dependent.
  • Reinventing library code.
  • Utility with business rules: move it to a service.
  • SimpleDateFormat in a static field: not thread-safe.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Precompile regex: keep a static Pattern, not String.replaceAll in hot loops.
  • Reuse formatters that are immutable.
  • Avoid boxing in helpers used in loops.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a certificate expiry job and its test.

  • The job asks an injected Clock for the current time.
  • The test fixes the clock to check the boundary day.
  • No sleeping or date-dependent failures.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Configuration layer holds the classes and files that set up beans, security, web options and properties for the application.
  • @Configuration marks a class whose @Bean methods create beans managed by the container.
  • Properties: values live in application.properties or YAML and are read with @Value or @ConfigurationProperties.

Worked Example 1

Test with a property override.

Worked Example 2

Profile bean.

Practice Exercise 1

Web configuration.

Practice Exercise 2

Typed properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How configuration is processed:

  • ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration classes and registers bean definitions.
  • CGLIB proxy: a full configuration class is subclassed so calls between @Bean methods return the singleton.
  • Environment: property sources are ordered; command line and environment variables beat files.
  • Auto-configuration: Boot adds beans with @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so your bean wins.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options:

  • @Bean: explicit creation.
  • @Import and @ComponentScan: compose configs.
  • @Conditional variants: @ConditionalOnProperty for feature flags.
  • @ConfigurationProperties: typed binding with @Validated.
  • @PropertySource: extra files.
  • YAML profiles: sections per profile.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • WebMvcConfigurer: implement it to add interceptors, CORS rules, formatters and resource handlers without losing Boot defaults.
  • Profiles: @Profile("dev") and application-dev.properties switch settings per environment.
  • Type-safe config: @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app") binds a group of keys to one class.

Senior Notes

  • @EnableWebMvc turns off Spring Boot MVC auto-configuration; avoid it unless you want full control.
  • Proxy beans: in a full @Configuration class calls between @Bean methods return the same singleton.
  • Secrets: keep passwords out of source and read them from environment variables or a vault.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • @EnableWebMvc in Boot: disables defaults such as Jackson settings.
  • Hard-coded values: move them to properties.
  • Wrong property name: app.pageSize versus app.page-size works with relaxed binding, but a typo silently gives the default.
  • Committed secrets.
  • Component scan too wide: slow start.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (never commit real secrets)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=
# set DB_PASSWORD in the environment;
Boot maps it with:
# spring.datasource.password=
# use the environment variable SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD instead

# OUTPUT:
# SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD overrides the file value at startup

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Startup tuning:

  • Narrow scans to your base package.
  • Lazy init (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true) trades startup for first-request time.
  • Remove unused starters.
  • Check the report with --debug to see conditions.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: dev, test and prod environments.

  • application.properties holds common values.
  • application-dev.properties uses an in-memory H2 database.
  • Production gets its database settings from environment variables.
  • Tests run with @ActiveProfiles("test").

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Exception layer is where the app turns errors into clean responses, with custom exceptions and one global handler.
  • @RestControllerAdvice plus @ExceptionHandler catches exceptions from all controllers in one class.
  • Status codes: map not found to 404, validation to 400 and conflicts to 409 instead of a raw 500.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test of the 404.

Worked Example 2

Throwing from the service.

Practice Exercise 1

Global handler.

Practice Exercise 2

Validation errors.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How an exception becomes a response:

  • DispatcherServlet catches an exception from the handler and asks its HandlerExceptionResolver chain.
  • ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver finds a matching @ExceptionHandler in the controller, then in @ControllerAdvice beans.
  • ResponseStatusExceptionResolver handles @ResponseStatus and ResponseStatusException.
  • DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps framework errors such as a missing parameter to 400.
  • If none match, the error goes to the container and Boot /error.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Handler options:

  • @ExceptionHandler with several types.
  • @ControllerAdvice(basePackages) to limit scope.
  • ResponseEntityExceptionHandler base class for standard Spring errors.
  • ProblemDetail with extra properties.
  • spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true turns on RFC 7807 for built-in errors.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom exception: UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException carries a clear message from the service.
  • ProblemDetail (Spring 6) gives the RFC 7807 error format: type, title, status and detail.
  • Validation errors: MethodArgumentNotValidException holds the field errors to return.

Senior Notes

  • Resolver chain: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver runs before ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and the default resolver.
  • Do not leak stack traces or SQL messages to clients; log them and return a safe message.
  • Handler order: the most specific exception type wins, and @Order sorts several advice classes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Catching Exception for everything: hides bugs and returns wrong codes.
  • Returning 200 with an error body.
  • Leaking stack traces: keep server.error.include-stacktrace=never.
  • No logging in the handler for 500 errors.
  • Checked exceptions that do not roll back transactions.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and behavior:

  • Exceptions are costly to create; avoid using them for normal flow such as a login check on every call.
  • Override fillInStackTrace for high-volume business exceptions if profiling shows a cost.
  • Keep handlers small; do not call the database in them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a checkout API.

  • Out of stock gives 409 with the item name.
  • Invalid input gives 400 with field errors.
  • Unknown order gives 404.
  • A traceId property is added to every problem so support can find the log line.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Separation of concerns means each class has one clear job: controllers handle HTTP, services hold business rules and repositories talk to the database.
  • Benefits: code is easier to read, test, change and reuse.
  • Typical flow: Controller calls Service, Service calls Repository, and data moves in DTOs and entities.

Worked Example 1

Service unit test with a mock repository.

Worked Example 2

Controller slice test.

Practice Exercise 1

Three layers in one flow.

Practice Exercise 2

Wrong versus right.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring supports layering:

  • Stereotypes: @Controller, @Service, @Repository mark the role of each class.
  • Dependency injection: each layer receives the layer below as an interface or bean.
  • AOP proxies: cross-cutting work such as transactions, logging and security is applied around services, so it is not repeated in each class.
  • Filters and interceptors handle web-wide concerns outside controllers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to organize code:

  • Package by layer: controller, service, repository folders.
  • Package by feature: order, customer folders, each with its own layers.
  • Hexagonal or clean style: domain in the center, adapters at the edge.
  • Modules: separate Maven modules enforce dependencies.
  • ArchUnit: tests that check the rules.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Thin controllers: bind input, call one service method and return a response; no SQL or business rules.
  • Services own transactions and rules, such as checking stock before an order.
  • Dependencies point one way: web to service to data, never a repository calling a controller.

Senior Notes

  • Layer leaks: HttpServletRequest in a service or an entity in a JSON response couples layers.
  • Testing by slice: @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories and plain unit tests for services.
  • Over-layering: a service that only forwards calls adds noise; keep layers only where they add value.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Fat controller: rules and queries in the controller.
  • Anemic everything: services that only forward calls.
  • Circular dependencies between services.
  • Transaction in the controller.
  • Entities as API models.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and maintenance:

  • Layers add little runtime cost; proxies are cheap.
  • The real cost is extra mapping code, so keep it simple for small apps.
  • Clear layers let teams work in parallel and speed up tests.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team moves a fat controller into layers.

  • The query and rules move to OrderService.
  • Persistence moves to OrderRepository.
  • The controller only maps HTTP to a service call.
  • Result: tests drop from slow integration tests to fast unit tests.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • AJAX means the browser sends a request in the background with JavaScript and updates part of the page without a full reload.
  • Spring side: a @RestController or a @ResponseBody method returns JSON instead of a view name.
  • Browser side: call the endpoint with fetch() (or XMLHttpRequest) and update the DOM with the result.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test of the JSON endpoint.

Worked Example 2

Send the CSRF token from the page.

Practice Exercise 1

JSON endpoint and fetch call.

Practice Exercise 2

POST JSON from the browser.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens on an AJAX call in Spring MVC:

  • Browser: fetch sends an HTTP request in the background and never navigates.
  • HandlerMapping finds the method; RequestMappingHandlerAdapter invokes it.
  • Arguments: @RequestBody is read by an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson).
  • Return value: @ResponseBody (implied by @RestController) skips view resolution and writes JSON directly.
  • Browser again: JavaScript reads the response and changes the DOM.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

AJAX styles with Spring:

  • JSON API: script builds the HTML.
  • HTML fragment: return a Thymeleaf fragment (products :: rows) and insert it.
  • Htmx: attributes in HTML call fragment endpoints.
  • Server-sent events: SseEmitter pushes updates.
  • jQuery $.ajax: older code uses it.
  • Async Spring: return Callable or DeferredResult for long calls.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • HTTP method and body: use GET to read and POST with @RequestBody to send JSON, and set Content-Type: application/json.
  • Status codes tell the script what happened; return 400 for bad input and 404 for missing data.
  • Partial views: you can also return an HTML fragment (for example a Thymeleaf fragment) and insert it into the page.

Senior Notes

  • CSRF: with Spring Security, AJAX POST calls must send the CSRF token in a header, or they get 403.
  • CORS: a page on another origin needs allowed origins configured, or the browser blocks the call.
  • Message conversion: HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) turns objects into JSON, chosen by the Accept header.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common AJAX mistakes:

  • No Content-Type header: Spring returns 415 Unsupported Media Type.
  • CSRF token missing: 403.
  • CORS not configured: the browser blocks the response, although the server ran the code.
  • Returning a view name from an AJAX method: the script gets HTML or a 404 template error; add @ResponseBody.
  • Not checking response.ok in JavaScript.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Small payloads: return DTOs and page long lists.
  • Caching: add Cache-Control or ETag with ShallowEtagHeaderFilter for rarely changing data.
  • Compression for large JSON.
  • Debounce search-as-you-type calls in the browser.
  • Async handlers free servlet threads during slow work.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: live username check on a sign-up form.

  • On each pause in typing the page calls GET /api/users/exists?name=abaji.
  • The controller returns {"taken":true} using an indexed query.
  • The page shows a message with no reload; the server still checks again on submit.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • AJAX means the browser calls the server in the background with JavaScript and updates part of the page, with no full reload; Spring MVC serves it with ordinary controllers that return data instead of a view name.
  • @ResponseBody (or @RestController) tells Spring to write the return value straight into the HTTP response body instead of resolving a view.
  • Request side: @RequestBody reads a JSON body, while @RequestParam and @PathVariable read query and path values.

Worked Example 1

Return 201 with a body.

Worked Example 2

One controller for pages and AJAX.

Practice Exercise 1

A controller that serves AJAX.

Practice Exercise 2

Test it with MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An AJAX call is an ordinary HTTP request; only the response handling differs.

  • Mapping: DispatcherServlet finds the handler through RequestMappingHandlerMapping.
  • Arguments: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads @RequestBody with a converter chosen by Content-Type.
  • Return value: the same class writes the result when @ResponseBody is present, picking a converter by Accept.
  • No view: the request is marked handled, so no ViewResolver runs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to shape an AJAX endpoint:

  • consumes / produces: limit the media types a method accepts and returns.
  • ResponseEntity: control status, headers and body.
  • @ResponseStatus: a fixed status for simple cases.
  • Async return types: Callable, DeferredResult or CompletableFuture free the request thread during slow work.
  • Streaming: StreamingResponseBody and SseEmitter for large or live output.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • HttpMessageConverter: Jackson (MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter) turns objects to JSON and back, chosen by the Accept and Content-Type headers.
  • Detecting AJAX: libraries often send X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest; fetch does not, so prefer content negotiation over header sniffing.
  • Status codes: return ResponseEntity so the client sees 201, 400 or 404 and can react.

Senior Notes

  • Error handling: use @RestControllerAdvice so failed AJAX calls get a JSON error body, not an HTML error page.
  • CSRF: with Spring Security, AJAX POST calls must send the CSRF token header, or they get 403.
  • Caching and size: set Cache-Control for read endpoints and return only the fields the page needs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • 415 error: the client sent the wrong Content-Type; set application/json.
  • 406 error: no converter can produce the Accept type.
  • HTML error page for AJAX: add a JSON error handler.
  • Missing @ResponseBody: Spring tries to resolve the returned string as a view name and gives a 404 or template error.
  • Missing CSRF header: POST gives 403.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning AJAX endpoints:

  • Payload size: return only needed fields with DTOs and enable server.compression.enabled.
  • Caching: add ETag or Cache-Control to read endpoints.
  • Threads: offload slow calls with async return types so Tomcat threads stay free.
  • Chatty pages: batch several small calls into one endpoint.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json
server.compression.min-response-size=1024
spring.mvc.async.request-timeout=20000

// OUTPUT:
// Responses over 1 KB are gzip compressed; async calls time out after 20 s

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a live search box.

  • The page calls /api/search?q=... after each pause in typing (debounce).
  • The controller returns at most 10 small DTOs.
  • The page shows results with textContent and ignores answers that arrive late.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the text format AJAX calls use to exchange data: objects in braces, arrays in brackets, keys in double quotes.
  • Jackson is the library Spring uses to turn Java objects (records, POJOs) into JSON and back.
  • Headers: send Content-Type: application/json with a request body and Accept: application/json to ask for JSON.

Worked Example 1

Parse JSON by hand with ObjectMapper.

Worked Example 2

Test JSON with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Request and response JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

Customize field names.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JSON conversion is done by Jackson through a Spring converter.

  • Read: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter.read calls ObjectMapper.readValue on the request stream.
  • Write: the same converter calls writeValue on the response stream.
  • Boot ObjectMapper: built by Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder with modules found on the classpath, such as the Java time module.
  • Records: Jackson 2.12+ supports records through their canonical constructor.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful Jackson options:

  • @JsonInclude(NON_NULL): skip null fields.
  • @JsonIgnoreProperties: hide or ignore several fields.
  • @JsonView: different field sets for different endpoints.
  • @JsonCreator: choose the constructor to read.
  • @JsonTypeInfo: polymorphic types (use with care).
  • Properties: spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion, spring.jackson.date-format, spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @RequestBody binds the JSON body to a Java object; a malformed body gives 400 (HttpMessageNotReadableException).
  • Field control: @JsonProperty renames, @JsonIgnore hides and @JsonFormat sets the date pattern.
  • Dates: Jackson in Spring Boot writes java.time types as ISO strings when WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS is off, which is the Boot default.

Senior Notes

  • Never expose entities directly: use DTOs, so lazy relations and internal fields do not leak or cause loops.
  • Unknown fields: Boot sets FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES to false, so extra JSON keys are ignored silently.
  • Security: never enable default typing for untrusted JSON; it allows gadget attacks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Infinite recursion: a bidirectional JPA relation (parent and child point to each other) overflows the stack; use DTOs or @JsonManagedReference with @JsonBackReference.
  • No default constructor: classes without one and without @JsonCreator fail to deserialize.
  • Lazy proxies: serializing an unloaded Hibernate proxy fails; map to a DTO.
  • Number precision: big numbers lose precision in JavaScript; send them as strings.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips:

  • Reuse ObjectMapper: it is thread-safe and costly to create.
  • Smaller output: use DTOs, skip nulls and compress responses.
  • Streaming: for very large lists use a streaming writer instead of building the whole list.
  • Afterburner/Blackbird: optional modules that speed up reflection access.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a dashboard posts a filter object and receives a summary.

  • The page sends JSON with the filter.
  • The server validates it with @Valid and returns a DTO.
  • A bad filter returns 400 with a field error map.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • fetch is the built-in browser function for HTTP calls; it returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object.
  • Basic call: fetch(url).then(r => r.json()), or with async/await: const data = await (await fetch(url)).json().
  • Options: the second argument sets method, headers and body, for example JSON.stringify(obj) for a POST.

Timeout with AbortController.

Worked Example 2

The Spring endpoint it calls.

Practice Exercise 1

GET with async/await.

Practice Exercise 2

POST JSON.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a fetch call travels:

  • Browser: fetch creates a Request, checks CORS rules and sends it with the network stack.
  • Promise: it resolves when the response headers arrive; the body is read later with json() or text().
  • Spring: the request reaches DispatcherServlet like any other, and the CORS filter or @CrossOrigin adds the headers.
  • Body stream: a body can be read only once; call clone() to read it twice.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

fetch option reference:

  • method, headers, body: the request itself.
  • credentials: same-origin, include or omit.
  • cache and mode: control browser cache and CORS mode.
  • signal: cancellation.
  • Body types: string, FormData, URLSearchParams, Blob.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Errors: fetch rejects only on network failure; a 404 or 500 still resolves, so check response.ok yourself.
  • Cookies: same-origin requests send cookies by default in modern browsers; for cross-origin use credentials: "include".
  • CORS: a call to another origin needs the server to allow it, for example with @CrossOrigin or a CorsConfigurationSource.

Senior Notes

  • Timeouts: fetch has none built in; use AbortController with signal to cancel slow calls.
  • CSRF: send the token in a header such as X-CSRF-TOKEN on POST, PUT and DELETE.
  • Preflight: a JSON POST to another origin triggers an OPTIONS request first, and the server must answer it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Assuming errors reject: check res.ok.
  • Forgetting Content-Type: Spring answers 415 for a JSON body without it.
  • Passing an object as body: use JSON.stringify, or the body becomes [object Object].
  • Not awaiting json(): it returns a Promise.
  • Setting Content-Type with FormData: let the browser add the boundary itself.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning fetch usage:

  • Parallel calls: Promise.all for independent requests.
  • Avoid repeats: cache results in memory or rely on ETag responses.
  • Cancel stale calls: abort the previous search when a new one starts.
  • Keep-alive: HTTP/2 on the server removes most connection costs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a React or plain JS front end on port 3000 calls a Spring API on 8080.

  • The browser blocks the call unless Spring allows the origin.
  • Configure CORS once, globally.

  • jQuery AJAX is the older library way to call the server: $.ajax(), plus shortcuts $.get(), $.post() and $.getJSON().
  • Callbacks: success runs on a good response, error on failure and complete always; modern code chains .done() and .fail().
  • Spring side is the same as for any AJAX client: a controller method with @ResponseBody or a @RestController.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside jQuery AJAX:

  • XMLHttpRequest: $.ajax wraps it and returns a jqXHR object that acts like a promise.
  • Defaults: the content type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and data objects are turned into query or form strings.
  • Response: with dataType unset, jQuery guesses from the response Content-Type.
  • Spring: sees a normal request; nothing is jQuery specific.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings you will use most:

  • url, type, data: what to send.
  • contentType, dataType: how to send and parse.
  • headers: extra headers such as CSRF.
  • timeout: milliseconds before failing.
  • async, cache, global: rarely changed.
  • statusCode: handlers for specific codes.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • JSON body: set contentType: "application/json" and data: JSON.stringify(obj); otherwise jQuery sends form-encoded data.
  • dataType tells jQuery how to parse the reply (json, html, text).
  • Form data: $(form).serialize() sends fields as name=value pairs that bind with @ModelAttribute or @RequestParam.

Senior Notes

  • CSRF setup: read the token from a meta tag and add it with $.ajaxSetup or beforeSend.
  • Legacy: new projects usually pick fetch; jQuery is still common in older Spring MVC and JSP apps.
  • Caching: IE-era GET caching is gone, but cache: false appends a timestamp parameter if you need it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Form-encoded body to @RequestBody: gives 415; stringify and set the content type.
  • Synchronous calls: async: false freezes the page and is deprecated.
  • Using the result outside the callback: the value is not ready yet.
  • Not stopping the form submit: the page reloads and cancels the call.
  • Missing CSRF header: 403 on POST.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and set up:

  • Global CSRF: configure once with $.ajaxSetup.
  • Global errors: use $(document).ajaxError for one handler.
  • Slim build: the slim jQuery build has no AJAX, so use the full build.
  • Debounce: do not fire a call on every keystroke.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: migrating a legacy JSP page.

  • Keep the existing jQuery code and add a @RestController next to the old controller.
  • Move to fetch page by page later.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Asynchronous form submission means sending the form data with JavaScript in the background and showing the result on the same page, with no full reload.
  • Steps: listen for the submit event, call preventDefault(), collect the fields (FormData), send them, and show the reply or the errors.
  • Server side: a normal handler with @Valid; on errors it returns 400 and a JSON list of field errors instead of re-rendering the form.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The cycle of an async submit:

  • Intercept: the submit handler calls preventDefault().
  • Collect: new FormData(form) reads every named field.
  • Bind: Spring binds multipart or urlencoded fields to a bean (@ModelAttribute style) or reads JSON with @RequestBody.
  • Validate: the Validator fills a BindingResult or throws MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • Respond: JSON with the saved data or the errors.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • JSON body: @Valid @RequestBody.
  • Form fields: @Valid with a bean and BindingResult.
  • File plus fields: @RequestPart with MultipartFile.
  • ProblemDetail: Spring 6 supports RFC 7807 error bodies with ProblemDetail.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • FormData sends multipart/form-data and supports file upload; to send JSON instead, convert with Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)).
  • Validation: @Valid with a BindingResult or a MethodArgumentNotValidException handler gives field names and messages.
  • Feedback: disable the submit button during the call to stop double submits, and show a success or error message.

Senior Notes

  • Server is the authority: client checks help the user, but always validate again in Spring.
  • Progressive enhancement: keep a working normal POST form and add JavaScript on top, so it still works without scripts.
  • Idempotency: protect against duplicate submits with a token or a unique constraint, since users retry on slow networks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Bean fields not bound: input name attributes do not match the property names.
  • Multipart size limit: raise spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size.
  • No user feedback: errors are logged but not shown.
  • Setting Content-Type by hand with FormData: breaks the boundary.
  • Trusting client checks: bypassable with any HTTP tool.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and usability:

  • Disable the button while pending.
  • Upload progress: fetch has none; use XMLHttpRequest upload events if you need a bar.
  • Limits: set max file and request size.
  • Debounce field-by-field checks such as username availability.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a sign-up form that checks the email while the user types and submits without reload.

  • A GET endpoint answers availability.
  • The POST creates the account and returns 201.
  • A unique database constraint is the final guard against races.

  • Dynamic page updates mean changing part of the visible page, such as a list or a message, after an AJAX call, without loading a new page.
  • Two styles: the server returns JSON and JavaScript builds the HTML, or the server returns an HTML fragment (for example a Thymeleaf fragment) that is inserted into the page.
  • DOM update: use element.textContent for plain text and innerHTML only for trusted markup.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the update reaches the screen:

  • Data arrives as JSON or an HTML string.
  • DOM change: JavaScript edits the DOM tree; the browser then recalculates layout and repaints only what changed.
  • Server fragments: Thymeleaf renders the selected fragment through FragmentExpression handling, returning only that markup.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Update techniques:

  • textContent: safest for text.
  • createElement and append: build nodes without parsing strings.
  • Template element: clone a prepared HTML template.
  • insertAdjacentHTML: fast insert of trusted markup.
  • Libraries: htmx or a front-end framework when pages get complex.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Fragment return: a controller can return "items :: list" to render just one Thymeleaf fragment as the response.
  • Partial refresh: after a POST, re-fetch the list or append the returned item, so the page matches the server.
  • Loading state: show a spinner or disabled state, and handle failures with a visible message.

Senior Notes

  • XSS: never put server or user text into innerHTML unescaped; use textContent or escape the data.
  • Polling or push: for live data use timed polling, Server-Sent Events (SseEmitter) or WebSocket.
  • Back button and URLs: updates by AJAX do not change the URL; use the History API when state should be linkable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • innerHTML with user text: XSS.
  • Stale state: the page shows an item the server rejected; update only after success.
  • Lost event handlers: replacing HTML removes listeners; use event delegation on the parent.
  • Rebuilding the whole list for one change.
  • No error path: a failed call leaves the spinner on.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Batch DOM writes with a document fragment.
  • Update only changed rows.
  • Paginate large lists on the server.
  • Event delegation instead of one listener per row.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order status board that refreshes every 5 seconds.

  • Poll a small JSON endpoint.
  • Update only changed rows.
  • Switch to SSE if polling load grows.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • REST API integration means a page, or a Spring service, consuming JSON endpoints over HTTP: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove.
  • From the browser: JavaScript calls the REST endpoints with fetch; the Spring MVC app can serve both the page and the API.
  • From Spring: server code calls other APIs with RestClient (Spring 6.1+), WebClient or the older RestTemplate.

Worked Example 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside a REST integration:

  • Server: @RestController methods are found by RequestMappingHandlerMapping and run through message converters.
  • RestClient: built on a request factory (JDK client, Apache or Jetty), applies converters and interceptors, and retrieve() turns error statuses into exceptions.
  • Declarative clients: an @HttpExchange interface plus HttpServiceProxyFactory generates the client for you.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choosing a client:

  • RestClient: synchronous, fluent, the modern choice in Spring 6.1+.
  • WebClient: reactive and non-blocking, from spring-webflux.
  • RestTemplate: older and in maintenance mode.
  • OpenFeign: declarative, from Spring Cloud.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Verbs and codes: GET 200, POST 201, DELETE 204, bad input 400, missing 404; map each to the right @GetMapping, @PostMapping and so on.
  • RestClient: build it once, then .get().uri(...).retrieve().body(Type.class); it throws RestClientResponseException on 4xx and 5xx.
  • Serialization: the same Jackson converters handle request and response bodies on both client and server side.

Senior Notes

  • Resilience: set connect and read timeouts, add retries with backoff and a circuit breaker (for example Resilience4j) for remote APIs.
  • Security: pass tokens in the Authorization header and never log them; secure the API with Spring Security.
  • Contract: document the API (OpenAPI) and test integrations with MockRestServiceServer or WireMock.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • No timeouts: a slow remote hangs your threads.
  • Creating a client per call: build once and reuse.
  • Ignoring error statuses: handle 4xx and 5xx explicitly.
  • Logging secrets: tokens in logs.
  • Wrong verb: a GET that changes data, or POST used for reads.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Connection pooling via the HTTP client.
  • Parallel calls with virtual threads or CompletableFuture.
  • Caching of slow, rarely changing replies with @Cacheable.
  • Pagination instead of huge lists.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a checkout page that needs payment status from a partner API.

  • The page calls your own endpoint.
  • Your service calls the partner with a timeout and a fallback.

  • Flow: the controller puts data in the Model and returns a view name; Thymeleaf finds the template and renders HTML.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Thymeleaf renders a page:

  • Controller returns a view name and fills the Model.
  • ThymeleafViewResolver creates a ThymeleafView.
  • Template engine: the template is found, parsed into a tree of events and cached.
  • Processors: each th: attribute has a processor that changes the tree using the Spring EL context built from the model.
  • Output: the result is written to the response writer.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax overview:

  • Text: th:text, th:utext, inline [[...]].
  • Logic: th:if, th:unless, th:switch, th:each.
  • Links and forms: th:href, th:action, th:field, th:object.
  • Attributes: th:attr, th:class, th:classappend.
  • Reuse: th:fragment, th:insert, th:replace.
  • Utilities: #strings, #dates, #lists.

Name 0.00

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Expressions: variable ${...}, selection *{...}, message #{...}, link @{...} and fragment ~{...}.
  • Natural templates: the placeholder text inside a tag shows when the file is opened directly and is replaced when rendered by the server.
  • Escaping: th:text escapes HTML, while th:utext does not and is a risk with user data.

Senior Notes

  • Versus JSP: Thymeleaf needs no servlet container to preview and is the Spring Boot default, while JSP support in Boot is limited.
  • Layouts: reuse parts with th:fragment and th:replace, or with the Layout Dialect add-on.
  • Security: the Spring Security dialect gives sec:authorize and CSRF hidden fields in forms using th:action.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Missing namespace: add xmlns:th="http://www.thymeleaf.org" for editor help.
  • Using th:utext with user data: XSS.
  • Null navigation: use user?.name to avoid errors.
  • Wrong template folder: a template outside templates is not found.
  • String compare with ==: works in SpEL for strings, but compare numbers with the right types.

  • Lean models: pass only what the page needs.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Auto-configuration at work:

  • ThymeleafAutoConfiguration runs when TemplateMode classes are present.
  • Beans created: SpringResourceTemplateResolver, SpringTemplateEngine, ThymeleafViewResolver.
  • Properties: read from ThymeleafProperties (prefix spring.thymeleaf).
  • Back-off: defining your own bean of a type makes Boot skip its version.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Main properties:

  • spring.thymeleaf.cache, prefix, suffix, encoding, mode.
  • spring.thymeleaf.check-template and check-template-location.
  • spring.thymeleaf.enabled to turn it off.
  • spring.thymeleaf.view-names and excluded-view-names to limit which views it handles.
  • spring.thymeleaf.reactive.* for WebFlux.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
spring:
  thymeleaf:
    cache: false
    prefix: classpath:/templates/
    suffix: .html
    view-names: "pages/*,home"
    excluded-view-names: "legacy/*"

# OUTPUT:
# Only view names pages/* and home are rendered by Thymeleaf

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Plain Spring MVC (no Boot) needs three beans: SpringResourceTemplateResolver, SpringTemplateEngine and ThymeleafViewResolver.
  • Prefix and suffix: spring.thymeleaf.prefix and spring.thymeleaf.suffix change where and what templates are found.
  • Template mode: HTML is the default; TEXT and JAVASCRIPT modes render emails and scripts.

Senior Notes

  • Cache: keep caching on in production, because parsing templates on each request is slow.
  • Dialects: add extras (Spring Security dialect, Layout Dialect, Java 8 time) by declaring them as beans or adding the dependency.
  • Check mode: spring.thymeleaf.check-template-location warns when the templates folder is missing.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Caching in dev: edits do not show.
  • Template in the wrong folder or with the wrong suffix.
  • Using @EnableWebMvc in Boot: turns off MVC auto-configuration, including static resources.
  • Mixing JSP and Thymeleaf without view resolver orders.
  • Wrong encoding: accents look broken.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cache on in production.
  • Template cache TTL can be set per resolver with setCacheTTLMs.
  • Devtools disables the cache and reloads on change automatically.
  • Compression for HTML responses.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
<!-- In dev, template edits appear after saving and rebuilding, with no restart of the page cache -->

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: rendering HTML emails with a second engine.

  • The web view resolver handles pages.
  • A separate engine with a classpath resolver for mail/ templates renders email bodies as strings.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Template resolution is how Thymeleaf turns a view name such as home into a real template file, using the prefix, the name and the suffix.
  • Default result: the view name users/list becomes classpath:/templates/users/list.html.
  • Who does it: ThymeleafViewResolver picks the view, and the template engine asks its template resolvers to locate the file.

Worked Example 1

Two resolvers in a chain.

Worked Example 2

Debug the resolved view.

Practice Exercise 1

Name to file mapping.

Practice Exercise 2

Render only a fragment.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution step by step:

  • View name: the controller returns users/list.
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver and then ThymeleafViewResolver (by order) accept the name; redirect: and forward: are handled here without a template.
  • Engine: TemplateEngine.process asks resolvers in order; the first one that finds the template wins.
  • Prefix, name and suffix are joined: classpath:/templates/ + users/list + .html.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolver choices:

  • SpringResourceTemplateResolver: Spring resources (classpath:, file:).
  • ClassLoaderTemplateResolver: from the classpath.
  • FileTemplateResolver: from the file system.
  • UrlTemplateResolver: from a URL.
  • StringTemplateResolver: the name is the template text.
  • Options: order, resolvablePatterns, checkExistence, cacheable.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Resolver chain: several resolvers can be added with an order; each can claim names by resolvablePatterns and pass the rest on.
  • Forms of a name: a plain name uses the prefix and suffix; redirect: and forward: prefixes skip the template and issue a redirect or forward.
  • Fragments: "file :: name" in a controller or th:replace resolves another template, then selects one fragment inside it.

Senior Notes

  • Other sources: resolvers exist for the classpath, the servlet context, files, URLs and even strings or a database.
  • Not found: a missing file gives TemplateInputException, shown as a 500 error with the template name.
  • Case and path: names are case-sensitive on Linux, so Home and home differ; keep one convention.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Leading slash in the view name: /home may fail on some setups.
  • Wrong case of file names.
  • Template next to Java code under src/main/java: not copied to the classpath.
  • Missing checkExistence in a resolver chain: the first resolver throws instead of passing on.
  • Returning a path with suffix: home.html becomes home.html.html.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cache resolved templates (default on).
  • Restrict patterns so each name is checked by one resolver.
  • Avoid checkExistence on the hot path when not needed, since it adds a lookup.
  • Small fragments rendered by selector avoid building a whole page.

# application.properties
logging.level.org.thymeleaf.TemplateEngine.CONFIG=DEBUG

# OUTPUT:
# Logs the resolvers and their order at start up, which helps to find
# why a name is resolved from an unexpected place

Scenario: per-tenant themes.

  • A custom resolver looks for themes/tenant/name.html first.
  • If missing, the default template is used.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A fragment is just a part of a parsed template that the engine can locate by name or selector.

  • Lookup: ~{file :: name} asks the SpringResourceTemplateResolver for templates/file.html.
  • Markup selectors: the engine looks for an element with a matching th:fragment or a CSS-like selector.
  • Context: the fragment runs with the same model variables, locale and request as the page.
  • Parameters: the arguments become local variables inside the fragment.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants:

  • th:insert: inserts the fragment inside the host tag.
  • th:replace: replaces the host tag with the fragment.
  • th:include: deprecated.
  • Selectors: ~{file :: #id} or ~{file :: div.card}.
  • Same file: ~{:: name} refers to the current template.
  • Without wrapper: a fragment can be inside th:block to avoid an extra tag.
codeExamples:
inserted inside
replaced
// OUTPUT: //
...
(insert keeps the host div) //
...
(replace removes the host div) //
...
(selector by id)

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Parameters: a fragment can take arguments, as in th:fragment="alert(type, msg)", and the caller passes them like a method call.
  • Selectors: ~{file :: #id} or a CSS-like selector can include any element, not only one with th:fragment.
  • Conditional include: ~{} is the empty fragment and ~{::} is a no-op, which lets you pick a fragment with a ternary.

Senior Notes

  • Rendering: the fragment is resolved by the same TemplateEngine used for the page, so it sees the same model and locale.
  • Caching: in production the parsed template is cached, so fragment lookup is cheap; turn spring.thymeleaf.cache off only in development.
  • Fragment expressions as arguments: pass markup into a fragment with ~{::selector}, which gives a layout-like effect without extra libraries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong path: including .html or a bad folder gives TemplateInputException; write fragments/footer.
  • Wrong fragment name: a typo gives an empty output or an error.
  • Insert vs replace: using insert leaves nested duplicate tags.
  • Parameter count: calling with the wrong number of arguments fails.
  • Template mode: do not put a fragment of a different mode (text, javascript) in an HTML page.
codeExamples: // OUTPUT: // WRONG: TemplateInputException: Error resolving template [fragments/footer.html] // RIGHT: footer is rendered

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cache on: keep spring.thymeleaf.cache=true in production so templates are parsed once.
  • Small fragments: include small, focused pieces; an enormous page of nested fragments adds lookup cost.
  • Fragment lookups in loops: including a fragment inside a long th:each repeats the lookup, so keep loop bodies simple.
  • HTTP caching: cache static parts at the browser or CDN level.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.thymeleaf.cache=true
spring.thymeleaf.prefix=classpath:/templates/
spring.thymeleaf.suffix=.html

# OUTPUT:
# templates are parsed once and served from the cache (set false only in dev)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: an admin portal with one fragments/ folder holding header, sidebar, pagination(page) and alert(kind, text). Every page reuses them, and a design change touches one file.

Fresher Notes

  • Layout: one master template (menu, header, footer, CSS) that every page reuses, so each page only supplies its own content.
  • Two ways: plain Thymeleaf fragments passed as parameters, or the thymeleaf-layout-dialect library with layout:decorate.
  • Goal: change the site menu in one file and see it on every page.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The layout dialect works as a decorator.

  • Step 1: the content page is processed and its layout:fragment sections are collected.
  • Step 2: the layout named in layout:decorate is loaded.
  • Step 3: content sections replace the same named sections in the layout; the layout head is merged with the page head.
  • Step 4: the merged tree is rendered with the model of the request.
codeExamples: // OUTPUT: // Orders - Shop

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • layout:decorate on the html tag chooses the layout.
  • layout:fragment defines or fills a slot.
  • layout:insert / layout:replace include a fragment where the fragment can itself be decorated.
  • Default dialect-free layout: pass fragment expressions as parameters.
  • Nested layouts: a layout may decorate a bigger layout, for example admin on top of main.
codeExamples:
Admin menu
// OUTPUT: // page -> admin layout -> main layout, three levels merged

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Layout dialect: the page declares layout:decorate="~{layouts/main}" and fills slots with layout:fragment="content".
  • Plain approach: the layout is a fragment with a content parameter; each page calls it with th:replace and passes ~{::main}.
  • Title merging: the layout dialect can combine page and layout titles with layout:title-pattern.

Senior Notes

  • Dependency: the dialect is a separate artifact (nz.net.ultraq.thymeleaf:thymeleaf-layout-dialect), and Spring Boot registers it automatically when it is on the classpath.
  • Processing order: the content page is parsed first, then decorated into the layout, so model data is available in both.
  • Choice: use the fragment approach if you want zero extra dependencies and the dialect if you want a Tiles-like decorator model.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing namespace: without xmlns:layout the editor warns, though it still works.
  • No dependency: layout:decorate is ignored and the page renders without the layout.
  • Slot name mismatch: content in a slot that the layout lacks is dropped.
  • Script placement: page scripts must go in a slot defined near the end of the layout body.
codeExamples:
Orders

// OUTPUT: // the output has an empty content area; fix the name to "content"

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: the decorator step adds a small cost per render, and template caching hides it. For the best speed in hot pages use plain fragment layouts, which need no merge step. Keep the layout light and avoid database calls in it by using @ControllerAdvice with @ModelAttribute for shared menu data, cached in a service.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a shop with three areas (public, customer, admin). One base layout holds CSS and scripts, and two child layouts add sidebars. Each page only writes its main content and is about ten lines long.

  • sec:authorize renders an element only if the expression is true, for example hasRole("ADMIN") or isAuthenticated().
  • sec:authentication prints data about the current user, such as sec:authentication="name".

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The extras module registers a SpringSecurityDialect.

  • sec:authorize: evaluates a Spring Security web expression through the WebSecurityExpressionHandler for the current request.
  • sec:authentication: reads a property of the Authentication object from the SecurityContext.
  • CSRF: a RequestDataValueProcessor adds the hidden token to forms generated by th:action.
  • Boot: auto-configuration registers the dialect when the jar is on the classpath.
codeExamples:
Role: roles

// OUTPUT: (admin user) // Role: [ROLE_ADMIN]

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • isAnonymous() / isAuthenticated() / isFullyAuthenticated() for login state.
  • hasAuthority and hasRole for permissions.
  • sec:authorize-url checks a URL against the filter chain rules.
  • #authorization / #authentication utility objects for use inside expressions.
  • #authorization.expression to compute a boolean for th:if.
codeExamples: Users Log in // OUTPUT: (anonymous) // Log in link only; the Users link is hidden

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • CSRF: a form with th:action gets the hidden CSRF token added automatically when Spring Security is active.
  • Namespace: add xmlns:sec="http://www.thymeleaf.org/extras/spring-security" to the html tag for editor support.
  • Expressions: sec:authorize-url hides a link when the user may not call that URL.

Senior Notes

  • Not a security control: hiding a button is only a UI courtesy; the server side must still protect the URL with authorizeHttpRequests or @PreAuthorize.
  • Security context: the dialect reads the Authentication from the SecurityContextHolder of the current request.
  • Boot 3: use the springsecurity6 artifact for Spring Security 6; the older springsecurity5 one does not match.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong artifact: springsecurity5 with Spring Security 6 shows nothing or fails.
  • UI only: forgetting server side rules lets users open hidden URLs.
  • Role prefix: hasRole("ADMIN") checks ROLE_ADMIN; use hasAuthority for exact names.
  • Plain HTML form: a form with action instead of th:action has no CSRF token and POST returns 403.
codeExamples:
<!-- WRONG: no CSRF token added -->
<form action="/logout" method="post"><button>Out</button></form>
<!-- RIGHT -->
<form th:action="@{/logout}" method="post"><button>Out</button></form>

// OUTPUT:
// WRONG: 403 Forbidden (Invalid CSRF Token)
// RIGHT: logout succeeds

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: the dialect evaluates expressions per request using the existing context, so the cost is small. Avoid many sec:authorize-url checks in loops, because each one runs the matcher chain. Compute a boolean once in the controller or a th:with variable for repeated use.
codeExamples: // OUTPUT: // the role is evaluated once and reused for both buttons

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a back-office app with roles USER, MANAGER and ADMIN. Menus, buttons and columns change by role in the template, while SecurityFilterChain rules and @PreAuthorize enforce the same rules on the server.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Unit test: checks one class in isolation, with no Spring context, no server and no database, so it runs in milliseconds.
  • Tools: JUnit 5 to structure the test and Mockito to fake collaborators.
  • Arrange, act, assert: set up the data, call the method, then check the result.

Worked Example 1

Controller as a plain object.

Worked Example 2

Run only unit tests with Maven.

Practice Exercise 1

A pure unit test.

Practice Exercise 2

Fixed clock.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A unit test is run by JUnit alone.

  • Discovery: the JUnit Platform finds classes and methods marked with @Test.
  • Instance: a new test object is created per method.
  • Mocks: Mockito creates subclasses or inline mocks at runtime with ByteBuddy.
  • No container: no ApplicationContext starts, so no beans, proxies or auto-configuration exist.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful styles:

  • Plain JUnit: for pure logic.
  • MockitoExtension: for classes with dependencies.
  • @Nested: to group scenarios.
  • @ParameterizedTest: for tables of cases.
  • AssertJ: fluent, readable checks.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Plain objects: a controller or service is a normal Java class, so you can create it with new and pass mocks to its constructor.
  • Constructor injection makes this easy; field injection forces you to use @InjectMocks or reflection.
  • Test pyramid: write many fast unit tests, fewer slice tests and few full integration tests.

Senior Notes

  • No framework behaviour: a unit test does not check @RequestMapping, validation or JSON conversion, because no DispatcherServlet is involved; use MockMvc for that.
  • Determinism: inject a Clock or supplier instead of calling LocalDate.now() so time based logic is testable.
  • Naming: a name like shouldReturnEmptyWhenUserMissing describes behaviour and reads well in reports.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Starting Spring for plain logic: remove @SpringBootTest and use new.
  • Testing the mock: an assertion that only checks a stubbed value proves nothing.
  • Shared static state: tests that depend on order are flaky.
  • Real time or random: inject a Clock or a seed.
  • Many asserts about unrelated things: split the test.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: thousands of unit tests should finish in seconds. Keep them free of I/O and sleeps, run them in parallel when they are independent (junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=true) and run them first in the build so failures show early.
codeExamples:
# src/test/resources/junit-platform.properties
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=true
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default=concurrent

# OUTPUT:
# independent test classes run on several threads (varies by machine)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a team keeps business rules in plain service classes, covers them with hundreds of unit tests that run in the commit stage of the CI pipeline, and keeps only a few slow tests for the full application.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller test: checks request mapping, parameter binding, validation, status codes and the view or JSON response.
  • @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, advice, converters, filters) and gives you an auto-configured MockMvc.
  • Collaborators such as services are replaced with @MockBean, so no database is needed.

Worked Example 1

Test a view controller.

Worked Example 2

Not found handling.

Practice Exercise 1

GET test with a mocked service.

Practice Exercise 2

POST with validation failure.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How @WebMvcTest works inside.

  • Context: it uses a type filter that keeps only @Controller, @ControllerAdvice, @JsonComponent, converters, filters and WebMvcConfigurer.
  • Auto-config: only web related auto-configuration is applied.
  • MockMvc: built on the context and driven through the real DispatcherServlet, handler mappings, argument resolvers and message converters.
  • Mocks: @MockBean beans are registered in the context in place of real ones.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • @WebMvcTest(controllers = X.class): limit the slice to one controller.
  • @Import: add a security config or a converter that the slice skipped.
  • @WithMockUser, csrf(): for secured endpoints.
  • ObjectMapper: autowire it to build request JSON.
  • @TestConfiguration: add small test beans.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Perform and expect: mvc.perform(get("/x")) followed by andExpect(status().isOk()) and checks on the view, model or body.
  • JSON: send a body with contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content(json) and read it with jsonPath.
  • Validation: post bad data and expect status().isBadRequest() or model().attributeHasFieldErrors.

Senior Notes

  • Slice limits: @WebMvcTest does not load @Service or @Repository beans, so a missing @MockBean shows up as a context failure.
  • Security: Spring Security is active in the slice, so add @WithMockUser and csrf() for POST requests.
  • Stubbing: use when(service.find(1L)).thenReturn(...) to control what the controller sees.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing @MockBean: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException for the service.
  • 403 on POST: add csrf() and a user.
  • Using @SpringBootTest everywhere: slow, when a slice is enough.
  • Hand-written JSON strings: they break on rename; serialize with ObjectMapper.
  • Not checking the failure path: test 400, 404 and 500 mapping too.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: slices start much faster than the full context. Contexts are cached by configuration, so many test classes with the same @MockBean set share one context. A different @MockBean set in each class creates a new context each time, so put shared mocks in a base class or a @TestConfiguration.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a REST API has a controller test for every endpoint covering success, validation error, not found and forbidden. These tests act as living documentation of the contract, and they catch changes in status codes and JSON fields before release.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Service test: checks business rules in a @Service class, with the repository replaced by a mock.
  • Setup: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), @Mock for dependencies and @InjectMocks for the class under test.
  • No Spring: the test is a plain JUnit test, so it needs no context and runs very fast.

Worked Example 1

Capture the saved entity.

Worked Example 2

Constructor injection keeps tests simple.

Practice Exercise 1

Happy path.

Practice Exercise 2

Error path.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the service test works inside.

  • MockitoExtension: before each test it creates fields annotated with @Mock, then builds the @InjectMocks object (constructor first, then setter, then field).
  • Strictness: the extension uses strict stubs, so unused stubbing fails the test.
  • No proxies: annotations like @Transactional and @Cacheable do nothing here.
  • After: mocks are reset and the extension checks for unused stubs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • BDD style: given(...).willReturn(...) and then(mock).should().save(...) from BDDMockito.
  • Answers: thenAnswer to return the argument.
  • InOrder: check the order of calls.
  • lenient(): allow an unused stub in a shared setup.
  • Real collaborators: use a small fake or in-memory repository instead of a mock when behaviour is simple.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Stub with when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(user)) and verify with verify(repo).save(any()).
  • Exceptions: assert business errors with assertThrows(OrderNotFoundException.class, () -> svc.get(9L)).
  • Captors: use ArgumentCaptor to inspect the entity the service passes to save.

Senior Notes

  • Transactions (@Transactional) are proxy behaviour and are not active in a plain unit test; test rollback in an integration test.
  • Strict stubs: Mockito reports unused stubbing, which keeps tests honest, so remove stubs that are not needed.
  • Do not mock the class under test and do not mock simple value objects; mock only collaborators across a boundary.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Mocking everything: a test that only repeats the implementation breaks on every refactor.
  • Field injection in the service: @InjectMocks may leave a field null; use constructor injection.
  • Ignoring the return value: forgetting to assert the result.
  • Unused stubs: UnnecessaryStubbingException.
  • Testing the repository query with a mock: use @DataJpaTest for real queries.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: service tests are the cheapest valuable tests and should run in milliseconds. Avoid Thread.sleep, build test data with small builder methods, and keep a single shared fixture class for reusable objects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a payment service has rules for limits, currency and duplicates. Each rule has its own test, and the repository and the gateway are mocked. The tests document the rules and protect them during refactoring.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Integration test: starts the real Spring context and checks that controller, service, repository and database work together.
  • @SpringBootTest loads the whole application; add @AutoConfigureMockMvc to call it with MockMvc.
  • Database: use an in-memory H2 database or a Testcontainers container so tests do not touch real data.

Worked Example 1

Test properties.
codeExamples:
# src/test/resources/application-test.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop

# OUTPUT:
# the test profile uses an in-memory database that disappears after the run

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Naming convention.

Practice Exercise 1

Full flow with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 2

Real server on a random port.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How an integration test runs inside.

  • Bootstrap: @SpringBootTest finds the @SpringBootConfiguration class and starts the full context.
  • Cache: the ContextCache reuses contexts that have the same key (configuration, profiles, properties, mock beans).
  • Transactions: TransactionalTestExecutionListener starts a transaction before the test and rolls it back after.
  • Web: MOCK mode uses a MockServletContext; RANDOM_PORT starts embedded Tomcat.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • @DataJpaTest: a repository slice with an embedded database.
  • @Testcontainers: a real MySQL or PostgreSQL in Docker.
  • @DynamicPropertySource: point properties at the container.
  • @Sql: load test data from a script.
  • @MockBean: replace external clients such as a payment gateway.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • webEnvironment: MOCK (default) uses a mock servlet; RANDOM_PORT starts a real server and you call it with TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient.
  • @Transactional on a test class rolls back each test, which keeps data clean for the next one.
  • Profiles: @ActiveProfiles("test") loads application-test.properties.

Senior Notes

  • Context caching: Spring reuses a context between tests with the same configuration, so avoid unneeded @MockBean or @DirtiesContext, which force a rebuild.
  • Real server rollback: with RANDOM_PORT the test and the server run in different threads, so test rollback does not apply and you must clean data yourself.
  • Speed: keep few integration tests for key flows and cover details with unit and slice tests.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • @DirtiesContext everywhere: rebuilds the context and slows the suite.
  • Data left behind: tests depend on each other; roll back or clean up.
  • Real external calls: mock or stub third-party services.
  • H2 differences: SQL that works in H2 but fails in MySQL; use Testcontainers for critical queries.
  • Hard-coded port: use @LocalServerPort.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: the largest cost is context start-up. Keep configurations identical across test classes so the cache is reused, use slices where possible, share one container for all tests with a static field, and run integration tests in a separate build phase with Failsafe.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: before each release the pipeline runs integration tests for the main journeys, such as register, login, place order and pay. They run against a containerized database and a stubbed payment gateway, and they catch wiring and mapping errors that unit tests cannot see.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • JUnit 5 is the standard Java test framework; it is made of Platform, Jupiter (the API you write) and Vintage (for old JUnit 4 tests).
  • Basics: mark a method with @Test and check results with assertEquals, assertTrue and assertThrows.
