  • Spring Boot: spring-boot-starter-test already includes JUnit 5, Mockito and AssertJ.

Worked Example 1

Assert an exception.

Worked Example 2

Grouped assertions.

Practice Exercise 1

Lifecycle and assertions.

Practice Exercise 2

Parameterized test.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JUnit 5 is modular.

  • Platform: launches test engines and reports results to Maven, Gradle or the IDE.
  • Jupiter engine: discovers @Test methods and runs the lifecycle.
  • Extension model: callbacks such as BeforeEachCallback and ParameterResolver let extensions like SpringExtension inject beans into test parameters.
  • Per-method instance: a fresh object for each test unless @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) is used.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • @Disabled, @EnabledOnOs, @EnabledIfSystemProperty: conditional tests.
  • @RepeatedTest(n): repeat a test.
  • @Timeout: fail slow tests.
  • @TestMethodOrder: control order when you must.
  • @Tag: group tests for the build.
  • @MethodSource, @EnumSource: more parameter sources.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lifecycle: @BeforeEach and @AfterEach run around each test; @BeforeAll and @AfterAll run once and are static by default.
  • Parameterized: @ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource or @CsvSource runs one test for many inputs.
  • Readable reports: @DisplayName and @Nested group and describe tests.

Senior Notes

  • Extensions: @ExtendWith adds behaviour; SpringExtension (inside @SpringBootTest) and MockitoExtension are examples.
  • Instance per method: JUnit creates a new test class instance for every test, so fields are not shared between tests.
  • Assertions: assertAll reports all failures together, and AssertJ gives fluent checks such as assertThat(list).hasSize(2).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Mixing JUnit 4 and 5 imports: org.junit.Test is ignored by Jupiter.
  • Non-static @BeforeAll: fails unless PER_CLASS.
  • Test order dependence: tests share state.
  • Swapped arguments: assertEquals(actual, expected) gives confusing messages.
  • Catching exceptions manually: use assertThrows.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: enable parallel execution for independent tests, tag slow tests and run them in a separate stage, and avoid heavy work in @BeforeEach; move expensive setup to @BeforeAll when tests only read the data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: the build runs mvn test on every push. Failing tests block the merge, reports are published by the CI server, and tags let the nightly build run slow tests that the normal build skips.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Mockito creates fake objects (mocks) so you can test a class without its real collaborators.
  • Core calls: mock(Type.class) or @Mock, when(...).thenReturn(...) to stub and verify(...) to check interactions.
  • Default: an unstubbed mock method returns null, 0, false or an empty collection.

Worked Example 1

ArgumentCaptor.

Worked Example 2

Spy on a real list.

Practice Exercise 1

Stub and verify.

Practice Exercise 2

Argument matchers and void methods.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Mockito works inside.

  • Creation: it generates a subclass or uses inline instrumentation with ByteBuddy, so the mock intercepts every call.
  • Recording: a call inside when(...) is remembered as the ongoing stubbing, and thenReturn attaches the answer.
  • Matching: on each call it looks for a matching stub, newest first.
  • Verification: every invocation is stored, and verify compares the list with the expected calls.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • thenReturn / thenThrow / thenAnswer: result, exception or computed value.
  • Consecutive calls: thenReturn(1, 2, 3).
  • verify modes: times, never, atLeastOnce, atMost.
  • Deep stubs: RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS for chained calls.
  • BDDMockito: given, willReturn, then.
  • MockedStatic: mock static methods inside a try-with-resources.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Matchers: any(), eq(5) and anyString(); if you use a matcher for one argument you must use matchers for all of them.
  • Void methods: use doThrow(new X()).when(mock).method() or doNothing() instead of when.
  • Spy: spy(realObject) keeps real behaviour and lets you stub only some methods.

Senior Notes

  • Mock vs @MockBean: @Mock is plain Mockito; @MockBean replaces a bean inside the Spring context.
  • Limits: Mockito cannot stub static methods by default; mockStatic exists but is a design smell in most cases.
  • Over-verifying ties tests to implementation details; verify outcomes and important calls, not every call.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Stubbing a final or static method without inline mock maker or mockStatic.
  • Mixing matchers and values: eq() for the rest.
  • Stubbing a spy with when: it calls the real method; use doReturn.
  • Mocking value types like String or a DTO: create real ones.
  • Verifying getters: verifies implementation, not behaviour.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: creating mocks is cheap but not free. Use @Mock with the extension rather than creating mocks in loops, avoid deep stubs in hot tests, and prefer small real objects for plain data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a notification service calls an email client and an SMS client. Tests mock both, check that the email is sent when the user prefers it, that the SMS is never used, and that a failure of the email client is handled with a retry.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MockMvc sends fake HTTP requests to your controllers through the real DispatcherServlet logic, without a network or server.
  • Flow: mvc.perform(request) returns a ResultActions that you check with andExpect(...).
  • Builders: get, post, put, delete from MockMvcRequestBuilders and matchers from MockMvcResultMatchers.

Worked Example 1

Standalone set-up.

Worked Example 2

Read the result.

Practice Exercise 1

GET with parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect after POST.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How MockMvc works inside.

  • Request: the builder creates a MockHttpServletRequest with path, params, headers and body.
  • Dispatch: the request goes through the filter chain (if registered) and DispatcherServlet.doDispatch, which uses the real handler mapping, argument resolvers, validators, return value handlers and exception resolvers.
  • Response: a MockHttpServletResponse records status, headers and body.
  • Result: MvcResult gives access to the handler, model, view and response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Setup: @AutoConfigureMockMvc, webAppContextSetup, standaloneSetup.
  • Default request: defaultRequest(...) and apply(springSecurity()).
  • Filters: addFilters(...) in a manual build.
  • Spring 6.2 and Boot 3.4: MockMvcTester offers AssertJ style assertions.
  • Multipart: multipart(...).file(...).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request details: add param, header, contentType, content, cookie and sessionAttr.
  • Result checks: status(), content(), jsonPath(), view(), model(), header(), redirectedUrl().
  • Debug: andDo(print()) writes the full request and response to the console.

Senior Notes

  • Three set-ups: auto-configured through @WebMvcTest or @AutoConfigureMockMvc; webAppContextSetup for a full context; standaloneSetup(controller) for a quick isolated test.
  • Not a real server: no port, no real servlet container features such as error pages from the container, so some behaviour differs from production.
  • Async: for Callable or DeferredResult results use asyncStarted() and then asyncDispatch(result).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Expecting a followed redirect: check the redirect URL instead.
  • No content type on POST body: gives 415.
  • Missing Accept header: may give 406 for JSON.
  • Forgetting charset or encoding for non-ASCII text in content().string.
  • Assuming container behaviour: error pages and some filters are not part of MockMvc.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: MockMvc is fast because it skips networking. Keep the set-up small (@WebMvcTest over full context), reuse one MockMvc per class, and avoid print() in the normal run since it makes the output very long.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real world: a team documents its REST API with tests. Each MockMvc test checks status, headers and JSON fields, and the same tests can feed Spring REST Docs to generate accurate API documentation.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @WebMvcTest is a test slice annotation that starts only the web layer (controllers, advice, filters, converters) and not services or repositories.
  • MockMvc is auto-configured and injected with @Autowired; you call mockMvc.perform(get("/x")) without a real server or port.
  • Collaborators such as services are replaced with @MockBean (or @MockitoBean in newer Spring), so the test checks only the controller.

Worked Example 1

JSON endpoint check.

Worked Example 2

Not found mapping.

Practice Exercise 1

Minimal controller slice test.

Practice Exercise 2

Missing mock fails the context.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

@WebMvcTest is a slice: a meta-annotation that limits auto-configuration.

  • Meta-annotations: it carries @BootstrapWith(WebMvcTestContextBootstrapper), @ExtendWith(SpringExtension) and @AutoConfigureWebMvc.
  • Type filter: a TypeExcludeFilter keeps only @Controller, @ControllerAdvice, @JsonComponent, Converter, Filter, WebMvcConfigurer and similar beans.
  • Auto-config: only the imports listed for the slice are applied, so no DataSource or JPA.
  • MockMvc: built from the web application context and wired to the DispatcherServlet with no network.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • @WebMvcTest with no class scans all controllers.
  • @WebMvcTest(controllers = {A.class, B.class}) targets several.
  • @AutoConfigureMockMvc(addFilters = false) skips security filters.
  • @MockBean / @MockitoBean, @SpyBean for collaborators.
  • @Import and @TestConfiguration for extra beans.
  • @WithMockUser for authenticated tests.
  • Properties via properties = ....

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Target one controller with @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) so the context stays small and fast.
  • Assertions use andExpect(status().isOk()), content() and jsonPath() from the MockMvc result matchers.
  • Not included: @Service, @Repository and @Component beans are not scanned, so a missing mock gives a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.

Senior Notes

  • Security auto-configuration is applied, so requests may return 401 or 403 unless you add @WithMockUser or a test security config.
  • Custom beans needed by the slice (a converter, a config class) must be added with @Import.
  • Speed: slices share a cached context when the configuration is identical, so keep mock sets consistent across test classes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing @MockBean gives UnsatisfiedDependencyException; add a mock for each constructor dependency.
  • Expecting JPA: repositories are not loaded; mock them or use @DataJpaTest separately.
  • 401/403 surprise: add @WithMockUser, csrf() or import your security config.
  • Using @SpringBootTest for everything makes the suite slow.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Slices start in a fraction of the time of a full context because few beans exist.
  • The context cache is keyed by configuration, so share the same @MockBean set across classes via a common base class.
  • Avoid @DirtiesContext unless state truly leaks.
  • Run with parallel test classes only if tests do not share mutable mocks.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team has 120 controller tests and the build takes 9 minutes because each uses @SpringBootTest.

  • Move controller tests to @WebMvcTest with a shared base class.
  • Keep a handful of @SpringBootTest tests for the critical flows.
  • The controller suite drops to about a minute.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • @SpringBootTest loads the full application context, as if the app were started, so it tests real wiring of controllers, services and repositories.
  • webEnvironment controls the server: MOCK (default, no real port), RANDOM_PORT and DEFINED_PORT start an embedded server.
  • Slower than slices, so use it for a few end-to-end checks and use @WebMvcTest for most controller tests.

Worked Example 1

Override a property in a test.

Worked Example 2

Test profile.

Practice Exercise 1

Full context with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 2

Real HTTP on a random port.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How @SpringBootTest builds its context:

  • Bootstrapper: SpringBootTestContextBootstrapper finds the @SpringBootConfiguration by searching up from the test package.
  • Environment: MOCK creates a mock servlet web application context; RANDOM_PORT starts the embedded Tomcat on port 0.
  • Properties: the order is test properties, command-line args, then application.properties files.
  • Caching: the merged context configuration is the cache key.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • classes = App.class picks the configuration explicitly.
  • webEnvironment: MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT, NONE.
  • properties inline overrides.
  • @ActiveProfiles, @TestPropertySource, @Sql for data.
  • @AutoConfigureMockMvc, @AutoConfigureTestDatabase.
  • @Testcontainers with @ServiceConnection.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • RANDOM_PORT with TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient sends real HTTP requests; inject the port with @LocalServerPort.
  • @AutoConfigureMockMvc adds MockMvc to a full-context test when you want speed without a real server.
  • Profiles and properties: use @ActiveProfiles("test") or @TestPropertySource to point at a test database.

Senior Notes

  • Context caching: Spring reuses a context across test classes with the same config; @MockBean or @DirtiesContext create new contexts and slow the suite.
  • Real databases: prefer Testcontainers over H2 when behavior must match production, wired with @ServiceConnection in Boot 3.1+.
  • Transactions: @Transactional rolls back in MOCK mode but not with RANDOM_PORT because the server runs on another thread.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Using it for unit logic: slow; test services with plain JUnit and Mockito.
  • Shared database state between tests; clean with @Sql or roll back.
  • Rollback assumption with RANDOM_PORT: data stays committed.
  • Hard-coded port: use RANDOM_PORT and @LocalServerPort.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Each new context costs seconds; reuse it across classes.
  • Limit @MockBean variety, since each combination makes a new context.
  • Use spring.main.lazy-initialization=true in tests to start faster.
  • Consider Testcontainers reuse and a singleton container for the suite.
codeExamples:
# src/test/resources/application-test.properties
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
logging.level.root=WARN

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Context start time: 3.4 s -> 2.1 s with lazy initialization

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: before a release, a smoke test boots the real app against a Postgres container and walks through create order, pay, and fetch.

  • Uses RANDOM_PORT and TestRestTemplate.
  • Catches wiring, serialization and migration issues that slices miss.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Controller mocking means testing a controller in isolation by replacing its dependencies (services) with mocks, so only the web logic is verified.
  • @MockBean puts a Mockito mock into the Spring context; when(...).thenReturn(...) defines its answers.
  • verify checks that the controller called the service as expected, for example verify(service).save(any()).

Worked Example 1

Capture the argument.

Worked Example 2

Stub an exception.

Practice Exercise 1

Stub and verify.

Practice Exercise 2

Standalone setup without Spring.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How mocks enter the controller:

  • @MockBean: the test context post-processor replaces or registers a bean definition with a Mockito mock of that type.
  • Injection: the controller receives the mock through its constructor, just like the real service.
  • Reset: mocks are reset after each test method by default.
  • Standalone: @InjectMocks uses Mockito reflection, no Spring.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mockito features useful here:

  • when().thenReturn(), thenThrow(), thenAnswer().
  • doNothing().when(mock).delete(1L) for void methods.
  • verify(mock, times(1)), never(), verifyNoMoreInteractions().
  • ArgumentMatchers: any(), eq(), argThat().
  • BDDMockito: given().willReturn().

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Two styles: @WebMvcTest with @MockBean, or standalone MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(controller) with @Mock and no Spring context.
  • Stubbing errors with thenThrow(...) lets you check that the controller or advice maps the exception to the right status.
  • ArgumentCaptor captures the object the controller built from the request so you can assert on its fields.

Senior Notes

  • Do not over-mock: asserting every call couples tests to implementation; verify only meaningful interactions.
  • Strict stubs: Mockito reports unused stubs with MockitoExtension, which catches dead test setup.
  • Standalone setup skips advice, converters and validation unless you add them (setControllerAdvice, setValidator).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Mixing raw values and matchers in one call: eq(1L) with a literal fails with InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
  • Unstubbed call returns null or empty, producing confusing 200 responses with empty bodies.
  • Mocking the controller itself, which tests nothing.
  • Stubbing after perform.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and hygiene:

  • Plain Mockito tests with standaloneSetup start in milliseconds.
  • Use the same @MockBean set across classes to keep the context cached.
  • Enable strict stubs (MockitoExtension) to remove unused stubbing.
  • Keep verify calls to meaningful interactions.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the payment controller must return 402 when the service reports a declined card, without touching any payment gateway.

  • Stub the service to throw CardDeclinedException.
  • Assert status 402 and a clear message.
  • Verify that no receipt email was triggered.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request testing builds an HTTP request with MockMvcRequestBuilders (get, post, put, delete) and sends it with perform.
  • Request data is set with param, header, contentType, content, cookie and path variables in the URL template.
  • Goal: prove that mappings, binding of path, query, header and body values, and content negotiation work.

Worked Example 1

File upload.

Worked Example 2

Debug with print().

Practice Exercise 1

Query, path and header.

Practice Exercise 2

JSON POST with ObjectMapper.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

What happens inside perform:

  • Builder: a MockHttpServletRequestBuilder produces a MockHttpServletRequest with URI, params, headers and body.
  • Dispatch: MockMvc runs the filter chain, then the DispatcherServlet in the same thread.
  • Mapping: HandlerMapping finds the method, argument resolvers bind path, query and body, and message converters read JSON.
  • Result: a ResultActions object exposes the response for matchers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Builder options:

  • Verbs: get, post, put, patch, delete, options, head.
  • param, queryParam, formField (6.1+), header, cookie.
  • accept, contentType, content, locale.
  • sessionAttr, flashAttr, requestAttr.
  • principal and with(postProcessor).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Path variables: get("/users/{id}", 5) expands the template with the arguments.
  • JSON body: set contentType(APPLICATION_JSON) and pass a string, or serialize an object with ObjectMapper.
  • Form and multipart: use param for forms and multipart("/upload").file(...) for uploads.

Senior Notes

  • Missing content type gives 415 Unsupported Media Type; a missing @RequestParam gives 400.
  • CSRF: with Spring Security, POST tests need .with(csrf()) or they return 403.
  • Print on failure: andDo(print()) shows the full request and response for debugging.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing Content-Type gives 415.
  • Wrong param kind: param for a JSON body parameter never binds.
  • Hand-written JSON with escaping errors; use ObjectMapper.
  • Forgot csrf() on secured POST gives 403.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and reuse:

  • MockMvc requests are in-memory and take about a millisecond.
  • Create small helper methods or a request factory for common headers.
  • Use defaultRequest on the builder for headers sent on every call.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API reads a tenant from a header and a page size from a query string.

  • Test missing header (400), invalid size (400) and valid case (200).
  • Prevents regressions in binding defaults.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Response testing asserts the result of perform with andExpect and matchers for status, headers, content type and body.
  • Common matchers: status(), header(), content(), jsonPath(), view(), model() and redirectedUrl().
  • jsonPath reads values from the JSON body, for example jsonPath("$.items.length()").value(3).

Worked Example 1

Redirect after POST.

Worked Example 2

Read body into an object.

Practice Exercise 1

Status, header and JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

View and model.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How matchers work:

  • ResultMatcher: a functional interface taking an MvcResult; andExpect runs it and throws AssertionError on mismatch.
  • jsonPath: uses Jayway JsonPath on the response string; a path that finds nothing fails.
  • content().json: uses JSONassert for lenient or strict compare.
  • Async: for Callable or DeferredResult use asyncStarted() then asyncDispatch(result).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Matcher families:

  • status(), header(), cookie().
  • content(): string, json, contentType, xml.
  • jsonPath() with value, exists, isArray, hasJsonPath.
  • view(), model(), forwardedUrl(), redirectedUrl(), flash().
  • Hamcrest matchers like hasSize and containsString.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status helpers: isOk(), isCreated(), isBadRequest(), isNotFound() read better than raw numbers.
  • Whole-body compare: content().json(expected) compares JSON leniently by default, ignoring field order.
  • View tests: for MVC pages use view().name("home") and model().attribute("user", ...).

Senior Notes

  • Strict vs lenient: content().json(json, true) is strict and fails on extra fields.
  • Extract the result with andReturn() when you need to deserialize the body and assert in plain Java.
  • AssertJ style: Spring 6.2 adds MockMvcTester for fluent assertions, but classic matchers remain the common choice.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • String equality on JSON breaks on field order or spacing.
  • Wrong path: $.items[0] vs $[0] for a root array.
  • Lenient json hiding extra fields when a contract needs strict.
  • Dates: compare formatted strings, which depend on Jackson settings.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and clarity:

  • Combine several matchers in one chain to reuse a single request.
  • Use andDo(print()) only when debugging; it is noisy.
  • Use @AutoConfigureMockMvc(print = MockMvcPrint.NONE) to silence default printing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a public API contract says paged results have content, page and total.

  • One test locks these fields and the content type.
  • Any rename in a DTO fails the build before clients break.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Exception testing checks that errors thrown by controllers or services are turned into the right HTTP status and body, usually by @ExceptionHandler or @RestControllerAdvice.
  • Stub a failure with when(service.find(9L)).thenThrow(new NotFoundException()) and assert status().isNotFound().
  • @WebMvcTest includes @ControllerAdvice beans automatically, so the real error mapping is exercised.

Worked Example 1

Resolved exception type.

Worked Example 2

Method not allowed.

Practice Exercise 1

Not found mapped by advice.

Practice Exercise 2

Unhandled exception.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How exceptions flow in MockMvc:

  • The handler method throws.
  • DispatcherServlet asks its HandlerExceptionResolver chain: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver (your advice), ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • If one resolves it, the response is built and no exception escapes.
  • If none does, the exception propagates out of perform because MockMvc has no container error page.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • @ExceptionHandler in the controller or in an advice.
  • @ResponseStatus on the exception class.
  • ResponseStatusException thrown directly.
  • ProblemDetail via ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled.
  • Test helpers: getResolvedException(), assertThatThrownBy.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Error body: assert the JSON that your advice returns, such as jsonPath("$.message"), or an RFC 7807 ProblemDetail with $.title.
  • Framework exceptions map to codes by default: MethodArgumentNotValidException to 400, HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException to 405.
  • Unhandled exceptions surface from MockMvc as a ServletException (NestedServletException in old versions) instead of a 500 response.

Senior Notes

  • assertThrows trap: with MockMvc an unhandled exception is thrown by perform, so wrap the call in assertThatThrownBy to test it.
  • resolvedException() returns the exception that a resolver handled, letting you assert its type.
  • Do not leak stack traces: assert that the body has no trace field in production-like config.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • assertThrows around a handled exception: nothing is thrown, the test fails.
  • Advice not in slice: a plain @Component advice-like class is not picked up; use @ControllerAdvice.
  • Catch-all handler hiding bugs as 500 with the same body.
  • Wrong handler order when two handlers match; the most specific type wins.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and quality:

  • Keep one test per exception type in the advice.
  • Make error bodies stable with a shared record such as ApiError.
  • Log server errors once, in the advice, not in every catch block.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: mobile clients depend on error codes.

  • A test table checks each exception type against its status and code.
  • When a developer adds a new exception without a handler, the test for 500 fails and flags it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Validation testing sends valid and invalid input and asserts that Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotBlank, @Size) rejects bad data with HTTP 400.
  • Constraint annotations on a DTO are checked when the controller parameter has @Valid or @Validated.
  • Failure type: a bad @RequestBody throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring maps to 400 by default.

Worked Example 1

Valid request passes.

Worked Example 2

Form field error.

Practice Exercise 1

Invalid body returns 400.

Practice Exercise 2

DTO validator unit test.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The validation path:

  • Argument resolver: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor reads the body, then calls the Validator because of @Valid.
  • Binding result: violations become FieldError objects; with no BindingResult parameter the controller call is aborted with MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • Resolver: DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver sets 400, or your advice builds the body.
  • Validator: Hibernate Validator, auto-configured by Boot when spring-boot-starter-validation is present.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • @Valid vs @Validated (groups, class-level for parameters).
  • Constraints: @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Pattern, @Positive, @Past.
  • Custom @Constraint with a ConstraintValidator.
  • BindingResult after the parameter for manual handling.
  • Nested objects need @Valid on the field.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Check field errors: with an advice returning a map, assert jsonPath("$.errors.name"); for forms use model().attributeHasFieldErrors("user", "name").
  • Unit-test the DTO alone with Validation.buildDefaultValidatorFactory().getValidator() to test constraints without MVC.
  • Path and query constraints need @Validated on the controller class and give ConstraintViolationException (400 in Spring 6.1+ with HandlerMethodValidationException).

Senior Notes

  • Missing @Valid means no validation at all, a silent bug that only a negative test finds.
  • Test both sides: one valid request expecting 201 and several invalid ones, each with a single broken field.
  • Custom validators that need beans work in @WebMvcTest only if their dependencies are mocked or imported.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No @Valid: constraints silently ignored.
  • Nested object without @Valid: inner fields not checked.
  • Starter missing: no validator bean, annotations do nothing.
  • Primitive defaults: int age is 0 when absent; use Integer with @NotNull to detect it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Validator creation is costly; Boot shares one bean, so do not build factories per call.
  • Cheap constraints first; avoid database checks inside a validator on hot paths.
  • Unit-test constraints with a shared static Validator for speed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a registration form is rejected in production because a new field had no @Valid.

  • Add a negative test per constraint.
  • Parameterize bad inputs so each broken field is covered.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Security testing checks that endpoints reject anonymous users and allow the right roles, using spring-security-test with MockMvc.
  • @WithMockUser runs a test as a fake logged-in user: @WithMockUser(username = "admin", roles = "ADMIN").
  • Expected codes: 401 for unauthenticated REST calls, 403 for an authenticated user without permission, and a redirect to login for form login.

Worked Example 1

Role forbidden.

Worked Example 2

JWT resource server.

Practice Exercise 1

Anonymous vs admin.

Practice Exercise 2

CSRF on POST.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the test security works:

  • Filter chain: MockMvc built with springSecurity() (automatic in Boot) adds the FilterChainProxy before the DispatcherServlet.
  • @WithMockUser: a TestExecutionListener stores an Authentication in the SecurityContext before the test.
  • Post-processors: per-request changes put the user in the repository used by the filters.
  • Failures: ExceptionTranslationFilter turns AccessDenied into 401, 403 or a redirect.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools:

  • @WithMockUser, @WithAnonymousUser, @WithUserDetails.
  • user(), httpBasic(), csrf(), jwt(), opaqueToken(), oauth2Login().
  • SecurityMockMvcResultMatchers.authenticated() and unauthenticated().
  • formLogin() request builder to test login.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request post-processors: .with(user("baji").roles("USER")), .with(csrf()) and .with(jwt()) shape a single request.
  • Setup: @WebMvcTest applies the security filter chain when your SecurityFilterChain bean is imported with @Import.
  • Method security: @PreAuthorize can be tested with @WithMockUser in a @SpringBootTest or slice that enables it.

Senior Notes

  • CSRF: POST, PUT and DELETE return 403 without .with(csrf()) even for an authorized user.
  • Silent pass: forgetting to import the security config in a slice tests the default config, not yours.
  • Custom principal: use @WithUserDetails or a custom annotation with @WithSecurityContext when your code reads a custom user type.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Security config not imported in a slice: the default rules apply.
  • Only testing allowed paths: always add a denied case.
  • csrf missing: 403 hides the real status.
  • Role prefix: roles = "ADMIN" adds ROLE_ automatically; authorities does not.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and maintenance:

  • Prefer slice tests with @Import(SecurityConfig.class) to full contexts.
  • Create a custom meta-annotation like @WithAdmin for repeated setups.
  • Use a password encoder with a low cost in tests to reduce time.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an audit finds that a DELETE endpoint was open to any logged-in user.

  • Add a matrix test: anonymous, USER and ADMIN against each endpoint.
  • Fail the build when a new endpoint is missing a rule.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is a common logging API; your code logs through it and a backend such as Logback does the real work.
  • Usage: private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class);, or the Lombok annotation @Slf4j.
  • Levels from low to high: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; Spring Boot logs at INFO by default.

Worked Example 1

Lombok shortcut.

Worked Example 2

Guard for costly arguments.

Practice Exercise 1

Logger in a controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Logging an exception.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How SLF4J works internally:

  • Facade: LoggerFactory finds a provider on the classpath through ServiceLoader (SLF4J 2.x) and asks it for a logger.
  • Logback: the provider returns a ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger that checks its effective level.
  • Spring Boot: LoggingSystem configures Logback at startup, and jul-to-slf4j and log4j-to-slf4j bridges route other libraries into it.
  • Parameterized message: formatting happens only after the level check passes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax and variants:

  • Levels: trace, debug, info, warn, error.
  • Fluent API (SLF4J 2): log.atInfo().addKeyValue("id", 1).log("done").
  • Markers for tagging, MDC for context.
  • Lombok @Slf4j or @Log4j2 annotations.
  • Group levels in Boot: logging.group.web=....

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Placeholders: log.info("User {} logged in", name) builds the message only when the level is enabled, so avoid string concatenation.
  • Exceptions: pass the throwable as the last argument, log.error("Failed {}", id, ex), to log the stack trace.
  • Set levels in application.properties: logging.level.com.shop=DEBUG or logging.level.root=WARN.

Senior Notes

  • Facade: SLF4J has no output of its own; the binding on the classpath (Logback in Boot) decides format and destination.
  • MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) adds per-request data such as a request id to every log line.
  • Never log secrets such as passwords, tokens or full card numbers, and be careful with personal data.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • String concatenation in log calls; use placeholders.
  • Logging then throwing the same exception, producing duplicate stack traces.
  • Swallowing the exception: log.error(e.getMessage()) loses the stack trace.
  • System.out.println in services instead of a logger.
  • Sensitive data in messages.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Disabled levels cost almost nothing with placeholders.
  • Guard expensive argument creation with isDebugEnabled() or use lambdas in the fluent API.
  • Heavy DEBUG logging in production slows throughput and fills disks.
  • Use a sampling or async appender for noisy paths.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: tracing a failed checkout across services.

  • A filter puts a correlation id into MDC for each request.
  • Every log line carries it, so support can grep one id.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Logback is the default logging backend of Spring Boot (through spring-boot-starter-logging) and the native implementation of SLF4J.
  • Appenders decide where logs go (console, file, rolling file) and encoders or layouts decide the format of each line.
  • Configuration can be simple properties (logging.file.name, logging.level.*) or a full logback-spring.xml in src/main/resources.

Worked Example 1

Rolling file appender.
codeExamples:
<appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
  <file>logs/app.log</file>
  <rollingPolicy
      class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy">
    <fileNamePattern>logs/app.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.%i.log</fileNamePattern>
    <maxFileSize>10MB</maxFileSize>
    <maxHistory>14</maxHistory>
  </rollingPolicy>
  <encoder><pattern>%d %-5level %logger{30}
  - %msg%n</pattern></encoder>
</appender>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// logs/app.log, logs/app.2026-10-07.0.log, ... (14 days kept)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

MDC request id.

Practice Exercise 1

Properties-only configuration.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.shop=DEBUG
logging.file.name=logs/app.log
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-history=14
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size=10MB

# OUTPUT:
# logs/app.log created;
com.shop logs at DEBUG, others at INFO

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

logback-spring.xml with profiles.
codeExamples:
<configuration>
  <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder>
      <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss}
      %-5level [%thread] %logger{30}
      - %msg%n</pattern>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <springProfile name="dev">
    <logger name="com.shop" level="DEBUG"/>
  </springProfile>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
</configuration>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// 10:00:01 INFO  [main] c.s.ShopApplication - Started ShopApplication

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Logback works inside Spring Boot:

  • Starter: spring-boot-starter-logging brings logback-classic, log4j-to-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j.
  • LoggingSystem: LogbackLoggingSystem loads logback-spring.xml (or defaults) and maps the logging.* properties.
  • Pipeline: Logger, then level check, then Appenders, each with an Encoder that formats the event.
  • Additivity: child loggers pass events to parent appenders unless additivity="false".
codeExamples:
# Boot default console pattern is built from these properties
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS}
%-5level [%thread] %logger{36}
- %msg%n
logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG

# OUTPUT:
# 10:00:01.123 DEBUG [http-nio-8080-exec-1] o.s.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet - GET "/hello"

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration options:

  • Properties: logging.level.*, logging.file.name, logging.file.path, logging.pattern.*, logging.logback.rollingpolicy.*.
  • XML: appenders, loggers, springProfile, springProperty.
  • Alternative file with logging.config=classpath:custom.xml.
  • Include Boot defaults with <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/base.xml"/>.
codeExamples:
<configuration>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/base.xml"/>
  <springProperty scope="context" name="app" source="spring.application.name"/>
  <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="DEBUG" additivity="false">
    <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
  </logger>
  <springProfile name="prod">
    <root level="WARN"><appender-ref ref="FILE"/></root>
  </springProfile>
</configuration>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// dev: Boot defaults plus SQL logging; prod: WARN to file

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefer logback-spring.xml over logback.xml, because the -spring name lets you use <springProfile> and Spring properties.
  • Rolling files: RollingFileAppender with SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy rotates by day and size and limits history with maxHistory.
  • Pattern tokens: %d date, %-5level level, %thread, %logger{36}, %msg%n, %X{key} for MDC.

Senior Notes

  • AsyncAppender moves disk writes to another thread so request threads are not blocked; set a queue size and a discard policy.
  • JSON logs (for ELK or cloud) can use an encoder such as the logstash-logback-encoder, or the structured logging support in Spring Boot 3.4+.
  • Runtime levels: change a level without restart through the Actuator /actuator/loggers endpoint.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • logback.xml with springProfile: it fails; use logback-spring.xml.
  • Duplicate lines from additivity true plus an extra appender.
  • Log files never rotate because no rolling policy is set.
  • Two backends (Logback and Log4j2 starters) giving a conflict; exclude one.
  • Editing logs at DEBUG in production leaking data.
codeExamples:
<!-- WRONG: line printed twice (additivity default true) -->
<logger name="com.shop" level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></logger>
<!-- RIGHT -->
<logger name="com.shop" level="INFO" additivity="false">
  <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
</logger>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// WRONG: each message appears twice; RIGHT: once

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tuning:

  • Wrap file appenders in AsyncAppender with a queue size such as 512 and discardingThreshold.
  • Avoid %class, %method and %line in patterns; they capture stack traces and are slow.
  • Keep production at INFO or WARN.
  • Set immediateFlush carefully; false is faster but risks losing the tail on a crash.
codeExamples:
<appender name="ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">
  <queueSize>1024</queueSize>
  <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>
  <neverBlock>true</neverBlock>
  <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
</appender>

<!-- OUTPUT -->
// Request threads enqueue events; a worker thread writes to disk

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: production disk fills in a week because of one chatty DEBUG logger.

  • Use the Actuator loggers endpoint to lower the level without restart.
  • Then add rolling limits so it cannot happen again.
codeExamples:
# management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=loggers
curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.shop.search \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"configuredLevel":"WARN"}'

# OUTPUT:
# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# com.shop.search now logs at WARN

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request logging records what came in: method, URI, query string, selected headers, client address and optionally the body, so you can trace and debug traffic.
  • Where: a servlet Filter (sees everything, including errors before MVC) or a HandlerInterceptor (sees only requests mapped to a handler).
  • Quick start: register CommonsRequestLoggingFilter and set the logger org.springframework.web.filter.CommonsRequestLoggingFilter to DEBUG.

Worked Example 1

Log the body safely.

Worked Example 2

Test that the filter logs.

Practice Exercise 1

Built-in filter bean.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom filter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a logged request travels:

  • Container: Tomcat builds HttpServletRequest and runs the filter chain.
  • Filter: OncePerRequestFilter checks a request attribute so it runs once per request.
  • Wrapper: ContentCachingRequestWrapper fills its byte buffer only while the downstream code reads the stream.
  • Consequence: the cached body is empty before chain.doFilter, so log after the chain.
  • Interceptor: preHandle runs after the handler is chosen by HandlerMapping, so unmapped requests never reach it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for request logging:

  • CommonsRequestLoggingFilter: setters for query string, headers, payload, client info, prefixes and suffixes.
  • Custom filter: full control over masking and format.
  • HandlerInterceptor: access to the handler method for logging the controller name.
  • Tomcat access log: server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled=true gives one line per request without code.
  • Spring Boot 3.x HTTP exchanges: HttpExchangeRepository with Actuator records recent exchanges in memory.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled=true
server.tomcat.accesslog.pattern=%h %t "%r" %s %b %D
server.tomcat.basedir=logs

# OUTPUT:
# 127.0.0.1 [08/Oct/2026:10:15:02 +0000] "GET /api/users HTTP/1.1" 200 312 14

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • OncePerRequestFilter guarantees one execution per request, even across forwards and error dispatches.
  • Body caching: the request stream can be read only once, so wrap the request in ContentCachingRequestWrapper and read the cached bytes after the chain runs.
  • Selective logging: log headers and URI always, but body only for small payloads and never for sensitive paths.

Senior Notes

  • Never log secrets: mask Authorization, cookies, passwords and card numbers before writing a line.
  • Size limit: cap the logged payload (for example 1000 characters) and skip multipart and binary content types.
  • Order: register the filter with a high precedence so it sees requests before security rejects them, but after the correlation id filter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes:

  • Logging passwords: mask fields and skip login paths.
  • Reading the body in the filter: the controller then gets an empty stream; use the caching wrapper.
  • Logging the cached body before the chain: it is empty.
  • Logging multipart uploads: huge memory use; skip by content type.
  • INFO level for everything: use DEBUG for bodies.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: the wrapper copies the body, so memory grows with payload size; set a cache limit.
  • Async logging: use an async appender so disk I/O does not block request threads.
  • Guards: check log.isDebugEnabled() before building large strings.
  • Sampling: log bodies for a small percentage of requests in production.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: support receives a complaint that an order was rejected. With request logging plus a correlation id, the team searches the log by id and sees the exact payload and path.

  • Step 1: user gives the id from the error response.
  • Step 2: search logs for that id.
  • Step 3: compare the logged request body with the validation rules.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Response logging records the status code, selected headers, body size and optionally the body that the application sent back to the client.
  • Why wrapping: the response body is written straight to the output stream, so you wrap it in ContentCachingResponseWrapper to keep a copy.
  • Key call: after logging, you must call copyBodyToResponse(), otherwise the client receives an empty body.

Worked Example 1

Missing copyBodyToResponse.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test.

Practice Exercise 1

Response logging filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Log the body for JSON only.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the response wrapper works:

  • Buffering: ContentCachingResponseWrapper returns a stream that writes into a FastByteArrayOutputStream instead of the socket.
  • Headers: it also holds back content length, so headers are not committed early.
  • Copy: copyBodyToResponse() sets the content length and writes the buffered bytes to the real response.
  • Status: getStatus() is valid after the chain, including error codes set by sendError.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Filter with wrapper: sees final bytes and status.
  • ResponseBodyAdvice: sees the controller object before the message converter; good for logging a DTO.
  • Interceptor afterCompletion: gives the status but not the body.
  • Header logging: res.getHeaderNames() works without a wrapper.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order of work: call chain.doFilter first, then read getContentAsByteArray(), log, and finally copy the body back.
  • Status and timing: log getStatus() together with the duration so one line tells the whole story of the exchange.
  • ResponseBodyAdvice is an alternative that sees the controller return value before conversion, but it does not see error pages or static resources.

Senior Notes

  • Streaming: wrappers buffer everything in memory, so skip large downloads, SSE and file streaming endpoints.
  • Content type: log text and JSON bodies only; for binary content log just the length.
  • Compression and ETag: body wrapping can interact with filters that write the response, so keep the order explicit.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing copyBodyToResponse: empty body for the client; put it in finally.
  • Wrapping streaming endpoints: SSE and downloads stall or use huge memory; skip them with shouldNotFilter.
  • Logging errors twice: the advice and the filter both log; keep one.
  • Reading bytes as the wrong charset: use the response character encoding.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Memory: the whole body lives in memory until copied; this doubles peak usage for large responses.
  • Latency: clients cannot start receiving data until the controller finishes.
  • Mitigation: log only the size and status in production, and the body in test environments.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a partner says the API returned wrong data last night. Response logging with size and status for every call, plus bodies in a short-retention debug index, lets you compare what was sent with what the partner reports.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Exception logging means recording failures with enough context (request, user, correlation id, stack trace) to find the cause, without logging the same error many times.
  • Central place: a @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods is the single point where controller exceptions are logged and converted to responses.
  • Log levels: expected client errors (400, 404) are WARN or INFO without a stack trace; unexpected server errors (500) are ERROR with the full stack trace.

Worked Example 1

Duplicate logging anti-pattern.

Worked Example 2

Test the handler.

Practice Exercise 1

Central handler with levels.

Practice Exercise 2

Add request context.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Exception flow in MVC:

  • Throw: the controller throws and DispatcherServlet catches it in processHandlerException.
  • Resolvers: HandlerExceptionResolver beans are asked in order: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver (your advice), ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Unresolved: the exception propagates to the container, which forwards to /error (BasicErrorController).
  • Interceptor: afterCompletion still receives the exception.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • @ExceptionHandler per class: local to one controller.
  • @RestControllerAdvice: global, can be limited by package or annotation.
  • ResponseEntityExceptionHandler: base class that handles standard MVC exceptions and returns ProblemDetail.
  • @ResponseStatus: maps an exception class to a status.
  • Logger args: markers and structured arguments for searchable fields.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Log once: log in the handler, not in every layer, and do not log and rethrow, or the same stack trace appears three times.
  • Pass the exception last: log.error("msg {}", id, ex) prints the stack trace because the last argument is a Throwable.
  • Catch-all: a handler for Exception.class prevents leaking stack traces to the client and guarantees the failure is logged.

Senior Notes

  • No internals to clients: return a ProblemDetail with a safe message and the correlation id, keep the stack trace in the log.
  • Filter exceptions: errors thrown in filters never reach @ControllerAdvice, so they need their own logging or the error page path.
  • Alerting: ERROR logs feed alerts, so keep that level for real defects only.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Swallowing: catch (Exception e) {} hides failures; log or rethrow.
  • e.printStackTrace(): bypasses the log format and levels.
  • Message only: log.error(e.getMessage()) loses the stack trace.
  • String concatenation: use placeholders.
  • Leaking details: return a safe message to clients.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and noise control:

  • Stack traces cost: filling a trace is expensive; do not log full traces for expected 4xx errors.
  • Flooding: a failing dependency can write thousands of identical traces; use rate limiting or a logging filter.
  • Custom exceptions: override fillInStackTrace only for control-flow exceptions you never log.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: at 02:00 the nightly import fails with a 500. The handler logs one ERROR with the stack trace and the correlation id; the client also receives that id in a ProblemDetail property, and the on-call engineer finds the line with one search.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Correlation id is a unique value (often a UUID) attached to a request so every log line, across all classes and services, can be tied to that one request.
  • Header: clients or gateways send it, commonly as X-Correlation-Id or X-Request-Id; if it is missing, the server generates one.
  • Flow: a filter reads or creates the id, puts it into MDC, adds it to the response header and removes it in a finally block.

Worked Example 1

Propagate to a downstream service.

Worked Example 2

Test the header.

Practice Exercise 1

Correlation filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Print it in logs.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss}
%-5level [%X{correlationId}] %logger{20}
- %msg%n

# OUTPUT:
# 10:15:02 INFO  [6b1c2f6e-77a1] c.e.OrderService - order created
# 10:15:02 INFO  [6b1c2f6e-77a1] c.e.PayClient - calling payment

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Mechanics:

  • Entry: the filter reads the header or generates a UUID.
  • MDC: the value is stored in the thread-local map of the logging backend.
  • Output: the log encoder reads the map for each event and prints %X{correlationId}.
  • Exit: the response header is set and the key is removed in finally.
  • Boot 3 tracing: with Micrometer Tracing, traceId and spanId are placed in MDC for you.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Header names: X-Correlation-Id, X-Request-Id, W3C traceparent.
  • Generators: UUID, ULID or short random strings.
  • Error bodies: include the id as a ProblemDetail property.
  • Async and messaging: copy to message headers.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Log pattern: include %X{correlationId} in the logback pattern so each line prints the id without any code in the business classes.
  • Propagation: copy the id into outgoing calls (RestClient, WebClient, messages) so the next service logs the same id.
  • Response: return the id in a response header and in error bodies so support can ask the user for it.

Senior Notes

  • Validation: accept only a safe format and length from the client, otherwise log injection and huge values are possible.
  • Early filter: give the filter the highest precedence so even security failures carry the id.
  • Tracing: with Micrometer Tracing the trace id plays this role and is placed in MDC automatically; a manual id is still useful for simple apps.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No cleanup: the id leaks to the next request on the same thread.
  • Trusting input: unvalidated headers allow log forging with newlines.
  • Wrong order: a security filter running first rejects the request without an id.
  • Not propagated: downstream services create new ids and the trail breaks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cost: an MDC put and remove is a few map operations, negligible.
  • UUID generation: UUID.randomUUID() uses a secure random; fine at normal rates, use a faster generator at extreme volume.
  • Log size: a 36 character id on each line adds storage; shorten if needed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a checkout call passes through the gateway, the order service and the payment service. All three print the same id, so one search shows the full path and which hop was slow.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a per-thread map of key-value pairs offered by SLF4J; the logging framework can print these values on every log line.
  • API: MDC.put("user", "abaji") adds a value, MDC.get reads it, MDC.remove and MDC.clear delete it.
  • Use: set request-wide data (correlation id, user, tenant) once in a filter and print it with %X{key} in the log pattern.

Worked Example 1

Propagate MDC to async threads.

Worked Example 2

Test the MDC value.

Practice Exercise 1

Set and clear MDC.

Practice Exercise 2

Closeable form.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • Facade: org.slf4j.MDC delegates to an MDCAdapter supplied by the backend.
  • Logback: LogbackMDCAdapter keeps a map per thread and copies it into each ILoggingEvent when the event is created.
  • Printing: the layout pattern %X{key} reads from that event map.
  • Thread pool effect: the map belongs to the thread, not the request.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

API and options:

  • put / get / remove / clear: basic operations.
  • putCloseable: scoped value.
  • getCopyOfContextMap / setContextMap: transfer between threads.
  • Pattern: %X prints the whole map, %X{key:-default} adds a default.
  • JSON: Spring Boot 3.4 and later supports structured logging formats that include MDC, and Logstash encoders do the same.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss}
%-5level [%X{user:-anon}] %msg%n

# OUTPUT:
# 10:15:02 INFO  [anon] application started
# 10:15:03 INFO  [abaji] order saved

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • ThreadLocal: MDC is stored per thread, so a value set in the request thread is visible to every class that runs on that thread.
  • Always clean up: servlet containers reuse threads, so remove keys in a finally block, or values leak into later requests.
  • Try-with-resources: MDC.putCloseable(key, value) removes the key automatically at the end of the block.

Senior Notes

  • Async boundary: a new thread (@Async, executors, CompletableFuture) does not inherit the map, so copy it with a TaskDecorator.
  • Virtual threads and reactive code: ThreadLocal assumptions break in reactive pipelines, which use Reactor context instead of MDC.
  • JSON logs: structured logging prints MDC entries as separate JSON fields, which makes them searchable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Forgetting remove: pooled threads reuse stale values.
  • Assuming async propagation: new threads start empty.
  • Storing objects: values are strings only.
  • Clearing too early: MDC.clear() in a nested method removes the outer filter values.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cheap: map operations per request; Logback copies the map per event only if the event is enabled.
  • Copy cost: getCopyOfContextMap allocates a new map; avoid in tight loops.
  • Keep it small: five to ten keys is typical.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a multi-tenant system sets tenant and user in a filter after authentication, so every line from services and repositories carries them; support filters logs by tenant to debug one customer.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Performance logging measures how long each request takes and logs it, so slow endpoints can be found before users complain.
  • Simple tool: a HandlerInterceptor stores the start time in preHandle and logs the elapsed time in afterCompletion.
  • Output: one line per request with method, path, status and milliseconds, for example GET /api/users 200 12ms.

Worked Example 1

Time a method with StopWatch.

Worked Example 2

Test with MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Timing interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where time goes in a request:

  • Filters: security, encoding, logging.
  • Mapping: HandlerMapping lookup.
  • preHandle: interceptors before the handler.
  • Handler: argument resolving, controller body, return value handling.
  • Conversion: message converter writes JSON or a view renders HTML.
  • afterCompletion: interceptors, in reverse order, always.

An interceptor therefore sees most of the time, a filter sees all of it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to measure:

  • Interceptor: per request, path based.
  • Filter: includes everything.
  • AOP: @Around advice on services to time business methods.
  • @Timed and Micrometer: metrics with percentiles.
  • Server-Timing header: sends the duration to the browser dev tools.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Clock: use System.nanoTime() or Spring StopWatch, not wall-clock time, because nanoTime is monotonic.
  • Request attribute: keep the start time in request.setAttribute, never in a field of the singleton interceptor.
  • Threshold: log everything at DEBUG and slow requests (above a limit such as 500 ms) at WARN so the slow ones stand out.

Senior Notes

  • afterCompletion always runs, even after an exception, while postHandle is skipped on errors, so the timing belongs in afterCompletion.
  • Filter vs interceptor: a filter also measures security and serialization time; an interceptor measures mostly handler time.
  • Metrics instead of logs: Micrometer timers give percentiles and dashboards, logs give the individual slow cases; use both.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Field for start time: shared singleton, concurrent requests overwrite it.
  • postHandle only: skipped when the handler throws.
  • Wall clock: currentTimeMillis can jump.
  • Ignoring async: for Callable or DeferredResult the first preHandle returns early and a second dispatch follows.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Overhead: two nanoTime calls and one log line, tiny.
  • Thresholds: log only slow requests at WARN to cut volume.
  • Slow causes: N+1 queries, remote calls, large payloads, GC pauses.
  • Next step: once a slow path is known, use a profiler or tracing to find the cause.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
logging.level.com.example.web.TimingInterceptor=INFO
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true

# OUTPUT:
# WARN  TimingInterceptor : SLOW GET /api/report 200 1840ms
# INFO  StatisticsLogger  : 52 JDBC statements executed (N+1 suspected)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the team sets a 500 ms budget. A WARN line shows /api/report at 1840 ms; statistics reveal 52 queries for one request, a join fetch cuts it to 2 queries and 90 ms.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready endpoints (health, metrics, loggers, info, env) to an application; you add it with spring-boot-starter-actuator.
  • Exposure: over HTTP only health is exposed by default; others are enabled with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include.
  • Base path: endpoints live under /actuator, for example /actuator/health and /actuator/metrics.

Worked Example 1

Custom endpoint.

Worked Example 2

Secure it.

Practice Exercise 1

Enable endpoints.

Practice Exercise 2

Change a log level live.
codeExamples:
# request
curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.orders ^
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" ^
  -d "{\"configuredLevel\":\"DEBUG\"}"

# OUTPUT:
# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# (com.example.orders now logs at DEBUG until restart or reset with null)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Actuator plugs into MVC:

  • Auto-configuration: WebMvcEndpointManagementContextConfiguration creates a WebMvcEndpointHandlerMapping.
  • Mapping: that mapping resolves paths under /actuator to endpoint operations, ahead of the regular controllers.
  • Endpoint beans: @Endpoint classes are discovered and their operations become web operations.
  • Technology neutral: the same endpoint can also be exposed over JMX.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration choices:

  • include / exclude: pick endpoints by id, or * for all.
  • enabled per endpoint: management.endpoint.X.enabled.
  • base-path: change /actuator to something else.
  • server.port and address: bind to localhost or an internal port.
  • Info contributors: build, git, env and java details.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/ops
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,loggers
management.server.port=9090
management.server.address=127.0.0.1
management.info.env.enabled=true
info.app.name=orders-service

# OUTPUT:
# GET http://127.0.0.1:9090/ops/info -> {"app":{"name":"orders-service"}}

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Loggers endpoint: /actuator/loggers lists levels and a POST changes a logger level at runtime without a restart.
  • Separate port: management.server.port moves the endpoints to another port, which can be firewalled from the public.
  • Info: /actuator/info shows build and git details when the build plugin and properties provide them.

Senior Notes

  • Security: expose only what you need, and protect the rest with Spring Security, because env and heapdump can reveal secrets.
  • Custom endpoint: annotate a bean with @Endpoint and its methods with @ReadOperation or @WriteOperation.
  • Integration with MVC: web endpoints are served by the same DispatcherServlet through a dedicated handler mapping, so filters and interceptors can apply.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • include=* in production: exposes env, heapdump and more.
  • Unsecured: anyone can change log levels.
  • Blocked by security: the default Spring Security chain returns 401 for actuator paths.
  • Wrong path: forgetting the base path after changing it.
codeExamples:
# WRONG
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

# RIGHT
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=env,heapdump

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/env -> 404 (not exposed)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and operations:

  • Cost: endpoints are idle until called, but health checks run on a schedule from probes.
  • Metrics scrape interval: 15 to 60 seconds is common.
  • Heavy endpoints: heapdump and threaddump pause or burden the JVM; restrict them.
  • Separate port: isolates probe traffic from user traffic.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoint.health.cache.time-to-live=10s

# OUTPUT:
# repeated health calls within 10s reuse the cached result

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: during an incident the team raises one package to DEBUG through /actuator/loggers, reproduces the problem, then resets it to null, all without a restart.
codeExamples:
# raise
curl -X POST localhost:9090/ops/loggers/com.example.orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"configuredLevel\":\"DEBUG\"}"
# reset
curl -X POST localhost:9090/ops/loggers/com.example.orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"configuredLevel\":null}"

# OUTPUT:
# 204 No Content, 204 No Content

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Health monitoring reports whether the application and its dependencies (database, disk, message broker) work; Actuator exposes it at /actuator/health.
  • Status: the overall status is UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE or UNKNOWN; DOWN maps to HTTP 503.
  • HealthIndicator: a bean implementing this interface adds your own check, such as calling a payment service.

Worked Example 1

Unit test an indicator.

Worked Example 2

Integration test.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom indicator.

Practice Exercise 2

Configuration.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,db

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/health/readiness -> {"status":"UP"}
# GET /actuator/health/liveness  -> {"status":"UP"}

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How health is computed:

  • Contributors: every HealthIndicator bean becomes a contributor named from the bean name (without the suffix).
  • Aggregator: SimpleStatusAggregator picks the worst status by order DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE, UP, UNKNOWN.
  • Mapping: HttpCodeStatusMapper turns DOWN and OUT_OF_SERVICE into 503.
  • Auto-configured indicators: db, diskSpace, ping and others when their classes exist.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • AbstractHealthIndicator: override doHealthCheck and exceptions become DOWN automatically.
  • CompositeHealthContributor: group nested checks.
  • Custom status: management.endpoint.health.status.order.
  • Availability states: ApplicationAvailability and AvailabilityChangeEvent change readiness programmatically.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Details: management.endpoint.health.show-details controls whether component details are shown; keep it restricted in production.
  • Probes: /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness serve Kubernetes probes when enabled.
  • Groups: health groups let you decide which indicators make up readiness (for example the database) and which do not.

Senior Notes

  • Cheap checks: a slow indicator makes every probe slow and can restart healthy pods; use timeouts and keep the check light.
  • Liveness vs readiness: liveness says the process should be restarted, readiness says it should receive traffic; do not put external dependencies in liveness.
  • Reactive: use ReactiveHealthIndicator in WebFlux, and the health contributor naming comes from the bean name.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Slow indicator: a remote call without timeout blocks the probe.
  • Dependencies in liveness: a database outage restarts all pods.
  • Details always shown: leaks host names and versions.
  • Swallowing exceptions: returning UP on error hides problems.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Caching: management.endpoint.health.cache.time-to-live applies to each indicator.
  • Probe period: every 10 seconds is typical in Kubernetes; the check must finish well within the probe timeout.
  • Async checks: run expensive checks in the background and expose the last result.
codeExamples:
# Kubernetes
# livenessProbe:  httpGet /actuator/health/liveness   periodSeconds: 10
# readinessProbe: httpGet /actuator/health/readiness  periodSeconds: 5

# OUTPUT:
# pod receives traffic only after readiness is UP

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: the database goes down. Readiness (which includes db) turns DOWN, so the load balancer stops sending requests, while liveness stays UP and pods are not restarted needlessly. When the database returns, traffic resumes automatically.
codeExamples:
# GET /actuator/health/readiness during outage
# HTTP/1.1 503
# {"status":"DOWN"}
# GET /actuator/health/liveness
# HTTP/1.1 200
# {"status":"UP"}

# OUTPUT:
# no restarts, no traffic until the database is back

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Metrics are numeric measurements of a running application (request count, latency, memory, pool usage); Spring Boot uses Micrometer as the facade, much like SLF4J for logging.
  • MeterRegistry is the central bean; you create meters from it: Counter (only goes up), Gauge (current value) and Timer (duration and count).
  • Automatic: with Actuator, MVC requests are recorded as http.server.requests, and JVM, CPU and datasource metrics are added too.

Worked Example 1

Gauge for a live value.

Worked Example 2

Test a counter.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom counter and timer.

Practice Exercise 2

Enable Prometheus.
codeExamples:
# pom.xml: micrometer-registry-prometheus
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics,prometheus
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/prometheus ->
# http_server_requests_seconds_count{method="GET",status="200",uri="/api/users"}
42.0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals of Micrometer:

  • Registry: MeterRegistry stores meters keyed by name and tags; registering the same id again returns the existing meter.
  • Composite: Boot creates a composite registry that forwards to every backend on the classpath.
  • Binders: MeterBinder beans register JVM, system, Tomcat and datasource meters.
  • MVC timing: WebMvcMetricsFilter times each request and records http.server.requests.
  • Naming: dotted names are converted to each backend convention, such as http_server_requests_seconds in Prometheus.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Meter types and options:

  • Counter: events that only increase.
  • Gauge: a value that goes up and down; the registry holds only a weak reference to the object.
  • Timer: count, total time and max for short durations.
  • LongTaskTimer: for jobs that run long.
  • DistributionSummary: sizes such as payload bytes.
  • Observation API: one instrumentation point that produces both metrics and traces.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Browse: /actuator/metrics lists names and /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests shows count, total time and max.
  • Tags: dimensions such as uri, method and status let you filter and group one metric.
  • Export: add a registry dependency (for example Prometheus) and expose /actuator/prometheus for scraping.

Senior Notes

  • Cardinality: never tag with unbounded values (user id, raw URL); each unique tag set creates a new time series and can exhaust memory.
  • Percentiles: enable histograms or publish percentiles on timers to see p95 and p99, which averages hide.
  • Annotations: @Timed on a controller or method works when a TimedAspect bean is registered; MVC requests are timed automatically.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • High cardinality tags: user id or full URL with ids.
  • Gauge on a temporary object: garbage collected, then the gauge reports NaN.
  • Creating meters in a loop with new names: memory growth.
  • Counter for a value that decreases: use a gauge.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: a counter increment is a lock-free add; timers are slightly more costly.
  • Histograms: each bucket is a series, so enable them only for key timers.
  • Cache meters: hold the meter in a field instead of looking it up on every call.
  • URI tag: MVC uses the path template (/users/{id}), which keeps cardinality low.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true
management.metrics.distribution.slo.http.server.requests=100ms,500ms,1s
management.metrics.tags.application=orders-service

# OUTPUT:
# http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{le="0.1",uri="/users/{id}"}
120.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an alert rule fires when the p95 of http.server.requests for /api/checkout stays above 800 ms for five minutes, and a dashboard shows the order counter by channel to spot a drop after a release.
codeExamples:
# PromQL
# histogram_quantile(0.95,
#   sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{uri="/api/checkout"}[5m])) by (le))

# OUTPUT:
# 0.93 (varies) -> alert fires, team checks the latest deployment

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerMapping is the DispatcherServlet strategy that finds the handler (and its interceptors) for a request; the result is a HandlerExecutionChain.
  • Defaults: RequestMappingHandlerMapping handles @RequestMapping controllers; others handle simple URL mappings, bean names and static resources.
  • Custom: you write your own by implementing HandlerMapping or extending AbstractHandlerMapping, and register it as a bean.

Worked Example 1

Add an interceptor to the chain.

Worked Example 2

Test it.

Practice Exercise 1

Minimal custom mapping.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it with a handler.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the DispatcherServlet uses mappings:

  • Discovery: at startup it collects all HandlerMapping beans and sorts them by order.
  • getHandler: for each request it loops, and the first mapping returning a non-null HandlerExecutionChain wins.
  • AbstractHandlerMapping: calls your getHandlerInternal, then adds matching interceptors and CORS setup.
  • Adapter: getHandlerAdapter finds an adapter whose supports returns true and calls handle.
  • No match: 404 through noHandlerFound.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Implement HandlerMapping: one method, getHandler.
  • AbstractHandlerMapping: adds order, interceptors, CORS.
  • AbstractUrlHandlerMapping: register handlers by URL pattern; SimpleUrlHandlerMapping is the ready-made form.
  • RequestMappingHandlerMapping subclass: custom RequestCondition for annotated controllers.
  • Path matching: Spring 6 uses PathPatternParser by default.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: the DispatcherServlet asks each mapping in order and the first non-null result wins, so set a suitable setOrder(...) value.
  • Adapter needed: whatever handler object you return needs a HandlerAdapter that supports it, for example HttpRequestHandlerAdapter for HttpRequestHandler.
  • Return null when the mapping does not apply, so the next mapping gets a chance.

Senior Notes

  • Rarely needed: most needs (versioning, header or host matching) are solved with @RequestMapping conditions or RequestCondition, not a new mapping.
  • Extension point: for custom matching on annotated controllers, subclass RequestMappingHandlerMapping and override getCustomTypeCondition or getCustomMethodCondition.
  • Registering: define the bean with a lower order value than the default mappings if it must take priority.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No adapter: returning an unsupported handler type gives ServletException: No adapter for handler.
  • Order too high: default mappings answer first.
  • Returning an empty chain instead of null: blocks later mappings.
  • Not a bean: an unregistered instance is never consulted.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cost: each request walks the mappings, so keep getHandlerInternal fast and non-allocating.
  • Order: put the most frequent mapping first.
  • Lookups: precompute a map of paths at startup.
  • Prefer annotations: the built-in mapping uses an optimised registry.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a company migrates an old servlet-style application. Old /legacy/** URLs must keep working through existing HttpRequestHandler classes, while new endpoints use annotated controllers. A custom mapping at order 0 routes the old paths, and everything else falls through.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerAdapter is the strategy interface that lets DispatcherServlet invoke any kind of handler; a custom one teaches Spring MVC to call a handler type it does not know.
  • Two methods: supports(Object handler) says whether the adapter fits, and handle(request, response, handler) runs it and returns a ModelAndView.
  • Registration: declare the adapter as a @Bean; the servlet finds every HandlerAdapter bean in the context.

Worked Example 1

Adapter bean plus name-based mapping.

Worked Example 2

Call through MockMvc.

Practice Exercise 1

Define a handler interface and an adapter.

Practice Exercise 2

Test the adapter alone.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the adapter is used per request:

  • Init: DispatcherServlet.initHandlerAdapters collects all HandlerAdapter beans and sorts them.
  • Lookup: getHandlerAdapter(handler) loops through them and returns the first with supports true.
  • Invoke: ha.handle(...) returns a ModelAndView or null.
  • Defaults: without custom beans the servlet loads the adapters named in DispatcherServlet.properties.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • Handler type: any object a HandlerMapping can return.
  • Order: adapters are consulted in Ordered order.
