  • Wrapping: delegate to RequestMappingHandlerAdapter to add behaviour around annotated controllers.
  • Return: null for a written response, or a ModelAndView for view rendering.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Lookup order: DispatcherServlet asks each adapter in order and uses the first one whose supports returns true.
  • Built-ins: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter (for @Controller methods), HttpRequestHandlerAdapter and SimpleControllerHandlerAdapter.
  • Return null from handle when you wrote the response yourself, so no view is rendered.

Senior Notes

  • When to build one: rarely; bridging a legacy handler interface or a function-style handler is the real use case.
  • Pairing: a custom adapter needs a HandlerMapping that returns your handler type, such as BeanNameUrlHandlerMapping.
  • Prefer alternatives (interceptor, argument resolver, router functions) when you only need to change how arguments or results are handled.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Too broad supports: return true steals annotated controllers.
  • No mapping: an adapter without a matching HandlerMapping is never reached.
  • Wrong return: returning a ModelAndView after writing the body causes a view error.
  • Replacing the default: declaring a bean named handlerAdapter can disable the defaults in some setups; keep the standard ones.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Cheap supports: it runs on every request, so use instanceof only.
  • Order: put the hottest adapter first.
  • No allocation in the hot path; keep the adapter stateless.
  • Streaming: write directly to the response for large payloads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a migration keeps 200 legacy Action classes while new code uses @RestController. One adapter runs the old actions inside the new application, and they are retired one by one.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • ViewResolver maps a logical view name returned by a controller (such as report) to a real View object that renders the response.
  • One method: View resolveViewName(String viewName, Locale locale); return null to let the next resolver try.
  • Custom resolver lets you render formats such as CSV, PDF or a database-stored template that the default resolvers cannot.

Worked Example 1

Unit test of the resolver.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc check.

Practice Exercise 1

A resolver for names ending with .csv.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How resolution works:

  • After the handler: DispatcherServlet.render gets a view name from the ModelAndView.
  • resolveViewName: loops over the sorted viewResolvers and takes the first non-null View.
  • Render: view.render(model, request, response) writes the output.
  • Missing: if none resolves, a ServletException says it cannot resolve the view name.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • UrlBasedViewResolver: prefix and suffix (JSP, Thymeleaf, FreeMarker).
  • BeanNameViewResolver: looks up a View bean by name.
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver: combines resolvers by media type.
  • Custom: any lookup logic, such as a database or a tenant folder.
  • Redirect and forward: names starting with redirect: are handled by the base class.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Chain: DispatcherServlet holds all ViewResolver beans sorted by Ordered; the first non-null result wins.
  • View interface: render(Map model, request, response) writes the output and getContentType() names the type.
  • Defaults: InternalResourceViewResolver accepts every name, so it must have the lowest priority.

Senior Notes

  • Ordering: implement Ordered or call setOrder; a greedy resolver placed first hides all others.
  • Content negotiation: ContentNegotiatingViewResolver picks among candidate views by the requested media type.
  • REST controllers skip view resolution because @ResponseBody marks the request as handled.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong order: a catch-all resolver with a low order number hides yours.
  • Not returning null: throwing for unknown names breaks the chain.
  • Locale ignored: pass the locale to caches and keys.
  • Stateful View: a View is shared when cached, so it must be thread safe.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cache: AbstractCachingViewResolver keeps resolved views per name and locale; extend it for costly lookups.
  • Production: keep caching on; turn it off only in development.
  • Few resolvers: every extra resolver adds a lookup per request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting app lets users save templates in the database. A custom resolver loads them by name, caches them, and the controllers only return the template name.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom argument resolver is a class that fills a controller method parameter (such as the logged-in user) from the request, so the controller stays free of plumbing code.
  • Steps: write a marker annotation, implement HandlerMethodArgumentResolver, and register it in WebMvcConfigurer.addArgumentResolvers.
  • Result: a method like show(@CurrentUser User u) receives the object directly.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc success and failure.

Worked Example 2

Resolving a Pageable-like parameter.

Practice Exercise 1

Marker annotation and resolver.

Practice Exercise 2

Register and use.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside a request:

  • InvocableHandlerMethod: for every parameter it calls resolvers.supportsParameter.
  • Composite: checks each resolver in order and caches the winner per parameter.
  • resolveArgument: your code runs and its result is passed to the controller.
  • Order: annotation-based built-ins first, then custom resolvers, then catch-all resolvers.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • By annotation: clearest and safest.
  • By type: good for value objects like Paging.
  • Named value: extend AbstractNamedValueMethodArgumentResolver for required and default handling.
  • Binder access: use the WebDataBinderFactory to convert and validate.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • supportsParameter checks the annotation or the parameter type; resolveArgument builds the value.
  • Source of data: headers, cookies, the session, a SecurityContext or a database lookup.
  • Fail early: throw a clear exception, such as ResponseStatusException with 401, when the value is missing.

Senior Notes

  • Reuse: one resolver replaces repeated lookup code in dozens of controllers.
  • Order: custom resolvers run after the built-in ones that match specific annotations, so avoid parameter types Spring already resolves.
  • Thread safety: the resolver is a singleton; keep it stateless.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Overlapping support: claiming String everywhere steals other parameters.
  • Per-user state in a field: the resolver is a singleton.
  • Returning null for a primitive parameter causes an error.
  • Reading the body twice: the stream is gone after the first read.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cheap support check: annotations are cached by Spring after the first lookup.
  • Expensive values: cache per request with a request attribute.
  • Avoid database calls when a token claim is enough.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API with 80 endpoints needs the authenticated user. One resolver reads the verified token and every controller declares @CurrentUser User user.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerMethodArgumentResolver is the Spring MVC strategy interface that turns one method parameter of a controller into a value from the current request.
  • Contract: supportsParameter(MethodParameter) and resolveArgument(MethodParameter, ModelAndViewContainer, NativeWebRequest, WebDataBinderFactory).
  • Everything is a resolver: @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @RequestBody, Model and HttpServletRequest each have a built-in resolver.

Worked Example 1

Standalone MockMvc with a custom resolver.

Worked Example 2

Required value handling.

Practice Exercise 1

Resolve a Locale-like value from a header.

Practice Exercise 2

Inspect parameter metadata.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • Setup: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter.afterPropertiesSet builds the default resolver list plus custom ones.
  • Composite: HandlerMethodArgumentResolverComposite wraps the list.
  • Call: InvocableHandlerMethod resolves each parameter, then calls the method by reflection.
  • Defaults order: annotation resolvers (@RequestParam, @PathVariable), type resolvers (Model, HttpServletRequest), custom ones, then catch-all fallbacks.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful base classes and helpers:

  • AbstractNamedValueMethodArgumentResolver: required, default value and conversion.
  • MethodParameter: annotations, generic type, index and name.
  • NativeWebRequest: headers, parameters, cookies and native request.
  • ModelAndViewContainer: add model attributes from a resolver.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Used by RequestMappingHandlerAdapter through a HandlerMethodArgumentResolverComposite.
  • First match wins: the composite caches the resolver chosen for each parameter, so supportsParameter runs once per parameter.
  • WebDataBinderFactory lets you bind and convert values, for example with createBinder.

Senior Notes

  • Related contract: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler is the mirror interface for results.
  • Subtypes: extend AbstractNamedValueMethodArgumentResolver to get required and default value handling for free.
  • Debugging: set a breakpoint in InvocableHandlerMethod.getMethodArgumentValues to watch each resolver run.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrong registration time: a resolver added too late is ignored.
  • Primitive null: returning null for int fails.
  • Order surprise: a built-in already supports the type.
  • No test: standalone MockMvc needs setCustomArgumentResolvers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • supportsParameter runs once per parameter, so it can inspect annotations freely.
  • resolveArgument runs per request, so keep it fast and cache costly lookups.
  • Fewer resolvers means a shorter scan on first use.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a multi-tenant SaaS needs the tenant in 60 endpoints. A resolver reads the header, checks it, and the services receive a Tenant object.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Custom return value handler processes a controller result of your own type and writes the response, so controllers can simply return a domain object such as a report.
  • Steps: implement HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler and register it in WebMvcConfigurer.addReturnValueHandlers.
  • Mark handled: call mavContainer.setRequestHandled(true) when you wrote the response, so no view is looked up.

Worked Example 1

Controller using the type.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc assertion.

Practice Exercise 1

A handler for CsvResult.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How it runs:

  • Invoke: ServletInvocableHandlerMethod.invokeAndHandle calls the controller method.
  • Dispatch: the composite finds the handler for the return type and calls handleReturnValue.
  • Handled flag: if requestHandled is true, no view is resolved.
  • Otherwise: the container is turned into a ModelAndView and rendered.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • By type: a domain class like CsvResult.
  • By annotation: a method annotation such as @PlainText.
  • Wrapper: delegate to an existing handler after transforming the value.
  • Streaming: return a StreamingResponseBody for large output instead.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • supportsReturnType usually tests the return class, such as CsvResult.class.isAssignableFrom(...).
  • handleReturnValue receives the value and a NativeWebRequest; get the servlet response with getNativeResponse.
  • Headers: set content type and Content-Disposition before writing the body.

Senior Notes

  • Alternative: a custom HttpMessageConverter is better for content-negotiated types, while a return handler suits special flows.
  • Order: custom handlers run after most built-ins, so a type already handled (such as String) is not intercepted.
  • Streaming: write directly to the output stream for large downloads instead of buffering in memory.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Missing handled flag: a view lookup follows and fails.
  • Headers after body: set them before the first write.
  • Wrong support check: an exact class check misses subclasses.
  • Not registered: an unregistered handler is silently unused.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Stream: write row by row to the writer, not one big string.
  • Buffer size: let the servlet container buffer; call flush only when needed.
  • Compression: enable server compression for text exports.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: finance downloads statements as CSV from 15 endpoints. All of them return CsvResult and one handler sets headers and streams the rows.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler is the strategy interface that processes the value a controller method returns: it chooses a view, writes the body or sets headers.
  • Contract: supportsReturnType(MethodParameter) and handleReturnValue(Object, MethodParameter, ModelAndViewContainer, NativeWebRequest).
  • Built-ins: RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor (for @ResponseBody), ViewNameMethodReturnValueHandler and HttpEntityMethodProcessor.

Worked Example 1

Support check.

Worked Example 2

Test the handler in isolation.

Practice Exercise 1

Inspect return handlers at startup.

Practice Exercise 2

A handler that adds a header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Internals:

  • Composite: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlerComposite holds the ordered list.
  • selectHandler: loops and returns the first whose supportsReturnType is true; async handlers get priority for async values.
  • Default list: ModelAndView, Model, View, ResponseBodyEmitter, HttpEntity, HttpHeaders, Callable, DeferredResult, view names, @ResponseBody, then catch-alls.
  • Custom: added after the specific built-ins and before the catch-alls.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controller return types and the handler that serves them:

  • String: view name (or body with @ResponseBody).
  • ResponseEntity: HttpEntityMethodProcessor.
  • ModelAndView: ModelAndViewMethodReturnValueHandler.
  • void: default view name or handled request.
  • Callable and DeferredResult: async handlers.
  • StreamingResponseBody: streaming handler.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Composite: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlerComposite picks the first handler that supports the return type.
  • ModelAndViewContainer carries the view name, the model and the requestHandled flag.
  • Async types such as Callable and DeferredResult have their own handlers.

Senior Notes

  • Order matters: an annotated @ResponseBody result is taken by the body processor before a view-name handler.
  • Mirror of HandlerMethodArgumentResolver: one side reads input, this side writes output.
  • Debug: breakpoint in ServletInvocableHandlerMethod.invokeAndHandle to see the handler chosen.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Wrapping the composite: replacing the whole handler list drops the built-ins.
  • Wrong support: using a type a built-in already handles.
  • Ignoring void: a null return with no handled flag falls to a view.
  • Blocking in async: do not block inside async return handling.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Selection cost is a short loop per request; keep supportsReturnType trivial.
  • Message converters are the usual cost; register only needed ones.
  • Streaming types avoid large buffers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a team sees unexpected 404 errors after returning a custom type. Debugging invokeAndHandle shows no handler supports it and a view lookup follows. Adding a handler fixes it.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Formatter converts between a String and an object in both directions, using the Locale: parse(String, Locale) and print(T, Locale).
  • Use it for request parameters, form fields and view output of types such as money, phone numbers or dates.
  • Register with FormatterRegistry.addFormatter inside WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters.

Worked Example 1

Controller using the formatter.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test of good and bad input.

Practice Exercise 1

A money formatter.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where formatters work:

  • Registry: FormattingConversionService stores formatters as converters (String to T and T to String).
  • Web: WebDataBinder uses it for request parameters, path variables and form binding.
  • View: Thymeleaf and JSP tags call it to print values.
  • Boot: WebMvcAutoConfiguration adds all Formatter beans.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Formatter bean in Spring Boot, no config class needed.
  • AnnotationFormatterFactory: annotation-driven, like @DateTimeFormat.
  • Built-ins: @NumberFormat, @DateTimeFormat.
  • Boot properties: spring.mvc.format.date sets the default date pattern.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Formatter vs Converter: a formatter is locale aware and text oriented; a converter is a one-way, type-to-type function.
  • Errors: throw ParseException and Spring reports a binding error or a 400 response.
  • Annotation driven: AnnotationFormatterFactory powers annotations like @DateTimeFormat and @NumberFormat.

Senior Notes

  • Spring Boot registers any Formatter bean automatically in the web conversion service.
  • Thread safety: formatters are shared, so do not keep a SimpleDateFormat field; use DateTimeFormatter.
  • Limit: formatting applies to bound parameters and form fields, not to JSON bodies, which use Jackson.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Shared SimpleDateFormat: not thread safe.
  • Swallowing errors: returning null on bad input hides problems; throw ParseException.
  • Expecting JSON effect: Jackson does not use formatters.
  • Ignoring the Locale: decimal separators differ between locales.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Create once: build patterns and regexes as constants.
  • Cache: the conversion service caches the converter found per type pair.
  • Keep parse cheap: it runs on every bound request.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop accepts prices as 12.50 INR in query strings. One formatter makes every controller accept Money and the same text is printed in the views.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Converter is a functional interface Converter<S, T> with one method T convert(S source); Spring uses it to turn one type into another, such as String into your own class.
  • Register with registry.addConverter in WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters.
  • Where used: @RequestParam, @PathVariable, @ModelAttribute binding and property placeholders.

Worked Example 1

Test through MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Use the ConversionService directly.

Practice Exercise 1

String to Status enum, ignoring case.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Mechanics:

  • GenericConversionService stores converters in a map keyed by source and target type.
  • Lookup: finds the closest match, walking the class hierarchy of both types.
  • Boot: WebConversionService adds all Converter, GenericConverter and Formatter beans.
  • Cache: the found converter is cached per type pair.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Converter: one pair.
  • ConverterFactory: one converter per subtype of a base.
  • GenericConverter: many pairs, access to field annotations.
  • ConditionalConverter: choose at runtime with matches.
  • Lambda: pass the types explicitly with addConverter(String.class, Status.class, fn).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Family: Converter (one pair), ConverterFactory (a type hierarchy, like all enums) and GenericConverter (many pairs, with type descriptors).
  • ConversionService is the entry point; WebConversionService is used in Spring MVC.
  • Null: returning null means "no value"; throw IllegalArgumentException for invalid input.

Senior Notes

  • Spring Boot adds every Converter bean to the conversion service automatically.
  • Generics: a lambda loses generic info, so use a class or anonymous class when registering by bean.
  • Versus Formatter: use a converter for pure type mapping, a formatter when locale matters.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Lambda bean: generics are erased, so the bean cannot be registered.
  • Returning null for a primitive target.
  • Wrong exception: let it throw a clear IllegalArgumentException, which becomes 400.
  • Expecting JSON effect: Jackson needs its own deserializer.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Stateless: converters are shared singletons.
  • Fast lookup: use a static map for code-to-object conversion instead of a database call.
  • Avoid chains: converting through an intermediate type costs twice.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a list page filters by ?status=blocked. A converter turns text into the enum for all endpoints and unknown values give a clean 400 response.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerInterceptor runs code around controller execution: preHandle before, postHandle after the handler and afterCompletion after the response.
  • Register it with InterceptorRegistry.addInterceptor in WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors, with addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns.
  • Veto: preHandle returns false to stop the chain, so the controller is not called.

Worked Example 1

A simple API key check.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test.

Practice Exercise 1

A timing interceptor.

Practice Exercise 2

Register with path patterns.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Execution flow:

  • HandlerExecutionChain: the mapping returns the handler plus its interceptors.
  • applyPreHandle: runs each preHandle in order; if one returns false, earlier interceptors get afterCompletion and the chain stops.
  • Handler: the controller runs via the adapter.
  • applyPostHandle: reverse order, only if no exception.
  • triggerAfterCompletion: reverse order, always for the ones that passed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Path patterns: addPathPatterns and excludePathPatterns use Ant-style or parsed patterns.
  • Order: .order(n) on the registration.
  • HandlerMethod: read annotations on the target method.
  • WebRequestInterceptor: a servlet-neutral variant.
  • Lambda: HandlerInterceptor has default methods, so a lambda gives only preHandle.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Typical uses: logging, timing, authentication checks, locale and tenant setup.
  • Order: interceptors run in registration order going in and in reverse order coming out; use order(int) to change it.
  • afterCompletion always runs for interceptors whose preHandle returned true, even after an exception.

Senior Notes

  • Interceptor vs Filter: a filter is a Servlet feature around the whole servlet; an interceptor knows the handler method and lives inside Spring MVC.
  • Handler object: cast to HandlerMethod to read annotations on the controller method.
  • Async requests: use AsyncHandlerInterceptor when the handler may run on another thread.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Instance state: storing request data in a field is not thread safe; use request attributes.
  • Not registered: a @Component alone does nothing.
  • Static resources: patterns may also catch them; exclude as needed.
  • No response after false: returning false without writing a response gives an empty 200.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Narrow patterns so cheap requests skip the interceptor.
  • No blocking calls in preHandle.
  • Metrics: use Micrometer built-in timers rather than custom timing in production.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: every API call must carry a correlation id. An interceptor reads or creates it, puts it in the logging context, and clears it in afterCompletion.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HandlerExceptionResolver turns an exception thrown during a request into a response; the method is ModelAndView resolveException(request, response, handler, ex).
  • Return value: an empty ModelAndView means "handled, response written"; null means "not mine, ask the next resolver".
  • Built-in chain: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver (@ExceptionHandler), ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.

Worked Example 1

Controller that throws.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test.

Practice Exercise 1

A resolver mapping an exception to 409.

Practice Exercise 2

Register it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Resolution flow:

  • Catch: DispatcherServlet.processHandlerException receives any exception from the handler.
  • Loop: each resolver in the list gets a chance; the first non-null ModelAndView wins.
  • Defaults order: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver.
  • Unresolved: the exception is rethrown to the container, which shows its error page.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • AbstractHandlerExceptionResolver: base class with shouldApplyTo and logging.
  • Order through setOrder.
  • JSON body: write with ObjectMapper to response.getWriter().
  • Error view: return a ModelAndView("error/conflict").
  • Spring 6 ProblemDetail: @ExceptionHandler methods can return it directly.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Register by overriding extendHandlerExceptionResolvers in WebMvcConfigurer to add yours to the list.
  • Order: implement Ordered when the resolver is a bean, so it runs before or after the built-ins.
  • Response: write status and body yourself with response.sendError or response.getWriter().

Senior Notes

  • Prefer @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler for most cases; a custom resolver is for cross-cutting low-level handling.
  • Not visible to exceptions thrown in filters, which occur before DispatcherServlet.
  • Logging: log in the resolver once, and return null so later resolvers still render the error.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Returning an empty ModelAndView without writing gives an empty response.
  • Returning null after writing: later resolvers may write again.
  • Wrong position: placed after the built-ins, it never sees exceptions they handle.
  • Swallowing the cause: always log the exception.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cheap type checks first, then return null quickly.
  • Log once: avoid logging the same exception in several resolvers.
  • No heavy work in the error path, since errors can spike under load.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a platform team wants all unexpected exceptions logged with the correlation id and answered with one JSON shape. A resolver placed first does this for every controller, while specific @ExceptionHandler methods stay available as a second layer.

Fresher Notes

  • Proxy pattern: a stand-in object with the same interface as the real one that adds behavior (transactions, security, caching, logging) before or after the call.
  • Spring uses it everywhere: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize and AOP advice all work through proxies.
  • Two kinds: JDK dynamic proxies (interface based) and CGLIB proxies (subclass based, the Spring Boot default).

Worked Example 1

Self-invocation pitfall.

Worked Example 2

Custom timing aspect.

Practice Exercise 1

A hand-written logging proxy.

Practice Exercise 2

Spring proxy is visible at runtime.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring wraps beans in proxies after they are created.

  • Creation: a BeanPostProcessor checks whether any advisor (transaction, cache, aspect) matches the bean and, if so, returns a proxy.
  • JDK proxy: built with java.lang.reflect.Proxy for interfaces.
  • CGLIB proxy: a generated subclass; the default since Spring Boot 2 (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true).
  • Call path: proxy, then advice chain (interceptors), then the target method.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Proxy options and variants:

  • @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true): force CGLIB.
  • @Scope(proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS): a scoped proxy so a singleton can hold a request or session bean.
  • @Lazy on an injection point: injects a lazy-resolving proxy.
  • ProxyFactory: build a proxy programmatically.
  • AspectJ weaving: no proxy, bytecode is changed, so self-invocation works.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Self-invocation: calling this.save() inside the same bean skips the proxy, so the annotation has no effect.
  • Visibility and final: CGLIB cannot override final or private methods, so advice is not applied to them.
  • Injected bean is the proxy: the object you get from @Autowired is the proxy, and AopUtils.isAopProxy can confirm it.

Senior Notes

  • Proxy creation: a BeanPostProcessor (AbstractAutoProxyCreator) wraps matching beans after initialization.
  • Interceptor chain: each proxied call runs an advice chain, so keep advice cheap and ordered with @Order.
  • Design choice: for self-invocation use a separate bean, AopContext.currentProxy() or AspectJ weaving.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Self-invocation: this.method() bypasses advice; move the method to another bean.
  • final classes or methods: CGLIB cannot proxy them.
  • Private methods: advice is not applied.
  • new instead of injection: new OrderService() has no proxy at all.
  • Injecting the concrete class with JDK proxies: causes a cast failure; inject the interface or use CGLIB.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • A proxied call adds a small cost (an advice chain walk), usually microseconds.
  • Many aspects on one bean multiply that cost, so use narrow pointcuts.
  • Startup: proxy class generation happens once per bean type.
  • Prefer @Around only when you need it; @Before is cheaper to reason about.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a payment service needs a transaction, an audit log and a rate limit. Instead of putting that into the method, each concern is a separate advisor, and the proxy chain applies them in order, leaving the method with business code only.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Template Method: a base class defines the fixed steps of an algorithm and lets subclasses or callbacks fill in the varying steps.
  • Spring examples: JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, TransactionTemplate and JmsTemplate handle the boilerplate and call your code in the middle.
  • Benefit: resource handling (connections, statements, cleanup) is written once and cannot be forgotten.

Worked Example 1

Overriding a filter hook.

Worked Example 2

TransactionTemplate.

Practice Exercise 1

Classic abstract class.

Practice Exercise 2

JdbcTemplate with a callback.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The pattern inverts control: the framework owns the algorithm and you supply the variable steps.

  • JdbcTemplate.query: gets a connection from DataSourceUtils, creates a PreparedStatement, runs it, maps rows through the RowMapper and always releases resources.
  • Errors: SQLException is translated by SQLExceptionTranslator.
  • Transactions: the connection is the one bound to the current transaction.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of the pattern:

  • Abstract class with final template method: subclasses override hooks.
  • Callback interfaces: RowMapper, PreparedStatementCreator, TransactionCallback.
  • Lambdas: functional callbacks need no subclass.
  • Hook with default: optional steps have empty default bodies.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Callback style: Spring prefers callbacks such as RowMapper over subclassing, so no inheritance is needed.
  • Hook methods: in AbstractController-style classes and OncePerRequestFilter you override doFilterInternal while the base class runs the skeleton.
  • Exception translation: templates convert vendor exceptions into the DataAccessException hierarchy.

Senior Notes

  • Hollywood principle: the framework calls your code, not the other way around.
  • Strategy versus template: template method varies steps through inheritance, strategy swaps a whole algorithm through composition.
  • Thread safety: templates are thread safe, so declare one as a singleton bean and reuse it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Template method not final: a subclass can break the order.
  • Too many hooks: the base class becomes hard to understand; prefer callbacks.
  • Deep inheritance: hard to follow; compose with strategy instead.
  • Swallowing exceptions in callbacks: the template cannot clean up properly if you hide them.
  • Creating a new template per call: create it once as a bean.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Templates add little overhead; the cost is the SQL or remote call.
  • JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate sends many rows in one round trip.
  • setFetchSize controls how many rows the driver loads at once for big queries.
  • RestTemplate should share a pooled HTTP client with timeouts.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a company needs to import files from three sources (CSV, XML, API). The import steps are the same (open, parse, validate, store, report). One abstract Importer holds the flow and each source overrides only parse.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Repository: a collection-like abstraction that hides how domain objects are stored and loaded, so services work with objects, not SQL.
  • In Spring: annotate an interface or class with @Repository; Spring Data generates the implementation from JpaRepository.
  • Purpose: one place for persistence code, easy to mock in tests and to swap databases.

Worked Example 1

@DataJpaTest.

Worked Example 2

Mocking in a service test.

Practice Exercise 1

A Spring Data repository.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom @Query.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How Spring Data repositories work:

  • Scanning: @EnableJpaRepositories (auto-configured in Boot) finds interfaces extending Repository.
  • Proxy: a JpaRepositoryFactory creates a JDK proxy backed by SimpleJpaRepository.
  • Query methods: PartTree parses names like findByCityAndAge into JPQL criteria at startup.
  • Translation: a PersistenceExceptionTranslationInterceptor converts exceptions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax and variants:

  • CrudRepository: basic CRUD.
  • JpaRepository: adds flush, batch delete and paging.
  • PagingAndSortingRepository: paging and sorting only.
  • Query keywords: And, Or, Between, Like, OrderBy, Top.
  • @Query with JPQL or native SQL, and Specification for dynamic filters.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Query methods: findByEmail and existsByName are derived from the method name.
  • @Repository effect: it marks the stereotype and enables persistence exception translation to DataAccessException.
  • Keep it thin: no business rules in repositories; put them in the service layer.

Senior Notes

  • Proxy based: Spring Data creates a JDK proxy backed by SimpleJpaRepository and a query lookup strategy.
  • Testing: use @DataJpaTest for repositories and mock the repository in service tests.
  • Repository versus DAO: the repository speaks the domain language (aggregates), the DAO speaks tables and rows.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Business logic in the repository: keep it in services.
  • Misspelled property in a method name: the app fails at startup with PropertyReferenceException.
  • Returning entities with lazy collections to the web layer: use DTOs.
  • Missing @Modifying on update queries.
  • findAll() on large tables: use paging.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Use projections to fetch only needed columns.
  • Use pagination or a Slice to avoid count queries.
  • Avoid N+1 with @EntityGraph.
  • Use saveAll with batch size for bulk writes.
  • Use existsBy instead of loading an entity just to check.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an e-commerce app keeps OrderRepository, CustomerRepository and ProductRepository. The service places an order by loading the customer and products, building the aggregate and saving it once. Tests swap the repositories for mocks or an in-memory database.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Service layer: a layer of @Service classes between controllers and repositories that holds business logic and transaction boundaries.
  • Why: controllers stay thin (HTTP only), repositories stay thin (storage only), and logic is reusable and testable.
  • Flow: controller calls service, service calls repositories and other services, and the result goes back as a DTO or entity.

Worked Example 1

Rollback demo.

Worked Example 2

Service unit test.

Practice Exercise 1

A service with a transaction.

Practice Exercise 2

Thin controller.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How the service layer works inside Spring:

  • @Service classes are singleton beans found by component scanning.
  • If a method has @Transactional, the bean is wrapped in a proxy with a TransactionInterceptor.
  • The interceptor asks the PlatformTransactionManager to begin, then commits or rolls back (runtime exceptions roll back by default).
  • Repositories called inside join the same transaction through the thread-bound resources.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • @Transactional attributes: readOnly, propagation, isolation, rollbackFor, timeout.
  • Interface plus implementation when you need several implementations.
  • Facade services that combine several services for a use case.
  • Domain events through ApplicationEventPublisher to decouple side effects.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • @Transactional belongs on service methods, so several repository calls commit or roll back together.
  • No web types: a service should not use HttpServletRequest or ResponseEntity.
  • Constructor injection: inject repositories through the constructor so the class is easy to unit test.

Senior Notes

  • Read-only: mark queries @Transactional(readOnly = true) to give the provider a hint.
  • Exceptions: throw domain exceptions and map them in @ControllerAdvice.
  • Anemic model risk: if services only forward calls, move rules into the domain objects.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • @Transactional on a private or self-invoked method: no effect.
  • Checked exceptions: they do not roll back unless rollbackFor is set.
  • Catching exceptions inside: the transaction commits because nothing was thrown.
  • Transaction in the controller: too broad; keep it in the service.
  • Field injection: use the constructor.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Keep transactions short; do not call remote services inside them.
  • Use readOnly = true for queries.
  • Avoid loading entities you only need to count or check.
  • Cache stable lookups with @Cacheable.
  • Move slow side effects (email) to @Async or events after commit.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a bank transfer service debits one account, credits another and writes a ledger entry. All three succeed or none do. The controller only converts HTTP to a call and the result to a response.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DTO (Data Transfer Object): a simple object that carries data between layers or over the network, separate from the JPA entity.
  • Why: it hides internal fields (passwords, ids), avoids lazy-loading surprises and lets the API change without changing the database model.
  • Java 17: a record is an ideal immutable DTO.

Worked Example 1

Validation failure.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test of the response shape.

Practice Exercise 1

A record DTO with validation.

Practice Exercise 2

Mapper method.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DTOs sit at the boundary of the application.

  • Inbound: an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) reads the body into the DTO; @Valid triggers validation before the method runs.
  • Service: maps the DTO to an entity (or domain object).
  • Outbound: maps the entity to a response DTO that Jackson writes as JSON.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Mapping options:

  • Manual mapping: simple and explicit, good for small projects.
  • MapStruct: an annotation processor that generates fast, type-safe mappers.
  • ModelMapper: reflection based, less code but errors appear at runtime.
  • Spring Data projections: interface or class based, selected directly in the query.
  • @JsonView / @JsonIgnore: filter fields without a second class (less flexible).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Request and response DTOs can differ: the create request has no id, the response has one.
  • Validation: put @NotBlank and @Email on the request DTO and use @Valid in the controller.
  • Mapping: convert by hand, with a static factory, or with MapStruct.

Senior Notes

  • Jackson serializes records directly with Spring Boot 3.
  • Over-posting: binding a request straight onto an entity lets a client set fields like role; a DTO prevents it.
  • Projections: Spring Data interface projections can return DTO-like views straight from a query.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning entities: leaks fields and causes lazy-loading or recursion errors.
  • One DTO for everything: the same class for create, update and response makes optional fields confusing.
  • Forgetting @Valid: the annotations on the DTO are never checked.
  • Mapping inside the controller: push it to a mapper or service.
  • Mutable DTO with setters everywhere: prefer records.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Fetch DTOs directly with a projection to avoid loading full entities.
  • Small response DTOs mean smaller JSON and faster serialization.
  • MapStruct has near-zero runtime cost, reflection mappers are slower.
  • Do not map large collections eagerly if you can page them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a mobile app needs a list screen (id, title) and a detail screen (all fields). Two DTOs (BookSummary and BookDetail) serve them, and the entity can change columns without breaking the app.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DAO (Data Access Object): a class that holds all database access code for one entity or table, behind an interface.
  • Purpose: separate persistence from business logic so the storage technology can change.
  • In Spring: a DAO is a @Repository bean that uses JdbcTemplate, EntityManager or Spring Data.

Worked Example 1

SQL injection mistake.

Worked Example 2

Testing with @JdbcTest.

Practice Exercise 1

JdbcTemplate DAO.

Practice Exercise 2

Using the DAO from a service.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a DAO works with Spring:

  • The DAO is a singleton @Repository bean with an injected JdbcTemplate or EntityManager.
  • The JdbcTemplate obtains the connection bound to the current transaction through DataSourceUtils.
  • PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor adds a proxy that converts exceptions of @Repository beans.
  • Results are mapped to objects with a RowMapper or by the JPA provider.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

DAO implementation styles:

  • JdbcTemplate: full SQL control.
  • NamedParameterJdbcTemplate: readable named parameters.
  • SimpleJdbcInsert: inserts and returns generated keys.
  • JPA EntityManager: object mapping.
  • Spring Data: generated implementation.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Interface plus implementation: StudentDao and JdbcStudentDao, so tests can use a fake.
  • Exception translation: @Repository turns SQL exceptions into DataAccessException subclasses.
  • CRUD methods: findById, findAll, save, update and delete.

Senior Notes

  • Closer to storage: DAO methods map to tables and statements, while repositories map to aggregates.
  • Parameters: always use bind variables, never string concatenation, to prevent SQL injection.
  • Transactions: DAOs join the transaction started by the service layer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • SQL concatenation: opens SQL injection; use placeholders.
  • Leaking connections when using raw JDBC without try-with-resources.
  • Business logic in the DAO: keep it in the service.
  • queryForObject on missing row: throws EmptyResultDataAccessException; use query with a list.
  • One DAO method per screen: design around the entity.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Use batch operations (batchUpdate) for many rows.
  • Select only the needed columns.
  • Index the columns in where clauses.
  • Use a connection pool (HikariCP) and keep transactions short.
  • Set a query timeout for risky queries.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a legacy reporting module uses hand-tuned SQL with window functions. A ReportDao keeps that SQL in one place using JdbcTemplate, while the rest of the app uses Spring Data. Services depend only on the DAO interface.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • PRG (Post-Redirect-Get): after a successful form POST, the server answers with a redirect and the browser then loads the result with a GET.
  • Problem solved: refreshing the page after a POST would resubmit the form and, for example, create a duplicate order.
  • In Spring MVC: return redirect:/orders/5 from the controller method.

Worked Example 1

MockMvc test of the redirect.

Worked Example 2

Forgotten redirect.

Practice Exercise 1

Basic PRG controller.

Practice Exercise 2

Query parameter with redirect.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How PRG works in Spring MVC:

  • The controller returns redirect:/path; ViewResolver creates a RedirectView.
  • RedirectView sends a 302 response with a Location header and no body.
  • Flash attributes are saved by FlashMapManager (SessionFlashMapManager) in the session with a short expiry.
  • On the next request, DispatcherServlet reads the flash map and puts it into the model, then deletes it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Redirect options:

  • redirect: prefix: the common way.
  • RedirectView: explicit object, can set setStatusCode (for example 303).
  • ResponseEntity with Location: for APIs.
  • addAttribute: values go to the URL.
  • addFlashAttribute: values go to the session for one request.
  • forward: prefix: a server-side forward, not a PRG redirect.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Status code: the redirect is normally 302 (or 303 See Other); the browser then issues a GET.
  • Flash attributes: RedirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute keeps a message across the redirect without putting it in the URL.
  • Validation errors: on errors, return the view directly (no redirect) so the form shows the messages.

Senior Notes

  • How flash works: FlashMapManager stores attributes in the session and removes them after the next request.
  • URL attributes: addAttribute appends values to the redirect URL as query parameters.
  • REST APIs do not need PRG, they return 201 with a Location header instead.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Returning a view after a successful POST: refresh resubmits.
  • Redirecting on validation errors: the BindingResult is lost.
  • Using addAttribute for large objects: they appear in the URL; use flash.
  • Expecting flash data on a second refresh: it is shown once only.
  • Redirect to user-supplied URL: an open redirect; validate the target.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and scaling notes:

  • A redirect costs one extra round trip, which is small compared with a duplicate order.
  • Flash attributes use the session; in a cluster use Spring Session or sticky sessions.
  • For heavy flash payloads store an id and reload on the next page.
  • Use a relative redirect (contextRelative) behind proxies to avoid wrong host names; set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework when needed.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.forward-headers-strategy=framework
spring.session.store-type=redis

# OUTPUT:
# redirects built behind a load balancer use the public host and scheme

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a checkout form posts the order. The controller saves it, flashes "Order placed", and redirects to the confirmation page. The customer can refresh or bookmark that page safely, and the browser Back button does not warn about resubmission.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Measure first: use Actuator metrics (http.server.requests), logs and a profiler before changing anything.
  • Common hot spots: slow database queries, N+1 selects, big responses, blocking calls and too little caching.
  • Layers to tune: the web server (threads), the Spring MVC code, the database and the network.

Worked Example 1

Pagination.

Worked Example 2

Timing a request in a filter.

Practice Exercise 1

Enable metrics.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics
server.compression.enabled=true
server.tomcat.threads.max=200

# OUTPUT:
# GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests ->
# {
    "name":"http.server.requests","measurements":[{"statistic":"COUNT","value":42.0}]
}

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Caching a method.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Where time goes in a request:

  • Container: accept, parse headers, queue for a worker thread.
  • Filters and DispatcherServlet: handler mapping, interceptors, argument resolution.
  • Controller and service: business code and calls to the database or other services.
  • Serialization: converting the result to JSON or rendering a view.
  • Usually 80 percent or more is spent waiting for the database or remote calls.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tuning settings:

  • Tomcat: threads.max, accept-count, max-connections.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled and min-response-size.
  • Keep-alive and HTTP/2: server.http2.enabled.
  • Hikari: maximum-pool-size, connection-timeout.
  • Virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled (Java 21).
  • Cache: Caffeine through spring.cache.type.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.tomcat.accept-count=100
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.min-response-size=1024
server.http2.enabled=true
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
spring.cache.type=caffeine

# OUTPUT:
# Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path ''

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Thread pool: Tomcat handles one request per thread, so tune server.tomcat.threads.max to match load.
  • Compression: server.compression.enabled=true shrinks JSON and HTML responses.
  • Caching: use @Cacheable for read-heavy data and HTTP caching headers for static content.

Senior Notes

  • Virtual threads: Spring Boot 3.2 with Java 21 can enable spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true for blocking-heavy apps.
  • Pagination: never return unbounded lists; use Pageable.
  • Load test: verify with a tool such as JMeter or Gatling, and compare p95 and p99 latency, not only the average.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Guessing: optimizing without measuring.
  • Unbounded queries: returning every row.
  • Blocking calls without timeouts: one slow service holds all threads.
  • Huge session objects or heavy work in filters.
  • Logging at debug in production or logging large bodies.
  • Caching without invalidation: stale data bugs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance work checklist:

  • Define a goal (for example p95 under 200 ms at 500 requests per second).
  • Load test with a realistic data size.
  • Fix the slowest query, then re-measure.
  • Add caching for stable data with an expiry.
  • Scale out only after the single instance is efficient.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a product listing endpoint took 1.8 seconds. Profiling showed 101 queries (N+1) and a 4 MB JSON. Fixes: join fetch, a summary DTO, pagination and compression. The response dropped to 90 ms and 40 KB.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Request path: DispatcherServlet runs filters, handler mapping, interceptors, argument resolvers, the controller and message converters; each step costs time.
  • Keep it short: do little in filters and interceptors, and keep controllers thin.
  • Do work once: avoid repeated parsing, repeated lookups and repeated serialization.

Worked Example 1

Streaming a large file.

Worked Example 2

Interceptor that skips static paths.

Practice Exercise 1

Async controller.

Practice Exercise 2

ETag support.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Request processing steps and their cost:

  • Filter chain: every filter runs for every request.
  • HandlerMapping: finds the controller method, with a fast lookup of exact paths.
  • Interceptors: preHandle and postHandle around the call.
  • HandlerAdapter: resolves arguments (path variables, @RequestBody) and calls the method.
  • Return value handler and message converter: write the response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques:

  • Async return types: Callable, DeferredResult, CompletableFuture.
  • @Async services with a bounded executor.
  • Streaming: StreamingResponseBody, SseEmitter.
  • HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag, ShallowEtagHeaderFilter.
  • Parallel calls: several remote calls with CompletableFuture.allOf.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Async: return Callable, DeferredResult or CompletableFuture to free the container thread during slow work.
  • Return less: use DTOs or @JsonView to serialize only the needed fields.
  • Conditional GET: ETag and If-None-Match let the server answer 304 without a body.

Senior Notes

  • Message converters: Jackson is fast, but reuse the auto-configured ObjectMapper, never create one per request.
  • Interceptors versus filters: filters run for every servlet request, so put heavy logic only where needed.
  • Streaming: for large files use StreamingResponseBody or Resource instead of loading a byte array.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Heavy work in filters or interceptors on every request.
  • Unbounded executor: @Async with the default setup can pile up tasks; configure a pool and queue.
  • Blocking inside an async task on the same small pool.
  • Reading the body twice: the request stream can be read only once; wrap it if you must.
  • Building a big String in memory for a download.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Reuse the shared ObjectMapper; disable features you do not need.
  • Return smaller payloads with DTOs and compression.
  • Use @JsonView or sparse fields for big objects.
  • Avoid reflection-heavy conversions in hot paths.
  • Check the order of filters; cheap rejections (auth, rate limit) should come first.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a report endpoint called three slow back-end services one after another (900 ms in total). Running the calls in parallel with CompletableFuture and adding an ETag for repeated requests reduced a typical call to about 350 ms, and repeated polls to a 304 response.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Biggest cost: in most MVC apps the database is the slowest part, so tune queries before tuning Java code.
  • N+1 problem: loading a list and then one query per row; fix it with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
  • Connection pool: Spring Boot uses HikariCP; size it so threads do not wait or overload the database.

Worked Example 1

DTO projection.

Worked Example 2

Counting queries in a test.

Practice Exercise 1

N+1 and its fix.

Practice Exercise 2

Pool and batch settings.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug

# OUTPUT:
# HikariPool-1 - Start completed.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How database time is spent in an MVC app:

  • Connection: taken from HikariCP; waits if the pool is empty.
  • Statement: parsed and planned by the database, and an index decides the cost.
  • Round trips: each query costs network latency, so many small queries add up (N+1).
  • Hibernate: flushes changes at commit and keeps entities in the persistence context.
  • Open-in-view: keeps the session open until the response is written.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for each problem:

  • N+1: join fetch, @EntityGraph, @BatchSize, default_batch_fetch_size.
  • Large reads: projections, Slice, streaming with @QueryHints fetch size.
  • Writes: jdbc.batch_size, order_inserts, saveAll.
  • Locking: @Version for optimistic locking.
  • Caching: @Cacheable or Hibernate second-level cache.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Indexes: add them on columns used in where, join and order by, and check with EXPLAIN.
  • Projections and pagination: select only needed columns and never load whole tables.
  • Batching: set spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size for bulk inserts.

Senior Notes

  • Open Session in View: enabled by default, it keeps a connection through view rendering; set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false for busy APIs.
  • Transactions: keep them short and use readOnly = true for queries.
  • Second-level cache and @Cacheable reduce repeated reads, but add invalidation work.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Missing index: a full table scan on every call.
  • EAGER fetch everywhere: loads far too much; use LAZY and fetch on demand.
  • IDENTITY ids with batching: Hibernate cannot batch inserts; use a sequence.
  • Big pool: hundreds of connections can overload the database.
  • Long transactions: remote calls inside them keep locks and connections.
  • LIKE with a leading wildcard: cannot use a normal index.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance steps:

  • Log slow queries and run EXPLAIN on them.
  • Add a composite index in the order of the where columns.
  • Replace loops of queries with one query using in.
  • Use a read replica for heavy reports.
  • Archive or partition very old data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an admin page listing 50 orders with their customers and items made 151 queries and took 2 seconds. Fixing it with an entity graph, a summary projection, an index on customer_id and open-in-view=false brought it to 3 queries and 60 ms.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Connection pool: a set of ready database connections that requests borrow and return, because opening a new connection per request is slow.
  • Spring Boot default: HikariCP is the default pool, configured with spring.datasource.hikari.* properties.
  • Borrow and return: a request takes a connection when it first needs the database and gives it back when the transaction ends.

Worked Example 1

Test with a small pool.

Worked Example 2

Turn off open-in-view.

Practice Exercise 1

Configure Hikari in application.properties.
codeExamples:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=app
spring.datasource.password=secret
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000

# OUTPUT:
# HikariPool-1 - Start completed.

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Read the pool through a bean.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HikariCP keeps physical connections in a concurrent bag and hands out proxies.

  • Borrow: getConnection() takes an idle entry from a thread-local list or the shared bag, or waits up to the connection timeout.
  • Proxy: the caller gets a wrapper whose close() returns the real connection to the pool instead of closing it.
  • Spring: DataSourceTransactionManager or JpaTransactionManager binds one connection to the thread for the whole transaction.
  • Housekeeping: a background thread retires connections older than max-lifetime and keeps minimum-idle ready.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Main Hikari options:

  • maximum-pool-size: upper limit of connections.
  • minimum-idle: idle connections kept ready.
  • connection-timeout: wait time for a connection.
  • idle-timeout: when extra idle connections are closed.
  • max-lifetime: keep it below the database or firewall limit.
  • leak-detection-threshold: log borrowed-too-long connections.
  • pool-name: readable name in logs and metrics.
codeExamples:
spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name=shop-pool
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=15
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=15
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=2000
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1740000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=15000

# OUTPUT:
# shop-pool - Start completed.
# (fixed-size pool: minimum-idle equals maximum-pool-size)

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • maximum-pool-size caps open connections; if all are busy, threads wait up to connection-timeout and then fail.
  • Open Session in View keeps a connection tied to the request until the view is rendered; spring.jpa.open-in-view=false frees it earlier.
  • Leaks: a connection that is never closed stays borrowed forever; leak-detection-threshold logs suspects.

Senior Notes

  • Sizing: a small pool (often 10 to 20) beats a huge one, because the database can only run so many queries at once.
  • Long calls: never hold a connection while calling a slow remote service; keep the transaction short.
  • Metrics: watch hikaricp.connections.active and pending through Actuator and Micrometer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Oversized pool: 200 connections overload the database; use a small pool and queue.
  • Slow remote call inside a transaction: the connection is held; call the service first, then open the transaction.
  • Open Session in View: hides lazy loading and holds connections during rendering.
  • Manual connections not closed: use try-with-resources.
  • max-lifetime above the database limit: causes sporadic closed-connection errors.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning approach:

  • Measure first: watch active, pending and acquire time.
  • Size from the database: a rough start is cores times 2 plus disk spindles, then test.
  • Shorten transactions: that raises throughput more than a larger pool.
  • Fixed size: equal minimum-idle and maximum-pool-size avoids resizing spikes.
  • Set open-in-view to false for APIs.
  • Statement cache belongs to the driver, for example prepared statement caching.
codeExamples:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics
# then query:
# GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active
# GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending
# GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.acquire

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# {
    "name":"hikaricp.connections.pending","measurements":[{"statistic":"VALUE","value":0.0}]
}

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API slows down under load and logs show Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.

  • Pending threads are high, active equals the maximum.
  • A thread dump shows threads inside a remote payment call within a transaction.
  • Fix: move the remote call out of the transaction and disable open-in-view.
  • Result: active connections drop and the timeouts disappear without enlarging the pool.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Cache: stores the result of a costly call so the next call with the same input returns the stored result.
  • Spring abstraction: enable it with @EnableCaching and mark methods with @Cacheable, @CachePut and @CacheEvict.
  • Cache name and key: each cached value lives in a named cache under a key, by default built from the method arguments.

Worked Example 1

Verify with a spy.

Worked Example 2

Caffeine with expiry.
codeExamples:
spring.cache.type=caffeine
spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=500,expireAfterWrite=10m

# OUTPUT:
# Entries expire 10 minutes after they are written, at most 500 are kept.

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

A cacheable service method.

Practice Exercise 2

Evict on update.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring caching is applied by an AOP proxy around your bean.

  • Interceptor: CacheInterceptor wraps each annotated method.
  • Key: a KeyGenerator builds the key, by default from the arguments (SimpleKey).
  • Flow: look up the key in the Cache from the CacheManager; on a hit return it, on a miss call the method and store the result.
  • Self-invocation: a call inside the same object bypasses the proxy, so nothing is cached.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Annotation options:

  • value / cacheNames: which caches to use.
  • key: SpEL expression such as #id or #p.id.
  • condition: cache only when true, checked before the call.
  • unless: do not cache when true, checked on the result.
  • sync: one thread computes per key.
  • @CachePut: always run and refresh.
  • @CacheEvict: remove one or all entries.
  • @Caching: combine several.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Proxy based: caching works through a proxy, so calling a cached method from the same class (self-invocation) skips the cache.
  • Providers: the default is a simple ConcurrentHashMap; use Caffeine or Redis for expiry and size limits.
  • condition and unless: condition decides before the call, unless decides on the result, for example to skip null.

Senior Notes

  • Stale data: always pair a cache with an eviction or time-to-live policy, or users see old values.
  • Cache stampede: many threads miss at once; sync = true lets only one compute the value.
  • Serialization: with Redis, cached objects must be serializable, and a class change can break old entries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Self-invocation: move the method to another bean.
  • No expiry: the default map grows forever; use Caffeine or Redis with time-to-live.
  • Mutable cached objects: callers change the cached instance; return immutable data or copies.
  • Wrong key: same key for different meanings; build it explicitly.
  • Caching in a transaction: a rollback can leave a cached value that was never committed.
  • Forgot @EnableCaching: annotations are silently ignored.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Hit ratio: track hits and misses; a low ratio means the wrong data is cached.
  • Size limits: use maximumSize and expireAfterWrite in Caffeine.
  • Local versus distributed: Caffeine is fastest per node; Redis shares data between nodes but adds network time.
  • sync = true prevents stampedes.
  • Record stats: recordStats exposes metrics to Micrometer.
codeExamples:
spring.cache.type=caffeine
spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=1000,expireAfterWrite=5m,recordStats
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=metrics
# GET /actuator/metrics/cache.gets?tag=result:hit

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# {
    "name":"cache.gets","measurements":[{"statistic":"COUNT","value":8421.0}]
}

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a product catalogue page calls the database for the same 500 products thousands of times a minute.

  • Cache product reads by id with a 10 minute expiry.
  • Evict the entry when an admin updates a product.
  • Result: database load drops sharply and page latency falls.
  • Risk handled: expiry limits stale data if an eviction is missed.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HTTP caching: headers such as Cache-Control let browsers and proxies reuse a response without asking the server again.
  • Cache-Control max-age: tells the client how many seconds the response stays fresh.
  • Validators: ETag and Last-Modified let the client ask "has it changed?" and get a small 304 Not Modified.

Worked Example 1

Test the header with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Enable the shallow ETag filter.

Practice Exercise 1

Set max-age on a response.

Practice Exercise 2

Conditional GET with an ETag.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HTTP caching is decided by response headers and honoured by browsers, proxies and CDNs.

  • Fresh: within max-age the cache answers without contacting the server.
  • Stale: afterwards it sends a conditional request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since.
  • Server: compares the validator; if equal it returns 304 with no body.
  • Spring: HttpEntityMethodProcessor writes the headers, and ServletWebRequest.checkNotModified evaluates preconditions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Spring options:

  • CacheControl: maxAge, noCache, noStore, cachePublic, cachePrivate, mustRevalidate, staleWhileRevalidate.
  • ResponseEntity: .eTag(), .lastModified(), .cacheControl().
  • WebRequest.checkNotModified: returns true when a 304 was already prepared.
  • ShallowEtagHeaderFilter: automatic, body based.
  • Interceptor: WebContentInterceptor sets rules per URL pattern.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • CacheControl in Spring: ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(10))) sets the header.
  • ShallowEtagHeaderFilter computes an ETag from the response body and returns 304 when it matches, but the body is still built.
  • Deep ETag: use WebRequest.checkNotModified before doing the work, so the expensive call is skipped.

Senior Notes

  • Private data: use private or no-store for user data, never let a shared proxy cache it.
  • Vary: if the response depends on a header such as Accept-Language, add Vary so caches keep separate copies.
  • Static assets: use long max-age with versioned file names, and short or validated caching for HTML and APIs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Caching private data publicly: add private or no-store.
  • Missing Vary: a cache serves English to a German user.
  • Weak validators: an ETag that never changes serves stale data.
  • Caching error responses: avoid long max-age on 4xx and 5xx.
  • Confusing no-cache and no-store.
  • Spring Security defaults: it adds no-cache, no-store to secured responses, which you override per endpoint only if safe.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips:

  • Long max-age plus versioned URLs for assets.
  • Short max-age plus ETag for API reads.
  • checkNotModified early to skip database work.
  • stale-while-revalidate hides refresh latency.
  • CDN respects s-maxage for shared caches only.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a mobile app polls /api/config every minute and the payload is 40 KB.

  • Add an ETag from a config version number.
  • Use checkNotModified before loading the config.
  • Result: most polls become tiny 304 replies, saving bandwidth and database reads.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Response compression: the server compresses the body (usually gzip) so fewer bytes cross the network, and the client unpacks it.
  • Negotiation: the client sends Accept-Encoding: gzip and the server answers with Content-Encoding: gzip.
  • Spring Boot: switch it on with server.compression.enabled=true; it is handled by the embedded server, not by MVC.

Worked Example 1

Integration test of the header.

Worked Example 2

Compare sizes.

Practice Exercise 1

Turn on compression.
codeExamples:
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,text/html,text/css,application/javascript
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# OUTPUT:
# Responses over 1 KB of those types are gzip encoded when the client accepts it.

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Check with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Compression is done by the embedded server before bytes leave the connector.

  • Tomcat: the connector has compression settings that Spring Boot fills from server.compression.*.
  • Decision: enabled, client sent a matching Accept-Encoding, the type is in the list and the body is large enough.
  • Headers: it sets Content-Encoding, removes Content-Length and adds Vary: Accept-Encoding.
  • MVC: message converters write plain bytes; they know nothing about compression.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • server.compression.enabled: master switch.
  • mime-types: which types are compressed.
  • min-response-size: smallest size to compress.
  • excluded-user-agents: skip some clients.
  • Reverse proxy: nginx gzip on or brotli.
  • Filter: a custom servlet filter for non-Tomcat setups.
codeExamples:
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,application/xml,text/html,text/plain
server.compression.min-response-size=2KB
server.compression.excluded-user-agents=BadBot

# OUTPUT:
# Only listed types of 2 KB or more are gzip compressed.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • mime-types: server.compression.mime-types lists which content types to compress; JSON, HTML, CSS and JS are typical.
  • min-response-size: tiny bodies are not worth compressing; the default threshold is 2048 bytes.
  • Already compressed: images, video and zip files gain nothing, so leave them out.

Senior Notes

  • CPU cost: compression trades CPU for bandwidth; a reverse proxy such as nginx often does it better.
  • Double compression: do not compress in both the app and the proxy.
  • Security: compressing secrets next to user input on HTTPS can enable BREACH-style attacks; weigh this for sensitive pages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Compressing in app and proxy: wasted CPU or broken double encoding.
  • Compressing images: no gain.
  • Forgetting Vary: caches serve compressed data to clients that cannot read it.
  • Wrong size check: tests with tiny bodies show no compression.
  • Setting Content-Length manually then compressing.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Compress text formats only; JSON often shrinks by 80 percent or more.
  • Use level 5 or 6 for a balance; very high levels cost much CPU for little gain.
  • Cache compressed static files rather than compressing on each request.
  • Prefer brotli at the CDN for static assets.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a reporting API returns 2 MB JSON to remote offices on slow links.

  • Enable gzip for application/json.
  • Download time falls from seconds to under one second.
  • CPU rises slightly, so move compression to the proxy if the application becomes CPU bound.
codeExamples:
# before: 2.1 MB in 7.4 s on a 2 Mbps link
# after gzip: 240 KB in 1.0 s

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Content-Encoding: gzip

Fresher Notes

  • Static resources: CSS, JavaScript, images and fonts served as files; Spring Boot serves them from /static, /public and /resources on the classpath.
  • Goal: make them small and cacheable, so pages load fast and the server does less work.
  • ResourceHandlerRegistry: in a WebMvcConfigurer, addResourceHandlers maps URL patterns to locations and sets caching.

Worked Example 1

Test the cache header.

Worked Example 2

Link versioned URLs in a template.

<link rel="stylesheet" th:href="@{/css/app.css}">

<!-- OUTPUT -->

spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.content.paths=/**

Practice Exercise 2

Manual resource handler.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Static files are served by ResourceHttpRequestHandler registered by Spring MVC.

  • Mapping: /** maps to the static locations, with the dispatcher handling dynamic URLs first.
  • Chain: a ResourceResolverChain finds the file (versioned, encoded, path) and a ResourceTransformerChain can rewrite content.
  • Headers: it adds Last-Modified, supports range requests and applies the configured Cache-Control.
  • Links: ResourceUrlProvider produces versioned URLs for templates.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Fixed version: strategy.fixed.version=v2 gives /v2/js/app.js.
  • Content hash: hash of file contents.
  • Custom locations: spring.web.resources.static-locations.
  • Webjars: /webjars/** for library files.
  • Disable: spring.web.resources.add-mappings=false for pure APIs.
codeExamples:
spring.web.resources.static-locations=classpath:/static/,file:/var/www/assets/
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.fixed.enabled=true
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.fixed.paths=/js/**
spring.web.resources.chain.strategy.fixed.version=v2
spring.web.resources.chain.compressed=true

# OUTPUT:
# /v2/js/app.js is mapped to /js/app.js, and app.js.gz is served when present.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Cache period: spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=365d gives a long browser cache.
  • Versioned URLs: VersionResourceResolver adds a content hash like app-3f2a.js, so a long cache is safe and changes still show.
  • Gzip variants: resourceChain(true).addResolver(new EncodedResourceResolver()) serves pre-built .gz files.

Senior Notes

  • CDN: in production put a CDN or nginx in front, so the application server does not serve files at all.
  • Minify and bundle: use a build tool; Spring does not minify for you.
  • Resource chain cache: it is on by default in production profiles and caches resolved paths, avoiding repeated lookups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Long cache without versioning: users keep old files after a release.
  • Hand-written links: bypass the version resolver; use th:href with @{...}.
  • Serving large media from the app: consumes threads.
  • Wrong security rules: static paths blocked by Spring Security.
  • Forgetting resource chain cache in development, which hides changes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Serve through a CDN with the content hash in the name.
  • Pre-compress at build time (gzip or brotli).
  • Bundle and minify files, and use HTTP/2 to reduce request overhead.
  • Use immutable in Cache-Control for hashed files.
  • Keep images in modern formats and sizes.
codeExamples:
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.max-age=365d
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.immutable=true
spring.web.resources.cache.cachecontrol.cache-public=true

# OUTPUT:
# Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, public, immutable

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a landing page loads 3 MB of assets and users complain it is slow.

  • Minify and bundle the JS and CSS, and compress images.
  • Enable content hash versioning with a one year cache.
  • Put a CDN in front.
  • Result: repeat visits download almost nothing, first visits are smaller.
codeExamples:
# before: 3.1 MB, 42 requests on every visit
# after:  0.9 MB first visit, 0.05 MB repeat visit
