beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Async request processing: the servlet thread is released while the work continues elsewhere, and the response is written later.
  • Why: a container thread is a limited resource; freeing it during slow work lets the server handle more concurrent requests.
  • Return types: a controller can return Callable, DeferredResult, WebAsyncTask, CompletableFuture or a streaming body.

Worked Example 1

Test async with MockMvc.

Worked Example 2

Return a CompletableFuture.

Practice Exercise 1

A Callable endpoint.

Practice Exercise 2

Configure the executor and timeout.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Spring MVC builds on Servlet 3 asynchronous support.

  • Start: the handler returns an async type; WebAsyncManager calls startAsync() and the servlet thread returns to the pool.
  • Work: a Callable runs on an executor; a DeferredResult waits to be completed.
  • Dispatch: when a result exists, the container dispatches the request again to the DispatcherServlet.
  • Finish: the stored result is treated as the handler return value, and handling continues from there (converters, views).
  • Filters: they run again on the second dispatch unless registered for the first only.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Async variants:

  • Callable: Spring runs it for you.
  • DeferredResult: you complete it.
  • WebAsyncTask: Callable with custom timeout and executor.
  • CompletableFuture and ListenableFuture: completion by the future.
  • ResponseBodyEmitter, SseEmitter, StreamingResponseBody: multiple writes.
  • Reactive types (Flux, Mono): supported when WebFlux types are on the classpath, still on the servlet stack.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Servlet 3 async: Spring calls request.startAsync(), returns the thread, and later dispatches the request again to write the result.
  • Thread pool: Callable runs on a Spring task executor; configure it with WebMvcConfigurer.configureAsyncSupport.
  • Timeout: spring.mvc.async.request-timeout ends waiting requests with a 503 by default.

Senior Notes

  • Not faster: async does not make one request quicker; it only improves how many requests are in flight.
  • Security and context: thread locals are not copied automatically; the security context is propagated, but your own thread locals are not.
  • Executor: the default executor is simple and unbounded; set a bounded pool with a queue for production.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Blocking inside the async pool without limits: pool exhaustion.
  • Using a thread local set on the request thread.
  • No timeout: requests wait forever.
  • Filters not async-capable: custom filters must support async or the request fails.
  • Believing it speeds one request.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use a bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with a queue and a rejection policy.
  • Set spring.mvc.async.request-timeout.
  • Keep Tomcat max-connections high enough for waiting requests.
  • Use TaskDecorator to copy context such as MDC.
  • Measure queue size and rejected tasks.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a report endpoint calls a slow partner API (3 s) and the server has 200 Tomcat threads.

  • Synchronous: about 66 requests per second at most.
  • Async with a pool sized for the partner limit: threads are free for other requests.
  • Result: other fast endpoints stay responsive during partner slowness.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Callable: a controller method returns java.util.concurrent.Callable<T>, and Spring runs it on another thread while the servlet thread is freed.
  • Result handling: the value the callable returns is treated as the controller result, so view names, bodies and status work as normal.
  • Simplest async option: you do not manage the thread or the completion yourself.

Worked Example 1

Exception handling.

Worked Example 2

MockMvc test.

Practice Exercise 1

A simple Callable.

Practice Exercise 2

Callable with a view.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a Callable return value is processed:

  • Handler: CallableMethodReturnValueHandler passes the Callable to WebAsyncManager.startCallableProcessing.
  • Submit: the Callable is submitted to the AsyncTaskExecutor; the request enters async mode.
  • Result: the outcome or exception is saved on the manager and the request is dispatched again.
  • Replay: the saved value goes through the return value handlers as if the controller had returned it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and hooks:

  • Callable<String>: view name or body.
  • Callable<ResponseEntity<T>>: control status and headers.
  • CallableProcessingInterceptor: beforeConcurrentHandling, preProcess, postProcess, handleTimeout.
  • Executor: set through AsyncSupportConfigurer.setTaskExecutor.
  • Timeout: setDefaultTimeout.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Executor: it runs on an AsyncTaskExecutor; by default a simple one that creates a new thread per task, so configure a pool.
  • Exceptions: if the callable throws, the exception is dispatched back and handled by @ExceptionHandler as usual.
  • Interceptors: CallableProcessingInterceptor can hook before and after the work, and on timeout.

Senior Notes

  • Who completes it: the callable is completed by the pool itself; if another system or event completes the work, use DeferredResult.
  • Timeout: set one, or a hung callable keeps the request open until the container times out.
  • Blocking calls: the callable still blocks a pool thread, so size the pool for the blocking work.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Using request-scoped beans inside the callable: the request may be gone; read values first.
  • Relying on thread locals such as a transaction.
  • Ignoring the default executor: a new thread per call.
  • Sharing non-thread-safe objects such as Model across threads carelessly.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use a bounded pool; size it for the blocking work, not for CPU count.
  • Prefer separate pools for different slow dependencies.
  • Use timeouts on the downstream calls too.
  • Do not use it for very fast work; the hand-off costs more than it saves.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: PDF generation takes 2 to 4 seconds and uses a library that blocks.

  • Return a Callable that generates the PDF on a dedicated pool of 5 threads.
  • Servlet threads stay available for normal pages.
  • When all 5 are busy, requests queue, then get 503 on timeout, which protects the server.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • DeferredResult: a controller returns a DeferredResult<T> object now, and any other thread completes it later with setResult.
  • Use case: the answer depends on something outside the request, such as a message, an event or another service callback.
  • Servlet thread freed: the request stays open, but no container thread is held while waiting.

Worked Example 1

Test completion.

Worked Example 2

Error result.

Practice Exercise 1

Complete it from another thread.

Practice Exercise 2

Long polling queue.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DeferredResult is a handle to a result that will arrive later.

  • Handler: DeferredResultMethodReturnValueHandler registers it with WebAsyncManager.startDeferredResultProcessing.
  • Waiting: the request is in async mode with a timeout; no thread works on it.
  • Completion: setResult stores the value and triggers an async dispatch on the calling thread.
  • Output: the dispatch runs the normal return value handling and writes the response.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Constructors: no args, timeout, timeout plus fallback object.
  • setResult / setErrorResult: one-time completion.
  • setResultHandler: advanced hook.
  • hasResult, isSetOrExpired: state checks.
  • Callbacks: onTimeout, onError, onCompletion.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • setResult and setErrorResult: call one of them exactly once; later calls are ignored and return false.
  • Timeout: new DeferredResult<>(5000L, fallback) returns the fallback value if nobody completes it in time.
  • Callbacks: onTimeout, onError and onCompletion let you clean up queued requests.

Senior Notes

  • Memory leak: keep waiting results in a bounded, concurrent collection and remove them in onCompletion.
  • Thread safety: setResult can be called from any thread, but your own shared state needs its own safety.
  • Long polling: a classic use; clients wait on a request until news arrives, then ask again.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Never completing it: the request waits until timeout.
  • No cleanup: stored results leak; remove them in onCompletion.
  • Unbounded queue of waiting clients.
  • Completing twice: the second call returns false.
  • Doing slow work inside the setResult caller: the dispatch runs there.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cap the number of waiting requests and reject extra with 429 or 503.
  • Use a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by topic or user.
  • Complete results on a worker pool so a slow response writer does not block the event source.
  • Raise Tomcat max-connections for many idle waiting clients.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a payment page waits for a bank confirmation that arrives by webhook.

  • The browser calls /payments/42/status and gets a DeferredResult stored by payment id.
  • The webhook handler calls setResult for that id.
  • After 25 seconds without news the client gets "pending" and asks again.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • WebAsyncTask: a wrapper around a Callable that adds a per-request timeout, a chosen executor and timeout callbacks.
  • Return it from a controller method, just like a Callable, and Spring runs it asynchronously.
  • Why: a plain Callable uses global settings; WebAsyncTask lets one endpoint have its own limits.

Worked Example 1

Test the timeout path.

Worked Example 2

Cleanup callback.

Practice Exercise 1

Timeout with fallback.

Practice Exercise 2

Dedicated executor.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

WebAsyncTask is a Callable plus settings.

  • Handler: AsyncTaskMethodReturnValueHandler unpacks it.
  • Executor: it resolves the executor from the task, a bean name or the default.
  • Timeout: the task timeout replaces the default, and timeoutCallback is used when it triggers.
  • Execution: then it follows the same path as a Callable, with an async dispatch for the result.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Constructors and callbacks:

  • (Callable): default timeout.
  • (Long timeout, Callable): custom timeout.
  • (Long timeout, String executorName, Callable): named bean.
  • (Long timeout, AsyncTaskExecutor, Callable): direct executor.
  • onTimeout, onError, onCompletion: callbacks.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Constructors: new WebAsyncTask<>(timeoutMillis, callable) or with an executor name or object.
  • onTimeout: register a callable that supplies a fallback value when the time limit passes.
  • onError and onCompletion: run code on failure or when the request finishes.

Senior Notes

  • Executor bean: pass a bean name such as "taskExecutor", so slow endpoints use a separate, bounded pool.
  • Fallbacks: a timeout does not stop the running callable; it only answers the client, so make the work cancellable if possible.
  • Choose carefully: if events complete the work, use DeferredResult instead.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Assuming the timeout stops the work: it does not interrupt the thread.
  • Wrong bean name: fails at request time.
  • Timeout longer than the proxy timeout: the proxy closes first.
  • No fallback: the client gets 503.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Give each slow endpoint its own small pool so one dependency cannot starve the rest.
  • Set timeouts below gateway timeouts.
  • Return a fast fallback or a "try later" status.
  • Record timeouts as a metric.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an export endpoint normally finishes in 2 seconds but sometimes hangs on a slow database.

  • Use a WebAsyncTask with a 5 second limit and a dedicated pool of 4.
  • On timeout, return 202 Accepted with a job link.
  • The rest of the application is not affected by the slow query.

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Streaming response: the server writes the body in pieces as data becomes available, instead of building it all in memory first.
  • Types: StreamingResponseBody, ResponseBodyEmitter, SseEmitter and a Resource for files.
  • Benefit: large exports and downloads use little memory, and the client starts receiving data early.

Worked Example 1

Test streaming.

Worked Example 2

Stream a file without loading it.

Practice Exercise 1

Stream a CSV.

Practice Exercise 2

Server-Sent Events.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Streaming writes through to the servlet output while the handler runs.

  • StreamingResponseBody: StreamingResponseBodyReturnValueHandler starts async mode and runs the body on the task executor.
  • Emitters: ResponseBodyEmitter sends objects through message converters one at a time.
  • Transfer: with unknown length the container uses chunked encoding and flushes buffers.
  • Completion: the request ends when the body returns or complete() is called.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • StreamingResponseBody: raw bytes.
  • ResponseBodyEmitter: JSON objects or text, many sends.
  • SseEmitter: events with id, name and retry.
  • Resource and InputStreamResource: files and streams.
  • Range support: ResourceRegion for partial content.
  • Flux: with reactive types, text/event-stream.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • StreamingResponseBody: you get an OutputStream and write to it from an async thread, so the servlet thread is free.
  • SseEmitter: sends Server-Sent Events with text/event-stream, good for progress and live updates.
  • Content length: with streaming the length is unknown, so the response uses chunked transfer encoding.

Senior Notes

  • Flush and size: write in sensible buffers and flush when the client should see data, but not after every byte.
  • Client disconnects: writing to a closed connection throws IOException; stop the work and release resources.
  • Database cursor: stream rows with a read-only transaction and fetch size, but keep the connection open only while writing.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Building the full list first then returning it: no memory gain.
  • Not closing cursors: the database connection leaks.
  • Ignoring IOException from a disconnected client.
  • Proxy buffering: nginx buffers events; set X-Accel-Buffering: no.
  • Transaction ended too early: lazy loading fails while streaming.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Use buffers of 8 to 64 KB.
  • Set the JDBC fetch size, for example 500, for large reads.
  • Run streams on a bounded executor, as each holds a thread.
  • Compress text streams, but flush at useful points.
  • Set timeouts and handle client aborts.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: finance downloads a 1 million row CSV and the application ran out of memory.

  • Switch to a streaming endpoint reading rows with a cursor.
  • Write each row to the output stream, flush every few thousand rows.
  • The download starts immediately and memory stays flat.

cheatNotes: MVC - Model-View-Controller design pattern for web apps
DispatcherServlet - Front controller that routes all incoming requests
web.xml/WebApplicationInitializer - Registers DispatcherServlet
@Controller - Marks a class as a Spring MVC controller
@RestController - @Controller + @ResponseBody combined for REST APIs
@RequestMapping - Maps a URL/HTTP method to a handler method or class
@GetMapping - Shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = GET)
@PostMapping - Shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = POST)
@PutMapping - Shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = PUT)
@DeleteMapping - Shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = DELETE)
@RequestParam - Binds a query/form parameter to a method argument
@PathVariable - Binds a URI template variable to a method argument
@RequestBody - Deserializes the HTTP request body into a Java object
@ResponseBody - Serializes the return value directly into the response body
@ModelAttribute - Binds form data to a model object
Model/ModelMap - Carries data from controller to view
ModelAndView - Combines model data and view name in one object
ViewResolver - Resolves logical view names to actual view templates
InternalResourceViewResolver - Common ViewResolver for JSP views
@SessionAttributes - Stores model attributes in the HTTP session
@Valid/@Validated - Triggers bean validation on request data
BindingResult - Holds validation errors right after @Valid argument
@ExceptionHandler - Handles exceptions thrown within a controller
@ControllerAdvice - Global exception/handler config across controllers
HandlerInterceptor - Pre/post processing hooks around controller calls
Data flow - DispatcherServlet -> HandlerMapping -> Controller -> ViewResolver -> View
Lambda expression - Concise syntax for implementing functional interfaces
Functional interface - Interface with exactly one abstract method
Stream API - Functional-style operations on collections (map/filter/reduce)
Method reference (::) - Shorthand for calling an existing method as a lambda
Optional<T> - Container object to avoid null checks
Default methods - Interface methods with a body using the default keyword
Static methods in interfaces - Utility methods callable on the interface itself
forEach() - Iterates a collection using a lambda
Collectors - Utility class for reducing streams (toList, groupingBy, joining)
java.time package - New date/time API (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Duration)
